HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Tuesday, 15th March, 1927.
The Third Session of the Second Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 15th March, 1927, in the Seventeenth
year of the Reign of King George V, was
opened by the Governor (His Grace the
Duke of Abercorn, K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.)
in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.
LOCAL BILLS.
Mr. Speaker laid upon the Table
Report from the Examiner. of Petitions
for Local Bills, that he has certified that
the Standing Orders have been complied
with in the following cases:
Portadown Urban District Council.
Carrickfergus Harbour.
Methodist College, Belfast, and Edgehill Theological College, Belfast.
Newry (Northern Ireland) Rates
and Streets.
River Bann Navigation.
Antrim Electricity Supply
(Petition for Bill).
Mr. Speaker laid upon the Table
Report from the Examiner of Petitions
for Private Bills, That in the case of the
Petition for the forthcoming Bill the
Standing Orders have not been complied
with.
Antrim Electricity Supply Bill.
Ordered: That the Report be referred
to the Joint Standing Orders Committee.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering witn
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hatn
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parlia
ment, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
hat he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to acquaint
King's Speech
King's Speech
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Speaker]
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate to hear His
Grace's Speech on behalf of the
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament;
of which I have for greater accuracy
obtained
The Speech is as
a copy.
follows:
-:
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
It is a matter of profound gratification that such a considerable improvement has taken place in regard to
Unemployment. To-day the number
registered at the
the Employment Exchanges as out of work is 37,125 as
compared with 64,000 a little over a
year ago. This improvement has been
most marked in the Linen Industry,
and has been reflected in the important
shirt and collar manufacturing trade
in Londonderry. A year ago I referred to the financial assistance which
my Government was rendering to the
advertising of Ulster linen in the
United States of America and I am
glad to know that this effort is bearing
fruit. Further contributory causes
towards the improvement have been the
stabilization of foreign exchanges and a
widespread recognition of the fact that
prices have now fallen to a firm level.
I am also glad to observe that the
Shipbuilding Industry is sharing in the
revival in trade. My Government
is continuing the Loans Guarantee
facilities to foster further trade whereever possible.
I earnestly pray that those engaged
in the various industries of Northern
Ireland will use their utmost endeavours
to
ensure that the improvement in
the volume of employment will be
maintained.
Proposals will be laid before you with
the object of according to Road
Authorities further powers in connection with the improvement of the roads
generally and particularly in relation
to widening and rounding-off corners,
with the object of reducing risks of
road accidents to the lowest possible
dimensions.
was
As it not found possible to
complete the necessary arrangements
to admit of legislation being introduced
during last Session in regard to the
minor difficulties which have arisen in
the interpretation and administration
of the intoxicating Liquor Act, I
trust that the Bill which is now to be
laid before you will receive your earnest
consideration.
A Bill will be submitted to you to
deal with the evil of the worrying of
sheep and cattle by dogs.
It is also proposed to bring the
existing arrangements for the provision
of funds for the erection of labourers'
cottages by Rural District Councils
more into harmony with the system
which is already in operation in
connection with the provision of capital
funds for Urban housing and Local
Government services generally.
Other Bills will be laid before you
dealing with the following matters: ---
To make provision regarding Unemployment Insurance.
To protect persons engaged on
painting work against the
dangers of Lead Poisoning.
To amend and consolidate the law
relating to Workmen's Compensation.
To extend the powers of Railway Companies with regard to
the owning and running of
omnibuses.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
15 MARCH 1927
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
My Government has caused an expert
investigation of the potentialities of
Coastal Harbours to be undertaken
with a view to the development of the
Fishery Industry of Northern Ireland,
and has set up a Departmental Committee to inquire into the marketing of
Agricultural Produce.
I
that
pray
deliberations may,
your
under the Divine blessing, result in the
happiness and contentment of the
people of Northern Ireland.
Debate on the Address.
Mr. MILLER (in morning dress): It
is my duty and privilege to move:
"That an humble Address be presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as followeth-
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to Your Grace for the Speech which
Your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."
It
Before doing so I should like, as this is
the first time that this House has met
since His Majesty was graciously pleased
to confer upon the Prime Minister a
Peerage of the United Kingdom, to congratulate him upon the signal honour
that has been bestowed upon him.
has always been an idea of mine that the
Leader of this House should have a sear
in the House of Lords, and now that
that House is going to be reformed 1
think it would be a good thing if he
would see that the Prime Minister of
Northern Ireland should in future have
a seat in the House of Lords, in the same
way as the Lord Mayor of Belfast and
the Mayor of Derry have seats in our own
Senate. He would then be able to tell
our grievances to the House of Lords,
and his presence would form another tie
with the Mother Country.
I would also like to congratulate the
Prime Minister and the Minister of Home
Affairs on the success of their recent tour
through Ulster. We were all very
pleased to see them, and we were gratified
at the fact that the Prime Minister heard
at first hand what the people had to say.
Before we had a Parliament here we
used to say in rural Ulster :
"To the sky, 'tis high,
To the Czar, 'tis far,"
To Westminster, 'tis impossible to get
there at all. In fact the majority of the
Members at Westminster did not know
whether Ulster was a town or a province.
I knew of one man who insisted that
Ulster was a town; he did not know there
was such a thing as the Province of
Ulster.
Those of us who listen to the words of
wisdom that fall from the lips of the
Prime Minister from time to time did
not expect anything sensational in the
King's Speech on this occasion. We are
all familiar with the story of the
Creation. We are told that the Creator
of the universe, having spent six days in
bringing order out of chaos, rested on the
seventh day; that He looked upon the
work, and saw that it was good. We are
not told the length of the days, but we
do know that our Prime Minister, after
spending six years in bringing order out
of chaos in Northern Ireland, and in
forming the machinery to carry on our
Government, stood in the frontier towns a
few months ago, looked upon the work
that he had done, and saw that it was
good. And he determined to rest in the
seventh year, which we are now beginning, so that the work that has to be
done in the seventh year, the year of
rest, is not going to be very strenuous.
It is to be more of a Sabbath day's work
than anything else. But even on the
Sabbath day certain things have to be
done, and so in the Gracious Speech
which we have heard to-day there is
nothing sensational; there are just a few
things to enable us to carry on.
It is gratifying to learn from the
Gracious Speech that the burden of unemployment has been greatly lessened,
and that the two staple industries-shipbuilding and linen-are on a fair way to
getting on their feet again. I regret,
however, that the Gracious Speech has
not been able to say the same thing about
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Miller]
our rural staple industry, Agriculture.
What with rates and taxes and the price
of labour, agriculture is in a very bad
way at present, and those engaged in the
industry are looking to the Government
to try to help them to get things into
a better way of working.
We understand from the Gracious
Speech that premier place is to be given
to a Roads Bill, to enable the local
authorities to improve the roads and to
cut off and to straighten out corners.
Owing to the dimensions of present-day
traffic it is very necessary that that
should be done. I understand that one
of the things aimed at is a cheaper,
easier and not so cumbersome way of
acquiring land which is wanted for public
purposes. That to my mind is a very
important thing. The matter was
brought to my notice lately in connection
with one of our County Councils. Some
three years ago our County Council took
advantage of the fact that there was a
derelict building in the centre of my
native town. They decided to run a road
through this house and some back
gardens, so as to cut off two very
dangerous corners, one a right angle and
the other an acute angle, ending in a
bottle neck, where it was impossible for
two vehicles to pass. All the preliminary
matters in connection with the proposal
were passed unanimously by the County
Council, and the County Surveyor told
me that he hoped to start the work in
April. Unfortunately some people got
the idea that there was a gold mine u
some of the back gardens, and they asked
so much for the ground that the County
Surveyor became frightened, especially as
County Councils become very economical
in the last days of their existence. The
County Council passed resolution
dropping the proposal. The Government
had agreed to give a loan of £2,500, but
the greed of certain people stopped the
whole thing, with the result that the
72 per cent. from the Ministry of Labour
was lost to the county. I think, therefore, that a Bill that would enable land
to be taken for public purposes, without
the payment of an exorbitant price, is
very much wanted at the present time.

sure there is no Member of this House
I am
who has not been having conversations

We then come to the industry about

agricultural industry-and there are
three matters mentioned in the Gracious
Speech which directly or indirectly affect.
the farmers. In the first place, we are
going to have a tightening up of the law
so as to obviate the destruction of sheep
and cattle by dogs. This will be very
welcome I am sure, especially in some
parts of the country where the people
have suffered enormously through dogs at
certain times banding themselves together
and killing sheep right and left.
The second matter that is of interest to
agriculture is the very prompt way in

own county of Tyrone-that as soon as he
got back to Belfast he would set up a
Commission of Inquiry with reference to
the great dfference between the price paid
to the producer and the price paid by the

selling knows that there is a tremendous
difference in those two. The Prime
Minister promised that he would have
inquiries made, and he has done so very
promptly. I think if he had added
horticulture it would have been well--
though perhaps agriculture includes horticulture because I think anyone who is
interested in horticulture must know that
in this case there is even a greater discrepancy between what the producer gets
and what the consumer pays.
The third matter that affects the agricultural community is the provision of
funds for the building of labourers'
cottages. Most rural councils at the

present time are very dilatory in looking

Various other Bills are foreshadowed in

Mr. BLACK (in morning dress): I
rise to second the Motion which has been
so ably moved by the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Miller).
At the outset I wish to associate myself
with the expression of the pleasure of all
of us at the honour which his Majesty
has seen proper to confer on the Prime
Minister (hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-an honour which we regard as done not
only to the Prime Minister personally
but to the Province of which he is the
chief citizen. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
The substantial diminution in the
amount of unemployment which is recorded at the very outset in His Grace's
Speech must be a matter of profound
satisfaction and gratification to every
Member of this House, and to every
member of the community. In my judgment the greatest calamity which has
befallen Northern Ireland since this Parliament was established was the wave of
acute and long-continued industrial
depression which has swept over us.
do not think I am speaking too strongly
when I say that at times it threatened
almost to engulf us. One thinks back to
the causes of this depression. They are
not to be found in anything for which
this Government, or the Parliament of
this part of the country, can be held responsible. They are not to be found in
anything for which the employees or
employers of Northern Ireland can be
held responsible. They are not to be
found in any conditions which could have
been controlled, or averted, or in any way
dealt with by this Parliament or by the
Imperial Parliament. They are to be
found in world-wide conditions, and,
although it was possible for the Parliament of the United Kingdom or for the
Parliament of Northern Ireland to do
something to alleviate the evils of unemployment that this long depression
brought in its train, yet those measures,
whether it be the extension of the benefits
that were
covenanted under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, whether it
be helping trade under the Loans
Guarantee Act, these measures were
merely palliatives and did not strike
at the root of the matter. And, just
as the cause of this depression was a
world-wide cause, so when we look to the
passing away of the depression we find its
cause in world-wide conditions too. It is
is a great satisfaction to find that competent observers, financiers, statesmen,
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
and men of business, detect at the present
time the passing away of the industrial
depression which has overcast not only
this country but practically the whole of
the civilised world, and we hope that we
are now entering upon the beginning of
an era of prosperity which will correspond in length and in intensity to the
era of depression through which we have
already passed. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Unfortunately the industrial depression hit us in Northern Ireland very hard,
because two of the industries in the
Kingdom which suffered most were the
linen industry and the shipbuilding industry, and those are two of the chief
industries upon which the people in
Belfast and the Urban Districts in
Northern Ireland depend for their sustenance. We learned with great gratification at the outset of the Gracious Speech
that there are already signs of a decrease
in unemployment in the linen industry,
and the same may be said about the shipbuilding industry. It is common knowledge that already a great many orders
have been placed with the leading firm of
shipbuilders in Belfast, that the yards are
becoming busy again, that six months'
hence, humanly speaking, every slip will
be occupied, and the work will be going
on as it was going on in the best times in
Belfast. It is with great satisfaction that
we note this in the Gracious Speech.
My excuse for dwelling on this is that
I think it is one of the chief matters of
vital importance, and it is of vital importance not only to industrial districts, such
as Belfast and Londonderry, but also to
the agricultural districts. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I venture to say that
when the towns become prosperous again,
when the buying powers of the people in
Belfast, in Londonderry, in Lisburn, and
in Portadown increase you will find that
prosperity reflected in the prosperity of
the country too. We are all one community. We in the cities cannot live
separately from the people in the country.
The interests of the city and the interests
of the country are not different.
are ultimately the same interests, and once
we get prosperity back to the city I
venture to say again we will be getting
prosperity back to the rural districts.
They
All the legislation which is adumbrated
in the Gracious Speech from the Throne
can, I think, be regarded as non-contentious legislation in the sense that the
matters which are dealt with are none of
the matters which form part of the great
contentions of party politics. In a Parliament such as ours, which has not to deal
with wide matters of foreign policy like
the Imperial Parliament, there are great
opportunities for useful legislation on
'domestic matters, just such type of legislation as is outlined in the Speech from
the Throne. And there will always be
that opportunity. We will never be able
to say that our work in that respect is
done, because with the progress of science,
the progress of knowledge, the progress of
arts, and the progress of human affairs
we will be finding that our life and the life
of the community is gradually getting
more and more complex, that there will
be more matters arising which have to be
provided for and dealt with by legislation, particularly of the type which is
foreshadowed in the Speech which has
been addressed to us to-day.
An excellent illustration of that is the
progress which has been made in the
motor industry. That industry is only
about thirty years old, but it is not too
much to say that it has entirely revolutionised the use of the roads in the community. The roads in the community
were originally built for horse traffic.
They were built for light traffic, for sparse
traffic, for slow moving traffic, and only
with a view to that. But nowadays what
do we find? The roads are used for busy
traffic, for fast traffic for which they were
never originally designed. That is a
matter that has to be dealt with because
it is common knowledge that the change
in the type of traffic on the road has inade
the dangers of the road a thousand times
greater than ever they were in the old
times.
Now Parliament can deal with matters
of this nature in two ways. They can
deal with the traffic itself. They can
prescribe and control the type of vehicle,
they can make regulations regarding the
speeds of vehicles. In the second place
they can deal with the roads themselves
and not the traffic on the roads, making
the roads more adaptable and suitable
for the traffic. In the last Session of
Parliament we passed through an Act
dealing with the first of these mattersvehicles used on the road, the safety of
the roads, and the construction and regulation of the vehicles. I venture to say
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
15 MARCH 1927
that this is not the last word on the subject, and if any of us live twenty or
thirty years more we will find, owing to
the new and fresh conditions that have
arisen and that experience has taught us,
more legislation on the same lines will be
needed. In this Session it is proposed to
introduce a Bill dealing not with traffic
on the roads but with the roads themselves.
Anyone connected with the roads in
Northern Ireland sees the necessity for it
-sees how necessary it is to give the road
authorities some powers to improve these,
to make them suitable for the new type of .
traffic which is using the roads.
Legislation of this kind will presumably
have to confer on local authorities power
to take some land compulsorily either for
widening a road
road or the rounding of
corners. The Legislature has always been.
properly jealous of any taking away of a
man's property compulsorily, but in a
matter of this nature where the good that
is done to the community will far outweigh the small injury which will be done
to owners of land in rural districts by the
knocking off of small corners in order to
round off the roads, that is a proper
power that should be given to local
authorities. But there is one thing I
hope will be provided for in whatever
Bill is introduced. It has been a remarkable thing in all Acts of Parliament which
have been passed giving compulsory
powers to take land that the tendency has
been for the expense of the acquisition.
almost to outweigh the value of the land
acquired. I hope something will be provided in this Bill so that when local
authorities do have to take lands they will
not be put to outrageous expense not only
in paying for the lands but paying for
the machinery by which the lands are
acquired. (Hon. Members: Hear hear.)
Another aspect in which the growth of
motor traffic has revolutionised things in
the country is the effect it has had on railway traffic. I do not need to dilate on
that or speak of the advantages the
obvious advantages-which motor traffic
on the roads has over the railway; how
the railway only carries people from a
fixed station to a fixed station along a
fixed course and at a fixed time; how the
omnibus is more mobile and can take up
a man here and drop him there on the
road and can be turned from one road to
another and use parts of the country that
have not yet been open to the railway.
Great good has been done to the community by the development of the omnibus traffic in recent years. Unfortunately, that traffic has led to injury being
done to the railway traffic. Now, it has
come almost the fashion to regard the interests of railways and the interests of
omnibus owners as entirely antagonistic
-to regard railway traffic and road
traffic as antagonistic. I venture to think
that that is in some degree a mistake, and
that the road traffic could well be made
by enlightened administration to be the
feeder of the railways. Railways carrying
people over long distances more satisfactorily than chars-a-bancs can do, could
be made to assist the road traffic. I welcome in the Gracious Speech the suggestion that legislation will be introduced
which will enable railway companies to
add to the facilities of the travelling
public by running omnibuses which will
link up their lines of railways, which will
act as feeders to the railways and which
will provide them with facilities which I
venture to think ought to have been provided long ago-facilities for bringing
people to their stations. I venture to
think that that will be wise legislation
and legislation which gives one hope of
the stopping of what almost threatens at
the present time to be the break-up of the
railway system, which would be a disaster
to the community, for whatever one may
think of the respective merits of railways
and omnibuses the railways have contributed, do contribute and always will contribute, a great deal to the comfort and
well-being of the people of the country.
Another subject dealt with in the
Gracious Speech on which legislation
becomes necessary from time to time to
adapt itself to changing conditions is the
Workmen's Compensation Acts. When
the Workmen's Compensation Acts were
first introduced, the policy was a simple
policy. It was simply a policy that the
workman should be compensated for any
accident which arose to him out of and
in the course of his employment. That
seemed a simple thing, and to the
framers of the early Workmen's Compensation Act it seemed a simple thing.
It was considered by those who introduced the earlier Acts to be SO
simple that no lawyer would get any
employment. It was to be a pure layman's Act. Experience has taught us
that so far from being a simple thing it
was anything but simple, owing to the
way in which the various matters regarding accidents and the way in which people
Debate on Address

[Mr. Black]
had to be compensated had to be dealt
with. They are highly complex, and
accordingly from time to time it has become necessary to amend the Workmen's
Compensation Acts to deal with all those
conflicting things. The first Act of
1897 was an Act of ten Sections. The
Act under which we are still working in
Northern Ireland-the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1906-was an Act of 17
Sections. The Act passed in 1925, which
was a codifying Act, is an Act of 51
Sections, showing that experience has
taught that you to have to add to these
matters, that you
you have to include
matters which were overlooked in the
earlier Acts dealing with a complicated
subject. As conditions become
complex so they will have to be legislated
for.

In a matter such as Workmen's Compensation it is in the highest degree
essential that our legislation here should
be kept on strictly parallel lines with
legislation in England. There is no
why our legislation here in
a matter such as that should be
behind English legislation, and I
welcome the suggestion in the Gracious
Speech that we will have legislation on
this subject. The legislation I take it
will be grounded and founded on the 1925
English Act, and I welcome the suggestion that the legislation will be legislation
of a codifying character. There is nothing I think that is worse for the community than when you have to look not
at one Act or one code but a long series
of Acts which it takes a skilled lawyer to
unravel. I take it with regard to this
Workmen's Compensation Bill that the
Bill will simply be a codifying Bill embodying such things as have been shown to
be necessary by experience in the working.
of the existing Acts, and that no change
will be made in the existing policy of
these Acts--in the enlightened policy,
I may say so, which provides for the compulsory insurance of men at their work
against accident happening in the course

There is a reference to an Act being
brought in to amend the Intoxicating

same way as the Workmen's Compensation Acts. A code was gradually built
up.
As Parliament has seen the necessity for amending or extending the Acts
something further has been added. But
there is this difference between the two
Acts. The Workmen's Compensation

takes not only a lawyer but a lawyer who
has been specialising in these matters to
form any real conception of the position.
with regard to anything in the slightest
degree off the beaten track in connection
with those Acts. The latest of these Acts
is our own, the 1923 Act. That Act to a
certain extent initiated a change of
policy. It is not difficult to realise the

We need not be surprised that here and
there in the framing of the Act something
was overlooked, something not actually
provided for, some loophole left, something which a little experience shows
requires some amending Act. Anyone
who has practised at my profession must

1923. Anyone can see what the intention

have been brought before the legal profession but also before those who had
to do with the actual administration of
the Act, and they have also found

may well be made the subject of an

The PRIME MINISTER: We have
been able to carry that on under even
more stressful conditions than existed
across the Channel, because our proportion of
unemployment was always
somewhat higher than theirs. Then
the termination of this period
the unemployment scheme has proved
that the men and women are ready
to step into their places. They were
around the factories and around the
yards and were easily absorbed once more
into the industries to which they were
born and bred. That is one of the good
effects of the Unemployment Insurance
Acts.
Another gratifying feature is this.
The pessimistic expressions with regard
to it in the past were all to the effect
that these people were being spoiled and
ruined through being on the unemployment list, that they would never be able
to regain their old vitality and skill, that
they would lose the traditional energy of
the Ulster working man and the Ulster
working woman. What are the facts of
the case? Since we met this time last
year 26,000 places have been thrown
open to those people and 26,000 people
have walked into them and taken up the
employment to which they were born and
bred. I venture to say that if those
other places that are still vacant according to our returns were offered to these
unemployed there would not be a man or
woman walking the streets. It is for
us, therefore, to encourage in every possible way that we can the industries which
go to absorb the unemployed who are unemployed through no fault of their own.
I would like to say that the Government will continue as it has done in the
past to help in every possible way the
development in these great industries. My
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) will do
everything in his power under the Loans.
Guarantee Act to foster it and attract
orders to our yards. Then there are, of
course, the satisfactory reflections that
over and above those two industries there
is a large number of allied industries which
also immediately begin to feel the effect
of the turn in the tide. All this has
really nothing or very little to do with
either the Government or this House or
with politics, but it is a matter for
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
15 MARCH 1927
keenest satisfaction on all sides of the
House that the hammers are once more
heard in the yards and that the looms
are beginning to go full steam again. I
am sure there is no one who will take
particular credit about that, except to be
most thankful, as the hon. and learned
Member for South Belfast (Mr. Black)
has said, that these happy days have once
more returned to us.
Then may I turn from matters that
affect industry in the towns to some of
those questions which more closely affect
our country areas? I was particularly
pleased with the tour to which my two hon.
Friends have referred and my visit to
the local authorities, and with what I saw
in every part of Ulster. The self-sacrificing, voluntary work that is done by
those who represent the county councils
and the other local authorities is beyond
praise. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Í admit I was agreeably surprised by the
extraordinary ability with which they
carry on their work, with their local
knowledge and their interest in everything for the good of the local people. I
am talking without regard to class or
creed. I found in every one of the local
authorities an anxiety to do their best
for the people whom they represent.
have also to add that I was struck very
much with the ability and the energy, not
to mention the courtesy, of the local
officials. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
They seemed to me to have a personal,
close interest in the whole locality that
was beyond all praise. And when I consider the wonderful asylums and the
hospitals and other local institutions, how
well they are managed and how much
keen local interest is taken in them, I say
that we here in Ulster may be proud of
our local institutions. We should be
most cautious to do nothing that would
damp down the ardour of the men who
carry on the local authorities, and we
should be careful to do nothing that
would add to their difficulties or burdens
by putting more upon the rates. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
When I was visiting, or had waiting
upon me various deputations, I found
that there were two points agitating the
minds of the people in the country districts that I would very much like to
have cleared up to-day, so that they will
not have to be referred to again. I
realise that it is much more difficult for
farmers and others living at a long
distance from the Capital to keep in
touch with the finances of the country
than for the dwellers in the city. The
papers take longer to reach them. Some
of them cannot afford to subscribe to more
than a local paper that comes out once a
week, or it may be that the matters to
which I am referring to-day are not reported in the country papers to the same
extent as they are reported in those that
are edited here in the city. But I did
find two questions that seemed to puzzle
the minds of the farming community, or
a certain section of them at all events,
and I would like to have these cleared up
to-day.
In many quarters I find that the cost
of administration has got mixed up with
the cost of our local services. In other
words, people in those far away country
districts have got an impression that the
cost of our administration is mounting
up unnecessarily from year to year, and
they have an idea that if we could only
stop this gradual growth of administrative expenses the moneys so saved
could in some way be spread over agricultural or local needs. Now, Sir, I wish
to be most careful and convincing on this
point to-day. I have here before me the
figures relating to the actual expenditure
on administration as shown in our Appropriation Accounts. Everybody knows
quite well that the question of our local
services covers Unemployment Insurance,
National Health Insurance, Old Age
Pensions, Widows' and Orphans' Pensions, Grants-in-Aid of Agriculture, and
SO on. That must be kept entirely
separate from the cost of administration.
Let me take for comparison the year
1924-25. I take that particular year because I think everybody will agree that
we should be permited at least two-and-ahalf or three years prior to that in order
to get settled down to a standard which
is fitting for the running of our Civil
Service.
In 1924-25 the total amount of the
salaries paid was £367,000. For the year
just concluding, 1926-27, it will be
£409,000, an increase of £42,000, or
something under 12 per cent. I have seen
it stated that we have gone up as much
as 60 per cent. It is easy for those who
are not fully acquainted with the real
facts of the case to spread about a rumour
which almost raises, if I may use the expression, cupidity in the minds of people
who do not know any better, and who are
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
bound to get a shock. Therefore, I think
it is well that I should make this perfectly
clear that it is something under 12 per
cent.
That can be accounted for in a very
reasonable manner. There was an increase of staff naturally necessitated by
the exceptionally large numbers of unemployed, and by the passing of the
Widows', Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act. Both of those
account for £19,000. The transfer of the
Council of Ireland services to us accounts
for a further £16,000, and the remainder,
which is only £6,000, is attributable to
the cost of the Census, and to the natural
increments payable to the whole of the
Civil Service. Those three sums bring us
back to the 1924-25 figures, and show that
except for the extraordinary number of
unemployed, and except for these other
unexpected events, there has been practically no change in the cost of administration since 1924-25. Of course it is
right to say that with a revival of trade,
and with the large number that have been
absorbed from the unemployed list, the
number that my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) will require in the Ministry of
Labour will be much lower during the
coming year, and naturally we will be
able to make a considerable saving in that
direction.
Then there is another point, the second
point, upon which there is so much misunderstanding. The Colwyn Committee
being satisfied that our establishment is
fair and reasonable, and we on the other
hand being satisfied that the existing permanent staff is necessary to carry out the
administration of the various services, the
present numbers may be accepted as a
fair standard. If the Joint Exchequer
Board determine at any time that our
staff expenditure is on the whole higher
than that existing in Great Britain, or if
they are led to believe that we could
manage with a lesser staff, they will not
allow us to spend the money in other
ways, but will insist on the Imperial Contribution being correspondingly
creased. I hope I have made this so clear
that everybody will be able to understand.
it in future, that owing to the arrangements come to through the Colwyn Committee, the Joint Exchequer Board,
taking into consideration the formula that
is laid down by them, could not permit
the money that might possibly be saved
on the administration of Departments
inthat go to form the Government, to be
spread over, or taken away for, any other
causes.
Therefore, it is really too bad of anyone to hold out to poor people in whatever part of Ulster they may reside that
there is a nest egg, a golden sack, ready
for them to put their hands into, if only
we could cut down the services, because
that is not the case. Owing to the formula, that money would have to be surrendered. If it is possible to make a
saving, owing to the formula, it is bound
to go back into the contribution that we
make towards the Imperial Services.
Now I would like also to point out
once more the difficulty there is in carrying out an improvement on the figures
which I have just given here to-day. We
are
sometimes compared with Great
Britain in this matter. It has been
realised that in Great Britain there were
a large number of services naturally
started during the war, and those Departments that were necessarily created
during the war were the field of the
Geddes axe. They were the field where
any savings might possibly be carried out
by a Chancellor of the Exchequer at
Westminster. But our Parliament was
established, and our Government was set
up, a considerable time after the war,
without any relation whatever to the
extra necessities of the war period. We
were established, if I may use the expression, at bed rock.
We were started off afresh with what
was considered by the Treasury on the
other side, by the Joint Exchequer Board,
and by the Colwyn Committee, to be a
fair and just service to carry on our proportion of what was after all the old
United Kingdom Parliament. Therefore, it is not possible for us to carry out
in an equivalent way those economies
which have been pressed for on the other
side. And that, I think, is the explanation that everybody should give to those
who feel that something further might be
done to narrow the staff that is necessary
to carry on our Government. However,
it will be reassuring to the House to know
that when our Minister of Finance introduces the Estimates for the coming
year he will be able to show a considerable all-round reduction which will justly
earn new laurels for him and the largest
and the principal Department of our administration.

15 MARCH 1927
I think it would be proper if I referred
further to my visit to the country districts. I noticed the great improvement
that has been effected during the past
twenty years. I noticed a better tone
and a happier tone amongst the farming
classes. I observed, as everybody must
observe, better roads, cleaner fields,
better-trimmed hedges, and an anxiety
upon the part of the people to bring
themselves into line with modern conditions.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Agriculture, knows better than any man
how slow and uphill a task it is to make
people break with old traditions, but undoubtedly, gradually, slowly, but surely,
we are going to capture many markets
that at present are debarred to the Ulster
farmer. That will take time. Now that
our industries have found their feet, the
policy of the Government will be to pay
particular attention during this coming
year to what, after all, is our greatest industry-agriculture and fisheries. Coupling that, of course, with the drainage of
the Bann, we propose that the fishing
villages all round our coast, the little
shelters, harbours, that require to be
assisted here and there, fishing itself, and
agriculture will be carefully looked after
by the Government, and particularly by
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale),
who has set up, as was stated in the
Gracious Speech, a special committee to
deal with these points, which, if they
were once settled would greatly improve
the farming industry.
What a pleasure it must have been to
everybody to read the complimentary
letters that appeared in the London Press
during the past few days as to the way
in which Ulster eggs and butter and
other agricultural produce were exhibited
at the exhibition in London. What a
change from ten, fifteen or twenty years
ago, to see that there we were actually
earning, and justly earning, the praise
of those who are so well able to judge!
Our Chief Whip, who takes SO much
interest in horse flesh, asked a question
the other day of the Secretary of State
for War with regard to the breeding of
light horses in Northern Ireland. And
what was the answer he got? He got the
answer that the Government of Northern
Ireland encourages the breeding of light
horses by granting subsidies for stallions.
Of the total number of light horses purchased for the Army during the current
financial year over 55 per cent. were purchased in Ireland, and over half of those
were purchased in Northern Ireland.
It is the same all along the line. I had
evidence of it myself with regard to cattle,
and we all know what is going on with
regard to grading-we see on every hand
signs of an improvement which we all
most cordially welcome.
The policy of the Government then will
be to carry on and to help all we possibly
can. It cannot be too often emphasised
that an order of, say, a 20,000 ton ship
in our yards is infinitely more valuable
than 20,000 speeches made in any part
of Ulster-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-that 20,000 tourists coming into our
area are far more valuable than 20,000
disgruntled letters written to the Press.
What we as a Government are going to
aim at as much as possible is less
speeches-
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
closure on them.
Put a

trying to help it in every way we possibly
Therefore the policy of the Government will be to carry on as we are doing,
and, as has been referred to by the mover

is so that we may carry on in this way

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
programme for the Session purposely.
We think Ulster will be delighted to know
that there is not to be anything further in
the way of legislation of an acrimonious
character. We hope that all will be discouraged who attempt to throw the apple
of discord into our midst when we are
just going to take advantage of these
peaceful times so hardly earned. Let us
have a year at all events of peace and
quiet in our midst, so that all may pull
their full weight and get on with the
business that lies to our hands.
After all I venture to say our credit
in Ulster never was as high as it is today. We owe no man anything. We
have had a succession of Budgets with
balances on the right side. A peaceful,
happy, and contented Ulster does undoubtedly attract orders to Ulster.
Where you find disturbance, where you
find acrimonious discussion going on
people on the other side are very apt to
say "Well we will not give our order to
Ulster," but when all is peaceful and
happy that is the best guarantee not only
of getting orders but also of attracting
tourists into our midst. Therefore, the
policy of the Government, as I say, will
be to work as hard as we possibly can, to
ask everybody else to work as hard as they
possibly can, and in that way to bring back
something of the old prosperity that used
to be attached to the name of Ulster.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr KYLE: I want, if I may, to congratulate the mover and the seconder of
the Address to the Throne. After what
has been said about speech-making one
feels a little bit dilatory about making
speeches. I wish I could feel as sanguine
as the Prime Minister in regard to the
subject of unemployment. It is very welcome to notice the difference between the
figures for unemployment at the present
time and, say, twelve months ago, but it
is also a bit distressing to notice that in
Belfast, for example, our rates are going
to go up 9d, 8d of which is due to the fact
that there are so many people denied unemployment insurance benefit that they
have had to go for the first time to the
Poor Law authorities. So that, while one
recognises the very satisfactory progress
that has been made in regard to the
diminution of the figures, one cannot help
but realise how important the problem is
still and also that very little has been
suggested or is suggested-in fact nothing
is suggested in the Gracious Speech from
the Throne-as to any proposals of the
Government to remedy the affairs as they
exist to-day where there are round about
37,000 people on the registers, not taking
into account the numbers who are not on
the registers at all.
I do not think the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Miller) in
moving the Address to-day was very
happy perhaps in some of his phrases. I
notice that in the tour which has been
mentioned the farmers in the constituency
which he represents-at least according
to the reports in the Press the Tyrone
farmers did not evidently think everything in the garden was lovely as our
hon. Friend would have us believe.
There is one thing no doubt in the
Address that we do welcome and that is
the setting up of a Committee of Inquiry
into the marketing of agricultural produce (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and I hope the right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale)
will see that there are at least some
Labour representatives chosen to act on
that Committee. We have raised this
matter from time to time in the House,
and now we raise it again in the hope
that the right hon. Gentleman will see
to it on this occasion that it is done.
There is no doubt that it is necessary,
because one remembers the fact that
last year another hon. Member for
Fermanagh and Tyrone, who is evidently
a higher authority on temperance than he
is on the price of potatoes, was discussing
this matter-you remember that at that
time last year potatoes were selling in
Belfast at 6d per stone, that is £4 a ton,
and the farmer at that time was getting
30s a ton for his potatoes, so that
obviously there is a leakage, and a very
considerable leakage, somewhere. Do not
let the Prime Minister and his Government think that they are going to make
the suggestion that an increased price
should be paid by the consumer in the
towns to give the farmer a better price.
There is surely room for the farmer to
get a price and for the consumer to pay a
little less than he is paying now-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-if common
sense and intelligence are used in the
matter.
There is another matter I would like
to mention in connection with the Loans
Guarantee, which has been mentioned by
the Prime Minister, and to make hon.

and hon. Gentlemen on the other side

Mr. GRANT: That is a bad argument.
Does that not show our broad-mindedness
over here?
Mr. KYLE: I welcome the proposal
to bring in a Measure to deal with the
evil of lead poisoning. By doing so we
are only getting into line with France,
with Belgium, with Poland, with Czecho
Slovakia, with Spain, and with Sweden.
Our Government are intending to do this,
though I would not be hopeful that our

hope our Government will go further towards the ratification of further conventions. Particularly I would ask them
to pay attention to the hours of labour
convention passed at Washington in 1919.
This lead poisoning convention was passed
in 1921, and the British Government,
composed of Tories like our hon. Friends
opposite, have refused to ratify that convention, with the result that their representative of the Home Office has resigned
his position, his official position, because
he could not stand up to the disgrace
which the British Government
brought on the name of Britain by refusing to ratify their own convention. I
hope our Government will go further, and
that they are not going to follow this
disgraceful lead of that hard-faced gang
of Tory tricksters on the other side.

simple thing. Obviously, it would be a

If an alteration in the

Australian Government's legislation with
regard to Workmen's Compensation to
realise how easy and possible it is to
guarantee to the worker, who meets with
an accident in the course of his employment, full wages. That has been done
by the State in Australia. The State
does not look for the extraordinary profits
that the insurance companies receive.

There is mention in the Gracious
Speech from the Throne of the necessity of
making provision in regard to Unemployment Insurance. A Commission has reported on the other side of the water, and
it has issued what is known as the Blanesburgh report. I want to say on behalf of
the Labour Party here that we are going
to oppose the findings of the Blanesburgh Committee being put into operation in Northern Ireland, and I will tell
you why. In Britain the unemployment
figures are round about 10 per cent. unemployed. In Northern Ireland the
figures are down to about 12 or 13 per
cent. of our population. Obviously conditions that would be fair with 9 or 10
per cent. unemployed would not be so
fair or so accurate if there were 13 per
cent., or even 15 per cent, unemployed
such as exists in the Northern area.
That is one of the reasons why we will
oppose the findings of the Blanesburgh
Committee being put into operation here.
There is no doubt that we will be told, as
has been said by the hon. Member for
South Belfast (Mr. Black), that we should
attempt at all times to follow on parallel
lines with Great Britain. I suggest that
in certain things we can follow on parallel
lines with Great Britain, taking into
account, as the umpire says, all the
circumstances of the case. We want to
follow on parallel lines so far as the
Ministry of Agriculture is concerned-co
far as the establishment of an Agricultural Wages Board is concerned. We are
penalising our agricultural labourers in
the Six Counties who are not being paid
the wages
which an hon. Member returned to this House some little time ago.
It is true that some honourable people in
the Six Counties do pay the wages which
the hon. Member gave to me in this House,
but the great bulk of the farm labourers
in the Six Counties are very much below
the level which was then stated. Some
are working for 18s a week, and some are
working for 15s a week. Others are
working for 30s 6d a week, which is the
highest in the Six Counties. It is all very
well to talk about parallel lines, but give
us parallel lines so far as the ordinary
workers in agriculture are concerned.
There is one very grave matter which I
think will probably be the subject of an
Amendment to the Address, and that is
the hardships which people are suffering
from owing to the passing of the Rent
Restriction Act. We will have to have
some amending legislation in regard to
that matter. I am sure hon. Members
on the opposite side have received, as I
have received, innumerable complaints
about the treatment that landlords are
meting out to people in regard to the
rents they are being charged for houses.
I hope that during the Session we may be
able to do something along that line and
mitigate that evil.
There is another matter that has been
the subject of discussion in this House
before, and I think it is surely of sufficient importance to warrant mention,
that is the overdue reform of the poor
law. It is some two years since the
Local Government Commission was set
up, and their Report was to be presented
before we broke up. I do not know that
the Report has yet been issued, and surely
something should be done about the reform of the poor law. I noticed that the
Prime Minister, in his speech, mentioned
the subject of the Drainage of the Bann.

I would like to know what the Government intend to do with the harbour at
Killough. Mention has been made that
an expert examination of the potentialities of the coastal harbours is to be undertaken. That was done by the Commission
which the Prime Minister set up two or

be any necessity to have any further

There is no necessity for any further

Another matter, which I have already
mentioned, is the Reduction of Hours
Convention at Washington in regard to
a 48-hour week. If we could get established in Northern Ireland a 48-hour
week it would mean a reduction of an
hour or two per week to 20,000 people.
That is surely something well worth while.
If it was done in Britain it would mean
a reduction of hours to 3,000,000 people.
I want to challenge the statement made
by the hon. and learned Member for South
Belfast (Mr. Black) that the unemployed
numbers could not be helped by anybody,
and to tell him that he had better think
again, because the increase of the hours
of labour for the miners in Great Britain
has meant that there are 30,000 more

would have been had the British Government not for the first time in history increased the hours. I hope my hon.
Friend the Member for South Belfast
will think again regarding that matter.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The mines
would have been closed in any event.
Mr. KYLE: It would not be a bad
job for some of them. I want also to

another matter which may not seem of
tremendous importance, but which, whe
there is talk of legislating on parallel

Guardianship of Infants Act.
It was
passed by a Tory Government, so there
is no reason why this Tory Government
should not accept what the Tory Government on the other side of the water has
done. Legislation affecting the position
of married women has also been passed
by the Conservative Government in
Britain, and there is no reason under the
sun why it should not be adopted by our
Northern Government.
Lastly, what I would suggest to them
if they have to keep on parallel lines with
Britain is that they have to abolish the
barriers that they have set up so far as
local government is concerned. They
deliberately put up a barrier to keep back
democratic candidates, to keep back the
poor man from having the same chance
as the rich man. That is the literal
truth. There has been set up the barrier
that a man must put down £25 before he
can be nominated as a candidate for the
Belfast City Council. We have seen how
rich men, business men, grocers, butchers,
and tinkers have dragged down the good
name of Belfast till it is what it is to-day.
If the Government are following on
parallel lines we want them to remove
those restrictions which they have set up
so that men of their own class may represent the common people instead of allowing the common people to represent themselves.

It is
I rejoiced to hear the rebuke which
the right hon. Gentleman delivered to so
many of his followers when he was

a very honest vindication of the unemployment grants. He stated that it was all
nonsense to say that these people who

quite true that every great Measure of

Measures that was ever passed. One of
the reasons that some people, who did not
want to defend it, gave for its existence

these islands, because you could not have
people hungry and cold, without food,
without shelter, without hearth and home,
without wrecking society to its very
foundations and destroying the whole
fabric on which society is built.
Therefore, I say it was not only an
essential thing from the human point of
view, but it was an absolute necessity for
the safety of the land. In addition to
that, this is not a grant from the State
at all, as some people imagine. Why is
the State feeding this one? Why is it
making grants to that one? It is nothing
of the sort. The working classes subscribe their share; the employers of
industry subscribe their share, and the
State augments it by giving a contribution. It is a combined and co-operative
effort by all those who are engaged in the
essential industries of the country, to save
people from the ravages caused by
depression in trade, in order that they
may live while unemployment exists.
Not only do I think it justifiable in these
times of abnormal unemployment, but 1

continuance of the Unemployment Fund
to deal with all the people who are out of
employment and who are willing to work,

constantly reading speeches about Imperial

Government are lacking in their duty

the
I end as I began, by saying I regard
this Speech from the Throne as a most
innocuous document, and that it contains
nothing worthy of attention here. It will
be passed through this House, as all these
things are passed, but they are merely
window-dressing. Nothing has been done,
and nothing is suggested, to deal with
the fundamental evils that lie at the root
of our industrial conditions, and it will
be our duty while we are here to continue
to protest against this Parliament being
used as a sort of smoke screen for the
Government. It is not really a Parliament as we understand other Parliaments.
It simply exists here as a recording and
registering agent to another Parliament.
It is incapable of taxing its citizens, and
unwilling or incapable of legislating for
them.
In a few weeks we will rise again and
Parliament will disappear, and so the
game of sham and humbug goes on until
the men who believe in realities will
ultimately get sickened at the lifelessness
and lack of spirit of this institution.
While Parliaments are tottering and falling in every part of Europe and parliamentary institutions are becoming a byword, and while others are pointing out
that Parliaments are no longer effective
instruments for the expression of democratic will, nothing will kill this Parliament except the parliamentarians themselves.

I earnestly pray that those engaged
in the various industries of Northern

to ensure that the improvement in the
volume of employment will be maintained
That is a very important part of the

coming over the country.

question of bringing the clubs into line.
with the public-houses.

There is just one other point I would

Bill or Regulation should be brought in to

Again, I would join with the Leader of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Thomas Henderson]
-I do not know what to call it. I know
one thing, that the man who makes
these statements has no love for the Prime
Minister of the Province of Ulster. He
says:-
"Though fifteen thousand drunkards,
the sod of Ulster tread,
And twenty thousand ragged boys
and girls are craving bread
.

I want to ask the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Grant) and the hon. Member
for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Elliott),
is it not a fact that those children are
craving bread through unemployment,
and not through strong drink? I do not
know whether the Prime Minister or any
Member of the Government has looked
into this matter, but these charges are
being continually levelled at the Government. I am one of the Government.
(Laughter.) What happens? If it is
true that these people are starving
through strong drink, do the people who
are talking not realise that in Belfast
they have a remedy?
I
The remedy was provided by the
Government in the Education Act, which
says that if a child goes to school hungry
or ill-clad, and the schoolmaster's attention is drawn to it, he immediately finds
out the cause by sending an inspector to
the home. If the father is unemployed,
an effort is made to help the child by
giving it books, and in other ways. I am
speaking now for the city of Belfast.
am pleased to say it was this Government
that brought in the Education Act. It
would be a good thing for the citizens of
Ulster if the Education Act were enforced
in its entirety all over Ulster, but unfortunately the city of Belfast is the only
centre that has put the Measure fully into
operation. If the statement that I have
quoted is true, the temperance people can
put those 15,000 drunkards into jail immediately for starving their children. I
am trying to defend the Prime Minister
in his absence against the attacks of his
so-called friends, who are continually
blackguarding him, and making statements to the effect that all the starvation
in Ulster is purely and simply attributable
to strong drink.
My contention is that if there are
15,000 or 20,000 ragged children, their
condition is due to unemployment. These
people who are running about blackguarding the Prime Minister are clergymen, Members of Parliament, and other
things. (Laughter.) I want to protest
in this House against one part of this
statement, and I do not care whether it
is broadcast over Ulster or not.
As a
Member of the Orange Institution, I want
to protest against the Orange Order being
dragged into this question. That is a
matter that should be kept out of the
controversy. It is only because it is referred to in this statement that I mention it in this House. The Orange Institution has enough troubles of its own
without being used as a shuttlecock, and
the members are not going to allow themselves to be made tools of any longer.
Let these people, instead of talking
about the starving children, draw the
attention of the local authorities to the
15,000 who are taking strong drink and
in consequence are starving their children. Let them get the Education Act
put into force, and those men will be put
away until they stop taking strong drink.
I would appeal to the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant) and to the
hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott) to use their great influence
with the clergymen to induce them, instead of running from one hall to another
talking about temperance reform, to come
into the neighbourhood that the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant)
and I represent, to try to do something
for the poor people who are downtrodden,
and to assist the Prime Minister in
solving the unemployment problem. Let
temperance reform take a back place until
the more vital and more important unemployment problem is solved. I believe
that if they do that they will be doing
a nobler thing than they are doing at
present in trying to keep back and to
humbug the Prime Minister when he has
a thousand and one other troubles to
contend with.
I notice that the Government intend to
bring in a Bill for the purpose of rounding-off dangerous corners. I want to ask
the Minister of Home Affairs, or the
representative of the Minister, if he is
satisfied that the taking off of dangerous
corners throughout Ulster will serve any
useful purpose? As one who has been on
a good number of roads in Ulster, I want
to make it clear that the taking-off of
dangerous corners is not going to solve
the traffic problem of the future. I am
quite satisfied that the workers of Ulster

at the present time. I must admit that
the
Government have done a certain

As the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr Devlin) has said, there is not a big
lot for us to deal with here. The fact of

they would settle the whole of the things

I do not want to take up the time of
the House any longer. (Hon. Members:
Go on.
1.) All I would like to say is that I
would suggest that the Minister of

The Prime Minister says that the

remind me of the lady who was always

had a dog called Fido, and Fido was lying
on the mat. The wife started to get a
Fido, Fido,
bit uneasy, and she said
Fido, is that you?" as he crawled up to

his room.
His pal asked "What did you
do?" and he said "I just suddenly
thought it best to go and lick her hand.'
I believe the Government are sleeping in
regard to the tourists who are coming
into Ulster, and I believe everything
should be done to encourage tourists to
come to Ulster. The present system gives
no encouragement to anyone. Even the
roads are no encouragement to an
Englishman, or a Scotsman, or a Welshman to come into Ulster and enjoy himself motor driving. I must admit there
has been a great deal done during the
past two or three years, and I want to
say in reply to the hon. Member for

present now, that the Belfast Corporation
have done more during the last eight
years than was done for the past thirtyeight years, and the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews)-I must give him credithas always tried to help them.
I do not altogether agree with the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
in the speech he has delivered. I as one
Member of this House do not like to hear
the word "Papish" being used, and I
believe the time has come when all right

"Papishes" or anything like that should

At the same time there were other

the Throne. All I can say is that looking

whole thing could then be carried out

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. T. Henderson]
more quickly and more effectively in the
best interests of the Province of Ulster.
There will be Amendments galore here.
There is one particular Bill dealing with
the worrying of sheep by dogs and there
will be five or six Amendments brought
in by the hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone (Mr. Elliott), and we will

Mr. ELLIOTT: I should like to preface any remarks I have to make on this
occasion by adding my congratulations to
those of right hon. and hon. Gentlemen
who have already spoken to the mover
and seconder of the Address for the very
efficient way in which they have discharged their duty.
While the King's Speech opens with a
very optimistic view of unemployment, I
cannot help thinking that this Speech will
be read throughout agricultural Northern
Ireland with a great deal of dissatisfaction and disappointment. We have
heard over and over again from the Prime
Minister, other Members of the Government, and other hon. and right hon.
Gentlemen in this House the importance
of our agricultural industry. I have
searched this Gracious Speech to-day to
find if there is anything on which the
agriculturists of Northern Ireland can
base any hope or from which they can get
any light for the future, and I fail to
find anything. It is quite true that we
find in this Gracious Speech from the
Throne that a Bill is to be passed in connection with the worrying of sheep by
dogs. This is in my opinion a very
necessary Bill and no one who is in any
way conversant with what is taking place
in rural Ireland can be other than gratified by the fact that the Government
have at last promised to bring in
legislation to deal effectively with what is
a great menace to the people, particularly
those in engaged in sheep farming. I
welcome that Bill, and I would like to
'assure the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Thomas Henderson) that
his time will not be taken up here by any
Amendments that I propose to Table in
connection with the Bill dealing with the
worrying of sheep by dogs.
Now in the recent tour of the Prime
Minister through rural Northern Ireland,
accompanied, as he was, by the Minister
of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), I
cannot help thinking that the Prime
Minister heard many views expressed by
the agriculturists of Northern Ireland
which opened his eyes and made him see
the agricultural industry in a light he
never saw it in before. I am here to say
that agricultural Northern Ireland is
passing through a stage of the acutest depression that the agricultural community
ever suffered from. I had hoped that in
the Gracious Speech from the Throne
there would have been some mention of
ameliorative measures which would have
been introduced here whereby the agriculturalists of Northern Ireland would be
enabled in some way or other to carry on.
We all know and I think the Government
realise at last that agriculturists are up
against it, that they are no longer able
to make ends meet, that the present demand for rates, for rent, and for taxes is
so oppressive that they cannot possibly
carry on any longer.
It is quite true that at last the
Government have realised the necessity for setting up a Departmental
inquiry in order that cognisance may be
taken of the fact that the prices of agricultural commodities as supplied to consumers in this industrial city and other
places is not at all in keeping with the
amount the farmers receive for their
produce. This is not a brain wave of the
Government. This matter was discussed
in the last Session of Parliament, and
I joined with the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Geo. Henderson) and the
other hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) in presenting those facts, but
the Government then turned a deaf ear
to our appeals. It has now dawned on
the Government that something must be
done, and I am encouraged to persevere
in asking the Government for further
support in connection with the agricultural industry, because I am convinced
that if we can keep hammering long
enough at the Government and strong
enough and shouting loud enough we will
be able to get something done for rural
Ireland.
Compare the prices that are being
charged in Belfast for agricultural commodities with the prices that the farmers
are receiving for their produce. It is
appalling. To-day in rural Ireland

farmers are receiving £3 a ton for

to-day. Other hon. Members will know

commodity. All the other commodities.
are simply on the same basis. I hope
that when this Departmental Committee
is set up by the Minister of Agriculture
it will consist of all shades-labour representatives, agricultural representatives
and consumers,
as well as those who
handle the stuff-the middlemen. As a
middleman myself I want to see the
middleman getting a fair crack of the
whip. I strongly object to the middleman getting all the profit on agricultural
produce. The man who did the honest
hard work and brought the stuff with the
help of God into existence should get a
fair crack of the whip. It is only now
that the Government have been aroused
to the fact that something must be done
for our agricultural industry. I suggest
to the Minister of Agriculture that this
Departmental inquiry should be made.
very wide in scope. It should not be
like some other committees set up. They
have been sitting behind closed doors for
weeks and weeks and months and months,
and one forgets almost that such a Committee was set up at all. If there is anything to be done to save the agriculturist of Northern Ireland it must be
done immediately, and I suggest that the
Minister of Agriculture should get in
touch with those interested and get this
Committee set up immediately.
I would like to say that I sympathise
in some measure with some of the expressions of opinion that have come from
the Benches opposite. It is all very good
for the Minister of Labour to tell us that
only 37,125 are unemployed as compared
with 64,000 a little over a year ago. I
am quite satisfied that the figures the
right hon. Gentleman has supplied are
perfectly correct as far as the registers
are concerned, but I would like to say
that in Cookstown we never have had
more applications to see if anything can
be done to get men re-established on the
Unemployment Exchange than we have
had during the last fourteen days. Many
of those people were formerly on the unemployment register but they have been
turned down by the committees and they
are no longer unemployed so far as the
right hon. Gentleman is concerned, but
they are receiving outdoor relief, and in
Cookstown to-day there are more unemployed and more poverty and distress than
there were twelve months ago. I feel
that if something cannot be done for
Cookstown and that area through the
right hon. Gentleman's Department we
are going to have a very lean time indeed.
I have put several cases before the right
hon. Gentleman, and I would like to
assure the House that there is no person
more in sympathy with the unemployed
than the Gentleman who presides over
the Ministry of Labour. He is always
willing to turn a sympathetic ear to any
matter which any Member puts to him,
but really the state of affairs in Cookstown is appalling. This morning I had a
letter from a man who has been turned
down because he is not able to satisfy
the members of the committee that he is
genuinely seeking work. That man has
unemployment stamps to his credit. I
would impress on the Minister of Labour
that those men who have stamps to their
credit should not be turned down lightly
if they are able to produce any evidence
at all that they have been looking for
work. I am sorry not to be so optimistic
on this matter as the right hon. Gentleman, and I would like if he or his Parliamentary Secretary would come to Cookstown some day and meet these men and
hear their grievances first hand. If they
are convinced that these men are getting
a fair crack of the whip I will be perfectly
satisfied.
There is another matter in connection
with rural Ireland, and is that the grants
in connection with labourers' cottages are
going to be put on some kind of basis.
am not sure.

They should not have preferential treatment, and there should be no class legislation. I hope that this Amending Bill

Debate on Address
16 MARCH 1927
"That an humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor as followeth:-
--
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our humble
thanks to your Grace for the Speech
which your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."-(Mr. Miller.)
Mr. DEVLIN: On a point of order-
Mr. SPEAKER: I will just put the
Question.
Question again proposed.
Mr. DEVLIN: I desire to raise a very
important constitutional question in relation to the rulings which you, Sir, gave
yesterday. I am not quite clear, and I
do not think, if I may say so with all
respect, that you are quite clear yourself
as to what precisely is the power of this
House in relation to reserved services and
the right of hon. Members of this House
to discuss either legislative, administrative, or financial matters that affect this
House. You stated yesterday that the
Post Office was a reserved service, but if it
is a reserved service I would like to call
your attention to an incident and a statement that took place here lately in
Northern Ireland. On the 15th February, during his tour in Northern Ireland,
the Prime Minister, at Strabane, made
the following reply to some references
that were made to the necessity for a new
Post Office in the town. He said-
"Sir Dawson Bates has taken a note
of what has been said, and will convey
it to the Minister of Commerce, who is
in constant touch with the Imperial
Authorities on the subject of Post Office
matters."
Now, I would like to know, if the Government are in constant communication with
the Post Office authorities in London, and
I merely take this as a typical case, and
if it is within the power of the Government to deal with these Post Office
matters, as clearly the Prime Minister did
in the declaration which he made at
Strabane, are we not permitted in this
House to discuss Post Office matters even
if these matters are a reserved service? I
would be very glad to have your ruling
on that.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps it
would assist you in giving your ruling on
the subject, Mr. Speaker, if I explain
that I think on reflection that the answer
I gave on the occasion quoted by the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) was a proper one.
The Department over which my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Barbour) presides advises
the Government on the other side when
that advice is asked for. Anything
special that is brought to the
notice of the Government on the other
side by this Government is purely in an
advisory capacity. Nothing is borne on
the Votes of this House in regard to the
Post Office, and, therefore, I presume it
is impossible to raise any questions as to
the personnel or as to the cost of buildings
which are borne on the Votes of the
Imperial Parliament. All we are able to
do in all these cases is to advise the
British Government what we think ought
to be done, in the case of a new building
where it ought to be placed and so forth.
Whether that advice is taken or not is
entirely a matter for the Imperial
authorities.
Mr. DEVLIN: I take it that if the
Northern Cabinet, or the Prime Minister,
or the Minister of Commerce is empowered
or has a right to give advice upon these
matters to the Imperial Government, if
they are the creatures of this Parliament
and owe their positions to this Parliament, this Parliament ought to be permitted as one of its privileges and rights
to criticise the advice which its Cabinet
Ministers give to the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. SPEAKER: I stated yesterday, as
the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) will recollect, that it was difficult sometimes to
draw an exact line between where a reserved service could not be mentioned in
this House and where possibly it could.
The hon. Member will notice that there is
a question on the Notice Paper to-day
dealing with some Post Office matter
which he has asked, and which on consideration I allowed because I know that in
some matters advice is sought from Members of the Government here. Generally
speaking, the Post Office, of course, is a
reserved matter and cannot be discussed
in this House in the way in which it can
be discussed in the Imperial House on the
Estimates. Therefore, I think it must be
a question for an individual case to arise,
and a ruling must be sought as to whether
it is within our competence or not to
discuss it here. There might be a par-

My final word will be one on behalf of
the agriculturists of Northern Ireland.
We all know—and I would like to impress

I have had appeal after appeal from
