purchase annuities, and who do not seem
to get any sympathy, at least very little
sympathy, from the Ministry of Finance.
I mentioned one case to the Minister a
few days ago, where an annuity was due
on the 1st December, and where a process
was sent out to recover that annuity on
the 16th or 19th February, I forget
which date. It is all very good to say
that we have got rid of the old landlords,
but I do say that in the old landlord days
if any landlord had issued a process
against his tenant for rent that was not
three months due he would have been
bundled out of the country. I put up
this case to the Minister, and I am sorry
my constituent had not a better record,

able to tell me that it was not the first
occasion on which this gentleman had to
be processed. I would like to remind
the right hon. Gentleman that the rule
of seventy times seven is not enough to a
lot of men, and I think during this acute
period of agricultural depression there
should not be any hard and fast rule,
and that when a man's rent is not
paid inside three months he should
not be processed, but he should get
a little time for consideration. I
hope that some practical sympathy will
be extended to agriculturists, because I

rent or annuity. It is not the want of
will; it is simply the want of means. We

sympathy. They can show that practical
sympathy by at least giving an extra
three months' credit to those who do
not feel able to pay at the moment,

In regard to the general question of the
condition of agriculture, I know that
agriculture is in a depressed condition.
That is common knowledge. It is not
necessary to ring the changes upon the low
prices of produce, because they are open
to every one who reads the newspapers to
observe. It is a deplorable thing that it
should be so. We must not forget that
these prices are regulated by economic
conditions. The fact that the retailer is
charging too much in Belfast, as compared
with the price he pays for his produce
from the farmer, is not the determining
factor in the farmers' price. It is the
competition of foreign countries and the
competition of the Dominions who are
bringing their produce into the only
market we have outside ourselves-Great
Britain. It is a factor such as this that
determines the prices which the farmers
have to submit to. Therefore, when hon.
Members, and particularly the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson),
attack the setting up of a Departmental
Commission to examine into these things,
and expects this Committee apparently to
determine definite and settled prices for
farmers' produce, he is asking something
that is beyond all human power to bring
into operation, because economic conditions are just as definite and as certain
as the laws that govern the universe, and
cannot be changed by any artificial
methods. But in that respect, let me

Mr. DEVLIN: We will discuss education later on. We will deal with it
specially.
Mr. POLLOCK: I say it is proof of
the liberality——
Mr. DEVLIN: No, it is not.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I rise to clear two
points that have been raised during the
course of this debate. My hon. Friend
the Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke) has
referred to the leaseholders, and I would
like to clear up a misunderstanding which
apparently exists, that the Prime Minister
and my Parliamentary Secretary had
given a specific pledge that the Government would deal with this matter. What
the Prime Minister stated was that he is
going to investigate the whole subjectmatter. I cannot conceive of a more
difficult or more technical subject than the
question of these short leases which are
falling in. At the same time one has to
be careful in removing any injustice not
to create two or three other injustices to
take its place. The Prime Minister has
consented to set up a Committee to investigate what I would describe as a most
difficult and thorny subject.
In regard to the question of police
barracks, which has been raised by my
hon. Friend the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford), I would like to take this
opportunity of thanking him for the
letter he gave me before he went away,
which contained some very valuable suggestions. In fact, the Government have
already acted on one of those suggestions
and closed a certain barrack. I refer to
Whitehouse. I would like hon. Members
to appreciate that we have a great deal
of difficulty in regard to the whole question of police barracks. For my part I
think the police are so popular in Ulster
that nobody wants a police barracks removed from their midst.
•
Take, for example, the question of Rock
Barrack, which was raised by the hon.
Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr.
Elliott). That, I am glad to say, is a
very peaceful district. During the bad
period through which we passed it was a
very disturbed area, but if things continue, as I hope they will continue,
peaceful, I am advised by the Inspector-
General that the ordinary police duties
could be properly carried out from
the surrounding sub-districts. When I
tell hon. Members that there are no fewer
than five sub-districts round that area
within a radius of from four to six miles
they will appreciate that that area is on
the whole fairly well policed.
.
However, as my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance has pointed out, we
get a certain allowance for a certain
number of police, and at the present time
we have more police than the number we
are supposed to have under the Colwyn
Award. Therefore, it is absolutely necessary that we should look round to see in
what way we can reduce the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. At the present time recruiting is suspended. In regard to these
specific cases the Government do not wish
to act in any hasty manner. They will
not close police barracks without the most
careful consideration. I should be only
too glad to discuss the pros and cons in
regard to any of these police barracks
with any Member of this House.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Could the right
hon. Gentleman say what will be the constitution of the Committee to investigate
the grievances of expired leaseholders?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid it
is a little premature.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Will it have the
approval of this House?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would be
delighted if my hon. Friend would consent
to serve on the Committee. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's remarks about
closing police barracks, I would like to
suggest to the Government that these
barracks should not be closed without
first of all the people of the district having
an opportunity of expressing their opinion.
I was informed that, before any police
barrack would be closed, the people in
the locality would have an opportunity of
stating their case. I understand this
barrack is going to be closed without the
people having this opportunity. I hold
that is not at all democratic. It is autocratic. I contend the people of the
district should have an opportunity of
expressing an opinion as to whether the
police barrack should remain or not.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure my
hon. Friend expresses the feelings of his
constituents, and I would be very glad to
discuss the matter with him. What I do
say is that if one is to take a vote in an
area in regard to any police barrack, I
venture to suggest the vote will be
entirely in favour of retaining the barrack.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Is it in order that I
should be asked to consult with the right
hon. Gentleman the Minister of Home
Affairs about the closing of a barracks
that he has already authorised to be
closed? Is that not prejudging the case?
Mr. KYLE: They want you to convince them that it is necessary.
UNEMPLOYMENT.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I desire to move this amendment to the
Address:
At the end to add the words
"But
humbly regret that while reference is
made in the Gracious Speech from the
Throne to the decrease in the number
of the unemployed, no mention is made
of the intention of the Government to
carry out its first duty to the people,
namely, the provision of means for
obtaining food, clothing, and shelter
for the people of Northern Ireland."
I regret very much that it falls to my
lot to have again to move an amendment
of this character. When I undertook
this duty first I certainly was not of the
opinion that it was going to become something of a hardy annual. I am afraid
that is what has become, inasmuch as
I have had to move an Amendment in
almost precisely similar terms on three
occasions in recent times.
I was wondering since yesterday as to
whether the optimism that was shown by
the Government Front Bench was justified or not. I certainly hope it will be,
because if that optimism is justified it
will not be my duty to move a similar
amendment on a subsequent occasion.
But I regret very much to have to disagree with the people who give expression
to those thoughts. Since I have been a
Member of this Parliament I have been
at a loss to understand the mentality of
the Gentlemen opposite in regard to this
problem of unemployment. I think I
described it on a previous occasion as the
Government following a Micawber policy
of waiting for something to turn up.
Certainly, as far as I have been able to
observe, the problem has never been dealt
with in anything approaching a scientific
fashion. No expert diagnosis has in my
opinion been undertaken up to the present
moment. I do not believe that the
favourable period has arrived about
which the Prime Minister was so eloquent
yesterday. I think we are asked to
assume far too much.
The Prime Minister quite clearly,
definitely, and unambiguously stated that
26,000 people had obtained employment.
I want to challenge the right hon. Gentleman, and I want to challenge the
Parliamentary Secretary to produce
some evidence that 26,000 people
have been absorbed in employment.
I can quite understand that the
unemployment figures have been reduced by 26,000. But I should point
out that it is an entirely different
matter to suggest that 26,000 people have
obtained employment. I have some definite
knowledge as to whether 26,000 people
have obtained employment or not. The hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin),
my colleague, yesterday pointed out that
it was necessary in Belfast to increase the
rate by 9d in the pound. Now, it is
scarcely necessary to point out that a
penny in the pound on the rates in
Belfast brings in a sum of about £7,000.
Out of that increase of 9d in the rates of
Belfast, 81d is going for poor-law purposes. If you multiply £7,000 by 81 you
get a sum of £60,000 for poor-law purposes in Belfast. I suggest that it is
simply a question of transferring people
from the unemployment register to the
poor-law register, otherwise it would be
unnecessary for the poor-law to ask for an
increase in the rates in Belfast by 81d in
the pound, necessitating an expenditure
Debate on Address-
Unemployment
16 MARCH 1927
of approximately £60,000 per annum for
poor-law purposes in Belfast.
Now, objection may be taken to my
attitude, but I am not prepared to accept
the Prime Minister as being an authority
on this question. Either discreetly or
indiscreetly, in November, 1923-I hate to
be referring to this, because I do not as
a rule indulge in platitudes-I have
referred on two or three occasions to a
statement made by the Prime Minister in
November, 1923. There is some sinister
coincidence, because at that time the
numbers of unemployed were approximately what we are told to-day-37,000and the Prime Minister stated in blunt,
plain language that he would solve the
problem of unemployment. The figure
at that stage was 37,000. Not only did
he not solve the problem of unemployment, but the figures of unemployment in
the Six Counties increased to 70,000. In
view of that am I not justified in coming
to the conclusion that we cannot accept
the optimism of the Prime Minister
without inquiry, and without some reservation. What guarantee have I got that
the Prime Minister is an authority on the
question?
We are told that the expected revival
in the shipbuilding has taken place. Now
it would interest the right hon. Gentleman who is in charge of this debate to
know that according to the most unimpeachable authority-and I am not
quoting this from any Labour or Socialist
paper-the slip accommodation in Great
Britain and Northern Ireland is sufficient
to build 3,000,000 tons of shipping.
We are expected to believe that the revival
of shipbuilding has come. Would the
right hon. Gentleman
be interested
to know that, according to the authority I am quoting, in September
last there were on the stocks in British
and Irish shipyards tonnage to the extent
of 774,797 tons, and the orders placed
since then have been approximately
750,000 tons, or, in other words, the tonnage that was under construction and the
orders that have since been placed amount
to 1,500,000 tons, or exactly half the
quantity British and Irish shipyards are
capable of building. Where is the
revival?
We are asked to believe that the boom
has arrived, and according to the authority from which I am quoting they are
certainly not as optimistic as the right
hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister is.
Now it might be as well when I am quoting this for this purpose to give the
opinion of a gentleman who, I understand, is an authority on this question.
This gentleman tells us:
If now there are signs that the tide is
beginning to turn, with an improvement in the freight market, which may
prove only temporary, those associated
with the industry, ready as they are
to hope for the best, suggest that the
contracts that have recently been
placed, which amount to about 750,000
gross tons, should not be accepted as
evidence that the industry is on the
high road to conditions of abounding
prosperity. If the position is examined,
the following facts are established:
One; that is the one I have given-
—
(1) Slips are available for about
3,000,000 tons, and plenty of labour
to maintain a rapid output could be
secured as it was secured in 1919, when
that record of tonnage was established.
(2) On September 30 last the vessels
in hand amounted to 774,797 tons, but
progress on 107,498 tons had been suspended for one reason or another,
leaving only 667,299 tons on which
work was proceeding. The fresh
tonnage begun during the preceding
three months was only 63,327 tons.
(3) The new orders which have since
been placed amount to about 750,000
tons, and by the end of the year there
may be a few others, but inquiries on the
part of shipowners do not suggest that
many additional contracts will be con-
Icluded in the immediate future.
And at the termination of the article we
get this:
With the knowledge of all these conditions it is hardly surprising that
leaders in the shipbuilding industry,
though they are more hopeful than they
were a few months ago, are disinclined
to indulge in optimistic forecasts.
As I pointed out, that is not from a
Socialist daily. It is not from a Labour
daily. It is not from a person who
preaches pernicious doctrines to the proletarian class. This article was culled
from the "Northern Whig " of December
Debate on Address
Unemployment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
7th, 1926. It is reprinted from the "Daily
Telegraph." I am sure, therefore,
my statement will not be challenged when
I say it is unimpeachable authority.
Apart from this gentleman's testimony,
what do we find the British Government
doing or what is the opinion of a
committee of inquiry established by
the British Government in connection
with the problem of unemployment?
a
Anybody who has taken an interest in
this problem-and I regret to say there
are very few people who take an interest
in this problem, judging by the amount
of attention I am getting at the present
time and the overwhelming attendance of
Members on the Government benches-profound interest is being taken in this great
social question-one of the most baffling
problems that have ever confronted
Government. It is scarcely possible to
get five people on the Government benches
to interest themselves in this problem. It
might be interesting to Members opposite
to know that a Labour Administration
appointed a committee of inquiry during
their tenure of office, and the majority of
the people composing that committee of inquiry were not Socialist or Labour. Quite
recently we have had the result of these
gentlemen's deliberations. Some of the
gentlemen who composed the committee,
were very eminent statisticians and economists. I believe Lord Balfour was one
member of that committee, Sir Josiah
Stamp was another one of the most
eminent economists in Great Britain. They
have come to the conclusion that within
the next two years there is no likelihood
of the numbers of unemployed in Great
Britain falling belcw 600,000. A very
respectable organ of public opinion, "The
Nation," in connection with that matter
states:
-
It is being decidedly optimisticmore optimistic than we think is justified-to assume that unemployment
will fall over the next year or two below
the million mark.
What justification in view of that testimoney is there for the Government suggestion that the problem has been solved
or is on the high road to solution in
Northern Ireland? I suggest that the
Prime Minister was taking credit for putting into employment every person who
has emigrated, every person who has been
put on out-door relief, and the hundreds
that at the present time are filling the
infirmary wards of the Belfast Institution
and probably many other institutions
throughout the Six Counties. The Prime
Minister is taking credit for having
placed all these in employment.
I listened with very much interest to
some speeches delivered in this House,
particularly to the speech delivered by the
hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh.
I understand from his observations
that we have got a state of unprecedented unemployment in Cookstown, and I am told on reliable
authority that the Prime Minister got a
somewhat hostile reception from the
farmers of Tyrone, due to the social and
economic conditions existing there.
I believe that the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) will be able to
tell us that there was a threatened revolutionary outburst in Aghadowey, and I
understand that it was only prevented by
his restraining genius. Whether that is
absolutely correct or not, I am not in a
position to say at the moment, but that
is what I was told on fairly reliable
authority. Under those circumstances
we are asked to believe that the position
is materially improved in Northern Ireland. I want to be quite candid: I
positively and absolutely refuse to believe
it. I am quite convinced that there may
be a small improvement, but it is not the
improvement that is claimed. In point
of fact, what has happened is this, that
large numbers of people have been disqualified from receiving unemployment
benefit and have been put under the poorlaw for the purpose of getting
maintenance.
The seconder of the Address in Reply
to the King's Speech (Mr. Black) told
us that in one yard in Belfast all the slips
were likely to be occupied in the very
near future. It is with very much
diffidence that I attempt to argue a point
of law with that Gentleman, because I
believe he is an authority on legal
matters, but the hon. Member for North
Belfast who sits below the gangway and I
used to belong to a very ancient and
honourable profession before we forsook
it to follow the somewhat doubtful profession of politics, and we can claim some
knowledge as to the present state of industry. I can claim some knowledge of
the present state of industry, and I know
this from my own experience, and from

reliable information that has been
supplied to me that in the Belfast shipyards it would require not less than about
150 per cent. of the work that we had at
the busiest times for the purpose of providing employment for 100 per cent. of
the men.
You may marvel at that statement, but
that condition of affairs is due to
the fact that revolutionary changes
have taken place, as a result of which
labour is being displaced by up-todate methods to such an extent that to
expect a continuance of employment in
Belfast, Belfast will find it necessary to
supply 50 per cent. more tonnage for the
purpose of keeping the people employed.
In view of the information which I gave
you in connection with the tonnage that
the British yards are capable of turning
out, you must agree that the ordinary
course of supply and demand, which is a
fetish of some of the Gentlemen opposite,
has not given you the ships to build in
the Belfast shipyards. The ordinary
course of supply and demand has not done
that, because you claim, as a Government,
to have brought that work to Belfast as a
result of your Loans Guarantee Acts; and,
if you have done so, then that proves very
conclusively that the ordinary operation
of the law of supply and demand has not
brought the orders for these ships.
Suppose that next week or next month
it happens that the British Government,
with their much greater financial standing
in the markets of the world, improve their
Trade Facilities Acts, where is your muchboosted boom or revival in shipbuilding?
I would ask the attention of the Government to this fact. I have already mentioned the tremendous labour-saving
devices that have been brought into
operation. I have described one under
the control of the Belfast Corporation, in
connection with the discharge of coal at
the Musgrave Channel into the electricity
station. The coal is brought out of the
hold of the ship and deposited into the
boilers in the electricity station, and after
the coal has been consumed the ashes are
deposited, without the human hand
touching it in the whole course of the
operation. Now, I would ask for somet
inquiry into that question. I would ask
you not to adopt the attitude that everything in the garden is lovely, that trade.
has now revived, and that for the future
everyone is going to be employed.
I know that my colleagues, who have
studied this question, and I are absolutely convinced that there can be no
solution of the problem of unemployment
so long as you have got Capitalism. For
six long years the people of Northern Ireland, and particularly of Belfast, have
experienced that,
that, and no scientific
attempt has been made on the part of the
Government to grapple with that
problem. I think it was the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
who, in a speech which he delivered some
time ago, tried to liken Northern Ireland
to Denmark. I wonder if he looked for any
information before he made that speech,
because the information I have got in
connection with Denmark and Holland
certainly would not bear out his contention. What attempt, for example, has
been made to do something for the rural
areas? The right hon. Gentleman knows
that the people are deserting the rural
areas and coming into the urban centres.
According to the statistics published by
the Department of the Minister of Agriculture, the ploughed area in 1914 was
637,000 acres. From 1914 to 1918, when
it became necessary to destroy as many
Germans, Austrians and their Allies as
we could possibly destroy, the ploughed
area in Northern Ireland increased to
856,000 acres. But immediately it was
no longer necessary to kill Germans and
Austrians, then we reverted to the lackadaisical and reactionary policy, so far as
agriculture was concerned, and according
to the statistics presented by the right
hon. Gentleman in 1925, the ploughed
area in Northern Ireland was 54,546
acres less than in 1914.
What attempt has been made by the
Government to provide employment in the
agricultural districts? Ploughed land gives
more employment than land under grass.
I am sure the right hon. Gentleman
knows something about Denmark, and it
would be very illuminating if he would
attempt to contrast the conditions in
Denmark and Holland with the conditions
that obtain in Northern Ireland at the
present time. I want to say that I
believe the Government have not dealt
with this problem in the way it should be
dealt with, and that no attempt has been
made to diagnose the problem at all, to
find out what could be done. I believe
that a good deal could be done. The hon.
Member for Antrim and I, some time ago,
asked for an inquiry into the question of
agriculture, and we were treated with

I feel that some inquiry should be

Speaker, we have no control over external

I might make for the purpose of developing international trade would possibly be
ruled out of order. I would not be

would I be able to suggest that closer relations should be established with Russia,
so that Russia might purchase some of the
agricultural and industrial machinery
that we can manufacture in exchange for
some Russian commodities. I am not
permitted to deal with these things, because they are outside the scope of our
Parliament. The only thing the Government have control of we find they have
neglected the home market.
Take the constituency that I represent
in the Belfast Corporation. I believe
there are something like 2,314 houses in
Smithfield Ward, the most unsanitary,
the most disease-infested ward in the city
of Belfast. Some of the right hon.
Gentlemen opposite would not keep their
horses in the houses to which I refer, and
yet people are condemned to live in them.
Take the present figures for unemployment. You say there are 37,000 people
in receipt of unemployment benefit, and
assuming that each one of those 37,000 is
paid £1 a week, I find that you could
have rebuilt all the houses in Smithfield
Ward at a cost of £500 each, and have a
balance of £800,000 for any purpose you
like. You have got absolutely nothing to
show for approximately £40,000 of unemployment benefit which you spent last
year, and for the multiple of it if you
spread your calculations over the last five
or six years during which you have been
distributing the unemployment benefit.
The right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock)
appreciates the significance of that, because, speaking in the debate on Supply
on 22-3-1922, he said:
Those students of the subject who are
best entitled to speak take a very
serious view of the situation. I do not
pursue the subject further than to express my belief that the taxpayers will
not continue indefinitely to provide
money to maintain those who are not
producing, and that some more radical
method will have to be adopted to cope
with the disease.
Would the right hon. Gentleman answer;
the question, what more radical method
has he suggested since 1922 to grapple with
the whole problem? I believe that is a
pertinent question. The Minister of
Finance knows that the Government have
done nothing, and the Government deserve the severest condemnation of the
taxpayers of Northern Ireland for not
having attempted to do something to
solve this very acute problem. In moving
this Amendment I want to say this, that
whoever else the Government may fool
they are not fooling me, because I have
attempted to penetrate below the surface
of this matter, and I am certainly not
so optimistic about a trade revival as the
Prime Minister and the Gentlemen who
occupy the Benches opposite. I am glad
to know that the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) is back, because he will be able either to corroborate
or to disprove the statement that I made
a short time ago when I said that I understood a revolutionary outburst had taken
place at Aghadowey, and that only the
restraining influence of the hon. Member.
prevented a sporadic outburst on that
occasion.
Question proposed, "That those words

Again many of those cases, I think the

But know it is perfect nonsense to
you

and the Socialist system, which the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) has been

Capitalist system goods are produced
primarily for profit and not for use.
Under the Socialist system, as we conceive
it, goods will be produced for use and not
for profit. Goods will be produced for use
primarily and because people require
them. We want to see goods made because people require goods. We want to
see clothes manufactured because people
have got to wear clothes. We want to see
bread made because people require bread
and not to enable other people to make a
profit out of it.

In 1918 I was in the shipyard, and
when a ship was being plated there were
from six to eight helpers employed with
one plater. Those helpers were employed
from the first operation with the plate
until it was placed on the ship. What is
the process to-day? That same plate is
lifted by mechanical power. It is carried
by cranes from one bay to another until
it is transferred to a machine to be
punched. Instead of eight helpers and
a plater being engaged at that machine
you have only one man who is sitting down
and works at the plate. Under the new
system he can do two plates faster than
one could be done under the old system.
That is due to the introduction of up-todate machinery which expedites the work
of shipbuilding. I do not object to that.
but what I want you to understand is
that there you have eight men displaced.
What provision have you made for that
class of worker who is displaced? What
reasonable opportunity has he of being
absorbed into work? You will be getting
ships produced by modern machinery with
less and less human labour attached to
the work, and from that point of view 1
do not think that the industry will ever
employ the same number of men as
previously.

Mr. DEVLIN: Thank you very much,
Mr. Speaker. What I want to say is that
constantly there are challenges to us from
the other side to come forward with alternative policies. You cannot bring an
alternative policy in regard to unemployment because the Government have no
policy at all on this question. Paying the

Government's policy because it was the
policy of the British Government before
this Parliament was established. Beyond
the payment of unemployment allowances
by the Government they have never
brought forward a single proposal, nor
has there emanated from them a single

unemployment is to be grappled with in
the future.
I must confess that my interest in this
question is not precisely the same interest
as that of some other Members of this
House. I am to a large extent more
interested in the question of poverty,
avoidable poverty, than I am on the question of unemployment insurance, because
those who are insured will be always
secure in receiving at least a modicum of
help during the period of unemployment.
But look at the tremendous surplus population who are either struck off the list of
those who receive the unemployment
allowance or who have never been on the
list, the poor people living in the slums.
and in the back streets and alleys of our
city, who neither breathe fresh air, nor
hope, nor find themselves brightened by
a single glimpse of sunshine. Nothing
has been done to deal with that section
of the community.
The poor-law system has been condemned. I understand that question is
to be grappled with in England. You appointed a Poor Law Commission and they
have been sitting now for eighteen
months. I expected to find in the King's
Speech some reference to what you proposed to do in relation to poor-law reform.
It is absolutely essential that something
should be done. I want to repeat here
what I have said often before. This
Government has claimed constantly, and
claimed indefensibly, that the status of
the insured unemployed person here was
equal to the status of the insured person
in England. In England vast sums of

to augment the unemployment allowance.
The burden has not been as great in
Northern Ireland, nor has the treatment
of unemployed persons been nearly as
generous in Northern Ireland as in
England.

Debate on Address
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of order.
I would also like to lodge my protest
against a late sitting. The House sat 46
days out of 365 last year, and the sittings
lasted on an average three hours, so
that we were not overworked by any
means. To-day very important questions
have come up in this House, and the
Government have not given to them the
serious attention that they deserve. The
Opposition have sat here very attentively.
They pay close attention to all the
questions that are brought forward for
the benefit of the people of the Six
Counties. But have the Opposition received any consideration? None whatever. The Government have adopted a
system of relays. They and their
supporters have gone down to the tearoom and to the smokeroom; they have
spent their time anywhere about the
building but on the Benches of the House.
There are one or two exceptions, but I do
not desire to mention them specifically. I
certainly do protest against rushing and
boring the Amendments to the Address,
Amendments of grave importance to the
people under our jurisdiction. I say that
the time has arrived when we as a Parliament, and especially the Government, will
have to devote more time to the questions
that come up here. We must cease this
rushing process. I make my protest
accordingly.

I be in order in moving, "That this

Amendment to the Address after the
ordinary time for the rising of the House.
That, I thought, was unusual, as it certainly was, and, as subsequently transpired, it was not persisted in.
I did not mean to associate myself in
any way with the hon. Member's remark
about the attendance of Ministers in the
House. I think the attendance in this

Members during the debates is extraordinarily high and far better in proportion
than it ever is at Westminster. It is not
reasonable to expect that Ministers, all
Ministers, should be in their places
during the speeches of all Members, and
I do not think that in ordinary circumstances a Member has any complaint if a
Department whose affairs are under discussion is represented on the Front
Bench. Of course, we suffer from some

Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move as an
Amendment to the Address at end to add
the words:
But humbly regret that in the
Gracious Speech from the Throne no
mention has been made of the intention
of the Government to amend the Rent
and Mortgage Interest Restrictions Act,
so that adequate protection shall be
afforded to tenants in Northern Ireland.
Before proceeding with the Amendment
I would like to congratulate the mover
and seconder of the Address. This is the
first time I have had an opportunity of
extending my congratulations to them.
In connection with the Speech from the
Throne I do not think sufficient has been
put forward, and the Amendment that I
am moving if included in the Address
would put a stop to something that is
happening every week in the city of Belfast and throughout the Six Counties.
The question was really touched upon by
the mover of the Address (Mr. Miller),
because he referred to overcrowding in
the rural areas. On behalf of the city
people I am going to prove conclusively,
I hope, that the Rent Restrictions Act is
not what the Minister of Home Affairs
predicted it would be. Unfortunately,
the Act is not so watertight as to give the
protection which is necessary. When the
Act of 1925 was being put through thirtytwo Amendments were put in by the
Opposition, and I am sorry they were not
accepted'. If two of those Amendments
which I moved myself had been accepted
the position to-day would not be as it is.

up to

ing obtained the house he went into

My hon. Friend rather suggests that

of houses for the working

As a result of the operation of these Acts

I am sure my hon. Friend (Mr.
Beattie) has not overlooked the fact that

That applied particularly to working
men who had saved up sufficient money

to build two houses, one to be used by

We know, of course, in Belfast that, as

of building houses, are not prepared to go

The
houses became decontrolled there would
be nothing on earth to prevent the landlords from rushing up the rents.
Minister of Home Affairs on

We are told that more houses have
been built, but we must remember there
is no control on new houses, and the
owners can charge and are charging any
rent they can get for them. We were
also told in the House to-day that there
is a considerable number of houses to be
let in Belfast. That is perfectly true,
but why is that so? It is because the
people cannot afford to pay the rents
asked for these houses. That is the
position we are in at the moment. There
are houses to let for some people, but they
cannot afford to pay the rents asked.
I would like to point out that there is
a great improvement in trade in Northern
Ireland and we are all delighted to see
it. In the King's Speech we were asked
to do all we possibly could to foster
friendly relations between employer and
employee so that this improvement in
trade might continue. We who represent
the Trade Unions are in this position.
We want to keep up that improvement
in trade and we want to see more orders
coming to Northern Ireland, but if we
are to keep up that improvement in trade
and pay a higher rent for our houses we
shall have to get higher wages.
That
simply means that orders will be driven
away from Northern Ireland altogether.
Therefore the Government should consider this question from the point of
view that if we are to compete successfully with our competitors on the other
side in shipbuilding and other industries,
we cannot have a reduction in wages and
at the same time pay the high rents at
present being demanded.
The Minister of Agriculture is going to
set up a Committee to inquire into the
question of the difference between what
the farmer receives for his produce and
what the consumer pays for it. That is
something we all want to know. Why is
Debate on Address--
Rent Restrictions Act
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
not a Committee set up to inquire into
the difference between the rents paid under

asking to-day? Is it not a fair request
that a Fair Rent Court should be set up to
decide this whole question? There is
nothing unreasonable in asking the Government to do this, and I think that even
in their own interests they should do it.
There are people, including the Government, who are just as anxious as the Opposition to see that fair play is extended to
all people, but the Government ought to

I sincerely hope that hon. Members will
realise my position on this question. I
have already said I supported the Motion

I did not know that this Amendment was
coming forward. My opinion on the
matter has not changed since 1925, and I

to prevent people being annoyed by these

subjected. Hon. Members have given

Ireland rents have been increased by 300

upon the Government the absolute necessity of doing something to ensure that this

The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I think we can congratulate
ourselves that this debate has been carried
on with a sincere desire on all sides of the
House to meet this appalling shortage of
houses for the working classes. We have
had Bills in this House and we have discussed the matter on various occasions and
we still admit that so far as the city of
Belfast is concerned there are not enough
houses for the working classes, that is, at
rents they can afford to pay. But I think
the House will be wise to begin at the beginning with regard to this question.
After all, it has to be borne in mind all
the time that the control of rents was
brought in as a war measure, and the war
now having been over practically nine
years it is not unnatural that the whole
people should look to getting rid of these
war restrictions and getting back to the
old system of supply and demand.
Before the war I think Belfast was
looked upon as one of the cities in the
United Kingdom where good houses were
provided for the working classes at reasonable rents. I will not go further than to
say reasonable rents. I think that is the
reputation the city had prior to the war.
That was accomplished without any control and without any pressure being
brought to bear by any Government. It
came in a natural way, and it must be very
carefully remembered that continuity of
control may have the effect of stopping
building, because it is always the case that
where restrictions are put on there is a
disinclination to build amongst the class
that build houses. They say, "There is no
use building houses because the Government will come along and refuse to allow
us to get a fair return for our money."
The mover of the Amendment spoke as
though in the City of Belfast the landlord
class was wealthy; in fact, so well-to-do
that after all, rents did not mean very
much to them. I can assure him that if he
was in the same position that I am in and
received the grave complaints that I have
received during the past number of years
with regard to poor landlords, and especially poor landladies who were persuaded to put their money into a few
small houses as their only source of livelihood he would completely change his attitude. In some cases landlords and landladies have been lying out for years and
years of practically any return whatever
on their investments, and I dare say-although I am not so well acquainted with
the figures as is the Minister of Home
Affairs-that as soon as ever the restrictions come off there are some of these
poorer landlords and landladies who are
desirous of attempting to make up some
part of what they have lost during the
past number of years.
But do please all realise the difficulties
that the Government are in. On the one
hand you have cases of tenants, real hard
cases, brought forward where rents have
been increased, and on the other hand we
are inundated with cases where landlords
have only got one house, or perhaps two,
three, or four houses on which to subsist
for a livelihood. Therefore we are face to
face with a very grave problem in that
regard.

21 MARCH 1927
t
The question that arises is, what has
happened in the case of houses that have
been decontrolled? My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
assures me, and, of course, I agree, that
in the higher rented and best houses there
has been a reduction in rents since decontrol took place. He assures me that
he can prove there has been a reduction
since decontrol took place. What we
hope is that when 1930 is reached the
number of small houses built in the city
will be so great that when decontrol of
those smaller houses takes place there will
also be a decrease in rent. But that is a
long way off yet. The Government are
keeping a watchful eye on all these things,
and we are naturally well informed with
regard to the meetings of the various
associations, whether they are acting for
the smaller class landlords or the tenants.
Therefore, we are fully informed with
regard to the problem.
But the whole point is this.
How can
we as a Government do more to help on
the building of the type of houses that
the ordinary working man can afford to
pay the rent of? That is really the
problem. What I am particularly
anxious to do is to find out if anybody
can evolve a better plan than the plan
the Government has so far adopted, with,
I think, considerable success, in respect
of small houses.
I remember speaking on this subject
once before, and I have already spoken
to those in the Belfast Corporation, whose
duty it is to take a special interest in this
question of small-house building, and so
far, I understand, the 500 superficial feet
house has not been built. I understand
there are plans and models to be seen, but
so far none of them have actually been
built. Of course, it is quite true, as the
Minister of Home Affairs has pointed out,
that when this proposal was before the
House on a former occasion the hon.
Member opposite (Mr. Beattie) blocked it
in every way he possibly could. His
argument was that the 500 superficial feet
house was not a suitable one for the working classes. Therefore, it was decried in
this House. In other words, when we do
make an attempt to help all we possibly
can hon. Members on the opposite side
immediately come along and do all they
possibly can to prevent the Government
taking steps in that direction.
I do not think this question should be
brought into the political arena at all.
I think it is far too serious a question for
either side to claim credit for doing this
or the other, or for one side to try to
prevent us doing a certain thing. If hon.
Members would put up a better plan than
the plan we have so far successfully
carried out I can assure them that the
Government will be only too delighted to
do all they possibly can to assist them.
Between now and 1930 we may be able to
change our plans. We give a substantial
grant to the Belfast Corporation and the
Corporation add to that grant, and in
some districts the local authority has
agreed not to charge rates on new houses
for a certain number of years-I think
five.
150 houses a month is something to congratulate ourselves on. 5,000 houses
already erected with Government assistance is nothing to be ashamed of, and I
certainly think we are getting on. If
anybody can throw out a suggestion that
will be more suitable for expediting the
building programme the Government
will be only too delighted to do everything it can to help them, but do believe
me when I say that a continuity of
restrictions of any kind upon building
may just defeat the very object we have
in view, and that is to encourage local
authorities and ordinary individuals in
the building trade to put up as many
houses as they can, believing that in the
long run the ordinary law of supply and
demand is far better than putting restrictions on, except in very exceptional circumstances, such as the war necessarily
entailed.

I understand quite well that the
Government are in an extremely difficult
position, which arises from the fact that
in 1925 they took no notice of a series of
Amendments which Members on this side
moved when the Rent Restrictions Act
was submitted to the House. I suggested
on that occasion that the Government
were acting as friends of the landlords,
and I see no reason to alter that opinion.
I still believe that they are the friends
of the landlords. I can still see no justification as to why an Amendment should
have taken place in the Rent Restrictions
Act until we had a normal situation. It
is quite evident from the statements made
by the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Beattie),
who initiated this discussion, that we
have not anything like a normal situation
at present, because if we had a normal
situation the one-house owner who is
taking advantage of the Rent Restrictions
Act, 1925, could not charge the exorbitant
rents being charged at the present time.
I know similar cases myself; in fact, a
very near friend of mine--how near I
will not tell you-was recently living in
a house which had to be vacated as the
result of the one-house owner claiming it.
They paid 9s 6d a week in rent for the
house from which they were evicted, and
they are now paying precisely £1 a week
for a house next door which is a similar
sort of house. There is not a scintilla of
difference between the two houses. When
they had the protection of the Rent Restrictions Act they were paying 9s 6d, and
immediately they lost the protection of
that Act the rent was increased to £1
a week.
It is obvious that these things do not
count with right hon. Gentlemen at all.
They are absolutely indifferent to the
people who are now being charged exorbitant rents. I am quite definitely of
opinion that the people who are responsible for house building will never allow
the position previously existing to return
to Belfast. I say that without hesitation,
because house builders and estate agents
are scientifically organised at the present
time. The law of supply and demand is
never going to operate the same as prewar. I have got good reason to be convinced of that, because I am of the definite
opinion that these people will never
permit sufficient houses to be built that
the supply should exceed the demand.
Therefore, I have no hesitation in making
this statement. I do not know whether I
will be in the House in 1930. I am absolutely indifferent. If you have any regard
for the tenants in 1930 you will have a
Rent Restrictions Act. Your houses of
£8 valuation and under will be decontrolled in 1930. I am perfectly
certain that you will not have a normal
situation in 1930. If the present Act on
the Statute Book is not amended there
will be an outcry amongst the tenants of
houses of £8 valuation and under, and it
will be absolutely essential for the Government, if they are responsive to the grievances and injustices of the tenants, to alter
the present Act in 1930 if not before it.
Too many things are taken for granted.

houses. He told us during the course of

I am
perfectly satisfied if he comes with me he

I do not believe it is sufficient to argue

brought about as a result of war conditions. How often have I heard the
argument employed on the opposite side
that the economic situation entirely depends on the aftermath of those war
conditions. How often have we been
told that in regard to unemployment.
What is true of unemployment is true of
housing. If you have got a state of
affairs existing which is due to war conditions, and that state of affairs has not
altered it appears to me you are not
justified in altering any Acts similar to
the way you did in 1925. I do not
believe it is necessary for me to say anything more except this; that it appears.
to me to be an inopportune moment to
give house-owners an opportunity to increase rents when wages are coming down.
A case might be made out if wages were
on the increase, but when we have a state
of affairs where labourers in the shipyards and other places are only getting
37s a week, who formerly had £3 16s a
week, I think any unbiassed
person would
surely come to the conclusion that this
is not a fit and proper moment to give
landowners and house-owners an opportunity of making it more difficult for
people to live on their present wages, and
make both ends meet. I hope, even at
this stage, the Prime Minister and the
gentleman responsible for this discussion
will reconsider the whole matter in such a
way that they will make up their minds
to take some action to protect the interests of the tenants in Belfast and Six
Counties.

Mr. BLACK: The passing of the Rent
Restriction Acts was a necessity. The
present continuance of those Acts is a
necessity, and their continuance for some
time in the future is a necessity too.
How long that is necessary it is impossible for one to say. Under the present
1925 Act houses up to £26 valuation are
protected down to the year 1930. What
the position will be in 1930 it would require a prophet to tell. It will be for
Parliament itself in 1930 to consider the
question again and to decide whether the
Acts still need to be continued in the interests of the community. In the English
Act of 1920 protection was only given for
one year. After that, in the Acts which
continued it was only continued for one
year. The Government during the last
Session took a step in advance in regard
to these smaller houses, and instead of
continuing for only one year they continued it for five years, in the first instance, to 1930.
It is impossible to say until we get to
1930 what the position will be, and it will
then be for this House to consider in how
far the continuance may still be a necessity. It may be necessary then to
continue the Acts in full force as
they are to-day, or it may be possible
to continue them in some lesser or weaker
form, or it may be possible to do away
with them altogether. I do not think it
contributes anything to this great problem in 1927 to try to discuss whether or
not the Acts should be continued in 1930.
I have said that the passing of the Acts
and the continuance of the Acts was a
necessity. What was that necessity? The
necessity was to cope with what was a
great and admitted evil. The evil was
that by reason of the shortage of houses
excessive rents were being charged to
tenants, and, in addition, landlords were
availing themselves of their common law
powers to evict tenants for the purpose of
extorting higher rents from new tenants,
or, perhaps, of selling houses to get the
benefit of the higher prices that were obtaining when these Acts were passed.

were only symptoms of a disease. The

the only way to solve this was to get
houses built to let-houses to let.

aggravate the disease itself. Fair rent
may do something to alleviate the

advantage would be to enrich both

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) At best

What effect would it have on the
shortage of houses? What individual
would invest his money to build houses
to let if he knew he was likely
to be dragged into a Fair Rent Court to
have a rent fixed that might seem good to
the court, but which was not the rent he
contemplated when he built the house?
Nay, more, what urban authority would
build houses under the circumstances?
Would Belfast Corporation or any town
in Northern Ireland venture to build
houses? They properly, in the interests
of the ratepayers, would not invest money
in the building of houses when they knew
they might be faced with a Fair Rent
Court to fix a rent which would not recoup them for their outlay. Or would
hon. Members opposite, members of rich
and powerful trade unions, advise their

they as landlords then would be dragged

might be fixed from which they would
not get an economic return.

absurd. If that happened at the beginning when builders were few surely the

compete with one another would give the
tenants some of the benefit. Anyone who
knows what happened knows that is ex-

Agricultural Research Station Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): The House, I am sure,
would like to know some of the facts
which led up to the establishment of this
Research Station.
The Department of Agriculture and
Technical Instruction when it commenced
operations in Ireland in 1900 rightly devoted its energies to increasing crop production. How well it succeeded in this
work is proved by the great increase in the
average yield of crops which has been
brought about during the period 1900-26.
For example-one example alone-the
average yield of potatoes in Ulster has
increased by 2.1 tons per statute acre.
Although during the past twenty-six
years the improvement of stock and
stock products has not been neglected,
they have not received the same attention
as has been paid to the crop side of agriculture. Since the inauguration of the
Northern Ministry of Agriculture we
have been trying to give our technical
research and educational work a new
direction. A very large proportion of the
agricultural income of Northern Ireland
is derived from the sale of stock and
stock products, such as eggs, butter and
things of that sort. As this aspect of
agriculture has in the past had relatively
little attention paid to it, it offers by far
the most promising avenue for improvement and development.
At present our markets in England and
Scotland for stock and stock products are
being challenged from all quarters. Store
cattle are arriving in increasing numbers
from Canada, whilst shipments of eggs,
butter, and, in some instances, bacon are
arriving from all our Dominions and
from foreign countries and are increasing
at an extraordinarily rapid rate.
During the past five years the technical
and research staff of the Ministry have
been trying in face of considerable difficulties to develop the animal husbandry
side of the industry. One of our great
difficulties has been the lack of experimental facilities. In England and Scotland it has been found necessary to
establish special research institutes with
large experimental farms for the purpose,
in spite of the fact that both England and
Scotland abound in large farms carrying
large numbers of stock of all descriptions.
Northern Ireland possesses relatively few
large farms, and it is impossible to secure
on smaller farms the facilities for experimental work which are needed.

As
agricultural conditions are
totally different from those in Great
Britain, hon. Members will appreciate the
fact that the research problems which
confront us in Northern Ireland are quite
distinct from those which are being investigated across the Channel, and hence
the great necessity for having a special
research station in Northern Ireland.
may point out in this connection that in
Northern Ireland there are 104,410 holdings and 2,450,790 acres of crops and
pasture, while in Scotland there are only
76,161 farms and 4,705,197 acres. Thus
with double our cultivated area Scotland
has something less than three-fourths of
the number of holdings which we have in
Northern Ireland, which makes it, of
course, very much more difficult to carry
on our experimental work.
the
The Executive Council of the Ulster
Farmers' Union, which has frequently
had the matter under discussion, addressed
a communication a short time ago to
the Government stressing the need, in
the interests of our Northern stockowners,
for a thorough investigation of
numerous problems relating to animal
nutrition. The Council, however, did
not content themselves merely with pointing out the need for such an investigation,
but, with commendable enterprise, submitted a concrete proposal for the estab-
Research Station Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Archdale]
lishment of an Agricultural Research
and Experimental Station for Northern
Ireland. As it deserved, the proposal
received careful and sympathetic consideration by the Government, and ultimately
a definite arrangement-embodied in the
Schedule to this Bill-was made for the
establishment of a Research and Experimental Station at Hillsborough.
The main, although not the sole, purpose of the Hillsborough Research Station
is to provide facilities for experimental
and research work on the nutrition of all
classes of farm stock. It is proposed, for
example, to develop still further the experimental work which has already been
accomplished in the production of baby
beef. This work has been taken up in a
most encouraging manner and put into
practice by a large number of our farmers,
and in this direction we are probably
making more progress than any other part
of the United Kingdom.
Very
A further problem which the Station
proposes to tackle is that associated with
the nutrition of the dairy cow. Dairying
can be made to pay only by developing the
cow as a milk-producing animal.
material progress has been made, but the
development of the cow as a producer
must go hand in hand with a better knowledge of how to feed her. The development of the cow from a 400 gallon animal
to an 800-1,000 gallon animal is not a
simple proposition. Such development is
being attended by a number of very serious
difficulties, such as a shorter period of usefulness, sterility, abortion, and a greater
tendency towards disease, such as tuberculosis. There is good reason to suppose
that these troubles are very intimately
connected with feeding, and that if we
knew more about the nutrition of dairy
cows we should be in a much better position to overcome these difficulties. It is
hoped that the Hillsborough experimental
farm will become a training place and a
centre for the production of Grade A
(Tuberculin Tested) Milk.
Northern Ireland has always held a
prominent place in the English bacon
market. We can hold and develop this
position only by improving the quality
of our bacon. This is mainly a question.
of feeding. It is common knowledge in
the bacon trade that feeding determines
the quality of the finished product, but
no exact knowledge or reliable information is available as to which feeding stuffs
are harmful from a quality point of view
and which are beneficial. It is hoped
that both the farmers and the bacon
merchants will join together at Hillsborough in the solution of this problema problem of great economic importance
to Northern Ireland.
Experimental work at present in progress indicates that both the number and
size of the eggs laid by a hen are directly
influenced by the type of feeding, and
that it is possible by nutritional means to
shorten to a considerable extent the
period between hatching and maturity.
Hitherto, with the facilities available at
Stormont it has only been possible to
carry out the experimental work with
small groups of birds. Under such circumstances the work is exceedingly slow.
It is the intention to develop the work at
Hillsborough with large experimental
lots which will make it possible to obtain
results much more quickly, and, above
all, to work out the results from an
economic point of view.
to
Although the main object of the
Station is to provide facilities for the development of the animal side of the agricultural industry, it is intended
utilise the land as far as possible for crop
experimental work, and particularly for
demonstration and experimental work or
cultivation. It is proposed in connection
with the experimental work, to which the
whole farm and its stock will be devoted,
to keep a detailed and accurate system of
cost accounts, which will enable those in
charge of the experimental and research
work to translate these results into
economic terms.
The experimental farm will not be a
place for training students in the sense of
the Cookstown and Greenmount Agricultural Colleges. It will, however, provide a direct and close link between the
research and experimental workers and
the farmer, and in this connection it is
earnestly hoped that every farmer in
Northern Ireland will not only visit the
Station at least once a year, but will not
hesitate to give those in charge the benefit
of any advice or criticism he has to offer.
The lands known as the Great Park
at Hillsborough, comprising over 900
acres, have been transferred by the Imperial authorities to our Ministry of
Finance. About 420 acres of this area

e


will be devoted to forestry under the care
of the Ministry of Agriculture, and 485
acres will be handed over for agricultural
research and experimental purposes to the
Board of Trustees to be created under
this Bill. This station will not be in any
sense a Government institution. It will
be controlled and managed by a Board
of nine Trustees, consisting of representatives of the Ministry of Agriculture, the
Agricultural Faculty of Queen's University, the Ulster Farmers' Union, and the
Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society.
As hon. Members will observe from the
terms of the agreement, the Government
propose to provide a capital sum of
£30,000 for the erection of new and the
reconditioning of existing buildings, as
well as for stocking and equipping the
station. It is estimated that when fully
established an annual income of £3,000
will be needed to run the station, and
with a view to providing such an income
it is proposed to create, by annual grants
until 1931-32, an Endowment Fund of
£60,000. I beg to move.

five years would give a return of about

The hon. Member who has joined issue
with us in this work has pointed out the
deplorable condition of agriculture. Well,
admitting all that, it is the Government's
business to try some practical method to
bring agriculture from the condition in
which it finds itself to-day into something
like prosperity, and it is by practical
measures, such as research work, and by
the provision of approved methods, which
my right hon. Friend and his Department
are endeavouring to carry out, that that
result can be attained. By no artificial
methods can improvement be achieved.
You cannot do it by doling out money
to farmers. It can only be done by
improving the productiveness of the soil,
and increasing the value of the products
of the farmers. It is towards that object
that this research farm is being established, and I have no doubt that in the
end it will show a return for the money
expended. Those are the facts of the
case, and I do not think that those who
have really any concern for farming can
find anything to criticise in the effort the
Government is making to help the
industry.

The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move,
That this Bill be now read a
Second time." I apologise to the House
for having to introduce this small Bill.
It arises from the fact that when we set
up our Ministries in the first instance
we coupled together the Ministers of
Agriculture and Commerce, and in the
second instance we coupled together the
Ministries of Education and Commerce in
order to fit in the Parliamentary Secretaries and to save the public as much as
possible. This Bill, as regards Clause 1,
merely rectifies the error which neces
sarily was created when the change took
place, and everybody will understand
that now, instead of combined Ministries,
it is simply the Ministry of Agriculture
in one instance and the Ministry of
Education in the other.
With regard to Clause 2, it has reference to such members of the Cabinet as do
not accept salary or any of the supplementary sum voted by the Committee of the
whole House, and it is an order that that
sum should be divided amongst those
Ministers who do receive Cabinet salaries.
Since we first established our Ministeries
the saving amounts to £1,600. I beg to
move.

Tuesday, 22nd March, 1927.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BELFAST-LONDON MAILS.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the position at present in relation to the transmission of the mails from London to
Belfast; what steps, if any, have been
taken to expedite transmission and ensure
a prompt and regular delivery of letters
in the city and whether, in view of the
rumoured closing by the London, Midland
and Scottish Railway Company of Fleetwood as a passenger and mail port and
the consequent resulting disadvantage to
Belfast, he can say what he proposes to do
to meet the demand of the citizens of
Belfast for a better passenger and mail
service from and to London.
COMMERCE
The MINISTER OF
(Mr. Barbour): For some time past my
Ministry has been in close touch with the
postal authorities and the London, Midland and Scottish Railway Company,
with a view to securing an acceleration of
the services at present used by the Post
Office for the conveyance of mails between
Belfast and London. As the hon. Member is doubtless aware, apart from certain
special late-fee arrangements, mails posted
in London up to about 3 p.m. each day
-the actual hour being dependent upon
the locality in which they are postedare conveyed to Belfast via Fleetwood,
and are due for arrival in Belfast at 6-30
a.m. every week-day except Mondays.
Arrival at this hour ensures the inclusion
of such mails in the first delivery in
Belfast, commencing at 7-30 a.m. When,
however, owing to the late arrival of the
Fleetwood steamer, connection with the
first delivery fails, the mails are held
over for the second delivery, starting at
10-45 a.m. The great bulk of the letters,
however, are posted in London too late
for conveyance via Fleetwood and, consequently, are forwarded via Stranraer
by the mail train which leaves Euston at
8-40 p.m.
In addition to Northern
Irish letters, this train carries the
very heavy mails destined for the
Midlands and North of. England,
and Scotland, and the present hour
of departure from Euston is the
earliest that would permit of these mails
being included. Letters conveyed via
Stranraer are due to reach Belfast at
9-30 a.m. but, although there has been a
marked improvement in this respect of
late, the Railway Company has not been
able, for various reasons, consistently to
maintain the scheduled time of arrival.
Recognising the practical impossibility of
securing an earlier dispatch of the bulk
of the letters from London than 8-40 p.m.,
as at present, the efforts of the London
Midland and Scottish Railway Company,
the Post Office, and my Ministry, have
been directed to an investigation of the
possibility of acceleration on the journey
between Euston and Belfast, and more
particularly on the portion between Carlisle and Larne.
While this investigation has revealed
certain respects in which the service
might be improved, it has established the
fact that acceleration to the extent required is not immediately practicable
without heavy capital expenditure.
Another aspect of the question which
has been strongly impressed upon my
Ministry is the importance of securing
a service which will ensure a sufficiently
early arrival in London to allow of
Northern Irish letters being included
in the first London delivery. Letters at
present carried from Belfast to London
via Stranraer are due at Euston at 7-15
a.m., and normally fall into the second
London delivery commencing at 9-15
a.m. Inquiry has shown that, in order
to secure inclusion of these letters in the
first London delivery, arrival at Euston
must be not later than 5-50 a.m. Unfortunately, such an arrival could only
be obtained by a correspondingly earlier
departure from Belfast, which would
militate against the value of the service
from the passenger and mails poins of
view.
After the most careful consideration
of the matter, from all points of view,
the Government has come to the conclusion that the only practical solution
of the difficulties under present conditions is the utilisation for the time
being of the Kingstown-Holyhead service

In regard to the last part of the question, the hon. Member will have

3 p.m., except in so far as such mails

that, in the case of mails circulating in
the reverse direction, a much earlier
arrival at Euston is necessary than could
be afforded via Fleetwood or Heysham.
I have no reason to suppose that the
new Heysham service will be less attractive than the existing Fleetwood route
from the point of view of passenger
traffic.

COST OF ADDITIONAL POLICE
IN BELFAST.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
circumstances leading up to the action of
the Ministry in charging the Corporation
of Belfast the cost of a number of
additional police drafted into the city;
whether he is aware that the Corporation
has repeatedly protested against police
being brought into the city on the ground
that they were wholly unnecessary, and
what steps he proposes to take to relieve
the Corporation of this financial burden.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Section 4 (2) of the
Constabulary Act (N.I.), 1922, provides
that where an additional force of police is
stationed in any county or county.
borough, half the cost of such additional
force, calculated at a prescribed rate,
falls on the local authority concerned.
This principle was merely a continuation of the old arrangements which were
in operation under the R.I.C. regime.
The additional force referred to is the
number of police stationed in the county
or county borough-as the case may beover and above the number allocated to
such county or county borough as "free
quota."
The entire cost of the free quota falls
on the Government, in contrast to the
arrangement which obtains in Great
Britain, under which the Government
assumes responsibility for, approximately,
only half of the total cost of the police in
each county, etc.
The free quotas assigned to the various
counties and county boroughs in Northern
Ireland were fixed in 1924 after consultation and agreement with the representatives of the local authorities at conferences held in the Ministry of Home
Affairs.
The free quota allotted to Belfast at
the time was 998, and the establishment
of police in the city when at full strength
is 1,273, from which it will be seen that
as a maximum the Belfast Corporation
cannot be financially responsible for more
than 275 men.
In the R.I.C. days the free quota was
only 900, and the total establishment
1,233, so that the Corporation were liable
for the cost of up to 333 men as a
maximum.
The amounts paid by the Belfast Cor
poration to the Government during the
years immediately prior to the transfer
of services approximated to £30,000 a
year, so that the principle is not, as the
hon. Member's question might suggest, a
new one.
It is no doubt a fact that the claims
made by this Government on the Belfast
Corporation during the earlier years of
administration under Northern Ireland
arrangements were comparatively limited,
primarily due to the fact that during the
years 1922 and 1923 recruiting for the
R.U.C. had not been completed and the
police work in the city had to be discharged by Special Constabulary.
It may be added, however, that the
Government feel that the Corporation are
morally liable for the cost of the additional Special Constabularly employed
during those early years, and this
matter is being pursued.
Representations have been made to me
by the Corporation against this charge,
but it has never been suggested that the
additional force charged for was wholly
unnecessary.
I may add, however, that the entire responsibility for deciding what force of
police is required in any locality rests
upon me after consultation with my
expert advisers, and while I am at all
times ready to give the most earnest consideration to any suggestions made to me.
on the point by the local authorities concerned, I cannot admit the suggestion
underlying this question that I should
necessarily accept the views of the local
authorities on the matter.
In all the circumstances I can hold out
no hope of any alteration being made in
the existing arrangements.

SALE OF CHINESE LIQUID EGGS.
4. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
quantities of Chinese liquid eggs in tins
are being imported into Belfast and sold
to food purveyors; whether he knows
that statements have been made alleging
that such eggs are harmful to the health
of the community, and what steps he
intends to take to stop this traffic.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that Chinese liquid eggs are imported
into Belfast, and it is believed that these
contain a high percentage of preservative.
Under the Public Health Acts the
Corporation as sanitary authority have
power to examine all articles of food exposed for sale, and if any such articles
are found to be unsound, or unfit for
human consumption, to have them condemned by a justice and destroyed.
The importation of eggs which contain
preservative will be prohibited after the

REMOVAL OF THE 'STATENDAM"

""
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he is aware that the Statendam" is
going for completion to Holland, and
what action he is prepared to take to
ensure that the liner will be completed
in Belfast.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the first part
of the question is, I regret to say, in
the affirmative.
""
As the hon. Member is no doubt aware,
a guarantee of approximately £250,000
was given under the Loans Guarantee
Acts, in respect of the construction of the
hull of the vessel. On learning from the
builders that there was a possibility of
the "Statendam being taken to Holland for completion I made an offer to
the owners-the Holland-America Linethrough Messrs. Harland & Wolff, that
this Government was prepared to give all
the facilities in its power in order to
ensure completion in the Belfast yards.
I understand, however, that the reason
for the decision to complete the liner in.
Holland is that a group of Dutch financiers have undertaken to provide the
capital moneys necessary for this purpose
on condition that the work shall be carried out in Holland.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to know
whether the Minister is aware of any connection between the Wilton Engineering
Slipway Co. and the firm of Harland &
Wolff, and what interests Harland &
Wolff are going to gain by the removal
of the "Statendam" to Rotterdam?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not aware of
any connection, if any, existing between
Messrs. Harland & Wolff and the firm
mentioned, Messrs. Wilton. It is the
first time I have heard a suggestion of the
kind, and, therefore, I am not in a
position to offer any opinion as to whether
Harland & Wolff will or will not benefit
by any arrangement entered into.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
Harland & Wolff are going to work in conjunction with the Wilton Engineering Co.
in the finishing of this ship?
Mr. POLLOCK: I have no knowledge
of that.

for this Government.

CLASS III. No. 6.
BORSTAL INSTITUTION, REFOR-
MATORY AND INDUSTRIAL
SCHOOLS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding One Thousand Six Hundred and
Seventy-five pounds be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending
31st March, 1927, to defray the expenses
of the Borstal Institution, Reformatory
and Industrial Schools and places of
Detention (8 Edw. VII, c. 59 and 67,
4 and 5 Geo. V, c. 58); and certain
capital expenditure under 14 and 15 Geo.
V, c. 13, s. 1, and 16 and 17 Geo. V,
c. 22.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The intróduction of this Estimate is rendered
necessary by the acquisition by the
Government of the Malone Reformatory
School for the purpose of combining a
Borstal Institute and a Protestant Re-.
formatory.
The House will recall that, when the
Bill giving power to the Government to
acquire the school was introduced, I
explained then that since the Northern
Government took over, we had to send
Borstal boys over to England. An opportunity occurred of acquiring Malone
School, and in the future this institution
will be used as a Borstal Institution and
also as a Reformatory. I may, however,
point out that as I explained before, the
cases will be segregated. We took over
the school on the 1st December, and it is
to meet the expenses for the three months
that this Estimate is introduced.
I might point out to the House that as
regards Borstal cases, the cost is borne
entirely by the State, and as regards
Reformatory cases, the cost will be borne
half by the State and half by the local
authorities concerned.
As regards the Borstal cases, we have
made provision for 15 cases of this description. The remaining Borstal cases,
22 in number-are still in England, but
we hope to get them over at the end of the
present month, and we will have altogether 37 Borstal cases.
This Estimate also makes provision for
the 35 Reformatory cases. I might point
out that this Estimate is not an additional
charge on the Exchequer, but it is in substitution of portion of the charges already
voted by this House in respect of Borstal
and Reformatory boys for whose maintenance we either pay the British Government or the Malone Training School, and
I am quite satisfied that the maintenance
of the Borstal inmates and the maintenance of the Protestant Reformatory
boys will certainly not exceed what was
paid in the past.
With regard to the staff, the Government have been fortunate in being able to
retain the services of Mr. Watson
formerly headmaster of the school. During the course of his service he has shown
himself to be a man who possesses every
qualification for this very responsible
office. We have retained all the old staff,
with the exception of three, and we have
appointed eight new officers. Three of
these take the places of those who have
left, and the other five are to meet the
extra requirements in respect of Borstal
cases. It might interest the House to
know that six out of the eight men are
men who bore the highest character in
the Army, and served there as non-commissioned officers.
I think hon. Members will appreciate
that if Borstal treatment is to be a
success, it is absolutely necessary that it
should be officered by men, who not alone
possess human sympathy, but also the
capacity for control. The whole Borstal
treatment is the antithesis of prison
treatment. It is an attempt by the State
to try to give boys who would otherwise be
destined to a life of crime a chance, not
alone of reforming, but of making good
and becoming good citizens. In this connection we propose to form an organisation on similar lines to that of the Borstal
Association which has done such
cellent work in England. This associa-.
tion will be a purely voluntary one. One
of its objects will be not alone to help a
boy when discharged to get a job, but to
assist him in other ways in after life, and
if any hon. Members of this House are interested in this form of social work, and
will let me know, I will be only too glad/to
avail myself of their services.
I beg to move.

Mr. BARBOUR: The Service for
