for
The Irish Land Act of 1903 and the
Northern Ireland Land Act of 1925 give
power to the Land Commission and
the Land Purchase Commission
Northern Ireland to authorise the
cutting of turf on the holdings of
tenant-purchasers by any occupiers of
land in the neighbourhood of a holding
for whose requirements such turf appeared
to be necessary, and regulations could be
made setting out the terms as to payment
and other conditions under which such
rights could be exercised. These powers
have been transferred to the Ministry of
Finance, in so far as they are exercised on
estates which have been sold, and are
subject to Land Purchase Annuities.

In-
A case has now actually arisen on the
Madden estate in County Fermanagh,
where certain of the tenant purchasers
presented a memorial asking that turbary
rights might be granted to them.
quiries were made into the matter by the
Land Purchase Commission on behalf of
the Ministry, and it was recommended
that fresh supplies of turf should be
secured for these people at a reasonable
rent. It was discovered, however, in the
course of investigation on the spot that
Supply-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

in order to make the scheme practicable
it was essential that an existing track
should be repaired and an addition made

the bog area. The making of this road
and the fencing of it was estimated to cost
about £200, but the difficulty is that
Land Purchase funds cannot legally be
made available for such a purpose once
the estate has been sold.
It would have been impracticable to
ask the people, who are applying for the
facilities and are all in poor circumstances, to pay for the outlay, and accordingly it was decided in the special
circumstances to ask this House to vote
sufficient money to defray the expense.
The tenants will be required to pay to
the owners of the land on which the road
is built a nominal annual sum for the use
of the right of way, and to the owners of
the turbary a small annual rent. The
total annual amount is 10s per allotment.
Regulations have been made by the
Ministry of Finance setting out the exact
conditions on which the facilities are
granted and safeguarding the various
parties interested. On account of their
wide experience, arrangements were made
for the Land Purchase Commission for
Northern Ireland to draw up the entire
scheme, which affects almost 110 tenants,
and to supervise the construction of the
road and the applotment of turbary.
Recoupment of its outlay will be made
from the money provided under this.
Estimate, and I should like before I close
to express my appreciation of the assistance which the Land Purchase Commission has given us in carrying out this
work and in making the necessary

to 1926; the Unemployment Insurance

as amended by the Economy (Exchequer Relief) Act (Northern Ireland), 1926; the Unemployment Insurance (Agreement) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1926; the Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions

Advances to Workpeople for Fares
under the Labour Exchanges Act,
1909; Fees and Expenses of members.
of Trade Boards under the Trade

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): This Supplementary Estimate
is rendered necessary, either because of
circumstances over which we here have no
control, or else owing to action which has
been taken by this Parliament. If hon.
Members will refer to Sub-head A, they
will see that the additional amount asked
for is £2,000. This is for the provision
of additional temporary staff at the
Employment Exchanges for the current
financial year, 1926-27, for which unemployment was calculated at 20 per cent.,
but which has worked out at a higher
percentage, namely, 21.5 per cent.
In January, 1926, when the original
Estimate was framed, the total unemployment in Northern Ireland was 64,000 or
26 per cent. In April it had fallen to
52,000 or 22 per cent., and the hopes
upon which we based the Estimate appeared as if they were going to be
realised. But, unfortunately, early in
May, the disastrous dispute occurred in
the coal industry, with the result that
within the first two weeks of that tragedy
the unemployment figures here increased
by 8,000. These figures remained more
or less stationary until about July, when
a slow but gradual improvement took
place, and it has been continuous from
that date
to this. At the same
time, owing to this retardation of
the improvement which was expected, we
have had to deal with a larger percentage
of unemployment than we estimated for,
and the amount under this Sub-head is in
order to provide the money required to
pay for the additional staff.
We
Sub-head J is to provide for the payment of the Medical Referee Service,
which we established here on 1st January,
1927, up to 31st March of this year.
have already appointed one permanent
doctor who is proceeding to carry out this
work with the assistance of certain other
doctors, who have been engaged on a
temporary fee basis. I may say that the
cost of this Service will be recovered from
our Health Insurance Funds by way of
Appropriation-in-Aid.
Sub-head U1 is a pretty large item of
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
£23,628. This is rendered necessary by
the fact that owing to the establishment
of this Parliament and the Free State it
has of course been necessary to apportion
the funds of our various Approved
Societies as between the three areas, and
this has been a prolonged and difficult
task. A committee was established for
the purpose of carrying out the change,
and was called the International Apportionment Board. On that Board Sir
Alfred Watson presided as chairman and
Sir Walter Kinnear, a distinguished
British Civil Servant, served upon it.
We here were represented by Major
Conacher, of my Department, and Sir
Joseph Glynn represented the Free State.
The work was completed upon the 30th
September, 1925, and this sum is asked
for to pay for the cost of carrying out the
necessary work.
The other item which I wish to refer to
is Sub-head V, namely, the Receipts
Appropriated in Aid, £30,550. This has
been rendered necessary by several causes.
The first is the fact that under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1925, the State
Grant to the Unemployment Fund was
taken for estimating purposes at approximately 8d. Subsequently the Economy
Bill reduced the rate to 6d from 5th
April, 1926, the resultant loss to the Funds
by way of State Grant being £94,000.
A deficiency in the Appropriation in Aid
amounting to one-eighth of this £94,000
was a sum of £12,000. There was a
further sum, due to the fact, as I have
already explained, that unemployment
in Northern Ireland during the present financial year amounted to 21.5 per
cent., whereas in the original Estimate it
was taken at 20 per cent.
There are three small savings. One under
Sub-head B was due to the fact that the
travelling and subsistence expenses in connection with our Contributory Pensions
Act did not amount to as much as was
anticipated. Then again, there was a
small saving under Sub-head L because
of the fact that fewer cases were referred
to the Courts of Referees, and there was
less publicity work done during the year.
The manufacture and sale of Insurance
Stamps and the payments of Contributory
Pensions Orders amounted to £1,000 less
than was anticipated. This leaves the
net Vote now asked for £54,098.

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: 1927?

Mr. BARBOUR: It is customary for
me when moving an Estimate for Public
Works and Buildings to preface my remarks by reminding hon. Members that
this Estimate provides for three distinct
types of expenditure. Thus Section 1
may be referred to as the "Imperial" part
of the Estimate, providing as it does for
expenditure which is repayable by the
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
United Kingdom to the Northern Ireland
Exchequer. Section 2 provides for Works
Services, which are neither chargeable
against Imperial funds nor against any
Northern Ireland Department, but are,
so to speak, common Northern Ireland
services. Section 3 deals with services
which are carried out on behalf of
Northern Ireland Departments, and the
cost of these is, of course, recoverable from
the other departmental Estimates. The
items in this particular part of the Estimate have, therefore, already come before
you or are included in this batch of
Supplementary Estimates.
Coming to the details of the Estimate,
I should first of all emphasise as regards
Section 1 that no additional money is
sought. It has not been necessary to do
so, inasmuch as the provision made in
the original Estimate for work at
Stormont has proved to be more than
sufficient to provide for the work which
is being carried on there, and for other
"Section 34" works which are now in-
Icluded in this Estimate. Of these the
item of £4,075 in sub-head B is required
for the furnishing of Mr. Speaker's residence at Stormont, which was completed
and occupied by Mr. Speaker in October
last. The other three "Section 34" ser.
vices require some comment.
Provision for the new Law Courts building should not normally appear in a
Northern Ireland Estimate as, being in
respect of a Reserved Service; the cost of
its erection should not be the concern of
this Parliament, as it is the direct expenditure of the Imperial Parliament of
Westminster. It has, however, been
decided to accommodate in this building,
not merely the Supreme Court, but also
such of the headquarters' staffs of our
Northern Ireland Ministries as must of
necessity on the grounds of administrative
and public convenience generally remain
in the city, that is to say, the Ministry of
Commerce, the Stamp Office, the Estate
Duty Office, etc. To this extent the cost
of departmental accommodation in the
Law Courts is dealt with in the same way
as the cost of providing accommodation at
Stormont, and is, therefore, a Section 34
charge payable by Northern Ireland but
recoverable from Imperial funds.
The
total cost of the building is estimated at
£543,500, which includes £55,000 for the
purchase of the site. It is estimated that
a sum of £185,250 represents the "Section
34" charge, and this will in due course
fall to be provided in this Estimate as the
work proceeds. The money to be voted
this year is limited to the proportionate
part of the purchase price of the site,
namely, a sum of £19,500. As a matter
of general interest I may say that the
sketch plans have been agreed with the
Imperial Authorities, and the Imperial
Office of Works anticipate that a sum of
£40,000 will be spent during the coming
financial year. This expenditure will be
entirely on piling and foundation work,
which will be begun in the early summer.
In the meantime the working drawings
are in hand.
As regards the next item in Sub-head
D, I mentioned in May last when moving
the original Estimate, the grant of
£10,190 which the Imperial Government
agreed to make for the purpose of reconditioning the avenue, fences, hedges, etc.,
at Stormont. The work was commenced
during the current financial year, and it
is anticipated that of the total amount
£4,380 will be spent this year.
The third item in the Sub-head arises
out of the Belfast Custom House reconstruction, the total cost of underpinning
and partial reconstruction of which will
be in the neighbourhood of £56,000.
This building was not transferred to the
Northern Government, being occupied
solely by Imperial and Reserved Departments, and normally any Works Services
in connection with it would be provided
for by the Imperial House of Commons
and not by us. It has, however, been
arranged that in the reconstructed building space will be provided for the
Stationery Office-a Transferred Service.
for which accommodation must be provided under Section 34, and on the basis
of the accommodation to be allocated to
the Stationery Office a total of approximately £6,000 will fall to be paid by
Northern Ireland, but will be recoverable
from Great Britain under Section 34. Of
this amount, £1,000 is required during
the current year.
I now turn to Part II of the Estimate,
Sub-head E, new works, alterations, etc.
A full explanation appears under that
Sub-head as regards the proposed adaptation of premises at Ormeau Avenue for

All concerned have been

Government. They produced two plans,
one of which was for a building faced

might harmonise as much as possible with
the characteristics of the City Hall and
other stone-faced buildings in the city.
When the settlement was finally
reached, we compromised with them by
agreeing to pay half of the difference in
the cost between the stone-faced building
and the brick building, so that we should
have a really fine edifice in the city. That
difference was something like £27,000,
and we agreed to pay £13,500 if they
would meet us by providing a stone-faced
building instead of a brick building. To

that that decision was arrived at only a

aware, it takes some considerable time to
take out the quantities. Therefore, we
need not expect very much in the way of
some little time to come.

With regard to the Parliament Buildings, which will also cover the Civil Service with the exception of the small
number referred to by my right hon.

unemployed.
In answer to the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) who asked why
we required Law Courts in Ulster, I
would like to point out that in the old
days, before the Act of 1920 was passed,
the centre of legal activities, so far as the
Courts were concerned, was the Law
Courts in Dublin. We had none here.
The temporary resting place of our
Judiciary is, of course, the headquarters
of the Antrim County Council, and we are
occupying their valuable building at considerable inconvenience to them. It is in
order to hand back to them their property
that we are anxious to get on with the

Mr. ROBB: The subjects to be taken
Oral Answers

23 MARCH 1927
in the junior certificate examination are
not the same as in the senior, because

certificate has been obtained the pupil

PATRICK THORNBURY-
DEPORTATION ORDER.
6. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that a Deportation Order was issued
against Patrick Thornbury, a citizen of
Belfast, on or about the 25th December,
1926, prohibiting him from entering the
city from Dublin, where he had been engaged for some months past as a school
teacher; whether it is a fact that this
young man returned home for the school
vacation on a number of previous occasions without interference, and while in
the territory of Northern Ireland was a
peaceable and law-abiding citizen; and,
if so, whether he will state why he was
treated like an undesirable alien or criminal on the occasion mentioned; and if,
previous to the issuing of the Deportation Order, he had ever been adjudged
guilty by an established Court of Justice
of any infraction of the law which could
justify an arbitrary deprivation of the
inalienable right of citizenship; and
whether he will have the Deportation
Order withdrawn.
The MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates); An Order
under 23 A of the Regulations under
the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922, was made
by me on the 1st December, 1926, prohibiting Patrick Thornbury (an ex-internee
who has for some considerable time been
employed as a school teacher in Dublin)
from entering or residing in the city of
Belfast or the Counties of Antrim or
Down. This Order was served upon
Thornbury on the 15th December, 1926,
in Belfast, this being, as far as is known,
the first occasion on which he had entered
the prohibited area since the Order was
made.
Thornbury had not, prior to the issue
of the Order, been convicted of any offence
by any Court. Such a conviction is not
a condition necessarily precedent to the
issue of an Order of Exclusion from a
portion of Northern Ireland. As stated
in the Order, he was suspected of being
about to act in a manner prejudicial to
the preservation of the peace and the
maintenance of order in Northern Ireland.
I considered the case very carefully before deciding to make the Order and was
satisfied that the issue of the Order was
desirable for the preservation of the peace
and the maintenance of order.
It would be contrary to established
practice and against the public interest
to disclose the information at my disposal,
but I am not at present prepared to revoke the Order against him.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not think that imprisonment

Sir DAWSON BATES: That is &
matter entirely for the competent Court
which dealt with the case.

Gentleman not think the time has

The matter is regulated by Section 5
of the Public Roads (Ireland) Act, 1911,
which requires that every locomotive
used on the public road shall be constructed on the principle of consuming
its own smoke, and renders every person
using any locomotive not consuming its
own smoke, so far as practicable, liable
to a penalty, and several prosecutions
have recently been instituted under this
Section. This provision is obviously
very necessary for preventing nuisance
in the public streets, and, in any event,
I have no power to suspend the provisions
of an Act of Parliament as suggested by
the hon. Member.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Supplementary Estimate for the Special Constabulary, which I have the honour to
introduce to-day, relates solely to Class
"A" that is, the Specials on whole-time
engagement. When the original Special
Constabulary Estimates were introduced
last year the total strength of Class "A,"
including 60 members of the Force employed on Customs Duty, was close on 400,
while the strength to-day is under 100.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the
disbandment of a Force of approximately
4,000 men, which was commenced in
Supplementary Estimates
Supply-

December, 1925, is a problem of very considerable dimensions. Barracks had to be
evacuated and stores withdrawn to base;
while comprehensive arrangements had to
be made for the sale, during the current
year, of large quantities of material which
had accumulated during the life-time of
the Special Constabulary in its active
form.
The programme of disbandment which
was framed early last year has, I am
happy to say, been completed according to
schedule, and additional provision is only
now required for a few items of expenditure which could not, in the conditions
prevailing, be estimated more accurately.
Hon. Members will see from the Estimate
that a token Vote of £10 only is required
to defray the additional cost of this
Service during the year. The proceeds
from the sale of surplus stores has been
considerably greater than I anticipated,
but financial procedure does not permit of
the utilisation of any additional moneys
received from this source to make good deficiencies in other directions. It is
necessary, therefore, to bring to the notice
of the Committee those items which have
been under-estimated at the time the
original Estimate was put forward.
As regards the item of "Allowances,"
the provision voted by the Committee at

Sub-head "Rent and Rates" for which

on the evacuation of premises commandeered for the Special Constabulary.
Hon Members will appreciate the difficulty of estimating accurately the amount
necessary to settle all these compensation

met by the Department during the year,
and I do not think there is any other
item that calls for attention. I beg to
move

in arriving at that conclusion our legal

The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
hon. Member for North Belfast is somewhat under a misapprehension. This
settlement of a dispute was not a matter
for my right hon. Friend to tender a sum
d of money to the trustees of the hall. This
was purely a legal affair where a legal
claim was made by the trustees of the
hall, and the question then for my right
hon. Friend and for myself and for the
Members of the Cabinet was to decide
whether it was better to come to an
amicable settlement than to go to the
Courts. It was merely a question if the
case was carried to the Courts whether
the damages against the Government
would be much heavier than the amount
arrived at. There was no question of a
solatium. It was a mere matter of legal
cost, and it was settled, in our opinion,
more satisfactorily than if it had gone
into court. I think my right hon.
Friend acted perfectly correctly.

The hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Grant) says what should have happened was that the hall should have been
razed to the ground; but really I think
that is an absurd proposition. To raze
the hall to the ground in an illegal way
would simply have brought a very heavy
charge on the City of Belfast, because
it would have been malicious damage.
What benefit would accrue to anybody?
I do think under all the circumstances
we have got over a very nasty period.
Feeling is better; everybody is desirous
of allowing the past to be forgotten,
and nothing should be raised now of an
acrimonious character. I am quite satisfied that the Cabinet-we had Cabinet
responsibility in the matter-I am quite
satisfied that the Cabinet did the right
thing in coming to a settlement out of
Court. Had we gone into Court the damages given against us might have been
very much greater.
Question put, and agreed to.

certain Grants in Aid (16 Geo. V, c 4

and sale of imported coal during the
stoppage in the Coal Industry.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In approaching the consideration of the first item on the Supplementary Estimate now before hon. Members, it may not be out of place if I review
the development of events since October
last, when the sanction of the House was
sought for the purchase of coal by the
Government. Hon. Members will remember that at that time, as a result of
the breaking down of negotiations for a
settlement of the coal dispute, the increasing demands on the Continental and
American markets were forcing up prices
and freights to such an extent that
merchants were daily becoming more reluctant to risk the placing of forward contracts, which would have involved them
in serious losses in the event of a sudden
termination of the dispute. The result
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
to
was a tendency on the part of the
merchants to restrict purchases
quantities covered by definite orders.
The Government realised that the
merchants could not be expected to undertake the extensive risks involved in
placing forward contracts under the
market conditions then prevailing, and
that if the essential needs of the community were to be safeguarded it would
be necessary for the Government to undertake the purchase of a supply of coal.
Accordingly, my Ministry was authorised
to make arrangements on the lines
indicated to the House at the time the
proposal to purchase coal was approved.
An agent was appointed to act in consultation with the Ministry of Commerce
to purchase coal and arrange sales to local
merchants at a price to be determined by
the Ministry after taking into account all
expenditure prior to such sale, including
an agency fee payable to the agent in
respect of his services, namely buying
coal, chartering steamers, arranging discharge, etc. The agent further had to
undertake the financing of the transactions. On the 8th October the agent was
authorised to negotiate for the purchase
of American coal for immediate shipment.

Mr. BARBOUR: I should have

Ireland owes a great deal for his courage
in going ahead and entering into very
serious commitments, not only in respect
of Continental coal but also of American
coal, which he brought over and

and a very much better range of employment to be maintained in Northern Ireland than was the case in a great many

As I was saying, the agent was
appointed on the 8th October, and the
agent was forthwith authorised to enter
into negotiations for the purchase of
American coal. It was decided that the
Government would take the major risk of
purchasing in America, leaving merchants
as free a hand as possible to import from
Continental ports, where, of course, the
risk, owing to the shorter time of transit,
was of a very much less serious character.
It was found impossible to obtain shipment in October, but on 14th October
acceptance of four cargoes, amounting in
all to approximately 20,000 tons for shipment in November was authorised. The
agent secured a further shipment of 6,000
tons for shipment in the same month. As

On the 6th November, in view of the
reopening of negotiations for the settlement of the coal dispute, the agent cabled
his American representative to suspend
further purchases. At that date the
Government's commitments were 61,536
tons, or approximately ten days' normal
supply, for the whole of Ulster for that
period of the year. That being so it was
necessary to ensure that all hospitals,
institutions, schools, and public utility
undertakings were fully supplied before
offering the coal to the industrial and
private consumer.
As hon. Members will recollect, the
negotiations which opened early in November led to a settlement in the coal dispute,
the immediate result of which was that
prices commenced to slump and merchants
and institutions were reluctant to buy for
December or January delivery. On the
24th November all restrictions on the
export of coal from Great Britain were
removed, and accordingly it became necessary for the Government to dispose of its
coal purchases on the best terms obtainable. As a first step the Associated Coal
Merchants of Belfast were invited to make
offers for the whole of the coal purchased
by the Government-the total as I have
said amounting only to ten days' normal
supply for winter consumption in Northern Ireland. The merchants, however-I
am very sorry to say-were not prepared to
make any offer. In the meantime, fortunately for us, two of the vessels chartered missed their loading dates and
arrangements were made for the cancellation of the cargoes amounting to 10,500
tons at a cost of £5,489, so that relieved
us of the necessity of taking up 10,500
tons
It became obvious at this time that, resulting from increasing importation from
Great Britain and the steady fall in prices
from day to day-Scotch coal delivered to
household consumers on 30th November
was sold at the rate of 80s a ton; on the
1st December 70s, showing the rapidity of
the fall; on the 13th December 45s, and
on the 15th December 40s-and so it became obvious that American coal arriving
in December and January could be disposed of only at a heavy loss. It was
decided, therefore, that the agent should
he empowered to negotiate for the cancellation of all commitments in cases in
which the ships had not already sailed
In addition to the two ships which had
already missed their sailing dates, and to
which I have already referred, negotiations for the cancellation of five ships and
cargoes were completed on the 17th
December at a total cost of £41,107, including coal and freight, or in other words
£1 11s 7d per ton of cargo in order to
affect the cancellation. The total purchases actually made amounted to 61,536
tons, of which only 25,036 tons arrived in
Belfast, the remainder being cancelled.
As regards the coal which actually
arrived in Belfast, namely, those 25,036
tons, a further effort was made, but without success, to induce the Belfast Associated Coal Merchants to make an offer
for these cargoes. As it was obviously
impracticable for the Government to set
up its own retail selling organisation it
was decided to offer this coal to the agent,
and eventually the following arrangement
was concluded: In consideration of the
agent waiving his claim for the commission of 2s 6d per ton on all the purchases
made by him on behalf of the Government this commission would have
amounted to £7,692-all cargoes
of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Government coal arriving at Belfast were
sold to him at 20s per ton, the Government being relieved of all charges over
and above the actual c.i.f. price of the
cargo. This meant, in effect, a loss of
31s 7d per ton on this portion of the
transaction. When it is recalled that before the last of these cargoes arrived in
Belfast the price of coal had fallen to
practically the normal level, and that
American coal was being offered at 21s
per ton c.i.f. Belfast on 21st December,
it will be appreciated by hon. Members
that the Government adopted the best
means possible of minimising the losses
involved in the transaction.
I have endeavoured to lay before the
Committee the fullest and most open
statement I could give, so as to place hon.
Members in possession of full information
on all the essential details of this transaction. Hon. Members will, of course,
realise that we had only one incentive in
entering into the transaction at all, and
that was to insure against not only the
ordinary householder in Northern Ireland
but also our industrial concerns being exposed to the very grave risk of being
actually without coal for a period. The
extent to which we entered into the transaction, as I have explained, amounted
only to the provision of ten days' supply,
and the fact that the loss on even such a
short quantity of coal as this has
reached such a substantial figure affords to
hon. Members, I think, some sort of indication as to the very great extra cost imposed on our whole industrial and
household community in the Six Counties
arising out of this industrial dispute.
Had these conditions continued the
Government would have come out without
a loss on the transaction, but I think, although we are faced with this heavy
charge, it is infinitely preferable that an
early termination of this most unfortunate dispute happily occurred. The
Vote which is now asked for is one of the
results of that development. I beg to
move.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move a reduction
in this Estimate of £100 to call attention
to the absolutely unwarranted waste of
public money in these transactions. I do
not think the Committee have ever
listened to such an exhibition of incapacity as has been shown by the Government in this particular connection. One
would almost say that they had done this
thing deliberately in order to show how
futile the Government can be in attempting to do something for the good of the
whole community. One would look to
them as having some idea of making
purchases for the community and sales to
the community for the benefit of the
whole community. I think it would be
well to pay some attention to this particular aspect of the case. The Minister,
I noticed, started on the 12th October.
The Minister said that on that date this
House granted permission, as it were, to
the Government to purchase coal.
We
want to go a little further back than the
12th October. On the 4th May last,
three days after the dispute started, I
asked a private notice question as to what
steps the Government intended to take
to prevent the exploitation of the needs
of the people in the necessities of life.
The Minister replied that a Bill was to be
introduced, and as a matter of fact it was
introduced on the 6th May and passed on
the same day. The Prime Minister himself said on that day that the Bill was to
prevent the effects of greed or panic.
On that same day (6th May) the
Minister of Commerce stated in reply to
a question by my colleague the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie)
that it had been intimated to his Department that prices had been increased, and
that he had issued instructions fixing
maximum prices at which coal might be
sold by merchants. It was not until
October 20th in this House that any statement was made that the Government
intended to have bulk purchases. We
want to contend from these Benches that
the Government had the power from the
6th May to make whatever purchases they
liked, and it was not until it was too late,
following on the policy that the British
Government as usual adopted, that they
attempted to take any action. The
Minister on the 20th October said that
the Government had decided to buy coal
which private enterprise had failed to
provide. Apparently nothing had been
done from the 6th May, or let us say the
20th May, when the House rose.
The
House reassembled on the 1st June for a
few minutes and then adjourned until the
12th October, and apparently nothing
had been done in the whole interim by the
Government to take steps to ensure that
the people of the Six Counties might be
provided with coal.

ahead, and also for the heating of school
buildings, hospitals and so on.

any other way. So long as my right hon.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think
it is unnecessary to impart any heat in
regard to the discussion of this very important subject, although it is a coal
question we are considering. It is well
for us to try to get into our minds
certain essential facts in regard to the
transaction we are considering here this
afternoon. The transaction resulted in a
loss of something over £90,000, which we
are called upon as a Committee to vote
to-day as a Supplementary Estimate.
There is one thing I would like to state
at the outset, that is, that I am one of
those who have never been in love with
the idea of a Government undertaking
the purchase of coal or any other commodity. As a whole, things of that
character are better and more efficiently
dealt with by private enterprise and by
those who have a thorough and competent knowledge of the particular things.
they are dealing in.
I quite recognise there are times, in
the interests of the community, when
great emergencies arise such as the great
war and such indeed as the circumstances
arising in connection, with this coal
dispute, when it is necessary for Governments to interfere in order to help the
industries of the country and to help
those who need the commodities necessary
to carry
on life in a reasonable way.
There is one thing, perhaps, that the
Committee is losing sight of and that
those who have criticised the Government
up to the present seem to forget. On
20th October last in this House this
whole question was discussed and debated,
and certain decisions were arrived at with
the full knowledge and concurrence not
only of the supporters of the Government
but of the Opposition. May I recall the
debate that took place on 20th October
in connection with this very matter
which, I think, will clear up the question
that the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) was in some difficulty about?

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The point

been that they would have suffered immense losses. They took certain risks as

of the people.

What are the facts? The neglect of
the Government to purchase coal at the
proper time has resulted, not only in a
loss of £92,000 to £94,000 to the people
of Northern Ireland, but it has enabled
private contractors and merchants to buy
and to carry on for a period of six months,
and to sell at exorbitant and impossible
prices to the poor of the country, coal
which if the Government had bought, as
we suggest they should have bought, and
sold at reasonable prices, the people
of Northern Ireland in addition to being
saved this great loss of £94,000, would also
have been saved having to pay, as most
of them had to pay, exorbitant and unfair
prices for coal during that period.
I do not want to labour the point any
further. The whole ground has been
pretty well covered, but I say that the
conduct of the Government in connection
with this matter is absolutely indefensible

You say,
Why did we not start in May to buy
coal?", I say that if we had started in
May to buy coal the consequences would
have been absolutely fatal." The strike
was necessarily a matter of very indefinite
duration, and the risk at the close of the
strike always stared every coal importer
in the face. The moment the Government had stepped in to assume the responsibility of supplying coal to Northern
Ireland, that moment the ordinary coal
importer would have drawn out, and
consequently we should have found ourselves involved in the supply of the total
coal requirements of the Province.
In the earlier days you could get coal
from the Continent in the course of two
or three weeks. That would have meant
that we would have been committed to
three weeks' supply instead of ten days'.
As the strike went on and the winter
requirements became larger, we then had
to turn to America, and drawing coal
from America meant that we would have
had to buy six, seven or eight weeks ahead
in order to make sure of getting our supplies. The Americans knew very well
the straits we were in and they were not
disposed to sell small quantities at reasonable prices. They wanted to ensure, as
far as they could, continuing business.
The result would have been that at the
time the strike ended, instead of our being
committed to only ten days' supply, we
would probably have been committed to
eight or ten weeks' supply being shipped,
or on ships coming to this port. So 1
think, bad and all as it is, it was an
ordinary business transaction.
I should be very much surprised if our
business people in Belfast did not study in
every way they could to have at least
ten days' supply. I expect some of them
tried to have as much as two or three
weeks' supply of coal in their yards if
possible, because of the desirability of the
continuity of operation. I think there
is no demand more necessary to provide
for than the ordinary small householder,
so that he could keep the ordinary necessities of life going.

Mr. BARBOUR: The Resolution before you provides for a charge upon
moneys provided by Parliament of the
cost of payment of subsidies under the
Labourers Cottages Bill to Rural District
Councils executing schemes under the
Labourers Acts which are lodged on or
after 1st April, 1927, and not later than
31st March, 1930. This charge will take
the place of that already in existence
under Section 1, Sub-Section (2) of the
Labourers Acts (Northern Ireland), 1923,
under which annual loan charges of
Rural District Councils in respect of
Labourers Acts schemes have hitherto
been subsidised by the Government to
the extent of 36 per cent. Under this
Bill it is proposed to repeal that Sub-
Section as regards new schemes and to
provide in lieu thereof the payment of a
subsidy of 40 per cent. of the annual loan
charges of Rural District Councils.
It is desirable that I should explain
to the House that the financial scheme
under which the Labourers Acts are
administered was formulated over 20
years ago at a time when advances could
be obtained at a much lower rate of
interest. Accordingly the operation of
the fixed percentage grant which was laid
down so far back as 1906 has produced
some curious anomalies in that owing to
the rise in the value of money this grant
no longer represents the total assistance
which is really being afforded for the
construction of these houses.
It has been arranged, therefore, that
in future advances for the erection of
labourers' cottages will be made from the
Government Loans Fund, thereby eliminating the various anomalies which arose
as the result of issuing stock at the extremely low price necessitated by the low
rate of interest payable. This, of course,
entails a readjustment of the fixed percentage grant which has hitherto been
paid, and having regard to the fact that
the increased cost of borrowing money
has been accompanied by a corresponding
rise in the rents receivable in respect of
labourers' cottages it has been decided
349 Labourers' Cottages (Loans)

23 MARCH 1927
Committee
that a Government grant of 40 per cent.
of the loan charges will have the result
of fairly distributing the financial responsibility as between the local authorities
on the one hand and the Government on
the other. I beg to move.

whereas the other people are labouring

very lowest

Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES-MOIRA
RURAL DISTRICT.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
over thirty sites purchased for the erection of labourers' cottages by the Moira
Rural District Council have been sold to
farmers in that area; whether he can state
how many sites are available for the erection of labourers' cottages in the area controlled by the Moira Rural Council, and
whether he can say if it is the intention
of this Council to proceed with the erection of these cottages.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Moira Rural
District Council Order of 1912 provided
for the erection of 68 cottages in the rural
district. This scheme was deferred owing
to the outbreak of war, and as the Council
did not proceed with the erection of the
cottages before the 31st August, 1924, the
scheme lapsed under the provisions of the
Labourers (Ireland) Act, 1918.
Section 15 of the Act of 1883 requires
that sites acquired under schemes which
have lapsed shall be reconveyed to their
former owners or be sold by public
auction. Up to date about thirty of the
sites acquired under this scheme have
been so disposed of.
The Rural District Council cannot now
legally proceed with this scheme, but if
the Council are of opinion that further
cottages are required in the district they
can formulate a further scheme under
which the remaining 38 sites could be
made available if still considered suitable
and such additional sites as might be
necessary could be acquired.
The question of proceeding with a new
scheme has been under consideration by
the Council during the past two years,
but no definite decision has as yet been
arrived at.
CANADIAN FLOUR FUND AND
PRINCE OF WALES'S FUND.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the "Canadian
Flour Fund" is in any way subject to
control or supervision by any Department
of the Government; if so, can he give any
details as to this Fund; how much of it
has been expended upon the purpose for
which it was intended; and can he say
upon what person or persons rests the
responsibility for its administration; and
if a balance sheet will be published.
The following question also stood on
the Paper in the name of Colonel Woods:
3. To ask the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the "Prince of Wales'
Fund" is in any way subject to control
or supervision by any Department of the
Government; if so, can he state the name
or names of those responsible for its
administration; whether this Fund was
created by public subscription for the
benefit or relief of sufferers from causes
directly attributable to the Great War;
what amounts have been expended upon
such persons; and what is the amount of
the balance remaining unexpended.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the hon.
and gallant Member's permission I will
answer his two questions together.
The administration of the "Canadian
Flour Fund" and of the "Prince of
Wales' Fund" in Belfast is not subject
to control or supervision by any of the
Departments of the Government of Northern Ireland.

From inquiries which have been made
it is understood that these two Funds are
administered by a body of Trustees appointed prior to the transfer of Services
to the Government of Northern Ireland
by the Central Committees established
for the administration of the Funds
generally in the United Kingdom.
The Trustees in question are-The Lord
Mayor of Belfast for the time being, who
also acts as Chairman and Treasurer; Sir
Crawford McCullagh, Mr. J. H. Stirling,
and Sir Frederick Moneypenny.
The Funds are, it is understood, administered for the benefit of the deserving
poor and of ex-Servicemen in Belfast, and
about £200 a week is distributed.
It has also been ascertained that the
accounts of the Trustees are audited annually by a specially appointed independent
Accountant.
Owing to the limited time available it
has not been possible to obtain certified
copies of the Accounts, but the Lord
Mayor has courteously agreed to furnish
me with a copy of the Accounts for the
last year, and on receipt of this I will,
if the hon. and gallant Member so desires, furnish him with a copy. It is
understood that the Trustees are desirous
of affording to any person interested full
information as to the manner in which the
Funds are administered.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
reply, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman whether he considers that it is not
within the purview of his Ministry to
inquire into all public funds such as
these, not only in the interests of those
for whom they are intended, but also of
those who administer them? For instance, is he aware that a secretary is
employed at a salary of somewhere about
£250 or £260 a year, that this man refuses
to interview applicants for relief at his
place of business, and that he has no
other known place at which applicants
can call?
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid this is
developing into a speech.
Colonel WOODS: I would like the
matter to be put clearly on behalf of the

those who make applications.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am certain
that the Lord Mayor will be only too
glad to give the hon. and gallant Member
any information that he requires.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman to use his influence with
the Lord Mayor with the object of securing the publication of a balance sheet, and
thus satisfy everyone concerned?
TAILORING TRADE..
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state how many
inspections have taken place during the
past twelve months of firms engaged in
the wholesale and retail tailoring trade;
and whether any of those inspections have
resulted in it being proved that certain
employers engaged in that trade have not
been paying the legal minima laid down.
by the Trade Board in that industry.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The figures which are available relate to the calendar year 1926,
during which sixty-two firms in the retail
branch of the tailoring trade and nine
firms in the readymade branch were inspected. Eighteen of the former and
four of the latter were found to be paying
to certain of their workers rates of wages
which did not conform to those laid down
by the Trade Boards, and arrears of
wages amounting to £74 2s 9d and
£9 Os 6d respectively were collected by
the Ministry and paid over to the workers
concerned.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman satisfied that satisfactory conditions
obtain in these workshops? In other
words, is he satisfied that the legal
minima are being paid, quite apart from
the returns that are made?
Mr. ANDREWS: So far as I know the
law is being complied with, but if my
hon. Friend knows of any cases where it
is thought that the law is not being complied with, and if he will report them to
me, I shall be indebted to him.

Mr. ANDREWS: The conditions in
regard to pensions for widows of men
who were over 70 years of age on the 4th
January, 1926, are not within the
regulation-making power of the Ministry
of Labour.
Under the provisions of the Act such
widows are not entitled to pensions if
there is not living at the time of the
death of the husband at least one child
under the age of fourteen. In this respect the widows in question are in the
same position as widows of men who died
before the 4th January, 1926.
Contributions under the Pensions Act
would not have been paid in respect of
the husband in either class of case, and
the pensions which are allowed if there
are children are in the nature of a gift.

Mr. BEATTIE: I desire to move an
Amendment that the Vote be reduced by
£1,000. In doing so I feel it is my duty
as a representative of the city of Belfast
to call the attention of the public and the
taxpayers to what I would describe as the
maladministration of services under the
jurisdiction of the Government.
I feel that the business has been neglected
owing to absence of business ability in regard to some of the services under the
control of the Government. I heard a
story on one occasion that if a man had
been executed for his business abilities he
would have died innocent. I think that
rightly applies to the Government on this
occasion. As far as my experience goes,
if they had been executed for govermental
abilities they would have died innocent.

I do not dispute generally the statements made in the Committee's Report,
which, after all, were based on facts as
disclosed to them, but I do take exception
to the statements that have been made
here and elsewhere that it is due to either

loss occurred. For my part I am perfectly
satisfied that every step which could be
taken at the time and which ought to
have been taken by us, was taken, and
I will go further-I say that if the same
circumstances arose to-day, and if the
same considerations were in my mind as
were before me during the months of
November and December, 1924, I would
still hold my hand and refuse to give the
contract to the firm concerned, even if I
was conscious of the fact that by my delay
and by my refusal a possible loss might
ensue.
Now I would like to explain as briefly
as I can the situation as it appeared to
me at the time, and here I would ask the
indulgence of the Committee to remember
that incidents of this character must not
be judged in the light of future events in
cold blood, but should be judged by the
circumstances from day to day which
operated in the mind of the responsible
official or Minister who had to deal with
this matter.
In November, 1924, sixteen approved
firms were asked to tender for the supply
of Constabulary uniform for the year 1925-
26, and these firms were informed that
their tenders must be received at the
Ministry by the 5th November, 1924.
Tender forms were sent to them of a
pattern which have been in use for several
years in Northern Ireland, and I understand were generally similar to the forms
which were used for Royal Irish Constabulary contracts. These tender forms
contain a Clause under which the person
tendering undertook to keep his offer open
for a period of six weeks from the appointed day-that is six weeks from the
day appointed for the reception of
tenders.
This Clause has been the subject of remark and criticism both here and elsewhere. It is perfectly obvious why such a
Clause was inserted. It frequently happens
that perhaps twenty or thirty tenders
come in on a particular contract. Some
of these firms are new ones, and it is to
enable the Government to make the necessary inquiries in regard to these different
firms that that particular Clause was inserted. It is a Clause which had been in
operation for some time, and it had never
Supply-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
been the experience of this Ministry that
any firm attempted to evade its undertaking in this respect. We have been
criticised because we did not take steps
at the very outset to satisfy ourselves that
this Clause was legally binding, but, as I
have already pointed out, the question
never arose because the firms who had
been in the habit of tendering had never
attempted to evade it. Even if it had not
been legally binding, surely it was a moral
obligation that any decent firm would
comply with. However, there it was, and
we confidently expected that the firms in
our approved list would adhere to their
terms.
I suggest that honour still exists in
commercial transactions. A person who
pleads the Statute of Limitations for a
debt which he owes is not held in high
esteem, nor is a contractor who pleads a

The tenders were received on the 5th
November, 1924, and were examined by
the various officers responsible for this
duty in the Ministry. On the basis of
their examination, investigation and
previous knowledge of the contractors, it
was recommended that the tender of a
firm "A" be accepted. The papers came
to me for formal approval on the 12th
November, 1924, but here I would like
to say that some time earlier information
from private sources had reached me to
the effect that this particular firm "A"
had been concerned in a transaction regarding a contract for the disposal of old
constabulary clothing where some serious
irregularities had taken place.
The allegations made to me were made
confidentially and were from such a source
that I could not ignore them, and were
sufficient to cause me to hold my hand in
connection with this contract. As I had
no documentary evidence in support of
these allegations, and as the parties who
could have cleared the matter up were unwilling to come forward and substantiate
the allegations, the only course open to
me was to have private inquiry made
through the police. These inquiries took
some time, and had to be made in a most
delicate way. I was kept fully informed
-and I would like to stress this pointby the officers of the Ministry of the risk
I was running in allowing the question of
the contract to remain over, and I was
also aware of the representations which
had been made by firm "A" during the
early part of the month of December as
to the rise in the price of wool and as
to their possible inability to carry out the
tender had we accepted it, but I was still
unable to satisfy myself that the allegations referred to were either untrue or
exaggerated, and in any event I did not
suppose that a firm who had been so long
connected with Government contracts
would repudiate the terms of their
tender.

We took steps to obtain competent legal

for one moment that I did the thing

--my then Parliamentary Secretary and
I were fully satisfied that the tender of a
firm which acted so dishonourably should
not be accepted, as they were not fit to
be on the list of Government contractors,
and accordingly we decided to accept the
next lowest tender, which, as already
pointed out, meant an excess cost of approximately £3,600 over the amount
specified in the original tender. Whether
the firm in question would not have taken
some other pretext for getting out of their
tender had it been accepted is open to
question. It was certainly not a case of
a firm whose word was as good as its bond.
We had its word but had not the bond,
and it withdrew from its offer.
I do ask this House to consider could
any responsible Ministry overlook such
conduct, and treat the firm as reputable?
If this had happened to any private
Member of this House what would that
private Member do? Would you enter
into a fresh contract with the firm when
the ink of his repudiation was scarcely
dry? I do suggest that at least as high
morality is required in Government as in
contracts by private individuals. I would
like to tell the House that I personally
am satisfied that our action in connection
with this tender has constituted a very
sound lesson to all contractors who deal
not only with this Ministry but possibly
to contractors who have to deal with other
Ministries.
If it once became known or understood
in certain trade and business circles that
the Ministry of Home Affairs was prepared or inclined to admit irregularities
of any description in connection with
public contracts, it would be impossible
ever to check or to control abuses. Complaints have often been made which have
been difficult either to substantiate or to
refute as to irregularities in connection.
with Government contracts.
I do say
this, we cannot entirely disregard these
complaints, though it is often hard to get
evidence that will carry conviction.
I hold the view that all Government
contracts should be above reproach, and
that no firm should ever be afforded the
smallest opportunity of even hintingmuch less alleging the possibility of any
irregularity.
I may point out in connection with the
various contracts that the Ministry has to
deal with some of the shrewdest firms in
the United Kingdom, and so far as I and
my officials can help it, we will never allow
any incident or complaint to pass unchallenged which might reflect in any way on
the propriety of the manner in which
contracts are dealt with in the Ministry.
I would ask the House to remember
that in dealing with matters of this kind
we have to consider principles besides the
immediate financial advantage. May I
give an illustration ?
Some short time
ago we had occasion to advertise for a
contract. A certain hour was fixed for

came in two hours after the time had expired for receiving tenders requesting that
their tender should be considered. If I

meant a saving to the public purse, but
what would have been the effect on other

in in time? What confidence would they

I had done that certainly I would have
been spared this very unpleasant debate.
especially having regard to the personal

stration and in the cost of Government

the last Budget speech of the Minister of

notified the Government of the advance
in price. Immediately after that the
Government notified the firm that their
tender had been accepted, actually after
it had been withdrawn.
A great deal has been made out of the
fact that this firm, had they acted
honourably, when they saw the notice
printed on the tender that the tender was
to be kept open for six weeks should have
struck that out in red ink, and then the

At that particular time, if I remember
aright, the Inspector-General had complete control of some 3,000 Royal Ulster
Constabulary, some 5,000 full-time “A”
Special Constabulary, and some 30,000
"B" Special Constabulary. It is difficult
for an ordinary Member of this Committee

Labourers' Cottages (Loans) [Money]
Resolution reported:
That it is expedient to amend the
Labourers Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
in its application to certain loans and
advances under the Labourers Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1883 to 1923, by
authorising a charge upon moneys provided by Parliament in respect of the
payment of the sums hereinafter mentioned to the councils of the several rural
districts in Northern Ireland by whom
loans may be borrowed in pursuance of
schemes approved for the provision of
cottages and allotments, in any case
where the petition for the scheme is
lodged with the Ministry of Home Affairs,
on or after the first day of April, nineteen hundred and twenty-seven, but not
later than the thirty-first day of March,
nineteen hundred and thirty;
And that the sum payable as aforesaid
in any financial year to the council of a
rural district shall be a sum equivalent
to forty pounds per cent. of the annual
loan charge of the council, or, if the
period for the repayment of the loan is
shorter than thirty-five years, a sum
equivalent to such less percentage of the
annual loan charge as may be determined
by the Minister of Home Affairs with the
approval of the Ministry of Finance, but
so, however, that no payment shall be
made in respect of any portion of the
annual loan charge which arises from expenditure causing the total capital cost
of the scheme to exceed three hundred
and fifty pounds for each cottage to be
provided, or from the payment of
interest, so far as it exceeds interest at
the rate in force, on the date of borrowing, for similar borrowings from the
Government Loans Fund;
And that, in relation to the schemes
for the provision of cottages and allotments, where the petition is lodged with
the Ministry of Home Affairs on or at
any time after the first day of April,
nineteen hundred and twenty-seven, the
provisions of sub-section (2) of section
one of the Labourers Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, shall not apply.

Oral Answers to Questions.
ENTERTAINMENT TAX.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether, in view of the action of
the Irish Rugby Union in deciding to
have both home International matches
played in Dublin this season in consequence of the Entertainment Tax, is he
prepared to abolish this unjust tax.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This matter continues to
receive my careful consideration, but the
hon. Member will understand that I cannot anticipate my Budget statement.
I should perhaps add that I am given
to understand that the primary reason
for having both matches in Dublin this
season was not the tax difficulty, but the
desire of the Rugby Union to attract a
larger gate, in order to meet heavy expenses incurred in connection with the
Dublin ground. For this purpose Dublin is, of course, more central than
Belfast.

2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked
the Minister of Labour whether he can
LIVE STOCK REPLACEMENT LOAN
SCHEME.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether the
Government will now withdraw the condition restricting cheap loans to farmers to those who have lost stock in a
particular period and make these loans
generally available for the whole of the
farming community.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Archdale): The Live Stock Replacement Loan Scheme was put into operation
to meet a very special emergency, and the
loans are confined to farmers who have
had losses of live stock since October,
1924.
I could not undertake to extend the
provisions of this special Scheme to
farmers generally. Any such wholesale
extension of credit facilities would involve serious questions of policy and
finance and would, furthermore, necessitate the setting up of elaborate administrative machinery.
I may add, for the information of the
hon. Member, that in addition to these
Live Stock Replacement Loans the
Ministry grants loans to farmers for the
following purposes:-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Archdale]
(a) the purchase of agricultural
machinery and implements;
(b) the purchase of pure-bred sires.
The Ministry is also about to issue a
Scheme under which loans will be given
to farmers in mountainous districts for
the erection of wire fencing.
Further, the Ministry
the Ministry of Finance
under the Landed Property Improvement
(Ireland) Acts grants loans to farmers for
the erection of dwelling-houses, out-offices
and silos, and also for such field works as
drainage and fencing.
Moreover my Ministry, in conjunction
with the Ministry of Finance, has evolved
a special supplementary Scheme under
which loans are granted to small farmers
on simplified conditions for the erection
of small hay barns, byres, dairies, as well
as for the equipment of poultry farms.
If the hon. Member wishes I shall be
very glad to let him have copies of these
Schemes.

CUSTOMS SERVICE.
Prime
4. Mr. KYLE asked the
Minister whether, in view of the necessity
in the interests of our wholesale trading
houses to prevent delay in the delivery
of goods in the Irish Free State owing to
customs restrictions, he is prepared to
approach the British Government and the
Government of the Irish Free State to
ascertain whether they would be agreeable
that a small joint committee of traders,
North and South, should be set up and
asked to report on the possibility of an
arrangement being entered into between
the Government of Great Britain, Irish
Free State, and Government of Northern
Ireland, which might result in obviating
unnecessary and wasteful delay and would
mutually benefit the people of North and
South.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I'have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply.
As the hon. Gentleman is aware,
matters appertaining to the Customs service are reserved to the Imperial Parliament under the Government of Ireland
Act, and correspondence or negotiations
with the Government of the Irish Free
State in regard to such matters fall to be
conducted by the appropriate Imperial
Department. If, therefore, the hon.
Member will state the precise nature of
the difficulties which he has in mind, 1
will be glad to consider whether it would
be practicable for my Ministry to make
representations to the Imperial Authority
concerned with a view to their solution.
LAND PURCHASE.-APPOINTED
DAY.
5. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Prime Minister whether he will state
what steps, if any, the Government is
taking to impress on the Imperial Government
the necessity for having the
appointed day (under the Northern Ireland Land Act, 1925) declared on all
estates before the next gale day, and
will the Government make the necessary
financial provision involved in putting the
Act into operation on all estates in
Northern Ireland before that date.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
reply to this question.
Having regard to the large amount of
preliminary work which is necessary, I
am satisfied that it is physically impossible for the appointed days for all estates
to be declared before the next gale day.
I would refer the hon. Member to a reply
given by the Under Secretary of State
to the Home Office in the Imperial House
of Commons on the first of the present
month, which shows that the Land Purchase Commission is dealing expeditiously
with the matter, and that very considerable progress is being made. I understand that on the 21st instant no fewer
than 2,791 holdings had been definitely
vested in the Commission.

Mr. DEVLIN: I beg to remove a reduction of this Vote by £100, for the
purpose of calling attention to and
having some information from the Government as to what is the precise position
in regard to the mails. We have now
for a period of nearly five years had our
mail system conducted upon lines
which I think no one in this House or
out of it could possibly defend. For
reasons which I have never heard adequately stated, the Government changed
the whole system by which the mails
Morrison, Hugh Smith
Mulholland, Captain The Hon. Henry
George Hill
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh McDowell
Robb, John Hanna
TELLER FOR THE AYES-
Captain Dixon.
O'Neill, Patrick
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr Beattle
were carried between Northern Ireland
and England some five years ago, and
from then until now the gravest inconvenience has been caused not only to
the general public, but especially to the
business classes of the community. Now,
whatever may have been said for this
change some few years ago there is nothing whatever to be said in defence of
it for the last three or four years, and it
seems to me to be another example of
the ineptitude of the Government. Instead of finding out as they ought to have
found out as capable business men apart
altogether from their business as Cabinet
Ministers charged with the duty of
looking after the interests of the community-apart altogether from that it
seems to me to be a most extraordinary
thing that the Government have allowed
this system to go on all these years.
Now what is the explanation that the
Government gave for the change that has
taken place within the last few days?
This is the explanation given to a
"Belfast Telegraph" representative:
The change in the route is being
made because letters from the North
and North-West were being brought as
far as Lisburn by the Holyhead service,
with the result that all the towns
served in connection with this route
were receiving their London letters
somewhat earlier than in Belfast.
Quite a number of firms had accordingly made arrangements to have their
letters directed to Lisburn, and were
sending daily by motor to Lisburn so
that they might have access to their
mails at an earlier hour than was
possible by the Stranraer route.
This step was necessitated by reason
of stockbrokers and the large number
of people who transact business in
public issues finding time of extreme

moment in the reception of their mails.
Many of the issues of stock close per

Letters by the Stranraer route to
London seldom reach the Metropolis in
time for the first delivery.
The only proposal before the Postmaster-General for the moment in connection with the Stranraer route involved an increased annual charge
upon Northern Ireland of £12,000 in
respect of mails; while the utilisation
of the Holyhead route avoids such
increase.
Now the question I want to put to the
Government is this: If the Government
on the 25th March decided to make this
change and if that decision was based
upon the experience they gathered from
the inconvenience caused to the general
public and to the commercial interests of
the Province, why was that step not taken
a number of years ago? I have no doubt
-I think it has been stated alreadythat one of the reasons was that you could
not safely allow the mails from Northern
Ireland to pass through parts of the Free
State, but it seems to me a rather inexplicable circumstance that although the
mails for Belfast were carried through an
inconvenient course, yet the mails were
delivered in places like Lisburn, Portadown, Lurgan and other centres, and we
had the extraordinary position of men who
should have got their letters the first
thing in the morning in Belfast having
to send special messengers to Lisburn,
having to have their letters addressed to
Lisburn and having to have their clerks
waiting in Lisburn when the mail was delivered there to carry it to Belfast in
order to have it in time to enable them
to send replies to London and elsewhere.
In my judgment that was an arrant
ute piece of hypocrisy, because while you are

So far as I can arrive at a decision the
legal position under the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920, with regard to reserved
services is that this Parliament has no
power to make laws with regard to any of
the Reserved Services, and, since many of
them closely affect the people of Northern
Ireland, the Act provides for the direct
representation of Northern Ireland in the
Parliament of the United Kingdom,
which, of course, has power to legislate
about them. Since we have no power to
make laws on these matters, they are not,
prima facie, proper subjects for discussion
here except possibly by means of certain
forms of resolution, such as an Address to
the Crown. A further exception would,
I think, arise where the Government of
Northern Ireland had themselves undertaken any action or proceeding in respect
of any reserved matter; but before discussion would be in order it would have
to be shown that such action or proceeding had in fact been taken. In such a
case, however, a Minister could always
quite properly avoid giving information
on the ground that the matter was confidential and that the responsibility
rested, and rested alone, with the United
Kingdom Government.
It is in view of that last exception that
I allowed the hon. Member to proceed,
because I think it does appear that the
Government have taken some action with
regard to the mail service.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

anxious to risk the mails going through

I have been in close touch with
my colleagues and with the London Midland and Scottish Railway Company for
a long time past with a view to endeavouring in some way to secure a fast route
directly between Belfast and London.
The difficulties are very great. We have
tried every way-Larne and Stranraer,
Heysham, Liverpool. We have gone into
the question with Sir Josiah Stamp himself in London, and we have had special
representatives of the London Midland
and Scottish Railway over here with the
necessary information as to the difficulties
of linking up our mails with the fast mail
that leaves Crewe.
The difficulties in the way are manifold,
and it was quite clear to us that at all
events for some time to come-it might be
as long as two years-it would be impossible to improve upon the Holyhead route.
In the meantime a great deal of representation, indeed pressure, has been
brought to bear upon us by the business
community to facilitate the mails, and to
get the mails somehow to London as
quickly as possible. I would like to explain to the House that the difficulty in
getting the mails through to London is
much greater than the difficulty in getting
the mails from London to Belfast.
That
is to say, it would have been possible, I
believe, for us to secure that the Larne
and Stranraer train would have arrived
in Belfast, I think, at 9-10 a.m., possibly
9 o'clock, which would have synchronised
with the delivery of the mails coming
through from Holyhead, but that would
not get over the difficulty of getting the
Belfast mails delivered in London in time
for the very first delivery.
The Holyhead route gets the mails to
London at something like 5-50 a.m., and
the Larne and Stranraer route gets the
letters into London somewhere about
7-15 a.m. Those two hours make all the
difference, and it has been pointed out to
us, amongst other things, that when
Belfast people and those who are served
by the Larne and Stranraer route desire
to apply for any of the many loans that
are issued from time to time their applications, when going to London, are sometimes ruled out because on opening the
first mail the promoters find the issue is
already over-subscribed and they post a
notice up to that effect and will not take
any more applications into consideration,
with the unfortunate result that on many
occasions apparently the Ulster people
have been denied getting an allotment of
a loan and have to go into the market
and buy it a few days afterwards possibly
at a premium. That is one of the
strongest reasons brought to bear upon
us to make use at all events of the most
rapid and businesslike route in the meantime. When an All-Red Route, of which,
I am still strongly in favour, can be provided by the London Midland and
Scottish Railway Company then it will be
possible for us even to beat the present
system which we have inaugurated in reverting to the Holyhead and Kingstown.
route.

a police sergeant who was shot. He happened to be a Roman Catholic, and he
was shot in the discharge of his duty. It
was outside my district, but the coroner
in whose district it happened was an old
man, and he was afraid to hold the inquest, so he asked me to do it, and I did
it.
In the police barracks there was not
sufficient room to hold the inquest, and a
very respectable Roman Catholic in that
little town offered his drawing room and
we went down and held the inquest in his
house. The jury, which was a mixed
body, found a verdict of deliberate
murder.
That was bad enough. Two days afterwards a man was shot in the neighbourhood of Garvagh in my coroner's district.

Mr. GEO. HENDERSON: I wish to
draw attention under this Vote to the

Land Act, 1925. While this is a Reserved Service I was glad to learn from
the Prime Minister that in connection
with all these Reserved Services the Imperial Government were very anxious for
suggestions from the Government of
Northern Ireland, and that these suggestions were listened to sympathetically by
the heads of the Departments administering the Services. I think it will be admitted on all sides of the House it would
be very desirable if this Act were put into
operation universally on all estates before
the next gale day. The Minister of
Finance, in his answer to-day, said that
up to the present time 2,791 holdings had
been dealt with by the Land Commission.
He quoted these figures as testifying to
the progress made in the administration of
this Act up to the present time. This Act
has been almost two years in operation.
I think it came into operation in May,
1925. At a recent date 2,791 holdings

there are about 28,000 holdings still to
be dealt with under the Act. I would
like to know when we are likely to get

of this Act with the necessary co-operation between our Government, the Imperial Government and the Department

Labourers' Cottages (Loans) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read
Mr. POLLOCK: This Bill, which
consists of one clause, is the natural
sequel to the Money Resolution which my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) submitted
a few days ago. As was claimed by my
right hon. Friend at that time, the introduction of this Measure is solely on
account of economic factors, that is to
say, it does not in any way affect or
change the policy of the Government in
regard to the provision of labourers'
cottages. I do not suppose that the House
will expect that I will amplify to any
great extent the details which my right
hon. Friend gave in moving the Money
Resolution. But it must be, I think,
obvious to hon. Members that the
machinery which was devised in the year
1883 has become practically obsolete, or at
any rate antiquated and cumbrous to-day,
and it is necessary to bring the working
of the Labourers' Cottages Acts more
up to date.
The Bill, therefore, is an attempt to
readjust matters as between the Government and the local authorities and the
labourers, and it does not change any important principle beyond the fact that it
makes equitable distribution as between
the parties concerned, because of the
changes that have taken place in the
conditions in more recent years. And let
me say that if any Member is concerned
as to what advantage would accrue from
the Government policy in respect of this
matter, he has only to consult the reports
of the Local Government Board and their
successors, the present Ministry of Home
Affairs, to learn what a transformation
has been made in the country by the
operation of these Acts. Indeed, apart
altogether from this, those of us who go
through the country, as
many hon.
Members do, must have noticed the
change that has taken place in the comfort
and convenience of the labourers'
tages that are provided all over the
country by the operation of the Labourers'
Acts. The Government hope this will be
continued and that the facilities which
are given by this Bill will contribute to
the result we all have in view. I beg to
move.

Dogs Bill.
