Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving the
Second Reading of this Bill I would like
to say that the subject with which it
deals has given the Government very
serious concern, having regard to the representations that have been made by
farmers and other sheep breeders in reference to the destruction caused to their
flocks by dogs. Under the Dogs Act,
1906, an attempt was made to deal with
this very serious question. The Act provides for the making of Orders specifying
the hours during which dogs are allowed
to be at large, and I might point out
that in the Six Counties, Orders have
been made by various county councils
under which dogs are not allowed to be
out between sundown and sunrise unless
under control.
Hon. Members who are familiar with
this question will realise the defects in
this Act. First of all, the owner of the
dog which destroys sheep must identify the
dog, and here may I point out that it is
common knowledge that dogs with this pro-
Dogs Bill-
Second Reading
28 MARCH 1927
[Sir Dawson Bates]
pensity for killing sheep usually carry on
their operations 6 and 7 and even 10 miles
away from their own home. In the
second place, if the owner of the sheep
is able to bring an action, it frequently
happens that the owner of the dog is
not a mark for damages, and hon.
Members will also appreciate how difficult
it is for the police to enforce the law in
regard to dogs being at large at night.
As the law now stands, the owner of the
sheep is entitled to kill a dog for the purpose of saving the sheep's life, and it frequently happens that when the farmer
sues the owner of a sheep who has shot
his dog while pursuing the sheep, the
farmer is sued in his turn for having destroyed the dog. I have known a case
where the judge gave a verdict for the
owner of a sheep against the owner of a
dog, and in the same court the owner of
the dog got damages against the owner
of the sheep for the destruction of his
dog. Apart altogether from the loss the
farmer suffers from the actual destruction of his stock, he suffers very frequently
from the injury done to the sheep by
dogs chasing the sheep during the lambing
season.
I think it right to assure this House at
the outset that this Bill does not in any
way seek to encourage the indiscriminate
or wanton destruction of dogs, but what
it does seek to do is to provide a safeguard for the farmer whose stock has
been unlucky enough to be the subject of
attention from wandering dogs. Most
hon. Members are aware that it is a wellknown fact that once a dog has tasted
sheep's blood, it can never be cured of
the habit of killing sheep, and from that
time it becomes a nuisance to the whole
community.
With the assistance of the Farmers'
Union, whose help I much appreciate, I
have been able to obtain some authentic
information in regard to the losses incurred by farmers in the last year or two,
caused by the killing or chasing of sheep
by dogs. I do not propose to weary this
House by going into lengthy statistics,
but I would like to quote two cases to
show the hardship from which farmers
and other sheep owners are suffering at
the present time.
In the last two years, on one mountain,
a gentleman had six sheep and 42 lambst
killed by dogs. In 29th April, 1926, 15
lambs were killed in one night on another
mountain grazing in the vicinity. The
same gentleman had 15 lambs killed in
the same period, and in addition to the
sheep which were actually killed he had
a large number of lambs born dead,
which could only be accounted for by the
in-lamb ewes being chased over the rough
ground. This gentleman brought an
action against the owner of one of the
dogs, which he was able to identify and
which had killed 42 lambs, but the only
result was that he himself had to pay
costs amounting to £14 though he won
the case, as the owner of the dog was not
in a position to make payment of any
sort.
With regard to the effect of this Bill,
it is proposed that it should be a valid
defence to an action brought against a
sheep-owner in respect of the destruction
of the dog if the animal was actually
engaged in either chasing or worrying
sheep or cattle. But as a safeguard
against indiscriminate shooting of dogs by
individuals who think that dogs should
not be allowed to exist, or by farmers who
may bear malice towards their neighbours,
the individual who shoots a dog must,
within 48 hours, give notice to the police
that he has shot the dog, and this provision will, I think, safeguard the law
abiding dog.
Within the last few years, I am glad to
say, and I think the Minister of Agriculture will bear me out, there has been
a general increase in the number of sheep
raised in Ulster. Sheep raising, especially by the small farmer, has, I understand, become quite a profitable occupation, but owing to the ravages of dogs
many sheep owners have either given up,
or are contemplating giving up, this very
important industry.
It has been represented by certain
people that this is a cruel measure
towards dogs, but I would suggest to hon.
Members that nothing could be more
cruel to the unfortunate ewe with lamb
or cow in calf than their chasing by dogs
whose owners do not take the trouble to
look after them. I hope hon. Members
will agree that this is a right and proper
Bill, and one that is in the interests of
agriculture. I beg to move.

sheep and cattle, and this is particularly
so in the case of the average individual

cattle or sheep or horses.
The first clause of the Bill says

of a dog to prove that the dog

is "chasing." A man may have a

this Bill he can destroy the dog. That is
a very harsh thing from the dog owner's
point of view,
f
I agree with the hon. Member (Mr.

He will try to protect dumb animals.

a man should go from the city into the

know perfectly well-because they have

[Mr. Elliott]
At the present time a great many

Sir DAWSON BATES: With the
leave of the House, I should like very
briefly to deal with the points that have
been raised during this debate. With
regard to the question of including
poultry, I think it would be impracticable
to do so in this Bill. Most of the damage
that is done is done at night, and, as we
all know, poultry are in a very safe place
at night. Taking everything into consideration, and having consulted my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, I do not think, on the whole, it
is necessary to extend the scope of this
Bill to include poultry.
With regard to the question of poison,
that is another matter on which I would
not like to give an undertaking in connection with this Bill. I think the laying
down of poison is a very dangerous practice. I know that, when I discussed this
matter with the farmers, they told me
they did not like the idea of poison, and
they are driven to it as a last resort.
Most of the farmers are dog lovers. I
would remind my hon. Friend that poison
is laid down for other purposes than the
destruction of dogs; it is laid down in
connection with vermin.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I do not like to interrupt the right hon. Gentleman, but I
would like to point out that I was referring to the laying of poison on pasture
lands.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
whole question of the laying of poison,
whether on pasture land or any other
kind of land, can be taken separately.
However, I undertake to go into the
whole question of the laying of poison,
to see if it is necessary to bring in legislation in regard to the matter.
Regarding the remarks of my hon.
Friend, the Member for East Belfast,
(Mr. Beattie), I would like to assure him,
as I did when I was moving the Second
Reading of the Bill, that this is not a
vindictive Measure directed against dogs.
I do not believe that the farmers have the
feelings towards dogs that he seems to
think, and, from the practical point of
view, I think he will find that farmers
are not in the habit of wandering about
their fields with guns ready to shoot dogs.;
they are very much more busily occupied.
I do think that this Bill as it stands
should be read a Second time.

29 MARCH 1927

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 29th March, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
D
the
O
BREACHES OF THE LICENSING
ACTS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
the number of prosecutions against
licensed publicans in Northern Ireland
for breaches of the Licensing Acts during
year ending 31st December, 1926;
the number of convictions, and the number of endorsements of the licences.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The number of prosecutions in Northern Ireland against
licensed publicans during the year 1926
was 215; the number of convictions during the same period was 144, and the
number of endorsements on licences was
13.
INFANT MORTALITY IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
for the second year in succession the
death rate in Belfast has gone up, and,
further, is he aware that the infant mortality in Northern Ireland is greater than
in England or the Free State, and could
he state what steps his Department are
taking to reduce these alarming figures.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The death rate
in Belfast for the year 1926 was 15.2 per
thousand, as compared with 14 per thousand in 1925 and 14.3 per thousand in
1924. No general inference can be
drawn from the rate in any one particular
year as compared with another, but from
an examination of the figures for a series
of years, I may state that the death rate
in Belfast has shown a decided tendency
to decline.
I am aware that the infantile death
rate in Northern Ireland is higher than
in England or the Free State, but substantially lower than that of Scotland.
In this case also there is a marked tendency towards improvement.
Grants are made by my Department to
local authorities and voluntary agencies
to assist them in carrying on maternity
and child-welfare work. Perhaps I
might refer the hon. Member to the reports of the Local Government Department of the Ministry for the years ended
31st March, 1725, and 31st March, 1926,
in which a general account is given of the
activities of the Ministry in promoting
the health of the community.
Having regard to the important influence which a pure milk supply exerts
on the health of the community, and particularly that of children, the Ministry of
Home Affairs, in conjunction with the
various local authorities, have been endeavouring, by all means possible, to
ensure purity in milk.
I may also state that it is the intention
of the Government, at an early date, to
introduce legislation which it is hoped
will have the effect of improving the milk
supply in Northern Ireland.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman give an assurance that he will
issue circulars to the various local bodies
asking them to provide free milk to expectant mothers, and thereby do something to reduce this infantile mortality!
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid I
cannot give an undertaking now. After
all, this is only one of the elements in
connection with the question.
Mr. KYLE: It is a very important one.
GUARDIANSHIP OF INFANTS.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister whether he is aware that a Measure
providing for the recognition in law of
equal guardianship of infants has been.
passed by the Imperial Parliament, and
when he proposes to have this non-contentious Measure introduced in this
House.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government have
considered the desirability of fulfilling
their pledges of equal treatment with
England by the introduction of legislation
which would place mothers of Northern
Ireland on an equal footing with mothers
in England as regards custody and guardianship of their children.
The ATTORNEY GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): The Prime Minister has
asked me to take this question, and with
the permission of the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) and the hon.
Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr.
Elliott), who has a similar question, I
will reply to both questions together.
As regards the introduction of legislation on lines similar to the Imperial
Measure entitled Guardianship of Infants
Act, I would refer the hon. Members to
the statement made by the Leader of the
Senate on the 3rd November, 1926, in
reply to a question put by Senator Leslie.
The statement still expresses the Government's attitude in the matter.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman, the Attorney-General, tell us
what that statement was, and whether or
not the Government are prepared to
follow on parallel lines with Britain in
this non-contentious matter?
It was
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The
hon. Member will find the answer in
Hansard, col. 326, in the year 1926.
With regard to the second portion of the
hon. Member's question, I would point
out to him and the House that this is not
a question of following on parallel lines.
with Great Britain, because this Act
which is sought to be put into force in
Northern Ireland is entirely dependent
upon another Act which was brought in
in the Imperial House in 1925.
entitled the Separation and Maintenance
Act, 1925. Under that Act the magistrates in England have got summary
jurisdiction to make orders for separation
between husband and wife, and it was
consequent upon the passing of that Act
that this particular Act that is referred
to in the question was passed. The
Government have considered whether it
would be practicable or necessary to put
the former Act into force in Northern
Ireland, and have come to the conclusion
that it would not. Accordingly, the
putting into force of the Guardianship of
Infants Act has no basis under our law
as it stands at present.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell the House whether or not
the parents, both father and mother, of
children in Britain are recognized in law
as equal guardians? That is the position
we want recognized here. Do I gather
from his reply that it is not the intention
of the Government to recognize the father
and the mother as equal guardians of the
children?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: It is
impossible to deal with this question
exhaustively in answer to questions of this
description. I have nothing to add to
what I have already said.

Question of Rights and Privileges.
if
Mr. DEVLIN: On a point of order,
that is the proper method by which this
question is to be raised, I desire, as I am
informed by you that you are the final
Captain Dixon.
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattie
judge in these matters, to raise the question
of the position of this House in regard to
reserved services and matters germane to
them. I have been somewhat surprised
at the rulings which have been given by
the Chair as to the right of Members of
Rights and Privileges
Rights and Privileges
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
this House to discuss matters that are
eminently germane to the business of this
House. If I may say so with all respect
I regard you as the official custodian of
the interests of this Northern Parliament
and the jealous guardian of the privileges
of this Parliament, and therefore I would
take it that you would regard it as your
primary function to protect the Members
of this House in their discussion of all
those matters that affect their constituents
and the area
which this Parliament
controls and that you would by no means
narrow the powers of Members of this
House to discuss these questions.
Now, the questions are the Customs,
Excise, Land Purchase, the Post Office,
and Soldiers' and Sailors' Land Trust
administration.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The last is Imperial.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, they are all
Imperial in a sense.
Mr. POLLOCK: Oh, no.
Mr. DEVLIN: They are all Imperial
in a sense.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN: Well, we have been
ruled out of order repeatedly when raising
these questions, and I say that this would
cease to be a Parliament worthy of the
respect of any section of the intelligent
public if this Parliament was denied the
right to discuss those questions. The
first and most vital question is taxation,
and Customs and Excise are reserved
services. Therefore, if Customs and
Excise are reserved services according to
the rule of Mr. Speaker we are not
entitled to discuss the taxation of Ulster
because you cannot have it both ways.
You cannot permit us to discuss a question
of taxation because it is a reserved service
and refuse to allow us to discuss other
matters that affect the conduct and
government of Northern Ireland and tell
us that they are reserved services.
This question has to some extent been
raised by the controversy that arose yesterday over the mails question. My position,
and I think the position of many Members
of this House, is that we do not quite
understand where we are, or what our
rights and privileges are. Now, there is
no analogy whatever between this House
and other Parliaments in what is known
as the Commonwealth of Nations within
the British Empire, for every Parliament
in the British Empire is a free Parliament with complete and absolute control
over its whole domestic affairs and the
right of taxation in every form. Really
they are absolutely free Parliaments, and
the only binding link between Parliaments is the binding link of the Crown.
We are in an entirely different position.
Another Parliament imposes our taxation.
Another Parliament collects our taxes.
Another Parliament administers our Post
Office, our Land Purchase and such
services as the Soldiers' and Sailors'
Land Trust. These may be reserved
services, or called reserved services, but
they are services in which our people are
profoundly and deeply interested.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Hear,
hear.
Mr. DEVLIN: Therefore I say not for
any British Parliament nor any British
Speaker of a British Parliament but the
Speaker of our Parliament to endeavour
to narrow our rights and privileges in this
House is a matter which I think is
worthy of reconsideration, Mr. Speaker,
at your hands since you are the
final arbiter on this question. I would
therefore like if we could have a clear and
definite statement from the Chair; or
what I would prefer still further with the
leave of this House, that we ought to be

The Prime Minister stated-which I
think everybody who understands the
constitution of the British Empire
should have known-that the position
of this Parliament is by no
unique. There are quantities
similar examples all over the Empire
of Parliaments which are not Sovereign
Parliaments and which can only legislate
in regard to certain definite matters and
not with regard to all matters. I might
almost say that it is the foundation stone
of the British Empire-subordinate Parliaments with superior Parliaments controlling them.
Mr. DEVLIN: Not in their own
country.
Mr. SPEAKER: That is the position
here.
Mr. DEVLIN: This is not subordinate Parliament.
Mr. SPEAKER: This is a subordinate
Parliament within the United Kingdom,
just as the Parliament of Ontario is a subordinate Parliament within the Dominion
of Canada.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would just like to
ask you this one question, Mr. Speaker.
Has the British Parliament the right to
legislate for us on questions that are not
reserved ?
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes. The position
is that the British Parliament has a complete right legally to legislate over matters
with regard to which this Parliament also
has power, to legislate, but that, if I may
say so, is a constitutional fiction, because,
except, I take it, by agreement, such a
thing would probably never be done. The
same power exists, as far as I understand,
with regard to all the Dominions and
Colonies. In theory the Imperial Parliament is supreme and has power to legislate
over all matters in any of them. But in
practice the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin)
knows that our Constitution is not a
written one—it is, of course, a power
which is very seldom, if ever, exercised.
Mr. DEVLIN: You have stated, and
I agree with you, that it is a mere constitutional fiction that certain Parliaments
have a right to pass legislation over other
Parliaments. I want to call your attention to the fact that lately in the House of

how has he made it a fact with all his

Mr. SPEAKER: When I said it was
a fiction what I meant was that, certainly
in my view, it was a thing which would
be extremely unusual and would only, as a
rule, be done with the knowledge and
consent of the subordinate Parliament. I
think it would be very unusual.
Mr. DEVLIN: It was done. I think
it was an agricultural Bill.

I have given the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews)
some little notice of the question I intend
to raise to the end that he might be able
to give us a answer. I want to raise again
the question of a reciprocal arrangement
with the Free State so far as the payment
of Unemployment Insurance benefit is concerned. It seems to me that it is a first
principle of insurance that if a person
pays contributions he pays those contributions in order that he may receive
benefit for paying them if he needs it.
That is so widely and so well accepted that
it seems to me that I do not need to
develop the point further than merely to
state that it is a first principle of insurance
that a person pays premiums so that he
may, if need be, get benefits.
I want to point out that in certain
parts of the Six Counties people pay
premiums, both employers and workers,
and yet when the worker gets out of work
he is not entitled to draw Unemployment
Insurance benefit. That is in consequence
of the fact that the worker who works in
the Northern area may reside in the Free
State across the street, or vice versa, and
it is the fault, I think, of rather faulty
draughtsmanship both on the Free State
part and on our part in this particular
connection. I want to say that, in the
opinions of those of us who deal with
matters of insurance and who are trade
unionists, there is no difficulty in this that
cannot easily be overcome. It is purely
a question of administration, and to
strengthen my case in that respect I may
say that I noticed that Mr. McGilligan,
the Minister in the Free State who correth sponds to our Minister of Labour in
Northern Ireland, has stated that he has
submitted a scheme to the Northern
Ministry of Labour. That scheme has not
yet been made public so far as I know,
and I would plead with the Minister that,
if this statement is true and a scheme has
been submitted to his Department, he
should make that scheme public so that
those of us who are interested in this particular question may see whether or not
it is a practical thing to be brought into
pe operation as between the Free State and
ourselves in regard to this rather import-
Se ant matter.
This statement has been made by the

hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) himself,

Free State Ministry and his Department
and that nothing had been done. Ι
thought it was rather singular that
after twelve months from the first

we are two years from that date and still
nothing has been done to obviate an obvious injustice. I do not think there is
any Member of this House who really
wants to see people who have paid for

Unemployment Insurance being denied

they require it.
It is not sufficient for the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) to reply as he
has done on more than one occasion when
I have raised this question in other places;
it is not enough for the right hon. Gentleman to say that the Free State benefit
differs from ours.
We on this side are
quite aware of that. It is not enough for
the right hon. Gentleman to say that they
do not pay widows' pensions in the Free

Let us assume that 4d out of the contribution goes for pensions. Is it a physical
impossibility or is it an impracticable

Unemployment Insurance?
I am not now asking that the same

is a voluntary thing, but this Unemployment Insurance is compulsory both on
employer and employee. It is deducted

in it, and, therefore, I think it makes all
the stronger the argument in favour of

the Minister of Labour here not submit

believe these difficulties could easily be

itiated this discussion, and, in

We have not asked you to confer the

on someone who lives in the Free State,

the way of Health Insurance.
All that we have asked you to do is to
make a reciprocal arrangement, so that if
any person from Derry or Belleek has
occasion to go temporarily into the Free
State, he may by some means get credit
when he comes back to Northern Ireland
for the number of weeks during which he
was employed in the Free State. I know
what the argument will be. I will be

the Free State is smaller than that of
Northern Ireland. That is probably
true; I think it is true. Supposing that
a person only pays a ninepenny contribution when in the Free State, and that he
is employed there for three weeks, would
it, for example, be beyond the ingenuity
of the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Labour to arrange, when that
person came back, that he should get
credit for two stamps under the arrangement we have in Northern Ireland?
Probably the price of three stamps in the
Free State would be approximately the
price of two stamps in Northern Ireland.
Is the problem so difficult that the Parliamentary Secretary, for example, could
not disentangle it? Is it so complex that
it could not be dealt with? We are asked
to believe that it is terribly difficult.
I do not profess to have a profound
knowledge of the intricacies of finance, or
of the international exchange of trade, or
the bills that are necessary in order to
balance trade between one country and
another. Years ago, when I was interested in economics, I read a good deal
about those things, and I want to suggest

Colonel WOODS: I was very pleased
to hear from the Minister of Labour an
expression of policy regarding strangers
coming into this country to take the work
of Ulster people. I only wish that he anu
his colleagues had thought of this earlier.
I wish to draw the attention of the House
to the serious condition of the staple industry of Belfast and the Six Counties.
I do not know that we have a sufficient
representation of the linen industry in
this House. I think there are only three
Members directly connected with the
linen industry, but I know they are all
very deeply interested in it
There is one matter that has, I think.
escaped the attention of the Ministry of
Agriculture, but to lead up to what I
want to say I shall first of all point out
the position of the farmers who grow flax
in Northern Ireland. It has been the
practice for many years for farmers to
bring their flax in carts to the market
towns. They usually brought in the load
for the purpose of selling it and used the
money provided by the sale to buy their
ordinary supplies for the week or whatever length of time was necessary.
buyers who went from the linen houses in
Belfast and elsewhere to buy flax always
waited to the end of the market, and the
farmer who did not want to cart his
goods back again was willing to take the
price of £7 or £7 10s for something worth
a market price of £12 or £14.
The
A
There has been no organisation
amongst the farmers as far as I know,
and the result is that the flax industry
is going out of Ireland.
It is going
abroad, that is, the control of the raw
material is going out of the country into
the hands of people who might readily
prove to be enemies of the State.
supply comes in from Belgium, and from
Holland, and an increasing quantity
from Russia. The control of the Russian
flax, of course, is in the hands of the
Bolsheviks. I believe they have an
interest in the flax that comes from
Holland and Belgium. You can easily
understand what would be the position
in this country if the control of the raw
material for its staple industry went out
of it altogether.
I suggest to the Government that they
should make an arrangement with and
between the producers and the consumers
of flax such as they have extended to the
new industry of sugar beet. It is not
beyond the ability of the Government to
do this, and it would be of inestimable
value to the people of this country. We
all know the importance of the linen trade.
We know that, perhaps, it has not been
handled in the wisest way in the past, but
I think it is really up to the Government
now to see that the control of the raw
material be kept in this country. For
instance, since 1913 the supply of flax in
Northern Ireland has fallen by half and
there is a smaller acreage under cultivation of flax than there was ten years ago.

Farmers are getting no encouragement to

The merchants and the spinners will

Prices are soaring now, and what is to be
the result? Prices for the finished article
of linen in this country will get so high
that the linen trade will be destroyed.
That is the point of view I want to put
before the House, and I want to ask the
Government's earliest consideration of this
particular matter. I know the right hon.
Gentleman the Minister of Commerce
will look into the matter and give it his
best attention. I am sure he will earn
the gratitude of every man, woman, and
child in the country if he is able to control
the price of flax and thereby save the
trade of Ulster.

our social reform. Does that mean step
by step with Tory England, or step by
step with England? I am not a very
good poltitical prophet. If I were I
would not be occupying the modest position which I do in this House, but I
would venture to prophecy that there will
be a Socialist Government in power even
at the next General Election.
Will you
walk step by step with them? No answer
from the Ministerial Bench! I am very
anxious to know whether that is to be a
definite and enduring policy, or whether
your love for social reform is only shown
when the Tories in the English Parliament are passing these Measures. If it
is to be the enduring policy of the Government then I rejoice at it, because then you
would be getting real Measures of social
reform. We would not only have the
widows and orphans of insured persons
receiving pensions, but we would have
pensions for widows and orphans whether
the husbands were insured or not, which.
in my judgment, would be a far more
humane and far more defensible method
of dealing with this problem than the
somewhat half-hearted and half method
by which this problem is being solved today.
That is all I have to say except this
that I trust the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Andrews) will agree to the suggestion made by my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle),
that there should be a conference again
with the Minister in Southern Ireland.
If that scheme was like Mahomet's coffin
hanging between Heaven and earth I
would bring it down to earth and examine
it, and explore through it so that this
grievance would be redressed. That I
trust will be the commencement of what
will be more constant conferences between
Northern and Southern Ireland. I think
it is all to the good, apart altogether from
the question of partition or the union of
all Treland or any of those considerations,
that there should be, as far as possible, inter-communication between
Northern and Southern Ireland.

interests are very much alike.

nary taxes. I mean taxes.

I am thankful for the interruption putting me right,
but I really mean taxes. I do say that I
was amazed that the Minister of Finance
should put it forward as a financial proposition that the farming community that
produces the big half of the wealth of this
Province does not bear its fair share of
taxes. I want to say to the Minister of
Finance that the farmers are liable for
Income Tax, and any of them who are
liable have to pay. That is a principle that applies to all parts of the community. I do not know any other people
in the business or manufacturing world
who are running after the collector of
Income Tax offering him money for the
payment of which they are not liable.
There is the other side which I want to
put very seriously before the House.
When the farmer comes to sell his produce
he has got to sell it to a firm, and the
first four shillings of every pound profit
that firm makes has to go in Income
Tax. The firm buys the farmer's produce with that four shillings looking over
their shoulder every time. The same
thing applies to the man who sells his own
produce, so that, therefore, while the
farming community may not directly bear
a very big lot of the Income Tax, yet indirectly I say the farming industry does
bear its share of that taxation.
It is
impossible for an industry producing
wealth to escape the burden of heavy
taxation.
I believe, as I said in this House during
this Session before, that we have reached
the point when the first duty of any
Government is to reduce expenditure. I
do feel, and feel strongly, that the industries of this country cannot continue
to bear the expenditure they are asked
to bear at the present time. I had the
privilege lately of listening to an address
by Dean Inge, who, I believe, is a very
famous student of history. He was dealing with the causes that led to the decline
of the Roman Empire, and he gave it as
his opinion that the two main causes of
the decline of that great Empire were
exceptionally high taxation and a low
birth rate. I do not know so much about
how our birth rate stands, but I think the
facts stand out that
we are the most
heavily taxed country probably in the
world at the present time. I do not know
that I agree with the very reverend gentleman's diagnosis of the causes, but I certainly think his opinion is worthy of respect, because he is a great authority on
history and a great student of history. I
would probably put the causes in another
place, but at any rate I do feel that the
first duty of the Government at the present time is by some means to reduce the
burden of taxation on industry. I believe that the greatest fillip that could
be given to industry would be given by a
reduction of taxation.
The Government have appointed, and
I am very glad that they have done so,
a Committee to inquire into the difference
between what the producer gets and what
the consumer pays. In this respect, under
our present system I think the greatest
safeguard of the consumer is that we have
competition. Competition is really what
keeps down profiteering. It does look on
the face of it as if there was profiteering
going on. I know in some cases the difference between what the farmer gets for
his produce and what the consumer pays
in the city of Belfast seems to be very
hard to account for, but I do feel that it
is very largely due to overhead charges.
If you take the retailers of farm produce
in the city of Belfast there is not a street
where there is not keen competition in
the retail of these articles. I say that
under the present system the only security
-at least the best security-the consumers can have is keen competition.
I am glad also that the Governinent

grapple with this question in a very

Horticultural Produce (Sales on
Commission) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): Last year the Imperial
Government introduced a Horticultural
(Sales on Commission) Bill which was
strongly supported by the National Farmers' Union and by the National Federation of Fruit and Potato Trades Associations, representing growers and wholesale
traders respectively. This Bill became
law in December, 1926.
The Bill now before this House, which
applies to all kinds of horticultural produce, that is, vegetables, fruit, flowers
and plants, is identical in wording with
the British Act and will, I feel sure,
commend itself to hon. Members equally
in the interests of producers and wholesale
traders, while it should also prove of considerable assistance to the Ministry,
especially in connection with the grading
and packing of apples and other fruit.
I would like to mention that the Ministry has experienced very great difficulty
in getting apples properly graded and
packed in Northern Ireland. The following is an example of what actually takes
place. One grower of apples calls in the
county horticultural instructor to give
him advice as to the grading of his apples.
The horticultural instructor tells him the
kind of boxes to be used for packing;
gives him the names of firms from whom
these boxes can be procured; calls on him
when he has got the boxes, and helps him
to grade and pack the apples. The
apples are then dispatched to Belfast to
a commission agent. That grower has
two neighbours who also send consignments of apples to the same agent on the
same day. They do not grade their
apples, the apples are simply mixedlarge and small, rough and smooth-and
put into barrels without being graded
and packed in the manner recommended
by the Ministry. All three consignments
arrive in Belfast on a certain market-day,
when the agent will probably have fifty
other consignments of apples from North
of Ireland growers. Even if the apples
of the first grower are sold at a higher
price than the ungraded fruit of the other
two, he very often secures no benefit, as
the commission agent may average all the
sales on that particular day, and the first
grower may get exactly the same price.
for his graded and carefully packed
apples as his two neighbours get for their
ungraded, badly packed apples.
The result is that the first grower tells
the horticultural instructor that there is
no advantage to be gained by grading and
packing fruit in the manner recommended
by the Ministry, and that, therefore, he
will not in future take any further pains
or trouble. Much dissatisfaction exists
amongst fruit growers in Northern Ireland who market their fruit in Belfast,
because the commission salesmen, when
making returns to the grower for the
fruit sold, do not give particulars stating
the actual price realized for the fruit, or
details of the amount deducted for carriage, commission and porterage.
understand that in the Dublin market the
fruit is sold by auction and the auctioneers return to the growers complete

statements giving the particulars mentioned above, and because of the methods
adopted by the salesmen in Belfast a
large proportion of the better quality
fruit produced in Northern Ireland is
sent to Dublin
The need for giving full particulars to
growers was emphasized at a meeting of
the members of the wholesale trade and
the horticultural instructors, which was
held at the time of the fruit show in
Belfast, in November, 1925, but apparently no change has been made in the
meantime.
The matter again cropped up at a
meeting held in Portadown on the 25th
August, 1926, at which fruit growers and
members of the wholesale and retail trade
associations were present. At that meeting the Chairman of the County Armagh
Agricultural Committee, proposed a resolution asking the Government of Northern Ireland to bring in a Bill similar to
that which, at that date, had just been
passed by the House of Lords in England,
and this resolution was passed unanimously.
There is no doubt whatever that this
Bill will be welcomed by fruit growers;
will remove existing causes of dissatisfaction, and will prove of considerable benefit
to the fruit growing industry.
This Bill provides, under penalties,
that the salesman must keep, in respect
of horticultural produce consigned to him
for sale on commission, certain records
such as names of consignors of the produce
and of every purchaser, and the price
paid, and must furnish the consignor with
an account showing (1) the actual price.
paid for the produce, (2) the salesman's
commission and details of any charges
made for services in connection with the
sale, and (3) details of the amounts, if any,
paid by the salesman on behalf of the
consignor in connection with the sale.
Particulars of this nature are at present
being given by live stock auctioneers in
Belfast in connection with sales of cattle,
sheep and pigs.
The Bill, however, further provides
that the Act shall not apply unless the
consignor sends to the salesman, before
the sale, an advice note specifying the
nature and description of the packages
consigned and the contents of each package.
Power is also to be given to a consignor,
within ten days after delivery of the
account which I have mentioned, to have
the salesman's books, so far as they relate
to this consignor's produce, inspected by
an accountant possessing qualifications
prescribed by the Ministry of Agriculture.
Any horticultural produce consigned
for sale is to be regarded as having been
consigned for sale on commission, unless
at or before the sale, the consignor gives
the salesman a direction in writing to the
contrary, or the consignor and salesman
have entered into an agreement in writing
to the contrary. Any such agreement
may relate to a particular consignment,
or generally to all consignments forwarded by the consignor who signs the
agreement.
We propose that this Bill should take
effect from 2nd May, 1927, so as to be
in time for the fruit sales in County
Armagh and elsewhere.
I beg to move.

Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman the Prime Minister tell us the
business for to-morrow and next week?
The PRIME MINISTER: To-morrow
there is a Motion on the Paper by the hon.
Member for County Down (Mr. Patrick
O'Neill), and I presume that that will
take the whole day. It is not proposed
to take any business except that tomorrow. On Thursday the Sitting will
be purely formal in order to receive the
Assent to the Bills that have been passed
before the end of the financial year. On
Tuesday next there will be the Committee
stage of the Horticultural Produce Bill,
and then we hope to begin the Estimates.

FITTINGS OF KING LINE SHIPS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if the internal fittings of the nine ships for King
Line, now being built in Harland &
Wolff's Belfast Yard, are being manufactured across the water, and if he will
state why this work is not done in their
Belfast workshops.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
question.
The information in my possession is
to the effect that the main engines,
machinery and all equipment which can
be produced in Northern Ireland are, in
fact, being produced here. I may say,
however, that the guarantee given by the
Government does not cover the full cost
of the ships, and my Department does
not, as a general rule, regard itself as in
a position to question any action of the
shipbuilders in regard to that part of the
expenditure which must necessarily be
incurred across the water, and the cost of
which is not defrayed out of the Guaranteed Loan Account.
I am informed that in this case a
certain sub-contract has been placed with
a firm across the water with the object
of gaining experience of a type of work
which has not so far been carried out at
the Belfast shipyard. As, however, the
work in question is being carried out by
Belfast labour under this sub-contract,
the question of employment in this area is
not affected.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to ask the
Minister is he aware that all the plumbing work and all the blacksmith work for
these nine ships under the King Line is
being carried out across the water; and
is it a fact that the 600 rail stanchions
that are being manufactured by Messrs.
Dickie, of Ayr, are being manufactured
under unfair conditions.
have no
Mr. POLLOCK: I, of course,
knowledge whether these sub-contracts to
which my hon. Friend refers are not
being carried out under fair conditions.
I am sure the hon. Member will realize
it is not likely to come within my province to know anything of the conditions
with regard to sub-contracts.
But even
in regard to the other matters of plumbing and such like, to which he refers, I
have orly to repeat what I said in reply
to the question, that is to say, we only
guarantee the shipowners in respect of
a certain percentage of the cost of the
ship. We are under no obligation,
and certainly have no right, to interfere
with the shipbuilders with regard to the
method of carrying out the contract.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that the 600 rail stanchions, blacksmiths' work that I spoke of, are part
and parcel of the hull of the ship, and as
the Loans Guarantee is to cover the hull
of the ship, it is bound to cover the
stanchions referred to by me, which are
being made at Dickie's, of Ayr?
Mr. POLLOCK: The guarantee does
not cover the hull of the ship. It does
not enter into any particulars of any
part of the ship that has any connection
at all with the financial aspect of the
matter. As to whether provisions of the
stanchions to which my hon. Friend
refers falls within the amount that was
guaranteed I cannot possibly ascertain.
It is impossible to make any division or
separation in regard to what we have
guaranteed or not guaranteed. I would
suggest to my hon. Friend that the less
discussion--or the less information I offer
in the matter will be to the advantage of
our negotiations with regard to this
question.

NORTHERN IRELAND HARBOURS.
2. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can give any
information regarding the report on
Northern Ireland Harbours by the expert
brought over from Scotland by the
Government at the end of February.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE :
(Mr. Barbour): The Harbours of Ardglass, Killough, and Ballycastle were inspected on 23rd and 24th February by
Mr. Gordon Nicol, Engineer to the Aberdeen Harbour Authority and Consultant
to the Fishery Board of Scotland. Mr.
Nicol was supplied with data relating to
each of these harbours and undertook to
furnish in the first instance a preliminary
report on the possibilities of each, based
upon these data and upon his personal
observations. This Report has not yet
been received.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon.
Gentleman say when we may expect it?
Mr. BARBOUR: We wrote to Mr.
Nicol expressing a desire to get the
Report at the earliet possible moment.
He is quite aware of our desire to get it
as soon as possible.
BOY CLERKS IN CIVIL SERVICE.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the number of boy clerks admitted to the Civil
Service of Northern Ireland during the
financial year 1926-27; what percentage
of marks is necessary to pass the entrance examination successfully; whether
additional qualifications are required,
and, if so, of what do they consist; and
whether any case has occurred wherein
the formality of a writen examination
has been waived.
Mr. POLLOCK: There is no class in
the Civil Service known as "boy clerk."
If, however, the hon. and gallant Member refers to members of the clerical class
recruited by competition in the financial
year 1926-27, open to youths between the
ages of 17 and 19, the answer to the first
part of his question is 19; to the second
and third parts, that candidates who
obtained 60 per cent. of the maximum
possible aggregate marks in the written
examination were required to appear before a Selection Board which chose a sufficient number to fill the existing vacancies, and that candidates so chosen by the
şelection board were required to furnish
to the Civil Service Commissioners satisfactory evidence of nationality, age,
health and character; and to the fourth
part, that no persons were admitted to
the clerical class in the year 1926-27
without a written examination except ex-
Service temporary clerks who were
accorded established status.

reply of the right hon. Gentleman, might

SUGGESTED STATE BANK.
.
4. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether his attention has been
directed to the address delivered, on the
26th January, 1927, at the Portrush Urban Council meeting, by Mr. J. C. Lyle,
C.V.O., who said that the natural drains
of the country, the rivers and the streams,
were choked and obstructed, artificial
drainage neglected, factories closed and
all sources of true wealth neglected and
ignored, the reason given being the lack
of cheap credit, while there was an appar
ently inexhaustible store of credit in the
bank reserves for any useless project
which could be manipulated so as to make
a money profit for the promoters; and
whether, in view of the way trade and
industry are handicapped by the banks,
he is prepared to take steps to establish a
State Bank.
Mr. POLLOCK: I regret to say that
my attention has not been called to the
address referred to by the hon. Member,
and I am, therefore, not in a position to
express a considered opinion on the conclusions reached by Mr. J. C. Lyle. If
the hon. Member will be good enough to
place me in possession of a copy of the address I will be pleased to give it my careful consideration.
I
add that, in so far as my
may
Ministry has had occasion to approach
the banks with a view to assisting trade
and agriculture in the matter of
guaranteed loans, we have found that
they are quite ready to grant reasonable
credit facilities.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether he is aware that
the statements made by Mr. Lyle are incorporated in this question, and therefore he cannot plead ignorance or lack of
knowledge of what was really in the mind
of Mr. Lyle?
JAMES FISHER, BELFAST-—
SENTENCE ON.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he refused to
give an interview to James Fisher, of
11 Blackwood Street, Belfast, who was
recently sentenced to three years' penal
servitude, and on, as alleged, a forged
affidavit, in connection with the will of
the late John Fisher, of Ballynagarrick,
Co. Down; whether Henry Corley, the
late District Probate Registrar, made the
probate of John Fisher's will, and sealed
both will and probate with the seal of
the High Court of Justice (King's Bench
Division) in the District Probate Registry, Belfast, on the thirteenth day of
January, 1902, Susanna Fisher, widow
of the deceased, the executrix, being
illiterate.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): James Fisher, of
11 Blackwood Street, Belfast, was sentenced to three years' penal servitude in
January, 1923, on conviction of throwing
a corrosive fluid on two persons one of
whom was a child of about seven years of
age.
The conviction was obtained on
the clearest evidence of the injured parties
and other witnesses.
Numerous petitions on behalf of Fisher
from himself and his relatives were received, and the case was carefully reconsidered on several occasions, but I could
find no mitigating circumstances which
would justify me in recommending any
interference with the ordinary course of
the law.
In August, 1926, I received a request
from Fisher for a personal interview regarding his conviction. His letter contained accusations of perjury against witnesses at his trial, of malpractice against
his own solicitor, and of forgery and fraud
against other persons, and it was obvious
that an interview to discuss charges of
this nature could serve no useful
purpose.
As regards the second part of the
question, the matter referred to is outside the province of the Government of
Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Minister be
prepared to receive this man mentioned
in the question without prejudice?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, Sir.

BELFAST CORPORATION
CONTRACT.
8. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether it
is a fact that his Department refused
to give an undertaking to render immune
from surcharge the members of the Improvement Committee of the Belfast Corporation when, on November 16th, they
decided to place an order with the proprietors of Lislea Quarries for 3,000 tons
of setts, because the price charged was
in excess of a tender submitted by a
Welsh firm; whether, as a result of his
Department's action, the Welsh firm not
only got an order for the 13,000 tons
originally allocated to them, but also the
3,000 tons intended for the Lislea firm;
whether this is consistent with his Department's attitude as disclosed by the
Public Accounts Committee's Report
which shows that out of an order for
21,000 yards of cloth, 13,000 yards was
placed with a firm who tendered at
8s. 11d. per yard, whilst an order for
only 15,000 yards was placed with a firm
which tendered at 8s. per yard; whether
he is aware that an order for 16,000 tons
of setts would keep all the quarries in
Northern Ireland busy for a period of two
years; and whether it would not have
been more advantageous to have had this
order placed in Northern Ireland than
be paying unemployment benefit to settmakers and quarrymen; and whether he
will state if the "attrition" test given
by the Belfast Corporation is justified in
view of the absence of attrition when the
setts are placed in the streets; and
whether it is the case that one of the
principal streets in Belfast has been
paved with Newry setts and has proved
satisfactory for many years, although
Newry setts have now been refused for the
reasons mentioned.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In view of the
obvious misunderstandings which have
arisen in connection with this matter, I
welcome the opportunity afforded by the
hon. Member's question of publicly
stating the true facts in connection with
this particular contract.

poration applied to the Ministry for

works. A public inquiry was held into
the application by the Ministry's Engi

neering Inspector on the 4th August last,
and following his Report the Ministry on
the 25th idem approved of the necessary
borrowing and of the works involved, but
in expressing its approval the Minstry,
in accordance with its general policy,
pressed the Corporation to purchase

been indicated during the course of the

setts are as good as the best Welsh setts
and are substantially cheaper.
Following the receipt of this letter the
Corporation invited tenders for the purchase of 16,000 tons of granite setts, as
a result of which it was found that the
Welsh firms tendered at 54s per ton,
while the Northern Ireland firms
tendered at 60s 6d per ton.
In spite of this difference in price the
Corporation proposed to divide up the
contract and to purchase 13,000 tons of
the Welsh setts at 54s per ton, and 3,000
of the Northern Ireland setts at 60s 6d
per ton.
After carefully considering the matter
the Ministry wrote on the 16th December
last to the Corporation approving of the
arrangements proposed to be made in the
above respect. Apparently the Corporation felt some doubt as to the effect of
the Ministry's approval, and wrote specifically to the Ministry on the 28th of that
month inquiring if the Ministry's letter
constituted approval to the Corporation
purchasing 3,000 tons of Northern Ireland setts at 6s 6d per ton over the price
quoted for Welsh setts.
In response to that letter, and with
the object of encouraging local industry,
the Ministry replied on the 30th December
specifically intimating to the Corporation
that the Ministry approved of the Corporation's proposals, and a letter was received on the following day from the
Town Clerk acknowledging the receipt
of the Ministry's letter, and intimating
that it placed the position beyond all
doubt.
The Ministry's letter was considered
at a meeting of the Improvement Committee of the Belfast Corporation on the
11th January, 1927, and apparently
some doubts were expressed as to whether
the approval of the Ministry would protect the Corporation from legal action if
any ratepayer chose to test in the Courts
the propriety or validity of the purchase
of local setts at the higher price.
The attention of the Committee was
drawn at the time to the fact that in a
recent case in Great Britain somewhat
similar action taken by the Ministry of
Health had been successfully challenged
in the High Court.
Following this decision the Corporation
decided to ask if the Ministry could indemnify the Corporation against any
legal proceedings and the effects thereof
which might take place if the tender were
accepted.
The Ministry has no power or authority to give such indemnification. As
will be understood from what I have
explained above, the Ministry had gone
to the fullest lengths possible within its
jurisdiction to encourage the placing of
the contract in Northern Ireland and to
satisfy the Corporation as to its position.
in the matter, but the Ministry has no
power to give any binding undertaking
in advance as to what course the Local
Government Auditor may find himself
called upon to adopt.
It has been definitely laid down by the
Courts on several occasions that the Local
Government Auditor is an independent
officer, and it would be illegal and improper for the Ministry of Home Affairs
to attempt by any undertaking to fetter
his statutory discretion or to issue to him
any instructions as to what action he
should take with regard to any items of
expenditure by a local government
authority.
It will be apparent to the hon. Member
from the above statement that the
Ministry adopted every course within its
power to encourage the purchase of local
supplies in this particular instance.

the operation of the 1923 Act, and if
possible to elicit from the Government a
statement of their policy regarding these
schools, particularly so in view of their
experience of the working of this Act up
to date. Prior to the passing of this Act
all schools in Northern Ireland had a
grant for the building and general maintenance from the old National Board,
which was equivalent to two-thirds of the
total cost. Under this Act no such
grants are available unless on conditions,
and the conditions are such that they are
not acceptable to the schools under
Catholic management.
It is hardly necessary for me to point
out to the Government that schools so fixed
find it most difficult to carry out the
duties entrusted to them, and I should
like to point out that, so far as appointments to these committees are concerned,
under no circumstances will the Catholic
people allow their schools to be managed
by any other than the clergy of their
Church. I think it is well to make that
statement clearly here to-day so that
there should not be any misunderstanding about it. Statements to the contrary
have been made, but they are quite contrary to the facts and are not supported
by any authority. Not alone are the
Catholic schools so fixed, but also, I
understand, quite a large number, if indeed, not a larger number, of the Protestant schools are placed in a similar way. I
have not, of course, any right and do not
speak for them, but I should like to
draw the attention of the House to the
way in which this Act has been received
by the schools managed under all denominations.
This Act was conceived in the very first
year of the first Session of this Parliament. Then a Committee was set up to
inquire into the educational services in
Northern Ireland. The hon. Member
for West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn), who
I am sorry is not in his place to-day, was
appointed as its Chairman, and, I suppose,
because of that fact it has since been
known as the Lynn Committee. That
Committee sat for nearly two years, and
on its findings the Bill of 1923 was based.
In its various stages through this House
the then Minister of Education, Lord
Londonderry, stated that where it differed
if at all with the recommendations of
the Lynn Committee was not in principle
but only in detail.
That Bill in its course through the
House had not the benefit of the opinion
of any Catholic Member because there
were none then in the House, but the
Catholic people feel indebted to at least
one hon. Member, that is the Member
for the University (Dr. Morrison), whom
I am glad to see in the House to-day.
During its course he had the courage to
state their view, though I understand
that in doing so he had not the support
of the rest of the House. This Act was
passed in 1923, and had to be amended
the following year in order to satisfy the
claims of the Protestant Churches with
regard to the teaching of religion in the
schools.
The Act came into full force and effect
in September, 1924, and in order to see
how it has been received we have got to
look at some of the figures relating to
what has occurred since. Up to the end
of the last financial year--31st March,
1926-only six of the 2,006 schools in
this area had been transferred to the education authorities, and even up to the
end of last year-that is, to the end of
December, 1926-only 90 schools had
been transferred to the local authorities
and 80 had appointed four-and-two com
mittees. That was exactly 4 per cent.

As I stated before, the Act was based
the recommendations of this Committee. The Minister of Education at
various stages during the course of the

had departed as little as was possible
from the recommendations of this Committee. Therefore, I think the opportunity exists in this for the Government.
without in any way compromising or

Mr. McALLISTER: This Motion has

On the last ocasion, with regard to the

To my

You hold the views you do on divergent

understand how you can hold those views,
but if you hold those views conscientiously
have we any right, if we had the power,
to treat you unjustly with regard to those
views, to ask you to violate your conscience because you hold those views?
That is a perfectly indefensible position.
A man is the custodian of his own conscience, and no one can legislate for him
in violation of that conscience.
There is also another aspect, the financial question, and the question of justice.

The Act of 1923 was promoted on account
mainly of three factors. It was found, in
fact, that the taxation revenue of this
province would not be sufficient to effect
the extensions in educational facilities
which the increasing view of the community in educational ideals demanded, and
that being so it was necessary that the cost
of such extensions should be put upon the
rates.

Whatever it is it had to
be put on the rates. Another factor was
that there was, if not universal at any rate
very widespread, dissatisfaction with the
system of management of schools by school
managers, and the only remedy that was
suggested for that was that the management of schools should not be, as in the
past, in the hands of single managers,
but that there should be handed over to
local authorities or some form of local
control the management of schools generally. There was possibly a third idea
behind all this legislation and that was an
increase in public interest in educational
matters. Prior to the Act of 1923 and
prior to the establishment of this Government the whole of the elementary education administration was centralised in a
Board in Dublin. It was very remote
from the people. The administration and
the provision of education was carried out
remote from the people and they did not
in fact feel the interest that it was hoped
they would feel when it was brought more
closely to them.
The Act of 1923 aimed at meeting all
these objections to the existing constitution. In one respect at any rate the Act
succeeded. One has only to read
in the newspapers of Northern Ireland the accounts of the proceedings
of the local education authorities
to see that a very real interest has been
aroused over the Six Counties in the sort
o of education that is given and the way in
which that education is served and given
to the children of the people.
The Act created local education authorities and it devolved upon them the provision and management of schools, but it
did not exert any compulsion upon the
manager or owner of the school to transfer his school to the local authority. Now
that was probably done for two reasons.
In the first place it was recognised that if
all the schools were at once transferred to
these new bodies without experience they
would probably be so terribly overburdened that they would make a great
many mistakes. In the second place it
was recognised that there would be many
persons who would be unwilling to transfer their schools because they were distrustful of the capacity and the power of
these newly-formed bodies of inexperienced men
to administer their schools.
Accordingly the Act did provide that the
managers and owners of schools should be
allowed, if they so wished, to continue to
manage the schools themselves.
Turning from that to the finances of the
Act, the State had hitherto borne all the
cost of teachers' salaries. The State still
continues to pay all the cost of teachers'
salaries, but with regard to grants that
were made to owners these grants were in
three classes. Prior to the passing of the
1923 Act schools got from the Government a grant towards their lighting, heating and cleaning. It was intended that
that grant should be equal to a half of the
actual cost, but under the Regulations as
they were framed and administered-that
is the old state of affairs prior to the
passing of the 1923 Act-prior to that the
grant in fact did not amount to more than
on the average a quarter of the actual cost
for lighting, heating and cleaning.
That arose in this way. The Treasury
in England had allowed a sum of £20,000
for this purpose. That sum was fixed
prior to the war. The costs of materials
for lighting, heating and cleaning rose
during the war, but the £20,000 did not
rise during the war, and had to be spread
over all the schools making this demand,
and as a result not one-half, but only
one-fourth of the cost was paid. That
was the state of affairs before the 1923
Act.
So far as lighting, heating and cleaning are concerned, under the 1923 Act
every voluntary school is entitled as a
right to get from the local education
authority one full half of the cost for

lighting, heating and cleaning, so, as far

The second class of grant is the grant
towards maintenance, that is, towards the
repair and replacement of equipment
such as, in the words of Section 15 of our
Act, should ordinarily be met from year to
year out of the ordinary income of the
school. Prior to the 1923 Act voluntary
schools, of which the hon. Member spoke,
received no such grant at all. They did
not get it. Under the 1923 Act they can
get it, but subject to a condition, and as
it is a condition which applies also to the
maintenance grant I will deal with that
condition in both cases subsequently.
The third class of grant is ordinarily
called the building grant, that is, a grant
for extensions or new wings of schools.
The hon. Member who moved this Motion
spoke as if, as a matter of fact and as a
matter of course, those who wished to
build a new school received from the
Treasury in England two-thirds of the
estimated cost of the new school or the
extension. That is not so. It is quite
true that the Treasury in England made
grants for building purposes-I call them
building purposes generally. But those
grants were always very grudgingly
made. For some years after 1900 no
grants at all in fact were made.
Treasury always protested against the
principle of making them, and for some
years they stopped them altogether.

But later on pressure from Irelandled, I may say, by my right hon. Friend,
the Prime Minister-was brought to
bear upon the Treasury, and the Treasury
was induced to agree that for a period of
six years they would continue to make
grants which were limited in amount and
which, in fact, were restricted to what
were called fairly urgent cases. That
was the situation at the outbreak of the
war, that the Treasury in England had
for a period of six years agreed to make
a limited grant for these building purposes. When the war broke out, all
building grants of all sorts stopped.
Accordingly when this Government was
set
up the situation was that the

restricted grants, as the House will see,

the
The foundation of the 1923 Act is that
grants in similar cases, grants for building and grants for extensions to schools,
shall be made in the future out of the
rates of the local education authorities
which are set up under that Act, of such
proportion as the Ministry shall approve
of the proposed expenditure of such building. It is the policy of the Ministry
to approve of the proportion of two-thirds
of the total cost as was the rule, so far
as it was a rule, under the old system
of the Commissioners of National Education. The policy of the Act was this,
that these grants come out of the rates,
and as the grants for maintenance which
are available come out of the rates the
local authorities which supply those
grants shall be given some modicum of
control in the management of the schools.
That is to say, that the person who
provides the money shall have some say
in the way in which it is spent.
It is a maxim that there shall not be
taxation without representation, and the
neglect of that maxim was the origin
of one of the tragic incidents in English
history. The way that maxim has
been applied in the 1923 Act is this, that
where any voluntary school asks from
the local education authority a grant for
maintenance or building, and where that
grant is approved generally, in exchange
for the grant the school shall give some
Measure of control to the local authority
in the management of the school.
That Measure is definitely laid down in
regard to maintenance. It is not so definitely laid down with regard to building, but the principle will probably work
out in practice as it has hitherto been
carried out.
In both cases there is a Management
Committee of four and two. That Committee consists of four representatives of
the school or the managers of the school,
and two representatives of the local
authority. I have never been able to see

that is the position, I do not see any difficulty in their paying for it. But if they
wish to preserve the continuity of educational policy which has been pursued in
particular schools up to that date, I
cannot see that they have any grievance
when the body that is to be set up to
continue that management is to be a body
on which they are to have a two to one
majority of the nominees.
Those are the principles upon which
the Act is framed. I can see no injustice
in any part of that Act. It is a most
democratic Measure. It merely enforces
the principle that those who contribute
by making these grants should be given.
some measure of control. But we are
asked now to go back on all that, and to
scrap it. Even if a better case were made
out than has been made out, what is to
be said of all the schools that have been
transferred, of all the schools that have
been handed over to four and two committees? Are we to go back now and tell
them that a different situation has arisen,
that they have lost their time, that the
transfer was all a mistake, and that they
could have had far better terms if they
had not transferred? On the ground not
only of expediency in that regard, but on
the ground of general principle-the
principle of the Act that where local
contributions are asked some measure of
local control should be given, the Government must resist this Motion.
As the hon. Members who have moved
and seconded the Motion have referred to
the fact that this question in fact was
raised at the time that the Bill was being
debated in this House, I may point out
that so solid was the opinion of the House
on that occasion that a division was not
even challenged on it, and there has been
no evidence whatever that the opinion of
the majority of the people of Northern
Ireland has changed since the Act of 1923
was passed, or that there is any solid
ground on which the Government can now
reverse the policy then adopted.

One of the purposes of this Act was to

infinitesimal section of schools has been

of schools actually transferred to local

educational authorities. That is about
eight per cent. The hon. Gentleman
thought he made a good point when he

tiations for transfer to the local authorities were proceeding in December, 1926.
We have no reason to believe that the

ing indictment of the Act from that point

I want to say a word, before I proceed
to deal with one or two other matters in

managers are perfectly justified in trying
to retain control over these schools. One
would imagine that managers of schools,
whether Catholic or Protestant, are merely
creatures to be used in times of emergency,

forget that when laymen took very little
interest in education-whether they
took an interest or not they took very

spiritual and religious interests. to
the fundamental necessity of having
sound, efficient education, not only
religious but secular education, for the

in individual managers and you will

of individual managers the great body of
managers of schools of all denominations
have discharged their duties efficiently in

And, therefore, I think they are

created and what they have built. And
I feel that at the present time it is a

one safeguard of the religious interests of
their community is to see that the children of their denomination are brought up
in their faith, and, therefore, they desire

Now the hon. Gentleman says—and it

unless we consent to transfer the schools
to the local authority we are denied that
grant.

Grants to Schools

HOUSE OF COMMONS

badly paid. It was for the purpose of

work they were doing, because they were

You need not be afraid of introducing

The PRIME MINISTER: I had not
intended to intervene in this debate, and
the necessity for doing so is very small
after the admirable exposition that my
hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry, has just made to
the House. I think everybody will admit
that he explained the difficulties and was
able to justify the smooth working of the
Education Act. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Now let me say that the whole time I
represented an Ulster constituency in the
Imperial Parliament the demand from the
Ulster people was for a democratic education system in our area. Year after
year the same demand came from the
people here that they wanted to have an
Education Act which was more in our own
hands than in the old days. Very shortly
after we had the power to do so the Londonderry Act was passed by practically the
unanimous approval of every Member of
this House. I am here to say that so far
as we, the Government, can judge the
Act is proving a great success. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
The hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) quotes a certain number of
schools as having been transferred, and
the inference he draws from the smallness
of that number is that the Act is not
proving the success which we hoped it
might be. He also went on to say that
the Act has now been in operation for
three years, and that this is the only result that had been attained. But he
utterly ignores the facts, first of all, that
the Regional Committees' powers have
been only transferred to them-I think
we call it the appointed day—at the outside for two years, and, in some instances,
for a very much shorter time. The
truth of the matter is that it takes a considerable time for the Regional Committees to get to work and to prepare
their schemes, and we are not at all disappointed at the results attained so far.
My hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Robb)
informs me that negotiations are proceeding daily for the transfer of new schools
of other schools rather to the Regional
Committees' authority, and, therefore,
far from any charge being made against
the Act, I think everybody is satisfied
that it is proceeding along a normal
course, and that, eventually, practically
all the schools that desire to come under
the scheme will be transferred to the
Regional Committees.
Now, I want just to touch upon the
reiterated charge that a differentiation
has been made between Protestants and
Roman Catholics in this Londonderry
Act. Nothing could be further from the
case. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There is no discrimination, and I would
point out that had even an indirect at-

tempt been made to discriminate between

whether the Acts that we pass here come
within the ambit of our powers. I hope
hon. Members on all sides of the House
realize that a scrutiny takes place of all

Therefore, when this Act was sent
forward in the ordinary way, before receiving the Governor's Assent, it had to
pass those eagle scrutinies, and we may
rest assured that there is no truth whatever in the charge made by the hon.
Member for West Belfast. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Another point the hon. Member (Mr.
Devlin) tries to make is that because prior
to
1923 the Government-the then
Government of the day-made grants to
schools of the nature that has been mentioned by the mover of this Motion,
therefore, we ought to do the same thing.
That would be absolutely to scrap the
whole Act. It would be a retrograde
move. It would be taking away from
the local authorities the power to control
their own schools, and would be going
back once more to the old state of affairs
when the grumble was that the central
authority mismanaged the education of
the people. But, over and above all that,
is it not far better for us in this democratic age to allow the local people to see
to the education, and to take an interest
in the education of their own children?
Is it not far better to encourage those
living in the country districts, both men
and women, who are intensely interested in
their own local affairs in other directions,
to add one more to the voluntary labours
they perform on behalf of the State, on
behalf of other people as well, and that
they should also take up this great question of the education of the youth of
Ulster ?
That is the reason why these Regional
Committees have been appointed, and
they are doing their work well. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I have had an
opportunity of observing some of the new
schools that have sprung up, and there is
no comparison between the new schools
that have cropped up as a consequence of
this Act and the schools which do not
come under the purview of my hon. and
learned Friend's Department. I wonder
have Members of this House or members
of the public gone into some of the old
clerically-managed schools and observed
the conditions under which the children
are taught, and then I wonder have they
gone into one of the new schools, such as
are to be found just outside Lisburn or
up near Ardoyne-I have forgotten what
the name of the particular school is, but
I had the privilege——————
Mr. POLLOCK: Everton School.
The PRIME MINISTER: The new
Everton School in the city of Belfast.
Any person in Ulster who has the slightest
doubt as to the progress that is being
made has only got to go to these schools
to which I have referred either the one
at the gates of__Larchfield, outside
Lisburn, or this Everton School-and
have a thorough examination of the
conditions under which the little boys and
girls are taught there. Therefore, it is
absurd for the hon. Member (Mr. Patrick
O'Neill), who has moved this Motion, to
suggest to us that we are going back w
the bad old days.
I may say, in conclusion, that the
Government has no intention of interfering with the Act. We have no intention whatever of bringing in any amendment to the Act. We propose to give
the Act all the encouragement we possibly
can, and by precept and by speaking in
the country to urge the local people to
look after their own local children, and
in that way the Act is bound to be the
success that Lord Londonderry, in the
first instance, and his colleagues in the
Cabinet anticipated it would prove.
Nothing has been brought forward to-day
to show that we should budge in the
slightest degree from the attitude we took
up from the very start. The question of
the teachers has been raised. We have
not interfered with the teachers. The
teachers have been paid by the State.
Their salaries have not been reduced.
As a matter of fact their salaries have
been very largely increased since we took
up office.

There is no special virtue in that.

two points which were put forward by

That statement was, I think, refuted by
one of the Members of the Government,
and that counter-statement was accepted
by the hon. Member for West Belfast.

it was because they refused to do so when

was

schools, at anyrate throughout my region,
