Thursday, 31st March, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
WIDOWS' AND ORPHANS'
PENSIONS ACT.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he proposes to take steps
to extend the provisions of the Widows'
and Orphans' Pensions Act, so as to include in its scope all the widows and
orphans who are now excluded.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have nothing to add to the
statement which I made on the 24th inst.
in answer to a supplementary question
put by the hon. Member for North
Belfast.
NORTHERN IRELAND MAIL
SERVICE.
2. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime
Minister whether any communications
passed between the Members for Northern Ireland in the Imperial Parliament
and the Government with regard to the
mail service; whether he made known to
the Imperial representatives the negotiations which were being carried on with
the British Government in relation to the
change in the mail service; and, if so,
whether he will state what
was the
nature of these communications.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): No, sir; no communications
passed between the Members for Northern Ireland in the Imperial Parliament
and this Government respecting the subject.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not think that it is the duty
of the Government to acquaint those
Members representing Northern Ireland
as to the attitude of the Government in
relation to this mails question, so that
there could be no conflicting policies?
The PRIME MINISTER: There is not
any conflicting policy. Our colleagues in
the Imperial Parliament, I hope, will
continue to press for an All-Red Route,
and we, as a Government, are urging the
Imperial Government to do the same
thing.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that a statement has
been made that there is not the slightest
intention on the part of the Northern
Ireland Members at Westminster to allow
this matter to drop, and whether he is
aware that a meeting of Members of Parliament has been called at Westminster
for the purpose of asking the Postmaster-
General to alter the decision he came to
at the request of the Northern Government, to revert to the Holyhead-Kingstown route for mails?
The PRIME MINISTER: I have no
official information on that subject. 1
did see it in the Press.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not the duty of
the right hon. Gentleman to get into communication with those Members represen
ting Northern Ireland, and ask them not
to be urging a directly opposite policy
in the Imperial Parliament to that
adopted by the right hon. Gentleman as
the policy of the Government here!
The PRIME MINISTER: Of course,
that is a matter for them to judge. They
know what I desire on the matter, and
I am sure they will not press it too
strongly.
Mr. DEVLIN: But is not the right
hon. Gentleman well aware that at his request the Postmaster-General and the
Postal Authorities in London have agreed
to revert to the mails being carried by
Holyhead and that the Members of Parliament from Northern Ireland are advocating an entirely different policy!
Surely there ought to be some understanding between the Government and
those who represent Northern Ireland in
the Imperial Parliament in order that the
position may be made absolutely clear as
to what the intentions of Northern Ireland are in regard to the postal service!
No answer. Aha!

Paint (Protection against Poisoning)
Bill to which they desire the concurrence

Committee.

Electricity Supply Bill a Second time and

Opposed Committee.

Mr. DEVLIN: I do not think in the
history of Parliaments that there ever was
a more Gilbertian situation than that
which has arisen out of this mails question.
The right hon. Gentleman (the Prime
Minister) is the representative of Northern Ireland. He has been negotiating
with regard to the unsatisfactory condition of the mail service between Belfast
and England, and he has found after an
experience ripened by incidents of a most
disagreeable character that the system
which has been in operation for five years
has been a most unsatisfactory system not
only to the business circles of Northern
Ireland but to the interests of the community at large. For my own part I
congratulated the right hon. Gentleman
the other day on having at last seen the
necessity of taking steps to see that a
mail service of an effective character was
promoted for the people of Northern Ireland, and he requested-and I want this
to be specially emphasized-the Postmaster-General to revert to the service of
the mails via Holyhead. Suddenly, there
arose in the Imperial Parliament a bitter
and violent agitation against the Postmaster-General.
Now, what was the Postmaster-General
doing? He was actually carrying out the
suggestions of the right hon. Gentleman
and the Members of the Government.
Notwithstanding that, these Members
from Ulster at least some of themhave gone over there and declared that
this policy will not suit them, and have
brought all the pressure which they as
representatives of Northern Ireland in the
Imperial Parliament could bring to bear
upon the Postmaster-General to flout the
opinion of the right hon. Gentleman and
the right hon. Gentleman's Government.
The right hon. Gentleman, in reply to
the question I have put to him, says he
has had no communication with them,
but that seems to me a very extraordinary
attitude for the right hon. Gentleman to
take up.
One would naturally think
that when he adopted the attitude he has
adopted and made this request to the
In-
Postmaster-General he would have informed these gentlemen in London what
his attitude was and what the desire of
the Government was, and that, in consonance with the wishes of Northern Ireland
as expressed by the Prime Minister, they
would not only have sanctioned but supported the right hon. Gentleman.
stead of that they go over to London and
engage in the most violent agitation
against the reversion to the old policy,
although that reversion has taken place
at the request of the right hon. Gentleman. They do not, they say, intend to
let this matter drop, and I want to know
really where we stand in regard to it.
The right hon. Gentleman ought to tell
us exactly where he stands, because we
do not know. We do not know that the
Postmaster-General in London has stated
that he has adopted the new policy în
accordance with the wishes of the Prime
Minister. I think a more extraordinary
position was never heard of in the history
of any other State or any other Parliament than this. I feel it my duty,
therefore, to give the right hon. Gentleman an opportunity to give an explanation of a more elaborate and satisfactory
character than he has given in reply to
the question I put to him.
The PRIME MINISTER: As a rule
hon. Members who are going to raise a
matter of this kind give one some notice
in order that one may be prepared with
any fresh information that may have
come to hand. I really thought that on
the former occasion when the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) raised this point
I had satisfied him at all events of the
position that this Government took
up in the matter. I am still at a loss
to understand how the difficulty to which
the hon. Member refers has arisen.
Hitherto the practice has been that,
where a matter of any very great importance affecting the welfare of Ulster
was concerned, the Secretary to
Ulster Parliamentary Party generally
communicated with me or with one of
the Cabinet regarding the matter, saying
that they would like to know what was
going to take place and if they could
give their help in any way, and so on.

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I think
there is an opposite side to that question.
I did not intend to participate in this
discussion at all but for the fact that the
Minister of Labour has attempted to score
debating points, and if it comes to that,
many other debating points may be scored
from this side. You are complaining
that under the Widows', Orphans' and
Old Age Contributory Pensions Act you
are given no discretionary
powers.
Whose fault is that? The Labour
Government at Westminster had nothing
to do with the Act passed by the British
Parliament. We had little or nothing to
do with the Act passed in this House.
Mr. GRANT: You take enough credit
for it anyway.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: There
is no credit due to anybody for the
Measure on the Statute Book, as it is so
unsatisfactory. But if there is anybody
to blame for the fact that there is no discretionary power, then I submit it is the
Tory Government at Westminster that is
responsible for the Minister not having
discretionary power. Secondly, the
people responsible for promoting the
legislation in this House are the people
who are responsible for the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Labour, not
having discretionary power. So far as
this Act is concerned I would like to see
him having it, although I do not agree
that it would be a good thing.
(Laughter.) If you had waited until I
had finished my point I think you would
have been satisfied that there was no contradiction in terms.
If I go back to the original Act, which
was passed by the Labour Party, it gave
the applicant the right to extended
benefit, provided that he satisfied certain
conditions. When the Tory Party came
back they deliberately altered that Act.
They took away the right to make extended benefit payable at the discretion
of the Minister of Labour. There are
thousands of people in Belfast who can
bear eloquent testimony to that fact.
Practically the whole of the disallowances
of extended benefit at the present time
are due to the fact that the Minister of
Labour has discretionary powers. If the
Parliamentary Secretary denies that, I
am prepared to discuss the question with
him at any time, and to show beyond the
shadow of a doubt to any impartial person that my contention is absolutely
correct.
To come back to the point at issue. As
we are not permitted by your ruling, Mr.
Speaker, to discuss the advisability of an
extension of the present unsatisfactory
Act, my hon. Friend's remarks were somewhat circumscribed, and I noticed on
several occasions that he was perilously
near the border line. He had to be exceptionally guarded in his language, in
case he should step over the border line.
To come back to the point of issue, I
would prefer, even under this Act, unsatisfactory as it is, that you had discretionary powers. As the right hon. Gentleman knows, I called his attention to a
case two days ago in which he displayed
a considerable amount of sympathy, and
I believe if it had been left to his own
discretion he would have granted a pension, but the Act of Parliament, as it
stands at the present time, prevented the
right hon. Gentleman from granting that
pension, simply because the widow's
husband had died about six hours prior
to the 4th January, 1926, and had no
children under 14 years of age. It would
be much better if we had a Pensions Act
on a non-contributory basis, which would
give a pension to widows regardless of
whether the husbands were insured contributors or not.
When this Measure was before the
House-and it shows, to some extent,
that we had a precise prescience even in
small matters-I was able to anticipate
the unsatisfactory features of the
Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Act. A
number of those instances have actually
taken place, and it is due to the fact that
these people have been disallowed that
the Act is so unsatisfactory. If this
question appears to be largely a question
of the right hon. Gentleman scoring debating points I would like to inquire how
it is that if it is a splendid thing for him
to have discretionary powers he did not
take those discretionary powers under
the Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Act.
If he had the results would have been
much more satisfactory than up to the
present.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to bring
to the notice of the Minister of Labour
a statement he has made that I was in
favour of his powers being taken away.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 5th April, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
LOCAL BILLS.
Portadown Urban District Council Bill,
Carrickfergus Harbour Bill, Newry
(Northern Ireland) Rates and Streets
Bill.
Resolved: That the Chairman of Ways
and Means and Mr. Robert McBride be
appointed by this House, to join with the
Members of the Senate appointed by that
House, to constitute the Joint Unopposed
Committee on the said Bills.-(The Chairman of Ways and Means).
Oral Answers to Questions.
APPOINTMENTS TO THE CIVIL
SERVICE.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Finance whether his attention has been
drawn to the Press reports of the annual
general meeting of the Association of
Established Civil Servants in the Government of Northern Ireland, and whether
the statements made at that meeting were
in accordance with the facts, viz., that a
youth with a good record at the Bangor
Grammar School, matriculated at Queen's
University, Belfast, and passed the
written examination of the Northern Ireland Civil Service Commission last
March, and was refused by the Selection
Board; whether undue preference was
shown to the son of one of the members of
the Selection Board, who had not only
secured an appointment, but promotion,
before he had sat for any written examination; and whether he considers that
the Government is encouraging parents to
give their sons an expensive education
with a view to entering the Civil Service,
when scholarship and ability are subordinated to other considerations.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have the best authority for
informing the hon. and gallant Member
that the statements which he describes
were not made at the meeting of the
Association of Established Civil Servants
to which he refers. They did not, so far
as I am aware, appear in any Press report
of the proceedings, but seem to have
originated in a pseudonymous article in
one of the Belfast papers, the accuracy of
which has been denied by the conveners
of the meeting.
Before I deal with the two cases in
question, I think it well to explain to the
House that the procedure normally
followed in filling junior appointments in
the Service is to submit candidates to a
written examination in the first instance,
and subsequently to present those who
qualify at this examination to a Selection
Board, whose duty it is to choose from
such qualified candidates those who, in
their opinion, are best fitted for
appointment.
At present two types of Selection
Board are employed. One of these, on
which the father of the youth to whom I
will afterwards refer, sits, interviews
candidates for appointments common to
the Service generally, e.g., posts of clerk,
typist, etc.; the other, which is somewhat
differently constituted, and on which the
gentleman I refer to does not sit, interviews candidates for posts peculiar to one
Department. For example, Seed-testing
Assistants, Ordnance Survey Assistants,
etc.
The interview by the Selection Board
is very similar to the viva voce examination now included in many of the competitions for entrance to the Imperial
Service, and is intended to test the candidate's alertness, intelligence and general
outlook, as well as other personal
qualities of value for the post for which
he is competing.
This system of a qualifying examination
followed by selection has worked very
well indeed during the four years it has
been in operation, and has, on the whole,
been remarkably successful in securing
for our Civil Service a first-rate type of
officer.
Turning now to the alleged statements.
As regards the first, no examination was
conducted by the Civil Service Commis-

sioners for Northern Ireland in March,

Grammar School.
As regards the second statement, the
son of the member of the Selection Board,

a candidate for one of several vacancies
in a departmental post, not of a clerical

attractive from the point of view of

an entirely regular and proper manner
after a
qualifying examination and
selection by the Selection Board, in competition with other candidates. The
Board which made the selection was, as
I have already stated, not that on which
the young man's father sits. The youth
in question had previously been employed
in a casual capacity as a temporary clerk
in another Department, but there was no
question of promotion, and no connection
between his former and his subsequent
appointment.
There is no relation whatever between
the cases of these two youths. They sat
for different examinations and different
posts; one was finally rejected and the

circumstance alone, I think, disposes of
the inference contained in the last part of
the hon. and gallant Member's question
-an inference based on what he will no

assure him that both Selection Boards are

motive only the desire to secure the best

the members of the Boards is without
fear, favour or affection.

SECONDARY TEACHERS'
PENSIONS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Oral Answers

Education whether he will state the
number of Secondary Teachers in
Northern Ireland qualifying for pensions;
and, further, will he state the estimated
cost of putting these Secondary Teachers
on a pensions basis similar to that of
English Secondary Teachers; and how far
the increased contribution to pensions
offered by the teachers would meet the
difference in cost between the English and
the Irish scale.
Mr. POLLOCK: I propose to take this
question for my hon. and learned Friend
(Mr. Robb).
The number of Secondary and Preparatory Teachers who are serving in a
pensionable capacity at the present time
is approximately 538.
As regards the main difference between
the English and the Northern Ireland
Schemes of Pension for this class of
teachers, viz., the devaluation of past service in Northern Ireland, the estimated
cost of giving credit to Northern Ireland
teachers for the whole of their past service is possibly equivalent to a capital sum
of £150,000. This estimate was, however, made at a time when full details of
the ages, etc., of the teachers who would
come under the Pension Scheme were not
available, and until an adequate actuarial
investigation of the whole position has
been made it is impossible to say whether
it is even approximately correct. The
other main difference between the two
schemes, viz., the award in England of
a lump sum payment on retirement in
addition to the pension award, cannot be
stated in figures without an actuarial
calculation.
As regards the last part of the hon.
Member's question, there is no offer at
present before me by the teachers to increase their contributions over and above
the sum of 4 per cent. as laid down in the
Regulations relating to Superannuation.
The whole question, however, of an early
actuarial investigation of the scheme is
at present under consideration, but until
it takes place in would not be possible to
say what would be the Government's
attitude.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): This Resolution is the necessary precursor of a Bill which proposes
to amend the existing Loans Guarantee
Acts in the direction of extending the
limit of the aggregate amount of the
guarantees which may be given by the

statutory limit of £9,000,000 to

]
N
Hon. Members will remember that in
October last, Parliament authorized an
extension in the limit from £7,000,000
to £9,000,000, and the Return which
was recently circulated shows that a sum
of £7,297,070 has been used up, leaving
an available margin of £1,702,930.
The Advisory Committee have now
recommended the grant of further
facilities in respect of additional loans
for shipping purposes aggregating
£1,500,000, and these further guarantees will practically exhaust the Ministry's power under existing Statutes.
On the other hand, the Ministry's powers
to give guarantees extend up to 31st
March, 1928, and in order to leave a
margin available during the next twelve
months the Government has decided to
seek further powers from Parliament so
that the Ministry may be in a position.
to give such further assistance as the
circumstances may require.
I am glad to say that in the interval
between last October and the present
time, unemployment has assumed less
serious proportions, more especially in
connection with the linen
the linen industry.
There is, however, still room for improvement in the shipping industry, which has
derived so much benefit in the past from
the operation of these guarantees. Consequently, the Government feel that they
would not be justified in relaxing their
efforts to assist by this means, and the
Resolution which is now before the Committee accordingly proposes an extension
of the limit from £9,000,000 to
£10,500,000.
Possibly the Committee may be disposed to inquire as to what the future
policy of the Ministry might be in rerespect of these guarantees, and while it is
impossible to form any definite opinion
at the present time, still the hope is entertained that with the improvement
which has started, and which we trust will
continue to develop, it may not be at the
time the Act expires at the end of March
next found necessary to continue further
I facilities of this sort. I beg to move.

in that country. It seems to me, and I
think to most people, that the nonfinishing of that ship here has meant loss

of unemployment insurance benefit in

that boat to be finished in the Belfast
port, because it will mean, and continue
to mean, that a good many joiners, a

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Anderson]
wish to intrude in this debate except for
a moment or two. The hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has mentioned
various ways in which this Loans
Guarantee Act could operate, but he was
treading along very dangerous ground in
asking the Government to give advances
for the carrying on of business throughout
the country. That would be something
in the nature of a subsidy, and I am
afraid that if a Government started to
advance or to guarantee money in that
connection it would open up a way for a
great many schemes that would, perhaps.
land it in very great difficulties.
There is one thing that the Committee
dealing with this matter have always had
to consider, and consider seriously, that
is the question of security. In going
security for a loan, either to a bank or to
any other institution, we must be absolutely sure that we are not going to land
ourselves in difficulties at a later stage.
In regard to this Resolution that is now
before the Committee, I would like to ask
the Minister of Finance a question. We
are now proceeding to go security to the
extent of about ten million pounds. That
is a very heavy obligation for any Govern.
ment to undertake, and I would like to
know whether we have been released from
a single guarantee that we have given
under the Loans Guarantee Acts? Are
they all operative up to the present
moment?
Mr. POLLOCK: Do you expect me
to answer that right off?
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: If it
would involve a long statement from the
Minister, I can wait. I view with some
considerable misgivings the amount that
we are guaranteeing now. We are proceeding to go to the length of ten million
pounds, and I would like to know exactly
if any of those guaranties have expired,
or if any of them are likely to expire at
an early date.
There is one thing that this Committee must bear in mind in connection with
this matter, and it is this. I think it is
admitted on all hands that the shipyards
in the city of Belfast would have been
practically idle had it not been for the
responsibilities undertaken by this Government. Up to the present these guarantees have not involved the taxpayers of
Northern Ireland in any responsibility;
in fact, I take it, they have relieved the
taxpayers of a considerable responsibility
in some directions. I am sure that they
have relieved the Unemployment Fund
to a very considerable extent, and that
they will continue to relieve the Unemployment Fund of very considerable outlay. I believe that up to the present the
policy that has been pursued by the
Government in this connection has been
amply justified, but the course that they
intend to take in the future is another
matter altogether
I think I am right in saying that the
Imperial Government have given intimation that they are going to cease operations under the Trade Facilities Acts.
To my mind, that raises a very interesting point. If we continue that policy,
I hope that it will attract additional
business our way, because if the Imperial
authorities cease to give the guarantees,
and we are prepared to give them, I hope
the result will be that all the slips in
Belfast will be occupied for the next few
years. But the relationship of this
Government with the Imperial Government in regard to guaranteeing loans is
a matter, of course, that I cannot deal
with.
The Member for Antrim has mentioned the fact that up to the present the
operation of this Act has been confined
chiefly to the city of Belfast. Well, there
is only one other shipbuilding place in the
North of Ireland-that is, the city of
Derry--and I am quite aware of the
fact that if the shipowners there are
anxious to build ships the Government
are quite prepared to do the same thing
for them. It is well for the public to
know that, so far as the city of Belfast is
concerned, no question of favouritism
arises, becauses the Ministry have definitely and clearly intimated that any other
shipbuilding centre in the North of Ireland can have the same terms as the shipbuilders in the city of Belfast. From
that point of view, I think it is only right
for me to say that that criticism is not
fair criticism, and that the Government
are perfectly prepared to assist any other
place where the security is equally good.
The operation of this Act has been very
good up to the present, and I hope that
the sum now asked for by the Government will have equally beneficial results.

said loans.
Mr. POLLOCK: They are guarantees
of loans to shipowners. I am under the
impression that some-one or two of the

if I tell him that before a very great time

that by the year 1930 the amount for

to nearly eight millions will be reduced to
four million pounds, and as they are extinguished we cannot increase the amount
of our guarantees without coming to

must be fully advised of every transaction,
and of the nature of the guarantee that
is given. I hope that that will in the
meantime answer my hon. Friend's question. I will have further investigation

figures.
I am sorry that any comparison should
be made between Derry and Belfast. A's
a matter of fact, I believe my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour has interested himself as indeed we all have interested ourselves in that particular
case, and has endeavoured with all the
weight of his authority, and of the
Governent's authority, to induce the
owners of Derry shipyards to restart
building ships in Derry. But their own
large yard on the North-East coast has up
to quite recently been only partially
occupied, and, as in ordinary cases charity
begins at home, they were concerned
rather more to make some provision of
work in the Eastern yards rather than
restart operations in Derry. However,
we offered them all the advantages in case
of suitable securities of the Loans
Guarantee system in the hope that we
might possibly induce these shipowners to
come to Derry. That is my reply to some
suggestion made that Belfast is preferred
before other places in the Six Counties.
The case to which my hon. Friend from
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) referred to is one
not new to me. But the Committee of
three very prominent gentlemen in Belfast
-men of very great business experience.
indeed have decided it would be quite
impossible under the conditions of the
Statute to open the door to such an enterprise as my hon. Friend has in mind.
The security would not be anything in
the nature of that which it is required to
be, to take care that the taxpayers of

do not think my hon. Friend is quite fair

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLASS I. No. 2
CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding nine thousand one hundred and thirty-five pounds
be granted to Hs Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on the 31st March, 1928,
for the salaries of the Department of the
Prime Minister, the salaries of the
Cabinet, and the Cabinet secretarial and
other expenses in connection therewith,
including the expenses of the Privy
Council office.-(Note-£3,000 has been
voted on account).
The PRIME MINISTER: There is
really very little that I can say to the
Committee on the subject of these Estimates. They were kind enough last year
to grant a supplementary sum of money
in order to assist in the upkeep and
dignity of the office for which I am deeply
grateful, and adding that amount on to
what had hitherto been voted the sum
total has reached a slightly larger amount
than it was last year. This sum is, if one
would turn to page 6 of the Estimates,
explained in some detail. There has been
under C1, which is the first item in that
particular part-Works Services-a decrease so far as rates are concerned that
is more apparent than real. The rates
there on the whole Stormont estate have
now been allocated to the various buildings which have been erected
upon it,
and, therefore, so far as the Cabinet
office is concerned so far as my residence
is concerned, it has been cut down to a
fair proportion of the £95 shown in the
Votes.
The stationery services were all practically stationary, that is to say, there
is no change in them.
The only other point, I think that requires some little explanation is under
Sub-head B-Travelling and Subsistence
Expenses. I am glad to say that so far as
actual travelling allowances to London
and throughout the country are
cerned it has very much decreased
during the past year-in fact during the
past two years-for the reason that there
conhas not been so many meetings on that
side to deal with matters of difficulty and
sometimes of controversy. Having got
into smoother waters the necessity for
holding meetings of the Cabinet or indeed
for my own approach to various British
Departments has not been what it was
before.
Then, on the other hand, it has been
thought proper throughout the Estimates
this year to show in a clearer way in their
appropriate Votes where the motor cars at
the charge of the State are actually used.
Although this is an increase it shows
clearly that the upkeep and running expenses, £150, and the wages of the motor
driver, £250, will, in future, be borne by
the Vote to show how the motor car is
being used, and what it costs per annum.
Hitherto, those items were under the
different heads, but now, I think quite
properly, each item as it is expended by
a Ministry is shown under that Ministry's
Vote. The actual change from last year
would be a saving if it were not for this
transfer to the Vote of these various
items.
I cannot think of any other particular
item, but if any hon. Member desires to
raise a question of any sort of course I
shall endeavour to give him all the assistance I possibly can. It will be realized
by the Committee that the Vote in a case
of this sort descends to a personal matter
more so than in the case of a Minister
over a large Ministry, where the question
of policy naturally arises with regard to
his Department. In my case, although I
am quite prepared to join in any question
of policy with regard to the Government,
not so much administrative criticism can
be directed. It is really more a personal
matter as to what the Committee thinks
the Prime Minister's salary and the upkeep of Stormont should be assessed at.
I will be very glad to answer any questions
that may be asked. I beg to move.
I

The PRIME MINISTER: The explanation is that to put down any hon.
Member simply as Whip would not be in
accordance with customary practice.
What happens at Westminster, as the
hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) knows, is that
the Whips of the party appear on the
Votes under Lords of the Treasury.
There may be five or six of them as Lords
of the Treasury, and then, holding that
position and receiving the salary as such,
they are eligible to act as Whips for the
Government Party, whichever Government happens to be in power. When we
were arranging the division of the
Ministries between the two Houses it was
felt that one Parliamentary Secretary
should be allocated to the Senate. That
is how it comes. He has to be carried on
the Votes, and I take the responsibility
of simply having him as Parliamentary
Secretary in my Department and carrying the Vote on my books, because there
does not seem to be any other appropriate
place in which to put him.

the most appropriate place for him would
be to put him out altogether? I must
say it is an extraordinary position to have

Estimates-
Old Age Pensions
HOUSE OF COMMONS
CLASS II. No. V.
OLD AGE PENSIONS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £946,400
be granted to His Majesty to complete
the sum necessary to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment
during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1928, for the payment of Old Age
Pensions under the Old Age Pensions
Acts (Northern Ireland), 1908 to 1925,
and under the Widows', Orphans', and
Old Age Contributory Pensions Act
(N.I.), 1925, and for Pensions under the
Blind Persons Act, 1920." (Note.-
£325,000 has been voted on account.)
Mr. BARBOUR: I am sure the subject
of this Estimate will provoke little controversy in this Committee, but there are one
or two items to which I would like to
draw the attention of hon. Members in
submitting it to them. They will doubtless have observed from the foreword to
the Estimate that there is a considerable
increase in the provision for the payment
of old-age pensions to persons
seventy. That is due partly to the fact
that owing to the first day of the financial
year falling on a Friday, there are fiftythree Fridays in the current financial
year, and partly to the fact that the
recent legislation both as regards normal
and contributory pensions is only now
beginning to have its full effect.
over
Under the Old Age Pensions Act of
1925, whereby the statutory condition as
to means was modified in favour of applicants for non-contributory pensions, the
total number of persons in receipt of pensions at the full rate of 10s. per week
under the non-contributory pensions
scheme has gone up from approximately
38,000 to roughly 44,300-an increase of
6,300 full-rate pensioners. A number
of these persons who became entitled to
full-rate pensions under the Old Age
Pensions Act of 1925 had, of course, been
previously in receipt of pensions at the
lower rates, so that, while the number of
full-rate pensioners has increased by this
figure of 6,300, the number of persons in
receipt of pensions at the lower rates
under the non-contributory scheme has
fallen from, roughly, 3,500 to about
1,000. It is expected, however, that the
number of these lower-rate pensioners
will again increase during the year as
fresh claims are submitted.
As regards the contributory pensions
payable to persons over seventy, there
are approximately 2,500 persons at present in receipt of pensions under the contributory scheme. This number is made
up of:-
(1) Persons who, prior to the passing of the Contributory Pensions Act
had not been entitled, by reason of a
means disqualification or some such
cause, to any pension whatever; and
(2) Persons who formerly had been in
receipt of pensions at modified rates
under the non-contributory pensions
scheme but who, on the passing of
the Contributory Pensions Act, were
found to have qualifications necessary
to entitle them to pensions under the
contributory pensions scheme and who
were accordingly transferred to that
scheme and are now in receipt of contributory pensions at the full rate of
10s per week.
It will be noticed, however, that Subhead "B" of the Estimate, which provides for the payment of contributory
pensions, shows a very considerable increase over last year's provision, whereas
the Estimate for non-contributory pensions (Sub-head "A") actually shows a
decrease in spite of the causes which, as
I mentioned at the outset, make for an
increase in the total cost of pensions this
year. The reason is that the figure of
2,500, which I mentioned as the number
of persons in receipt of contributory
pensions at the moment, does not by any
means represent the total number of persons over seventy in Northern Ireland
who have the necessary qualifications for
contributory pensions. It is estimated
that of the total number of 44,300 persons in receipt of full-rate pensions some
12,000 are persons who would be entitled
to pensions under the contributory
scheme but who, being also entitled to
full-rate pensions, irrespective of their
insurance qualifications, were
were granted
full-rate pensions prior to the passing of
the Contributory Pensions Act. It is
proposed that, during the year, these
persons shall be taken over gradually into
the contributory pensions scheme under
the administration of the Ministry of
Labour.
Perhaps I may say here that this transfer will be a benefit both to the pensioners
themselves and also to the Exchequer,

It is always our principle that the boy
is questioned by any Member who wishes
to question him, and then we, each of
us, endeavour to arrive at our own
opinion, independently, as to the suitability or otherwise of the boy, and I may
say it is really remarkable to what a very
great extent such opinon is almost unani-
The opinion of one member of
the Committee confirms that of the others
mous.
to a very great extent. If thirty boys
are submitted for twenty places it is necessary that ten candidates, who may have
qualified, should fail to secure appointments.
In the matter of this boy, McCrudden,
I, as Chairman of the Board, had before
me the positions which had been taken
by those boys in the examination. When
this boy went out I realized the impression
he had made on me, and I told the other
members of the Committee. I said,
"Well, now, just while you are forming
your opinion about that boy, I want to
tell you he took sixth place in the examination." I felt that I gave this boy
every justice, because his appearance was
very disappointing in view of the position
he had taken in the examination. There
is one thing I would like those who have
criticized this selection made by this
Selection Board to consider. It is that
while any individual is able to form an
opinion as to a single boy, I do not think
that hon. Members have had an opportunity of forming a comparative opinion
of him, having regard to the other boys
who were up for selection at the same
time. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In making selections, I feel I can give an
assurance to everybody that the Committee do their very best, impartially, to
select the best candidates for our Civil
Service.
I have given you the names of the
Selection Board which sits to consider
appointments common to the Civil Service
as a whole, but in regard to appointments
peculiar to a particular Department, such
as a semi-technical position, a special
Board composed of five members is employed. It is composed of either the
Chairman of the above Selection Boardthat is to say, myself-or a deputy; then
a representative of the Civil Service Commission who is on the general Selection
Board, or a deputy; Mr. J. V. Coyle,
or in his absence another member of the
general Selection Board nominated by the
Civil Service Commission; and two members appointed ad hoc by the Department
concerned, that is to say, by the Department to which the candidate under review
will be sent after selection.
The appointment for which Mr. Grant,
junior, was a candidate was that of

control of the Ministry of Agriculture.
The appointment being departmental the
interviews were conducted by the Special
Board, that is, the second Board. The
members of this Board on the occasion
when Mr. Grant's son was examined were
Mr. L. McQuibban, who acted as Chair

Mr. MCALLISTER: I suggest to all
sections of the House without criticizing
personally the Members of this Committee that its selection cannot be defended in this House or before any impartial body. It is constituted of six
members, three of whom are Members of
this 'House sitting as members of one
party. There is no representative of
any section of the Opposition, and I
would suggest to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) that he should appoint a Member of this House carrying
the confidence of the people whom we
represent. I would suggest the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
as a member of that Selection Committee.
You cannot expect a substantial
minority of the people to have confidence
in any body which has sway over so much
of material interest to them when they
have absolutely no representative upon
that Committee. I would urge the
Government as a matter of justice and
fair play, and if they wish to transform
their verbal gestures into something practical, to adopt the suggestion I have
made and appoint on that Committee
someone who will carry the confidence
not only of the public representatives
who sit on these benches but of the whole
community whom we represent in Northern Ireland. I think it is perfectly indefensible to say that out of six members
three should be selected from one side of
the House.
Whilst not for a moment suggesting
anything personal, I do not see that they
have any outstanding personal qualifications for that particular position upon
which their selection could be defended.
It must be for some other reason and,
therefore, I would urge the Government,
in all seriousness and in all earnestness,
if they want to secure the confidence of
the people of Northern Ireland generally,
to adopt the suggestion which I have
made. I think the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) by experience, by capacity, by ability, and by
his active interest in everything material
to Northern Ireland is, at least, equally
qualified to sit as a member of that Committee as any other selection you could
make.

by leave of the House I would like to
make a very short statement. The Bill
has been in the Library for some time
now, so that hon. Members have had
opportunity for studying it. I should
explain, perhaps, that a Private
differs from a Public Bill in this important respect-that when the House
is asked to give assent to a Public Bill
by Second Reading it adopts the principle
of the Bill, but in the case of a Private
Bill nothing of that kind takes place.
If hon. Members will look at the
Preamble of the Bill they will find set out
there a series of allegations which
go
the root of the whole Bill. In giving

assent to the principle of the Bill at all.

examines into these allegations of fact
and then recommends to the House
whether or not the vital stage—that is
the Third Reading Stage-should be
assented to by the House. I think that
meets the point of the hon. Member (Mr.
Beattie).

CLASS IV. No. 2.
NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £114,500
be granted to His Majesty to complete
the sum necessary to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment
during the year ending on the 31st of
March, 1928, to defray the Grant in Aid
of Benefits and Expenses of Administration under the National Health
Insurance Acts." (Note.-£35,000 has
been voted on account).
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I would ask
hon. Members to turn to page 98 of the
Estimates and they will there discover the
Vote which I propose submitting to the
Committee this afternoon. The excess
expenditure over last year which we are
asking the Committee to pass is due to
three things which I propose explaining
later to the Committee. While the increase in the Estimate shows a sum of
£14,500 over the amount spent last year
in reality the difference in the expenditure proposed is only £4,500. I propose, therefore, dealing with the increase
under the heads of those two amounts,
namely, £10,000 and £4,500.
For the benefit of hon. Members who
are not acquainted with the apportioning
of the Health Insurance funds, and as
I shall be dealing for a short period with
fractions, I would like to explain that the
Government's contribution to approved
societies is different from the flat rate of
contribution under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts. Until January, 1926,
the State contribution under the Health
Insurance Act represented two-ninths of
all benefits and expenses of administration incurred by the approved societies. I
want here to explain the nature of that
two-ninths. When the Health Insurance
Act first came into operation it was decided not to give a flat rate of contribution as a proportion of the Government's
payment to the approved societies, but
that all sickness benefit and all administration of insurance societies would be
paid as follows: The Government would
bear a proportion of two-ninths and the
approved societies would bear a proportion of seven-ninths.
Under the Economy Act, which came
into operation about the middle of last
year-probably about June and which
was brought into operation to relieve the
Exchequer of some of the charges that were
borne by it, the grant in aid of benefits
and administration by the Government
was reduced as from two-ninths, which
represented the contribution for all who
were drawing sickness benefit, to oneseventh for men and one-fifth for women.
This Act, as I have said, came into
operation about the middle of the year,
but the State grant of two-ninths had
already been issued and had been paid
up to March, 1927, and this represented
£10,000, one of the amounts to which I
have referred.
If hon. Members will look at page 98
where it says "Grant in Aid of Benefits
and Expenses of Administration," they
will discover that in the year 1926 the
total amount represented £135,000, while
we are asking the Committee to grant us
for this year a sum of £149,500. The
difference represents £14,500, but, as I
have said before, we have paid from
January to March the excess contribution representing two-ninths instead of
one-seventh for men and one-fifth for
women. Consequently, by deduction, we
drew that back for the whole year, and
that reduced the amount of last year's
Estimate by the sum of £10,000.
In reality the comparable figures which
I am asking the Committee to consider
to-day are £145,000 representing 1926,
and £149,500 for the current year. Those
show that the actual difference between
this Estimate and that of last year is
£4,500. I stated at the commencement
that I would deal with the expenditure
of £4,500 under three heads, as we have
given effect to it under three heads. The
higher expenditure on additional benefits
represents £2,500.
As hon. Members are aware, at the
second valuation surpluses were shown by
Estimates-
National Health Insurance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
approved societies greatly in excess of
those shown at the first valuation, and
the amount declared to be available for
distribution on additional benefits, both
cash and non-cash benefits, will represent
a sum of £500,000, including interest
under the State grant which will be
spread over a period of five years. This
new scheme came into operation in July,
1926, so that last year we made provision
for only nine months as against a complete year in the present Estimate.
Now, I come to the second heading,
that of the higher cost of administration.
This higher cost of administration is
occasioned partly by more numerous
schemes being administered than the
approved societies administered formerly.
There have been introduced by the approved societies schemes for dental treatment, surgical appliances, convalescent
homes and ophthalmic treatment. It is
also occasioned partly by a reduction in
the arrears that have accrued to
members during their time of unemployment. These are the benefits that have
been introduced and, consequently, they
have to bear a proportion of the State
cost for administration.
Then, under the third head I am dealing with a small proportion of the State
grant is calculated with reference to
the amount of contributions paid by employers and insured workers, and I want
to say to the Members of the Committee
that that is really the only portion of
contributions in connection with health
insurance that bears any relation to the
contributions under the Unemployment
Insurance Act. That is calculated with
reference to the contributions paid by employers and insured workers, and in view
of the more hopeful industrial outlook
and the improvement in trade generally
it is necessary to assume that a greater
average number of contributions will be
paid during the ensuing year.
additional State grant under this head
amounts to approximately £1,000.
The
This covers the entire Estimate, and I
thought it due to the Committee that I
should make this explanation. I feel
certain that there will be little or no
criticism levelled at this Estimate for the
reason that it is a grant in aid by the
Government towards not only the
penses of administration in connection
with approved societies but to make it
expossible, as I have outlined in my speech,
to increase the benefits to those who are
suffering as a result of sickness. I commend the Estimate to the Committee and
I feel sure that no definite criticism will
be levelled at a Vote of this character. I
shall be glad to answer any question that
may arise during the discussion. I beg
to move.
Mr. KYLE: I move a reduction in
this Estimate of £100. Before doing so
I want to congratulate the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Labour on
the very lucid manner in which he put
this Estimate before the Committee. I
move this reduction for two reasons. One
is that the Ministry have not attempted
during the year that has passed to get
into touch with the societies in Northern
Ireland to ensure that medical benefits
should be paid to people who are insured
under the National Health Insurance
Act.
I had occasion to refer to this twelve
months ago on these Estimates, and one
would have thought that during the interim something at least would have been
done by the Government to ascertain the
feelings of the people who are insured

I want to take this opportunity of saying publicly that the societies that
adminster this National Health Insurance
Act have been guilty and are guilty of very

all the large societies in Belfast-the

I represent are from the health point of

many occasions when my colleague (Mr.
Beattie) and myself are going through

we have noticed a large number of people

National Health Insurance
HOUSE OF COMMONS

benefit had been stopped. These people
satisfied the dispensary doctor and appeared to satisfy the resident medical
officers in the Belfast Workhouse that
they were sufficiently ill to remain in the
Infirmary wards. From that point of
view it would seem to follow that if we
are going to have an improvement or
revival in trade, as the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) anticipates, the sum
estimated for should be substantially

marked attention to this whole question.
It appears to me that it is necessary to
spend a huge sum each year in sickness,
disablement and sanatorium benefit
simply because the people have not sanitary dwellings in which to live nor
receive nourishing food. If the Prime
Minister and his associates would probe
into that problem we might find increased expenditure in regard to subsidies
for the building of houses. I am sure I
am expressing the views of Members on
both sides when I say we would much
prefer to see the money spent on subsidies
for building houses rather than it should
go on sickness and sanatorium benefits.
Fundamentally this is the most important question we have to solve, and if
the right hon. Gentleman would induce
the Prime Minister and his colleagues to
go deeply into this question they would
possibly find in some of the Estimates a
far larger sum being expended for purposes we consider beneficent and more
beneficial than the sum spent in sickness
and sanatorium benefits. It is well recognized that since the setting up of national
insurance hundreds of people in Belfast
suffer from the fell disease of tuberculosis.
We send them to a sanatorium for a short
time. Their health may improve during
the time spent there, but finally what is
the position? As soon as a slight improvement has taken place they are sent back
into the unsanitary dwellings out of which
they came with the result that the disease
becomes worse on the second occasion than
previously. I ask for a fuller and more
adequate consideration of these points. I
think if that were done it would be for
the better health of the people of Ulster
and Belfast generally.

disablement benefit was paid at the rate

88 6d a week, and that at the recent
valuation the great majority of these
societies indeed, all the societiesshowed a surplus. This is an answer to

the representation of Antrim. 83 per
cent. of Members are in approved
societies in Northern Ireland which have

likely to be distributed in increased

I would like the hon. Member to know

I now come to the hon. Member for
the Border Counties (Mr. Elliott). I
would like to say that we have few, if any,
complaints from the agricultural districts.
Indeed, I think it would be well if I informed the Committee as to the number
of complaints that have been made to the
Ministry of Labour by letter and by interview. Probably about two per cent. of
complaints have been made to the
Ministry of Labour during the past
twelve months. An investigation of a
large proportion of the complaints of the
insured persons shows that the matters
have been dealt with properly either by

coming into contact with the society.
Those to which a satisfactory solution
was not found were referred to the umpire, and 45 cases were dealt with in that
way. Of those 22 were decided in favour
of the applicants, and 23 in favour of the
society. On the whole, I am perfectly
satisfied with the way in which the work
is being carried on by the approved
societies. I receive many complaints myself, I get the necessary inquiries made,

always anxious to discharge their liabilities to the members connected with them.

The wise men.

Mr. GORDON: The wise men from

in the interests of neither the approved

policemen as resident magistrates.
never could understand what qualifications a policeman had for a judicial' position. These positions in the old days were
given to county inspectors and district
inspectors because of their services to
Dublin Castle in the time of the difficulties of the British Government, and
no doubt that somewhat indefensible
proceeding might have been justified from
their point of view. But now that we
have recognised systems of government of
our own, and that there is no necessity
whatever to reward those gentlemen, I
think we ought to adopt a different procedure altogether in relation to these
appointments.
The multiplication of laws which require subtle minds to interpret them and
the complications that arise in thoroughly
mastering and understanding those laws
are not the genuine functions of a man
trained in a semi-military or police occupation. Every Act of Parliament here
becomes more difficult as time passes.
Our legislation is largely legislation by
reference, which makes it all the more
difficult for the ordinary layman to understand. I think that when you are making
judicial appointments you ought to have
in mind the character from the legal
standpoint of the person who is to administer justice and to give an adequate
interpretation of those laws.
I have no objection to a policeman
being made a sergeant, or a sergeant
being made a head constable, or a head
constable being made a district inspector,
or a district inspector being made a
county inspector. That is the naturally
slow but certain progress through which
men engaged in this noble occupation
have to pass in going from the Valley of
the Shadow to the Promised Land. But
why should a policeman more than any
other person untrained get appointments

two subjects that were specially addressed
With regard to the remuneration
of the services of those who are in the
Senate I may say that the late Leader of
the Senate, Lord Londonderry, did intervene with regard to the Members there
to know whether we could make some

Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
the present Leader of the Senate whose
duty is is to safeguard the interests of
Members of that House approaches the
Government afresh on the subject my
colleagues and I will give it the most
careful consideration.
With regard to the Serjeant-at-Arms
and the Deputy Serjeant-at-Arms and
Black Rod, coupled together, I can only
say that having been given a Parliamentary institution of our own we were
bound and I am not talking now as
head of this Government but as a Member of this House-we were bound to
maintain such dignity at all events that
we here in Ulster would not be looked
upon as a third-class Parliament, but as
ranking amongst other Parliaments, at
all events as the representation of an
important Province of the kind demands.
I would be no party to agreeing to anything that would lower the dignity of this
House or the Senate.
It may be at the moment we are in rather
humble circumstances here, but it has to
be borne in mind that the British Government will be handing over to us in a few
years at all events proper housing for
both the Senate and the House of
Commons. Now, that building will also
include accommodation for the Civil Service, which will be gathered together
into one building from the many
scattered quarters in which it is at
the moment housed. The consequence
is that that building will be a very
substantial block, and will contain inside
accommodation for the Senate and for the
House of Commons. Now, part of the
duty of the Serjeant-at-Arms is actually
to maintain the buildings and look after
the fabric of the buildings, to maintain
the police inside the buildings, and to
see that good order is preserved not only
actually in the Chamber but throughout
the whole building. And these duties
are, I think, duties that can best be carried out by these gentlemen who have the
confidence of the House of Commons and
the confidence of the people. I do think
it is somewhat ridiculous for the hon.
Member to suggest that we here could do
without the two officers whose duties are
onerous, and whose duties require to be
carried out with the respect and dignity
attributable to any House of Commons in
any part of the Empire. I know the
attack is not a personal one. I know the

The first time I came here I asked
where the Division Lobby was, and I was
told, "Out there." I went out into the
Lobby and I found a public meeting of
officials, and I got lost. That is why I
say that this Six County area, with a
population of a little over a million,
should, by its very smallness, be a very
very powerful factor in enabling us to
make it prosperous and successful in
business and in commerce, in the happiness of the people and in the betterment
of their social conditions. We could do
that all infinitely better by sitting round
a table than by carrying on this Parliament as we do now. The pomp is for
outsiders, but outsiders take no interest
in it. The picturesqueness is to attract
people to it, but nobody is attracted.
The formalism is to lure the public, but
the public will not come here. Therefore, I say on those grounds I am not
only opposed to this extravagant expendi.
ture on this Parliament, but I shall vote
for the proposal made by my hon. Friend
(Mr. William McMullen).

institutions. I can assure the hon.
Member that one of the greatest difficulties in starting a new Parliament was to

indeed to say that no Ministers have sat
more consistently in their places than
the Ministers of Northern Ireland have
done since this Parliament was set up.
We are seldom absent from our places,

made to explain away or answer any of
the charges made against us.
This is

add to the dignity of what we hope will
be one of the finest Parliamentary institutions inside the Empire.

to make. The question the hon. Mem.
ber (Mr. Devlin) emphasized towards the

ine point out to the hon. Member when

under the Act of 1920 that they would
put us in a proper position to carry on
our Parliamentary Institutions. They
were to build the Parliament House, they
were to build the new Law Courts, and
they were to build administrative buildings, and do all that out of British funds.
What the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin)
is setting against this is a non-recurrent
charge. It is merely the carrying out of
the building of those institutions that
makes our contribution to the Imperial
Services look smaller than it really is.
That is the explanation of the whole
financial position. The British Government are carrying out their honourable
bargain under the Act of 1920 to supply
Ulster with her Parliament Houses. They
are bound to do it by their own Act of
Parliament, and instead of grumbling
and grousing about a thing of that sort
I think everyone in this House ought to
rejoice that they are going to set us off
on our career enshrined in a proper
building and with proper administration.

COST OF EXTRA POLICE IN
BELFAST.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been called to the further strong
protest at the meeting of the Belfast
Corporation on March 1st. against his
action in charging the Corporation part
of the cost of the extra police brought
into Belfast; whether it was stated that
this charge last year amounted to £36,000,
and was equivalent to a little over 5d in
the £ on the rates; and whether he proposes to take steps to meet the wishes of
the Corporation and remove this charge.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have read the
report appearing in the Press of the
meeting of the Corporation referred to,
but I can only refer to the reply which
I gave to the question raised by the hon.
Member on this subject on the 22nd
ultimo, to which I have nothing to add.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon.
Gentleman give us any valid reason why
Belfast is treated differently in this matter from other areas of Northern Ireland,
and can he also whether the Lord
say
Mayor stated at the last meeting of the
Corporation that the city had been unfairly treated? Would the Minister
also say whether he proposes to remove
this injustice?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not responsible for what the Lord Mayor may
have stated. I consider the Belfast Corporation has been treated extremely
fairly.
MANUFACTURE OF ILLICIT
SPIRIT.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will consider
the advisability in the promised Amendment of the Intoxicating Liquor Act,
1923, of making the penalties for the
manufacture and sale of illicit spirit, as
well as the possession of the same, more
drastic by making it mandatory for the
magistrates in cases of conviction to
award a period of not less than
month's imprisonment in addition to any
monetary penalty that may be inflicted.
one
Sir DAWSON BATES: The amendment of the law relating to illicit distillation is not within the legislative powers
of the Government, and cannot, therefore, be dealt with in the Bill referred to
by the hon. Member.
I may, however, point out that the
existing law provides for extremely
heavy penalties-a fine not exceeding
£500 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months, or both fine and
imprisonment.
BELFAST WATER BOARD-WAR
SERVICE (PAYMENTS) ACT.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the War Service (Payments) Act (Northern Ireland)
is applicable to the Belfast Water Board,
and whether it gives to that body full
authority to make payments to ex-
Service employees in respect of bonus and
increment of salary or wages as agreed
by the Commissioners.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The reply to
both parts of the hon. Member's question,
as I am advised, is in the affirmative, subject to the limitation that the amount
payable does not exceed the proportion
of salary or wages specified in any agreement made before the termination of the
late war.

GRANTING OF GOVERNMENT
LOANS.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state on whose
recommendation loans are granted by the
Government; for what purpose these
loans are granted, and what rate per
cent.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The purposes for which loans
may be issued by my Ministry from the
Government Loans Fund are fully set
out in the Schedule to the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Act, the terms
of which are, no doubt, familiar to the
hon. Member, having been passed by this
House as recently as November last; and
it is not possible for my Ministry to go
outside the purposes therein indicated.
Before any loan is made, my Ministry
consults with any other Government
Department which is in a position to
supply information that would be of
service in deciding whether a loan can
properly and with safety be granted.
The rates of interest charged are
periodically published in the Belfast
Gazette and vary from time to time in
accordance with the expense to Government of raising money for Ulster Loans
Stock, and also vary with the purpose and
length of the loan. The present rates
range between 53 per cent. and 5 per
cent.

Personal Explanation.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME
MINISTER.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I desire to make a personal
explanation to the House arising out of
the debate yesterday.
When we were
discussing the Votes I made the following
statement:
I believe that the hon. Member and
his colleagues
referring to the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin).
are anxious to do away with the Northern Parliament, and therefore take
every opportunity to throw out insinuations against our own Parliamentary
institutions in order to convey the
impression that it would be better to
have one Parliament for the whole of
Ireland. Of course, if the hon. Member says
he is not anxious to see Ulster
in a Dublin Parliament, I am prepared
to accept that.

CLASS II. Vote 10.
LOANS GUARANTEE CONTRI-

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £4,680
be granted to His Majesty to defray
the charge which will come in course
of payment during the year ending on
the 31st March, 1928, for the purpose
of making a contributory payment towards interest charges under Section 2
(1) (b) of the Loans Guarantee Act
(Northern Ireland), 1926."
Mr. POLLOCK: This Vote is intended
to cover small liability which our
Government entered into in order to
secure a very unsually large shipbuilding
contract for Belfast. The approximate
amount of that contract was £4,000,000.
Of that sum the shipowners undertook to
provide out of their own resources
£2,000,000. The British Government,
through the machinery of the Trade
Facilities Act, entered into an arrangement with the shipowners to guarantee
the lenders of £900,000, and our Government also entered into an undertaking of
a similar kind to the extent of £1,200,000.
The lenders required a small fractional
increase of interest from the shipowners
in respect of the Ulster guarantee, as
distinguished from the British guarantee,
and in order that the negotiations might
not break down and that we should
secure this enormously valuable contract
for Belfast, we agreed to bridge the
difference between the interest required
for the Ulster guarantee, distinguished I
say from that of the British Government.
The figures are here before the Committee,
and I feel that the Members quite understand the value and importance of the
issues that were involved in this very
important contract.
I feel also that the Members will agree
that an essentially good bargain was made,
because there can be no doubt whatever
that the large ships contemplated under
this contract, occupying possibly three
years in the building and employing a
very large number of men, will relieve
the unemployment register of such
numbers of workmen as will pay the small
contribution that we pay in respect of
this interest very many times over.
For this reason I am sure that the Com-
Imittee will commend the action of the
Government on the very important results that have been achieved. I do not
think there is any further information
that I can give, because hon. Members
are fully familiar with the nature of these
transactions. I beg to move.

that the prolonging of this discussion is
not going to get us very much further.

East Belfast, it is not fair competition,

Belfast shipworkers have a reputation to

work is done in other places the city of

I would appeal to the right hon. Gentle
man to go to the shipbuilders and to place
the facts he has got from the hon.
Member for East Belfast before them, and
I believe some good will come out of it.

The fact of the matter is we have got to

only pebble on the beach. We are not

transaction. With the permission of the
Committee I would like to give the figures.
We are guaranteeing £1,200,000, the

understand that if we are going to endeavour to fetter or to curb the shipowners in getting these ships built by laying down very stringent regulations such

shipowners may say, "No, we will not
place the order in Northern Ireland at
all, but we will place them across the
channel." That is why I have said we
must be careful that in fighting for the
shadow we do not lose the substance.
There is one other matter to which I
would like to refer. This small Vote
which the Committee is being asked to

Labour would use a little judicious pressure we might be able to get more men
employed.
I quite agree that this Vote of £4,680
is absolutely essential if we are to carry
on. I know that when it was suggested
in this House that a subsidy should be
given to shipbuilders the Minister of
Labour told us it was impossible. I take
it that this sum of £4,680, which is only
a portion of £18,000 the Government propose to give, is really in the nature of a
subsidy, and I am extremely glad that
the Government have decided by this
means to enable shipbuilders to obtain
orders for the Belfast shipyards.
Question put, and agreed to.

ble that in this group 10,441 payments are

Let me look at it from the financial
standpoint for a moment or two. From

Act came into operation-to 31st March,
1927, we have paid to widows no less a

a million.
But this Act is very wide in its usefulness and its ramifications, and on 2nd
January next we take on a fourth group,
namely, those who have become entitled
to old-age contributory pensions at 65.
It is estimated that these will number
approximately 7,000 persons, and we also
estimate that during the last three months

in the form of contributory pensions at 65
to our people who become entitled to them
a sum of £45,000. This, I think, gives
the Committee a fairly good idea of what
is taking place under this beneficent
Measure. I may say that the sum, for
some time at any rate, which will be
spent on these pensions will be an increasing one. For instance, next year it is
estimated that the sum will amount to no
less than £430.000.
There is just one other thing I would
like to say in this connection. Very often
we hear a good deal of talk about the cost
of administration, and it is said that the

those to whom Parliament intends it to
he paid is used in administrative costs.
I am glad to be able to tell the Committee
that on the benefits paid the administrative costs are rather less than four per
cent., and in relation to the contributions

the school pay to the Government.

£9,000 has been voted on account.)
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will
observe that the principal items included
in the Estimate now before them consist
of expenditure designed to aid various
branches of industry; thus we have
financial assistance for the Fishing Industry, and for the provision of better
harbour accommodation; grants in aid of
light railways, which in common with
other forms of rail transport are passing
through a period of acute depression; and
grants calculated to assist our great linen
industry, on the one hand by providing
supplies of raw material through the
propagation of pedigree flaxseed, and on
the other by helping to stimulate
the sales of the finished product in the
United States market.
In passing, I may explain that in laying
down the conditions under which the
various grants are made the general
policy of my Ministery is to render the
maximum assistance to industry with the
funds available, and at the same time to
impose the minimum interference in the
actual conduct of operations for which
assistance from Government funds is
made.
Excluding the provision made by way
of Supplementary Estimate to meet the
loss incurred in respect of Government
coal contracts it will be observed that the
expenditure proposed in respect of these
services during 1927-28 is less by some
£4,000 than the total sum provided in
respect of the same services during
1926-27. This saving is effected mainly
by the reduction in the amount provided
as a Grant-in-Aid of the Linen Publicity
Campaign and the disappearance of the
subvention in aid of wages in the coal
mining industry. I propose to refer to
the variations between the amounts provided last year and those included in the
present Estimate under their appropriate
heads, as these fall to be dealt with in the
course of my remarks.
Hon. Members will observe that in the
case of the Works Services the amount
provided under this sub-head is greater
by £2,910 than the provision made in the
previous year, and this is largely due to
expenditure at Ardglass in the hope of
benefiting the fishing industry there.
For the purpose of providing muchneeded additional space for the curing of
herrings we propose forthwith to fill and
surface the area enclosed by the new retaining wall built last year. The time has
also arrived when the harbour must be
cleared of a certain accumulation of silt.
and the expenditure on this item alone is
expected to run to about £600.
My Ministry does not propose to undertake any major works for the improvement of fishing facilities until the report
of the engineer, who inspected the
harbours of Ardglass, Killough and Ballycastle in February last, is available. This
report is expected at an early date.
Under grants in aid of harbour works
there is an increase of about £1,000.
and this is due to grants proposed in respect of works at Rathlin, Bangor and
Portstewart Harbours, amounting in all
to £2,450.
The token provision of £10 in last
year's Estimates in connection with the
proposed grant-in-aid to the Coleraine
Harbour has been repeated, as it is unlikely that the amount of the grant from
this Ministry, which is limited to £3,000.
will become payable during the current
financial year. The harbour works at
Coleraine are expected to cost approximately £60,000, towards which the

Ministry of Labour will make an unemployment relief grant, and any amount by

At Rathlin the Church Bay pier, which
is the property of the Antrim County
Council, has developed grave defects, and
measures must be taken this summer to
remedy these defects if the pier is to be
saved from total destruction. The estimated cost of this work is £3,000, half of
which will be borne by the Ministry of
Commerce, and half by the County
Council.
At Bangor there is a small grant of
£600 to the Bangor. Urban District
Council in consideration of the amount
which that Council proposes to expend on
improvements to that part of the harbour
works, known as the "Long Hole," which,
I am informed, is used mainly for fishing
purposes. The Council has prepared a
general scheme for the improvement and
development of the harbour, estimated to
cost approximately £10,500. The Ministry of Labour will also make a contribution by way of an unemployment relief
grant, and the combined grants from the
two Ministeries will not exceed £850.
There is a sum of £350 provided for improvements at Portstewart Harbour.
This is inserted at short notice, and is intended to meet the cost of the removal of
certain rocks at the entrance to the
harbour, which impede convenient access
to the harbour.
Hon. Members will be interested to
hear about the Census of Production,
which is being taken, and from which we
expect to receive a report shortly. The
amount of £335 is included this year on
the advice of the Board of Trade, which
is taking the census on behalf of the
Northern Government on an agency arrangement. The total cost of the work is
estimated at £3,000, of which a sum of
£1,745 has already been paid; that is to
say, in respect of work which has already
been completed. Publication of the
census has come definitely within sight,
and my Ministry is at present in communication with the Board in regard to
the form in which the returns so far
collated should be published.
The amount shown opposite the item,
grant in aid of linen research, namely
£3,000, represents the third annual instalment of a total grant-in-aid of £10,000,
Two instalments of £3,000 have already
been paid, and, under the original
arrangement, the amount of the present
instalment was fixed at £2,000. The
Association, however, have produced
estimates to show that their expenditure
will have exceeded receipts during
1926-27, by approximately £1,500, and
have expressed serious concern in regard
to the effect which this deficit might have
upon the carrying out of the programme
for the following year. In order to meet
this difficulty the Association suggested
that the third instalment should be increased from the £2,000 previously promised to £3,000, and that a similar
amount should be contributed from
Government funds in each of the following two years. It is, accordingly, proposed to accede to this request in so far as
the third instalment is for the present
year, but as to any grant that may be
made during the two following years,
these will have to be considered in the
light of circumstances as they may then
exist.
There is another item in connection
with the linen trade and that is the grant
which we have been making in aid of flax
development and more particularly the
bulking of pedigree flax seed. The amount
shown, namely £1,770, represents the
balance of the £10,000 which was originally approved as an advance to the Flax
Industry Development Society, Ltd., to
enable it to undertake the bulking of pedigree flax seed. It was anticipated that the
full amount of £10,000 would have been
advanced by the end of last year, but the
Society had not, in fact, qualified for the
payment of the full amount, and,
accordingly, the balance is included in
this year's Estimate. From the sowings
of pedigree flaxseed arranged by the
Society in Somerset last spring some 88
tons of seed have been derived. Of this
quantity an effort is being made to
arrange for the sowing of 25 tons in
Canada this year with a view to bulking
in that country. Under present conditions Canada appears to offer the best
opportunity in the whole of the Empire
for commercial bulking on a large scale,
and it is hoped that if the present effort
is successful Canada will, in the course of
a few years, be in a position not only to
meet its own requirements for seed, but
