The next item is the grant in aid of
the linen industry publicity campaign.
The amount of £5,000 represents the
final payment of the amount of £20,000
which was originally authorized, £10,000
having been voted in last year's Estimates
and £5,000 in the previous year.
The
progress reports which have been supplied
to my Ministry under the conditions
attaching to this grant show that, both
from the point of view of advertising and
publicity, the work of the expert Committee in New York in charge of the scheme
has been very thoroughly undertaken.
While it is yet too early to expect the
effects of the scheme to be reflected in
our export figures, the general opinion in
trade circles is undoubtedly favourable to
the work that is being done. Although
it is not possible to ascribe the degree of
present activity directly attributable to
the advertising campaign, it is significant
that unemployment in the damask weaving trade is practically non-existent in
Northern Ireland to-day.
Hon. Members will note that it is proposed this year to double the amount
which was voted last year as a grant in
aid to the Tourist Development Association. It is hoped that this Association
may be able to undertake, in part at any
rate, the work which has hitherto been
performed by the Ulster Publicity
Branch of the Ministry of Commerce. As
will be seen later it is proposed to terminate the activities of the Ulster Publicity
Branch.
I think the Committee will be in
general agreement with the Government
view of the value of the work being
carried out by the Ulster Tourist Development Association. Unfortunately, it is
not possible to procure statistics which
would show the effect of the Association's
activities on the volume of tourist traffic,
but it is generally admitted, I think, that
the results so far obtained are most
encouraging. The demands made on the
Association from overseas for tourist
literature are considerably greater than
the Association is able to meet. It is
hoped that the grant of £1,000 now proposed will, in addition to assisting towards the work which the Association is
taking over from the Publicity Branch,
enable the Association to meet those demands and continue its activities in an increasing degree.
There is, as hon. Members will see, a
small sum of £50 included to defray
the travelling expenses of the members of
the Fishery Advisory Council which has
been set up to advise my Ministry on
fishery matters. The Council, which
consists of representatives of the four
Boards of Conservators and of the more
important commercial fishery and angling
interests in the Province, was created as
a medium through which those bodies and
interests could give expression to their
views and afford advice to the Ministry
on matters affecting the administration of
the fishery services. The meetings so far
held have proved such a medium to be
excedingly valuable to my Ministry.
I now turn to statutory railway grants.
The provision under this Sub-head, I am
sorry to say, shows the very large increase
of £2,525. It goes entirely to meet the

This very large increase is due to the
fact that for some years past the working
losses of the company have been met from
moneys received by that company under
the Irish Railways (Settlement of Claims)
Act, 1921, leaving only the guaranteed
dividends to be provided by the Tyrone

The PRIME MINISTER: I only just
want to intervene for a few moments to
deal with the point raised by the
Leader of the Opposition to call
attention to the amount on the Paper
dealing with the grant proposed
to be made to Lough Swilly Railway. I
think it is only due to the Committee
that they should realize that although
this line runs almost entirely through
Free State territory the capital involved
in the line is held, I think, entirely by
Ulster people, by people who live in the
city of Derry itself-almost entirely.
have made inquiries on that point, and
I think anybody will be able to confirm
it who pursues the same course.
I
The truth of the matter is that this
Lough Swilly Railway is the only artery
out of the city of Derry into the Free
State, and it is used, of course everybody
is aware, for the distribution of Derry's
produce and manufactured articles into
Southern Ireland. Consequently, it is
not only to the benefit generally of the
Ulster people that this line should be kept
open, but it is also particularly a matter
of concern to the city of Derry itself,
because were that line to be closed it
would undoubtedly interfere largely with
the trade between Northern and Southern
Ireland. And I may say that the Free
State authorities take exactly the same
view. The grant made by my right hon.
Friend to assist them over this year is a
grant that has been followed up by a
similar grant by the Free State, both
Governments realizing how important it
is to keep this line open..

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
However, it has been made so far as
Northern Ireland is concerned on the
understanding that between now and the
beginning of the next financial year,
1928, some effort should be made by the
Government to call together all railway
interests in our area with a view to ascertaining whether it would be possible in
some way to assist the railway companies,
and if possible to induce them to bring
forward some scheme of amalgamation
that might possibly bring back some of
the prosperity that they used to enjoy.
It is a very complicated question, and one
that will require very delicate handling,
because the Government has no idea at
the back of its mind to force or coerce in
any way any of the railways inside our
borders. But what we do feel is that
these captains of industry who are on the
directorate of the various lines might do
a great deal to simplify an otherwise extraordinarily complicated and difficult
situation. We intend later on to invite
a conference of them all frankly to discuss
the whole matter with a view to ensuring
that none of our lines may have to be
closed down.
Supposing we had to confine our
energies entirely to those lines that traverse our own territory alone, it might
have been, possibly, that without giving
the assistance, a moiety of which I say is
granted by the Free State authorities,
this line might have fallen by the wayside,
whilst other lines were making a genuine
attempt to solve the difficult problem.
We, therefore, thought it was better for
us, at all events, to keep the line alive
and a going concern. We felt very cer-
We
tain that once the line was closed down
it would deteriorate very rapidly, running through the district it does.
hope the Committee will, therefore, support us in putting forward what we think
is a modest Estimate. It certainly is
very important to keep the line alive
during the period of investigation to
which I have referred.
With regard to the question of the

by the Leader of the Opposition, I
desire to point out to him that there is

have all ranks and creeds of all political

mention that the hon. Member for West

Ulster. The hon. Member (Mr. Kyle)
need have no fears whatever on that

there is no difference whatever made by
the Ulster Tourist Development Association. I am glad to see that the local
authorities are coming forward and
assisting in every way they can to make
the Association an even greater success
than it is at the moment, and I have no
hesitation in asking the Committee to
double the Government contribution and
to make it £1,000 this year, as against
£500 last year.

time, hope that Ardglass will continue
to be a very important centre of the
herring fishing industry.

Mr. BEATTIE: I am raising this
matter because of the answer given by
the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale) to the question put to the Prime
Minister by the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott). I take
exception to the answer on the ground
that it is the most discourteous reply given
to any question that has ever been presented in this House. I put a supplementary question to the Minister of
Agriculture, and judging from the answer
I received he has failed to recognise that
there is such a thing as an official Opposition in this House.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I
might ask the leave of the hon. Member
to point out to him, and I think the
Members of the Imperial Parliament will
be able to confirm what I say, that so
far as a Select Committee of the House is
concerned, it is usual to have on it representation of all parties in the House.
So far as a Departmental Committee set
up by a Department is concerned, however, politics do not arise at all, and my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) is
within his rights in appointing those
advisers who he thinks will be able to
give the best information to his Department on the subjects raised. There is no
obligation on the Minister to consult any
political Party in the House with regard
to a Departmental Committee as against
a Select Committee.
Mr. BEATTIE: Taking that as the
customary procedure in the Imperial

to having them represented thereon.

Oral Answers to Questions.
NORTHERN IRELAND CIVIL SER-
VICE-CONDITIONS OF SERVICE.
1. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. Elliott)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he can state when the Terms and Conditions of Service for Northern Ireland
Civil Service will be published, and what
has been the cause of the undue delay.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Regulations for controlling the
conduct of the Civil Service and prescribing the classification, remuneration and
other conditions of service employed
therein are in course of preparation, and
it is anticipated that they will be issued
before long. The delay which has
occurred is due almost entirely to the desire on the part of the Civil Service Commission for Northern Ireland to obtain
the benefit of the results of the discussions
which have been taking place in Great
Britain for several years past in regard to
the various questions involved. It is now
realized, however, that those engaged in
the revision and codification of the
numerous and scattered regulations and
instructions on matters concerned with
conditions of employment in the Imperial
Service are unlikely to conclude their
labours at an early date, and it has
accordingly been decided not to postpone
any longer the issue of Northern Ireland
regulations.
I may add that in actual practice no
serious difficulty has so far arisen through
the delay in question.

Ireland Civil Servants are not placed in

Mr. POLLOCK: I regret that I cannot give the declaration desired by the
hon. Member, as it would clearly commit
the Government definitely to a policy of
maintaining the Civil Service in Northern
Ireland on a basis of absolute equality
with that of London Departments, to the
exclusion of all local considerations
affecting the public interest.
I can, however, assure the hon. Member that when dealing with questions relating to the remuneration or other conditions of employment of Northern Civil
Servants due consideration has, and
always will be, given to their position as
compared with members of the Imperial
Civil Service.
I should remind the hon. Member of a
fact which is common knowledge, namely,
that the higher officers in our Departments are remunerated on a much lower
scale than that of officers holding similar
positions in Great Britain.
Mr. DEVLIN: If Civil Servants in
Ulster do the same work as Civil Servants in England, why should they not
be treated in a similar way?
Mr. POLLOCK: As a whole, the Civil
Servants in the employment of the
Northern Government are treated in the
same way as Imperial Civil Servants, but
it must be obvious-I am sure it is
obvious to my hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin)
who has asked the question that, in the
higher positions, the amount of work and
the amount of responsibility involved in
the Imperial Service is immensely greater
than that involved in our smaller area.
For that reason, therefore, the remuneration is necessarily very much lower with
us than it is with them.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Lead Paint (Protection against
Poisoning) Bill [S]
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I beg to move," That the Bill
be now read a Second time.”
In doing so I would like to say that,
although it is not so far-reaching in its
influence as many of the Measures which
I have had the pleasure of bringing before this House, at the same time the
Government feel that it is a very important Measure, because it aims at safeguarding the health and lives of many of
the industrial workers who are engaged in
the house-painting industry.
Lead Paint Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
The Bill is drafted in the same way as
the British Measure-which was passed at
Westminster last year, and which came
into operation in Great Britain on the
1st of January of this year-was drafted.
It may interest the House if I tell hon.
Members how opinion has ebbed and
flowed during the last fifteen or sixteen
years in reference to lead poisoning, which
produces the distressing and serious
disease known as plumbism.
The Imperial Government in 1911 set up two
Committees, one to inquire into the effect
of the use of lead paint in the building
painting industry, and the other in
connection with the painting of vehicles.
Both Committees investigated the problem very thoroughly, and examined a
great many witnesses, and they came to
the same conclusion, namely, that the
disease did exist in these two branches
of the painting industry to a serious
extent.
Secondly, they came to the conclusion
that the disease was mainly due to the
dust generated by what is known as the
Where you
dry rubbing down process.
want a particularly fine and glossy finish
the painter is required to rub down coat
after coat dry, and that process produces
a fine lead dust which is of a very poisonous nature. Thirdly, each of the Committees came to the conclusion that substitutes were available for lead, and that,
therefore, the use of lead paint, generally
speaking, should be prohibited.
In 1919 the Washington Conference
also explored this subject, and the result
of the findings of that Conference was
that a Bill was passed in the Imperial
House for the protection of women and
young persons by means of Regulations.
Then later on, in 1921, the problem was
again investigated by the International
Labour Conference at Geneva and a draft
Convention was agreed to, setting out
that white lead paint should be prohibited
for interior painting. I should point out
that this draft Convention was agreed to
largely through the influence of the delegates from Belgium and France. Belgium
and France produce a great deal of zinc,
which is a substitute for lead in paint, and
they were naturally interested in the conclusions of the Conference, which would
have turned a considerable amount of
trade in their direction.
We in Great Britain produce no zinc;
on the contrary we have a considerable
lead industry which gives a great deal of
employment, and most of our Dominions
-Canada, Australia, South Africa, and
India-all produce lead, and the lead industry is of considerable importance to
the British Empire. It is true that the
British delegates gave their consent to
this draft Convention, but a wrong impression has been, I think, created by
statements which have been made to the
effect that because a draft Convention has
been agreed to it is therefore necessary
that the countries should ratify that Con-
That is a misvention by legislation.
understanding. It is quite clear by
Article 405 of the Treaty of Versailles
that all the obligation which the delegates
had was that they should bring before the
responsible authorities in their own
country the terms of the draft Convention, and then it is for that country to
legislate or not on the subject as that
country's representatives think right and
proper.
The next point to which I would like to
refer is this, that in the same year that
the Geneva Conference was considering
this problem the Imperial Government set
up another committee to investigate it in
That
Great Britain.
called the
Norman Committee, and they were to explore ground which had previously been
travelled over by the two committees to
which I have referred, and which investi-
This new committee
gated it in 1911.
was
came to the conclusion that the position
had to a great degree altered, because of
the fact that waterproof sandpaper had
been invented, and it was therefore
possible not to have dry rubbing down,
but to replace that with wet rubbing down,
which prevented dust rising or being
created. On the contrary, instead of
dust being created, it was held that a
paste is produced which, of course, cannot
be inhaled, and therefore the liability to
lead poisoning is very much reduced. In
addition to that it was considered by these
two former committees that substitutes
that were efficient and durable and economical were in existence, but during the
war the use of lead paint was very largely
abandoned because lead had to be conserved for more important purposes.
These substitutes were used instead, and
it was found that they did not bear the
test of time, and were, therefore, not so
satisfactory, especially for exterior work
where painting was subject to weather
conditions, as was lead paint.

Lead Paint Bill-
26 APRIL 1927
Now, that rather changed the whole
position, and the British Government of
that date, notwithstanding this recommendation of the Norman Committee,
decided to introduce a Measure in the
Imperial Parliament-it was the Socialist
Government-totally prohibiting the use
of lead paint.

Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: My hon. Friend says
'Hear, hear." I wonder will he say
that when I have finished, because, of
course, if you prohibit the use of lead
paint you very seriously injure the lead
industry in Great Britain and other parts
of the Empire. That is undeniable. The
result of injuring the lead industry would
be that you would put a great many
people out of employment who at the
present time are working. If the thing
can be done without disturbing too much
the conditions of trade I think it is desirable that it should be done in that way
rather than in a more drastic direction.
This Bill which, as I have said, was
passed in the Imperial Parliament last
year deals with the matter to some extent
by prohibition and in other directions by
regulation. It is not necessary that I
should go through all the Clauses of the
Measure itself, because they are very
clearly set out here, and anyone who reads.
them is quite capable of understanding
them. Under Clause 1 the use of lead
paint is prohibited except in the form of
paste or paint ready for use. Again, in
the same Clause, dry rubbing down or
scraping lead paint is prohibited. Again,
in Clause 2, it is prohibited to use women,
young persons or children in the painting
industry where white lead paint is used,
so that you see in several directions the
stronger course of prohibiting the use of
lead paint is actually followed in this
Measure. In other directions also the
problem is dealt with by Regulations
which the Ministry of Labour will have
power to enforce.
Under Clause 1 you will see that spraying of lead paint can only be done under
very great precautions, and, again, there
is to be regular medical inspection. There
are to be facilities for those engaged in
the industry washing their hands, and,
during their period of work, protective
clothing has to be worn, and the clothes
temporarily laid aside have to be placed
in such a position that they cannot be in
Second Reading

any way saturated with paint. Then last,
but not least, there are to be distributed
to persons employed in this industry instructions dealing with the precautions
which ought to be taken by those using
lead paint. In Clause 3 there are provisions set out for the purpose of applying
the same procedure in making Regulations and Orders as exists in our Factory
Acts, and Clause 4 insists that registers
and returns shall be supplied. There are
other preventive Clauses in the Measure
which are quite easily interpreted.
All that I have to say in conclusion
is that this is an honest attempt to
deal with this problem in a reasonable.
way. It is hoped that it may be
sufficient, and if it is not sufficient the
Government will not hesitate to bring in
another Measure of a more drastic kind.
I, however, take this opportunity to appeal
seriously to employers and to workers' representatives and to workers to do everything possible to make this Measure, if it
passes this House, as I am sure it will, the
success which some of us at any rate
anticipate it will be. I make this appeal
on two grounds-one ground of human
sympathy, and the other of self-interest.
I beg to move. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Mr. KYLE: I would have welcomed
this Bill in a far heartier way if it had
been to carry out a long overdue reform
and one that was anticipated in the
King's Speech. It was stated there it
was going to be a Measure
to protect persons engaged on painting work against the dangers of lead
poisoning.
This Measure is only going partially to
do that.
Mr. ANDREWS: No.
Mr. KYLE: The Minister himself said
that.
Mr. ANDREWS: No.
Mr. KYLE: It is only going partially
to protect persons in the trade. We are
all agreed that there is this danger of lead
poisoning. It is a very serious illness that
painters suffer from, and I do not
think any question of the trade that
the Minister paid so much attention
Lead Paint Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
to should be placed before the life and
the well-being of the painter and his
family. We all know-at least the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
probably will know a good deal more than
some of us who are only lay personsof the evils of lead poisoning. When it
was mentioned in the King's Speech that
there was going to be a Measure introduced to protect painters or persons engaged in painting work against the
dangers of lead poisoning one would have
hoped that a more stringent Measure than
the Measure now before us would have
been submitted to us. The evils of lead
poisoning are such as would have warranted the Government in prohibiting
altogether the use of white lead in paints
for buildings. This regret has been
voiced in the Senate by Colonel Sinclair.
In the debate that took place there on
the Bill he said that he regretted the use
of lead paint was not to be prohibited
atlogether; that inspection would be a
difficult matter owing to the conditions in
the painting industry, and that a whole
army of inspectors would be necessary
under the Act to carry it out.
I only wish he had moved in this
direction. It would have enabled those
of us who are not very hearty supporters
of the Senate to point to one useful thing
that it had done; but, alas! no such luck,
and we are to continue in the rather cheap
opinion we have of this body which knows
better, but does not, apparently, dare to
amend a Bill. The evils of lead poisoning are so widely recognized among
civilized nations that as far back as 1921
90 delegates of 30 Governments met at
Geneva, under the auspices of the
International Labour Office, and under
the leadership of Sir Montague Barlow,
Sir Thomas Legge, and Mr. E. L.
Poulton, of the G.C., B.T.U.C., representing Britain, passed a Convention,
according to which each State ratifying it
-and Britain ratified it-undertakes to
prohibit the use of white lead in paint,
and to prohibit further the employment
of males under eighteen years of age, and
of all females engaged in any painting
work of an industrial character. These
prohibitions were to come into force in
1927.
Our Government should have been able
to profit by the rather painful experience
of the British Government in regard to
this Measure, because it was not merely a
coincidence that Sir Thomas Legge resigned the position he held at the Ministry of Home Affairs in Britain, because
he was a responsible person and had
pledged his word on behalf of Britain that
white lead should be prohibited altogether. He felt it was such an urgent

as I know. I remember during the war

Mr. DEVLIN: That is practically the

it was the impression conveyed to my

the fruit of the labours of this assembly,
the Geneva Convention, which has been
referred to by my hon. Friend the Leader
of the Opposition.
After all, those of us who have not
given careful study to this question are
bound to come to whatever conclusion our
intelligence directs from what has previously occurred. What did occur?
There was a Convention held in Geneva
at which there were 90 delegates from 30
countries. It must have have been a
matter of deep international concern
when it called for a close and searching
inquiry at the hands of these responsible
agents of their countries. After giving
it the most careful consideration they
came to the conclusion-unanimously, I
understand that lead poisoning was
widespread, and
and that more effective
action should be taken by the respective
Governments to deal with it. I prefer
that opinion to the opinion of my hon.
Friend the Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison). I also prefer that
opinion to the opinion of the lead
merchant to whom the hon. Member for
Down (Mr. T. McMullan) has referred.
And then, in addition to that, there

had the privilege and the honour of personal acquaintance with Sir Montague
Barlow. I know what a splendid and

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In submitting the
Estimate for the expenses of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary it is, I think,
appropriate that I should refer to the
great and very welcome improvement
which has taken place in recent years in
the condition of law and order in this
Province. And when I do so I would
like to bear testimony to the police forces,
not alone the Royal Ulster Constabulary
but the Special Constabulary.
emerged from a period of lawlessness that
swept over this Province, and I think at
the present time we may claim that there
is no more law-abiding part of His
Majesty's dominions than the Province
of Ulster. While I bear testimony to
the return of normal conditions I should,
I believe, fail in my duty as Minister of
Home Affairs if I were in a spirit of
undue optimism to relax in any way the
necessary precautions which the Government have taken and are taking for the
detection of crime and its prevention.
We have endeavoured in this Estimate to
effect economy in every branch of the
Force. I would like to remind the House
that sometimes economy becomes parsimony, and any attempt to starve
neglect our police forces on which the
peace of the community must depend
would I suggest be on a par with the
individual who saves money by not insuring valuable premises. But, so far as
economy can be affected without impairing in any way the efficiency of our police
force, that economy will be made.

I would like to point out that the great
bulk, roughly 85 per cent., of the cost of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary is confined to pay and allowances, and it
follows therefore that to effect economies
of a substantial character it is necessary
either to reduce the pay and allowances
or to reduce the numbers of the force.
As I have already said, I am prepared as
circumstances arise, and when I believe
the situation warrants it, to reduce still
further the numbers of the police, but
the Government is not prepared at the
present time to follow the suggestion
that has been made in certain quarters
that the pay and allowances of the police
force should be reduced.
I would like to remind hon. Members
that in 1919 the whole question of the
pay of the police forces in Great Britain
was referred by the Imperial Government
to a Committee, which was presided over by
Lord Desborough, and which was known
as the Desborough Committee. That
Committee recommended very substantial
increases to the pay. That the old rates
of pay had been entirely inadequate was,
and I think is, generally admitted on all
sides. Members are aware that as a result of the inadequacy of the pay a very
serious situation' arose in England-I
refer to the police strike which took place
in London.
The rate of pay as fixed in 1919 by the
Desborough Committee is common to all
forces in Great Britain-England, Wales
and Scotland-and those same rates were
subsequently applied to the Royal Irish
Constabulary by the Ross Committee,
which sat in Dublin. Since that time the
pay of the Royal Irish Constabulary, and,
subsequently, of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, has been similar to that which
exists in Great Britain.
My own view is that, when one considers the unpleasant and dangerous
nature of the duties which the police have
to perform, the responsibility which even
a junior constable has to exercise on very
many occasions and the strict discipline
which is absolutely necessary in a police
force, no one can suggest that the pay of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary is unduly
high. But if there was a higher rate of
pay in England and Scotland than we
have over here, one result would be that
we would not get the high class of men
that we look for in the Royal Ulster Constabulary, because the candidates for the
Force would prefer to go to England,
where, I may say, they would be
welcomed.

have stated, I am prepared as circumstances may arise to reduce the numbers,
but I feel and I hope hon. Members will

There is another matter to which I
would like to refer, and that is the question of barrack reconstruction, in regard
to which there has been a certain amount
of loose talk. I think I saw it stated.
some time ago that it was the intention
of the Government to embark on a
grandiose scheme, and to erect palatial
barracks at a cost of something like
£800,000. That idea is purely romantic.
I would remind hon. Members that the
condition of the barracks at the time we
took them over was far from satisfactory.
I think I am not using too strong language when I say that the condition of a
very large number of barracks in Northern Ireland was a disgrace. This partly
arose from the fact that the Government
of the day adopted the practice of taking
Estimates-
Royal Ulster Constabulary
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
buildings for short leases. There was
usually a term in those leases providing
that they can be terminated in a period
of five years, and the landlord was under
covenant to keep the buildings in repair,
but it frequently happened that the landlord did not act up to his responsibilities.
I can assure the House that the barracks
which we propose will provide nothing
more than is absolutely necessary for the
health and comfort of the police, and may
I say also for the efficiency of the Force,
because you cannot expect men to do
their duty properly and efficiently if they
are housed under unsanitary conditions.
The question of closing certain barracks
and of amalgamating others has given
the Government a good deal of concern;
but we have delayed the undertaking of
any substantial scheme in regard to rebuilidng or erection of new barracks until we get back to more or less normal
conditions. I have appointed a small
Departmental Committee to go into the
whole matter and to advise me in regard
to this matter; but I would ask hon.
Members to realize that it is a matter of
very considerable difficulty, because 1
find that when it is suggested or even
hinted that a certain barrack should be
closed all the local people object.
It has been suggested that we should
follow the principle which has been
adopted in certain parts of England and
Scotland-that is the institution of what
is known as the village constable. Personally, I think there are very great
difficulties in the
the way of adopting
such a course in this country, and
although I am not prepared at the
present time certainly not without very
careful consideration-to say definitely
that such an arrangement might not be
possible in certain localities, the view I
take at the present time is that the existing system of having a barrack with
four or five men which controls not alone
the particular village in which the barrack
is situated but the surrounding area, is
a more effective method of providing
suitable police supervision.
Following on the report of the Committee to which I have referred, it will be
necessary to consider very carefully the
effect of their recommendations, and I
can assure the House that before any
barrack is abolished or amalgamated with
another, such a course will only be taken
if in the opinion of my police advisers
adequate police supervision can be afforded
from the sub-districts.
I may remind hon. Members that we
have made substantial progress in regard
to the reduction of barracks during the
past five years. I find that in 1922 we
had no fewer than 283 barracks, and that
at the present time we have only 204, a
substantial and economical reduction.
No doubt the removal of a barrack from
any particular locality will be a matter of
regret to the people in the district, but
I do hope it will be realized that economy
is essential, and that usually it is not possible to effect savings without, perhaps,
affecting some particular interest.
I would like to refer to a matter to
which attention has already been directed
in this House, and which has been the
subject of a considerable amount of
criticism outside. I allude to the charge
which appears as an Appropriation-in-
Aid for the extra police force in the city
of Belfast. It has always been the practice
in connection with the management of the
old Royal Irish Constabulary-following
the period in which the Belfast Corporation had a police force of its own, which
had to be abolished owing to its unsuitability that the Corporation should
pay a certain small proportion of
the cost of the Royal Irish Constabulary. The way it was done was
this. The Government undertook to pay
for a certain number of police for each
county borough or each county, and the
particular number allocated to each
county and city was based to a large extent on the population, the rateable
valuation, and the acreage. The number
so allotted to each county borough or to
each county was known as the free quota.
I think there is a great deal of misunderstanding as to what the free quota really
means. That is really what the free quota
means. When the Government found it
necessary to station men over and above
that number in any particular locality, the
local authorities paid half the difference
of the cost between what is known as the
established number-that is the number
actually required having regard to existing conditions-and the free quota.
Prior to 1919 the free quota for
Belfast was 500. In 1919 the free
quota was increased from 500 to 900,
while the established number was
Royal Ulster Constabulary

1,233. To-day, the free quota has been
extended from 900 to 998, while the
established strength is 1,273. Therefore,
in practice, Belfast is better off to-day by
having 58 fewer men to pay for than in
the old days of the Royal Irish Constabulary, with, of course, the additional
advantage of having more men to do duty
in the streets.
But there is another advantage which
sight has been lost of. In the old days,
take for example, in 1920, I find that the
charge for each man over and above the

to be paid by the Belfast Corporation.
To-day, they are only charged one-half of

the time the transfer of the police service
was made to Northern Ireland

to re-open the whole matter.

suggested that Belfast is any more lawless than any other part of the country?
I have not been able to detect that there
has been any more lawlessness in Belfast
than in many parts of the country.
Speaking not on behalf of the Belfast
Corporation but as an individual member
of that body I believe that 1,000 police.
in the city of Belfast are sufficient and
adequate for all purposes. My personal
opinion is that those 275 policemen could
be profitably utilized in other directions
without allowing those members of the
force to be an additional burden on the
people and industries of Belfast. You may
remember that some time ago a great outcry took place in the city as the result
of a speech made by a prominent director
of Workman & Clark's. He pointed out
that owing to the excessive rates that
were levied by the Belfast Corporation it
was extremely difficult for the Belfast
shipyards to successfully compete with
shipbuilding firms across the channel. I
do not think it can be denied that the
heavier the rates are in any city the employing class to that extent find it very
difficult to enter into successful competition with firms across the channel and all
over the world.
You are aware of the attempts made
recently by means of the Loans Guarantee
Act to bring orders to our shipyards in
Belfast. Although it is not an unjustifiable thing for the Government to

The clear contemplation of this Act of
1922 is that the ordinary police work of
a town or county should be performed by
the free quota of that county or county
borough. That that was the intention of
the Act is clearly shown by the speeches,
which have been referred to by hon. Members opposite, of the then Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs
(Mr. Megaw), in introducing the Act,
when he spoke clearly of the free quota
being the normal police force, and the
additional force being police that were to
be brought in under exceptional circumstances. Accordingly, I submit that it is
absolutely clear that the intention of the
whole system is that the cost of the ordinary police work and the force necessary
in normal times in a county or county
borough is to be borne by the exchequer
of Northern Ireland, and that, if any
additional force is to be brought in because of any disturbance or default
arising in any particular community,
then that community should pay its share.
Taking that as the clear meaning of
the Act-that the free quota in a county
or county borough is to be the normal requirement of that county or county
borough for ordinary police work-what

The hon. and learned Member for
Armagh (Mr. Davison), who sits behind
me has fallen into a misconception in this
way: He assumes that if we increase the
free quota to Belfast the counties will be
placed under some liability to contribute,
a liability under which they are not placed
at the present time. But what is the
liability of the counties? Just as when
the Minister was dividing up his free
quota and allotted 998 to Belfast he
seems to have under-estimated the requirements, so in fixing the free quotas for
the counties he seems to have over-estimated the requirements, so that at the present moment the position is that in every
county in Northern Ireland the nominal
free quota is greater than the actual number of police required and stationed in the
county.
What Belfast is asking the Minister today is not to withdraw any of the free
quota from the counties, but to re-allocate
the free quota so as to assign to Belfast
what ought to be assigned to it under
Section 3 of the Act, and to assign to the
counties what ought to be assigned to
them under the same Section. If that is
done, we say you will find that you will
not have a number in the counties less than
the free quota, nor a surplus in Belfast
over the free quota, but you will meet the
ordinary normal requirements.
counties will have nothing to bear in the
way of rates for the police, and it will
leave Belfast next to nothing to bear for
the cost of the police. The numbers of
the free quota ought to be so re-allocated
that you will have Belfast with its fair
and proper and reasonable share of the
free quota.
The
That is the position. As I said at the
outset, I think difficulties have arisen
under some misapprehension. What I
am asking the Government to do is to
look into the matter again. The free
quota is allocated under Section 3 of the
Act.
Once it is allocated it is not like the
law of the Medes and Persians where no
change could be made. Under Section 3
ample power is given from time to time.
to alter the allocation. In my judgment
the very fact of the number in Belfast for
ordinary requirements in peaceable times.
being 1,273 shows that the present allocation is not a correct or a just allocation,
and that the time has come when the
matter ought to be reconsidered and a reallocation made.
I ask the Government to go into the
matter as early as possible, and call together the police authorities, and if necessary the civic authorities in Belfast. Let
them take into consideration what would
be a proper re-allocation of the free quota
among the counties and county boroughs
on the basis of the normal requirements
of police for those places. If that were
done I am confident we would find that
Belfast would not have to bear any additional burden such as it bears now, and
that the rate of 6d in the £ would be
removed from the city. I really cannot
see why the Government should not now
go into the matter again, arrange a
fresh allocation and endeavour to allocate on this basis, which is the only basis
you can adopt-the basis of the normal
requirements of the counties and county
boroughs. In that way you make the
free quota a fair one.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I have listened to this debate
with very great interest in order to ascertain, if I could, the true basis of the
grievance that the Belfast Corporation
have against the Government. I have to
take a very broad view of these affairs.
May I at the outset say that although,
of course, the responsibility primarily
falls upon the shoulders of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs, the
decision that was come to in the matter
was a Cabinet decision, which involved
all his colleagues, including myself. We
are emerging after some six years from a
time when it was very difficult, indeed,
to look even twelve months ahead.
common prudence the Inspector-General
advised my right hon. Friend to allocate
the police of Ulster in such a way as he
considered from a technical point of view
was the safest for the whole of Ulster.

No one denies that in the city of
Belfast property is probably one-half, if
not two-thirds, of the value of all the
property in Ulster. Nobody denies that
the city is large and requires care in the
disposition of the police force. When
it comes to an accurate allocation of the
force throughout the boroughs and Six
Counties every particular corner will
naturally fight its own battle, and I am
not at all surprised or disappointed at
the activity of those who are voicing the

[The Prime Minister]
sentiments of the Corporation in putting
forth their case here to-day. It is, of
course, sometimes lost sight of that in
balancing the amount of money the
Government has at its disposal from year
to year the greatest care has to be taken
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of

somehow rough and ready justice is done
between town and country, and the
attacks that have been concentrated upon
the Government in connection with this
particular item would make it appear
that the Government were in some

like to remove that entirely erroneous
impression. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I called for a few figures in order to
assure the Committee that there is no
picking out of the city of Belfast for unfavourable treatment. I asked for these
figures just to refresh my memory, and
when I give them the Committee will
realize that the sum of money under discussion to-day is a mere nothing. I
looked back over the past few years since
we came into office, and I find that recoupments to the Belfast Corporation in
connection with malicious injury damages
amounted to £1,238,573; grants for
Housing Scheme, £285,187; grants in
aid of unemployment relief schemes,
£424,385; grants in respect of health
services, tuberculosis, sanitation, &c.,
£250,960; grants in respect of roads,
£56,819, and £400,000 to which my right
hon. Friend referred in connection
with the Special Constabulary during
the trying times, making a grand total
of £2,655,924. Therefore, I hope that
the Committee will realize that the
Government has done its very best to
help the Belfast Corporation, and has
shown in every instance the utmost desire
to meet the special requirements of the
case and to help them through difficult
times.
Another point has to be carefully considered. There is grumbling about this
extra quota that has been fixed upon the
city. The amount of that extra quota is
spent in the City of Belfast, which is
practically the centre of the headquarters
of the R.U.C. When the great poverty
that exists throughout the counties at the
present time is taken into consideration,
when it is remembered that agriculture
has passed through such a very trouble-

am not quoting these figures to suggest

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I wish
to support the reduction moved. I feel that
probably no Estimate coming before the
Committee this year offers greater scope
for the economy axe than the Estimate
considered to-day. This force is costing
the country too much. By the
organization of the force I believe this
Estimate could have been reduced. The
one thing that would strike any person
looking at this Vote for the first time
would be the proportion of very highly
paid officers and officials we have as compared with the size of the force.
There
is surely room here for a business reorganization of this force, because, as has
been pointed out by the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) and others who
gave figures, the number of highly paid
officers and officials is out of keeping with
the size of the force and the duties it
carries out.
I also wish to support the reduction on
account of the way this Estimate is set
out. It has been pointed out to the Committee that it is very hard to know what
the pay
of these officers and higher
officials is. We have the pay set out, and
then we have allowances and travelling
expenses, and from the Estimate it is
very hard to get to know what the real
remuneration of these people is. This
may not be a popular thing to say. The
rates of pay of this force were fixed in
1919, which was at the very peak of the
boom.
I feel the time has come when these
rates should be reduced from the top to
the bottom, because I think it will be
admitted by hon. Members, that since
1919 there has been a considerable reduction in wages all round. That has been
an absolute necessity to keep our industries going. There has been a considerable reduction in the pay of skilled
artisans and tradesmen since 1919. We
have to look at these things comparatively. This should be part of the duties
of this Departmental Committee which
the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) has promised to set up. The time
has come when there should be at least
an inquiry into the whole system of remuneration from top to bottom, because
these scales were fixed at the boom period
of our prosperity in industry.
Wages
have suffered considerably since then..
I wish also to protest again against the
sums which have been appropriated in aid
in this Vote and are represented as economies. It has been pointed out that the
sum of £25,000 has been appropriated in
aid from the Road Fund. That should
have gone to the reduction of the rates,
because, as far as I can gather, not a
penny of the sum raised by the extra
duties on lorries last year has gone to the
relief of rates. It was appropriated for
this thing and for that thing instead of
going, as was intended, to the relief of
the local rates. I do wish to protest most
strongly against this amount being appropriated in aid of this Vote, against its
being taken from where it should go, and
being represented to the Committee as
economy.
I do not wish to detain the Committee,
but there are many items that could be
referred to if one wished to go through
the Estimate item by item. Take, for
instance, architectural and engineering
services page 61. There is a sum of
£3,750. As far as I can gather from the
Estimate there the proportion of these
architectural and engineering services to
the proportion of new work done is altogether out of all business thinking. One
really cannot disabuse one's mind of this
fact, that the report of the Public
Accounts Committee this year disclosed a
state of affairs connected with this force
which made many of us feel there
was a laxity and looseness about the
administration of this Department that
did not occur with regard to any other
Department in connection with our
services. That really makes us a little
bit suspicious about the way a great many
items in this account are set out and about
the looseness with which money is spent.
I feel that a proper reorganization of this
force on business lines would save thousands of pounds without impairing in any
way its efficiency.

Adjournment
26 APRIL 1927
'Mr. KYLE: I want to ask the Prime
Minister can he state to the House when
it is the intention of the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) to introduce the
Budget?
Mr. POLLOCK: I hope to be in a
position on Tuesday, the 10th of May,
to present to the House the statement
of income and expenditure for the year.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Prime
Minister inform me of the order of the
business for the remainder of the week?
The PRIME MINISTER: It is proposed to-morrow to take the Loans
Guarantee Bill, Second Reading, and
then to carry on with the Estimates for
Special Constabulary, Public Record
Office, Ministry of Agriculture, and so
on, as will appear upon the Paper. On
Thursday the final stages of the Lead
Paint (Protection against Poisoning)
Bill and the Loans Guarantee Bill will
be taken, and then Estimates as will
appear upon the Paper. Next week, on
Tuesday, the 3rd May, the Local Government (Contracts) Bill will be presented,
and the Estimates will be carried on. I
will give further information later on.
Mr. DEVLIN: Could the right hon.
Gentleman say what is the meaning of
this extraordinary delay in the presentation of the Budget?
Mr. POLLOCK: There is no exceptional delay, if I may say so; but we
are dependent upon the findings of the
Joint Exchequer Board in regard to
many matters of account, and it was not
convenient for that body to meet until
this week.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would
like to ask the Prime Minister whether
he is aware that very important legislation has been foreshadowed in the
British Parliament, and whether it is the
intention of this Government to follow
some of these important Measures. I am
sure the right hon. Gentleman is aware
of some of them.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think a
discretion must be given to the Government as to what legislation they introduce, but full notice will be given of it.
Mr. DEVLIN: Has the right hon.
Gentleman given serious attention to the
question of extending votes to women
over twenty-one ?
The PRIME MINISTER: That also
will engage our attention.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon.
Gentleman be moved by any other consideration than the fact that such a
Measure has been introduced in
England?
The PRIME MINISTER: I would
like to have a little notice of these
intricate questions.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Measure which it is my
duty to submit to the House for Second
Reading is the natural corollary of a
Money Resolution which the House
will remember was passed on the 7th of
this month. This Resolution authorized
an extension in the limit within which
guarantees may be given from nine to
ten million five hundred thousand
pounds. I then stated that guarantees
amounting in the aggregate to a
of £7,297,000 had been given by
sum
the Government. In actual fact from
this figure should be deducted the amount
of repayments made amounting
£767,000. Under the Act, of course,
these cannot be re-issued. It is right
that the House should understand
that while the guarantees amounted to
£7,297,000 there is an actual reduction
in the liability of the Government
by the sum I have mentioned. At that
time I mentioned that one of the objects
of the Money Resolution was an anticipation of the outcome of negotiations
which were then in progress directed to
the construction of five large motor ships
in Belfast. The money was estimated between three and four million pounds.

I am happy to be able to
say to-day that these negotiations
have ended satisfactorily-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and as
as a result
orders have actually been placed
for five large ships involving a large
amount of varied labour which I am sure
will be regarded as very satisfactory to
the House. Three of these are actually,
as I understand, either started or about
to be started, and as to the other two we
have an undertaking that they will be
put into work at a very early date. The
Government's guarantee in connection
with this large order, which I regard as
one of the most important shipbuilding

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With regard to the
Special Constabulary Estimates, hon.
Members will observe that there is a net
decrease of £82,000 as against last year's
expenditure. With regard to Class
YA," generally speaking, the expenditure in respect of that force has ceased.
The greater part of the expenditure appearing in the Estimates for Class "A" is
in respect of men employed on
Customs Duty, the cost of which is defrayed by the Customs Authority, and
appears as a Grant-in-Aid, and it is not,
therefore, expenditure in the real sense
of the world. The time of the men engaged on this Customs duty is paid for
by the Imperial Government.
the
Mr. DEVLIN: Then it is not on these
Estimates?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think if my
hon. Friend turns to the Grants-in-Aid
he will soon find it does appear.
There are a few members of the "A"
Special Constabulary still engaged at
Sprucefield, and, of course, they are disappearing by degrees as the stores are
disposed of. Hon. Members will appreciate that the non-essential stores are
being got rid of by degrees, and, therefore, practically speaking, the "A"
Constabulary Force, to whom we all owe
so much, has, in fact, ceased to exist.
With regard to the "B" Force, it will
be observed that an alteration has been
made in the conditions of service. In
many cases members of the force who
were most anxious to continue as members of the Special Constabulary found
it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to
attend the requisite number of drills.
In order to meet this difficulty, and in
order that we might not lose the valuable
services of these men, we decided to
establish a reserve category, whose
members would only be required to attend one annual parade a year, principally for the purpose of kit inspection,
receiving a nominal retaining fee of 5s.
The members of this Reserve Force would
have all the rights and privileges of a
member of the Special Constabulary, also
having the right to retain their kit, but
liable to be called upon to serve should
the necessity arise.
It has also been decided to reduce the
number of drills required for those remaining in the active category from 16
to 8 drills, at the same time reducing the
bonus payable from £3 to £2. We were
reluctantly compelled, in the interests of
economy, to make this cut in the bonus,
but even at a higher figure this bonus does
in no way represent anything in the
nature of payment for services rendered.
The force is entirely a voluntary one, and
I think I know the feelings of the "B"
men sufficiently well to state that this
small bonus, which is all that our Exchequer can afford, does not in any way
represent the real incentive which leads
members of the "B" Special Constabulary to continue as members of that force.
I know perfectly well that if the Government required the services of the "B"
Special Constabulary in an active sense,
every man in the force, whether on the
active or on the reserve category, would
answer the call without considering
whether they were to be paid or not.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Although there is not now, I am glad
to say, the same necessity for the active
co-operation of the "B" Special Constabulary Force, I think nothing is more
necessary to a community such as ours
than that we should have at our back the
help of an organized and disciplined body
of men, such as the "B" Special Constabulary. I hope, therefore, that the formation of this reserve will enable men,
who otherwise could not continue as
active members of the force, to continue
as members of the Special Constabulary.
I beg to move.

I have at all times voted in favour of
this Estimate. I do not intend to-day
to vote in favour of the Amendment-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-but it is
for quite a different reason from that of
the hon. Gentlemen opposite who say
Hear, hear." I can see quite easily

of the sea upon their backs, and they have
made up their minds to get rid of the "B"
Special Constabulary by the shortest possible means that they can adopt without
showing their hand. Originally they
paid these men a sum of £10; then they
cut them down to £7; then they cut them
down to £5; then they cut them down to
£3; now they have cut them down to £2.

necessary to keep the "B" Special Force
alive. But I am not going to vote for
the Government, just to show the position
that I occupy in regard to the attacks
made upon the Independent Members
upon every possible occasion from the

Government deride us; they say we have
no right to be in this House, and that we
misrepresent the people who sent us here.

that I was returned to this House, as I
have said before, by the votes of the
people, and so long as I am returned by
the votes of the people I shall come here
to do my duty. I am not an automaton

When I stood before my constituents I

to say that in future when I cannot agree

PUBLIC RECORD OFFICE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum, not exceeding £1,862, be granted to His
Majesty to complete the sum necessary to
defray the charge which will come in
course of payment during the year ending on the 31st March, 1928, to pay the
salaries and expenses of the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (13 and
14 Geo. V., c. 20.")—(Note-£600 has
been voted on account).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): This Estimate will be found
on page 47 of the Book of Estimates.
There is a net decrease of £85, which is
accounted for by the fact that in the
year 1926-27 a special sum was included
for the provision of furniture and fittings
to provide for accommodation for an increased number of documents, etc. The
actual figure was £200, and for the current year is £100.
Under Sub-head E, purchase of historical documents, a sum of £30 is provided, in order to enable the Record
Office to make an advantageous purchase
in the event of documents of value, relating to Ulster, being offered in a saleroom. The amount is small and is, of
course, only a nominal figure.
One other item may be referred to, and
that is under Sub-head A, salaries, wages
and allowances. There is no longer pro-

It is gratifying to be able to report to

trades unionist freedom from victimiza-

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I

important Measures.
I am sure the

proposes to introduce legislation dealing with a vast number of matters, and I did not at the moment appreciate the particular Measure to which
the hon. Member was referring. I

Government because of its slavish following of legislation in the Imperial Parliament, or something of that sort, and did
not pay much attention to it although I
gave a courteous reply. I said:
I think a discretion must be given
to the Government as to what legislation they propose to introduce. But
full notice will be given of it.

Thursday, 28th April, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
THE FLAX-GROWING INDUSTRY.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he has
seen a statement in the Press made by Mr.
Ritchie, one of the Department's inspectors, that he was afraid the flaxgrowing industry would die out of the
country; whether this statement expresses
the opinion of the Ministry on this.
important subject; and, if so, what steps.
will he take to prevent such a regrettable
result.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Mr. Archdale): I have seen a report in the Press of the statement made
by Mr. Ritchie regarding flax-growing.
Mr. Ritchie is not an officer of the
Ministry of Agriculture. The statements quoted do not represent the views
of the Ministry.
The Ministry is endeavouring to encourage flax-growing in Northern
Ireland-
(a) by raising new and selected
varieties of higher-yielding capacity
than the varieties now grown.
In this connection, through the offorts
of the Ministry, the Empire Marketing
Board has now made a Grant of £2,000
for the purpose of defraying the cost of
the propagation in Canada of pedigree
flax seed so that in future years an
adequate supply of such seed may be
available for Northern Ireland growers.
(b) by carrying out experiments
with the most promising new varieties
raised in Ireland and elsewhere and
also by manurial trials and demonstration plots at various centres;
(c) by providing the services of
Flax Instructors who advise growers
and scutch-mill owners on points of
difficulty.
In addition to the activities of the
Ministry of Agriculture in this connection, the Linen Industry Research Association receives from Northern Ireland
public funds, through the Ministry of
Commerce, an annual grant towards the
conduct of its work, the grant for the
current year being £3,000. Furthermore, advances up to a maximum of
£10,000 from the funds of the Northern
Government are being made through the
same Ministry to enable the Flax Industry Development Society to develop
stocks of pedigree flax seed for growers
throughout the Empire, including, of
course, growers in Northern Ireland.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if he has considered any scheme for safeguarding the
producers of flax, that is, by guaranteeing a minimum price?
con-

sidered it a good many times, but I am
afraid we have never yet been able to find
a solution.

Mr. ARCHDALE: Before I give details in connection with our Estimates for
Agriculture I think the House would like
to have a brief sketch of the work which
my Ministry is carrying out in order to
assist agriculturists throughout Northern
Ireland. As will be seen from letters in
the papers and elsewhere, there is a great
deal of ignorance throughout the whole
of Northern Ireland as to our work.
Our live stock is the most important
branch of the agricultural industry. The
export trade of cattle alone from Northern Ireland ports was in 1925 worth
£3,339,000. Cattle from Northern Ireland are now competing against Canadian
and Free State cattle, and the only way
we can hold our place on the British
market is by sending animals of the
best quality which will feed and fatten
quickly. Our cattle at present have a
good reputation, both in England and
Scotland, but unless we keep steadily improving our stock we will get ousted, as
both Canada and the Free State are
making every effort to improve their
stock and are spending considerable sums
in introducing pedigree sires.
The Ministry is also doing all that is
possible for improvement of cattle with
the funds at its disposal by the following
means:-
(1) By placing premium bulls in each
county under the Cattle Schemes of the
Committees of Agriculture.
The
(2) By assisting Milk-Recording Associations to procure pedigree sires.
Ministry contributes two-thirds of the
cost of these bulls up to a sum of £73,
the Association paying the balance.
(3) By helping breeders of pure-bred
Shorthorns to procure high-class pedigree
sires. The conditions are that three
owners at least of pedigree herds must
co-operate and purchase a suitable pedigree animal, and retain this animal for
five years, the Ministry contributing up
to £333 that is two-thirds of the price
up to £500.
(4) By purchasing and assisting
County Committees of Agriculture to
place pedigree bulls in the poorest
mountainous districts. These animals are
sold on considerably reduced terms to
applicants selected by the County Committees. If such an animal costs, say
£36, the applicant pays £12 in three
yearly instalments of £4 each.
I may say, with regard to that, that
the agricultural editor of one of the leading English papers was over here within
the last few weeks, and in the paper of
the 22nd April this is what he says about
our cattle:
It is extraordinary that so long as
well-bred bulls can be obtained at such
reasonable prices the problem of the
scrub bull should still be present.
Compulsory registration has worked
and is working well in Ireland, and
those who are in close touch with the
Irish store cattle trade are aware of
a very distinct improvement in the
stocks sent over here for sale. There
is no doubt that the quality of Irish
store cattle is vastly superior to that
of our own, and stock breeders in this
country ought to feel ashamed that it
should be so, considering the advantages and opportunities they have had
compared with the Irish breeder. The
fact is that now that Ireland has become in a more settled condition the
Government is organizing the cattle

breeding resources of the country on
a very sound basis, and we hope that
our Government will turn a deaf ear
to the opposition to a bull-licensing
scheme and put the compulsory registration of bulls on the Statute Book.
So that in England, at any rate, the
agricultural papers are in favour of what
we are doing here and what is being done
in the Free State.
In 1926 we had standing in Northern
Ireland 416 premium and subsidized
bulls; Scotland at the same time had 838
premium and subsidized bulls, and the
Irish Free State had 1,681 premium and
subsidized bulls.
Northern Ireland in 1926 had a cow
population of 260,000, including heifers
in calf. This means only one premium
or subsidized bull to 629 cows.
Critics have alleged that the Bull
Licensing Act has reduced substantially
the number of bulls in the country, and
that fewer bulls are being reared, but
these allegations are refuted by the
following figures:
The total number of bulls inspected in
the first year, 1923, was 6,838; of those
629 were rejected, leaving 6,209 licensed.
In March, 1926, the number of bulls
licensed was 6,639, that is an increase in
1926 over 1923 of 430.
These figures show that the number of
bulls actually licensed in 1926 (6,639)
was 430 more than was licensed in 1923,
and was only about 200 less than the total
number of bulls (6,838) inspected for
licences in 1923. This increase may
be attributed to the demand for
better bred bulls and to the higher
prices now being realized for animals
which have been licensed. Of these
6,639 licensed bulls 2,142 are pedigree or pure-bred animals, and 4,497 are
cross-bred or half-bred bulls, so that I
think that disposes of the argument that
pedigree bulls are ruining the country.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In regard to milk recording, there is
probably no branch of farming in which
greater development could be made than
in dairying. The total number of cows
de might with advantage be increased and
the yield per cow could be raised far
above the present level.
If the average
eede
and b
the
yield was increased by 200 gallons per
cow it would mean, at 6d per gallon, a
gain each year to the country of
£1,250,000.
Can this be done? It is certainly
possible when it is realized that in Sweden,
Denmark, and Holland the yield per
cow has gone up by 200 gallons, and that
in the Province of Friesland (Holland)
alone the yield of 100,000 cows has been
raised from 480 gallons per annum in
1896 to the present yield of 840 gallons
per annum.
Individual farmers in Northern Ireland
have, as a result of milk recording and of
breeding from selected cows, increased the
yields of their herds to 800 and 1,000
gallons, and in some cases 1,200 gallons
per cow, but this is by no means common;
indeed, as shown by the following figures
the dairy farmers of this country have
not taken up milk recording to any considerable extent. In 1926 there were
260,000 milk cows and in-calf heifers in
Northern Ireland. In 1927 there are
only about 12,000 cows out of that
260,000 under test for milk recording.
This means that something less than 5
per cent. of the cow population in Northern Ireland is under test as compared
with 24 per cent. in Denmark. We are,
however, making steady and increasing
progress. In 1922 we started with six
societies and 1,244 cows, and this year we
will have 62 societies, with about 12,000
cows being tested.
I would like to give the figures from
three Milk-Recording Associations in my
own neighbourhood. One is Fivemiletown, and out of 154 cows in the Milk-
Recording Association they increased the
average yield of 109 gallons per cow in
one year. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In Monea, which is quite close to me,
152 cows are in the Association. They
have increased since they began two years
ago, the average yield of those cows by
103 gallons per cow, and in Aghadrumsee, which is nearly on the borders of
Cavan, they have 199 cows under test
and they have increased in one year the
average produce of those cows by the
enormous amount of 264 gallons per cow.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not
believe there is a milk-recording society
in Great Britain which has increased as
much as that society of Aghadrumsee.

The records which have been kept prove
that there are many cows in Northern
Ireland which yield from 600 to 1,200
gallons. This shows clearly that if the
average for the whole country is 400
gallons there must be a considerable
number of cows giving much less than 400
gallons each, or, in other words, there
are a large number of cows which do not
pay for their keep, and which the farmers
are feeding at a dead loss.
Dairying is a key industry in Northern
Ireland, for on it mainly depend the pigraising and calf-rearing industries. To
help milk-recording we give the following
grants:-
1. 4s. per cow, each member contributing, in addition, 3s per cow.
2. A grant of £35 towards the salary
of the supervisor.
3. A grant of two-thirds the price of
a dairy bull (no grant exceeding £73).
4. A grant of £10 towards prizes for
the best cows.
The county committees also make an
annual grant of £10 to each Association.
We will have 62 Milk-Recording Associations in operation this year in Northern
Ireland.
In Northern Ireland there is a sheep
population of 530,000. These can be
divided into mountain sheep and lowland sheep. About two-thirds of
all the sheep in the country are
mountain or black-faced, and these
are usually grazed on a common run
or mountain as one flock, although those
on each mountain may be owned by halfa dozen farmers. The Ministry has been
assisting the agricultural committees of
the Six Counties in placing pedigree blackfaced rams in the mountainous districts at
reduced terms, usually at about one-third
of the cost price. These rams are procured
from home breeders and at the Scotch
sales. In 1926 there were 240 pedigree
subsidized rams standing in the mountainous districts of the Six Counties. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Lowland sheep are usually run in small
flocks, and each farmer keeps his flock
on his own farm. For lowland sheep a
scheme similar to the cattle scheme has
been adopted by several of the county
committees, whereby premiums are given
to pedigree rams, and, in so far as one
can judge, the scheme is working satisfactorily.
It will probably be interesting to hon.
Members to know that the effect of the
scheme in mountainous districts has been
to increase the value of the lambs from
these pedigree sires by from 10s to 15s
per head in 1926. I am glad to be able
to state that sheep-breeding has been one
of the few branches of agriculture which
has paid during these depressed times.
If more money were available to increase
the number of premium bulls and
premium rams to be placed throughout
the Six-County area annually, I have no
hesitation in stating that money spent in
this way would be productive ten-fold.
A scheme for the improvement of pigs
on the lines of the Cattle Scheme is in
operation in each county, and is giving
satisfaction.
In regard to the Horse Scheme, when
the Ministry started operations in 1922
there was no scheme for giving premiums
to stallions in Northern Ireland. The
Ministry during each year has secured
from two to three high-class thoroughbred stallions. These sires were sold to
applicants selected by the County Committees of Agriculture at one-third of the
cost price, a loan, which has to be paid
off in five yearly instalments, also being
given for two-thirds of this net purchase
price. We have probably as a good a
selection of thoroughbred stallions in our
area as could be found in any similar
area throughout the British Isles, and
this is corroborated by the gentleman who
acted as judge at the last show at Balmoral. The judge, I may say, is one who
acts for the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries and for the War Office in
selecting premium thoroughbred horses
at the Olympia Show held each spring.
He reported:
Generally speaking, the collection,
consisting of 13 stallions, cannot be
considered anything but
anything but distinctly
good. The horses were of a high class
all through, and should, humanly
speaking, be expected to leave their
mark on the country. I particularly
appreciated the condition they were
shown in; good, hard, healthy condition, which is so much better, from a

In connection with Clydesdales-the
only heavy breed of horse encouraged and
subsidized by the Ministry-a number of
pedigree stallions of this breed have also
been purchased, sold on reduced terms,
and placed in districts where suitable
stallions were not available.
After the rearing of store cattle the
production of poultry and eggs is the
most important branch of Northern Ireland agriculture. In no other part of
the British Isles is poultry-keeping
practised on a more extensive scale than
in the Six Counties, where the hens are
an important object of care and
attention on all classes of farms. The
following table shows the number of each
class of poultry per 100 acres of crops and
pasture in Northern Ireland, the Irish
Free State, England and Wales, and in
Scotland. The table is based upon the
most recent figures available.

So that we show the largest increase per
100 acres in the poultry population of
the British Isles. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Unfortunately, it is to be feared that
egg production on many farms is still regarded in a somewhat haphazard manner.
It is the Ministry's object, however, to
endeavour to bring about such an improvement in the standard of poultrykeeping on the ordinary farms of the
country as will enable the humblest
farmer to obtain results which will compare favourably with those of the scientific
breeder. The pecuniary advantage to be
derived from a closer attention to breeding cannot be over-emphasized.
If poultry keepers would only concentrate on producing eggs during the winter
months, from September to February,
when eggs are most scarce and prices are
highest, instead of producing the bulk of
their eggs during the period from March
to July, their profits would be considerably greater than at present. In 1904
-the first year for which export statistics
for all Ireland are available-the export
of eggs amounted in value to £2,044,208,
and in 1925 the value of the eggs exported
from Northern Ireland alone was
£1,927,065. The export of eggs from
Northern Ireland ports in 1926 was almost equal in value to the total amount
realized for eggs exported from the
whole of Ireland in 1904.
The success of this work is largely due
to our County Agricultural Committees
and their poultry instructors. The Committees have egg stations established in
every county, by means of which the
smallest farmer, or his labourers, can
procure eggs from pedigree laying strains
of birds at a price of 2s. 6d. per setting.
The poultry instructors who are all
women are responsible for supervising
these egg stations, and it is also their
duty to give lectures throughout their
districts.
There are three schools for which the
Ministry is directly, or indirectly, responsible. Two of these-the Ulster
Dairy School at Cookstown and the North-
West School at Strabane-are devoted
entirely to the training of girls in rural
domestic economy, namely, dairying,
poultry, cooking, laundry and sewing.
When the Ministry was established in 1921
three-fifths of the pupils at the Cookstown
School came from counties outside of
Northern Ireland; to-day the pupils are
all drawn from the Six Counties. The
school has its full complement of fifty
pupils and we have a waiting list of
forty-nine. The Strabane School in 1921
drew its pupils from Counties Donegal,
Derry and Tyrone; now it draws its
pupils from the Six Counties, The
school has its full complement of twentyfive pupils and has also a waiting list.
The chief object of these schools is to
provide a training for girls in the subjects
mentioned, in order that they may return
home and put into practice many of the
lessons they have learnt, and by doing so
make better wives. Some are trained to

The Greenmount College is confined
entirely to the training of young men in
agriculture and horticulture. It is
managed by a special committee appointed by the Antrim County Committee
of Agriculture, and each of the other five
Committees of Agriculture support it by
sending pupils and giving scholarships.
This college originally could accommodate
only twenty-five boys and was
filled, but since 1922 it has been enlarged.
Dormitory accommodation for twentyfive more students has been provided,
new class-rooms and laboratories have
been built and equipped, and at the beginning of last session 45 students were
enrolled. The Ministry hopes that before long this college will be full and have
a waiting list similar to the girls' schools.
This college provides a training in the
theory and practice of agriculture and
horticulture for farmers' sons, and the
majority of the students who pass through
it return to the land.
Since 1900, under the old Department
of Agriculture, the County Committees,
with their staffs, have been responsible
for the following schemes: The winter
class scheme, by means of which classes
in agriculture are held in selected centres
in each county during the winter months,
for farmers' sons who are actually engaged in working on their own or their
fathers' farms. In 1921 in the Six
Counties there were ten classes held and
153 students attended, and in 1926 there
were twenty classes and 300 students.
There were also experimental and demonstration schemes, by which experiments
and demonstrations are carried out on
farms throughout the Six Counties by the
instructors on the growing of different
varieties of oats, potatoes, turnips,
mangels, the manuring of crops and the
feeding of farm animals on different
rations to ascertain which gives the best
and most economical results. In 1921
there were 99 experiments and demonstrations carried out in the Six Counties,
and in 1926 there were 899.
In regard to horticulture, a similar
scheme was in operation in each county,
and this applied also in the case of
poultry and butter-making schemes.
They also have live stock schemes, by
means of which premium sires are placed
in each of the Six Counties for the improvement of the live stock.
In 1921 there were no premium stallions. In 1926 we had 13 thoroughbreds,
23 Clydesdales, 1 Irish draught and 1 half.
bred stallion standing for premiums in
the Six Counties.
In 1921 there were 265 premium or subsidized bulls. In 1926 they had increased
to 416.
In 1921 there were 22 premium rams.
In 1926 there were 261 premium rams.
In 1921 there were 70 boars. In 1926
there were 105 boars.
By means of poultry stations farmers
and labourers can get settings of eggs of
pure-bred strains at reduced prices.
