When the Ministry commenced to
function in 1922 it realized that in the
poor mountainous districts in each county
a special effort was necessary and should
be made to benefit those small farmers on
the poorest land. The Government gave
a special grant of £54,000 for the development schemes, chiefly for this purpose.
The grant was to cover a period of four or
five years, and it was decided to spend
portion of it on the following schemes:
Special instructors to be placed in the
poorest districts in each county. 12 instructors are now at work and have to
visit farmers and advise them re crops,
etc., carry out demonstrations in manuring land with artificial manures,
growing of better varieties of potatoes,
oats, etc., forming better pastures, and
getting premium bulls, boars, rams and
poultry stations placed in these districts.
Last year these special instructors carried

the
As the Ministry has occasionally-very
often, I am afraid-to meet criticism in
connection with its policy relating to the
disease known as black scab, it may be
of interest to hon. Members if I outline
very briefly some of the considerations
which influence our actions. In the first
place, when outbreaks of black scab are
discovered, the surrounding district must
be scheduled, and that necessitates the
placing of restrictions on the planting and
sale of potatoes grown in the area so
scheduled. The scheduling is necessary
for two reasons, firstly, to prevent the
spread of the disease in Northern Ireland,
and, secondly, to safeguard our export
trade, as those countries which purchase
potatoes insist, for their own protection,
upon the scheduling of a considerable area
surrounding places where black scab has
been found.
We have a valuable export trade, not
only with great Britain but also with the
Free State, France, Malta,
Malta, Spain,
Portugal and Greece. All these countries
impose stringent regulations governing
the import of potatoes. For example,
Scotland requires certificates to the effect
that potatoes imported from Northern
Ireland were not grown in a scheduled
area nor within one mile of any place
where black scab has been found. Most
of the foreign countries require somewhat
similar certificates, and if the Ministry
were unable to issue such certificates
trade would be impossible and merchants
would be unable to find outlets for a considerable proportion of
surplus
potatoes available for export. The danger
of black scab spreading to clean areas is
always present, and the only really
effective safeguard is the planting of
varieties that are immune from the
disease. Unfortunately, the ideal white,
long-shaped shipping potato to replace
the Up-to-Date variety is not in existence,
and that fact presents a real difficulty.
our
I might sum up the Ministry's
activities in relation to the potato industry and particularly with regard to
those growers who live in scheduled areas
by referring to three points:
:-
Every possible effort is being made to
discover the most suitable varieties for our
growers. Experiments are each year conducted centrally at Stormont-where we
are always glad to arrange for visitors
to see the plots and also at different
places throughout the scheduled areas.
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Archdale]
By these means new varieties are verv
thoroughly tested under widely differing
conditions, and those interested have
opportunities of seeing them while they
are growing and also while they are
mature.
Steps have been taken to distribute
seed potatoes at reduced prices to growers
in scheduled areas with a view to introducing the varieties most suitable for the
markets in which the produce must be
sold. Under this arrangement
last
season over 800 tons of seed were distributed in Counties Down, Tyrone and
Londonderry. Assistance is given in
finding markets for the potatoes grown in
the scheduled areas. A year ago merchants in County Down experienced
difficulty in selling Lochar potatoes-
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ARCHDALE- -and the merchants in South Londonderry were faced
with the problem of finding an outlet for
coloured potatoes of the Arran Victory
type in Great Britain, where in the past
only white potatoes have been in demand.
In both cases the Ministry's Marketing
Inspector interviewed British buyers and
was able to give marked assistance in the
disposal of coloured potatoes in British.
markets.
When the Ministry of Agriculture was
established in 1921 the Forestry Commission transferred 3,845 acres of forestry
lands to Northern Ireland. These lands
are situated in three counties and comviz:-Baronscourt
prise four centres,
(County Tyrone), 2,820 acres; Knockmany (County Tyrone), 468 acres; Castlecaldwell (Co. Fermanagh), 303 acres;
Ballykelly (County Derry), 254 acres,
making a total of 3,845 acres. Since then
the Ministry has acquired 72 acres at
Baronscourt, 582 acres at Newcastle
(County Down), and 442 acres at Hillsborough (County Down), making a total
of 4,941.
From 1922 to the present date the
Ministry has planted 2,129 acres. Planting at Knockmany and Castlecaldwell is
now completed and this autumn the Newcastle area will all be planted. At Ballykelly we have 140 acres of full-grown
timber, and each year from 10 to 20 acres
are sold and the land is planted up again
as the trees are cut.
During the past year the Ministry inspected about 20 tracts of land which were
offered for forestry purposes. Only some
of these were suitable, but the prices asked
for these lands were quite prohibitive.
The Government's policy is to acquire
additional areas for afforestation, and my
Ministry is anxious to hear of suitable
blocks of land that can be purchased at
an economic price. This year the Ministry
has inspected several areas and is now
negotiating for the purchase of some of
them.
Land for forestry purposes generally
is worth only from £2 to £3 per acre to
purchase outright, or from 2s to 3s per
acre to rent, although in exceptional
cases, where the land is good and well
sheltered, it may be worth a little more.
We have issued a forestry scheme to
assist farmers who wish to plant small
areas
as shelter belts, and young trees
will be sold to such farmers at cost price
from our own nurseries. Landowners
or those who intend to plant large areas
can secure a grant of £2 per acre for
planting and a grant of £1 per acre for
clearing scrub.
The Ministry of Labour assisted my
Ministry in procuring out-of-employment
labour to help in planting operations during 1925-26 and 1926-27, and up to the
31st March last £3,730 had been expended
in this way.

afraid I do not know at present. When
the Ministry was established in 1922, no

The Ministry approached
University authorities, and eventually it
was arranged that the University would
establish a faculty of agriculture and
would provide temporary buildings in
order that classes in agricultural science
subjects might be conducted. At the same
time temporary buildings for research
were lent to the Ministry by the University until permanent buildings would be
erected.
The Ministry have offered each year
six agricultural scholarships of the value
of £100 per annum for four years tenable
at Queen's University. There are at
present 22 students taking out the degree
course in agriculture at Queen's, and the
first set of students will complete their
course in this year 1927. Seventeen of
these are Ministry scholarships, 2 are
Gibson scholarships, and three are fee
paying.
For the erection of a permanent building to train such students and to carry
out research work in agricultural botany,
agricultural chemistry, animal nutrition,
dairy bacteriology, animal and plant husbandry, the Ministry gave a grant of
£36,000 to Queen's University. The late
Miss Riddel gave £5,000 and the
University provided a free site and gave
£6,000. In addition, the Ministry provides the teaching staff for the applied
science subjects, equipment, etc. It is
expected that this building will be
completed by October next.
as
There is no industry which has made
progress during the last 50 years which
does not owe its development mainly to
scientific research. Agriculture is the
industry which, above all others, requires
research most, but it has benefited least.
It is only during the last 36 years that in
Great Britain the State has granted funds
for education and scientific research
applied to agriculture, and in Ireland it
is only 26 years since the Department of
Agriculture was established and provided
with funds for this work. The funds
available, however, were extremely
limited compared with those provided by
other countries, such as the United States,
Canada, Germany, France, Denmark,
Sweden, Holland, etc.
At the outset my Ministry realized that
if agriculture in Northern Ireland was to
succeed, and if we were to hold our place
with competing countries, it was imperative that scientific research in certain subjects should be undertaken and carried
out on sound lines. As no buildings or
laboratories were available, the Ministry
had to proceed to get plans prepared and
buildings erected. This has all taken
time. As I have already mentioned,
Queen's University very generously placed
certain temporary huts at the disposal of
my Ministry which enabled us to make a
start with a seed-testing and plant diseases
division and a chemical and nutrition
division until the new buildings at Elmwood Avenue were available. The old
farm buildings at Stormont were adapted
to the purposes of a plant-breeding division and an animal diseases station, and
these adaptations were completed early in
1926 only. Provision was also made for
research in poultry at Stormont.
We have, therefore, now established
seven research divisions:
At Queen's University-1, seed-testing
and plant diseases division; 2, agricultural chemical division; 3, animal nutrition division; 4, crop and animal husbandry division.
At Stormont-5, plant-breeding division; 6, animal diseases division; 7,
poultry division.
Research work requires very great
accuracy and concentrated attention, and
a discovery or new line of development
which may benefit the agricultural community requires to be tested again and
again for several years before one would
be justified in publishing results, as in
agricultural problems the seasons,
weather and different conditions arising
may have a very direct influence on the
results. If one were to issue a report of
what was believed to be a new discovery
on the results of one year's work only,
without repeating the test and confirming
the results, it might be found that the
second and third years' trials did not
agree with the first, and the agricultural
community would not only be misled,
but, in future, would place no reliance or
confidence in either the published results
of research work, or in the Ministry's
advice.
The Ministry, therefore, laid it down
as a sine qua non that they would publish
no results on research or experimental
work until these had been confirmed
beyond yea or nay. It is only five years

since my Ministry was established, and we

yesterday. The Empire Marketing

£2,000 per annum for maintenance.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is a

hear).
One of the functions of each Research
Division is to advise farmers on technical
matters relating to the various aspects of
the industry. Such work is intimately
associated with research, and it could not
be adequately carried out without the
facilities which are provided in the
Last year
several Research Divisions.
advice was given in over 1,500 cases.
Hon. Members may be disposed to ask
what direct benefits the practical farmer
has so far derived from the research
activities of the Ministry, and I propose,
therefore, very briefly to refer to a few
examples. In the past it has been
customary to have cattle ready for killing
for beef at from 2 to 3 years' old. Such
cattle when killed weighed from 11 to 13
cwt. During the last few years, however,
a demand has arisen for smaller joints
from earlier maturing cattle. This demand is general not only in the British
Isles but also in America and on the
Continent. The Ministry realizing that
our farmers must change with the times
carried out experiments for several years
with the object of producing beef (baby
beef) from animals of from 7 to 9 cwt. each
and which were killed when from 12 to 18
months' old. The experiments proved
beyond question that not only can such
young animals, if properly reared, be
fattened for beef but that it is economical
to so fatten them. It is simply a matter
of applying (1) intensive methods of fattening, (2) of having the right type of
animals, and (3) of exercising intelligence
in the correct use of proper foods. Better
quality, is produced and the joints are of
the size now in demand. The production
of baby beef is now an ordinary practice
on many farms in County Down and elsewhere. Last spring two special auction
sales of these young fat cattle were held
in Belfast at which many animals were
sold to buyers from England and Scotland.
A
It is the practice of farmers to supplement the roots and fodder given to their
dairy cows with some form of meals.
large proportion of farmers used for this
purpose either ground oats or Indian meal
or a mixture of these two foods, viz.,
foods rich in starch, and many farmers
still follow this practice. Those who are
progressive, however, have availed themselves of the information placed at their
disposal by the Ministry and now use what
is known as a "balanced ration,'
" which
consists of proteins of albuminoids as well
as starch in the proper proportion to
nourish the animals and produce milk.
This ration is composed of a mixture of
cake and meal in the correct proportions.
Its advantages are briefly :--(a) increased
milk yield, (b) lower cost of production,
(c) better health of cows.
Those who are feeding their dairy stock
on a "balanced ration" are having extraordinarily good results compared with the
old method, and I may say that the
members of the Milk Recording Society
in my county are largely feeding their
cows on this ration, which has greatly
increased the average yield.
For more than twenty years farmers
relied to a large extent upon the use of
high-grade basic slag-a phosphatic fertilizer for the improvement of their
pastures. This manure was a by-product
from the manufacture of steel. Since the
war changes in the process of steel manufacture have taken place, with the result
that high-class basic slag has become very
scarce and practically disappeared from
the market. Farmers would have been
seriously handicapped if no substitute had
been forthcoming. The Ministry, foreseeing the trend of events, carried out
experiments in every county in Northern
Ireland, and these have proved conclusively
that equally good results can be ob

tained at less cost from a new fertilizer
known as rock phosphate. This is a raw
product imported from North Africa. It
is simply ground to a very fine powder
before it is applied to the land. At the
present time the price per unit of phosphate in rock phosphate is little more than
half the unit price of phosphate in basic
slag. Farmers realize the advantages of
the new fertilizer, and each year it is being
used in considerably larger quantities for
application both to grass land and to
turnips.
Perhaps I may be permitted to quote
one further case in which very material
benefits have been derived by farmers
from the result of research and experimental work. I refer to the potato crop.
During the decade 1891-1900 the average
yield of saleable potatoes in the nine
counties of Ulster was 3.7 tons per statute
acre. During the following decade 1901-
10, when the Department of Agriculture
was functioning, it was 5.2 tons, and from
1911-20 it was 5.8 tons per statute acre,
an increase of 2.1 tons per acre.
Taking the average acreage in Ulster,
namely, 250,000 acres, during the period
1901-20, and valuing the potatoes at £3
per ton, we find that the value of the increased yield during the period of twenty
years was approximately 27 million
pounds. Credit for this may be given to
the Department of Agriculture, which
made known the benefits to be derived
from (a) sprouting the seed, (b) applying
a proper mixture of artificial manures,
and (c) spraying the crop.
While it is yet too soon to expect me to
quote figures seeing that the value of the
research work carried out by my Ministry
approximates to millions of pounds, steady
progress is being made. Startling discoveries need not be expected, however;
but new and improved methods are
gradually being adopted, often without
the farmers themselves realizing the extent of them. Such developments do lead
to progress, and very largely in this dírection lies the hope for agriculture in the
future.
The Estimate that is now before the
Committee provides for the administrative expenses of the Ministry, salaries
and expenses of headquarter staff, maintenance of headquarter offices, and expenses of a general overhead nature.
There is an increase of £2,564 in the total
Estimate, of which £1,850 is attributable
to the salary sub-head, representing for
the most part automatic increments of
salary. The staff provided for is the
same as last year. Postage expenses show
an increase of £550, which is accountable
for most of the balance of the total excess over last year's Estimate. In travelling and subsistence expenses there is a
small increase of £200, to cover travelling
and removal expenses of officers, which
occur as a result of the development of
services. In rent, rates and fuel there is
a reduction of £230, and there is a slight
reduction in maintenance, renewals and
repairs.
With regard to stationery, books and
office supplies, there is an aggregate reduction of £110, and law charges show a
slight increase to cover the expenses of
prosecutions for infringement of the provisions of various Acts and Orders. The
increase under the sub-head of postage,
telegrams and telephones is inevitable as
the Ministry's work develops, and it has
increased largely since we took over the
Council of Ireland services. Incidental
expenses show an increase of £65, and we
require a slight provision for the purchase
of uniforms for the ship inspectors at the
ports. This year is the year for buying
great-coats for the inspectors, and this
sub-head shows a slight increase for that
reason. In connection with the Receipts
Appropriated-in-Aid, there was provision.
for a payment by the County Committee
of Agriculture, but that disappears as the
officer in question has come back to the
Ministry. I beg to move.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: I desire to move a

there is an increase, a small one, I admit,

some £2,500, and, as the Minister has

If we take item A, on page 16, the headquarter staff, we find there
officials, costing £8,300 in salaries alone.
To that would be added some part of the

item on the next page. In my opinion
this area of Northern Ireland is not getting a sufficient return for this amount.
In other words, the headquarter staff
might be run with half the officials, or
with two or three less than it has, and at

We have had a very interesting and
long explanation of the details of the
work of this Department during the past
twelve months, but I hardly think the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Agriculture, could have the credit that
he claims endorsed by any large section
of the community which he serves.
Indeed, I think he has taken credit on behalf of his Department for many of the
things that are due to a great extent, if
not solely, to the action of the farmers
themselves, and that the position would
not have been much worse, if any, had
there not been a Ministry of Agriculture
at all. With regard to the question of
afforestation, the Minister has told us of
the work that has been done in that respect, of the areas which have been or
are in course of being planted, and
he also told us that the Department were
anxious, or rather were willing, to
purchase suitable land for afforestation.
I have been wondering if he himself has
not considered that portion of the Mourne
Mountains, in the vicinity of Rostrevor,
which he himself should know very well
and which, in my opinion, is quite suitable for this purpose. I should like to
know from him whether he has made any
inquiries as to whether land as suitable
as some of the land he has taken is not
available there for this purpose.
With regard to the land the Ministry
have taken at Newcastle, County Down,
I understand that it belongs to the
Annesley Estate, and that previous to the
Department taking this land over for
planting the owners denuded it of timber
and sold it for commercial purposes.
That, in my opinion, is a thing this Committee should not endorse. It should not
allow individuals to cut down their plantations and then let them to the Department for the purpose of re-planting. I
think that is altogether wrong, and if the
facts are as I have stated I hope the
practice will not be pursued in the future.
The Minister also told us that his
Ministry were anxious to take an even
better quality of land than that which
had usually been offered. In my opinion
it is a mistake to plant land that is suitable for other purposes, either for grazing
or cultivation. I understand that at the
present time some negotiations are going
on for the acquirement of land in the
vicinity of Castlewellan, also on the
Annesley Estate, land which is quite
suitable for grazing and which is being
used at present for that purpose.
I
think it would be a mistake on the part of
the Department to take land of that
nature for the purpose of planting when
there is more suitable land available in
other neighbourhoods.
There is one other matter, indeed it was
the principal matter on which I intended
to speak. It is in connection with the
dismissal of an official of the Department.
The Minister is quite aware of all the
facts in connection with the case. I have

with, so far as I am concerned, most

district. He had been employed under
the old Department of Agriculture, and
when the Ministry of Agriculture was
established he decided to stay in the
North, although I understand he had
been offered a position under the Free
State Government. But, for some reason

Department dismissed him, most unjustifiably so far as I know, and I have been
supplied with many of the facts, at least
so far as the official is concerned. Without notice of any sort, and without complaints of any kind having been made
against him, he was summoned to the Department in December last. There most
of the officers in charge-the permanent
staff-six or seven of them-met him in a
room, and made many complaints against
him. He was taken quite unawares, of
course, as he told me, but to me the
charges did not seem to be such as would
warrant his dismissal. However, when he
told me of the matter I advised him to
ask the Department to set out the particulars of these charges so that he would
be in a position to meet them. He did
so, but the Department never gave him.
any particulars as to why he was dismised.
When this happened I wrote to the

he refused. He said it was a domestic
matter, in other words that it was a

ment that is not a fair way to treat a
public representative, and in this House
I now claim that the Minister should

Mr. ELLIOTT: I rise to support this
Vote, and of course to oppose the Amendment which has just been proposed by the
hon. Member for Down (Mr. Patrick
O'Neill). I have listened very carefully

forward by the hon. Member for Down

inspector in whom he is interested has
been dismissed. I do not know anything
at all about this inspector, but I understand that if a potato inspector, or any
other Civil Servant employed by the

Ministry, is dismissed and treated unfairly he has an opportunity of appealing
to the Civil Service Committee for redress,
if such is required. The gentleman referred to, I understand, had that opportunity of appealing, and I have not found
out yet whether he has appealed or not.
If he has appealed to the Civil Service
Committee, and they have turned down
his case, it would appear to me that the
action of the Ministry was justified. If

Committee to have his case reheard it
would appear to me that he had no case
to appeal on, so that if the hon. Member
for Down has no other reason or motive
for moving a reduction of this Vote I
certainly think that his case is a very
weak one.
I would like to congratulate the right
hon. Gentleman who presides over the
Ministry of Agriculture on the very lucid.
statement which he has put before us this

I would like to take this opportunity
also of congratulating the right hon.
Gentleman on the fact that he has been

While I do not agree altogether with

a good deal of the criticism that has been

House about bulls is due to ignorance of
the facts.

With reference to the selection of bulls,
it has been mentioned to me on more than
one occasion that when the inspectors go
round to inspect bulls for licensing they
do not take into account the pedigree of
the animal offered for selection, that they
simply go on the make, the shape, and the
quality of the animal as it appears before
them without any reference at all to the
record of the sire or the dam. I was in
conversation with the Ministry's inspectors not so very long ago, and I was
assured that that is not the case, and that
the Ministry's inspectors not only take
into account the quality of the bull offered
for licence but also any circumstances that
are brought to their notice with reference
to the milking qualities of the dam or
the milking strain of the sire. I would
like the Ministry to encourage that as
far as possible, and to see that bulls of
milking strain are the bulls licensed and
kept for service in Northern Ireland.

If we have County Agricultural Committees elected democratically by the people,
and who are the direct representatives of

have no fault to find with the inspectors;
I am sure they are qualified men, but I
know that a strange man who is brought
from one place to another is not acquainted with the soil there nor the nature of
it, nor the aspects of the country further
than what he sees. He has not the same
information as the local people. I think
the Ministry ought to consult the local

people as to the class of cattle that would

With regard to the schools and colleges
and experimental farms, I believe they
are doing good work. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). I do not think, however,
that it is getting to the poorer farmers
quickly enough. I would be glad if the
Minister would spend £1,000 or £2,000
more in this way. Get some of these
skilled men he has and put them down on
a 40-acre farm in the country, buy them
everything they need-five cows, two
horses and all necessary implements and
pay the interest on a debt of £500; plant
them seven miles from a market town
and three miles from a bog where they
can get their fuel, and let them show the
farmers of Co. Antrim or any other part
of the Six County area how they would
make that farm pay. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). Personally, I would be
quite willing to vote a couple of thousand
pounds extra if the Ministry would get
a man to go down and show farmers something in a practical way like that.
I hope that some such step will be taken.
It is not good enough to say that there
are schools at Greenmount and Lisburn.
The majority of our farmers are small
people with farms of from 15 to 30 and 50
acres, and it is difficult for them to make
money. I rejoice with the Minister that
the breed of cattle has improved and that
cows are giving increased milk. I am glad
to know that the poultry are appreciated
throughout the country and that so many
good results are accruing under his administration. I support this Vote with
all my heart. I believe that the Minister
is trying to do his best. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
should like to join in congratulating the
right hon. Gentleman on the full and
comprehensive statement he has given to
the Committee this afternoon. While it
was rather difficult to follow the mass of
.
figures he put forth I think he managed
in his speech to convey a good deal
of valuable information to the Committee with regard to this, our
most important industry. I should like
also to congratulate the right hon.
Gentleman on the valuable work carried
out by his Department in different ways
in regard to agriculture. I think in the
schemes for the improvement of live stock,
for the education of the agricultural comimunity and for helping the breeds of
poultry the Department is really carrying on in this community a valuable work
on behalf of agriculture. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
I suppose it is the right hon. Gentleman's misfortune that he has to present
this Estimate when his Ministry has fallen
on rather evil days. He has occupied the
position to-day rather of a manager of
works who probably has to justify to his
shareholders the installation of an everincreasing bit of machinery while the output is going down. It is, unfortunately,
true that with all these advantages and
all these schemes no matter where we look
the output of this industry is on the decline. Taking our dairying industry,
from statistics given not very long ago
by the Department we find that we are
only exporting from this area about onethird the butter we exported twelve years
ago. I think that is a very serious state
of affairs, because, as the right hon.
Gentleman said to-day, and said very
truly, our dairying industry is the key to
successful agriculture in this area.
I feel there is some justification for
putting the blame for this great decline
in our dairying industry on the policy of
our Agricultural Department in the past.
I believe myself that this policy is being
changed at the present time. I do not
know whether it is definitely changed or
not, but I feel there is a change in regard
to the policy of the Department in relation
to the dairying industry. In the past
the industry suffered from the fact that
the Department got a type of animal into
their minds that was intended entirely for
the production of beef. They forgot that
in encouraging and forcing this special
type of animal on this area serious harm
might be done to our dairying industry.
There is a great deal of truth in the statement that the Department in the past
has contributed largely to the decline in
dairying by introducing that type of
animal into their area.

Even last year it took very serious
pressure from this House to get the
Government to consent to appoint a Committee to inquire into the reasons for this
very serious decline in our key industry
in agriculture. I do not wish to make
complaints unnecessarily here, but I feel
that the success of that Committee will be
largely due to its personnel. I did take
the liberty to suggest to the Minister of
Agriculture the names of two gentlemen
I thought particularly fitted to sit on this
Committee. If they had been added they
would have been a great advantage to the
Committee. One of them is a man who
established a herd of cows in this community, two of which hold world records.
He has had experience of the industry
in America, he has travelled on the Continent, and he was responsible for the
establishment in his own district of a small
Co-operative Creamery that turns milk
into butter. When I tell this Committee
that the year before last that little Cooperative Creamery ran its business on
such successful lines that it was able to
pay suppliers of milk 1s 4d a gallon, I
think Members will recognize that if we
could only get the rest of the dairying
industry to be run on the same lines we
would largely solve the problem how to
make agriculture profitable. Last year
was not quite so good a year, but nevertheless that little Co-operative Society
paid to its suppliers of milk in the country
1s. 2d. per gallon. They turned the milk
into butter and the butter was sold in the
city of Belfast.
Dr. MORRISON : Did you see the
balance sheet?
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I did
not see anything. I got the information
from members of the Society, whose word
I can rely upon. There is no secret about
it. It is the Ballycarry Society, an Agricultural Co-operative Society that turns
milk into butter and sends the butter to
Belfast; and I am informed that the result of their efforts is as I have stated.
I do not want to say it is possible to carry
this scheme out as successfully over the
whole of the Province, because the people
at Ballycarry have an advantage in their
proximity to the city of Belfast. They
can sell their buttermilk there, but if we
could run the dairying industry on lines
that would give the suppliers of milk to
our dairies an average price of a
shilling or even less per gallon, we would
have solved the problem of agriculture.
The members of this Society have solved
the problem by stabilizing their supply.
They make it worth a man's while to produce a stable supply of milk the whole
year round, and they are able to supply
to their customers almost exactly the
same amount of butter and milk in
December as they do in June. If this
Dairying Committee is to be of any use to
the dairying industry it must begin with
the fact that the problem is to stabilize,
to a great extent, the supply of good
milk all the year round.
Mr. ARCHDALE: It is very hard.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I know
it is hard, but here is a little Society that
has done it, and another Society that has
done the same thing is the Belfast Cooperative Society. They have done it by
penalizing the man who does not give a
stable supply. The man who does not
give them a stable supply all the year
round is penalized in the price he gets.
I do not know whether it would be possible for the Government to do the same
thing, but some scheme of this kind must
be adopted, or some system of subsidy
must be given to encourage farmers to
produce a more stable supply of milk the
whole year round. I do think it is deplorable that in this area of ours, which,
it has been said, nature has made one of
the finest dairying places in the world, we
should at the present time be importing,
as, I think, the figures show, more butter
than we are exporting.
Then we come to the export of live
stock, and what do we find? We find
there has been a very serious decrease
during the last two or three years in the
export of live stock from Northern Ireland. The Minister of Agriculture referred to correspondence that has been
going on in the newspapers with regard
to this very important matter, and I think
it is well that this subject should be .
ventilated, because it is an important
matter that means a great deal to our
community. It has been said that there
is never smoke but there is fire, and I
think some of the figures put before the
Committee by the right hon. Gentleman
this afternoon go to prove that there is,
at least, ground for inquiry into the
question of whether the present system of
licensing bulls is not, at least to some
extent, responsible for the decrease in
young cattle and in our exports of live
stock. If you take the figures given by
Ministry of Agriculture 1016
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. George Henderson]
the right hon. Gentleman, he said, if I
took the figures correctly, that in 1923
there were licensed in this area 6,209
bulls, and in 1926 there were 6,639
licensed. That was an increase. Now
we have more bulls licensed and we have
less calves. Is that not so?
Mr. ARCHDALE: There have been
new diseases discovered amongst cows
which did not operate to the same extent
before-sterility in COWS and other
things.
But
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
the facts are that we had more bulls
licensed in 1926 than in 1923, and yet
we have fewer calves, and our exports of
livestock have decreased. From my own
experience I would be slow, in fact I
would be opposed to scrapping the compulsory licensing of bulls, because I think
it is important, as the Minister said, to
keep up not only the quantity but the
quality of our exports. At the same time
I do feel that there are grounds for an
inquiry, and, as the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has suggested,
there might be a little more give and take
with regard to this question. You will
find in most districts of Ulster that
generations of families have farmed in a
particular district, and these men get to
know the sort of stock that will best suit
their district. In my own district I
hardly know a farmer who was not
anxious to improve his stock and produce
the best calves possible. The only exception was in the case of a man who put
heifers to grass and sent them to the
market. He bought a cheap and inferior
bull to put with them, because if the
heifers were in calf they were good
enough to sell.
I would appeal to the right hon. Gentleman to see if there could be a little more
give and take, and in this connection
perhaps I should pay a little tribute to
the Department, because I did interfere
in the case of one small farmer.
He was
a most efficient farmer who had a small
herd of twelve cows, several of which were
almost dry. By grading up his stock he
was able to send to the Belfast Co-operative Society 135 gallons of milk per day.
He had a 1,500 gallon cow, and a bull
which he was anxious to preserve on account of the milking qualities its dam
possessed. He applied for a licence for
the bull, which was refused.
He appealed, and the refusal was upheld. I
made an appeal to the Department on
behalf of the man, and I understand the
Ministry have given him liberty to keep
the bull. If that is true I wish to pay a
tribute to them and to say that there
probably is a little give and take. I hope
the policy of the Department is changing
with regard to the licensing of bulls.
The other figures the Minister has given
go to show that the Ministry do not appreciate the importance of our dairying
industry. Take the premium the Department give to milk recording societies
which buy bulls. We find that the premium is limited to £73. These bulls
bought by the milk recording societies are
as a rule bulls that are bought for the
milk records held by their progeny. Take
the other class of bulls, for which the
Department give a subsidy of £253. I
gather that is more for beef than for milk
stock. Therefore, the balance seems to
be be still in favour of beef rather than of
milk.
There is another rather important point
about our dairying industry, and it is
that you cannot carry on that industry
without giving a considerable amount of
employment. On the other hand you can
produce beef without giving any very
considerable amount of employment,
and I think this is another reason why
the Department should not discriminate
between the dairying industry and the
beef industry. Again, take the question
of the Government's policy in regard to
cheap credit for farmers. I have tried to
impress on this Committee the importance
to our agricultural industry of cheap
credit. The policy in the past has really
been putting a premium on grazing rather
than on tillage. The policy of the
Government should be to give these loans
to the men who have lost stock.
If we
look at our tillage farming what do we
find? We find that tillage farming is
terribly on the decrease. I do not want
to suggest that the right hon. Gentleman or his Department can entirely
obviate that decrease, but again it is something that should give rise to most serious
thought on the part of the Government.
and on the part of any man interested in
the welfare of the community.
As the Member for West Belfast has
said, there is nothing that makes for
stability in a community like a healthy
and prosperous peasantry, and there
should be some scheme initiated by the
Government to help our tillage farmers.

I believe the Irish Free State are about

between the two Goverments and considerably more co-operation and consultation. I do not think there is any
industry that would have benefited more

the industry of agriculture. I would,

of Ireland.
With regard to the question of research, I certainly think there is a field
here in which important valuable work can

Every other industry has brought science

field that has been so much unexplored,

industry.
Take, for instance, the question of
pedigree flax. I was very much interested last year in three or four plots
that I saw in County Antrim, which

that from the ordinary Dutch
Dutch and
Riga flax seed. I am sorry that

Dr. MORRISON: There are one or
two broad general questions arising out
of this Estimate and the discussion that
has taken place in the Committee to
which I should like briefly to refer.
great deal of money is being spent with
the object of reviving the dairying industry in this country. The Member for
Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) has
given us a very rosy picture of the possibilities in this direction and of the
prices that can be secured for milk and
butter. I am sorry to say that I cannot
with him.
agree
I cannot agree with
the rosy estimate put before the House
by the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh in this matter. In looking over
the reports of the different co-operative
creameries that have been working in our
area I see that the average price paid for
milk last year was 7d per gallon-7d, 71d,
or 7d a gallon. I do not think that is
a remunerative price, or that farmers, if
they cannot get better, will be content.
I think if we cannot get a market for
milk and as far as I see, for the majority
of milk producers in Ulster at the present
time, there is practically no market-it
would be an unwise thing to be placing
our money in that work.
It seems to me it is a question of milk
or beef. There is no doubt that if you
improve the milking qualities of the cow
you injure the beef, and beef is a thing
that can be produced easily, and it can
be easily marketed in the best market in
the world. I think, myself, that in
trying to develop milk we are putting our
money on the wrong horse.
I should like to say that I agree very
heartily with the praise that has been
given to the Minister of Agriculture.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) He has
shown, so far as I can see, great sympathy
with the agriculturists in our area. I
can say here that I have very little
practical experience of what is going on,
but I know from some people actively
engaged in breeding and agriculture that
the Department is doing well in nearly
everything it touches. That is the testimony that I have heard again and again
from people very well qualified to give it.
In one or two cases where we had complaints I looked into the matter and
made inquiries and I found that the
action of the Department was right. And,
therefore, I am glad to give this testimony on behalf of the Ministry.
There is one thing I noticed in the speeches
to-day. They are more sympathic to the
agriculturists generally than some of the
speeches that I have heard in this House,
and I am glad to know it and recognize
it, because at the present time I think
there is a widespread feeling in rural
Ulster that the sympathies of Belfast
are not with the farming community
at the present time. I think there
is an element of truth in that, and
it arises from what we can see and
an easily explained cause. I think it
is a proper thing to consider what I
have heard stated by men within easy
access of the markets in Belfast that for
every load coming from the farmers placed
.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]
on the markets in Belfast by the farmer
and his horses he receives a pound more
than the agriculturist in rural Ulster
does, and, consequently, you will have a
prosperous, well-groomed cheerful farmer
in the vicinity of Belfast who is not to
be found when you get back to the
Hinterland, and you judge of the conditions of agriculture all over Ulster by
the effects you see on the farmers who are
wealthy and prosperous in the vicinity
of Belfast. I had a friend who had a
deputation with him very recently looking into
some stud horses. One of
them was a farmer in the vicinity
of Belfast with 60 acres of land.
He came down well groomed, well set
up, and prosperous as a country squire,
and he was able to tell him that
he was getting ls 5d a gallon for his
milk. The man to whom he told this
had a creamery within a mile of him,
worked by Belfast business men, and the
price was so low that he never dreamt
of sending milk to it.
I venture to say that the average price
in that creamery at the present time is
7d a gallon. I would like to suggest that
these things are hard for the rural farmer.
My honest conviction is this, that for 60
per cent. or 70 per cent, or possibly 80
per cent, they have no interest at the
end of the year on the capital invested
in the land, and they have no wages for
the worker owing to the depressed condition of agriculture at the present time.
I think they deserve the sympathy of
everybody. And as for the agricultural
worker my opinion is this, that he is the
hardest worker and the worst paid man
in the labour market. And if the Minister of Agriculture can do anything to
remedy these conditions for rural agriculture he will have done a noble work
for the prosperity of Ulster.

It is entirely a case of domestic discipline,

temporary official, liable to dismissal on

do not think there was any star chamber

as a transferred officer before the special

In reply to my hon. Friend (Mr.
Elliott) behind me, I am afraid I cannot
promise to add Cookstown or Coagh to
the list of places at which premium bulls
are selected. The opinion of the experts
of my Ministry is against such a step. I
acknowledge that when I was standing
at the last election I said that I was in
favour of Cookstown being chosen, and
would do my best to get it chosen, but
when I looked into the whole case with
the advice of the experts I found that it

out, so as to be able to choose premium
bulls which are of equal standard.
The hon. Member for Down (Mr.
Patrick O'Neill) referred to the question
of not taking agricultural land for
forestry. That is our opinion, and for
that reason we think the price we are
giving, which is more than the price given
in England, is a good one. The average
rent given for all land bought for
forestry in England is between 2s 6d
and 3s an acre, which works out at from
£2 10s to £3 for purchase outright. The
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) was inquiring on this subject,
too. The difficulty we have in Ireland
is that nearly all the land in Ireland is
owned by the small tenant occupier, by
the small proprietor. You have not the
large tracts of unoccupied land suitable
for forestry such as they have in Dorsetshire and Wiltshire, and other places in
England where they are establishing these
big places for forestry. I think I told
my hon. Friend the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) that we had only
planted 2,000 acres.
The total acreage
we have planted since 1922 is 2,189, and
we have offers out for about 1,000 more
acres. If we can get suitable land we
shall certainly buy it, but we are not
going to take for forestry land upon
which men can be put. I do not think
that would be economical.

difficulty about sugar beet is that last

My hon. Friend, the Member for

The two hon. Members for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford and Mr. McAllister) spoke
about the class of bulls in the poor districts. We do look into that, and we try
to have pure pedigree bulls put into the
poor districts. In a great many cases we
even supply bulls, under the auspices of
the county committees, to farmers in poor
districts. We pay nearly all the price,
and give them time to pay back the
balance of the money. Therefore, I think
we are giving all the help we can in that
connection.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
George Henderson) referred to the decrease in the number of cattle. Besides
cows and calves which had fluke last year,
owing to three bad seasons there has been
so much bad hay in Ireland that a great
many cows have gone astray. I believe
that has more to with the diminution than
anything else we can think of.
Two years
ago there was a very large export of cattle
from this country; and between the large
export, the deaths of cattle, and cows not
being in calf, the number of cattle at present is very low, but I am glad to say it
is increasing. There are now more incalf heifers which augurs well for the
rfuture.
The hon. Member (Mr. William
McMullen) spoke about cultivation during the war. There is no question that
it did not pay, and that is the reason it
was not continued. We are doing all we
can to encourage tillage, especially by
potato growing. There is no better way
of keeping land fit for cultivation than
by growing potatoes.

CIVIL SERVICE SELECTION
BOARD.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether it is a fact that the
Selection Board in connection with the
Northern Ireland Civil Service has been
abolished; and if so, whether he will state
the new methods and procedure to be
adopted in relation to appointments to
the Civil Service of Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not a fact that
the use of Selection Boards in connection with entrance to the Civil Service
of Northern Ireland has been abolished.
The Civil Service Commissioners are continuing to use such Boards to assist them
in assessing the merits of candidates
for permanent appointments, while the
Ministry of Finance is doing likewise as
regards candidates for temporary appointments. The Boards dealing with these
two classes of appointments, viz. :-
permanent and temporary, are appointed
by, and derive their powers from, the Civil
Service Cimmissioners and myself respectively. A recent change has, however,
been made in regard to the competition
for appointments of Junior Clerk in the
Service, the interview by a Selection
Board having been definitely incorporated!
in the examination. The marks awarded
to a candidate by the Board will, therefore, in future be aggregated with his
marks for other subjects for the purpose
of determining his final placing.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the Selection
Board remain as it was?
Mr. POLLOCK: Exactly.
Mr. DEVLIN: Has the right hon.
Gentleman considered the suggestions
made that there should be additions or
changes on that Board so as to give all
parties representation on it?
Mr. POLLOCK: No. I have not considered that. As I have mentioned in my
reply to the question, the Civil Service
Commissioners operate in matters relating to permanent admissions to the
Service, and it is only in the matter of

PRODUCTION OF BIRTH
CERTIFICATES.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware that forms
have been circulated among the parents
of children attending public elementary
schools in North Antrim, to be filled in
by the custodians of the registers of
births, with directions that, for each
school child, birth certificates shall be
sent to the principal of the school
attended by the child, the parents in each
case paying the cost of the same, whether
this has been done by order of the North
Antrim Regional Education Committee;
and, if not, by whom was the order
given; in how many other regions has a
similar order been made; and whether he
approves of such a burden being placed on
comparatively poor persons.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The Ministry
has ascertained from the North Antrim
Regional Education Committee that it is
not the case that forms have been
circulated among the parents of the
children attending public elementary
schools in the area under the control of
that Committee to be filled in by the
custodians of the registers of birth with
directions that for each school child a
birth certificate shall be sent to the
principal of the school attended by the
child, the parents in each case paying the
cost of same. The Ministry is not aware
of any region where such an order has
been made, and, accordingly, the last part
of the question does not arise.

SALARIES OF SECRETARIES.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will state the
salaries which the several secretaries of
the sub-commitees on School Attendance
in North Antrim received from public
sources for the discharge of public services, other than that of those secretaryships, during the year ended the 31st.
March, 1927.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to the
Ministry's records the salaries received
during the year ended 31st March, 1927,
by the several Secretaries or Clerks of
School Attendance Committees of the
North Antrim Regional Education Committee for the discharge of public services
other than those rendered to School
Attendance Committees are as follow:
The Clerk of the Cushendall School
Attendance Committee holds the appointment of Petty Sessions Clerk, in respect
of which he received a salary of £65.
The Clerk of the Ballymoney School
Attendance Committee holds the appointments of Clerk of the Ballymoney Union
and Clerk and Executive Sanitary Officer
of the Ballymoney Rural District Council, in respect of which he received from
the Union salary
salary and emoluments
amounting to £581 6s 8d, and from the
Rural District Council £401 5s Od.
The Clerk of the Portrush School
Attendance Committee holds the appointment of Clerk, Executive Sanitary
Officer and Registrar of Dairies under the
Portrush Urban District Council, in respect of which he received salaries
amounting to £475.
There is no record that the Clerk of the
Ballycastle School Attendance Committee
received salary from any other public
sources.
LOANS FOR ARTIFICIAL
MANURES.
8. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it would be possible, with the money at his disposal, to
issue loans to farmers for the purchase
of artificial manures for the grass lands
of Northern Ireland on the same terms
as loans are at present issued for the
replacement of live stock.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): In addition to the
special scheme of Live Stock Replacement
Loans the Ministry, as the hon. Member
is, no doubt, aware, grants loans to
farmers for the following purposes:-
(a) the purchase of agricultural machinery and implements;
(b) the purchase of pure-bred sires;
(c) the erection of wire fencing in
mountainous districts.
The Ministry of Finance under the
Landed Property Improvement (Ireland)
Acts also grants loans to farmers for the
renovation and erection of dwellinghouses, out-offices and silos, and for such
works as drainage and fencing.
Moreover my Ministry, in conjunction
with the Ministry of Finance, has
evolved a special supplementary scheme
under which loans are granted to small
farmers on simplified conditions for the
erection of small hay barns, byres, dairies,
as well as for the equipment of poultry
farms.
If the hon. Member wishes I shall be
very glad to let him have copies of these
schemes.
I regret that the Ministry has no funds
at its disposal out of which to issue loans
to farmers for the purchase of artificial
manures for grass lands. In any case,
owing to the impossibility of ensuring
that any such loans would be applied
solely for the improvement of grass lands
there would be serious administrative
difficulties in devising a practical scheme.

CLAUSE 1 (Regulations as to use of
lead paint.)
1.-(1) The Ministry of Labour may
make regulations for preventing danger
from lead paint to persons employed in
or in connection with the painting of

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1,
page 1, line 5, to leave out "may" ("The
Ministry of Labour may ") and insert
"shall."
It will be apparent to every Member of
the Committee that it is essential that the
word may shall be left out and the
word "shall" inserted. There is hardly
any legislation passed to-day of the
character of the Lead Paint (Protection
against Poisoning) Bill, in which it is left
to the discretion of the Minister as to
whether or not he should issue regulations. There is no point in the Measure
unless it is made compulsory for the
Minister to issue regulations. If we do
not get this word 'shall" inserted the
Minister may make regulations, but, on
the other hand, he may not. The likelihood is that he will not, as he is identified
and closely associated with the employers
of Northern Ireland.
I am sure the
whole Committee will see the importance
of not leaving it to the discretion of the
Minister of Labour, or any other person,
but of making it binding upon the
Minister to issue regulations for the prevention of poisoning from lead paint.
With these few words I move the deletion
of the word " may and the insertion of
the word "shall.'
""

undemocratic, I think quite unnecessarily

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause
1, page 1, to leave out lines 10 and 11
("except in the form of paste or of paint
ready for use.")
The danger of lead poisoning is admittedly great. That is admitted by the
right hon. Gentleman the Minister of
Labour to the extent that he is prepared
to introduce this Measure under which
he may issue regulations. If the danger
of lead poisoning is as great as to warrant
him introducing this Measure surely it is
so great that it would justify him prohibiting the use of lead compound even in
the form of paste or of paint ready for
use.
The lead that would be used in the
manufacture of the stuff would be
dangerous for work-people to handle. It
is not as if there were no substitutes that
would take the place of the paint made
out of this lead, and it is from that point
of view that I desire these words deleted-
Except in the form of paste or of paint
ready for use.
It is also from the point of view that the
Minister himself sees the dangers from
lead poisoning. If the dangers from lead
poisoning are as great as he and I both
agree they are then he ought to prohibit
the use of the lead compound in the form
of paste or of paint ready for use. What
is the difference between allowing a
painter to paint a building with white
lead paint or with a compound
manufactured from this lead and
allowing a painter to paint a building
with a standard article such as paint
ready for use? The paint is made from
the same substance. It seems to me that
there is no difference at all between allowing a painter to paint a building with
ordinary white lead paint and using, as
stated here, a paint ready for use.
same substance is in the paint.

Mr. ANDREWS: This is a
drastic Amendment, and the hon. Member
may not know that it goes beyond
even the draft Convention which was
agreed to at Geneva. The draft Convention proposed to prohibit the use of lead
paint only for internal work, but if this
Amendment, which the Government cannot accept, were to apply it would mean
that the use of lead paint would be entirely prohibited both for inside work and
outside work.
The hon. Member has
made the point that it suggests that this
paint should not be used in the form of
paste, but as a matter of fact it is when
dry that the lead is most dangerous
because of the dust penetrating the lungs.
I am glad to be able to tell hon. Members
that the danger arising from lead poisoning is greatly exaggerated. So far as I
know, since we took over our powers in
Northern Ireland in 1921 there has been
only one fatal case, and therefore to say
that the industry is to be fettered and
controlled to the extent suggested would
in my opinion not be reasonable.

CLAUSE 2 (Prohibition of employment of women and young persons in
painting buildings with lead paint):
On and after the nineteenth day of
November, nineteen hundred and twentyseven, it shall not be lawful to employ any
woman, young person, or child in painting any part of a building with lead
paint:
Provided that this section shall not
apply to the employment of-
(a) persons employed as apprentices
in the painting trade under arrangements approved by an order of the
Ministry of Labour made after consultation with the organizations, if
any, representative of the employers
and workers in the trade; or
(b) women or young persons in such
special decorative or other work (not
being work of an industrial character)
as may be excluded from the provisions of this section by an order of
the Ministry of Labour; or
(c) women who at the passing of this
Act are employed in any trade which
. involves as part of their occupation
such painting as aforesaid.
The CHAIRMAN: Clause 2, page 2,

Amendments, as it is conceivable there
may be agreement about one and not
about the other.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move the deletion
of paragraph (b). In doing so I am
quite aware of the opinion that exists
among a certain section of women,
hold that any work that man does should
be available for women, and it may be
thought that in moving this Motion I am
violating that particular canon of some
women's organizations. I want to say
quite frankly that I am opposed to women
and young persons working where I am
of opinion they are in danger, whether or
not it is going to curb the individual
liberty of the woman or of the child. I
am in favour in the same way of the
Factory Acts. The whole history of the
prohibitory legislation has been that it
has been found necessary in the interests
of the women and the children to pass
legislation specially to protect them.
Employers, as employers, have never
shown very great desire to save life or to
protect in the way they ought to have
done the life and well-being of the young

result that the State itself has had to
step in from time to time and limit hours
for example of women and young persons

Mr. BEATTIE: Salaries. To such an

Some inspectors tried other methods.
For example, an inspector called. at a
small school in North Antrim and told
the teacher he would be dismissed without pension unless he resigned, and
promised him special consideration by
way of pension if he did resign.
He
thereby induced him to write out and sign
his resignation, and the result was that
the school was closed and the teacher retired on a pension of a trifle over £20 a
year. That is the case as stated by the
ex-Teachers' Union. It is their case I
am endeavouring to present in the most
intelligible way, and my object in presenting it is to endeavour to assist this
down-trodden class of people.
Some teachers had to resign owing to
ill-health brought about by teaching in
unsanitary schools. In some cases
managers and inspectors collaborated to
secure the premature retirement of the
teachers, and in all these cases the pension is a disgrace to the State. We all
remember, at least I do, attending a little
school away out in the hills near Portglenone, and by no means was that school
sanitary. The conditions that the
teachers of that time had to endure were
deplorable. I understand that these
schools have all been closed. They were
closed prior to the Northern Government
taking over the system of education, but
by no means should we forget the people
who served the State at that particular
time when the schools were really a
disgrace.
The Northern Ireland Education Act
of 1923, Section 70, Sub-section (3), empowers the Minister of Finance to grant
to any pensioned teacher-
Mr. POLLOCK: What year, 1923 ?
Mr. BEATTIE:
Yes. This is your
own Act. Section 70 empowers the
Minister of Finance to grant to any pensioned teacher in receipt of a pension at
the appointed day such increase beyond
that authorized by the Pensions Increase
Act as will bring such a teacher's pension
up to an annual sum not exceeding £50.
Yet on the 1st April, 1926-only last
year-there were in Northern Ireland no
fewer than 209 ex-teachers of national or
public elementary schools with pensions of
less than £50 a year. Of this number
121 were scheduled for being denied any
increase under the Pensions Increase Act
of last year.
Owing to their great poverty a number
of ex-teachers were obliged to commute
their small pensions, and now they are
in dire distress. It is true that those who
are seventy years of age and upwards can
draw the old-age pension, but this can
not be done by those who have not reached
the Psalmist's inferior span. Some teachers
saved a little money, and those of them
who saved considerably are debarred
from participating in the advantages of
the Pensions Increase Act.
This is a
penalty upon thrift to which I am sure
the Minister will recognize we are opposed
in its present form, as being out of harmony with the spirit or even with the
letter of modern legislation.
The pensioned teachers designate this provision
as the "thrift barrier."
on
The pensions of teachers are proportionate to their years of service and their
average salaries for the three years preceeding their retirement. The teacher
who retired before the new scale of
salaries came into full operation merely
received a starvation pension based on
the salary that obtained during his
or her teaching days, but the teacher
who retired after the enjoyment of
the new scale for three years retired
a satisfactory pension. Let us compare
the following two cases in order to demonstrate this more clearly to the House. A
trained first-class teacher retired in 1916
on a pension of £96 2s 4d per annum, an
untrained third class teacher retired
recently on a pension of £160. No addition was made to the former's pension
under the Pensions (Increase) Acts because she had effected some savings. In
its incidence the pensions system is unfair. Sir William Vernon Harcourt once
said:-
Some people get less and some more
than they deserve, and the mean between the two is justice which nobody
receives.

That is really applicable to the exnational teachers in the case which I am
trying to present to the House. Teachers
retiring after 16th August, 1920, who did
not enjoy the benefits in full of the improved scales of salaries do not receive
any increases under either of the Pensions
(Increase) Acts of 1920 or 1926. Exteachers describe this proviso as the "time
barrier.
""
Mr. POLLOCK: The time barrier?
Mr. BEATTIE: That is the time the
Act came into operation and the time the
Government set out would be calculated
from that. All ex-teachers whose salaries
are less than £50-this is the power the
Minister has fully conferred upon him
under the 1923 Act-should have their
pensions raised to that figure, which is a
modest figure. Both the means barrier
and the time barrier should be swept
away. Ex-teachers who retired before
the improved salaries scales came into full
operation should be placed in as good a
position as regards pensions as if those
scales had been in operation before they
retired.
Let it be borne in mind that the expenses which such an Amendment of the
pensions system would involve would
gradually decrease as the present teachers'
pensions pass away until it reaches zero.
That is quite recognized by the Minister
of Finance. We do not think that these
old teachers will have any longer life than
the average individual, and so this will
not be a increasing but a decreasing liability. These poorly
poorly superannuated
teachers taught as a rule under wretched
conditions. They were underpaid. They
prophesied in sackcloth and lived on
husks. Their homes were situated in the
"Land of Bare." They never resided in
the land of Goshen, yet they did a
good day's work for their native land.
Those teachers fought the battle of life
under conditions which would have beaten
a weaker set of men.
Is it too much then for them to look
to the Government for the wherewithal
to provide some of the comforts of life
for their declining years? It is true that
a good deal has been done by the Pensions
(Increase) Acts, and the Old Age Pension Act, but the administration of the
pensions scheme and of those Acts has
produced a number of anomalies which
it devolves upon the Government
to
remedy, so that these aged servants of
the State may not go down to their graves
with the feeling harrowed into their souls
that they have been treated most unmercifully and unjustly by the State which
they served so faithfully.
Not a few public elementary school
teachers began their teaching careers in
workhouses, industrial, prison or training
schools. Their services were of public
utility and their work was under public
surveillance, yet in reckoning their
pensionable service this part of their
career is not included. A teacher, say,
taught five years in one of these public
institutions and thirty in an ordinary
school. Instead of having 35 years to his,
credit he has only 30.
This is the point I was very strong on
when the question of superannuation was
before the House, as in the Belfast Workhouse we had a teacher who as she was
employed all the time in the institution
was excluded from any benefit under the
Act. I think that was a very great hardship on that individual. I am endeavouring to show how some of those who were
servants of the State in the past are now
being neglected, and if it is is within the
power of the Minister of Finance to
remedy the injustice, I believe he should
do so.
It is from that point of view I
am presenting this case here to-day. The
services of this class of teachers I am now
speaking about were of public utility and
their work was under public supervision,
yet in reckoning the pensionable age of
teachers who were transferred from those
institutes the short time they spent
there was not calculated. As I was saying the teacher who taught five years in
one of those public institutions and thirty
in an ordinary school has only thirty
years to his credit, and if he retires he is
granted no pension unless he retires on
the ground of ill-health. This is a gross
injustice.

period.

he taught five years in one of these workhouse or training schools and 35 in an
ordinary school he would retire not on
full pension but on seven-eighths of full
pension, but if he taught the same time,
40 years, in an ordinary school he would
be awarded the full pension.
If you started to teach the same time
as a schoolmaster who lives next door
and one entered for a period a training
or industrial school and the other went
to an ordinary school you would some out
with seven-eighths of the pension and he
would come out with the full pension.
The services of both men would have been
equal as far as the State is concerned,
and because one has been reforming
persons of criminal inclinations-which is
a great service-I can see no reason why
he should be unjustly treated.
I come now to the class of teachers

Mr. POLLOCK: I may say at once
that the Government intend to resist this
Motion for reasons which I hope to
amplify at some length. The two subjects which have been introduced, that is
the pensions of older teachers who retired
before our scheme came into operation
and the pensions of secondary teachers,
are essentially different in character, although perhaps the whole question of edu
cation may be correlated or may be
regarded as correlated.
Following the hon. Member, who has
made his statement, I propose to deal with
the question of the elementary teacher
who retired before we became responsible
for our present educational existence, and,
perhaps, a little of the history of the case
in respect of this Department of the subject may help to enlighten the House in
regard to the position the Government
takes up.
There is no question whatever
that in what we are accustomed to call
the old days-although some of us, perhaps, regard them as very short in
retrospect that is when education in
Ireland was controlled by the Commissioners of Education, that is, by the Imperial Government, the teachers had
miserable salaries. No one attempts for
a moment or can attempt to controvert
that statement. The pensions naturally
sympathized with the salaries. They
were based upon the salaries. Therefore,
the pensions of these people were equally
miserable relatively miserable with the
salaries.

The British Government as time went
on-and I am speaking now of pre-war
days and money became less valuable,
Teachers' Pensions
Teachers' Pensions
3 MAY 1927
the British Government took the matter
into consideration, and, as a matter of
fact, in the year 1914, in the early part
of the year 1914, they decided to increase
the pensions of these older teachers who
were pensionable at that time.
The war
intervened and it was in October of that
A year, 1914, before this small increase became operative, and as the war went on
naturally the value of money became less
and less, and in the year 1920 the British
Government because at that period the
control of education was still in the hands
of the Commissioners of Education-gave
a small additional increase to these former
pensions. We followed that up in 1923,
or as soon as we assumed control with
many increases to these pre-war or pretransfer pensions, and then we reached
the Pensions Increase Act of 1926, to
which the hon. Member referred, which
placed the pensions of these old-time
teachers on the same basis as those of the
English teachers similarly situated.
Now I come, after giving a historical
exposition of the position of the pension
system, to the actual position of these
teachers as it stands to-day. There are
187 old teachers to-day whose pensions
are under £50. Of these there are 67
who are over 70 years of age, and, therefore, they receive a State grant under the
old-age pensions system. There are 18
who commuted part of their pension, and,
therefore, they are ruled out of any question of discussion, because they elected
to take a lump sum, and, therefore, they
cleared the authority of any further responsibility. And there were 36 that did
not apply for any increase at all, which
necessarily implies that their means were
quite sufficient, and, therefore, they did
not make any application. That left 66
possible cases of hardship. Of these 66 I
have had examined the pensioners who
were not in receipt of old-age pensions,
and who have not the means bringing
them to the limit of the Pensions Increase Acts. I have examined 58 of
these cases. The other eight were
recent disablement pensions.
Of the 58 cases examined 15 have an
income of £100 per annum or more inclusive of their own private means.
Fifteen have from £70 to £100 per
annum; 10 have £50 to £70, and 18 have
under £50 per annum. Of the 18 who
have under £50 per annum eight are now
eligible for old-age pensions by reason of
the recent removal last year, as hon.
Members will recall, of the thrift disqualification barrier. Four will be eligible
shortly; two are abroad; one is living with
relations, and the remaining three have
pensions of £43, £47, and £49. Therefore, although these pensions cannot be
regarded as amounts that will enable
these poor people to live in luxury, at the
same time it cannot be stated that they
are reduced to absolute privation. Now
the first and primary consideration with
regard to these people is that the Northern Government had no responsibility for
the acts of the Imperial Government
which have been referred to at such length
by the hon. Member; and it was quite
unnecessary to bring out into relief all
the derelictions, if they were such, of the
Commissioners of Education in this
House, because we had absolutely no responsibility whatever for the acts of the
Imperial Government until we undertook
control of education ourselves.
Now the hon. Member seems to be
labouring under the impression that this
pensions matter is a matter of very small
account. But when you take the question of responsibility and the financial
amounts involved in carrying out that
responsibility you will find that by comparison with Great Britain we have
actually, so far as the Government is concerned, done a great deal more for these
people than probably we would have been
called upon to do, for this reason, that on
the other side, which has been very frequently referred to, under the English
system the local rates pay towards
these teachers' pensions. The Government contribute a certain grant, but in
effect it amounts to this, that the local
authorities there who are responsible for
these things contribute practically half of
the whole cost, and the grant which the
Government gives supplementing their
expenditure is something in the neighbourhood, as I say, of little more than 50
per cent.
Where are we to-day in respect of that?
Our whole education system to-day so far
as the burden on the State is concerned
is out of all proportion to what we should
be called upon to bear. And, as a matter
of fact, because of these things the Colwyn
Committee in my judgment has been exceedingly generous when in taking 1923-
1924 as the standard year they have given
us an amount out of all proportion to that
which exists in Great Britain in the first
place. Then that leaves us with a burden

When we took over the education system

pre-transfer basis, obviously their pensions and the pensions of these older servants that emerged after that date were
increased proportionately. £700,000,
and the contributions, were quite unable

Now in order that the House may
understand or realize the responsibility in

which evidently the House has
appreciated up to the present I will
mention the position in which the English
pension scheme stands, and our elementary scheme is on the same basis.
The reason why I use the English scheme
is because we have no actuarial calculation. But this is based on the actuarial
figures and statistics. In 1913-1914 the
gross expenditure in England and Wales
on superannuation was £176,000. Now I
am not going to carry you through all the
subsequent increases. But in the year we
are now in, 1927-8, the £176,000 has
jumped to £4,100,000 and the progress of
increase going on from year to year as

upon this higher basis of pensionable
scales I have mentioned, reaches the

England. Now adapting that basis of
calculation on the population scale it
would mean that the Northern Government having made itself liable for the
teachers' pensions, because of the fact
that the fund, as I have said, was
insolvent when we got it, absolutely insolvent, having taken upon ourselves
that burden which would have required
£1,000,000 if you had made solvent the
old pension fund, but having, as I say,
taken over the responsibility of this fund,
we shall reach eventually the yearly payment of £300,000 to pay the pensions of
our school teachers in Northern Ireland-
£300,000 a year. That is the actuarial
basis-
Mr. KYLE: At what date?
Mr. POLLOCK: It comes up from
£4,100,000 by some millions to £9,600,000
in 1968. That will be the ultimate

Mr. BEATTIE: There was a fund.
