As a matter of fact we have got to get
teachers for our Northern Ireland secondary schools from Great Britain, simply
because we have not got the personnel in
our own area willing to take up the profession, because it does not offer sufficient
attractions to the young men of the
Province. With the exception of about
three all the secondary schools in the
North of Ireland are staffed by old
masters or old mistresses. It is quite
true that those masters and mistresses had
no pension rights when they entered the
profession, but there had grown up a
custom in secondary schools that masters
should not be displaced. That was not
to the advantage of the young people of
Northern Ireland, because, after all, the
men of Northern Ireland are men of
character equally with the men of any
other country, and character cannot be
instilled into children by old masters and
old mistresses, and until the State faces
its responsibilities in this matter I do not
see where we are to get that character in
the future. I do hope the Members who
represent the University, and who also
represent a considerable number of these
secondary teachers, will give the House
the benefit of their views on this particular Motion. Until the State is prepared to treat the secondary teacher at
least as well, if not better, than it treats
a policeman straight from the plough
without any training, we are likely to
continue in a bad way so far as our
educational system is concerned.
I have heard it stated, and read it in
the Press, that at one time an amalgamation took place of the pension funds for
elementary, secondary and technical
teachers, and that at the time that took
place there was a surplus in the funds of
the secondary teachers and a deficit in the
funds of the elementary teachers. When
the Parliamentary Secretary is replying
to this debate I would like him to say
whether that is so or not. I am glad the
Minister of Finance has corrected a statement he made on a previous occasion in
this House, when he stated he was not
aware that the secondary teachers had
made an offer to the Ministry of Education in regard to their pension. About
two days afterwards I noticed in the
Press a letter from a secondary teacher
in which it was catergorically stated that
the writer had been present at an interview which was attended by the Minister
of Finance at which this offer had been
made.
Mr. POLLOCK: Might I intervene ?
At the interview to which the hon. Members refers, a suggestion was casually
made that the secondary teachers were
willing to contribute one per cent. additional to their present pension contribution if the Government would agree to
reconsider the question of their pension.
The matter never went any further.
There was no offer made. It did not
come before me or before my Department,
but there was a suggestion made in the
casual way to which I have referred.

I do not think there are really very
many hardships in regard to primary
teachers' pensions. They seem to be fairly
well satisfied, but undoubtedly in regard
to secondary teachers' pensions some perfectly lamentable cases have been brought
forward. It is absurd that an old man
over seventy years of age who has spent
his whole life as a secondary teacher and
who has spent himself in the service of
his country should be compelled when he
retires to fall back on 10s a week old-age
pension in order to support himself.
have even heard of cases where
some of these teachers would get more
under the Old-Age Pension Act than
they get from the miserable pension given
them under the secondary teachers' pension
scheme. I do not think that is right.
When the pension scheme was first introduced it was laid down that the minimum
pension should be £120 a year, and I do
not think anybody in this House thought
that £120 a year was too much to give
to a man who had spent the whole of his
life as a secondary school teacher. Now,
I understand that in place of £120 per
year being the minimum £120 is the
maximum, and that it is laid down that
no teacher can have more than £120 a
year. I am
sure hon: Members must
feel that that is a very insufficient pension
for a man who has done the work
a secondary teacher has to do.

--and I think one of the very first

the worst treated body of people in

been doing our best to improve their
status. As far as I understand, at the

That is one of the things which
secondary teachers are exceedingly
anxious to get. Another thing, of course,
which they are anxious to secure is that
they should be able to work for and to
obtain a higher pension than they are
now able to get. The point has already
been made, but I would like to make it
again, that the secondary schools in
Northern Ireland to a very large extent
depend for their masters on Great
Britain. I am sorry to say that in the
University comparatively few art graduates there are comparatively few male
arts graduates in any case, but of those
arte graduates a very small number
indeed wish to take up the profession of
teaching. The majority of them are
training themselves for the Bar, for the
Ministry, or for other positions. Only a
comparatively small number of Queen's
University students take up the profession of teaching, and their numbers are
quite inadequate to fill the posts that
are vacant in the secondary schools of
Northern Ireland.
Consequently, we must bring over our
secondary school teachers from Great
Britain. I know some who have come
over here. They are quite satisfied as a
rule with the conditions under which
they work, with the schools, and with the
remuneration they are getting, but, as
soon as they become settled here and come
to investigate the conditions of pension,
and see what is awaiting them when their
active life is ended, they take the first
opportunity of a better offer in England
to go over there and leave Northern
Ireland. That is most disastrous, because, after all, anybody coming from
Great Britain over here does not just all
at once fall into our ways and habits.
The Northern Ireland character differs in
a good many ways from the character of
the people across in England, and it requires a year or two for a teacher coming
here to understand Northern Ireland, and
especially young Northern Ireland, the
boys of Northern Ireland. Then, just
after he has had three, four, five, or six
years here, when he has not only been
doing good work but teaching himself to
do good work and to understand the
Northern Ireland boys, our pension
system fails to hold him, and he goes over
to England where he can see a better
prospect at the end of his period of
service.
We are
That is a great hindrance.
spending here, as the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock) has told us, large sums on

I am quite sure he does not, because I

education, but I do think that this is a-
I do not like to call it cheeseparing policy
in regard to pensions, but it is penny wise
and pound foolish, or, to quote an old

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Johnstone]
a crown to the edifice of education which
we are endeavouring to build up here.
Without a good secondary education
primary education must be very largely
wasted. Primary education ends when
a boy comes to fourteen years of age,
and secondary education goes on until
he is seventen or eighteen. It is
during the period of secondary education that he acquires that extra
knowledge and training which are going
to make him afterwards a leader in
industry, a leader in business, and a
leader in everything. There is no use in
the training of privates unless you train
officers as well. The secondary schools
are here to my mind for the training of
the officers who are going to lead our
business to, I hope, a successful goal, and
if the secondary school teachers are not
well treated it means that you are going
to have a poor service, and that you are
going to lose largely the effect of the very
excellent primary school education which
you have at the present time.
I am very sorry to say I must vote
against this Motion-at least I am not
really sorry I have to vote against it,
because I do not think it is going to do
any good-but I do hope that this debate
will induce the Minister of Finance (Mr.
Pollock) to make very careful actuarial
investigation, and to consider further
whether it is worth while even wasting
a few thousand pounds a year he may
consider it waste; I do not-in order to
complete our education system in Northern Ireland, and to make the whole
system very much more efficient and
better than it is at present.

And we have hope of that. We had a

that a teacher who had served the full

that every teacher, no matter how long
he had served-two years, three years,
fifteen years or twenty years-should still
get £120 a year of a pension. The rule
says that a man who serves 40 years shall

£3 for every year he serves-

CIVIL SERVICE REGULATION.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. MCALLISTER: I rise to call the
attention of the House to the very unsatisfactory and unique, so far as my
experience goes, and indefensible regulation which has been introduced by the
Government into the system of selecting
candidates for the Civil Service of Northern Ireland. We on these Benches
have, on all occasions, advocated the
principle that merit, and merit alone,
should be the cause of success or failure,
and that the only test of applying that
principle of merit is by public examination. On a recent occasion we expressed
dissatisfaction with the Selection Committee, and I suggested that a representative from these Benches, representing
one-third of the people of Northern Ireland, should be nominated on that Committee, and I suggested my colleague and
Friend, the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), as a suitable candidate for the Committee, and one who
would carry the confidence, not only of
those whom he directly represents but of
all the people of Northern Ireland. The
reply to that has been the publication of
a new regulation.
Now the source of our complaint from
time to time has been that various
candidates for public examination have
got first and second places in this examination, and have failed to be appointed
for the position for which they sat in
examination. As president of the Old
Boys' Association of St. Malachy's
College, a position of which I am rightly
proud, my attention has been drawn to
the fact that two boys from that college
stood for public examination, which was
subject to the approval of the Government. These boys got first and second
places in the examination and were refused appointment to these particular
positions. Now, according to the Regulation existing prior to this a certain examination was necessary, and the
candidates were called before the
Selection Committee, and were rejected
or refused according as that Committee
decided. Complaints were made by us
that the boys attaining the highest results
in the examination were not appointed.
This is now got over in this ingenious
way.
There are three parts now in this
examination. First of all there are the
essential subjects for which certain
specific marks are given. In the second
part of the examination there are
optional subjects, of which it is necessary
to take two. But the third part of the
new Regulations contains those of which
I complain, and to which I draw the
attention of the House. They read thus:
1099 Civil Service Regulations
Civil Service Regulations 1100
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McAllister]
All the subjects in Part I, and two
subjects, but not more than two, in
Part II, must be taken up. Of the
candidates who obtain the highest
aggregate marks in Parts I and II a
certain number, to be determined by
the Civil Service Commissioners, in
relation to the number of situations
to be filled, and taken in order of
merit, will be summoned to Part III
(Interview), which will take place at
a later date than the other Parts of
the competition. The final lists of
candidates eligible for appointment will
be made up by uniting the results of
the three parts of the competition, and
those candidates who secure the highest
will be declared
aggregate marks
successful.
Now, therefore, before this Regulation,
the marks for the complete and distinct
subjects of examination for which the
various candidates stood were taken in
the aggregate and published.
The Selection Committee, for some
reasons and for some qualifications that
are entirely undisclosed, confer upon
themselves the right to add whatever
number of marks they like for the interview in order to outvote the marks for
the principal parts of the examination,
and thereby, to deprive of the appointment the candidate who, by every fair
test, has obtained the highest number
of marks in Parts I and II. They then
publish an announcement that a certain
candidate, who perhaps was the last in
Parts I and II, has gained the highest
marks-that is, by the addition of the
marks they have conferred upon him for
the interview-and they represent to
the public that the candidate who received the highest marks received the
position. I say that to any impartial
body of men, to any unbiassed public, to
any fair and just-minded people, that is
an absolutely indefensible position.
What is the nature of this interview?
Is it a question of appearance on which
the Selection Committee are to apportion
a certain number of marks? That is the
most grotesque test for candidates for
a public examination that I have ever
heard of. Is the public service of
Northern Ireland to be turned into a
manikin parade for men? Is it to be
turned into a cabaret?
Are you to apportion so many marks for knock knees as
against bendy legs? Of how marks
many
are you going to deprive men who have
flat feet? Is that going to be the test
that you are going to apply to candidates who seek to enter the public service
of Northern Ireland?
Mr. BARBOUR:
standards?
Are those your
Mr. MCALLISTER: No, those are
not the standards I want. I want merit,
not malformation. Those are shortly
the facts. Prior to these changes in the
Selection
regulations, the
Committee
boldly vetoed the man whom they did not
want to appoint; now they go about it
by the sinister method of adding a certain
number of marks to the candidate of their
own preference, and they deprive of the
appointment the candidate who has legitimately, fairly and honestly passed the
essential test that should be necessary to
enter the public service.

Mr. DEVLIN: I think the House will
realize that this is, perhaps, not the best

They selected twenty candidates; they

What happened then? The right hon.

In the matter of this boy, McCrudden, I, as Chairman of the Board, had

When this boy went out I realized the

while you are forming your opinion
about that boy, I want to tell you he
took sixth place in the examination."
I felt that I gave this boy every justice, because his appearance was very
disappointing in view of the position
he had taken in the examination.-
(Official Report, 5th April, 1927; col.
670, Vol. 8.)
Really, what is involved in that

I happened to say something on the debate
when my hon. and gallant Friend raised
this question on the Motion for the
Adjournment.

takes away from the popular mind a trust

deciding something by some machinery
other than by the normal machinery
which should test the capacity of boys for
these appointments. There ought to be
only two qualifications. Efficiency is one
and character is the other. Efficiency is
tested by the examination a young fellow
necessarily passes, and character should

If we do not make appointments on

Mr. POLLOCK: As one who was responsible for the original constitution of
this Selection Board, and the principle
underlying the whole scheme, I may, perhaps, be permitted to say something in
response to the fierce fulminations of the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin).
In the first place it was devised as being
the fairest and at the same time most
effective method of securing that the
young boys entering the Civil Service
should be of a character not only worthy
of the Civil Service but who would by
movement reach positions of importance
and responsibility in the Civil Service.
It has functioned for almost six years,
and I think that in all its experience it
has only had two complaints, and there
have passed through that Board possibly
hundreds of candidates-at any rate, a
large number. I do not wish to place
a figure on them. It has been the most
effective and serviceable method by which
entrants can be judged, and let me assure
the hon. Member opposite, who has so
fiercely denounced this body, that that is a
practice that obtains in almost every Civil
Service in the world. It is the method
that is adopted in the Imperial Civil
Service, and for what reason? Because
the passing of the educational test offers
no necessary guarantee that a boy is the
most suitable boy for entrance into the
Civil Service. Why? Because boys are
almost invariably crammed. Many of
them work up the essential subjects for
the examination and when they pass one,
two or three they are necessarily regarded
as brilliant boys. It does not follow at
all.
Mr. DEVLIN: Then why have examinations at all?
Mr. POLLOCK : To see that their
general education is up to a certain standard. There is no other method. I do
not say that every boy is crammed, but
there is a tendency-it is perfectly well
known; I am not suggesting anything
that is not common knowledge-for boys
do cram, and it is to avoid the possibility
of a boy who has crammed and has not
got the necessary manner, bearing and
intelligence being appointed that the
method is adopted to have these boys
present, in order, before the Selection
Board, to discover by interrogation
whether the necessary intelligence is there
to justify the appointment. Notwithstanding the fierce fulminations of the
hon. Member for West Belfast about some
mysterious cynical change, it has always
been the practice for each member of the
Selection Board to reach a conclusion by
marks. In other words, as a boy
passes before the Board he is interrogated
and certain marks are placed against him
and when these are added up they know
what the order of merit is.
Mr. DEVLIN: Do the boys understand they are passing in review on the
question of deportment?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not necessary
that a boy should be informed of that.
Deportment is essential and should be inherent in the mind of the candidates.
It is the duty of a Selection Board to see
that there is something more than a high
educational qualification to fit a person
for entrance into the Civil Service, and
that is the specific duty of this Board.

CLASS 4. No. 3.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £860,000 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1928, to defray the contribution to the Unemployment Fund, under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts, as amended by the
Economy (Exchequer Relief) Act (Northern Ireland), 1926, and the Equalization
Payment to the Northern Irish Unemployment Fund, under the Unemployment Insurance (Agreement) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1926.-(Note.-
£400,000 has been voted on account.)
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) Hon. Members will find this
Estimate on page 99, and they will see
that it is divided into two Sub-heads.
Sub-head A is the State's statutory contribution to the Unemployment Fund,
and hon. Members will observe that the
sum asked for is £3,000 more than last
year, the difference being due to the fact
that there are more people working.
The State's contribution will in consequence be higher. Sub-head B is the
Equalization Payment to the Unemployment Fund. It will be observed that the
amount asked is £410,000 less than
last year under this head. The benefit
of our Re-insurance Agreement which
some hon. Members opposite from time to
time have criticized unfavourably is very
apparent. The decrease this year in the
Estimate is due to the decrease in the
difference between the relative percentage
of unemployment in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. It is due to the Reinsurance Agreement, which I have already referred to, that this substantial
sum is available to keep our liabilities
here in parity with Great Britain.
This is the sixth occasion upon which I
have asked hon. Members to vote large
sums for the relief of unemployment
through the medium of our Unemployment Insurance Fund, and I never did
so with so much thankfulness and so much
pleasure before, because, judged from
every standpoint, the position is very
greatly improved. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I remember, in fact I do
not think I will ever forget, that on the
first occasion I had to introduce this
Estimate six years ago, shortly after we
took over our powers in April, 1922, there
were upon the live register,
either
as totally unemployed or on systematic short time, 100,000 of our people.
This time last year the figure was reduced
to 52,500, and to-day I am glad to be
able to tell the Committee that the number has been further reduced to 29,968,
a reduction since the beginning of the
year of no less than 20,000. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
It is gratifying also to know that the
fall since the beginning of the year, except during the holidays of Easter week,
has been continuous and has averaged
1,200. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Last week there was a fall of 1,479 and
this week there is a fall of 378. Another
gratifying feature is the fact that all
our principal industries have contributed
to this reduction. In the shipbuilding
industry the fall during the last three
months has been 8.3 per cent.; in the
linen trade 6.6 per cent.; in the building
trade 9.7 per cent.; in the shirt and
collar trade, in which Derry is so deeply
interested, 8.8 per cent.; in the distributive trades, 1.3 per cent.; in the food
and drink industry, 3.6 per cent. Hon.
Members opposite may say that these
satisfactory figures have been produced
by people being harshly cut off benefit.
Really that position cannot be substantiated.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. BEATTIE: It can be justified.
Mr. ANDREWS: Hon. Members
know quite well that a great many of our
mills-I have given the numbers before
so I need not repeat them to-day-which
were stopped altogether for many years
are now working full time. In addition
to that we know that many slips which
were idle for years are now usefully
occupied. Besides, it will interest hon.
Members to know that vacancies filled
at the Unemployment Exchanges during
last year numbered no less than 34,958,
and this year already, up to the 25th
April, 8,829 of our people have received
employment through the medium of these
Exchanges, which I would remind the
Committee were primarily formed for this
purpose.
I think it is interesting to compare our
position with Great Britain. I go back
to January, 1926, and I find the difference between unemployment in Great
Britain and here at that date was 13.6
per cent., while in January last the
difference was 7.1 per cent.; in February
of this year 5.8 per cent., and in March
of this year, which is the last figure available for comparison, 4.9 per cent., so
that we are gradually making up leeway.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Again
it is pleasant to know that the percentage
of unemployment here as compared with
the industrial area of Northern England
is just about the same. We are a little
more than in Scotland and we are two
to three per cent. less than in Wales.
That could not have been said a year ago.
Comparisons with different towns in
Great Britain are also a little instructive,
because sometimes we here are naturally
inclined to think that our people are
bearing a greater burden as regards unemployment than is being borne in other
places. I find in Belfast the percentage
of unemployment at the present time is
13.8 per cent.; in Sunderland 27.9 per
cent; South Shields 23.3 per cent.; Newcastle-on-Tyne 15.5 per cent.; Glasgow
13.6 per cent.; Sheffield 14.6 per cent.;
Hull 13.4 per cent. and Liverpool 14.8
per cent.
Now it is no satisfaction to us
to feel that others are also suffering, but
the fact that in the towns I have named
unemployment is even greater than here is
proof conclusive that this problem is
national, if not international, in its ramifications. Another figure which I have
been furnished with is particularly interesting. There are to-day 2,242 fewer
people unemployed in the whole of Northern Ireland than there were unemployed in Belfast alone at the beginning
of this year.
I would like to be quite frank with the
Committee, and if I may I would like to
tell the Committee what my views are
as regards the future. It is always a
dangerous thing to prophesy, but at the
same time I do feel that it is rather up
to me to tell hon. Members what my
views are for what they are worth. Let
me take the shipbuilding industry first.
We find that the percentage of unemployment in the shipbuilding industry, notwithstanding the fall which I have already
told the Committee of, is still very regrettably high, namely, 27.2 per cent.,
but I am hopeful-in fact I am more than
hopeful, I am confident-that the improvement which has already taken place
will be enhanced as the months of this year
go on, and I am reinforced in that opinion
by the speech, which some hon. Members
may have read, by Lord Kylsant on the
subject which appeared in to-day's papers.
He said he did not expect a boom, but it
was gratifying to feel that the position
had undoubtedly improved and he looked
forward with confidence to a still greater
improvement; at any rate they had made
good already to the extent that 22 out of
26 of the firm's slips were now occupied.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Only two vacant.
Mr. ANDREWS: My right hon.
Friend says I should have said 24 instead
of 22 out of 26. I am very glad to be
corrected. Only two slips are vacant
belonging to that great firm. In passing
I
may say that I do feel that the
people of Belfast and Northern Ireland
generally are very deeply indebted to
Lord Kylsant. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The energy which he has displayed, the courage which he has shown
and the enterprise which he has brought
about have been of the greatest advantage to us here in Belfast, and I think
it is proved conclusively that he is a
worthy successor, if I may say so, to those
great industrial magnates who for generations have controlled the destinies of those
great shipbuilding yards. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)


When I come to the linen trade I regret
that I cannot speak with the same amount

of confidence and certainty.
The percentage of unemployment in the linen
trade has been reduced to 7.9 per cent.,
so that in the first place there is not so
much room for improvement, but in the
second place the linen trade is so subjected
to foreign competition that it is almost
impossible to gauge the future, as we are
not in a position to know, for even a few
weeks ahead, how fierce this foreign competition may or may not become, and the
result is that our linen trade here being
subjected to these attacks from foreign
countries is in a more precarious condition
than in my opinion it would otherwise be
in. Whether it would be possible to have
that remedied or not I am not in a position to say. Speaking as Minister of
Labour I would welcome the day when
some protection was given to our employers
and our workers alike against the dumped
goods of foreign countries. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The shirt and collar trade in Derry is,
I think I may say, the sister trade of the
linen trade here in Belfast. Unemployment there has been reduced in that trade
to 6.5 per cent., and that again is a very
satisfactory position. I am told that the
prospects for that industry are fairly
satisfactory. The building industry shows
a percentage of unemployment of 26.7
per cent., notwithstanding the fall of 9.7
per cent. to which I have already referred.
I am hopeful that if the negotiations
which are proceeding in reference to wages
questions at the present time between employers and employed, and which in
Belfast at any rate are being conducted,
I understand, in the most friendly and
helpful way by both sides, are satisfactorily ended there will be an improvement
in this trade, especially if the wages are
stabilised for sometime ahead, giving those
requiring to build houses a certain
amount of knowledge that at any rate the
bottom has been reached as regards the
cost of building.
There are only one or two other remarks which I desire to make. I have
always endeavoured to lift, and appealed
to hon. Members to lift, this question
above that of Party. I have always felt
it should be put on a higher plane, the
plane of human sympathy and common
humanity (hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and I am not going to say anything
to-day of a Party kind. I have never
accepted personally a large measure
of
responsibility when trade was disastrously depressed, and when unemployment was cruelly rife in our midst; and
I am not going to take any credit for the
improvement that has taken place. But
I feel that when I say that I am entitled
to add that the Government, all along
the weary path, has done its best to encourage and to help private enterprise to
perform a great and indispensable public
duty, and that in addition to that we
have by every means within our power
done what was possible to help our people
here, unemployed through no fault of
their own, who were genuinely seeking
employment, and anxious to find it, and
who were passing through an unparalleled period of adversity. I beg to move.

The other point I want to ask is this:
SO
If we as a Parliament are going to follow
dead accurately the conditions in
England and Scotland as far as unemploy
ment is concerned it is time the Government took action to place the people in
the same conditions. Because while you
might go step by step with Great Britain
the opportunities in Great Britain are
more reasonably accessible for the finding
of other occupations than they are in
Northern Ireland. We have two industries shipbuilding and linen. It is not
reasonable to ask the shipyard worker to
go into the linen industry to seek employment. There is no linen lord or linen
employer who is inclined to accept a man
who has been in the shipyard for the last
ten years. Similarly no linen worker can
reasonably be expected to get work in
the shipyards. I say the opportunities
here are not so great as they are in England and Scotland. For that reason I
think it is unreasonable to lay down hard
and fast rules as they apply in England
for the unemployed worker in Northern
Ireland.

dissimilar, and if that industry disappears

Hear,
Our business is to see that the linen
industry is preserved as far as possible.
There is no doubt it is the finest material
in the world. (Hon. Members:
hear). It has been one of the boasts, not

Britain, and here in Ireland-that per

Minister of Labour to subsidise private
enterprise, to bolster up private enterprise, to assist private enterprise. I
agree that it is part of a Government's
duty to assist the people of the community, but they should not assist private
enterprise to make profits to the detriment of the community. That is one
point on which I disagree with him absolutely. I think it is not the duty of the
Government to help employers qua
employers.
But the Minister claims that is a thing
that he should be specially congratulated
about. If a Socialist advocated that
enterprise should be encouraged to the
end that people might find employment
there might be something in it, but here

is a stalwart for private enterprise-
Mr. ANDREWS: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE- -who is a stalwart for
Capitalism, and who seeing Capitalism
in a bad way and private enterprise in a
bad way takes public funds and uses
them to bolster up private enterprise.
That would be a perfectly good argument
from a Socialist, but I would put it up
that it is not a particularly brilliant defence of Capitalism that our right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour has suggested, and that he claims he should get
credit for.
The only other point I want to make is
that taking Northern Ireland's figures in
comparison with Great Britain's figures
we find that there is a larger percentage

Great Britain. That being the case,
before any parity arrangement is arrived
at the difference in the figures should be
taken into consideration. If the Minister
takes them into consideration I think it
will work out more to the benefit of
Northern Ireland than it has done
hitherto.

CLASS IV. No. 4.
UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £118,511
be granted to His Majesty to complete
the sum necessary to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment
during the year ending on the 31st of
March, 1928, for Grants to Local Authorities, etc., in Northern Ireland, for assistance in carrying out approved schemes to
relieve unemployment, and for expenses
in connection with training unemployed
persons for overseas settlement."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I would invite
the attention of the Committee to pages
100, 101 and 102 of the Estimates, where
they will observe that the Vote which I
beg to submit this afternoon is under two
sub-heads, namely: sub-head "A," Unemployment Grants to Local Authorities,
and sub-head "B," Richhill Training
Centre for Oversea Settlement.
I propose giving a short history of the
great public service rendered to the State
by local authorities undertaking works of
public utility to assist us in tiding over a
period of acute unemployment. Every
Member of the Committee will agree with
me when I say that unemployment is one
of the major problems of our industrial
system. In its economic aspect it re-acts
adversely upon the industrial enterpriser
and the business man as well as upon the
wage earner. I think it was the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) who, in his speech on the previous
Estimate, said that probably the wage
earner suffers most. Accumulated savings are soon exhausted, and his financial
reserve is not equal to a prolonged period
Unemployment Grants. 1150
Estimates-
4 MAY 1927
of idleness, and, consequently, he and his
family feel the pinch and suffer a degeneration of the standard of living.
The Government, through the Ministry
of Labour, called to its aid the local
authorities, and even although it meant,
in almost every case, increased taxation,
the public bodies nobly responded and
voluntarily undertook this new financial
responsibility, thus helping thousands of
our workpeople to weather the storm of
adversity. I believe that the whole
Committee will approve of my tribute to
local, urban and county authorities.
It is for the Committee to say whether
these grants must come to an end. If
there were no need to create further work,
if business and industry had recovered,
and trade had resumed its normal channels, these grants would not be required,
but while you have idle workpeople and
depression in the basic industries in the
country this Committee has a moral obligation which cannot be lightly cast aside.
For the information of the Committee
I will state what exactly has been done
since these schemes were first inaugurated.
The schemes were first brought into existence in May, 1922. 270 schemes were
approved of for Belfast and 522 for the
rest of Northern Ireland, making a total
of 792. The total cost of the schemes
represents £3,540,799 for Belfast and
£1,210,163 for the rest of Northern
Ireland, making a total of £4,750,962.
The grant sanctioned by the Government
for these schemes was as follows: for Belfast, £887,551; for the rest of Northern
Ireland, £326,454, making a total of
£1,214,005. There has already been
paid towards schemes in Belfast £692,577,
and to the rest of Northern Ireland,
£170,407, making a total of £862,984.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The number of men who have got
direct employment through these schemes
in Belfast represents 17,726, with an
average employment per person of 3
months, while in the rest of Northern
Ireland 10,376 men have got jobs averaging from 2 to 3 months. In all 28,102
men have been employed directly. Indirectly this number would be increased by
employment in the industries which
provided the material for the various jobs.
I can assure the Committee that the money
is spent to good advantage, and is only
granted to public bodies to carry out
work that would not be immediately
undertaken but for the fact that there is
so much unemployment. The amount
under sub-head A is for £150,000.
Now, I propose to deal with what my
experience in this Committee has taught
me is a controversial Estimate and which
will require all my resource of ingenuity
if I am not to enter into conflict with
those who, I fear, hold mistaken views regarding the training centre at Richhill.
Mr. BEATTIE: There is no doubt
about our views.
Mr. GORDON: I am sure we will hear
the hon. Member's views in a short time.
However, I propose to give a short history
of the work connected with this particular
centre. Let me say that it was to be
expected that the extended depression
and general unemployment would raise
new problems. Lack of opportunity to
gain industrial training and learn trades
sent a flood of youths annually into blind
alley or dead end occupations. We are
making an effort to arrest this. Young
men full of ambition and high in hope
start life as workers, but meeting failure
after failure in establishing themselves in
some trade or calling, their ambition and
hope go to pieces and they gradually sink
into the ranks of casual workers.
If we can help them by an organized
effort, and by training equip them with a
degree of efficiency that will assist them
to make good in some outpost of the
Empire-
Mr. BEATTIE: Why not Ulster?
Mr. GORDON- --we will be carrying
out a great national duty and satisfying
an ambitious desire in the hearts of some
young men who probably feel that opportunities might be offered them by virtue
of this training which they could not
otherwise embrace. In September, 1926,
the Department took over Richhill Castle,
Co. Armagh, for conversion into a farm
training centre with no other purpose in
view than to help our young men to receive a training which would make them
acceptable to the Dominion Governments
and fit them for agricultural work in the
Dominion for which they desired to be
trained. Centres of a similar character
have been established by the Imperial
Government in Brandon and Claydon,
and I have been in conversation with the
Unemployment Grants 1152
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
Australian representative, who has informed me that as soon as these men receive a course of training they are eager
to be taken overseas to commence farming
operations.
We are anxious to give our young
Ulster men a similar course of training in
agriculture. This course of instruction
will normally last for a period of three
months, and amongst the subjects in
which training will be given are general
agricultural operations, especially ploughing, milking, handling and care of horses
and live stock, tree cutting, fencing and
ditching. As I have already said, the
training will be of an elementary nature
but will satisfy those making the selection.
The estate comprises 192 acres. Sleeping and dining huts are provided for the
trainees. The sanitary conditions are
perfect. Wash baths are provided and,
as hon. Gentlemen will observe from the
Estimates, there is a hostel superintendent
whose duty it is to maintain order and
see after the cleanliness of the huts.
Mr. KYLE: Is that a stockbroker?
Mr. GORDON: Hon. Members may
rest assured that I will deal with any
points they raise at the end of the discussion. If they interpolate any question
during the discussion to which I can reply
at once I will not hesitate to do so.
Mr. KYLE: Is that a stockbroker?
Mr. GORDON: No, he is not. We
have no stockbrokers in existence down
there, nothing but practical men trained
in a practical way. My right hon. Friend
the Minister of Labour and I paid a surprise visit to the Richhill Training Centre
last week. We went down unexpectedly
and found the place clean, the trainees
perfectly content, and the training being
carried out in a most satisfactory manner.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I want
to tell the Committee that the reason I am
making such a comprehensive statement
is to anticipate some of the questions that
hon. Gentleman are likely to ask me.
The necessary farm stock and equipment have been purchased, and the
Canadian Government-I know the question of what the Dominions have done
will naturally arise has presented as a
gift a certain amount of farm machinery
of Canadian design, in order that the
trainees proceeding to that Dominion
may acquire a working knowledge of the
equipment used in that country.
All applicants for training must be
single men between the ages of 17 and 25,
except in the case of ex-Service men,
whose age limit is 31. Applicants must
be of good character and must pass a
medical examination.

When the training is completed the

would otherwise have to be met by the

the Government means that the men will

anticipate that about 100 trainees will

Forms of application are to be had at

the intending trainee is interviewed by a

report is satisfactory to the Dominion

ing entitled, "Our Foreign Policy in regard to the emigration of our youth from

Now, the Minister of Labour to-day
made a very powerful and very satisfactory statement upon the general question
of unemployment. He pointed out, and
we all listened to it with delight, that
there was a progresive decrease in the

this very moment when there is a decrease
in unemployment the Government come
forward and ask us to vote a large sum
for the purpose of training our youth,
not only our youth, but the best of our
youth, to go out to another country. 1
object to it on principle and I object to
it as a busines transaction. I say morally it is wrong to encourage emigration,
to encourage our people going to another
country when the proper place for them
is at home. And I object to it on the
financial ground.
Let me take the financial grounds first.
The value of a youth ought to be twenty
times more than the value of a COW.
What would be thought of the Government that would make a present to another country of cattle for that country
without any recompense for it? It takes
about £500 to train a youth up till he is
18 years of age, and you make a present
of this youth to another country for the
purely material benefit of that country.
You make a present of £500 cash spent on
the training of that youth, and you never
have, so far as I know, made any bargain
whatever with the Canadian Government
to recoup you for your expenditure, apart
altogether from the expenditure upon the
training of this youth before he entered
this college. I never heard a more monstrous transaction in my life than to give
this valuable asset to a great rich country
like Canada that can well afford to pay
for what it wants itself to develop agriculture. It does not pay for the training
of its agriculturists. Obviously, it has
not enough men to do its agricultural
work, and they come over here and they
ask us to set up a college and to pay for
it in the face of all the financial difficulties and the fiscal burden we have to bear,
and our people already borne down by
taxation, in order to train these young
men and make them a present to Canada.
I must say a worse bargain I could not
conceive.
What is the character of these emigrants? They are not the usual unemployed. They are not the surplus,
useless, wastrel section of the population.
The young fellow that wants to go into
the agricultural training college is usually
of the better type of citizen. He is a
young fellow that wants to get on.
He is
a young fellow with ideas in his head.
He has qualities that will make him an
effective citizen in his own country. And
yet he is offered the allurements of this
college in order to train him, not for the
purpose of being scientifically capable of
developing the lands of the Province in
which he was born, and the country in
which he lives, but to go out to a foreign
country to give his character, his training,
his help, and physical strength to Canada.
I do not see how that can be justified
at all.

1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the present
financial position of the Northern Ireland
Unemployment Fund; the total amount
of money borrowed; the total amount repaid, and the amount of debt on the
Fund.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY ΤΟ THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): My hon. Friend
the Minister of Labour has been detained
and consequently I am taking this question.
The "Suspense" debt, which was the
debt at the time when the re-insurance
agreement was made with Great Britain,
is £3,424,434. The "Parity" debt, which
is at present approximately £584,000, is
maintained under the agreement at the
same proportionate level as the debt on
the Great Britain Unemployment Fund.
BELFAST CORPORATION HOUSING
POLICY.
2. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is satisfied that
the present housing policy of the Belfast
Corporation is in accordance with the
Housing Acts under which the various
schemes were inaugurated, and whether
he will take immediate steps to have a
further inquiry into the administration by
the Corporation of the Housing Acts.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The housing policy of
the Belfast Corporation is a matter which
is altogether within the competence of
the Corporation provided that the provisions of the Housing Acts are observed,
and I am not aware of any particular in
which the Corporation have departed from
the provisions of these Acts.
There appears to be a certain amount
of difference of opinion within the Corporation as to the policy to be pursued
in regard to their future operations, and
until the situation is clearer I do not
consider that it would be desirable for me
to express any opinion thereon.
I am not aware of any circumstances
which would render an inquiry into the
Corporation housing policy either necessary or desirable at the present.

Gentleman aware that, although tenants
have been in these houses for five years,
they do not know their position and have
not received their title deeds?

hon. Friend will give me notice I will
inquire into it.

Gentleman say what is the position of
tenants who deposited £10 towards the

can be answered without notice, and I am
not sure that it is not a matter for the
Corporation.

Mr. DEVLIN: I practically exhausted
nearly every aspect of this question when
I was addressing the Committee yesterday, and I do not propose to occupy
very much of the time of the Committee
in adding to what I stated on that
occasion. I have no objection whatever
to persons emigrating either to Canada or
elsewhere if they choose to emigrate. I
am a strong believer in the individual
right of every citizen to do what he likes
for himself provided that he does not
encroach on the rights of others, and
therefore if any section of the community
or any individual believes that by emigrating to Canada he is serving his own
ends and promoting his own interests that
is a matter entirely for himself. My objection is to this subsidy for emigration,
to the seductiveness of this campaign, and
to the facilities which it gives to encourage the young men of the country to
leave the country, and to public money
being used out of the funds of Northern
Ireland to train and to equip citizens to
give their physical vigour and their
scientific training to another country.
As I stated yesterday, the prospects of
employment have considerably increased
during the past few months, and the
opportunities for employment will be
greater, I trust, if we are to believe the
rosy story told by the Minister of Labour
in his speech yesterday. For that reason
what we ought to do is not to make foreign
lands attractive to the young men, and
the best of the young men, of Northern
Ireland, but to try to make the homeland
attractive to them by giving them all the
facilities and training that can possibly
be afforded them to remain at home.
Why should this money not be spent in
the larger development and more efficient
equipment of agricultural colleges to train
Ulster youths to do agricultural work on
scientific processes and after training in
these colleges? What right have we as a
small State like Northern Ireland with
only about a little over one million of a
population and covering a very small area
to spend public money in training the
youth of Northern Ireland to go out and
give all that they have and all that they
are for the purpose of developing the
agricultural greatness and power of
another land? I do not know how far the
Canadian Government value this contribution we are making when we give them
youth and vigour and physical strength.
Surely they ought to pay and recompense Northern Ireland for the expenditure which Northern Ireland is called
upon to make for the proper equipment
and training of these potential agriculturists in that great country.
My own view is that the Government
have not given sufficient and mature consideration to this question or they would
have entered into some arrangement by
which the Canadian Government would
pay for the training of these trainees in
this Richhill College. This country has
been sufficiently depleted of its population
already. Taking the country as a whole.
we lost nearly four millions of our population in half a century. There was a
universal cry amongst all sections of
public-spirited and patriotic citizens
against this continuous exodus of the best
and most vigorous of our citizenship,
and if America is great, and if Australia
is great, and if Canada is great it is because of the contribution that Irish vigour
and Irish power and Irish strength gave
to the creation of the greatness of these
lands. That was all very good when econ-
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
omic conditions were of such a character
that people were compelled to go. There
are very few people who want to leave
their native land unless they must leave
it. There is an inherent and fundamental
and tenacious idea to cling to the home
and to the homeland, and therefore I say
I am opposed to this grant because it
is laying down a most vicious principle,
and that is that it is the function of
the Government to make emigration
attractive, to train young citizens by
equipment, by learning, and by scientific
knowledge to leave their country and go
to another country.
I am opposed to it on that ground first
of all, because morally I think it is indefensible. Nationally and racially it is
indefensible, and financially I never knew
of such a transaction. As I said yesterday, if you were asked by Canada to make
a present of capital to Canada you would
stand aghast, and say "How dare you ask
us to make a contribution of capital to
Canada?" But with human beings, the
cost of whose feeding and training and
clothing and education when they come to
be 20 years of age could be very modestly
estimated at £500, we make that contribution in money value alone apart from
the vicious principle of encouraging people
to emigrate. On that ground I am also
opposed to it.
I notice that there are some Members
for Derry here. I notice one Member particularly taking copious notes. I have
no doubt we shall have a valuable contribution from the hon. Lady (Mrs.
Chichester), whom we will be glad to
hear, or some of the other Members for
Derry upon this question. I have no
doubt that the usual encomiums will be
passed on the Government for their
prescience in seeing the value of this institution, but before these encomiums are
passed may I call the attention of the
Members for Derry to the following statement:
Mr. W. W. McCausland speaking on
the 11th of last month, when he was
re-elected President of the Limavady
Branch of the North-Derry Unionist
Association, referred with concern to the
increasing tide of emigration principally in the direction of Canada. He
thought the attention of the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland should be
invited to this loss of the young manhood of the Six Counties.
I commend that view of Mr. McCausland,
fresh and vigorous after being unanimously elected to be President of the
Limavady Branch of the North-Derry
Unionist Association, to the Members for
Derry, and I would also commend to the
Prime Minister the views which he holds
as a loyal, faithful, devoted and unchanging follower of the Government and supporter of his policy.

That declaration is a denunciation
emigration as emigration to Canada.
may be said for these people that they are
going out because they are not satisfied
with the conditions at home, but this is
a much more indefensible proceeding, because you are actually using public funds,
the funds of the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland already, as I have said, overburdened with taxation, heavy rates and the
almost unbearable financial burdens they
have to bear. You are voting a sum of
£8,000 which I have no doubt will be an
annual charge for the purpose of making
emigration attractive and equipping these
young men to go out there to Canada, a
country for which I have the greatest admiration; but the one thing I admire
about America and Canada is that they
give you very little. I do not know of
any overflowing generosity on the part of
either America or Canada towards

you.
I do not think that a rich country like
Canada, a country blessed by Providence
with natural advantages of the most
beautiful character, rich in resources
as Canada is, ought to ask us to spend the
money of the taxpayers of Northern Ireland to give them efficient agriculturists,
trained to go out there and to develop
their own rich land.
For these reasons I will vote for the
reduction of this Vote. My own view is
that these young fellows if they are
trained at all-and I am all for scientific
training in farming-have a very wide
and productive field in their own province.
I saw a letter in the "News-Letter" the
other day from a very distinguished agriculturist stating that it would be a good
thing if the Agricultural Department
would take a few farms of 40 acres, put
their instructors on these farms, give
practical demonstrations of farming, and
teach the young farmers how they could
make their farms pay, and how they could

make agriculture a financially successful
industry. That would be practical work
for the Department to do. My objection
to this Government is that they are always
trying to fashion themselves in picturesque form:-"We are doing something
great for the Empire, we are serving
some great purpose," and so on.
The whole thing is absurd in the present
condition of your finances. We cannot
afford to devote public money much
needed at home for our own purposes, nor
do I think it desirable. The one real asset
that the country or province possesses is
a young and vigorous population. Mark
you this, that the class of people who will
go to these colleges are the best type of
the young. I am not making any attack
upon them. When a young fellow makes
up his mind to go into an agricultural
college and train and equip himself and
prepare himself for a future life in a
foreign land, it shows he is not only enterprising but civic-spirited, and that is the
class of people I think we should
encourage to remain at home. For these
and other reasons I shall support the reduction of this Vote.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I had really no
intention of intervening in this debate,
but having listened to some of the remarks made by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin), and having heard
his invitation to enter into a discussion
with him on the merits of the Government's
proposals as against those put forward by
the Opposition, I made up my mind to say
a few words. I would like, first of all, to
ask the hon. Member for West Belfast
how he really can put forward the argument which he has put forward to-day.
after having heard the figures submitted
to the House in answer to a question this
afternoon. It does seem to me that the
bottom of his argument falls through
when we find that emigration from
Northern Ireland reached the very high
figure of something like 12,800 last year.
How can he possibly contend that the
figure given to us yesterday of 100 young
men, whom it is hoped to send from this
agricultural training school, can really so
very vitally affect the situation in
Northern Ireland?
Quite apart from that does it not seem
obvious that if there is, much as we may
deplore it, this constant drain on the
manhood of Northern Ireland-and I believe the best of the manhood of Northern Ireland; there has always been a considerable amount of emigration from
Northern Ireland-is it not better for this
Government to see that a certain proportion of these young men go out into the
world to seek their fortunes properly
equipped to seek those fortunes? It does
not seem to me an unreasonable argument. We ought to be proud that a
certain proportion of the emigrants from
these shores go out with a reasonable
prospect of finding employment and
reasonably equipped to carry out that employment satisfactorily.
There are other aspects the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) has touched. He
has referred to Canada as a foreign land.
I do not think Members on this side would
be willing to accept that view. Leaving
all those considerations aside the benefit
which we may confer on a portion of the
great Empire of which we are a part-it
does appear to me that we ought always
to remember first of all that there will
be amongst the young men of the nation
always a spirit of adventure. There will
be a call of the blood to go out away from
home to learn more of the world, and in
responding to that call for adventure they
will be able, I am quite positive, to
broaden their outlook and gain a wider
experience of life. If they do eventually
come back to the land of their birth they
will come back a great deal the better for
their experience, and if so they will be
better citizens of our State. It will be
said, of course, that we are showering
encomiums upon the Government, but I
do think the Government are doing good
work in assisting some of these men to go
out with a reasonable prospect of employment, so as to be able to fulfil, as I have
said, this call of the blood. Their outlook will be broadened and they will be
able to strike out for themselves. This
will benefit probably not only themselves
but their country.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I
want very briefly to support the Amendment to reduce this Vote. I cannot say
that I have heard one satisfactory reason
as to why this Estimate should be allowed
to go through the Committee. I listened
with very great care to the long statement
made by the Parliamentary Secretary
yesterday in introducing this Estimate,
and I must say that as usual he went to
great pains to put the Committee in pos-

session of the whole situation as he wanted
the Committee to see it, which is not
necessarily the situation as it exists. I
do not want to deal with that aspect of
the problem at the moment, but I think
it is perfectly obvious to anyone who has
given even cursory attention to the problem in Northern Ireland that it is an inadvisable thing that the State imprimatur
should be put on a scheme of this
character.
Anyone who examines the recent Census
returns that have been published will
realize right away that the countryside is
becoming depopulated and denuded, and
under the circumstances I am at a loss
to understand why people should be
trained for agricultural purposes for any
part of the British Dominions. The Parliamentary Secretary and the chief of the
Department will probably know that in
the year of the famine in Ireland the
country was capable of maintaining a
population of eight and a half millions.
Our portion of that eight and a half
millions would be over two millions, that
is, about the year 1845 this Province was
able to maintain a population of two
millions. We find at the present time,
according to Government policy, it is not
possible to maintain one and a quarter
million people.
That is somewhat difficult to understand
having regard to the fact that our potentialities for the purpose of producing
wealth are much greater to-day than they
were in the middle of the nineteenth century. Having regard to all its potentialities for producing wealth this portion of
Ireland should be able to maintain a
considerably larger population than in the
years previous to the famine. I think that
should be sufficient to show that there
is no case at the moment as to why these
boys should be trained for export to the
Dominions.
We hear a great deal of loose talk about
Empire settlement. We have got to ask
ourselves is this the best method of doing
this thing, even if we accept the inevitable that the Government are going to
do it. I understand the boys that are
being trained are, roughly, sixteen or
seventeen years of age, and I know it is
the habit and the policy of the Colonies
and of the United States of America only
to take emigrants who are absolutely
physically fit. Now what is our position?
The Chancellor of the Exchequer next
week when he comes to introduce the
Budget will probably deal with the cost
of our social services in Northern Ireland.
We are paying a considerable sum per
annum in old-age pensions. Our young
manhood and young womanhood is going
out of our Province, and we are being left
the aged and decrepit and the worn out,
with the result that our social services
cost much more than they otherwise
should. It is an unheard-of policy that
Canada or any other part should have
the pick of the basket, to describe it in the
vernacular.

The family is the unit, and if there is
any settlement to be brought about it
should be on the basis of the unit of the
family. I do not want to be misunderstood. I have no objection to the amount
we are paying in old-age pensions, but it
is unfair to leave the aged in Northern
Ireland while the young manhood is being
exported to Canada and other parts of the
British Dominions. We would probably
find from the point of view of our old-age
pensions and social services that we would
have a considerably smaller burden to
shoulder if there was a difference in policy
so far as the Government is concerned.

The last day this matter was discussed
here the Prime Minister asked us to consider it from the point of view that
Canada was an exceptionally large
country, and that thousands of square
miles of that country had not been settled
up to the moment. He said it was highly
desirable in view of the numbers of people
that were going to Canada from the
United States of America. It was necessary to stock Canada with British blood
for the purpose of ensuring that Canada
in real fact would be full of people with
British sentiment.


Under the present arrangement I am
at a loss to understand how that will take
place. I know three boys who emigrated
quite recently to Canada from the North
of Ireland. Since they went those boys
have married, and it might interest
the Committee to know the nationalities
of the three girls they married. The first
boy married a girl of French extraction.
the second married a young woman
German extraction, and the third married
a girl from the South of Ireland, who probably, had not a pronounced British
sentiment.

Thus we discover that the three young
men who left Northern Ireland have married girls who probably do not consider it
a desirable thing to have British senti..
ment. So far as Canada is concerned,
having regard to the old struggle and
quarrel that took place between the
French and the British as to who should
own Canada, if we are going to send
our young men out, and they are going to
marry girls of other nationalities, the
possibility is that the object which the
Prime Minister has in view is going to be
defeated. There would be much less
chance of that, if we are going to emigrate
at all, if that emigration was by the
family.
I would be interested this afternoon to
have information about how many of these
emigrants were males and how many
were females. I think our position in
Northern Ireland is much the same as that
in Great Britain with regard to the preponderence of females over males. If we
are to emigrate it should be by families.
I must say this with some reservation, because I think there is no more tragic picture than to see a family emigrating from
Belfast, or Derry, or any other place. If
there is one picture I am rather inclined
to feel sentimental and pathetic about it
is the picture of a large family compelled
by economic circumstances to go to
Canada or Australia, or any other placé,
for the purpose of getting a livelihood.
I have, unfortunately, seen those circumstances in Belfast and different parts
of Northern Ireland, and I think there
is no picture that touches one so much.
But if the Government's argument is right
that emigration is inevitable, then I submit the best method is not to export the
young manhood but to export by the
family. If that became the policy of the
Government the position I described in
regard to the three young men who married wives who had not necessarily a pro-
British sentiment might be avoided, and
there might be a possibility that succeeding generations of Canadians might be
more pro-British in sentiment than probably the off-spring of those matches I
have attempted to describe.

make a little criticism on the remarks of

I think there is a great deal to be said

or the Colonies it is a very large gift
indeed. I am told there are statistics to
the effect that the enormous sum of money
that we owe to America as a result of the
war has been paid and over already by
the stream of young and vigorous emigrants that have gone to America from
this country and from England since the
war ended. I find that many of the emigrants from Ireland are distinguishing
themselves in the Colonies.
At the pre-
It
sent moment I am reading a history of
young Ireland by a distinguished Irishman who went out there and occupied a
very high position in the State, Sir
Charles Gavan Duffy. I find that in
many important places in Australia you
have very influential Irishmen and they
are very prosperous. What I would like
the Committee to do in this matter is to
face the facts. I have been all my life
accustomed to face facts and to get rid of
theories, and to get down to the bed rock
and look at the position as it exists there
and is producing these things. In dispensary work I had for 30 or 40 years in
a large country district I was brought
face to face with these facts in a way that
the men on the other side can have no
knowledge of What were these facts?
I found that vast numbers of our people
were going to the States. Now I have a
certain amount or had a certain amount
of admiration for the United States.
is considerably less than it was. I do not
see why our people should go to the States
where it seems to me the only question
of importance is the Almighty Dollar, and
where religion and higher things seem to
my mind to take a secondary place,
when they had through the vigour and
courage of our ancestors the choice of the

America and to send it to the Colonies,

the same time be under their own flag?"
I hope hon. Members on the opposite

I did divert the stream. Now no longer
own
do they go to America, but they go to
Canada, to Australia, to South Africa,
and to New Zealand. I have sent, or
have been the means of sending, to these

healthy but I have also sent the sick. I
have sent young people who were
threatened with consumption. I have in

not live in this country. I got them

healthy, vigorous men in Australia at the
present moment.
I was in direct touch-I should tell the

Australia, relatives of my own, who employed a large number of people and who
could always take on men. On a farm
where they had perhaps fifty or 100 men
there were always one or two stragglers
they were glad to get rid of. I also wrote
to the Commissioners of these different
countries, and when I knew of a young
fellow or even of a family wanting to
emigrate, I said: "Do not bother your
head about the States."

HENDERSON:
I
Mr. GEORGE
want to say this, that while emigration
is deplorable I am afraid that, like the
poor, we are likely to have it always with
us. It is certainly very deplorable that
so many of our young people are not able
to find employment in this area. The
result of that state of affairs, as the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. W.
McMullen) has pointed out, is that there
is a great flood of young, vigorous life
from this country, and we are left with
the old and infirm, which means an added
burden to our social services.
I took exception to this Vote last year
on the ground that it was setting up
another institution in Northern Ireland
that would employ some more officials,
and I feel that at the present time we
have a sufficient number of officials to
work this area, and as many as we can
afford to pay. I find from the Estimates
this year that this institution is likely to
be a costly place. The salaries of the
officials in charge amount to £2,203, and,
like the Member for County Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) I find it very difficult to understand why it is necessary to pay a Bill of
£845 for farm hands and domestics on a
farm, where you have sixty or seventy
men that you are training for this work.
The Member for West Belfast (Mr. W.
McMullen) asked me something about my
experience of farming, and what staff it
would take to work an 190-acre farm.
From my experience I think that a staff
of six or seven suitable workmen, with
a domestic servant, should work a farm
of 190 acres fairly efficiently, if it were
well managed and well wrought.
While I say that emigration is to be
deplored, I feel that our loss may be very
often the emigrants' gain. I know a
great many emigrants who went to the
Colonies and who made good. I know a
great many others who went to the
Colonies and who had to come home
again, men who had not very much
capital and who were unable to find employment. If a great many of the
emigrants were prepared to work in our
own land under the conditions that prevail in Canada, and if they put the same
vigour into their work, I believe they
would make a livelihood equally well in
this country. They might not have the
same opportunities of becoming millionaires, to whom the Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) referred, but I feel that
if they put the same energy into their
work, and if they worked the same number of hours here as they do in Canada,
they would make their livelihood quite
easily. But the people at home will not
live under the conditions that prevail in
Canada, and they will not put the same
energy into their work as they do in the
Colonies.
I feel that if a farmer started with a
burden of £12,550, in addition to £1,508
for stock and equipment, he would need to
be a very good agriculturist to get a return for his money. I think this institution is costing more than it is worth.
The hon. Member for Derry asked why
should we not try to send these men out
efficiently equipped. Will the Government or any Member of this House say
that by taking a man off the streets of
Belfast and keeping him at Richhill for
three months, he will be efficiently
equipped for farm work in Canada? The
thing is totally absurd. I did put before
this Committee last year another method
by which I think the money could be very
much better spent than it is being spent
at present. You have too much capital
expenditure; your overhead charges are
far too high. If the Government want
to equip men for farm work in Canada
they should put them on farms in County
Antrim and County Down, and other
parts of this area, and the young men
would get a far more efficient training on
the farms than they get at Richhill.

I may say to the hon. Member for West

training centre is different from a farm.
My hon. Friend the Member for Antrim
Estimates-
Unemployment Grants
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
(Mr. George Henderson) seemed to refer
to it as a farm. A training centre is
different from a farm. If the Government was working this as a farm I venture to say that they would work it on
the lines indicated by the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson).
But this is a training centre, and of necessity it requires a greater amount of money
to run a training centre than to run a
farm. You require to have a man to
train the trainees; you have to have a
superintendent where you have a
siderable number of men in training;
and you have to have handy men
train them in putting up fences, and
there are other incidental works of a
skilled or unskilled character. Consequently, the cost of running a training
scheme is bound to be considerably more
than the cost of running an ordinary
farm.
conto
With regard to the hours of duty, I
want to say to the hon. Member for West
Belfast that they are from six o'clock in
the morning till half-past five o'clock in
the evening. The trainees are called at
six o'clock, have breakfast, start work at
seven o'clock, have the ordinary stopping
times to get food, and finally end at five
or half-past five o'clock according to the
particular job on which they are engaged
that day.
I may say in answer to the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) that we
are careful in our selections. Those whom
we select are the sons of artisans; they
are not the sons of farmers. We feel
that the sons of farmers will receive sufficient training on their own farms, and
there is no necessity for going to the expense of bringing them to a training
school. Therefore, we only take the sons
of artisans. If I might digress for a
moment, I might say that those put into
the farm training centres on the other
side of the water are largely taken from
the mining and industrial centres. I could
read statements made as to these centres
by Miss Bondfield, the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Labour Ministry in the
Labour Government; Dr. Shields, representing the Socialist Party, and other
Members of the English House of Com
mons. Their experience is that men engaged in a 42 to 50-hour week in industrial centres were so interested in the
work that they gave up their whole
Saturday evening, and sometimes Sunday
evening, for the purpose of doing a little
farming in their own vegetable gardens.
It was to stimulate that interest that
these men were called from the industrial
districts. It has been found that the
whole tendency of men reared in agricultural districts is to go into industrial
districts rather than remain in their own
areas for which they had the training.
Consequently, men were being sent out
to the training centres from the industrial
districts.

[Mr. Barbour]
The position is, however, different as

and on the "Belfast Gazette."
By way
of Appropriations-in-Aid of this expenditure, we have not only the receipts from
sales to Departments but also receipts
from sales to the public, and still more
important from the money point of view,
receipts from advertisements in
the
"Belfast Gazette.' As far as the
"Belfast Gazette is concerned, it is,
I am thankful to say, a thoroughly paying proposition as hon. Members will see
by comparing the estimated expenditure
under Sub-head "A" with the estimated

the
Other official publications of
Government of Northern Ireland are in
a different category.
On the issue of a
Blue Book as, for example, the annual
report on the work of a Department,
sufficient copies are printed to meet all
probable requirements, including sales to
the public. The Stationery Office as the
medium of sale must hold all the copies
not required by the Department for its
own use. Owing to the comparatively
limited circulation of such publications it
is not always possible to dispose of the
entire number of copies printed, with the
result that the cost of the unsold copies
must fall as a final charge on the
Stationery and Printing Vote. I think
the Committee is fully aware that another
cause of the loss on the production of
these publications lies in the fact that in
order to encourage the public to buy the
sale price is fixed at a figure which could
not, in many cases, cover the actual cost
of printing.
As for Imperial Stationery Office Publications (Sub-head "C") only a sufficient
number of these publications is taken into
stock to meet current requirements,
including sales to the public, with
the result that the gross cost of these
publications is more than offset by the
amount recovered in respect thereof as
appropriations-in-aid owing to the small
profit made on the copies sold to the
public. I may say for the information
of hon. Members that the entire cost of
the carriage and transit of supplies under
Sub-head "F" remains as a final charge
on the Stationery and Printing Vote.
The net total of the Estimate is accordingly made up of the loss on the production of Northern Ireland Official
Publications, plus the cost of carriage and
transit, less the profit made in the
"Belfast Gazette" and the slight profit
on Imperial Stationery Office Publications.

Coming now to the details of the provision made in the Estimate, we find that
there is an increase of approximately
£800 in the gross cost of Northern Ireland Official Publications, which, of
course, includes the Official Reports of
Parliamentary Debates. This increase is
entirely due to the fact that provision
is made this year for the printing of the
results of the Census taken last year.
was explained by the right hon. Gentleman the Minister of Finance in a reply to

include, in addition to the detailed tables
for each county, a general summary and
a topographical index, and will be comprised in nine volumes to be issued during
the latter part of the present year.
As
The reduction of £250 in the gross cost
of the "Belfast Gazette" is due to a saving
in printing costs. The only other itens
which call for special comment are Subheads D and E which make provision for
the stationery and printing requirements
of Public Departments. Here there is a
saving of about £700 in the case of printing and of £650 in the case of Stationery
and office supplies. I am glad to say

and the cutting down, wherever possible,

paper. If hon. Members will
compare
the total expenditure on stationery and

from these efforts to economize. I beg to


move.
