The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): This Estimate will be
found on page 131 of the book of Estimates. In approaching the consideration
of the Estimates now before the Committee, I do not propose to weary the
Committee with a recital of the multifarious duties with which the Ministry of
Commerce is concerned. The information
already afforded to hon. Members in the
Estimate for Harbour and Commercial
Services recently submitted to and approved by the House will have served to
indicate, at any rate in a general way, the
directions of the principal activities of
this Ministry. The Committee are aware
that these vary from the registration of
public companies to the administration of
fishery services; from the rendering of
general assistance to industry on tariff
questions, market conditions and trade
representation abroad, to the administration of railway services; from the registration of friendly societies and trade unions
to the administration of Electricity Acts,
as well as Acts relating to mines and
quarries, weights and measures, and
other matters.
Before turning to the details of the
Estimate now before the Committee, I
might mention that in the administration
of the fishery services a steady effort is
being made to develop what is admittedly
a valuable natural resource. By way of
illustration, the Ministry has extended
the scheme under which loans are granted
to bona fide fishermen, so as to include
assistance towards the purchase not
merely of nets, but also of boats and
engines. The additional opportunity
thus provided has already been availed
of by our fishermen to some considerable
extent, and altogether there are indications of a more active pursuit of fishing
as a calling around our coast.
As
Another feature to which I should like
to refer is the very considerable burden
of work thrown upon officers of my Department by the administration of the
Industrial Assurance Act of 1924.
hon. Members are aware, that Act deals
with complaints in respect of that class
of insurance which is usually conducted
by door-to-door collectors, the premiums
Ministry of Commerce

being small sums payable at intervals of
less than one month. It is open to parties
who consider they have a grievance under
any of these policies to take up the matter
with the Industrial Insurance Commissioner instead of proceeding by way of a
court of summary jurisdiction or the
county court. I am satisfied that the
Measure which was placed on the Statute
Book in 1924 has provided those classes of
the industrial community who are least
able to protect themselves with a readily
accessible and economical form of legal
redress for genuine grievances.
The activities of the Empire Marketing
Board recently set up by the Imperial
Government to stimulate trade in home
and Empire produce will be well known
to the Committee. The fullest advantage
is being taken by my Department of the
facilities thus provided for making the
qualities of Northern Ireland produce
more widely known in the British market.
Close touch is being maintained with the
Empire Marketing Board, and, with the
collaboration of the Ministry of Agriculture, two striking exhibits of Ulster produce were recently staged in London. I
am glad to be able to inform the Committee that we have had definite evidence
that those exhibits were beneficial to our
exhibitors there, and that the benefits
obtained were not wholly confined to the
British market. We propose to continue
this work during the current year, concentrating particularly on the exhibitions
organized by the grocers' associations and
kindred bodies, as these are visited by the
largest and most direct customers for our
goods. Officers of my Department and of
the Ministry of Agriculture attend these
exhibitions, and are ready to convey information and lists of Northern Ireland
suppliers to all inquirers.
As regards the normal day to day work.
of the Ministry, I do not propose to enter

letters of appreciation from various
centres bear witness to the services we set
ourselves to render to the mercantile
community of the Province.

of providing accommodation in the
Custom House for the Northern Ireland

having become available as a result of the

in the new Law Courts for Administrative Staffs of Northern Ireland Departments, who, by reason of the nature of
their activities must, on the grounds of
public convenience, be housed in the city.
Regarding the item of £1,900, which appears for the first time in the Estimate,
this requires some explanation.
When
to
the administration of the Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland was transferred
to the Northern Ireland Government a
revision of the 6-inch ordnance maps,
which are the statutory maps for Northern Ireland, was then in progress.
In
the interests of economy it was decided to
suspend the revision of these maps and to
proceed with the revision of the 25-inch
maps only. Accordingly, it has been the
practice in the past few years merely to
issue reprints of existing 6-inch maps,
but these maps are now rapidly becoming
obsolete, and, in consequence, cease
meet the requirements of the Land Purchase Commission, Land Registry, Commissioner of Valuation and the general
public. It has, therefore, become necessary to revise the 6-inch scale maps, necessitating the provision of additional accommodation and of photographic equipment at the premises of the Ordnance
Survey. The item has been included in
Section I of this Estimate, as it is considered a charge of such a nature as will
enable us to recover the amount of the
necessary expenditure from the Imperial
Government under Section 34 of the Act
of 1920.
Turning now to Section II of the Estimate, I have already referred to the inwill
crease appearing under this Section, and
an explanation of this increase
doubtless be welcomed by hon. Members.

penditure
in

The next item appearing under this
head is a provision of £5,000 in respect
of the Northern Government's contribution towards the cost of the erection of
the new Administrative Offices at Stormont. I may explain the necessity for
making such provision. The extent of
the accommodation at Stormont for which
the Imperial Government has accepted
liability under Section 34 of the 1920
Act is for a staff of 850 at Stormont and
250 in the new Law Courts, making a
total of 1,100. After a comprehensive
review of all the circumstances we were
convinced that this accommodation would
not likely prove sufficient to provide for
the normal discharge or the development
of social services that might take place.
It was decided, therefore, to ask that
accommodation should be provided at
Stormont at the expense of Northern Ireland funds, for a further 70 persons, and
the building at present in course of construction is designed to accommodate
that increased number. The total cost
of the extra accommodation, calculated
on the basis of a pro rata estimated cost
of that portion of the new building only,
which is designed for Departmental as
distinct from Parliamentary purposes, is
estimated at £30,000. This is, however,
only an approximate Estimate, and is
subject to variation according to the
fluctuation of building costs.
It was
agreed that the contribution should be
paid as and when required, and the provision of £5,000 is required to enable
payment of the first instalment to be
made. This is considered to be a more
desirable and economical course to adopt
than the alternative of having at a future
date to add to the original structure at
Stormont,

For various reasons, I am sorry to say,
delay has taken place in the progress of
the work of re-modelling the Belfast
Prison, so that the Estimates now put
forward are in the main re-votes. Unavoidable delay has again arisen in the
preparation of the plans for the erection.
of the warders' cottages, and this has
prevented a start being made on this work,
but it is anticipated that a contract for

Similar delay occurred in the provision of
new workshops within the jail itself, but
this work is now proceeding satisfactorily.
The progress on the remaining items
is contingent upon a completion of the
above works, and it is hoped that an
effective start will also be made on the
remainder of the work during the present
year. The installation of electric lighting in the prison has now been practically
completed.
I come now to the item known as
Ormeau Avenue or the purchase and
adaptation of premises for use of the
Ministry of Labour Headquarters. Hon.
Members will recall that in presenting

Government of premises in
of premises in Ormeau
Avenue to be used, for the time being

As stated in the footnote, the purchase
price has been fixed at a sum of £16,500,
and falls to be paid to the owners of the
property, who are the Imperial Government, as a final charge on Northern
Ireland Funds during the current financial
year, whilst until such time as the new
Administrative Offices at Stormont are
ready for occupation by Northern Ireland
Government Staffs, the Imperial Government has agreed to pay to the Government
of Northern Ireland an annual sum
equivalent to the rents hitherto payable
under Section 34 of the Government of
Ireland Act in respect of the existing
rented buildings. It will thus be seen
that the Imperial Government is con.
cerned in two capacities in this transaction
-firstly as the vendor of the building in
Ormeau Avenue, and, secondly as being
under a statutory liability to provide
temporary accommodation for the headquarters' staff of the Ministry of Labour
pending the provision of permanent
premises. It is anticipated that the
annual sums to be received from the
Imperial Government will be sufficient to
recoup to us the costs of adaptation, and
that the building can in due course be
sold for at least the amount we paid for
it.
The amount to be credited in respect
of these rents appears under Sub-head O
as an appropriation-in-aid of the Vote.

Hon. Members are aware that Malone
Reformatory has been acquired by the
Government, and now falls to be maintained out of public funds. With a view
to bringing this institution up to the
modern standard of efficiency, and also
to meet probable future requirements,
an examination has been carried out by
the Works Branch of the Ministry of
Finance. As a result of this examination it was discovered that the existing
system of gas lighting was very unsatisfactory, and that the machinery and fire
appliances in the institution were obsolete
and in a very poor condition. It is,
therefore, considered essential to instal
electric light and power driven machinery,
and at the same time to replace the existing fire appliances by more up-to-date
machines. New cubicles are also required. As this expenditure arises from
the fact that in Northern Ireland there
was no Borstal Institution corresponding
to that at Clonmel, it falls to be met out
of the No. 2 Capital Fund, as we call it,
or the £400,000 paid to us by the Imperial Government in respect of the cost
of capital construction necessary to provide Northern Ireland with buildings
for which no previous counterpart existed
in the province.
Hon. Members are aware that the
work on the provision of a new Central
Employment Exchange has been completed satisfactorily, and the building is
now in occupation by the Ministry of
Labour. As a result various buildings
throughout the city, which had been oc-

The scheme for the provision and equipment of a Training College and Hostel
at Stranmillis is making satisfactory

on the erection of a new Lecture Block
was commenced last year. A contract
has been placed for adaptations at Hampton House which, as hon. Members are
aware, was acquired for the purpose of a
Men's Hostel, and the work has already
commenced.
Stranmillis Public Elementary School,
together with the teacher's residence, has
been taken over by the Government for

in connection with the Training College.
The cost of acquiring the School for this

which I referred when speaking of the
Malone Training School.
The existing laboratory accommodation
at the Poultry Research Station has been
found to be quite inadequate for the
present requirements, and it is proposed
to utilize the existing storage accommodation as an extension laboratory. This
will, therefore, necessitate the provision
of alternative storage accommodation.
In addition, it will be necessary to provide
additional poultry pens to accommodate
the increasing number of birds which are
being put forward for entry at the egglaying competitions at this institution.
The work on the provision of farm
buildings and cottages at the North-West
Agricultural Institute, Strabane, has now
been completed, and this item disappears
from the Vote. Similarly, the main
works on the extension of Greenmount
Agricultural College have been completed,
except for a minor item in regard to the
purchase of farm implements, which will
be completed during the current financial
year. Further small alterations to improve existing accommodation for live
stock are required at the Ulster Dairy
School, Cookstown.

Details of a scheme for the improvement of Ardglass Harbour for the purpose of extending the fishing facilities of
the town are. fully set out. The progress
of works which were provided for last
year has been retarded owing to various
difficulties. A start has, however, been
made on the formation of the new curing
plots, which will, in all probability, be
available for the ensuing fishing season.
The necessary dredging operations at
Ardglass will be started shortly.

Mr. KYLE: I am sure the Committee

I want to suggest to the Government

of their own in connection with the Government buildings, instead of paying
premiums to insurance companies.
Mr. POLLOCK: We have considered
that question.
Mr. KYLE: I know that the Belfast
City Council did this some years ago, and
they found it was quite possible for them
to form their own insurance fund. They
were not alone in that respect, for, many
years ago, Bradford adopted the principle
of establishing an insurance scheme for
their public buildings. They found that
it paid them to have their own insurance
scheme, instead of paying premiums to
insurance companies that were not warranted by the risks involved through fire
or other causes. I am glad to learn that
the Minister of Finance has considered
that question. His consideration has
probably not induced him to fall in with
the idea, but I think the matter is well
worthy of exploration, as, in my opinion,
it would be the means of effecting

I
agree that it would be very desirable

charge of them, and some have been

Motion made, and Question proposed,

(Captain Mulholland.)
Mr. W. MCMULLEN:
There is a
matter that I want to refer to, briefly,
affecting the Department of the Minister
of Labour, and in the earlier part of the
evening I intimated to him my intention
to do this. Members of the House may
have seen in the newspapers this morning
a report concerning a strike in the building industry in Derry. I understand that
120 bricklayers are now involved in an
industrial dispute in Derry, and that
agents-two delegates came across from
England and Scotland from the Brick and
Stonelayers' Association, to make arrangements for the transfer of these men from
Derry to England and Scotland.
Now
this will create a very serious position so
far as house-building and other house construction is concerned. I want to find
out whether the Ministry of Labour has
intervened in the dispute that has taken
place in Derry up to the moment, and if
not what is the reason they have not intervened. As one who has a fairly extensive knowledge of negotiations, I would
not like to see a position of stalemate
developing there. It will retard the
building of houses and probably incidentally throw a large number of other
workers, such as builders' labourers, out.
When I am on this point perhaps the
Minister of Labour will give some information as to what the situation in
Belfast is at the present time. I observe
from the Press that the negotiations have
been prolonged. I do not think there
has been any successful outcome from
these negotiations at the moment. So far
as I am able to observe by the Press there
seems to have been a deadlock reached.
I hope that is not the situation. I would
like to give the Minister of Labour this
opportunity of dealing with the first
point I have raised, and also, he may give
us some definite information as to whether
his Department has intervened in the
negotiations that have gone on and with
what result.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is quite true
negotiations have been proceeding for some
time in both Derry and in Belfast between
employers and employees in the building
trade. I understand that these negotiations are still proceeding, and on an
occasion of this kind, under the circumstances, I am inclined to think that the
least said the soonest mended. The
Department has not directly intervened
in the discussions up to the present because we have found that it is the wiser
course for the Department to pursue,
namely, that we should leave it as far as
possible to the employers and the workers
to settle these difficulties between themselves, and the practice we follow is that
we watch the proceedings and then, if
either party approaches us in connection
with the matter we endeavour to find out
from the other party if our services would
be acceptable to both. That practice we
have followed in the past with a reasonable degree of success, and I can assure
the hon. Member that we will continue to
pursue that policy in the dispute which, at
the present time, I regret to say has taken
place. I sincerely trust, in the interest
of the whole community, as well as in the
interests of both employers and employed,
that the differences which at the present
time exist will be satisfactorily adjusted
at an early date.
Mr. KYLE: While I quite agree with
the right hon. Gentleman that it perhaps
is a case of the least said the soonest
mended, yet I think the matter so far
as the first part of my colleague's question
is concerned has not been answered. If it
is true that in consequence of the building
trade dispute in Derry bricklayers are
going to be taken from the North of Ireland to Britain, it will mean that a very
serious state of affairs so far as the building trade in the North of Ireland is concerned. And if a dispute takes place in
the building trade-which like the right
hon. Gentleman I hope, and we all hope,
will not take place so far as Belfast is

concerned what is going to be the position of the Ministry of Labour in this

From the point of view of the general
community, from the point of view of the
householders, and those people who desire new houses, as well as from the point
of view of business people who are building additions to their premises at the
present time, it will be most unfortunate
if this dispute takes place. I would
counsel the Minister of Labour to get his
Department interested, to find out how
little is the difference between employers
and employees in this particular dispute,
and to see if it is not possible to bridge
over what, after all, is the very narrow
chasm that divides the employers from
the workpeople in the building trade at
the present time. It will be an unfortunate development if 150 bricklayers
leave Northern Ireland for Britain, because it would leave the building trade
in Northern Ireland absolutely denuded
of bricklayers, without whom building
operations cannot be continued.

Mr. KYLE: I want to say how profoundly disappointed I am that the
Minister of Labour did not see his way to
2R
Lead Paint Bill-
Third Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
accept any of the Amendments which
were put down for the Committee stage
of this Measure. During the Committee
stage the right hon. Gentleman said that
the reason why the delegates of certain
countries, notably France and Belgium,
were in favour of the Convention was that
it was in the interests of those countries
to take that attitude, inasmuch as they
are interested in the zinc trade, as opposed
to the interests of the British Empire
in the lead industry.
I feel and I want to say it as emphatically as I can-that the right hon.
Gentleman was very ungracious, indeed,
to the delegates of France and Belgium
in this connection, and, so far as I am
concerned, I want to say that I would
have nothing whatever to do with the
statement imputing motives to France
and Belgium of the nature to which I
have referred. After all, a few years ago,
France and Belgium were the gallant
Allies of Great Britain in the World War,
and it seems to me that it is a most
wrongful thing for the Minister of
Labour to suggest that France and Belgium were in favour of the ratification
of the White Lead Convention because
they were interested in the development
of the zinc industry.
I went to some trouble to find out
whether or not France and Belgium had
actually ratified the White Lead Convention, and I found that they were not
amongst the countries which had ratified
it. I think, therefore, that as little as
the right hon Gentleman can do is to
say that he was mistaken in imputing
motives to. France and Belgium in this
connection.
This Convention, advocating the abolition of the use of white lead in paint, was
passed by a Conference that was held in
Geneva in 1921. According to this Convention, each State ratifying it undertook
to prohibit with certain specified exceptions the use of white lead in the internal
painting of
of buildings, and directed
the use of white lead in operations for
which its use is not prohibited on certain
detailed principles that are specified. It
prohibits the use of white lead by males
under 18, and by all females in work of
an industrial character.
The prohibition came into force in 1927,
and yet the right hon. Gentleman has
not seen his way to adopt the Convention
that was passed by a Conference at which
Great Britain was represented. The
countries that have signified their intention of ratifying the Convention are
ten in number out of thirty, and it is
certainly not too much to expect that the
Government of Northern Ireland, where
there are no great interests involved,
should be able to ratify a Convention of
this character.
A considerable amount of discussion
has taken place on this Measure in England, and as a result of the Bill which
was passed in the British Parliament-of
which this Measure is an exact copy-Sir
Thomas Legge, who was present at the
Conference at which the Convention was
passed, resigned his official position as
senior medical inspector of factories, which
shows how much he felt the action of
the British Government in not fulfilling
what he considered to be their pledge.
I feel very strongly that the Government of Northern Ireland ought, at least,
to have made a more gallant attempt, or
a more accurate attempt, to carry out the
wishes of the International Conference
held at Geneva. I want to repeat as
emphatically and as unhesitatingly as I
can that I repudiate the statement made
by the right hon. Gentleman during the
Committee stage of this Measure, that it
was in the interests of the countries referred to that zinc should be used instead
of white lead. Those are the right hon.
Gentleman's words, and yet, as a matter
of fact, we find that neither France nor
Belgium have actually ratified the Convention so far as white lead is concerned.
I think that tends to show the inaccurate
nature of the statement of the right hon.
Gentleman.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I do think that my hon.
Friend (Mr. Kyle) has tried to make a
mountain out of a molehill. I cast no
reflection upon either of those great
countries to which he has referred. I
only stated a fact when I said that those
countries have great zinc works, while we
in this country have none; and as a
matter of fact it is quite natural that
these countries should support an industry which is mainly their own, while
it is the duty of Great Britain, just in the
same way, to care for those industries
which are mainly hers and her dominions.
That is the position quite clearly as I see

it.

But may I point out, in reference to this
Convention, that a Committee of experts
was set up at Geneva to inquire into this
whole matter, and those experts unanimously recommended that white lead paint
should continue to be used. The statement which I made was very largely the
statement which was made by the Chairman of that Committee of experts. The
position is simply this: The hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) appears to wish to argue
that there has been a breach of faith on
the part of the British Government and
of our Government in not ratifying this
draft Convention which has been agreed
to by our delegates. The Treaty of
Versailles, under Article 405, made it
perfectly clear that all that the delegates
undertook to do was to recommend the
terms of the Convention to the responsible authorities in their own
country, and if it was considered by that
country that it was not desirable that the
Convention should be ratified either in
whole or in part the matter ended there,
and there was no breach of faith or no
want of honour displayed. That is the
position as clearly expressed as I can
express it and as I see it.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
the Third time," put, and agreed to.
Ordered: That the Clerk do carry the
Bill to the Senate and acquaint them
that this House has agreed to the said
Bill without amendment.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): I would ask the forbearance of the Committee if they do not
hear me very well, because I have been
suffering from a rather bad cold within
the last two or three days and am as
hoarse as a crow.
In the general survey of the Ministry's
work which I made in this Committee
recently, I covered the several activities
for which provision is made in the
Estimate for Agricultural Services now
before the Committee. Hence on this
occasion I will content myself with a very
brief reference to some of the main subheads of this Estimate.
While there are increases in the cost
of certain services, these increases are
more than counterbalanced by decreases
in others, so that the whole Estimate
shows a reduction of £424.
The increases occur under the following
sub-heads:-
Agricultural Research, £1,750; Improvement of Live Stock, £1,100; and
Forestry, £636, the principal reductions
being in respect of Seed Supply Schemes,
£3,000; Building Grant to Royal Ulster
Agricultural Society, £1,500; and Unemployment Relief Scheme (Forestry),
£1,288.
I should, however, state that in the
event of the Ministry during the current
year being able to acquire additional land
for afforestation it may be found necessary to ask Parliament to make further
provision under the last named sub-head.
Hon. Members are doubtless aware that
the scheme of loans for replacement of
live stock has recently been temporarily
revived. A statement as to the amount
which will be needed for this purpose
will be submitted to the House at a later
date.
Under Sub-head A, Agricultural Research, provision is made to meet the
charges for labour, lighting, heating,
etc., which will arise when the new agricultural buildings at Elmwood Avenue,
1255 Agricultural Services

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Estimates-
[Mr. Archdale]
in connection with Queen's University,
are occupied, and for the employment of
two additional research assistants, one for
the chemical division and one for the
plant diseases division, required, owing to
the increased number of inquiries received
from farmers-1,500 last year.
In connection with Queen's University,
the grant-in-aid-£23,507-for building
will be recouped from the Colwyn Grant.
In the Hillsborough Research Station
the trustees have been incorporated by
Act of Parliament, and are now in occupation of this station, which comprises
almost 500 acres in the Great Park at
Hillsborough. The aggregate provision
-£20,800-in the present Estimate-is
an increase of £500 over last year.
In regard to the improvement of live
stock, the additional amount included
under this head is needed (a) to augment
the sum hitherto available for subsidies
for the purchase of high-class bulls for the
use of breeders of pedigree cattle, and
(b) to provide for grants to eight new
Milk Recording Associations. Several
hon. Members have been making inquiries
about some of the grants to be made for
pedigree bulls, so I think I might enlarge
a little upon that subject.
The County Committees out of their
joint funds are spending £10,686 on
Live Stock Schemes, and this year 352
premium bulls are standing in the Six
County area. The object is that small
farmers should have the advantage of
these bulls for their cows at a low fee.
This scheme is, practically speaking, confined to the improvement of cross-bred
stock.
There are 61 Milk Recording Associations at work this year. The Ministry
assists these associations by providing
funds for the purchase of pedigree dairy
bulls; the subsidy given by the Ministry
amounts in each case to two-thirds of the
cost of the bull up to a maximum grant of
£73. The object is to improve the milking
strain of cross-bred cows belonging to
members of the Milk Recording
Associations.
There are a number of breeders of pedigree shorthorns in Northern Ireland.
The herds can be divided into two
classes:
:-
(a) Pedigree cattle that are bred on
dairy lines; and
(b) Pedigree cattle that are bred on
beef lines.
It is upon these breeders that the
Ministry and the country depend to produce pedigree bulls to take up the
premiums offered by the County Committees, as well as pedigree bulls for the
Milk Recording Associations. The
Ministry is spending a limited amount of
money each year to assist these breeders
of pedigree stock, both those who are devoting their attention to the production
of milk and those who are devoting their
attention to the production of beef. The
conditions are:
(a) That at least three owners of
pedigree herds, who have sufficient
cows, must combine to purchase a highclass stock bull approved by the
Ministry.
(b) That a subsidy to the extent of
two-thirds of the cost of the bull up
to a maximum grant of £333 is given
by the Ministry.
As the three or more breeders must have
sufficient cows to mate with this highclass stock bull, they are not required to
allow the bull to serve cows belonging to
other owners. Besides, there is the great
danger of introducing disease into pedigree herds.
By means of these schemes the Ministry
assists:-
(a) the poor small farmers;
(b) the more progressive men who
are gradually grading up their stock,
and who are members of Milk Recording Associations; and
(c) the pedigree breeders who produce each year the young bulls that are
selected for the county premiums and
for Milk Recording Associations.
Under Sub-head J, Forestry, the increase is due to the fact that since the
Estimates for last year were passed the
Ministry took over additional areas at
Baronscourt and Newcastle amounting
to over 510 acres, and that a further area
of 230 acres will be taken over during the
current year.
About 440 acres have also
been taken over at Hillsborough, making
in all a total of 1,180 acres.

In this Estimate
the expenditure shows a net increase of
£807. This increase is mainly due to the
decision recently arrived at to resume the
production of the 6-inch maps of Northern
Ireland. When the administration of
the Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland
was vested in the Ministry of Agriculture
it was decided, for reasons of economy, to
suspend the revision and production of
the 6-inch maps and to confine ourselves
to the 25-inch maps only. The view then
taken was that the purposes for which
6-inch maps were required might be met
generally by the issue of maps on the
25-inch scale the scale on which field revision is carried out. Arrangements were,
however, made for the reprinting from
existing plates of such 6-inch sheets as
might be specially required. Mainly as
a result of this change of policy it was
found possible to administer the service in
Northern Ireland with a staff of 36, as
against a personnel of 50 which had been
fixed as the appropriate establishment for
Northern Ireland at the time my Ministry
began to function.

Subsequent experience, however, has
shown that an adherence to this decision
is impracticable, owing to the fact that
the 6-inch map is the statutory map for
Northern Ireland and that it would not
be feasible to make the 25-inch
statutory map. Moreover, it was found
that up-to-date maps on the 6-inch scale
were essential to the work of various
Government Departments, notably the
Valuation Department and the Land
Purchase Commission. In the circumstances it was necessary that work on the
6-inch sheets should be resumed. Provision has, accordingly, been made in this
Estimate for the additional staff, etc.,
which is necessary to give effect to this
decision. Certain necessary initial capital
expenditure in this connection in the shape
of the provision and equipment of a
photographic studio at estimated
cost of £1,900 has been provided for in
the Estimate for Public Works and

Mr. KYLE: When I ask the House to
grant a Second Reading to this Bill,
which proposes to reduce the hours of
labour of a number of workpeople in
Northern Ireland, the House should try
to recall some of the vicissitudes of the
hours question in Great Britain and Ireland. In the 1840's the agitation for a
48-hour week and an eight-hour day was
started, and ever since then there have
been repeated agitations on the part of
the workers to secure that beneficial reform.
Recently the proposal has been placed
on a very different plane, because not only
has it been secured-that is the 48-hour
week and the eight-hour day-by the
majority of workers through their trades
union activities, but, in the case of the
miners, Governments have actually passed
laws regulating their hours; but, further,
it has become a matter of international
importance and is recognized as such in
the preamble to Section 13 of the Treaty
Mulholland, Captain The Hon. Henry
George Hill
Pollock, Right Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Captain Dixon.
of Versailles, as a result of which a Conference was held at Washington in 1919
attended by representatives of thirtynine countries. With the exception of exenemy countries and Russia every European country was represented. There was
an almost full representation of the South
American States, along with delegates
from China, Persia, and Siam, and
Canada, India, and South Africa, on this
occasion, took their places as separate
entities for the first time in an official
international assembly. 123 delegates
were present, 73 of whom were Government delegates, twenty-five representatives
of employers and twenty-five of workers.
These were assisted by a body of advisers
of whom twenty-three were women.
Hon. W. B. Wilson, Secretary for Labour
for the United States of America, was
President of this Convention, and the
Right Hon. G. N. Barnes, M.P., was one
of its Vice-Presidents. This Conference
adopted a Convention upon which this
Bill is based. I have not exceeded the
draft Convention by a hair's breadth in
the drafting of this Measure.
The
When the interests of the many and
diverse countries which passed this Convention are taken into account I think it
will be agreed that it is not too much to
expect this Parliament to grant a Second
Reading to the Bill. Since the Convention was passed the following
countries have ratified it: Bulgaria,
Czecho-Slovakia, Greece, India, Roumania, Belgium, British Columbia, Italy,
the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats
and Slovenes, Spain, and Sweden, and
Measures have been introduced in the
Parliaments of the Argentine, Bolivia,
Italy, Denmark, Germany, Norway,
South Africa, Luxemburg, Austria,
1275 Hours of Employment Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Kyle]
Brazil, France, the Netherlands, and
Poland to give effect to the Convention
that was passed at Washington in 1919.
One of the main reasons why I am introducing this Measure is because I mentioned it in the election address on which
I was returned to this House, and I now
take this opportunity of proposing the
Bill and asking the House to give it a
Second Reading. It seems to me that it
is a laudable thing that we should attempt
in Northern Ireland to establish the
48-hour week by law. It will also be
noticed, I am sure, by some Members of
the House that recently not merely a 48hour week but a 44-hour week has been
passed into law by some of the Australian
States in the British Commonwealth of
free nations, so that it is not too much to
expect that we in Northern Ireland should
similarly have a 48-hour week by law
established.
The general argument in favour of the
Bill is that it has been found by experience that almost as much work can be done
in a properly organized firm in 48 hours
as was done formerly in 55. You have
only to ask the opinion of those people
who control the main industry in Northern Ireland, that is the linen trade, as to
whether or not almost as much work can
be done in the 48 hours as was formerly
done in 55 in the mills and in the factories; and when you take into consideration that these mills and factories are
mostly worked by machinery, which has
got to be attended, I think it will be
agreed that almost as much work can be
done in 48 hours as was done in 55.
The classical example of the 48-hour
week in the engineering world is the firm
of Messrs. Mather & Platt, of Manchester,
who a good many years ago-many years
before the war-established a forty-eight
hour week when fifty-four was the ordinary working week in the engineering
trade. They found that they could get
as much-this is on record-and better
work done in their engineering shop in the
48 hours as was done formerly in the 54.
As a matter of fact, Rountree's Cocoa
Works of York, who have made a careful
and exhaustive study of labour conditions.
in relation to output, maintain that this is
so, and have recently proven by extensive
investigation that the working week
should not exceed forty-four hours, and,
accordingly, have adopted this working
week themselves in their huge factory at
York.
When I am able to inform the House
that the following trades all enjoy a 48hour week or less-boot and shoe manufacturing, 48 hours; building, 44 hours;
cooperage, 47 hours; furniture, 44 to 47
hours; leather, 48 hours; engineering and
shipbuilding, 47 hours; iron and steel
manufacture, 47 hours; general metal
trades, 47 hours; mining, 48 hours;
pottery, 47 hours; railways and road
transport, 48 hours; printing trade, 48
hours; docks, 44 to 46 hours; spinning
and weaving trades, linen, 48 hoursthey will be able to appreciate that this
is no drastic or revolutionary proposal.
Nevertheless this Measure would be a
boon to a large number of workpeople in
the Six Counties. I estimate the number
as being between 20,000 and 25,000, the
most important section of which is the
bleaching, dyeing, and finishing trade
Despite repeated attempts to reduce their
hours to 48, the workers in this trade are
still compelled to work 49 hours per week
in most of the bleach greens in tho
country. There are some exceptions, but
the majority of firms in the country in
the bleaching, dyeing, and finishing trade
work 49 hours. The workers have repeatedly asked the employers to reduce
these hours to 48.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews)
during a debate on a somewhat similar
Measure advocated trade union organization to reduce the hours of labour. These
workers have attempted it in this way.
but, owing to the strength of the employers' organization, had to give way
rather than enter into a trade dispute
which would have brought about a great
deal of suffering and hardship, and, per
haps, have done their trade an irreparable
injury. Now we appeal to this House to
remedy this injustice and hardship inflicted upon the workpeople and also to
protect the large number of people who
work in small industrial establishments
and who are not able on account of their
isolation to bargain effectively in this
matter.

Another argument that might be advanced is that with a reduction of hours
to 48 per week the roll of accidents would
undoubtedly decrease. The important
investigations carried on during the war

doubtedly low wages and bad conditions.
play a very important part in the sickness that affects industry, but long hours

Unor
In addition to all that I have said and
the arguments I have adduced there remains the more important argument to
me, and that is that, in addition to the
reduction that may take place in the
numbers of the unemployed as a result of
this Measure, this is a Measure calculated
to give more leisure to workpeople, to
enable them to live a more wholesome
life, to enable them to take a more useful
part in public affairs, to enable them to
live as their Creator intended them to
live, and not to be always bowed down
by their hours of labour. Science in industry has multiplied the productive
powers of man ten-thousand-fold. Surely
we are right to expect for the worker,
the producer, that this House will pass
this Measure to afford some slight relief
to a large number of the people of
Northern Ireland.
I do not think it is necessary for me to
add very much to what I have stated in
regard to the productive powers of industry, or to add very much to the facts
that have been adduced to the House regarding the possibilities of production
in industry. I think everybody knows that
men to-day can with the aid of machinery produce ever so much more than men
could ten, fifteen or twenty years ago;
and surely, as I say, it is right that the
working people should expect that their
hours of labour should be reduced to 48,
so that they might get some more leisure
as well as more results of the labour that
they give.
I now come to deal with the Measure
itself apart from the general arguments
in favour of the reduction of hours.
Clause 1 of the Bill lays it down that
subject to certain conditions and provisos, the hours of labour in any industrial undertaking shall not exceed eight
in any day or 48 hours in any week.
Sub-section 2 of Clause 1 defines what an
industrial undertaking is for the purposes
of this Bill. Broadly speaking, the
definition includes all workers except
workers in commercial departments,
domestic service, and agricultural
labourers, and follows the definition of
"industrial worker agreed upon by the
International Labour Office and submitted at Washington in 1919 for the
approval of the Conference. Do not
forget that the Convention which I have
mentioned was passed on the motion of
Great Britain, seconded by France.
on
Clause 2 of the Bill provides for exceptions to the 8-hour day where by law,
customs, or agreement between organizations of workers and employers, the hours
worked are one or more days less than
eight. The limit of eight hours may as
respect the workers affected by the law,
customs, or agreement, be exceeded
the remaining days if an agreement to
that effect is arrived at between such
organizations or representatives. That
makes provision for a state of affairs we
have in the North of Ireland. In almost
all trades the workpeople are free on
Saturday afternoons, and it is necessary
to make provision to increase the hours
beyond eight on the other five days of
the week to enable the workers to get the
half day off on Saturday.
Sub-sections 3 and 4 of Clause 2 deal
with shift workers, and make provision to

[Mr. Kyle]
suit workers transferring from night
shift to day shift, and also make provision
that in certain cases a worker may work
56 hours in a week. We know it may
happen that such workers may have to
work a further eight hours inside the
week. That happens in the shipyards.
It also happens in other places in the
North of Ireland, and in order that the
right hon. Gentleman may not meet us
with a small flaw in regard to this particular Measure we make provision that
in certain cases the worker may be allowed
to work 56 hours a week. Sub-section 6
of Clause 2 provides that in case of
accident, actual or threatened, the 48
hours a week may be exceeded to avoid
serious interference with the ordinary
work of the industrial undertaking.
or
Clause 3 lays down the conditions under
which overtime may be worked.
It lays
down the condition that at least time and
a quarter shall be paid for overtime. It
does not interfere with any custom
agreement more favourable that has been
or may be established. It does not prevent the payment of upstanding wages
covering periods of short time or overtime
in accordance with agreement made
between organizations of employers and
workers. That shows the modesty of this
Measure. We are not asking, as a
matter of fact, to establish by law the
actual trade customs of the majority of
the workers in Belfast. I am safe in
saying that the majority of the organized
workers in Belfast have a higher rate for
overtime than time and a quarter; yet,
we are asking the House to pass into law
an overtime rate of time and a quarter
where a 48-hour week obtains. Again,
we are very careful lest we might imperil
the passage of this Bill, because we make
provision that arrangements made by
employers who pay certain of their
employees wages for holidays and short
time may not be upset.
Clause 4 makes provision for helping
the enforcement of the Act by means of
notices posted in a conspicuous place in
the firm's premises. These notices will
state the hours at which work begins and
ends, when work is carried on by shifts,
the hours at which each shift begins and
ends. They will also state the intervals
allowed for meals and rest, which are not
to be reckoned as part of the working
hours.
Clause 5 lays down how questions
arising out of the Act may be determined.
It states the questions to be so determined
and the machinery by which they are to
be brought to final decision. The final
arbiter is the umpire or such other person
appointed by the Governor of Northern
Ireland for the purposes of the Act; that
is to say, it is necessary in a Bill of this
character to have some final authority,
and in this Measure we copy the Unemployment Insurance Act by asking the
Governor of Northern Ireland to appoint
an umpire, whose decision will be final.
If hon. Members will look at Clause 5
they will see how important it is that
the questions to be determined should be
specifically stated.
Clause 6 specifies the penalties and
proceedings, and makes it plain that if a
contravention of the Act is caused by an
agent of the firm without the knowledge
of the employer, then the agent is to be
held liable and not the employer. If an
employer can prove to the Court that he
has used due diligence to secure compliance with the Act he shall be exempt
from any conviction in respect of the
offence. Hon. Members, particularly
hon. Members opposite, will notice-
Mr. GRANT: There is no one in the
House except those opposite.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I acquaint the
hon. Member that I am present.
Mr. KYLE:
Hon. Members will see
how modest we are in the proposals
contained in this Measure, and particularly in this Clause: If an employer
can prove to the satisfaction of the Court
that he took due care to see that the
provisions of the Act were enforced the
actual person responsible-the agent of
the employer-will be liable.
Clause 7 deals with the application of
the Act, and lays down specifically the
workers who are not covered by the Act.
You will see Clause 7 provides that the
Act shall not apply-
(a) to members of the employer's
family where the only persons employed
are members of his family; or
(b) to persons holding positions of
supervision or management or employed
in a confidential capacity who are not
usually employed in manual labour,
and are in receipt of upstanding

You will see by that exactly the scope
of the Bill. I estimate, as I have said,
that the Bill will cover some 20,000 to
25,000 workers in the North of Ireland.
Some 10,000 to 15,000 of those workers
are employed in the bleaching, dyeing
and finishing trades. The rest are employed in small industrial establishments
in the North of Ireland. It will be
granting a boon to every one of the persons employed in the small industrial
establishments if this House will agree to
pass the Second Reading of this Measure.
The other Clauses of the Measure are
self explanatory and are not very important. Clause 11 specifies the date at
which the Act, if the House will pass it,
will come into operation. That date is
the 1st May, 1928. If reports are made
that any hardship will be involved in any
particular industry there is a provision
that this date may be postponed for a
further period of six months. I think
that this Bill is of so eminently fair a
character that it will be extremely difficult
for Members opposite to oppose carrying
the provisions of it into effect. The hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Lloyd-
Campbell) said the other evening that
negotiations should take place between
trade unions and organizations of employers to lay down hours of labour.
Broadly speaking, I agree with him.
Broadly speaking, that is what obtains,
but if certain people are so weak in power
that they are unable to get their employers to agree to a 48-hour week surely
the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Lloyd Campbell) will not say
that the people who work in those
small industrial establishments or in
the bleaching, dyeing, and finishing
trades should be asked to work 49
hours or 50 hours, or that the men
who work for some rural district councils
and county councils should be compelled
to work 50 hours because their trade
union is not powerful enough to bring
sufficient pressure to bear on the employers to reduce their hours to 48.
If any hon. Member opposite, and
particularly the hon. Member whom I
have referred to, believes the thing is just
and right then he should support the
Second Reading of this Measure. It has
been proved beyond the shadow of a doubt
of employers, speaking generally without
wanting to give offence to anybody, that
when this agitation was started for an
eight-hour day they opposed the project
and did all sorts of scandalous things to
hinder even such eminent men as Lord
Shaftesbury attempting to get a reform
of the Factory Acts, and to get some curtailment of the hours of labour for women
and young persons. Employers have
adopted that attitude from time immemorial.
Now we have actually got a majority
of workpeople enjoying a week of 48 hours
or less, and that being the case surely it
is not too much to expect that the other
workers who have not got the power
through their trade unions to compel
their employers to grant them this 48hour week will be assisted by this House.
The House will see that the time has come
when they should at least step in and
assist those people who are not able to
assist themselves.
We heard this afternoon that the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Agriculture, gave £1,000 to the Farmers'
Union to help them to bring his message
to the farmers of the North of Ireland.

The hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) has referred at considerable length to what is

I agree with the hon. Member (Mr.

two ways of lowering the cost of production. One is to lower wages and the other
is to increase output. I think the latter
course is the course that we will have to
adopt. By some method employers and
employees have got to get together, and,
in the same length of time and for the
same wages, produce more material. If
we can do that we lower the cost of that
material and will thus be able to go out
into the foreign market and meet the
competition of other countries. It will
be done by the two sides working together,
and, as I say, increasing production,
whether by improved machinery or by any
other method
It is a fallacy that is often cried out
from the housetops that if a man produces

of a job. On the contrary, if a man can
produce more, more trade will come to the

over the world, and from many of those

the trouble at home-call it what like

in this country-is that they have got to
put more work into their life and time and
have got to do it for the same money.
In other words, we have got to increase
the output of the country if we are going
to get back and retain the markets of the
world.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am taking this reply for my
right hon. Friend, the Prime Minister.
The statements made by the hon.
Member are substantially correct.
The trade in fertilizers and feeding
stuffs in Northern Ireland is closely interlocked with that of Great Britain, and
in the interests of both traders and far-
Oral Answers

mers it is most important that any legislation affecting or regulating the trade
should be identical in the two countries.
The Act to which the hon. Member
refers sets up a special committee to advise on the Regulations to be made in regard to this subject. Had separate
legislation been undertaken here on
identical lines it would have been necessary to have set up a separate Northern
Irish Advisory Committee, whereas by
virtue of our inclusion in the British Act
we have direct representation on the
British Committee, in the person of the
chief agricultural analyst for Northern
Ireland.
Moreover, no Regulations recommended
by this Advisory Committee can become
operative in Northern Ireland until laid
before this Parliament.
Thus the inclusion of Northern Ireland
in the scope of the Act not only has the
effect of keeping our progress in these
matters in harmony with the steps taken
in Great Britain, but also retains the
authority of this legislature and enables
us directly to benefit from the wider
knowledge and experience of an Advisory
Committee drawn from the whole of the
Kingdom.
Had it been possible to do so, the
proposed inclusion of Northern Ireland
in the British Bill would have been
brought to the notice of the House, but,
unfortunately, Parliament was not in
Session at that time and an immediate
decision was necessary. I should add,
however, that the extension of this
Measure to Northern Ireland in no way
precludes this Parliament from discussing
the subject or from dealing with any
further legislation which may be required.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the application of
this Measure to Northern Ireland was
not carried in the British House of
Commons, but was inserted in the House
of Lords, and would he be good enough to
publish the correspondence that has
taken place between the Northern
Government and the British authorities
in relation to this matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir. This is
entirely a Departmental matter, and
usually correspondence of that nature is
regarded as confidential.

Budget Statement, 1927-28.
Mr. POLLOCK : This is the sixth
annual summary of the expected revenue
and expenditure of the Province which it
has been my privilege to submit to Parliament.
When I presented my first Budget in
1922 we were faced with the difficulty of
interpreting the intentions of Parliament
as set out in the financial provisions of
the 1920 Act.
This was not altogether surprising in
view of the novel features of a scheme of
Devolution based on federal principles in
these islands.
It was only by the machinery of an
Arbitration Committee that these difficulties have been fully overcome, and I
am now happy to be able to state that our
arrangements with the Imperial Treasury,
through the operation of the Joint Exchequer Board, work smoothly and to
some extent automatically.
I am also bound to say that during the
intervening years the permanent officials
of the Imperial Treasury have
deavoured to facilitate our work, notwithstanding the difficult technical problems
with which they and we were often faced.
en-
A year ago when I stood in this place
performing a duty similar to that which
I am undertaking to-day I ventured to
call the attention of the House to the uncertainties necessarily attached to Estimates, whether of revenue or expenditure,
made under conditions of great industrial
disturbances such as then existed.
Hon. Members will recall that it was
in this month of May last year that a
relatively small band of extreme factionists startled the nation by action which
appeared to be aimed at the overthrow of
the whole structure of British civilization.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Does
that refer to Mr. Baldwin and his colleagues?
Mr. POLLOCK: A few days, however, sufficed to convince the actors in
this drama that the foundations of British
liberty were too deeply and firmly laid
to be uprooted by a small junta of revolutionaries. This is the point I want to
make and the reason why I have introduced the subject. The wounds which
were inflicted on the industrial life of the
country by the General Strike and the
protracted coal-mining disturbance were
too deep to be readily healed, and the
serious direct losses suffered by almost
every industry in the country could not
fail to be reflected in the returns of
national revenue.
The effect of these disturbed conditions
during the greater part of the year on the
revenues of Northern Ireland was more
noticeable on those sources of revenue
which, by their nature, are most susceptible to changes in industrial conditions,
that is Customs and Excise Duties and
Income Tax. This will be clearly seen
when I develop my statement.
Happily, those sources of our revenue
over which we exercise control, such as
Death Duties, Entertainment and Stamp
Taxes, Motor Duties, etc., are not so
directly and immediately re-acted upon by
industrial troubles. In fact, our Transferred Revenue taken as a whole continues
to show a very satisfactory expansion.

Death Duties and Motor Vehicle Duties

The interesting feature of this return
is the continued decrease in the use of
alcoholic liquors, and I propose to dwell
on that for a moment. If last year's
decrease stood alone, I should be inclined
to connect it with the exceptional industrial disturbances, but reference to
past years discloses a consistent and
regular reduction in the use both of
spirits and beer. The trade attributes
this reduction to the heavy duties and
consequent high prices of stimulants,
but whether it arises from this cause
from a natural change in the drinking
habits of our people must remain a matter
of speculation. The striking fact, however, remains that the people of Ulster
have consumed less alcohol during this
year, as represented by the very considerable sum of £270,000 of duty.
or
If we translate this reduction in duty
into the cost over the counter, we find
that the total reduction in the expenditure
of the people on alcoholic drinks must
have been at least £600,000 last year,
and probably more.
This continuous decline in the use of
spirits is very instructive.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: In 1914 the consumption in Ulster was 3/4 gallons per
head of the population. Last year's
return is one-quarter of a gallon per
head of the population, that is to say,
the people of this Province are consuming
only one-third of the quantities used in
1914. If we transform these fractions
into total quantity we find that in 1914
the consumption of spirits was about
937,000 proof gallons, whilst last year the
figures are only 310,000 gallons.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: Inland Revenue,

As regards the contribution to Imperial
Services, I would remind the House that
when I presented my statement last year
I estimated that we should have a surplus
of approximately £1,700,000 available
for that purpose, but having regard to
the severe economic disturbances of the
period under review and the heavy loss
of Customs and Excise revenue, it need
not be regarded as surprising that the
available surplus as between revenue and
expenditure only admitted of a contribution of £1,200,000.
Before taking leave of last year I
think it will give satisfaction, and perhaps
offer some encouragement to our manufacfacturers and traders, and indeed to all
those who are interested in the welfare
of the Province, if I refer to our trade
balance for the calendar year 1926.
From the information supplied to me
by the statistical branch of our Ministry
of Commerce, I am able to state that the
total imports of the Province amounted
to £54,800,000, while the exports
curiously enough are returned as
£54,600,000. There is thus a small
adverse balance of £200,000.
But when we take into account the
factors which are known as our invisible
exports, such as interest on investments,
revenue from shipping, expenditure in
Ulster by the Imperial Government, and
other items, we may safely assume that
the balance of trade is well on the right
side.
Taking everything into consideration,
therefore, notwithtsanding the depressed
condition of our principal industries
during the past year and despite our coal
difficulties and burden of unemployment,
we did not merely ride the storm but
weathered it with credit.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK : I come now to the
year upon which we have entered, and
which still largely lies ahead of us. I
propose to take first in order the Estimates of our expenditure, and when ↑
have enlarged on these will set out the

expenditure.
Transferred Expenditure-1927-28.
CONSOLIDATED FUND.
The first important items which confront us are those which are comprised
under the head of Consolidated Fund
expenditure and which do not appear on
the printed Estimates for ordinary
Supply Services. The first is the Road
Fund, estimated to reach £380,000.
Then we have to meet interest on borrowings amounting to £80,000.
This Estimate is influenced by two
important factors. Firstly, the Treasury
Bill rate, and, secondly, the advances
required by the Unemployment Insurance
Fund. As to the Treasury Bill rate, in
view of the recent reduction in the bank
rate I estimate in the meantime we shall
save approximately per cent, on temporary borrowings. In regard to the
second, that is, unemployment, the considerable reduction of unemployment,
with its effect on the finances of the Insurance Fund, will result in a diminution
of our temporary borrowings.
I propose this year to allocate
£297,000 to our various Sinking Funds,
and while dealing with this subject I will
take the opportunity of referring to our
Ulster Savings Certificates. I have
always had a very decided opinion upon
the necessity for Sinking Funds, and I may
point out that even during our years of
stringency we have never failed to make
the necessary provision for the essential
Sinking Funds, thus creating the permanency of those funds which in their
nature are of a disappearing character.

Public attention has recently been
focussed on the very large capital liabilities with which the British Government is faced in regard to National
Savings Certificates, and the present
occasion provides a suitable opportunity
for giving any reassurance which may be
necessary as to the steps we are taking
to provide against a corresponding
liability here in respect of Ulster Savings
Certificates. We started the Ulster
Savings Certificate at 12s. 6d., and in
twelve years it realizes the sum of £1.
Provisions, of course, must be made for
the full liability which lies ahead.
Hon. Members will recollect that
powers were obtained in the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Act, 1923, to
create a Sinking Fund for the purpose of
meeting the accruing charge in so far as
the interest on these securities is concerned. Up to the present time approximately £177,000 has been placed to the
credit of that fund, and provision is made
this year for the allocation of a further
sum of £63,000.
Interest on Ulster Savings Certificates
repaid and the payment of the statutory
salaries of the Speakers of both Houses of
Parliament and the Comptroller and
the Auditor-General will, in all, require
£24,000.
Before leaving the Consolidated Fund
Services, I wish to lay before the Committee particulars of certain new charges
which I propose to place on the Fund
this year.
The first relates to the question of agriculture, and I would say at the outset
that although I have been forced by
reason of financial stringency to refuse
the majority of applications which have
been made on behalf of the agricultural
community, I have been by no means
deaf to these appeals nor indifferent to
the necessity for offering help to fariners
in some practical form.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: I should like to
emphasize that word " practical." My
own personal view in respect to help does
not lie in that direction of grants toward
relief from agricultural rates. Doles are
bad at any time, but the distribution of
large sums of money among our farmers,
the vast mass of whom only get a few
shillings each, and others a pound or two,
has no good effects whatever, and is
simply squander-mania.
No, sir, the agricultural industry will
never be brought into a state of prosperity by a system of pauperization.
Real assistance to the industry can only
be given by educating the farmers in the
science of agriculture, by giving facilities
for procuring the purest and best types
of seed, as well as by the improvement
of stock and other productive measures.
The Government has done a great deal
in the past few years though the Department over which my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Archdale) presides, but we have
always been handicapped by the uncertainty of our financial position. Only
a few months ago my right hon. Friend
came to me with the request for the
necessary money to undertake a scheme of
providing pedigree stock. I had to object
to the expenditure at that time because I
could not see how the necessary few
thousand pounds could be spared, but we
are now able to afford some assistance,
and I propose to allocate from this year's
revenue the sum of £40,000 to be applied
over a period in the productive schemes
of the character which I have outlined.
This work will be carried out through
the agency of the County Committees.
Mr. ELLIOTT:
Hear, hear.

Each of these gentlemen has been indefatigable in his efforts to ensure the best

They have been with me again and

in order that these ex-Servicemen's

They have adduced some remarkably
good arguments which, I admit, I would

as

Services last year amounted to £1,735,000,
showing a substantial increase for the
year of almost £100,000. I am sorry to
say that the increase falls chiefly on the
Post Office Service, although Land Purchase also requires a larger amount, as is
to be expected owing to the development
of that great work.
The increase in Post Office expenditure
is common to the whole Kingdom, and
is chiefly attributable to the Telephone
Service and the necessity for additional
postmen. I am specially concerned in
regard to the Post Office, which, in the
year before last, was almost self-supporting, and which, I had hoped, would be
on a profit-making basis by this time.
The revenue, however, in this Service has
not kept pace with the additional requirements of the Service, but it is reasonable
to assume that the depression in business
has contributed in no small measure to
the reduction of receipts. There is not a
Service connected with the Government
that is more sensitive to conditions of
trade than the Post Office.
As regards Land Purchase there is an
increase of £25,000, bringing the total
cost this year to £279,000. This increase
is only the beginning of a continuing
additional charge which will arise from
the obligations which the Government
have undertaken in the promotion of the
great Land Purchase scheme in the interest of our farming community.
As the transfers from landlord to
tenant proceed the financial responsibility
of the Government will concurrently increase until in a few years it will reach
a maximum calculated at approximately
£325,000 a year, the major portion of
which will extend over a lengthy period,
not far from sixty years. If we capitalize
that we will find that the taxpayers of
Northern Ireland will provide about
£6,000,000 in order that the tenant
farmer may become the owner of his
land.
Outside of Ireland no such beneficent
scheme in connection with land tenure
has ever been undertaken, and if we may
judge from the remarks of my hon.
Friend, who claims to speak for the unbought tenants, there is no case where
less recognition has ever been expressed.
(Laughter.)
Mr. DEVLIN: What about the

While on the subject of expenditure
generally, I have noticed recently that
there has been a good deal of criticism of
the Budget figures of Northern Ireland,
on the lines that a Budget which shows
an expenditure of eleven millions per
annum is far too great for a Province
of the size of ours.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr.
POLLOCK: With this general
criticism, which is founded on no economic
basis, I must entirely disagree.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK : When comparisons
are made with twenty years ago, we forget
that we have now Services in being, on
which we are spending this year no less
than 3 millions, which were non-existent
even so recently as the year 1907, and
which were operative only to a very small
extent in 1914. I refer particularly to

Relief, Health Insurance Services, and
Contributory Pensions. I do not suppose
there is any Member of this Committee
who has the courage to stand on a platform and to suggest that any one of them

fore the war the Government spent something like £500,000 on education in

Thus about one-third of our total population is either in receipt of direct assistance from the State or, through the
medium of State schemes, is secured

Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

given at the present time; I have for the

Changes in Taxation.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have now reached
the point which probably will be found
of most interest to the Committee, that
is, the question of taxation. Several
minor changes are to be made in Great
Britain affecting Stamp Duties and
Death Duties. It is convenient from
every point of view that the laws governing these imposts should be the same in
Ulster as in Great Britain as a great
many commercial transactions as well as
the administration of estates are thereby
facilitated.
Finance Minister's Statement 1332
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
Firstly, I propose to grant relief from
the Companies Capital Duty in the case
of the amalgamation or reconstruction of
Joint Stock Companies. These duties are
at the rate of £1 per cent. on the capital
of companies.
The tendency in these modern days is
very distinctly in the direction of amalgamation of Joint Stock Companies
engaged in similar enterprises with a
view to more economical administration
and production. Such companies must
necessarily have paid Stamp Duties on
their original registration, and I feel it is
a hardship to impose additional Duties if
they desire to coalesce. I hope that this
concession will serve to remove any discouragement which may have existed in
the amalgamations of business concerns
where such combinations are regarded as
offering mutual advantages.
Secondly, in regard to Death Duties,
there are two small changes I propose to
make in the Finance Bill which will be
introduced very shortly.
This is a very technical subject, and
in order that hon. Members may understand its implication I will read the
exact nature of the proposed change-
I find that Mr. Churchill laboured under
exactly the same difficulty in the Imperial
House of Commons:
Under existing law, Legacy Duty and
Succession Duty are not charged on the
same property passing on the death of
a person. But circumstances can arise—
and, in fact, have arisen-where a claim
for one of the duties can be made by our
Exchequer, and a claim for the other
duty on the same property can be lawfully sustained by Great Britain or the
Irish Free State.
The Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
contained a provision which prevents
double taxation in respect of Estate
Duty in each area, but the Clause was not
drafted sufficiently widely to cover the
case
of Legacy and Succession Duty.
Clearly, however, the cases are analogous
and therefore I have made a reciprocal
arrangement with both of these Governments in order to avoid such an instance
of double taxation, and legislative
sanction to these agreements will be
sought. The loss to our Exchequerif it can properly be regarded as a lossis estimated at £2,000 per annum.
The other question of Death Duties relates to the charge on settled property,
and I propose to follow the Imperial
Chancellor in rectfying an oversight relating to the aggregation of free and
settled property for the purpose of assessment to duty.
to duty. At present, property
settled before 1894 is not aggregated
when passing on the death of the life
tenant with the other property passing
on the same death. There is no reason
for that distinction, and I propose to remove it.
The gain in revenue will be very
slight some £2,000 a year. You will
see, therefore, that these two changes
seem to balance each other.
As I look round the Committee I see
on both sides of the House a number of
hon. Members, who, when they were
freed from the wholesome restraint of the
Government Whips, have come to me
again and again, and almost with tears
in their eyes have pleaded for the reduction of the Entertainment Tax.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: So earnestly has this
matter been argued that I was often almost led to believe that this small tax was
responsible for the existing depression in
trade, and that if it were buried beyond
resurrection we would have no more need
for a Bankruptcy Court. (Laughter). I
have listened, I hope patiently, to the
plausible arguments which these deputations have so painstakingly discovered,
but owing to financial stress I have been
under the painful necessity of sending my
friends away unsatisfied.
It has been alleged that the Entertainment Tax offends against every canon of
sound finance, but in reality it is one of
the fairest taxes that has ever been devised. It is a universal tax; it is to be
found all over the Continent and in
America; it is a tax on those who seek
amusement, and as such is justifiable on
every ground.
The farthest I was able to go in years
past was to agree that when any relief
from the unexampled burden of unemployment appeared, the revision of this
tax would be considered.
But if such a tax has to be imposed I
think it is desirable that it should not
Finance Minister's Statement 1334
The Budget-
11 MAY 1927
be placed on the healthy outdoor instincts
of the people.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: I don't think a man
goes to a Rugby match so much for amusement as to cheer his friends and encourage his team to victory. So I propose to
entirely abolish the Entertainments Tax
on all outdoor sports-
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK-- -except such as involve the use of horses, dogs, or other
animals, or the use of mechanicallypropelled vehicles, and also to exempt in
the Finance Bill some indoor sports
where no money is awarded or paid to any
of the contestants as prizes or remuneration.
A few weeks ago I received a deputation-battalion would be the more correct
term-(laughter)-of cinema owners and
theatre proprietors, and had a lengthy
discussion with these gentlemen in regard
to the imposition of tax on their entertainments. The small picture houses in
the poorer parts of our cities, and those
who cater for the workers in the country,
are beyond question going through a difficult time. Most of them cannot make
ends meet. I have examined some ΟΙ
their accounts; they are not being run
extravagantly; they are not paying high
wages; and this tax has formed a high
percentage of their total expenses. Undoubtedly many of the amusement houses
in Belfast are suffering from internecine
competition and other causes.
That may
be because there are too many of them;
I do not offer any opinion upon that subject here. The salaries of artists, the
rent of films, are out of all proportion to
their receipts. But these considerations
do not apply to such a great extent to
the smaller type of house that I have
mentioned.
As I have said before, I have hitherto
been unable to hold out any hope to all
these importunate people because of the
heavy cost of unemployment relief. This
year, however, we see a break in the
clouds, and although only a glimmer of
the silver lining is visible I think that
some concession may safely be given-I
said some concession. Our liabilities are
still heavy. We must not, indeed, overlook that fact. The aftermath of the
Coal Strike is only beginning to be fully
felt, and we have many and heavy commitments in front of us. I think, however, that without endangering the
stability of our finances we could give
relief to the smaller entertainment houses
-to those which, as I have said, really
need relief, and so I propose to abolish
the tax on all admissions not exceeding
6d. That is to say, all those who attend
the smaller picture houses for which there
is an entrance fee of sixpence will be
under no tax.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the "Classic"
come down to that figure?
Mr. POLLOCK: I cannot predict
that. These two proposals will, it is estimated, cost the State £35,000 a year in a
full year; for the portion of the present
year during which the changes will be
operative the loss is estimated at £28,000.
The concessions will be operative
immediately the Finance Bill passes
through this Parliament.
Conclusion.
FINAL BALANCE.
The final figures for the year, after
adjustments have been made for the
various proposed changes in taxation I
have just outlined, are, therefore:

which I hope will be available for any

and, if finally realized, will automatically

Although we may congratulate ourselves that the indications for this year
are so comparatively satisfactory, yet we
must bear in mind that we have many
commitments ahead of us. We may in
the near future be called upon to embark
on a scheme for the drainage of the valley
of the Lower Bann.. Possibly similar
problems may have to be solved in relation
to Lough Erne. In addition there is the
growing cost of Land Purchase, and there
are other important commitments which
I need not enlarge upon. But I think I
Finance Minister's Statement 1336
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
have said sufficient to make it clear to the
Committee that the present conservation
of our financial resources is the only
policy which will enable us to reap a
harvest of prosperity in the years to come.
Notwithstanding this warning, which I
consider it my duty to give, yet when I
look back over the intervening years,
since our first accounts were made up, and
realize that these were years of unexampled commercial and industrial depression, and some of them racked with
serious political troubles, we have great
reason to thank God that we have been
able to accomplish so much, and to take
courage with the conviction that a brighter
future lies ahead of us.
Just as I conclude, let me say that it
would be very ungenerous on my part if
I should close my statement without offering any meed of praise to the splendid
officers of my Department who, for six
years, have worked so loyally and contributed so greatly to the happy regularization of our financial relations with the
British Government which has been so
recently accomplished. My only regret
is that I cannot individualize, as all have
worked so whole-heartedly; but whether
still with us, or whether close associations
with Ulster have been severed by retirement, it is only fitting that I should
publicly declare that as a Government
and as a people we appreciate their work
and fully recognize our indebtedness. I
beg to move.
