on
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): Hon. Members will find this
Vote on page 9 of the book of Estimates.
At first glance the administrative Estimate for the Ministry of Finance services appears to afford a good field of
criticism to the advocates of staff economy,
and each year it has been customary for
me, even at the risk of wearying the Committee, to draw the attention of hon.
Members to the variety of Services enumerated in Part I of the Vote for the
performance of which the Ministry is responsible. It will be appreciated, I am
sure, at the outset that this Estimate
includes the several staff groups which are
necessary for the administration of the
several grants, most of which have already
come before the Committee in the group
of ten Estimates accounted for by the
Ministry of Finance, most of which have
already been passed by the Committee.
In addition, the Estimate deals with many
administrative Services which are not
comprised in the ordinary definition of the
word "finance," and which were administered in pre-transfer days not by the
Treasury but by separate Departments
for which separate Votes were taken.
It is charged, for instance, with the
administration of the Services in Northern
Ireland formerly administered by the
Commissioners of Public Works in Ireland, the Commissioner of Valuation and
Boundary Survey for Ireland, the Commissioners of Charitable Donations and
Bequests for Ireland, the Teachers' Pension Office, the Office of the Registrar-
General of Births, Deaths and Marriages,
the Irish Land Commission (in part), the
National Savings Departments, the Irish
Branch of the Stationery Office, by the
Customs and Excise Department in
respect of Licence Duties, Entertainment
Tax and Old Age Pensions, and the Trade
Facilities Department. On former occasions, when moving this Estimate, the
nature of these varied functions was described at great length, and I would refer
hon. Members to the detailed statement
made in connection with the moving of
the Estimate for the year 1923-24.
On this occasion it is not intended to
lead hon. Members through the complex
statutory codes which give rise to these
Services, nor to enlarge upon the duties
of the Department in regulating the
financial business and the Civil Service
of the Government-duties which correspond generally to the functions discharged by the Treasury in relation to
the Imperial Government. My object in
making these preliminary remarks is
merely to emphasize at the outset that
the Estimate embraces a wide field, and
not only the expenses involved in controlling the financial business of the Government. The question of effecting reductions in staff is under constant review by
the Establishment Branch of the
Ministry, and the Estimates themselves
show evidence of this.
Turning now to the Estimate as a
whole, it will be seen that there is a considerable decrease in the net amount,
which is less by £15,995 than last year's
figure. As explained in the foreword to
the Estimates, this is due to a saving of
approximately £2,000 in staff costs, a
saving of approximately £10,000 in
old-age pension administration costs,
and a saving of approximately £5,000 in
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
respect of the Census.
Taking the staff
as a whole, the money provision is less by
approximately £2,000, excluding Census,
despite the increase over last year which
has arisen through the operation of increments, which is always a steady cause of
increase. The aggregate numbers in the
Headquarters and Treasury Division, as
shown on pages 10 and 11, remain as for
last year.
Both the Accounts Division and the
Works Division, shown on the following
three pages, show reductions in numbers
and in cash. The Accounts Branch, dealt
with on page 12, is among other things
charged with the collection of Land Purchase Annuities, and it is gratifying to
note that since 1923 there has been a
continuous reduction in the cost of collection, particularly during last year.
The amounts collected in the five financial years from 1923-24 to 1927-28 were
£661,000, £664,000, £668,000, £670,000
and £675,000 respectively while the staff
costs in those years were £4,090, £4,029,
£3,989, £3,711, and £3,282 respectively;
that is to say, the cost of collection per
£100 has been reduced from 12s 4d in
1923-24 to less than 9s 9d in the current
year. This satisfactory state of affairs
does, I think, bear out the statement
made that constant effort is made in the
direction of staff economy.
As regards the duties of the Works
Division, shown on page 13, these comprise not only the execution of the various
Works Services set out in the Estimate
for Public Works and Buildings, with
which the House is already familiar, but
also under an agency arrangement a very
considerable amount of work on behalf
of Imperial and Reserved Departments in
Northern Ireland. In addition, there are
a number of services which the Branch
performs for Northern Ireland Departments but which are not reflected in the
Works and Buildings Estimates. Among
those latter Services I may mention the
examination of schemes submitted to the
Ministry of Education by Local Education Authorities for the erection and
equipment of new schools and in some
cases the actual preparation of the plans.
and the supervision of the work; and Services in connection with railways, harbours, inland waterways and canals, in
respect of which officers of the Works
Division advise the Ministry of Commerce
on all technical points which arise.
There is also a very considerable amount of
work of a technical nature arising out of
the consideration of drainage problems
at the present time, and more detailed
surveys and borings are being undertaken
on the Bann. Moreover, all drainage
schemes brought before the Drainage
Advisory Committee by the County Councils have to be fully considered in their
technical aspects by the officers of the
Works Division.
I need not attempt to give here any
detailed account of the work done by this
Department in connection with works on
behalf of Reserved and Imperial Departments in Northern Ireland, as for example the works at the Customs and
Excise Offices, Post Offices, Inland
Revenue Offices, Registry of Deeds,
Land Registry, Probate Registry,
Ministry of Pensions Offices and Coastguard Stations. It will interest hon.
Members to know that the work of reconstruction of the Belfast Customs
House, which is at present in progress,
will involve a total expenditure of upwards of £56,000, and I am glad to say
that in spite of the great difficulty of the
problems presented it is proceeding
smoothly; the piling difficulties have
been satisfactorily overcome.
In addition to the Services which have
béen enumerated, the Works Division is
also responsible under an agency agreement for the work of erecting and maintaining the houses provided by the
Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust in
Northern Ireland. Up to the present
758 houses out of the 1,046 allocated to
Northern Ireland have been completed
and occupied, and 120 are in course of
erection and are expected to be completed early in the current financial
year. In addition, a fresh scheme is being
prepared for the erection of a further
140 houses in Northern Ireland, and it

I refer in particular to the non-contributory old-age pensions Service, in which

Government most concerned, namely, the

scheme devolves, of course, upon the
Ministry of Labour, and we have, therefore, to consider whether in future we
are to have two different pensions

the contributory and the non-contributory

Thursday, 12th May, 1927.
The House met at Three of the clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
THE BUILDING TRADE DISPUTE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is a fact that a greater
number of employers in the building
trade are paying the agreed rates to their
employees than the number of employers
in the Master Builders' Federation, who
are trying to enforce a reduction of
wages, and, if this is so, can he state
whether the Government is prepared to
permit this minority movement amongst
the employers to hold up a justifiable
settlement; to worsen the conditions of
the building trade workers; to delay the
erection of the Parliament House, and to
harass the community.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I regret that the difference of
opinion in the building trade on the
question of wages has not been adjusted,
and that work in this trade has consequently been interrupted. The hon.
Member will appreciate that a satisfactory settlement of such matters can
only be brought about by mutual agreement, and I am glad to be able to state
that I am informed that negotiations are
being resumed this afternoon between
the parties with hopeful prospects.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I would like to
know as to whether that specifically relates
to Belfast, and as to whether the right
hon. Gentleman has any information regarding the position in Derry.
Mr. ANDREWS: The answer to the
question relates to Belfast, and as to the
position in Derry I do not think at the
moment that negotiations are proceeding,
but I am hopeful that if there is a settlement in Belfast a settlement will follow
in Derry.
Mr. KYLE: The House will notice
that the right hon. Gentleman has not
answered the question that has been put
down in which it was asked whether it is
a fact that a greater number of employers
in the building trade are paying the
agreed rate, the rate of 1/9, to their
employees than the number of employers
in the Master Builders' Federation,
who are trying to enforce a reduction of
wages. The right hon. Gentleman has
not attempted to answer that question.
Mr. ANDREWS: As negotiations are
proceeding at the present time, I do not
think it is in the public interest that I
should attempt to answer the question
more directly.
Mr. KYLE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman say that the Government are
prepared to allow a minority movement
amongst the employers to upset the whole
building trade of the North of Ireland?
If it had been trade unionists the right
hon. Gentleman would immediately have
taken steps to see that some of us were
coerced. But when a minority movement exists amongst employers the
Government is prepared to allow this
minority to dictate to the rest.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have not the
power to compel either employers to
employ or workers to work who do not
wish to do so.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say whether the Government
thinks it is a wise thing that there should
be a section amongst employers allowed
to exercise such undue force in the State
at the present time?
Mr. ANDREWS: In view of the
peaceful negotiations that are proceeding
I do not think it is in the public interest
that I should answer that question.
THE INDUSTRIAL RESOURCES
COMMISSION.
2. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime
Minister what steps, if any, have been
taken to give legislative effect to the recommendations contained in the report,
dated 21st April, 1926, of the Commission on the Natural and Industrial
Resources of Northern Ireland on the
power resources of the country.
Oral Answers
The Budget
12 MAY 1927
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply to this question.
The majority of the conclusions at
which the Development Commission
arrived in regard to the power resources
of Northern Ireland do not call for
legislative action.
The hon. Member is probably aware,
however, that a Bill is before Parliament
seeking powers to develop the water
power of the Lower Bann River and to
distribute electricity through the greater
part of County Antrim and parts of
County Londonderry. The intention of
the promoters of the Bann Hydro-
Electric Scheme is to link up their system
with that of the City of Belfast.
Another scheme has been put forward
for erecting a transmission line from Belfast to Lisburn, and it is hoped to make
arrangements for this line to be so constructed that it may form the first section
of a ring main to encircle Lough Neagh.
The establishment of the Belfast-Lisburn
line as the potential first section of a
main transmission line will probably involve assistance from Government funds.
As the hon. Member, no doubt, appreciates
the difficulty in the way of electricity
development in Northern Ireland outside
the large industrial centres is the lack of
demand and the lengthy intervening
distances between urban districts where
only moderate loads may be anticipated.

the indulgence of the House, which I
have no doubt will be granted, if he can
give us economic arguments to convince
us that it is not an uneconomic proposition for the people of this country
to be so expensively governed. Those of
us who think so can at least lay this
unction to our souls that the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) has gloried in
the reductions he has been able to bring
about. Therefore, if these Services and
the cost of administration had been
based on such perfect economics as the
right hon. Gentleman suggests, he has
perfected still further this perfect
system, because, as I say,
he has
gloried in the reductions which he has
been able to bring about.
I do not know whether I am entitled
to discuss at all the proposals which
have been made here in regard to
the tax that is to be imposed on us so
far as
our tobacco is concerned. The
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) referred to it yesterday. I know that he is
not responsible for the taxation but,
nevertheless, we in Northern Ireland
have got to pay it. I think, instead of
increasing the tax on tobacco, it would
have been a much better thing if the
right hon. Gentleman had put the tax on
the shoulders of those who are more able
to bear it than are the users of tobacco. 1
realize of course that the Minister is not
a free agent in this respect. In regard

Gentleman raised, regarding the £5,000
which he hoped to obtain from the
brewers a sum amounting to £5,000 in
Northern Ireland-no doubt
my hon.
Friend (Mr. Gyle) who represents East
Belfast, and who is perhaps more interested
in this particular question than apparently he was interested in the question
of the hours of industrial workers, will
have something to say in regard to that
£5,000.
I must say I am amazed at the right
hon. Gentleman not protesting against
the juggling with figures which is going
to result in Income Tax payers paying
eighteen months' Income Tax in twelve
months. It means that on a subsequent
Budget Day he will have to face up to a
deficit which will be caused, no doubt, by
the fact that we are going to pay eighteen
months' Income Tax inside twelve months.
I am not surprised at Mr. Churchill
being responsible for this work of art,
because he is an artist amongst other
things, but I am surprised at the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock). I am
sure that if it had been done, or if it had
been proposed that it should be done, at
the Harbour Trust during the time he
was there his righteous indignation would
have been unbounded. I realize that I
am treading on very delicate ground. It
is hardly fair to blame the right hon.
Gentleman for a tax for which he is not
responsible, and yet we in Northern Ireland having to pay this tax, and, seeing
that our Imperial representatives are not
interesting themselves as much as
Iwould like to see them interest themselves in the question of taxation as far
as it affects Northern Ireland, I think we
owe a duty to the people of Northern
we

Ireland to refer to these matters in this

of view.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would they resign and
give us a chance?
Mr. KYLE: There are Members who
represent my point of view in the British

is that, as I say, one does not want to do

I come now to what is perhaps the
more pleasing side of the Budget statement. Those of us who have pressed,
and continued to press by question,
amendment, and debate in this House, by
meetings outside, and by attendance on
deputations, for the rebate of the Entertainment Tax on outdoor sports have good
reason to congratulate ourselves. Those
who run, those who play Rugger and
Soccer, can now feel that all their
attention can be devoted to the game and
not to vilification of the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Pollock). I am not saying he did not deserve it, but at long last
he has yielded to the importunities of
those of us who have been insistent and
consistent on this question. I might
just draw the attention of the House to
the fact that on this day two years agothe 12th May, 1925-I had the honour to
move an Amendment to the Budget of
the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock)
in which I pressed for this concession,
and that was the first time it had been
done in this House. I pressed for the
concession that has now been obtained.
Subsequently, other hon. Members of the
House did press for the same Amendment,
but I think we have a right to congratulate ourselves on the successful issue of
our efforts.
The right hon. Gentleman has spoken
of the need for a Sinking Fund. He has
allocated a considerable sum to what e
considers to be a laudable object. There
is a growing feeling in the community,
and expression has been given to it
many of the important reviews in Great
Britain, as to the real value or use of
the Sinking Fund. I want to suggest that
perhaps it is not so wise a thing as the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) has
stated. I know that all Conservative
financiers-and we must include our own
Labour Chancellor under that headbelieve in the allocation of very considerable sums to the Sinking Fund. That
has been meeting with a growing volume
of criticism, not from Labour people or
from Socialists so much as from financiers
-and responsible financiers in Great
Britain, as to the real value of allocating
so much money each year to the Sinking
Fund. I want to suggest that an inquiry
should be held, or that a Commission
should be set up to inquire into the
strangle-hold that financers have upon the
community. There is nobody who has
any knowledge at all of the economic
problems that face employers as well as
workers in Northern Ireland who is not
aware of the strangle-hold that financers
have upon the money market. Any
member of the Corporation, for example,
can tell you how difficult it is for the
Corporation to get money to erect houses.
We did see a statement that has never
yet been refuted, because it is impossible.
of refutation, that for a house that costs
£500 to build and the economic rent of
which is 9s. 9d. per week, 6s. 6d. of that
9s. 9d. goes to the financiers, and only
3s. 3d. goes to pay the cost of material,
the labour, and the land on which the
house is built.
I really think that we have a decent
case for inquiry into our financial system
here. We should have a Commission to
inquire into the disposal of the finances
of the Government. Workers can produce wealth in abundance. Employers
have loads of idle machinery-too much
of it. If it is the case-and it is the
case -that we can produce goods more
rapidly and more efficiently than ever
before, that we have loads of capital in
the form of idle machinery, and that
workless men and women are eager to
earn their living, the country should be
wealthy and prosperous, and yet it is
not as prosperous as any of us, on either
side of the House, would like to see it.
Some of us are convinced that the finan

cier gets more than a fair share of the
wealth that is created by the people, and
so we suggest that a Committee should
be set up to investigate the whole matter.
I suggest that we in Northern Ireland,
as a means of raising finance for social
reform, should impose a tax on bookmakers. I know that I am now on very
delicate ground. I know that many
sanctimonious people on both sides of the
House, in my party as well as in the party
of the Members opposite, will say that
that is a thing we should not handle.
But do not forget-you people who talk
like that that you have got a tax on
drink, which many of you think is immoral, too, and which many of you think
should be prohibited.
I suggest that instead of doing as they
have done in Great Britain and in the
Free State, where they have imposed a
tax on betting, you should form a register
of the bookmakers and raise some money
in that way.
It is obvious to every
person. Read the Press. Look around
in any large city; you will find that this
evil exists, and all the talk in the world
will not remedy that evil. You have got
to face up to it. Apparently you cannot
prohibit it without doing something which
I think no person wants to see done. In
considering it do not forget that already
there is a betting tax in England, the
home of non-conformity. You have a
tax on betting in the Free State, and I
suggest that there should be a registration of bookmakers in Northern Ireland.
I think that would be a better thing than
the betting tax.
Finally, I want to suggest that the
Government of Northern Ireland should
start a general insurance scheme. Regarding ordinary life insurance, vast sums
of money are taken from the people in
premiums each year, and only a very
small moiety is paid back to the policy
holders. The hon. Gentleman who represents the University (Dr. Morrison) is
not present, I am sorry to say, but, no
doubt, he could give me assistance in advocating that the Government should
start this business on their own, because
of the enormous sums that are collected
by these insurance companies, only a very
small proportion of which ever gets back
to the people who subscribe them.
Thousands of pounds go into the pockets
of directors every year.
I do not want hon. Members to take
my word for it that this is so, or even
to take the word of the hon. Member for
the University, but I want them to
examine the returns of these huge insurance societies, and they will find that
what I am saying is absolutely true, is,
indeed, less than the truth, because I believe, and always have believed, in being
moderate in putting forward requests
or suggestions of this nature. I know I
have been twitted by hon. Members opposite on my attitude, but it is better to
say you do not know when you do not
know than to pretend that you know what
you do not know. I had a maxim driven
into me very early in life, and it was this,
the more you know, the more you know
you do not know. The converse of that is
true, and I want to suggest to the hon.
Members who twit me in this House that
the less you know, the less you know you
do not know. That is the position of some
of the people who have twitted me in this
House, they are ignorant of their own
ignorance, if I may say so without giving
offence.
I want to suggest to the Government
that they should enter into competition
with the present insurance companies, as
has been done in Australia. If they do
so, they will compel these private companies to treat their policy holders much
more generously than they are doing at
present. Take the vast sums of money
that are paid every year by employers as
premiums for workmen's compensation. I
reckon that the sums paid by employers
could be halved if a proper State system
was introduced. Again, this has been
done in Australia, where it has enabled
them practically to halve the contributions of the employers and to increase
the benefits to the workpeople, with the
result that the workmen who get hurt at
their work in Australia get much greater
sums for smaller premiums paid by the
employer than are paid in this country
under the system of private insurance
companies. This would save
ployers an enormous sum of money each
year, and would enable them to pay
better wages or to reduce their costs.

I am sorry that this Government is not

worker in Northern Ireland our Govern-

ment ought to be represented in conferences of this nature. It has been

greater purchasing power. I think that
is a commonplace; everybody knows that.
Everybody knows that the worker who
gets increased wages has a greater purchasing power. Greater purchasing
power means more money for manufactured goods. That means more employment, and more employment means less
taxation.
Mr. POLLOCK:
That is Protection.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman
said that is Protection. He can call it
whatever he likes. We in this Party of
ours are not hidebound Free Traders, nor
are
we hidebound Protectionists. A
Socialist, obviously, cannot be a Free
Trader in the sense that a Liberal, for
example, is a Free Trader; everybody
knows that. We are inclined, just as
every sensible person is inclined, to Free
Trade as against Protection, because it is
obvious that if we had Free Trade
amongst all the nations of the world it
would be a distinct advantage to the
manufacturing nations such as Great
Britain and Northern Ireland.
More employment means less taxation,
and less taxation, national as well as
local, means reduced costs for our manufacturers, which again leads to a happier
and more contented people. The people,
if happier and more contented, will turn
to more active pursuits, and more intensive studies of the financial and other ills
that we endure at the present moment,
and so, by thought and reason, evolve a
higher, a saner, a better, and a nobler
system than the system that we live under
to-day. You can call that system by
whatever name you like. It does not
matter. I call it Socialism.
Mr. DEVLIN: I desire to join with
my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) in the congratulations which he has extended to the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock).
Whatever we may think of the right hon.
Gentleman's politics, we all recognize
that there is no more skilled financier or
abler business man, and I trust I may be
permitted to say at this stage of the proceedings how profoundly we regretted his
recent illness, and how deeply we rejoice.
to have him, in the fullness of vigour and
strength, amongst us again. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The right hon. Gentleman has had one
or two advantages in introducing this
Budget. He has had already the experience of the Budget of the Chancellor of
the Exchequer in Great Britain and of the
financial statement from the Chancellor
of the Exchequer of the Free State, so
that, whatever we may be lacking in these
islands, we rejoice in a multiplicity of
Chancellors of the Exchequer.
In coming to the question that will
absorb our attention to-day, I may say
that my memory takes me back to the
passage of the 1920 Bill under which this
House meets and operates; and it seems
to me an amazing commentary upon the
political prescience and wisdom of those
who then controlled the affairs of Ulster
that they accepted a Bill, which is now an
Act, by which they were prepared to
burden themselves with a contribution of
£8,000,000 to the Imperial Exchequer.
I have never been able to follow the
rather clever methods of those who conduct the finances of this country and of
England by which we have reached the
stage that, although we accepted the
burden of £8,000,000 as part of our
responsibility in connection with the 1920
Act, we are now paying nothing at all.
For my part I do not object to that.
I rejoice at it. It has always been my
ambition, and I have ventured to express
it on repeated occasions in this House,
not to make any Imperial contribution at
all. The Government thought otherwise,
and they have on many occasions, at
great Imperial functions and at other
picturesque periods, told us that the one
thing they were anxious for was to be
able to contribute to the upkeep of the
Imperial concern. They ought to take
up the position that I take up-and I am
perfectly frank in this matter-and to
state distinctly what their ideas are, and
if their ideas are consistent with their
action, namely, to pay nothing to the
British Exchequer. Now we are paying
nothing. We are getting the use of the
soldiers of the British Army and the
sailors, and the organization of defence,
for which we are paying nothing at all.
Therefore, I trust we will be able to
boast of how creditably the right hon.
Gentleman the Chancellor of the Exchequer has been able to relieve Ulster of
this burden of contribution, and at the

Mr. DEVLIN: Now I come to the next
question, and it is this. When one rises
in this House to discuss a Budget statement it is only then that one realizes how
impotent we are. I noticed that when
the right hon. Gentleman introduced the
Budget yesterday there was not a single
Member of the general public in the
galleries, and as far as this House was
concerned he had only half-a-dozen
Members behind him and a full and
serried gathering in front of him. What
is the moral we are to draw from this?
It is that the people are not interested
in our finances, because we are a household that has no control over its own
financial upkeep.
Another country imposes our taxes, or
practically all our taxes, and collects all
our taxes, and the vital things that count
in the affairs of this country are not discussable at all. Even if we were able to
discuss them we could not adjust them
or change them. For instance, we have
heard it stated on the platform and in
the Press that we are an ideally happy
community as compared with other parts.
of this island. I quite admit that the social
services here are an improvement on
those in Southern Ireland. No one more
deeply regrets than I do that there is not
a scheme of widows' and orphans' pensions
in Southern Ireland, and that the oldage pensions do not come up to our level.
But have we been told the whole story?
In Southern Ireland they have abolished
taxes on the breakfast table. The tax on
tea, which is one of the greatest burdens
borne by the working class, has disappeared altogether The taxes on sugar
have been considerably reduced. The
tax upon coffee has disappeared. Therefore, as a balance against the limitation
of their social services as compared with
ours very great burdens have been removed from the shoulders of the Southern
people. In addition to that in Southern
Ireland-I am not their spokesman or
defender-they have to maintain an army
and they have to pay for all their
machinery of defence, which we have not
to do, because it is done by the Imperial
Parliament. The fact of the matter is

that this Budget statement is like the
statement made by the Chancellor of the
Exchequer in England, it is more clever
than informative.
The only tax affected by the changes
made by the right hon. Gentleman is the
Entertainments Tax. I am very glad to
see that the continued pressure which
came from this side of the House has
ultimately had its effect. I sometimes
wonder whether we have any justification

fact that we are regarded not only as a
constitutional minority but as an organized band-I do not mean
to say
organized all together as an organized
band of pariahs and Parliamentary outcasts in whom there is no wisdom, who
can give neither culture, nor information,

Act (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-that

It was the same in regard to the
Motor Bill, as the right hon. Gentleman the Home Secretary knows. He
would not listen to a single suggestion

In fact, if you have this force behind you
you can not only make a Government do

I say why the right hon. Gentleman, not

never subscribed to the doctrine which I
hear sometimes put forward, not only
here but elsewhere, that it only cost the
country so much ten years ago and that
it costs so much now. I think that is not
a fair way to put things. But I do not
either subscribe to the argument of the
right hon. Gentleman that all the increase in the cost of Government has been
due to an extension of social services. I
do not agree with that, because last year
you raided the Health Insurance Fund,
and one of the justifications you gave for
it was that you wanted money to help
you to pay widows' and orphans' pensions. Remember, too, that your social
services are not based absolutely upon
grants from Governments. They are
partly paid by the people and partly paid
by the Government-the employers, the
workers and the State. Each of them
give their contributions for these social
services.
There is even this much misunderstood
question of the dole. There is a universal
idea amongst not always ignorant people
that this unemployed allowance is a sum
taken out of the flowing resources of a
golden State and handed over to people
who will not work. There was never a
grosser misrepresentation of the true
facts of the situation. This unemployment fund is built up partly by the
workers, partly by the employers and
partly by the State. It is mainly an
Insurance Fund. Therefore, to
say
the increase in our cost of Government
is largely due to the increase in our social
services would be to deny to the general
body of the people the credit to which
they are entitled of being contributors to
these funds.

as

hope that after the next Budget statement we will not only be able to congratulate each other upon the further

Craigavon): I rise in order to deal with
the closing remarks and the earlier remarks of the hon. Member who has just
sat down. My right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock), of course, will, with the permission of the House, deal with the detailed criticisms that have been made by
the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle)
and the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), but as I was in the British
House of Commons at the time that the
Bill granting us self-government was
passed, I think that perhaps the House
would bear with me if I call attention
to the real facts of the situation in regard
to the contribution that we make annually
towards the Army, Navy, pensions and
other services.
Hon. Members will realize that in the
1920 Income Tax throughout the
year
whole of Great Britain and Ireland, as
it then was, was at the rate of 6s in the £.
We were at that time contributing, I
think, something like £14,000,000 towards the Exchequer in Great Britain as
the United Kingdom. When the Treasury
were framing the White Paper on which
our financial relations were based-and
when I talk about our financial relations
I am talking about the financial relations
that would have existed between Great
Britain and the rest of Ireland had the
Act of 1920 been observed by the Free
State-that £14,000,000 gave then an
idea that in ordinary circumstances, with
a high rate of Income Tax and with the
tax that was then on commodities, it
would be fair for Ireland as a whole to
contribute towards the Imperial services.

portant factors that must be taken into

the original sum that was fixed in advance

That has all taken place in the normal

hon. Friend when the financial system was
being evolved in 1920. I remember well
when he and some of his able colleagues

tributes paid by every side of the House

out that the hon Member for West Belfast
(Mr Devlin) gets carried away when he

The PRIME MINISTER: We realize

to face the responsibility of the Government of Ulster, through no fault
of our own, through no desire of our
own, my colleagues and I are going to do
our very best for the people. We have
got to bear in mind that if our contribution is at the present moment £1,400,000
a year the time may come when Ulster
will be very grateful to its present
administration for not foregoing the
arduous task of paying that £1,400,000,
and I will explain to the House why.
There is such an equipoise in the Act of
1920 that if taxation was reduced to any
large extent if the Income Tax came
down to something like what it used to be
in the old days and we found it difficult
to carry on on account of the paucity of
revenue derivable from Ulster itself, then
the Act of 1920 provides that they would
be paying us a contribution instead of
our paying them a contribution, and, consequently, if we were to offer the British
Government to-day to take away altogether the contribution and to say: "We
will not ask you in future if you let us
The Budget-
General Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
off in the present;" why I think the
Chancellor of the Exchequer would jump
at it at once. He would say it was the
best bargain that possibly could be made.
Mr. DEVLIN: The same as he did last
year.
The PRIME MINISTER: Doubtless.
The hon. Member, with all his ability, is
not what I would call an expert as regards
finance any more than myself. But I
will make it thoroughly clear about the
contribution last year and this year.
What does this contribution go towards?
We have the full value of the British
Navy, and I think we all take the greatest
pride in contributing to the senior
service. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We have the full value of the British
Army (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and I am sure every county in Ulster is
proud of having representatives in the
British Army and of the pensions that
are paid to war heroes. I think we would
be doing less than our duty if we did not
go shoulder to shoulder with the rest of
Great Britain and Ireland in paying all
we possibly could towards the amelioration of their lot after all they have done
for us.
Then there is the ordinary debt. I do
not know how many thousands of millions
it goes into, but we as part and parcel of
Great Britain and Northern Ireland are
proud to help to wipe out that debt in
order that the whole country may benefit,
as well as Ulster itself.
Now, I come to another point the hon.
Member hardly realizes. He said last year
we paid no contribution and this year we
are going to pay no contribution. That
arises through a cause which is very
easily explained. The hon. Member
mixes up non-recurrent charges with
those charges which go on automatically
year by year. We pay £1,400,000. It
is true we got £868,000 as aid towards
the very difficult times through which
labour in this city and the rest of Ulster
was passing, but we hope that will be a
non-recurrent charge. We hope the
shipyards and the linen mills and other
industries in our area will go on prospering to such an extent that we will reach
the point I do not know what the point.
is called, but there seems to be a point
round about 22,000 when we get back to
self-supporting as far as unemployment is
concerned.
And then there is the other question,
of course, of the buildings which the Imperial Parliament charged itself with
building for the Ulster people, for this
reason, that when Home Rule was passed
and when the North had set up its own
Parliament and its own institutions we
were very different to Dublin. In Dublin
they had large public buildings, because
it was the centre of Government in Ireland in the old days. They had everything that was required. And in the
original Act as it was provided in 1920
there was £1,000,000 sterling applicable or allotted rather to Southeru Ireland and £1,000,000 sterling allotted to
Northern Ireland in order to enable both
to build their own Parliamentary Houses
and administration buildings and to get
under way.
Then it was pointed out, I
think, very clearly to the British Government that the million pounds to Dublin
was really an unnecessary gift, because
they had all these fine buildings to carry
on this work of Parliament in, whereas
in Northern Ireland we were beginning as
it were from the base. We had no public
buildings that could possibly contain the
Civil Servants moved up here for the new
centre, and the consequence was that the
Government changed that Clause and
put into the Bill an obligation to supply
us with law courts, to supply us with
Parliament Houses and with buildings to
hold the Civil Servants-all undertaken
by the British Government. And the
money which is at present appearing in
our Estimates from time to time is money
which is granted for this purpose of building. Consequently, this is a non-recurrent
charge. When these buildings are all
cleared out of the way and when
Unemployment Insurance Fund reaches
the stage of stabilising itself, then this
grant from the Imperial Treasury to us
lapses and still the old and original
idea of a contribution from Northern
Ireland towards each of these services will
have to go on.

have no hesitation in saying that if they

Southern Ireland would have been better

tory position. Dwindling as these contributions have been they are dependent

From the very start, when

ending March, 1922, was £2,820,000;

British Exchequer that they were not in

A Budget from my point of view
shows in a word or two the success or
failure of the Government which is
responsible for that Budget. The test of
the Budget is: do the people feel they
are getting satisfaction for their money,
or do they believe that they are being
governed by an expensive Government,
imposing on them an almost intolerable
and unbearable taxation? I think the
most hopeful friends of the Government
would come to the conclusion by that test
that the present system of government,
owing to its inefficiency and high expenditure, has been an utter failure.

probable cost of the

The next item is the £40,000 which the

I agree with the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) that this money would have
been more usefully expended at the
present time in relation to grants towards
the relief of local agricultural rates. We
all know agriculture is passing through
a very difficult period. We are hoping
we have nearly turned the corner and that
better times are coming for the farmers
of Northern Ireland, and this assistance
of £40,000 added to the present grant
would help to tide them over the serious
difficulties they at present experience. Or
if you could not see your way to do that
-I do not know how far you can vary
it-if you could vary it to this extent
to grant the £40,000 towards the small
farmers to improve their holdings by
building houses in the same way as at
present the labourers get grants to build

would be more usefully expended in that
way than in advancing it towards the investigation of pedigree stock at the
present time. I am afraid that instead
of helping the farmers, which is the intention of the Minister, it will not help
him, but will pass through the hands of
the big stock breeders, and purely pedigree stock will be used for export instead
of improving the stock of Northern Ireland. I make that suggestion. I do not
want to keep the House. I am only
pointing out these two things that occurred
to my mind. I join with the others in
congratulating the right hon. Gentleman,

Mr. POLLOCK: I am sure I cannot

out of 120,000 that are under £15 valuation, I believe. 20,000 would get 2s 6d.
That is the relief they would get from
rates-2s 6d each in the year. 34,000 would

a man and call it a grant-in-aid! How
far does that contribute to the improve.
ment of any farm in the country, small

argue that these small grants, amounting
in the aggregate to a large amountbecause of the number of agricultural
holdings in Ireland-that the aggregate

sum, if it had been applied to all the

In regard to the other matter, about
which there is apparently much misconception, I said yesterday in furnishing
the Estimate that a sum of £279,000 a
year was at present being expended by
and paid by the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland as the cost of the Land Purchase
Scheme, and that by the operation of the
Act of 1925, when completed, the liability
of the taxpayer of Northern Ireland
would amount to a sum of £325,000 per
annum, extending for a period not far
from 60 years. Now, I repeat that to
the hon. Member who made the statement, and I am sorry he is not here, but
I think in the interests of accuracy it is
well that even in his absence I should
clear up the matter.
Although the Imperial Parliament
carried out a great scheme of land purchase from the Ashbourne period until
to-day, it was the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland that were paying that part of it
that related to Northern Ireland. We,
therefore, got over the burden of all the
past from the Imperial Authority when.
the change was made, and the figures in
relation to that are easily explained. The
cost of the excess stock, from the
tremendous fall in the value of money,
and the cost of the bonus on all the land
of Ulster from the Ashbourne period
until to-day amount, together with the
cost of administration, to £279,000 a
year, and that covers the whole process of
land purchase from beginning to end.
The annuities we receive have nothing in
the world to do with it. The annuities
are simply the interest upon the vast sum
of money that was paid the landlords for
the land itself, and have nothing whatever to do with the burden the Government took upon their shoulders in respect
of the cost of excess stock and the bonus
to bridge the gulf between the landlord
and the tenant that we have undertaken
in respect of this recent Act affecting
about 28,000 unbought tenants. We
have undertaken to bear that burden to
bridge the gulf betwen landlord and
tenant, and we also undertook to pay a
quarter year's gale rent in order that the
scheme might not break down.
This Government did all of these things
added together, amounting to, as I say,
a sum of £325,000 a year when the full
scheme reaches maturity. I hope I have
made that clear to the House. The hon.
Member for Antrim, in discussing the
matter, evidently had a small and imperfect appreciation of what the Government has undertaken in respect of this
and their present responsibility. That
is all I have got to say on that matter. I
hope that will make the position
sufficiently clear to enable us at any rate
to get some credit for what we have done
in respect of the unbought tenants that
are at present in this position.
I fear that if I undertake to reply
to all the matters that have been raised
in the discussion, and raised in a perfectly
friendly way, I would occupy the time of
the House perhaps longer than Members

the same as ours, and it must be remembered that they have a much wider area.
Therefore, so far as government is concerned, we can claim at any rate that
we bear favourable comparison with any
other area or any other population in the
world. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

The hon. Member for Down (Mr. Patrick
O'Neill), in his criticism of the present
financial relations of Northern Ireland
with Great Britain, made some rather
curious remarks, or rather drew some
very extraordinary conclusions. He set
out to prove that, although we had paid
some twenty odd millions by way of contribution, we actually got it all back by
way of grants. As a matter of fact we
have not got it all back.
I think possibly the hon. Member corrected that and
said fifty per cent.-
-or some hon. Member said fifty per cent. As a matter of
fact those grants were simply a liability
of the Imperial Parliament, at the incidence of our career, in order to pay for
the restoration of law and order.
It was
not for anything inherent to the normal
condition of Ulster. It was simply a
condition that arose out of the changes
that were taking place in the Constitutional relations of the country and the
invasion, as we all know, of elements that
were badly disposed that resulted in the
destruction of an immense amount of
property. This was all the result of the
Imperial Parliament's policy and, therefore, they admitted liability, and paid it.
These grants, so called, were not by any
means anything that Ulster should have
been called upon to pay.
Let me remind the hon. Member that,
when he speaks of these grants which are
accruing now, they are undertakings that
were solemnly made under an Act of
Parliament of the British Parliament.
They undertook by that document to
provide us with buildings that would cost
large sums of money. My right hon.
Friend the Prime Minister endeavoured
to explain the matter earlier in the
day, but as it has been repeated since, I
would like hon. Members to get into their
minds that this money, if the terms of the
Act had been carried out, should have
been paid to us long since, or rather the

1. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state on what
terms a premium was granted for this
season by the County Londonderry Committee of Agriculture to Mr. H. R.
Morrison, of Meath Park, Coleraine, for
the services of his thoroughbred stallion,
"Lord Ashbourne"; whether this horse
was to attend at Magherafelt one day in
each alternate week; whether these
terms have since been changed by the
County Agricultural Committee, and if
so, why; and whether the change deprives
the Magherafelt area, covering an area
of 18 square miles, of the services of this
thoroughbred stallion, and what action he
proposed to take in the matter.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): Premiums to stallions
are granted under the Ministry's Horse
Breeding Scheme, copy of which I am
sending to the hon. Member. It will be
observed that County Committees of
Agriculture are empowered by the
Scheme to make such arrangements as
they consider desirable for the travelling
of premium stallions. I may say, however, that in selecting the thoroughbred
stallion "Lord Ashbourne" to hold a
premium in the County Londonderry
during the 1927 season the Londonderry
County Committee decided in the first
instance that the animal should stand at
Maghera and Magherafelt on one day
each week alternately.
In view, however, of the heavy rail
and other expenses involved, and of the
lack of demand for the services of this
stallion at Magherafelt in the previous
season, the Committee later decided that
the standing of the stallion at Maghera-
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.-
UMPIRE'S DECISION.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that the
Ministry has by decision of the umpire
laid it down that young men, having
served an apprenticeship to the trade of
engineering, must, even while drawing
standard benefit, seek employment as
labourers; whether he can state what
Section of the Unemployment Acts of
Northern Ireland empowers his Department to refuse standard benefit to skilled
craftsmen because they do not seek work
as labourers.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The umpire is an independent
officer appointed by the Crown, and is
free to rule on the merits of each individual case as he thinks right.
Section 3 of the Northern Ireland Unemployment Insurance (No. 2) Act, 1924,
provides that an applicant for unemployment benefit, whether standard or extended, must be genuinely seeking work.
In a particular appeal which came before him recently the umpire held that,
in order to satisfy this condition, the
claimant, a young man of 22 living in a
country town, unemployed since the completion of his apprenticeship and in
receipt of benefit for four months, who
was faced with the prospect of prolonged
unemployment due to depression in his
own trade, should show that he was not
restricting his efforts to find work in
that trade, but that he was looking for
suitable employment in any quarter in
which he was likely to find it.

ENNISKILLEN MILITARY
BARRACKS.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT (for Mr. Cooper)
asked the Prime Minister whether he can
state if any correspondence has passed
between the Imperial Government and
the Government of Northern Ireland relating to the transfer of the Enniskillen
Military Barracks, and can he state the
result of any such correspondence.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to reply to
this question.
Consequent on the withdrawal of the
military from Enniskillen a number of
buildings ceased to be required by the
War Department, and a communication
has been received from the Imperial
Government, proposing that the Government of Northern Ireland should consider
the acquisition of these premises. The
consideration of their suitability from
various points of view has been the
subject of inquiry by the Departments
concerned, but no final decision has yet
been reached, though it is hoped to do so
at a very early date, more particularly as
regards the possibility of using a part as
a county headquarters.
BANN DRAINAGE.
MAJOR SHILLINGTON (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Finance
whether the Government accept the recommendations of the Drainage Advisory
Committee on the question of the Bann
Drainage, as set out in the Interim
Report, which has recently been published; and what action it proposes to
take thereon.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Drainage Advisory Committee has expressed the opinion
that unless the drainage works can be
co-ordinated with the works for the provision of hydro-electric power, the cost of
carrying out an efficient drainage scheme
would, in present circumstances,
prohibitive; the Government's decision
on the matter will be guided accordingly.
be
The present position is as follows:-A
Bill entitled the Antrim Electricity
Supply Bill has been introduced this
Session. The promoters have not pressed
for the further stages to be taken in this
House pending the result of an application, which they are making to the Loans
Guarantee Advisory Committee, for a
guarantee for a portion of the works
expenditure. In regard to the grant of
such a guarantee, I am guided entirely by
the advice of the financial experts who
compose that Committee. It follows,
therefore, that although the Government
concurs generally in the views of the
Drainage Advisory Committee, it can
arrive at no final determination on the
Bann drainage problem until the fate of
the Electricity Supply Bill in this House
has been settled.

I protest upon that ground, first of all,

from the private Members of the House

no Parliament that works so little as this

Most of the Members of the Government

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Although I
do not propose, in moving the Estimates
of the Ministry of Education, to detain
the Committee with any such detailed
review of the whole range and sphere of
the Ministry's activities as I attempted
last year, I wish, by leave of the Committee, to adopt the same procedure in
moving them as I did on that occasion.
I shall endeavour to satisfy the Committee as to the general educational
policy of the Government upon the first
Vote, which covers the expenses of office
administration, because upon that Vote I
think that I shall be in order in touching
upon any and every matter pertaining to
policy.
On the second Vote I shall content
myself by simply moving the Vote; and
I shall be glad to make such reply as I am
able, if particular explanation of any item
in that Vote is demanded by any hon.
Member, or if any particular head of
expenditure contained in that Vote gives.
rise to discussion. I must add, of course,
that on the present Motion, the Motion
covering Vote 1, I shall be pleased to
give any information and explanation at
my disposal to any hon. Member who
desires to make inquiry upon any particular item of expenditure set out in that
Vote which, as I have already said,
covers the general expenditure of the
Ministry on office administration.
The total estimated cost of educational
administration stands at £1,866,529,
which shows a decrease upon last year's
figure of just under £10,000. Such a
variation upon so large a Vote is not a
matter of great importance, and I think
the Committee may assume from the
figures that there has been very little
change in the character of the administration. This, of course, signifies that
the progress of the administration of the
Education Act has been steadily maintained. We are passing through a
period where we look for steady continuance in the advance of the operation of
the Education Act and for the gradual
expansion of the activities of the local
educational authorities up and down the
country. The point which I wish to make
is that although expenditure shows this
small decrease, there has, in fact, been no
halting with the operation of the Education Act, and no lessening of the activities
of our local education authorities.
ESTIMATE OF LOCAL EDUCATION
AUTHORITIES.
It was inevitable that during the first
years of their existence the Estimates of
the local education authorities should be
approximate only. There was little or no
solid foundation upon which to build
them, and they were, so to speak, at first
a series of leaps in the dark rather than
forecasts of expenditure founded upon
well-informed premises. To begin with.
no one could tell how long it would take
before the machinery in a particular local
area would be in a condition to function
at all, quite apart from the fact that no
such machinery could operate satisfactorily or fully until a complete survey of
the field of its activities had been carried
out. I am happy to say that, though we
have by no means reached finality in these
matters, both we ourselves and the local
education authorities have gathered useful lessons from our experience of the
working of the Act, and are better able to
gauge the cost of local educational
administration.
Last year the local education authorities estimated their total expenditure at
£230,000, and the Ministry included in
the Estimate an amount of £135,000 to
cover the estimated share of that expenditure. As a matter of fact, in the year
1926-27 out of the estimated Grant-in-
Aid of £135,000 only £112,000 was
spent.
The schemes submitted by the local
education authorities for the financial
year 1927-28, which is covered by the
present Estimates, contemplate an expenditure amounting to some quarter of a
million pounds, of which about £230,000
would rank for the Grant-in-Aid from
Parliamentary funds. Presuming that the
whole of this £230,000 were spent, the
share to be met from Parliamentary funds
on the Ministry's Estimates would be
some £150,000. But, judging from the
experience of the two preceding years, we
are content to expect a total local
expenditure of, approximately, £195,000
qualified for the Grant-in-Aid, thus
making the State liability under this
head £130,000, and this is the figure
which appears in this Estimate.
Ministry of Education 1444
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
It will be seen, therefore, that while
the Ministry is actually estimating for
£5,000 less under this head than appeared
in last year's Estimate, the actual increase in liability for local expenditure
which is expected by the Ministry this
year is the difference between £112,000,
the amount which was actually spent in
1926-27, and £130,000, which is the
amount which the Ministry anticipates
that it will require for Parliamentary
Grants-in-Aid of local expenditure in the
year before us, namely, an increase of
£18,000. This foreshadows an increase
in local expenditure of £9,000 in the current financial year, so that the Committee
should really need no assurance from me
that the Act is in increased operation, or
that education in the country is not
standing still.
The Ministry anticipates a still further
expansion of the activities of local education authorities before the limit up to
which Grants-in-Aid may be given is
reached. At present the Belfast
authority alone has reached a total local
expenditure which exceeds the equivalent
of a shilling in the £ rate, at which subvention from Parliamentary funds ends;
but I am happy to say that fact has not
checked the energy or the activity of the
Belfast authority. I believe nothing is
more pleasing to the citizens of this great
city than the progress of the provision of
the means for the proper education of
their children.
So much at present for the activities of
our local education authorities in so far
as they affect the figures to be found in
our present Estimates, but I shall, I hope,
return to them again when I touch upon
our general policy before I sit down,
because, in my view, the whole of our
educational future rests in their hands.
It is theirs to make or to mar our entire
programme.
GENERAL EXAMINATION OF
ESTIMATES.
Now let us examine these Estimates
apart from local expenditure, not in detail, but in large divisions, such as office
administration, elementary education,
and the rest. We shall find, I think,
that expenditure generally is static, and
that room for variation is comparatively
narrow.
(1) ADMINISTRATION.
But
For instance, on the Vote we are
discussing, Vote 1, there is a saving of
£236. There has been a reduction in the
number of clerks and of inspectors.
There has been a reduction in the amount
estimated for special inspections.
this saving has been more than offset by
the normal yearly increases in salary of
the staff. Again, on the same Vote, what
has been saved owing to the existence of
cheaper travelling facilities and to the
reduction of mileage rates for inspectors
using their own cars on travelling allowances of inspectors, and of other officers of
the Ministry, and of members of the
Advisory Council-this saving, I say,
has been largely discounted by a rise in
the amount we shall have to spend on
maintenance and repairs, and an increase
in printing and stationery charges.
On the printing and stationery head it
is, perhaps, encouraging to note that
there has been a growing sale to the
general public of the Ministry's Annual
Report. Parliamentary publications are
proverbially dull and considered unattractive, but last year some 600 copies of this
Report were sold to the general public,
though I must add that this particular
subject of rejoicing partakes rather of the
nature of a Pyrrhic victory, as the cost
of production on the numbers sold still
exceeds the sale price of each copy of the
Report to the public.
I may add that the mass of general
printing which the Ministry calls for increases annually with the increase of
public interest in education. The setting
up of the new system, with all the changes
from the old, has, undoubtedly, led to an
abnormal and temporary output of circulars and forms and advertisements. As
the new system becomes stereotyped so
the numbers of these may be expected to
decrease; but we welcome that portion of
our stationery bill, which is due to the
general demand for information upon
matters of educational administration.
In our opinion it is money well spent and
essentially productive.

(2) TRAINING COLLEGES.
Our training colleges for elementary
teachers will cost us slightly more this
year in spite of the fact that there is a
decrease of £600 payable by the Ministry
in bonuses to teachers who began their

offset by the increase in the number of

upon the general application of compulsory education and the effective administration of that part of the Act which

I should like to take this opportunity

(3) ELEMENTARY EDUCATION.
I pass now to what is by far the largest
head of our expenditure, namely, that of
elementary education. Here there is an
apparent total increase of £3,000. But
the real increase is larger than this, because the figures in the Estimates last
year were an over-estimate in some directions. This year the Christian Brothers'
elementary schools have, for the first
time, come into connection with the
Ministry. This has entailed a very considerable increase in our expenditure in
grants, to meet the capitation grants in
respect of attendance at these schools,
their total coming to something like
another £10,000 a year.
The net increase on this part of the
Vote is, however, £3,000 only, as there
has been a revision of the Estimate for
salaries for
and assistant
principal and
teachers, and a saving on the capitation
grant and on fees for the teaching of extra
subjects, the present financial year being
the first year when the reduced rates of
payment will have their full effect.
The total cost of teachers' salaries we
estimate at over £1,400,000. While I
am not complaining of the burden which
the payment of the whole of the elementary teachers' salaries imposes upon the
State resources, and while I do not think
that this Committee would be ready, in
the present circumstances, to agree to any
amendment of the system, hon. Members
will readily realize that this heavy liability has a cramping effect upon the
Ministry's activities.
Of the £1,794,570 which the Committee is asked to vote for all forms of
educational services in the Province (including higher education, the training of
teachers, grants to Queen's University,
and grants to local education authorities),
no less than 78.4 per cent. is required to
meet the salaries of elementary school
teachers.
While I am dealing with elementary
education I may say that in this field
there is every sign that our local education
authorities are making good headway, not
only with the tasks that lie immediately
in front of them, but with that, perhaps,
greater task of earning the confidence of
the public and winning the trust of those
who, when our proposals first appeared
before them, were inclined to view the
educational future with deep misgiving.
At any rate, these authorities may boast
that they are busied with elementary
school accommodation; that they are
facing the building problem, the problem
of amalgamations, the problem of the concentration of local effort, and facing these
problems with no small success.
They are concerned, too, with a great
mass of work entailed by the growing
number of transfers of schools and by the
setting up of increasing numbers of school
committees for those elementary schools
whose managers are not handing over to
the public altogether, but are admitting
the public, on conditions, to a share in
the management. I dealt with this question so recently in the House that I will
not go into the matter again, but I can
assure hon. Members of every party that
the transfer of schools and the general rearrangement of elementary school management, contemplated under the Act, is
proceeding in a most encouraging manner.
These authorities are also taking steps
generally to establish beneficent schemes
for the medical inspection and treatment
of school children. I believe, personally,
that no part of the Education Act and
no part of our expenditure is more blessed
with the prospect of immediate return to
the Province than that which deals with
medical inspection and treatment
children.

Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
The figures which appeared in the
Report of the Ministry of last year are a
sufficient proof that the local authorities
have not shrunk from doing their duty in
enforcing school attendance. I am aware
that there are some who complain that
still more might have been done, that
steps, more stringent yet, might have been
taken. But I would rather proceed by
gentle measures. I would rather reach
our aim by evolution than by revolution.
I believe, that, by firm but reasonable
application of the law our local education
authorities will ultimately achieve what is
the only true solution of the problem of
securing school attendance. They will inculcate a habit of attendance; they will
make good attendance a custom; and,
in that way, they will bring about the
great reform without which our efforts
for the perfecting of our educational
system must fall far short of fulfilment.
I should like to give the House a few
figures which will, I hope, go far to show
that substantial progress has already been
made in the direction of securing a satisfactory habit of school attendance. Here
they are:-
In 1925 the average attendance in
Belfast was 86.4 per cent. of the average
number on the rolls; in 1926-the latest
figures-it was 87.4:
In Derry city the figure in 1925 was
87.8, and in 1926, 85.1 per cent., but that
fall was entirely due to local epidemics.
In County Antrim the 1925 figure was
86.1 per cent.; the figure for 1926 is 88.1.
In County Armagh there has been a
great upward bound from 79.8 per cent.
in 1925, to 87.5 in 1926. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
The County Down figures show a rise
from 83.7 per cent. to 86.6 per cent.;
County Fermanagh from 79.2 per cent.
to 83 per cent.; County Londonderry from
79.7 per cent. to 82.7 per cent., and
Tyrone from 82.8 per cent. to 85.2 per
cent.
We are very satisfied, and I think the
Committee will join me in congratulating
the local authorities on the results of their
administration. These figures, it is true,
are not yet quite equal to the English and
Scottish figures, but they are treading
upon their heels and do represent an
immense advance.
(4) SECONDARY EDUCATION.
The figures for secondary education
show very little change. There is, on the
face of it, a decrease of £1,400. On
closer examination, however, it would
appear that we are asking for nearly
£4,000 more than was spent last year, as
our requirements for that year were overestimated by some £5,000. There are,
perhaps, signs that industrial difficulties
have had the effect of slowing down the
expansion of the secondary school population, but I am happy to say that these
signs are disappearing, and we may expect
a substantial increase in our figures
during the current financial year.
Here I should like to record what I am
sure every Member of this House will
recognize with pleasure as an important
development in our educational system.
Our local education authorities, especially
those in the counties, are beginning to be
increasingly conscious of their duties in
respect of the provision of opportunities
for secondary education. One education
authority has actually embarked upon the
management of a secondary school of its
own. Long may it flourish! Another is
contemplating the same step in the immediate future. Others again have made
substantial contributions towards secondary schools within the areas of their control. There is no department of education
where the assistance of the local education authorities is more needed than in
that of secondary education.
I have spoken of the burden that lies
upon the State in connection with elementary education. Now it is common
knowledge that technical instruction has
long been in receipt of local assistance. It
was here that our local authorities first
proved their fitness to undertake educational administration generally. But
secondary education has remained practically entirely unassisted from local resources, while the State, responsible as it
is for the whole of the salaries of the ele
mentary teachers, cannot be expected to
undertake any greater liability than at
present for secondary education. In
England, it must be remembered, the
local authorities pay the whole of the
salaries of secondary teachers in schools
under their own management, and are re-

couped by a 50 per cent. grant from the
State. Schools which are not directly
managed by local authorities there, or on
whose governing bodies a local authority
has not the preponderating voice, receive
no salary grant. Their sole grants from
public sources are £2 per student between

authorities receive rate aid to the tune of

spends £9 7s 6d on each secondary school
pupil; the Ministry of Education for

which are, as a rule, under other than

per pupil.
SALARIES OF SECONDARY SCHOOL
TEACHERS.
Yet here in Northern Ireland we are
over and over again criticized in the Press
and on the platform for our parsimony
towards secondary education, and particularly in our dealings with secondary
school teachers, both in respect of salary
scales and of the pension scheme. We are
continually being told that we should have
established the Burnham Scale of salaries
here, as they exist in England.
Members: Hear, hear).
(Hon.
While we have not imposed any one of
the Burnham Scales for secondary teachers
(for I must remind the House that there
are more of these scales than one)—while
we have not imposed any one of these
scales as a minimum scale upon the
governing bodies of secondary schools, we
have certainly not forbidden the payment
of salaries equal to these scales, or even
above them. Quite the contrary. In
fact, there are at present a considerable
number of secondary teachers in receipt
of salaries in excess of the minimum scales
adopted by the Ministry-there are even
some in receipt of salaries in excess of the
Burnham Scale-presuming always that
Burnham Scale to be the one for teachers
in provincial schools.
When the Ministry was about to adopt.
certain minimum salary scales to apply to
teachers in recognized secondary schools,
it was necessary to consider first and foremost the general financial situation, both
of the State and of the schools themselves.
The Ministry could not undertake the
whole burden of secondary teachers'
salaries—it was already bearing the whole
cost of salaries of elementary teachers.
The local authorities obviously could not
by the mere dictation of the Ministry
have imposed upon them charges, of this
nature for secondary education at the
very outset of their career. There remained then to consider the financial
capacity of the secondary schools themselves. They alone must bear the responsibility for the salaries, with such
aid as the State could afford to give them.
The Ministry examined the general
financial conditions of the schools so far
as it could be discovered. It was at once
apparent that many of the schools-the
smaller schools, particularly in country
districts were in no position to pay the
Burnham rates. It would have been useless to prescribe minimum scales, which
would close the doors of many of the
schools in the Province. So the scales were
fixed-minimum, remember, not maximum
scales at the highest figure which in the
judgment of the Ministry, from the evidence at their disposal, they considered
the generality of the schools could bear.
THE MINISTRY'S MINIMUM
SCALES.
For
What are these minimum scales?
I doubt very much if the country at large
knows exactly what is being called in
question. What are they? For a man,
£210 per annum; and, for a woman, £200
per annum as a commencing rate, rising
by fixed annual increments, which are recouped in full to the schools by the State,
normally to £450 for a man and to £325
for a woman, with a further increase to
£500 and £375 respectively for teachers
holding first or second class honours
degrees or an equivalent qualification.
Besides that, provision is also made for
extra payment to headmasters and headmistresses of amounts varying from £50
to £200 a year.
Now I would suggest that these scales
are not so very parsimonious after all.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There
are few comparable professions which
give a man or a woman so good a start.
If the country can be convinced that
secondary schoolmasters and mistresses are
being underpaid, and if local education
authorities can be persuaded to make
grants to those schools which are in need
Ministry of Education
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
of assistance, I can assure this House that
the Ministry will not check their activities
nor prevent local authorities from lending their assistance. Far from it. The
Ministry will be ready to bear, within
the specified limit, its share of any such
assistance granted by local educational
authorities.
Apropos of the alleged insufficiency of
the remuneration and pensions of secondary
teachers, it is interesting to note that the
Ministry's inspectors report a remarkable
and general improvement in all departments of our secondary schools. Moreover, the number of highly qualified
University graduates, or teachers with
equivalent academic distinction, at work
in the schools is steadily increasing. There
are now, altogether, in the service of our
recognized secondary schools, 760 full-time
and part-time teachers, of whom no fewer
than 586 possess University degrees or
equivalent academic qualifications. Out
of these 586, 388 are University graduates,
of whom 212 have taken honours degrees.
That seems to me a sufficient ground for
claiming that there is a rise in the general
level of secondary education in Ulster.
SECONDARY SCHOOL EXAMI-
NATIONS.
I should just like to touch upon the
subject of our Secondary School Certificate Examinations for a moment-and,
indeed, our whole school examination
system, because we have inaugurated a
new scheme of examinations, which have
brought us hopeful and encouraging results and the success of which emboldens
us to hope for a general lightening
eventually of the burden of examinations
upon our elementary and secondary
schools.
We are anxious to see a system under
which our young people will be asked to
face but three public examinations during
the whole of their school career. They
will leave the elementary school after an
examination, the first school examination,
which will determine their placing when
they transfer to the secondary school and
upon the results of which scholarships
will be awarded by local education authorities.
After two or three years they will face
the second school examination, upon
which will depend the award of the junior
certificate, at the close of the intermediate
course, and the award of the local education authorities senior scholarships, and
this examination will, I hope, eventually
be much more of a school examination and
less of an external test.
After that will begin the two years'
secondary course proper, called the postintermediate course, when, instead of the
broad general education which he has
experienced hitherto, the pupil will
receive an education with some measure
of specialization in it, in literary, mathematical, scientific, or commercial subjects.
The third and final school examination,
that for the senior certificate, will mark
the end of school life and open the gates
of the University to those who are fortunate enough to be privileged to continue
their education.
We hope ultimately to secure such
general recognition for this examination
for the senior certificate that it will become the accepted channel from the
secondary school to the University, to the
junior ranks of the Civil Service and to
the Training College for teachers. It is
already accepted by local education
authorities in most cases for the purpose
of the award of their scholarships to the
University.
This final school examination should be
the first door to professional life. I am
well aware that these things have not yet
all been brought to pass, but I think that
the Committee is entitled to know the
direction in which we are travelling, and
travelling hopefully, which, as Stevenson
assures us, is even better than arriving.
are
TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.
That is what we are doing for those who
would enter the professions. What then
we doing for those whose life is
destined to be passed at the bench or the
drawing board, in the workshop or at the
plough? What are we doing to fit our
boys and girls for trade and commerce and
the future mothers of young Ulster to
undertake the duties of the home?
Technical instruction is estimated to
cost a further £3,000 this year owing to
the increased cost to the State of
teachers' salaries in increment grants and
allowances payable under the Salary
Regulations.
