It will be familiar to this Committee
that the attendance grant in respect of
technical school students is a fixed grant
of £42,000 per annum, divisible amongst
the schools in units of attendance, which
may move up and down in value according as the attendance has been decreasing
or increasing. In 1924-25 the unit of
attendance was worth 21s; in 1925-26 it
was 19s and we hope that the present
school year will show an even lower figure,
in spite of the effect of the continued depression in trade and industry.
I cannot speak highly enough in appreciation of the energies of the Committees
who are responsible for technical instruction, or their officials. The expansion of
instruction in our midst is
and is happily
technical
already remarkable
continuous.
This Committee will, I am sure, note
with approval that we are again making
provision for the award of trade scholarships to young persons engaged in industry. We are convinced that the conection between industry and technical
instruction cannot be too close, and that
the strongest characteristic of technical
instruction must be its reality, its practicality. The Ministry would be glad to
see the idea of these trade scholarships
further extended and provision for the
assistance of apprentices to the various
skilled trades within their areas made by
local education authorities. I feel sure
that local employers would gladly favour
this form of aid to their young craftsmen.
and readily release the lads for the period
of their courses. The time should come,
and come soon, when the engineering and
science laboratories and classes of our technical schools and colleges will be the recognized anterooms to the workshops of
industry. Through them every skilled.
craftsman will have passed in order to
gain a knowledge of science and art as
applied to industry before being finally
enrolled as a tradesman and actually using
scientific processes in the pursuit of his
handicraft.
THE PROBLEM OF THE
ADOLESCENT.
That is all that I feel called upon to
say on the present Estimates, but before
I sit down I should like to say something
upon the attitude of the Ministry upon
a question of educational policy which is
engaging the attention of those interested

in educational administration in Great
Britain, and which should also be occupying our attention here in Northern
Ireland.
Last year's Report of the Ministry
showed that in the school year 1925-26
there were some 167,000 children of compulsory school age on the rolls of our
public elementary schools. This gives an
average annual entry of between twenty
and twenty-one thousand children. We
may, I think, take these figures as fairly
representative of our child population,
though when the census returns are fully
published we shall be able to arrive at
more exact calculation.
Presumably, therefore, there are between eighteen and twenty thousand
adolescents in each year between 12 and
20 years of
age. This gives a total young
population of 140,000 to 160,000 between
the
ages I have named, and of 100,000 to
120,000 if we confine ourselves to the ages
of 14 to 20, the ages beyond the upper
limit of compulsory school attendance.
That is the extent of our problem, the
problem of the education of the adolescent, which we share with the rest of the
United Kingdom and the rest of the
Empire.
All these adolescents, it is true, will not
be able to enjoy the advantages of fulltime education. But, even
So, there
should be a far larger school population
than there is at present-particularly a
larger secondary school population. We
have to-day some 9,000 only on the rolls
of our secondary schools. There are some
22,000 on the rolls of our technical schools
and classes, but the great majority of
these are, of course, part-time evening
students. Though much has been done
more still must be done if we are to keep
abreast of the times, if we are to keep in
line with the other peoples of the world.
The least we can do--at present, maybe,
it is also the most we can do is to provide facilities, opportunities for those
who having passed the elementary stage
of education are ready to go further along
the road and to acquire those great
lessons which we think all our young folk
should have offered to them. The object
of any sound system of public education.
to-day should be to instil into our
children, first, the love of learning for the
pure love of knowing; then, the love of
learning for the material welfare that it
Ministry of Education 1456
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
alone can bring; and lastly, the love of
learning for the sake of the peace of the
world which widespread knowledge only
can ensure, and the greatest enemy of
which is the ignorance of the masses of the
nations of the world.
THE EDUCATION OF THE
ADOLESCENT.
How then are we to provide for the
adolescent? When should the elementary
stage of education be completed for the
average child and what should succeed
it? The Advisory Council, under the
Chairmanship of Sir Robert Lynn, has
this question under consideration at present. But I would ask this House and
the country at large, especially those who
are acting as members of a local education
authority, or of one of its Committees
or sub-Committees, also to turn their
attention to these important matters.
Here is the problem in its simplest and
most direct form. How are we to arrange
our system of public education to meet
the varying needs of the children whose
elementary course of education has closed?
Hitherto, in common probably with the
vast majority of peoples, we have been
content to keep children throughout the
whole of their years of compulsory schooling from six to fourteen-in the elementary school. At that age, and not
before, they have left the elementary
school whether they were to take up
immediately or to go on to another school
for a further course of study.
work
But, from time immemorial, the boy
in the preparatory department of the
secondary school--the child of parents
who could afford to give him the best
opportunity has started his secondary
course, not at fourteen, but at twelve.
Cannot we then so order our public
system of education as to give the
children of the great mass of the people
the same chance.
The average child should have his work
so arranged for him that he has covered his
elementary courses--that common ground
which is the foundation of all education,
whatever the ultimate aim of the pupil--
by the time he has reached his twelfth
year. That is the true dividing line.
where childhood ends and adolescence,
with all the differences of educational
needs of adolescence, begins.
Let us consider first the child who is to
go to the secondary school and then to the
University. He will need a course of
post-elementary education of at least five
years preferably six. He is probably
destined for one of the learned professions,
and he will not specialize in the narrower
sense until he has reached the University.
For him the existing secondary schools
are able to cater.
Next, we have the child whose wholetime education must cease at the age of
sixteen or thereabouts. He is destined
for commerce or for industry. He has not
the time at his disposal to devote the same
amount of his adolescent education to
purely intellectual training. Specialization or bias must enter comparatively early
into his post-elementary school life. But
he could at least have two years of liberal
post-elementary education before the
curve takes place. For him we have the
day commercial school and the junior
technical school, the one for the cadet of
commerce, the other for the cadet of industry. Both of these should provide a
four year course- two years of wide education-languages, mathematics, physical
training, handwork, and music with a
further two years' course definitely preparatory for the life's work of the pupil.
In this connection we are hoping to
develop a new type of junior technical
school, definitely leading towards our
greatest industry, agriculture, and so
helping, if may be, to check the increasing
number of lads who---for want of such
leading, or because our existing schools
lead definitely at present to commerce or
to the industry of the cities and townsswell the ranks of the workers in urban
occupation.
In the result the farmer has been left
short of labour to work his farm-our
countryside is threatened with depopulation and the whole of the future of the
Province is menaced. For we must at all
costs maintain the great industry of agriculture for which our Province has been
by nature so bountifully endowed, even
though shipbuilding, and engineering,
linen, tobacco, ropemaking, and
other great industries are still flourishing.
We are going to ask my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Agriculture, to help us
here, and I believe we shall not ask in
vain.

Ministry of Education
17 MAY 1927

ED
Lastly, we must be prepared to deal
with those children whom an unkindly
fate has robbed of the prospect of fulltime education beyond fourteen, when
compulsory schooling ends.
For them,
and they are unfortunately the great
majority of our children, we must endeavour to provide something which
hitherto we have not provided. We must
organize special facilities in connection
with our elementary school system which
will enable those children to enjoy a
definite post-elementary course of liberal
education, a course which will sharpen
their intellectual faculties and waken
their taste; which will give them not only
useful and necessary information, but an
appetite for further study and for reading;
a course which may lead them, at its close,
voluntarily to continue their education
for themselves at the evening classes at
our technical schools as part-time students
in the intervals which their work permits
to them.
That is the task immediately before
this country-the reorganization of educational opportunities during the last two or
three years of compulsory school attendance,
and the provision of greater
facilities for continued education for
adolescents between the ages of 14 and 20.
I am not now foreshadowing the extension
of the school age to 15 or 16. For that
we are quite definitely not yet prepared.
But even that possibility we must keep
well within view. The Education Act
has made it plain that any future
development of education must be linked
with local administration, assisted and
advised by the Ministry. When I present
Estimates that call upon the taxpayer for
over a million and three-quarters of money
for public education, I think I need have
no hesitation when I claim that the taxpayer is doing all that can be expected of
him now, and that for further expansion
we must look for assistance from local
resources.
I present these Estimates with a certain
feeling of wistfulness, for they are the
last which will have been prepared under
the scrutiny of Mr. David Frizzell,
Accountant to the Ministry since its foundation, and the controller of finance of
local education schemes. Mr. Frizzell
has intimated his wish to retire this summer, when he will have completed 45
years of service in the cause of education
in Ireland. During that long period he
has served his country with remarkable
ability and zeal. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) His ripe experience has been invaluable to our young Ministry. His
patience and his tact in helping those of
less experience than himself, his full grasp
of the working of the educational machine
and his lucidity in explanation have done.
more than I can say to set our new system
going. With these qualities he has always had such high ideals and such transparent honesty as not only maintained
but even enhanced the traditions of the
Civil Service. He will carry with him
into his retirement not only the respect
but the real affection of his colleagues.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I beg to
move.

There is just one other matter in connection with the Vote which I would like
to refer to, and that is with regard to the
appointment of inspectors. There are not
many, I think only one or two, Catholic
inspectors on the list. I need hardly
point out to the Committee,
because
they must be aware of it, that one-third
of the schools are under Catholic management. In my judgment there should be
at least that proportion of inspectors. 1
approached the Ministry with regard to
this, and it was their opinion also that
that should occur, but what happened?
During the past year two vacancies
occurred. Both of these inspectors who
retired were Catholics. On the appointments being made only one Catholic was
appointed. It is particularly with reference to the one not appointed I wish
to deal. I am not going to mention
names. In my judgment a very serious
injustice was done to this man. He was
the teacher in a small elementary school
in a country district. He went there only
a few years ago and the school was at its
lowest ebb. In the shortest possible time.
he brought it to its highest standard,
during which he pursued his University.
career, and I think he had a remarkable one.
He got his higher diploma in education
with honours, his B.E., his Master of
Science and his Master of Arts. That
man was suitable by age and suitable in
appearance in every way, but still he was

that on the Selection Board there was a

accent. (Laughter.) It is not a joke. I
believe there was no other reason given
but that. My own opinion is that the
only thing that barred his appointment.
was his religion. Of that I am satisfied.

districts higher than they are at the present time. In my own area-Magherafelt we are paying 10s. or 11s. in the £,

Dr. MORRISON: I have not very

for 16s, as the contribution of the

this. No hon. Member of this House
would be here if he had not the desire of
the country's good at heart-at least, I
take it to be so and we are grateful,
or should be grateful, for the preservation
of our country and our institutions. Most
of all should we be grateful to the men
who suffered physical disability and injury
in the country's defence and in ours. We
should leave no stone unturned or avenue
unexplored in our efforts to fulfil the
promises made to these men when they
left their homes, their employments, and
their all to go out in defence of their
country.
Many of us had friends and relatives
who went out to fight for their country.
Some came back; others did not; but most
unfortunate of all are those who came
back maimed in health, maimed in limb,
perhaps with lungs mutilated and burned
out by foul gas, and with every chance
of happiness in this world destroyed.
Those are the men for whom we seek the
protection of this House and of every
right-thinking man in the country to
provide that they will not only get assistance but that they will get the right
to work.

Again they say further down:
In most countries that participated in
the war it has been maintained that recourse must be had to legal obligations,
and that private employers, public
bodies, and Government services must be
compelled to employ a certain number, a
definite percentage, of war-disabled. This
solution, which has become necessary in
practice, is in conformity with equity.
The war-disabled fought not only in defence of the country and all its institutions but also to preserve its commercial,
agricultural, and industrial wealth.
They were disabled while serving the
whole country, and the debt which has
been incurred by the whole of society
should be borne by all. Employers of
labour should remember that they, too,
owe a duty to those whose knowledge of
warfare was not confined to the manufacture and supply of war munitions.
Of the countries that have put
measures of this kind into operation, the
first is our friend, the late enemy, Germany, who dealt with this problem by an
Order published in 1919, and enacted by
the Reichstag in 1920, making employment compulsory. Austria passed a
similar measure in 1920. Poland also
passed such a measure in 1921, and Italy
also in the same year. France, of course,
had a similar measure in different forms
since 1916. They had voluntary service
then, and it was made compulsory that
the State should employ war-disabled
men. These measures have all been
found workable, with a few flaws from
our point of view, perhaps, and these
have been taken into account in the drafting of the present Bill.
Great Britain dealt with the problem
in another way, and put into operation
in 1919 a voluntary employment scheme,
with which most hon. Members present
are familiar-the King's National Roll of
Honour.
The King's National Roll of
Honour was found after two and a half
years to have failed in its object. A
Select Committee of the House of Commons sat in June, 1922, and in September, 1922, made a Report, which they
conclude with:
So urgent is the problem that the
Committee recommend that their proposals should be carried into effect
forthwith, and the necessary legislation passed during the autumn session.

it is the natural result of memory faded
by the lapse of four years.
That was in 1922. How much more has
it faded since ?
Such an attitude of mind should not,
however, be permitted to influence the
action of the country towards the disabled.
I particularly draw the attention of hon.
Members to that.
Such an attitude of mind should not,
however, be permitted to influence the
action of the country towards the
disabled. If, therefore, sentiment and
sympathy cannot be revived by any
improved voluntary system within
reasonable time, there would appear to
be no other course open than to apply
compulsion.
Another Select Committee of the House
of Commons sat in 1923 on the
"Employment of Disabled," and they made an
interim report which endorsed the Report of the first Committee. I need not
read it as it only exactly endorses the
Report of the first Committee.
This Bill has the advantage of the experience of similar Acts in Germany,
France.
Poland, Austria, Italy and
Expert observers in the different countries
have pointed out the weakness or otherwise of their own Acts so that we might
benefit, and all the advantages have been
embodied in this Bill. Not only have we
chosen the best out of every foreign or
allied enactment, but we have inserted
every safeguard that the most important
employers of labour can suggest, and we
have satisfied the Labour Union leaders
that no rights or privileges of trades

[Colonel Woods]
unionists shall be imperilled in any way.
A similar Bill has received its Second
Reading in the Imperial House without
one dissentient voice. It is, and has
been, supported by every Member of the
Imperial House of Commons.
In case it is alleged that this Bill is
unjust, I would point out that the word
"compulsory" only applies to a very small
percentage. It is on those who would
shirk their duty that it is most insistent.
There is a Committee, and above the
Committee there is a Court of Appeal, and
they are all under the Ministry of Labour.
The first Committee is composed of three
representatives of employers, three representatives of employees, and three representatives of the disabled men. That is
very fair.
In fact it is against the interests of the disabled ex-Servicemen.
The Committee can exercise its authority
to prevent any ex-Serviceman from taking
undue advantage of this Bill, from acting
unjustly, or from shirking his work. On
his employer making complaint to the
Committee they have power to withdraw
such a man's certificate.
Then we have the Appeal Court, which
is to hear cases either of the men or of the
employers. Section 7 shows that the only
thing an employer has to do is to furnish
returns showing the numbers of persons
employed who are in receipt of remuneration and stating the number of disabled
men employed. It is no hardship on
employers in the least. Section 8 says:
An employer shall not be compelled
to employ or continue to employ any
particular disabled man who holds a
certificate in accordance with the provisions of this Act or any disabled man
who is not suitable for the purposes of
his establishment.
He cannot have foisted on him a man who
is a baker or a blacksmith unless he has
suitable work for him. He can go to the
Committee and show that there are no
suitable men available for him. In that
case he is exempt from the operation of
the Act. There is every possible safeguard put into the Bill. I do not see that
any honest man can find any reason to
complain that there is any real compulsion in the matter whatever. There
is no such thing as dragooning the employer into it. All he has got to do is to
come to the Committee and prove whether
he can or can not employ a man.
Then we have the very old grievance of
the ex-Serviceman that his pension is
taken into consideration when he is being
given employment. That is guarded
against here. If the Bill is passed it
comes into force on the 1st January
next. It is not made absolutely compulsory for at least two years, so as to give
employers time to fill the vacancies with
the necessary percentage laid down in
the Regulations made by the Ministry of
Labour. There is no hardship in that,
and it is made so that no person will be
put out of employment to make room for
a disabled ex-Serviceman.
To put the whole mattter in a nutshell,
the King's National Roll has failed owing
to various reasons, mainly because the
sympathy and sentiment for the disabled
soldier has died, stifled by business. As
a matter of fact it has now become a
struggle for money and position and the
survival of the fittest. The disabled man
has no one to look after him and it is the
duty of the Government to do so. There
is no sentiment in business; it is a kind
of "soldier's farewell." Sentiment was
the foundation stone of the King's
National Roll of Honour. The war is a
memory only to those who knew something about it; to others it was a time of
great prosperity now faded into the limbo
of ancient history. Unfortunately, it is
only human nature as we are acquainted
with it to strive for position and money
and forget the under dog. I would say
this, that if there is any feeling amongst
Members for those who did their best and
came out, unfortunately for themselves,
on the worst side, let them express that
feeling. Let there be no party considerations. Let their conscience dictate to
them what way they should act. Let
them act as if they had no party machine
guiding them in their action."
I would like to tell you about some
cases of disabled men who are unemployed. I was asked by a very prominent
gentleman in Ulster to give him some details of these ex-Servicemen for his information, following on speeches made in
England by a Field-Marshal regarding
the position of ex-Servicemen in Southern
Ireland. In the course of my investigations I found some exceedingly painful
cases. Hon. Members would hardly believe some of the stories if I told them.
There was the case of a man with a wife
and seven children, the oldest being 13
years, trying to live on a pension of 19s

intended to help and the second whether

The opinion of the Government is that

declined. I do not admit the accuracy of

When this Government took over its
powers on the 1st January, 1922, there
were 105 firms on the King's National
Roll. Two years later, on the 1st
January, 1924, there were 502 firms; two

date for which I have figures, the number

judged from this standpoint, there has
been a gradual increasing of the number
of firms registering. Let me deal with

1st January, 1922, there were 1,339 disabled men employed; on the 1st January,
1924, 2,988; on the 1st January, 1926,
4,552; and on the 25th April of this year
there were 4,921.

All this time, up to within the last few
months, we have been suffering from a
period of acute industrial depression, and
notwithstanding that industrial depression and scarcity of work for men of every
class there has been a vast improvement
as regards the number of disabled men
employed. On the 1st January, 1926,
there were 1,849 disabled men unemployed, and on the 25th April, the last
date I have a figure for, there were 1,134.
Therefore, between 1st January, 1926,
and the last figure we have got, no fewer
than 715 disabled men have obtained employment.
At this stage I am entitled to pay a tribute to those public-spirited, patriotic
men who have served upon the King's
National Roll of Honour, and who have
done invaluable work, with great perseverance and self-sacrifice, in obtaining
employment for these men. Yet we are
asked to scrap all this machinery. We are
asked to wipe off the slate this voluntary
effort, and to substitute for it a compulsory system. Obviously we cannot keep
two systems going at the same time. This
Bill must mean that men are to be employed compulsorily or else that they are
to be employed voluntarily. That is, in
my opinion, the position.
I should tell hon. Members what the
Government's record is in connection
with this matter. The Government is
upon the roll with a percentage of disabled men to the male staff of 17.3, and
to the total staff of 13.6. The Ministry
of Labour's record is this: the percentage
of disabled men employed in relation to
the male staff is 22.7.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: Therefore, practically one man out of every four employed
in the Ministry of Labour is a disabled
ex-Serviceman.

That proves conclusively that employers
are not looking on this matter in a niggardly way, that many are not seeking just
to qualify in order to get upon the Roll,
but that they are doing more and are endeavouring, as far as possible, to employ

Under those circumstances I do not think it can be held that

On

I do not want to weary the House by

Measure and a Measure that would not

stitution of the Committee which is to

Under the Trade Board Act, at

of which I happen to be a member,
there are requests made by
ployers to enable them to employ some

Board issues that certificate to say that

Mr. KYLE: I would like in the first
place to congratulate the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
(Mr. Robb) on the very admirable speech
he made yesterday afternoon. It was
idealism almost from start to finish, with
certain limitations, however. I would
have liked if he had thought fit to have
stressed the importance and the necessity
of the local authorities paying greater
attention to educational activities more
than he did yesterday. Probably the
Parliamentary Secretary did not think it
part of his duty to do so. But I do think
that the representative of the Ministry of
Education in Northern Ireland ought to
have stressed more than he did the
difference between the educational system
in Britain as compared with the education
system of Northern Ireland. While one
agrees that the 1923 Act is the Charter
of the education system in Northern Ireland, yet one feels that unless the Minister
is prepared to stimulate the local authorities to a greater degree than he has
hitherto done very much of the possibilities of the 1923 Act will be lost.
He told us yesterday that the total
Estimates for education amounted roughly
to an 8s. rate over Northern Ireland, and
out of that 8s. rate 7s. 9d. was provided
by the Government, leaving only a threepenny rate for the Six Counties to provide
for education. Well, if we compare that
figure of 3d. that is being paid by our
local authorities for educational purposes
with the sum that is being paid in Scotland and England, I think the difference
will immediately strike those local authorities who have. been limiting the amount
that they are striking for educational
purposes. It will strike their conscience
to the end that they might realize that it
will only be when the local authorities
as well as the Government are prepared
to strike a heavier rate than has been
struck up to now by those authorities
that we will get full fruition of the educational system, the possibilities of which
the Parliamentary Secretary laid before
us yesterday.

gathered that he was opposed to the

spoken in congratulating the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education upon the clear and succinct

I congratulate him upon the exhaustive
nature of the statistical statement he has
made, I cannot agree with him as to the
roseate picture which he painted of the
success of the Education Act in Ulster.
have no doubt that, when this educational
scheme was first fashioned, it was the intention of the Government, as indeed it
was the desire of all men of goodwill in
Ulster, to provide the people with a
system of education that would meet their
essential educational needs. But there is
only one test that can be applied as to the
success or failure of any scheme, and that
is the test of experience, and the experience of everyone has been that, to some
extent, the Education Act has been a
complete failure.
I do not propose to enter into the many
aspects of the question so eloquently dealt
with by the hon. and learned Member for
the University, but I rise for the purpose
once again of stating the position of those
whom we represent, and to put before the
Government frankly our view that this
Act will require to be modified and, if
necessary, a new Bill introduced to meet
the insistent demands of one-third of the
population of Northern Ireland. What
was the chief purpose of the Education
Act? It was to have the schools in
Northern Ireland transferred.
Tried by
the test of experience, as I say, the Act
has been a failure in that regard. Not 10
per cent. of the schools of any religious
persuasion have been transferred, and at
the present moment the voluntary schools,
which educate 33 per cent. of the Catholic
population and a considerable number of
the schools that represent a very large
section of the Protestant population, have
definitely and distinctly declared that
they will not be transferred.
The hon. and learned Gentleman may
say that they ought to be transferred;
that is a matter entirely for them. You
may say that there is no defence for their
attitude; that is a matter for you and
them. But what we have to deal with, as
men of the world, is not what this one
thinks or what that one thinks; we have
to consider what is as it is. In this respect we have a grave wrong perpetrated
upon an important and vital element in
the life of this community. I think it is
a grave injustice to those people whose
schools have not been transferred to deny
to them the elementary justice of giving
them the grant for maintenance and for
buildings which has been given to the
transferred schools.
An educational project is not a project
for the purpose of setting up machinery;
it is for the purpose of creating a more
satisfactory condition of educational
equipment, and whatever your views may
be, whether you dislike their opinions or
regard them as undesirable prejudices, no
matter what view you take of them, you
are putting the Catholic schools and the
Protestant schools that have not been
transferred in a position of complete inferiority as compared with the other
schools in Ulster.
Why does the Government take up this
attitude? May I further point out that
we are putting forward, when we make
this claim for our schools, not a claim that
has not been carefully considered and
sympathetically regarded, even by eminent Protestant authorities, some of whom
sat upon the Lynn Committee. One of
the recommendations of the Lynn Committee, upon which you are supposed to
have based your proposals which now constitute the Education Act, was as follows:
In the case of primary schools which
have not been handed over to the Local
Committees, or are not under a Management Committee (i.e., schools coming
under Class III), loans may be made
by the Ministry, but no aid should be
available out of State funds for repayment of interest and sinking fund; always provided that an exception may
be made in the case of existing vested
national schools, in which case aid may
be granted towards enlargement or
structural improvement, two-thirds of
the interest and sinking fund being paid
annually by the Ministry.
Now it is a strange thing to me that
although you have constantly proclaimed
on platforms and in Parliament that your
Education Act is the result of the
considered judgment of this Committee,
yet you extracted from your Bill this
Clause which proposed to do justice to the
voluntary and non-transferred schools,
and you accept all the other recommendations of the Lynn Committee.
That is a
thing that has never yet been justified by
the Parliamentary Secretary for Education, and I do hope and trust that if the

first place I raised this question before,

munity. All these fads of specialists of

I was glad to hear my hon. Friend the

ought to receive.

As hon. Members who sit on the
other side of the Committee justifiably
say, the greater number of the children
who attend the primary schools are the
children of working men who will have to
make their way in the world by their
own efforts, and who will have to depend
for their success in the world on the
education which they get in the ordinary
primary schools. The ordinary child at a
primary school only remains at that school
from, say, five to six up to thirteen or
fourteen. Those are few but precious
years, and I think it is of the greatest
importance to see that those years are
occupied as well as possible in putting
into the child's hand as well-fashioned
tools as we can to enable him to carve his
way in the world.
The essential tools are reading, writing:
arithmetic, a knowledge of English grammar, a knowledge of geography, ordinary
elementary subjects. If a boy is going to
be successful in the world those are the
essential tools that he should be equipped
with, and in my judgment it is essential
that you should equip him with as finely
wrought tools as possible. If one listens
to what is said by business men and employers in the city one hears them say now
that the boys who come from the National
Schools have had a too diffusive curriculum, that there are too many frills on
their education, that you cannot get boys
to count so well as the boys of twenty or
thirty years ago, that the boys now do not
write so well as the boys of twenty or

Then we come again to the question
of schools that will not be transferred.
I believe in the popular control of education. I believe if there is one thing more
than another which has helped to create
suspicion and prejudice in our midst, it
is every Church trying to herd its own
band of children to its own schools.
must say this with regard to the Roman
Catholic Church. I admire their honesty
and consistency, because they have always
frankly said, "We believe in a denominational system of education, and we will
not have anything else." Some of our
other Churches have paid lip service to a
popular system of education, yet have
been as denominational as the other.
I am sorry as a citizen that this Act,
which I think was conceived on generous
lines and right principles, could not have
been taken as a great national settlement
by all sections of the community. I was
sorry when the hon. Member for Down
(Mr. P. O'Neill) said on a recent occasion, in this House, that the Roman
Catholic Schools would not be transferred
in any circumstances, because I had hoped
that with the growing feeling of confidence in the community and with the
better feeling all round we might have
evolved out of this Education Act, with
some slight alterations, an educational
system that would be participated in by
every section of our community without
hurting anybody's convictions. Therefore, I was sorry when he sat down.
I do feel that the non-transferred
schools have at the present time less or
more of a grievance, especially with regard to grants. Before there was a rate
struck these schools were entitled to a
certain grant if they provided a certain
other amount. Now, that these sections
have to pay a rate for education purposes
is it fair that they should be placed in
a worse position than they were in under
the old system? We do not like coercion.
We will not be coerced. It looks to me
that this is a way of coercing people into
transferring their schools. If the coercion
was going to be a success I do not know
if I would be in sympathy with it, but
it is not going to succeed. If it is put
in for that purpose it is going to cause
some bitterness, and I think it would be
no injustice to put these schools, as regards building grants, in the position they
were in prior to the time the Education
rate was struck, because this section of
the community pays rates as well as other
people.
I was never very much in favour of this
country and this Parliament setting up
British standards, and saying, "We must
come up to British standards.' If this
Parliament is to justify its existence it
ought to try to set up its institutions in
keeping with the needs of this small area
and in keeping with what it can afford to
pay. I have said in this House before,
and I still maintain it is true, that this
small area cannot afford to live up to
British standards of Government. It is
said that in Ireland we have only onequarter of the taxable capacity of
England.

In presenting this Estimate, I may
refer to one of the most salient features
in it that we are asking for less this
year than last year.
a
The Committee will observe that there
is a decrease of £732. It will also be
observed on referring to the particulars
of the Staff in the Ministry of Home
Affairs that there is a reduction of 2,
namely, 157 as compared with 159 in last
year's Estimate. Apart from few
minor transfers in the staff of the various
branches of the Ministry arising from
differentiation of duties, the most important changes have occurred in the Roads
branch, and the branch in connection
with Police Administration and Maintenance. As regards the latter branch
we have been able to effect a saving of 8
officials, consequent on the reduction of
work owing to the disbandment and
reduction of the Special Constabulary
Force, but as against this, for
reasons
which I will explain later, we have found
it necessary to make provision for an increase of 5 clerks in the Branch which is
responsible for Road and Motor Traffic
Administration.
As Members of the Committee will see
from the Order Paper, it falls on me to
present after this Estimate the Estimate
for Grants to Local Authorities, and, in
the circumstances, I think it is due to the
Committee to make a general comprehensive statement involving policy and
covering the whole work of administration
of the Ministry.
As the Committee are no doubt aware,
the Ministry of Home Affairs is divided
into two main departments, one is what
is known as the Home Office, and carries
on in Northern Ireland the functions
exercised by the Home Office in England,
and includes within its operations the
general administration of law and order,
Prisons, Reformatories, Borstals, Industrial Schools, Asylums, and Police Services. The expression "law and order"
covers a multitude of operations. Apart
altogether from the question of the
arrangements necessary for carrying out
of magisterial duties, and the supervision
of the Petty Sessions Courts, the Ministry
finds itself called upon daily to deal with
questions arising out of the administration of a series of very important Acts
of Parliament affecting every-day life,
for example, the Intoxicating Liquor
Acts, the Poisons and Pharmacy Acts,
and the Protection of Animals Acts.
I would like to take this opportunity
of saying a word in regard to the operation of the Poisons and Pharmacy Acts.
As the Committee is aware, an Act of
this Parliament was passed in 1925 which
provided, in the first place, for the establishment of a Pharmaceutical Society for
Northern Ireland and for governing,
generally, the conditions under which
poisons and dangerous drugs may be sold
in Northern Ireland. The Society established under this Act has been working
in the closest harmony in past years with
the Ministry, and I would like to express
my appreciation of the work performed
by the members of the first Pharmaceutical Council. Not alone have they devoted
their time and their energy to improve
their own status as a Society and members
of a profession, but they have also
assisted the Government very materially
in ensuring that the laws regulating the
sale of poisons and dangerous drugs are
observed by all druggists and chemists
and other qualified persons who have been
in the habit of selling these commodities.
For this purpose an inspector was appointed, whose duty it was to make visits
to all establishments in Northern Ireland
for the purpose of examining their books
and records, and also to inspect those
traders who were licensed to sell poisons
and ascertain to what extent those who
were unlicensed were breaking the law.
In this connection I might point out
that despite the provisions of Section 4 of
the Intoxicating Liquor Act, it was found
that, prior to the appointment of this
Inspector, there was a considerable sale
of methylated ether for drinking purposes
by certain chemists and druggists, and as
a result of the inspector's supervision and
the action of the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society I am glad to say that
there has been an extraordinary improvement in connection with this, although
I regret to say that there are indications
that this pernicious practice is still going
on.
With regard to the administration of
the Reformatories and Industrial Schools,
this matter was discussed when I presented the Estimates in conncetion with
these matters. With regard to the
Prisons Service, I hope later on to present the Estimates, and I propose to defer

!
T
making a statement in regard to this
branch of my Department till then.
Turning now to the other branch of
the Ministry of Home Affairs—the Local
Government Branch--hon. Members will
appreciate that this branch is responsible
for the many and varied services which
come within the ambit of local government. There is one branch in this
division which is responsible for the administration of what is known as the Road
Services, particularly in relation to
Public Service Vehicles and for the collection of Motor Licence Duties and the distribution of the Road Fund. I think I
have already indicated that we have found
it necessary to increase the establishment
of this branch by five officials. This increase is due to the very heavy additional
and responsible work thrown on the Ministry by the Act passed last year-the
Roads Act.
Hon. Members are aware that this Act
established for the first time in Northern
Ireland, and, indeed, in any part of the
United Kingdom, outside London, a comprehensive and uniform system of control
and the licensing and inspection of public
service vehicles and their drivers. During
the months that have intervened this
particular branch has been engaged in
preparing all the necessary Regulations
which have to be issued under the Act.
I might point out that Part I of the Act,
which deals particularly with private
vehicles, is already in operation, while
Part II, which deals particularly with the
licensing of public vehicles, will come into
operation on, I hope, the 1st July.
In connection with the preparation of
the necessary Regulations, I would like to
say how deeply my Ministry appreciate
the invaluable help given to them by the
Roads Advisory Committee.
As explained before, the actual work of
inspection will be carried on locally by
members of the police appointed specially
for the purpose. I stated in this House
that it was the intention of the Government to turn inspectors into policemen,
not policemen into inspectors, and in order
that we might have the best possible type
and the most highly skilled men to carry
out this very important duty, I arranged
for a theoretical examination to be carried
out by an official from the Polytechnic
Institution, London, and subsequently a
practical examination carried out by inspectors from Scotland Yard. I desire to
emphasize again that any officers appointed
to administer this Act have been appointed solely on merit. In some cases
we had most excellent results, and several
gentlemen would have been appointed if
it had not been that, unfortunately, their
condition of health prevented the doctor
passing them. As hon. Members
appreciate, these officers, after they have
passed the probationery period, become
entitled to pension rights.
As I have said, we propose to bring the
second part of the Act and the new Regulations into operation on the 1st July,
but I might explain, so as to prevent any
misunderstanding in the future, that, as
hon. Members are aware, in future before
a vehicle can be used for public hire it
must undergo an examination at the
hands of the motor inspector, and no individual will be allowed to ply for hire
unless the vehicle he is driving is so
licensed and unless he himself has a
licence which can only be obtained as a
result of a medical and driving test.
Licenses will only be issued to those who
have attained the age of 21. Hon. Members will realize that there are, at the
present time, a large number of vehicles
on the road which have not gone through
this test. Of course the vehicles have
been tested by their owners, but that is
a different matter altogether.
Mr. BEATTIE: They have been tested
by the Corporation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: They have not
been tested by the Corporation in the way
I have in mind. I think my hon. Friend
misunderstands the position. The Corporation test is a very different thing
from the mechanical tests to which these
vehicles will be submitted. I think my
hon. Friend has mixed up two things.
think the Corporation are more concerned
with the type and size of the machine
than with the construction.
Mr. BEATTIE: And the capacity.
I
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes.
I am
perfectly well aware that a large number
of these vehicles are perfectly sound, but
hon. Members will appreciate that there
are also many vehicles on the road that
should not be there at all from the point
of view of the safety of the public.
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
We propose to allow the vehicles to
continue until, by degrees, they have all
been inspected, and as each vehicle is
inspected the owner will receive a licence,
or the machine will be ordered off the
road in the event of it not being in proper
condition. As regards the drivers, we
propose to issue driving licences of a temporary character, which to those who are
of the qualified age, will hold good
until the licence has been revoked as the
result of the necessary examination made
by our inspectors.
At the present time one hears a good
many complaints in regard to the disregard of the newly prescribed speed
limit. That applies particularly to motor
buses. Hon. Members are aware that,
following on the passing of the Motor
Act, we increased the speed limit of
Public Vehicles from 12 to 20 miles
where the wheels have pneumatic tyres.
We were assured at that time that if this
privilege was granted it would not
be abused. While there are many motor
drivers who adhere to this Regulation, a
great many drivers do not. It may be
stated here that 20 miles is not a sufficient
speed, but so long as the Regulation
exists so long must the law be enforced.
This Regulation is made, not for the
protection of one class of traffic, but for
the protection of the passengers using
these motor buses and for the public
using the streets. As the new inspectors
get to work we hope, by a system of
patrols, to try to do something more to
lessen the great danger which these passengers and the general public suffer as
a result of this excessive speeding.
With regard to the question of overcrowding, I hope that the inspection of
all the vehicles which will take place will
go a long way to remove another very
great danger from which the travelling
public are at the present time suffering. It
is one of the most serious evils with which
we will have to deal. If a machine is
insured and it is represented at the time
that the policy is taken out that it is for
the purpose of carrying, say, thirty passengers, and if at the time an accident
takes place it is carrying thirty-five
passengers, the policy is not worth the
paper it is written upon, and the passengers suffer accordingly.
I would like to say a word in regard
to the administration of the Road Fund.
I fear that the method of distribution of
the Fund is perhaps somewhat imperfectly
understood, and I hope the Committee
will bear with me while I again explain
the system.
The Road Fund, as hon. Members are
aware, is built up of motor licence duties
collected each year, as well as of the various
fines, fees and penalties. For convenience
and on the ground of economy the collection is carried out by the officials of the
County Councils, the County Councils
being reimbursed their out-of-pocket expenses in connection with the matter, and,
as a result, I think this practice has
rather created a tendency on the part of
certain individuals to allege that this is
a county rate, and that the sum so collected in each county should be spent
there instead of regarding it as a State
tax.
The motor vehicle is not confined to the
county in which it has its garage. The
owner of it uses all the roads in the Province, and I suggest that he is entitled to
have the money spent on the roads which
he uses most, and that spirit is, in a nutshell, the essence of the principle of the
Fund.
The roads in Northern Ireland are
divided into three classess. The first
class are the main trunk roads connecting
the most important cities and towns and
leading to important places of public interest. These roads are mostly used by
motorists, and to them, acordingly, we
give the greatest measure of assistance
from the Fund. Up to two or three years
ago we gave grants based on 50 per cent.
of the cost of maintenance or repair.
During the last two years we have increased that percentage to 60, even though
in England the percentage is still only
50. But over and above that we gave a
special increased percentage grant of 72
per cent. of the total cost in cases where
the Road Authorities concerned undertook
to carry out works of permanent or semipermanent reconstruction. That the
policy of the Government in its distribution of the Road Fund has been a right
one I think, is amply shown in the enormous improvement which has been
affected in some of our roads in Northern
Ireland, particularly in County Antrim,
County Down and County Armagh, consequent on the laying down of reinforced
concrete or other similar form of surfacing such as asphalt. There it has
Estimates
Ministry of Home Affairs
18 MAY 1927
been proved that it would have been impossible to have put down the ordinary
roads owing to the faulty foundations and
the heavy traffic they had to bear.
Mr. GEO. HENDERSON: Is that 72
per cent. of the total cost?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes.
Mr. GEO. HENDERSON: Total cost?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, the rest
is paid by the County Council. With regard to the second-class roads, these are
roads of secondary importance connecting up urban centres or populous rural
centres, or joining one main road with
another, while the third-class roads are
the ordinary roads of local importance.
As regards the second-class roads we give
grants of 30 per cent., and recently we
have instituted the principle of giving
grants of 15 per cent. in respect of thirdclass roads where they are used for motor
traffic.
To show the enormous extent to which
road traffic has developed in Northern
Ireland in recent years (which is largely
due to the rapid improvement in the condition of our roads), I might point out
that in 1922-23 the amount collected by
County Councils for motor licence duties
was no less a sum than £207,000. In the
following year this increased to £248,000,
while for the following years the amounts
were: 1924-1925, £287,000; 1925-1926,
£341,000; 1926-1927, £375,000. We have
not gone in for a Reserve in connection
with the Road Fund, but have utilized
these moneys solely for the purpose
indicated.
In connection with housing, I am glad
to be able to say that housing operations
in Northern Ireland, with the assistance
of the Government grants under the Acts
recently passed, are being very satisfactorily maintained.
With regard to the provision of houses
by local authorities, the total number of
houses approved
erection under
approved for
schemes promoted by the local authorities
up to 31st March, 1927, was 1,989, of
which 1,057 had actually been completed
on that date, and schemes involving the
erection of a further 190 houses are under
contemplation.
With regard to the private owners, we
find that since the passing of the first
Northern Ireland Housing Act in 1923,
no less than 5,339 houses were approved
for subsidy up to the 31st March, 1927,
and during the last financial year, 1,636
new houses were actually approved.
During the present financial year provision is being made for 1,500 new houses.
In this connection the Ministry have
had under consideration the question of
the type of house being erected by private
builders as compared with the local authorities. It has been found that while the
local authorities generally endeavour to
provide a house of the smaller type, which
could be let at a low rent, the private
builders, on the other hand, have generally confined themselves to the erection of
houses of a larger type which appear to
command a readier sale.
As the Committee is aware, the Acts
provide for a subsidy for any house of
the kitchen or parlour type between certain limits, i.e., a house with a floor space
of 550 square feet as a minimum and a
floor
space
as
of 950 square feet a
maximum.
It appears to the Ministry, apart altogether from the pressure of economic conditions, that the time will soon arrive
when there will be a sufficiency of the
larger types of subsidy houses-
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES-and that the
real need will be for houses bordering on
the lower limit prescribed by the Acts,
i.e., houses which can be let at rents more
nearly suited to the pockets of the working man.
The Ministry has already addressed
all the housing authorities in Northern
Ireland on the subject with a view to
directing their energies and the energies
of the private builders in their respective
areas in this connection, and the Government is at present considering whether it
would not be necessary to obtain Parliamentary sanction with the view to affording in the future a greater measure of
encouragement to the private builder and
the local authority who confine their
respective energies to the building of the
smaller classes of houses.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The operations of rural district councils in connection with the provision of houses for
the working classes have been fully maintained during the past year. Since the

I would now like to say a word or two
in regard to the question of poor relief.
Unfortunately, owing to economic conditions, it has been necessary to make
special provisions for dealing with outdoor
relief, particularly in Belfast and also in
one or two other centres in Northern Ireland. The Acts of Parliament, dealing
with this matter in Northern Ireland
make provision enabling the Ministry,
under exceptional circumstances of distress, to accord powers to Boards of Guardians to grant outdoor relief to ablebodied persons for certain periods. As
the Committee is aware, under normal
circumstances relief given by Boards of
Guardians is confined to relief given in
the workhouse, except in cases of illness,
infirmity, or in the case of a widow with
two children dependent upon her.
The depression in trade in Belfast made
it necessary for the Belfast Board of
Guardians and the Belfast Corporation.
to apply to the Ministry for Orders, under
Section 13 of the Local Government Act,
1898, authorizing them to grant relief
out of the workhouse to heads of families.
I would like to say that the Belfast Board
of Guardians have taken the greatest possible care and trouble in this connection,
and have endeavoured to the best of their
ability to cope with this very difficult
problem, the extent of which may be
gauged from the fact that in the first
week of April, 1926, the actual number
of people in receipt of outdoor relief in
the city of Belfast was 4,909, while in the
second week of March of this year the
number had increased to 9,818. Similar
conditions, although not to the same extent, have arisen in the course of the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I will.
regards the health services there is little
that calls for comment. Fortunately, we
have escaped the ravages of smallpox
which have been so noticeable in Great
Britain during the past few years. As the
Committee is aware, we have in Northern Ireland a system of free vaccination,
which is carried out by the local dispensary doctors with calf lymph supplied by
the Ministry, and on every outbreak in
Great Britain the Ministry have issued
warnings to the local authorities and the
local medical officers concerned, pressing
upon them the necessity of the people
complying with the laws, and I do not
think it would be unjustifiable for me to
say that the manner in which these laws
have been observed has resulted in the
present immunity which we enjoy from
this terrible scourge.
The Ministry has carefully followed the
developments on the Continent and in
Great Britain in connection with new
methods of treatment of tuberculosis, and
has kept in close touch with the Ministry
of Health in relation to the negotiations
which were carried on with Professor
Spahlinger regarding his system of treatment. It is a matter of regret that Professor Spahlinger has not, up to the present, found himself in a position to submit to expert test the principles of his
system of treatment. At the same time,
I may say that the Ministry has been
working in close touch with the Belfast
Corporation in connection with the socalled Ruppell system of treatment, which
has been recently instituted on an experimental basis by the Chief Tuberculosis
Officers of the Corporation. We are not
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
18 MAY 1927
yet in a position to indicate the relative
merits of this system of treatment.
Another branch of Local Government
administration to which I would like to
refer is the appeals in connection with
Old-Age Pensions. Under the Old-Age
Pensions Acts the Ministry has been constituted as an Appeal Tribunal in cases
where the Pensions Officer appeals against
a pension, or where the claimant has been
turned down by the Pensions Committee.
of
The Ministry decided during the past
year 3,153 appeals, an increase of 456
over the previous year's. Claims were
allowed in 1,576 cases, and 1,577 cases
were rejected. Many difficulties in dealing with these claims are experienced
chiefly due to the destruction
documents through fire in Dublin and
owing to the incomplete Church records
available. Further difficulties frequently
arise owing to the operation of the recent
Act passed in 1925, which excludes for
calculation purposes unearned income up
to £39 a year.
It has been found
that it is extremely difficult in many
cases to make a clear distinction
between earned and unearned income,
particularly in the case of agricultural
holdings, and the Ministry finds it necessary in the majority of such cases to have
personal investigations made by one of
its inspectors before deciding on the
appeals. As regards the "age" cases, the
Ministry's policy throughout has been to
try to assist all claimants who were
really entitled to the pension, if age
could be substantiated, and there again
inspectors are usually sent down and
every help is given to the claimant to
substantiate allegations as to age.

Prosecution of Omnibus Owners 1590
18 MAY 1927
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON : I
would like to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs to give this House an explanation
of the wholesale prosecution of the bus
owners of Belfast and district. I made
it my
business to-day to ask the Chairman
of the Police Committee of the Belfast
Corporation who was responsible for these
prosecutions that are taking place, and he
said that the Police Committee had no
knowledge that various bus proprietors
were being prosecuted for allowing their
buses to stand at certain places. I think
it is very unfair that these people should
be prosecuted in such a wholesale manner.
Mr. McClements, of Holywood, has
eighteen summonses in his window. He has
provided a waiting room at Oxford Street
for the convenience of the travelling
public, and his buses stop at that waiting
room for half a minute, when up
comes Sergeant Sweeney. If I were the
officer in charge I would try to find something more useful for Sergeant Sweeney
to do. If he would look after the criminals who have escaped it would pay him
better than prosecuting people who are
trying to render a service to the public.
As I
This man McClements has been summoned for keeping his buses half a minute
at his waiting room, and last night I
counted eighteen summonses displayed in
the window of that waiting room.
have said, the Chairman of the Police

says he has very little knowledge of any

convenience for the public who travel to
the outlying districts, and I do not know

the Minister of Home Affairs should put
a stop to it. It is a very serious matter
for the bus owners.concerned. They are
facilitating the public, and they have to

withdraw Sergeant Sweeney and the other
sergeant, and then get them to perform
more useful duties than they are at present discharging at the Sand
the Sand Quay,
wasting their time issuing summonses and

LAND PURCHASE CHARGES.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
will issue a detailed statement of the
Land Purchase Charges amounting to
£279,000, the amount of charges under
the Northern Ireland Land Purchase Act
(1925), and the amount standing to the
relief of the Northern Ireland taxpayers
in connection with Land Purchase, taking
into account the total receipts and the
total expenditure under the Acts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE: (Mr.
Pollock): The hon. Member will understand that in replying to this question I
must base my information in the main on
the figures given in the published Imperial
Estimates, and over which neither this
House nor my Ministry has any control.
The amount of £279,000, which is the
estimated charge against Northern Ireland revenues in respect of the Land
Purchase Commission for the year 1927-28,
is made up as follows:--

In addition, the cost of bonus arising
out of the Act of 1925 contained in the
amount of £86,000 given above is probably in the region of £4,000. The total
of these three items is, therefore, somewhat in excess of £60,000.
I do not understand the purport of
the last portion of the hon. Member's question, but if he refers
to the fact that the Land Purchase
Annuities in respect of agreements
entered into prior to the passing of the
Government of Ireland Act, are retained
in the Exchequer of Northern Ireland,
I may say that this arrangement, which
was made under the Government of Ireland Act and not under the Land Purchase Acts, as suggested by the question,
has nothing whatever to do with Land
Purchase as such.
The exact purpose served by the payment of the Land Purchase Annuities
into our Exchequer is set out in one of the
White Papers issued in 1920, in explanation of the provision of the Government
of Ireland Bill, which was then under
consideration. This is as follows:-
"The money derived from these
annuities will meet the additional expense incidental to the severance of the
two Irish Governments from Great
Britain and from one another."
There is certainly no receipt of any
money by the Government of Northern
Ireland applicable as a relief from the
burden of the cost of Land Purchase.
£279,000
I have no information as to what charge
has already accrued under the Northern
Ireland Land Purchase Act, 1925, but I
should surmise that the greater proportion
of the administrative charges amounting
to £51,000 is now incurred in the operation of this Act, whilst the cost of the
remission of one-quarter year's rent

BELFAST
CORPORATION.-PAY-
MENT FOR EXTRA POLICE.
6. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has had a conference with representatives of the Belfast
Corporation on the question of the payment by the Corporation of a portion of
the extra police brought into the city,
and if so, what arrangement has been
arrived at.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In accordance with
the suggestion made by the Prime
Minister in this House on the 26th ultimo
(Hansard, Vol. 8, No. 14, 876) when the
question of the payment by the Belfast
Corporation for extra force of police was
raised in connection with the Estimates
for R.U.C., representatives of the Corporation were invited to confer with the
Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance
and myself on the 13th instant on the
point at issue. This conference was held
on the date indicated and the question
was discussed at length. It was not
possible to arrive at a conclusion at the
meeting, and it has been arranged to hold
a further conference at a later date.
"B" SPECIAL CONSTABULARY,
FERMANAGH.
7. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether a large number of
the members of "B" Section of the Special
Constabulary in Fermanagh were called
upon last December to resign owing to their
failure to attend the stipulated number
of drills; whether they refused to resign
or to hand over their arms and equipment; whether the Minister has now
sanctioned the formation of a new
Reserve Section of the "B" men and
invited all the men who refused to resign to become members of the Section,
and retain their arms and equipment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact
that 103 members of Class "B" Special
Constabulary, County Fermanagh, were
unable to attend the prescribed drills,
and, accordingly, their services
technically terminated as from the 31st
December last
were
At that time no facilities were available
for the retention of suitable members of
the Force who were unable to attend
drills, but, as the hon. Member is aware,
a new scheme is now in operation under
which members of the "B" Class-Special
Constabulary-are allowed to transfer
into a Reserve category without any obligation to attend drills.
The men referred to were highly reported upon by the County Commandant
who strongly urged that their services
should be retained in the Reserve Section.
In all the circumstances this principle
was agreed to.
It is not a fact that the men refused to
resign or give up their arms and equipment as suggested.
There is no intention of permiting men
who refuse to resign or otherwise behave
insubordinately, to remain members of
the "B" Force in any capacity.
Mr. KYLE: Is it the intention of the
Government to form a Reserve Section of
the Special Police, the "B" Specials?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is this Reserve Section
created for the purpose of accommodating
those who were in revolt? Is that the
purpose for which they are created?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot
imagine the "B" Special Constabulary
going into revolt.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did these gentlemen
not refuse to resign and refuse to drill?
What exactly are they there for? Why
is there a special section created? Is this
a dumping-house for soldiers who will
not fight?
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will talk about this
on the Home Office Vote.

Mr. POLLOCK: The purpose of this
short Measure, which it is my duty to
submit for Second Reading to the House.
is to give effect to the alterations which I
dealt with in my Budget statement in regard to taxation. Clauses 1 and 2 give
effect to the concessions as regards Entertainments Duty. If I may recapitulate
these they are in effect: The remission of
Entertainments Duty on all payments for
admission to any entertainment up to and
including the sum of sixpence. Clause 1
of the Bill is designed to give effect to this
relief as from the 1st June next.
Clause 2 is designed to give effect to exemption from Entertainments Duty with
effect from the 1st June next of payments
for admission: First, to certain indoor
games or sports in connection with which.
Mulholland, Captain The Hon. Henry
George Hill
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham
TELLER FOR THE AYES-
Captain Dixon.
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattie.
no money is awarded or paid to any of the
contestants; and, secondly, to all outdoor
games or sports other than those involving
the use or participation of horses, dogs or
other animals, or the use of mechanicallypropelled vehicles.
It is necessary, I think, that I should
give some clearer explanation, or some
explanation at any rate, of Sub-section 2
of Clause 2 of the Measure. This Subsection is designed to ensure exemption
in those cases where a combination of
entertainments takes place. The previous
Acts are so drafted that exemption is
only given if, for example, the exhibition
is solely an agricultural one. The addition of anything else would make
the entertainment taxable. Clearly, it
would be wrong that the addition of an
outdoor game, which is itself exempt from
tax, should make the main entertainment,
viz., the Agricultural Show itself taxable.
I should, perhaps, here add that on the
Committee Stage I propose to move an
Amendment in order to provide that all
agricultural shows to which grants are
made by County Committees of
Agriculture with the approval of
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
19 MAY 1927
shall
the Ministry of
of Agriculture,
be exempt from tax provided that
the Ministry of Finance is satisfied that
the main purpose of the show is agricultural. The effect of the Amendment
will enable the promoters in such shows
to include such occasional items as pony
gymkhanas in order to attract a larger
attendance at these agricultural shows.
I come now to the question of Death
Duties. In the first place I will deal with
Clause 3, that is for repayment in case of
any alteration in duty. Clause 3 gives
effect to a small change in the incidence
of Death Duties on settled property in a
restricted class of cases. The House may
perhaps remember that in my Budget
statement I read the document in which
this was dealt with. I do not suppose I
can make the effect of this any clearer
than I did on that cccasion, but perhaps
it would be as well in connection with
this Clause that I should in
a few
sentences explain anew the exact financial
effect of Clause 3 of this Measure. It is
intended to remove an anomalous distinction between the assessment of free
and settled property to duty which has
existed since 1914 as the result of an oversight. At present property settled before
1894 is not aggregated (for purposes of
Estate Duty) when passing on the death
of the life tenant with free property also
passing on that death. There is now no
reason for this distinction, and as opportunity has been taken to remove it in
Great Britain the time is opportune for
a similar change in Northern Ireland.
Clause 4 deals with Death Duties and it
is intended to provide relief from a form
of double taxation. We have read from
time to time discussions in the papers in
regard to the hardships consequent on
3 double taxation in Southern Ireland,
Great Britain and ourselves, and as this
is a comparatively small matter it is
thought desirable that the present opportunity should be taken to remove this
disability. As I say, it is intended to
provide relief from a form of double taxation by which claims to legacy duty and
succession duty in two countries, that is,
either in Great Britain and in Northern
Ireland, or in Northern Ireland and in
the Irish Free State, may arise simultaneously in respect of settled property
passing on death. The Government of
Ireland Act, 1920, contains a provision
(Sec. 28) which prevents double taxation
in respect of estate duty, but this provision is not sufficiently wide to cover this
particular type of case. A reciprocal
arrangement to avoid double taxation in
this respect has been entered into with
the Governments of Great Britain and of
the Irish Free State. This Clause is intended to give legislative sanction to this
arrangement.
All that I have to say further in this
matter is that the rates of Entertainments
Duty are contained in the Schedule which
will be found on the last page of the Bill
and which will give hon. Members full
information as to the exact position which
this Measure takes. I beg to move.
Mr. GYLE: As one who accompanied
what, I think, was called a battalion
of cinema proprietors and amusement
caterers in the city of Belfast as a deputation, I wish once more to ask the
Minister of Finance if it would not be
possible for him to reconsider this matter regarding the Amusement Tax in the Six
Counties. It would not cost us very much
more to put us in Northern Ireland on
a par with Great Britain. I may point
out that when that deputation went to the
Minister of Finance facts and figures were
placed before him which showed that the
amusement caterers here were not in the
same favourable position as their brethren
in England. It was suggested that
there was rather an internecine war going
on between the cinema proprietors in
Belfast, and if that were removed their
business would be put on a purely business
foundation. It was also suggested at that
conference that there were far too many
cinemas, and that towns in England
similar to the city of Belfast should be
taken into consideration.
I have made inquiries which show that
we have not too many cinemas here as
compared with similar towns in Great
Britain. I will give you facts as regards
Sheffield, which has practically the same
population as the city of Belfast. In
that connection a suggestion was made
that Belfast was over-catered for in the
matter of entertainment houses. I will
make a comparison with Sheffield, and the
reason that town is selected is that I
understand the Chancellor caused a comparison to be made with that place when
considering the question of this tax.
Sheffield, including the township of
Ecclesall, has a population of 482,798.
Belfast, according to the return for 1926,
3E
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Gyle]
has a population of 415,007. Sheffield
has 66 cinematograph theatres and nine
legitimate and variety theatres. Belfast
has only 28 cinematograph theatres, one
legitimate theatre, and two variety
theatres. The seating accommodation in
the Sheffield theatres is more than threeand-a-half times that of Belfast. This
fact, taken in conjunction with the small
difference in the population, shows that
Belfast is not over-catered for.
I have here returns taken from the
books of a Belfast cinema for one week for
comparison with the rate of tax imposed
in other parts of the United Kingdom.
At this theatre in Belfast there were for
one week 3,510 admissions at 41d, which
works out at £65 16s 3d, and the tax at 11d
amounted to £21 18s 9d; 5,630 admissions
at 9d, which makes £211 2s 6d, and the
tax at 3d amounted to £70 7s 6d; 924
admissions at 1s 2d, which makes
£54 9s 8d, and the tax at 4d amounted
to £13 11s 4d. The total takings were
£331 8s 5d, and on that there was a tax
of £107 17s 7d.
The figures for the same theatre
if it were in England would
be: 3,510 admissions at 6d, making
£87 15s, and the tax would be
nil; 5,630 admissions at 10d, making
£234 11s 8d, with a tax of 2d amounting
to £46 18s 4d; and 934 admissions at
1s 3d, making £58 7s 6d, with a tax of
3d amounting to £11 13s 6d. The total
takings would be £380 14s 2d with a tax
of only £58 11s.
It will be observed when comparing
these figures that the entertainment
caterer in Northern Ireland is on the week
£49 58 9d worse off than his brother in
England on the same number of admissions
and at prices that are the same when the
price and tax are taken together, the
prices being 6d, 1s and 1s 6d. When the
tax free seat at 6d comes into force, as
I understand it will on 1st June, the
figure of £49 5s 9d will be improved by
£21 18s 9d. This will, however, still leave
the man in Northern Ireland £27 7s per
week, or £1,422 4s per annum, worse off
than his neighbour in England, Scotland
or Wales.
Those are the actual figures taken in
comparison with a town of similar size
in England, and we cannot see why the
Chancellor should penalise the industry
in Northern Ireland to the tune of almost
£1,500 a year, an industry that is worth
so many thousands of pounds in capital
value and in which so many people are
employed. We cannot understand the
reason the Chancellor cannot put us in
exactly the same position as we would be
if these theatres were in any other part of
the United Kingdom. I appeal to the
Chancellor of the Exchequer, and I ask
him will he reconsider this matter this
year. It is quite evident when he does
not answer me that he has no intention
of doing so.

2, paragraph 2, in connection with outdoor sports. He stated that all outdoor

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I want
to deal very briefly with the point raised
by the hon. Member who last spoke. I
believe it to be absolutely unfair on the

what he is pleased to call mechanicallypropelled vehicles. I presume that relates in the main to the mechanical hare.

sport up to the moment. The right hon.
Gentleman will probably appreciate the

I can quite understand that the

There is a further aspect of the matter
I want to comment upon. I have not
had an opportunity of seeing a display of
the mechanical hare. I would have gone
on one occasion but for the fact that the
prices were prohibitive. I would like to
see this sport democratized, and there
does not appear to me to be any great
chance of that being done if the Entertainment Tax is going to remain. The
Chancellor has spoken about giving
facilities to agricultural shows. If
facilities are to be given to agricultural
shows I do not see why similar facilities
should not be given to a sport in its experimental stage, as the finances of the
Northern Government will, perhaps, not
benefit to a very large extent by the imposition of this tax.
I think from my own observation that
this is a sport that can only be introduced
at very great cost, and if the Chancellor
is going to put a tax on that form of
sport the probability is that it will not
be patronized, with the result that it may
die in its birth throes. That, to me,
would be an unsatisfactory state of affairs,
because I want to see this form of sport
becoming substituted for the cruel and
inhuman sport practiced and engaged in
at the present time of chasing a live hare.
In the interests of humanitarianism it
Finance Bill-

would be as well, having regard to the

In regard to the Schedule of this Bill,
it appears to me to be unfair. Hon.
Members will observe that for a charge
of 7d it is proposed the rate of duty should
be 2d. The rate of duty will be
approximately one-third the charge for
admission. If one takes the trouble to

might be the point in it that a larger
number of people buy the more cheaply
