more highly priced. The Chancellor
might argue that it is in order to get the
maximum amount of revenue from the
cinemas and music-halls that this duty has
been divided in that way, but I hold that
it is absolutely unfair that the people who
can very poorly afford to go to a cinema
or a music-hall at the present time should
be charged approximately one-third,
while the people who pay, and are able
to pay, 15s, perhaps, for a seat in a
cinema or music-hall should be only
charged 2s, which is about one-seventh.
There should be some revision from that
point of view.
Owing to the unprecedented unemployment that exists at the present time it is
extremely difficult for any father or any
son who is existing on unemployment
benefit to have an opportunity of visiting
a music hall or a picture house. The
Biblical dictum is that man shall not
live by bread alone. These poor unfortunate people should have some opportunity of being able to patronize a cinema
or a music hall, but if the rate of duty is
going to be that which is suggested by the
Chancellor the possibilities of this are
extremely remote. Owing to the excessively democratic sentiments that have
been expressed from time to time by
Gentlemen on the Front Government
Bench I think one of the most fitting
gestures for the purpose of showing that
you really believe in democracy, and are
interested in the welfare of the people,
would be to cheapen their forms of entertainment, and to allow those people to go
to these cinemas and music halls at a
much cheaper rate than they will be able
to if you persist in the rate of duty proposed at the present time.

Mr. ANDREWS: The law as regards
workmen's compensation in Northern
Ireland is contained in five Acts of Parliament. It is obviously inconvenient and
at times embarrassing. The British
Government in 1925 consolidated these
Acts, and we propose in this Session of
Parliament to do the same thing. Hon.
Members will recollect that in 1923 we
passed the Workmen's Compensation Act
in this Parliament, and since then several
alterations have been made in the law in
Great Britain. This Measure which I
have the honour to bring before the House
to-day is to put us in step with Great
Britain in this matter.

I think it is desirable that I should
simply and as briefly as possible explain
to the House some of its main provisions.
Up to the present the court fees have been
paid by the general taxpayer, but the
Imperial Commission on National Expenditure came to the conclusion that as
employers were liable to pay compensation
so the employers might be expected to pay
the court fees. Clause 1 of this Measure
provides for that in future. Sub-section I
of Clause 2 is intended to amend two provisions contained in the 1906 and 1923
Acts. As the law stands a workman who
meets with an accident while under the
age of 21 years may apply for an increase
in the amount of his compensation on the
basis of what he would have been earning
on the date of the review if he had remained uninjured. The review cannot
take place until six months after the
accident, and it must take place before
the man is 21 years old. Hence a man
of the age of 20 years and 7 months is
unable to take advantage of the law, and
this Sub-section is to relieve that hardship.
Sub-section 2 of the same Clause has
been inserted at the request of his Honour
the Recorder of Belfast in order to render
the procedure under Section 14 of the
1923 Act more effective. The Sub-section
enables the Clerk of the Crown and Peace,
or on an appeal the judge, to fix in terms
of money what are to be the future weekly
payments to a workman whose case has
been referred to the medical referee for
Clause 5 gives priority payment to a
worker in case of the winding up of a
company; in other words a payment
nuder the Workmen's Compensation Act
is really looked upon as wages in this connection. Clause 6 deals with a disease
which is called silicosis and which is not
known here. It is produced by what is
called ganister mining or in the making of
silica bricks, and as we have neither of
these industries we have not heard of the
disease. It is simply inserted in case
these industries should start here so that
compensation will be payable in the same
way as it would be paid if the work was
done in Great Britain. Clause 7 extends
the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation Acts to the crew of any aircraft, the owner of which resides or has
his place of business in Northern Ireland.
Clause 8 is to give effect to the resolutions passed by the Imperial Conference to which I have already referred,
and which were to the effect that matters
of this kind should be dealt with all over
the Empire on the same basis; in other
words, if a man or woman were injured
here and then removed to one of the
Dominions the competent authority in
that other part of the Empire would in
such an event deal with the matter in the
same way as if he or she had remained at
home. The only other Clause to which
I need refer is Clause 9, and it confers
upon masters, seamen, apprentices to the
sea service and apprentices in the seafishing service or pilot the right of taking
proceedings for the recovery of Workmen's compensation in our Northern Ireland Courts.

Mr. KYLE: When I got this Bill
yesterday and read it I must confess that
I never read a more complicated Measure.
If it had not been for the somewhat lucid
exposition given by the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) I would have had
great difficulty in attempting to appreciate the Clauses of the Bill. We have
often referred in this House to legislation by reference, but I think I have
never seen in any Bill before the House
more references made to legislation than
are contained in this particular Measure.
I would have very much preferred to have
heard the right hon. and learned
Attorney-General introducing this Bill
and explaining the extremely complicated Clauses that are in the Measure. I
would esteem it a favour if the legal
Gentlemen who are in this House would
get up in their places and endeavour to
explain or make more clear the opinions
that the lawyers will have in the courts
in regard to this Bill-more clear than
the Minister of Labour has done in his
entirely admirable speech. Take Clause
3 which states:-
In the event of the death of any
person entitled as a dependant to money
paid into a county court under the
principal Act, then, if no direction has
been given as to the disposition thereof
for the benefit of other dependants in

entitled thereto, the court may, without probate or letters of administration,
distribute the sum amongst such persons as appear to the court, upon such
evidence as the court may deem satisfactory, to be entitled by law to receive
the same.

easy to understand. I would appreciate,
as I said before, if our legal friends who,
unfortunately represent the party opposite, and of whom we have none-

I would like to refer to Clause 7, which
raises what seems to me to be a totally
3F
1635 Workmen's Compensation Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Black]
different point, but to my mind a very
important point, indeed. The meaning
obviously of Clause 7 is that if a man
engaged in any flying work in connection
with aircraft and the aircraft were registered in the United Kingdom but the
owner has his place of business in Northern Ireland, any man injured in connection with that aircraft, whether it be in
Northern Ireland or not, should be entitled to get compensation as against his
employer.
I think the principle is quite right that
if an employer is resident in Northern
Ireland the man whom he employs should
be entitled to get compensation under our
compensation code, even if the accident.
happened in England, or Scotland, or
China, or Peru. That is what the Clause
seeks to carry out. It provides :
The Ministry of Labour may by order
extend the provisions of the Workmen's
Compensation Acts (Northern Ireland),
1906 to 1923, subject to such modifications and exceptions as may be specified
in the order, to such persons, being
workmen within the meaning of the
said Acts, employed as pilot, commander, navigator, or member of the
crew of any aircraft to which this section applies when outside Northern
Ireland, in such circumstances as may
be specified in the order.
What is provided for is compensation
for an accident happening outside Northern Ireland. It is a desirable thing
to provide, but I am afraid this Parliament has no power to provide for
that, that it is outside the powers of this
Parliament to legislate in regard to compensation for an accident happening outside Northern Ireland. The Section of
the Act that confers upon this Parliament powers to legislate is Section 4 of
the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
and it provides in regard to both the
Parliaments of Southern Ireland and
Northern Ireland that
they shall not have power to make
laws except in respect of matters exclusively relating to the portion of
Ireland within their jurisdiction.
Therefore, our only power to make laws
is in regard to matters exclusively relating
to the portion of Ireland within our
jurisdiction. I am afraid this Parliament has no power to make laws in regard
to compensation for accidents arising
outside Northern Ireland.
Exactly the same criticism applies to
Clause 9. What is designed by Clause 9
is this: If an accident happens at sea,
whether it be on the seas of England,
or Scotland, or on the high seas,
or in some foreign port, proceedings for
the recovery of compensation might be
taken in this country just as they might
have been taken before the Act of 1920
was passed and before we had a separate
legislature here. I think it is a right
and proper thing and a desirable thing,
but that also is a thing that I fear our
Parliament has no power to provide for.
The legislation to provide for these
matters must be legislation of the Imperial Parliament and not legislation of
our Parliament.
Take, for instance, an accident happening at Port Said, or Vancouver, or any
foreign port. That is not a matter exclusively relating to the portion of Ireland within our jurisdiction. This is
providing compensation for something
that happens abroad and it is clear to my
mind that the powers of our Parliament
are fettered by Section 4 of the Act of
1920, and that we have no power here to
legislate as in Clauses 7 and 9 of this Bill.
These are not academic points, because
I am aware of my own knowledge that
the matters have been raised in legal
circles. Persons who are concerned and
who may have to pay compensation in
regard to accidents happening in foreign
ports have considered these matters and
have taken advice on them. I would
suggest to the Ministry of Labour that
they should at once get into touch with
the Imperial authorities and seek to have
an Act passed in the Imperial Parliament. It is clearly within the Imperial
Parliament's power to deal with this
matter and we should not attempt to
deal with it when there is at least a doubt
-to my mind a certainty-that we have
no power to deal with these things.

Mr. BARBOUR: In asking the House
to give a Second Reading to this Bill, I
feel sure hon. Members will appreciate
that we seek to do little more than remove
an anomaly which has grown out of the
revolution in transport methods and
facilities that has been the feature of the
last twenty years. The railway companies had their origin at a time when
the element of speed was an almost negligible factor in road transport, due
partly to the type of road transport then
in use and partly to the condition of the
roads themselves. The railways, even in
the earliest stages of their development,
represented a new departure in the matter
of speed, and when most of the Acts
governing our railways were framed, our
legislators did not contemplate the extent to which the roads would become
highways of fast traffic, nor the advent
on the roads of a form of locomotion which
would throw out a challenge to the railways in those factors of speed, comfort
and convenience, to provide which the
latter were being constructed.
Thus it comes about that only in few
cases and to a very limited extent have
railway companies power in their governing Acts to use the roads for motor traffic
as an auxiliary to their rail systems.
Indeed a position of affairs has now been
created wherein the railway companies
are forced to stand by and contemplate
the diversion of a considerable share of
their traffic to their rivals on the roads.
In addition to that our system of rating
actually compels them to make a substantial contribution to the upkeep of
these very roads which they are precluded
from using to anything like the extent
enjoyed by ordinary citizens.
Although the development of road
transport in Northern Ireland has been
most marked in the last few years there
is no doubt that there are still many
districts which could be usefully opened
up by a well-organized combination of
road and rail services. I am sure hon.
Members will agree that it would be the
barest justice to free the railway companies from the restrictions which preclude
them at the moment from playing their
part in the further development of road
transport which will inevitably take place
during the years to come.
By this Bill it is proposed to confer upon
railway companies operating in Northern
Ireland the power to provide, own and
maintain omnibuses and road vehicles
generally for the conveyance of passengers
and merchandise, and it is intended to
secure for them these facilities in the
same broad and ample manner as they
are at present enjoyed by the ordinary
citizen. The Bill also makes the necessary
provision for ancillary powers in regard
to fares, the provision and equipment of
garages and workshops, and the borrowing powers necessary for the attainment
of these objects.
common
I need hardly assure hon. Members that
the railway companies will, in
with the owners of all other motor
vehicles, be subject to all those measures
of control provided for in the Motor
Vehicles (Traffic and Regulation) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1926, which will become effective in the near future. It is
simply an enabling Bill to put the railway companies, so far as the right to use
motor vehicles is concerned, in the same
position as any other trading community
or any citizen is in our area. I beg to
move.

have been struck, and every Member who

General himself should be answerable for

It is quite impossible that the Permanent Secretary should be able to control that force. No Civil Servant, the
head of a Department like the Ministry
of Home Affairs, can possibly be in a
position properly to answer for or control
the expenditure of the police force, and
I think an immediate saving would be
made if the Department of Police Administration and Police Maintenance
were wiped out, and the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, under the control of the
Inspector-General, made a separate Department in the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Under the present system if a question
arises in a police barrack in the country,
first the sergeant writes it out, it goes then
to the District Inspector, then to the
County Inspector, then to headquarters
and is dealt with by several officials at the
headquarters of the police. Then it goes
over to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
It is dealt with there by one of the clerks
in that Department, and it goes up
through the secretaries to the Minister.
Then possibly it has to start again through
the Ministry of Finance. Sir Russell
Scott in his Report suggested that
generally the responsibility on our
Departments was needlessly extended.
If that is true of the ordinary Departments how much more true is it of the
present system where we have this dual
system of control?
I believe we could effect an immediate
saving by adopting this suggestion. At
any rate it is worthy of consideration.
That saving will go on year by year and
you will have an immediate improvement

am absolutely convinced that the trouble

Mr. POLLOCK: This Bill is submitted
in order to give statutory effect to certain
proposals which were made in my Budget
statement, and which, owing to their
nature, are not of the character usually
embodied in Finance Bills.
I will go
through the Bill clause by clause.
In connection with Clause 1 hon.
Members may remember that the
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act
of 1923 provided for the application of
any surplus arising on the accounts in any
financial year. The surplus was to be
applied in the first instance towards the
reduction of any capital liabilities in connection with the public debt of Northern
Ireland, and for this purpose a Reserve
Fund was established. Each year so far
the Government has been in the fortunate
position of being able to show what I will
term a cash surplus, and consequently
there is a considerable balance in this
Fund at the present time,
I
1729 Financial Provisions Bill-

20 MAY 1927
Second Reading

In
uent
The necessity for the further legislation on the subject of the Reserve Fund
arises from the somewhat complicated
financial relations with the Imperial
Authorities under which it is not possible
in any year to fix what I will call the
actual surplus or deficit, as the case may
be, until matters of detail have been
settled by the Joint Exchequer Board and
the Imperial contribution finally fixed.
It is therefore proposed that these belated adjustments, whether in favour of
Northern Ireland or otherwise, shall be
adjusted, not in the cash accounts of
following years, but within the Reserve
Fund, and I am sure hon. Members
will agree that this is an eminently
sensible arrangement.
Coming now to Clause 2 it is unnecessary for me, I think, to deal with this
matter at any great length as hon. Members will recollect that, when making my
Budget statement, I dealt in some detail
with the important part played by Sinking Funds in National Finance, and
showed that it is a cardinal point in the
Financial Policy of the Government to
insist upon adequate provision being made
at all times for Reserve Funds and for
Sinking Funds in respect of various capital
liabilities which have been incurred.
Previous legislation has authorized me to
establish a Sinking Fund for the payment
of interest on Ulster Saving Certificates,
but so far the statutes have not enabled
me to make definite provision against the
ultimate repayment of the capital of
these Certificates, and this omission is
now rectified by this Clause in the Bill.
I do not propose to deal exhaustively
with Clause 3 which, as hon. Members
will see from the Bill, is concerned with
the special allocation of £40,000 from
this year's revenue, for the purpose of
providing assistance for the development
of the agricultural industry. I have
already stated that this money will be
applied principally towards schemes connected with the improvement of live
stock, and the actual details of these
schemes are at the present moment the
subject of consideration between my
Ministry and the Ministry of Agriculture.
I
the
may repeat, however, that
machinery provided by the County Committee of Agriculture will be utilized for
these schemes.
The last proposal contained in the Bill
is contained in Clause 4, and in this case
also has been fully dealt with on the
occasion of the Budget. As will be seen
from the Clause it embodies the proposal
that the ordinary housing subsidy of £80
per house shall be payable in respect of
houses erected for ex-Servicemen by the
Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust.
As a result of this concession the Government expect that the Trustees will be
able to erect at least 50 additional houses.
The total cost of this to the Government
is expected to be approximately £28,000
to £30,000 and will be paid direct from
the Consolidated Fund over a period of
three years.
That, I think, covers the whole range
of this small Bill, and I do not think I
have omitted anything that it is necessary for hon. Members to understand in
connection with it. Therefore, I beg to
move.

CLAUSE 2 (Exemption of certain
games, etc., from entertainments duty)—
(1) As from the first day of June, nineteen hundred and twenty-seven, entertainments duty shall not be charged
or levied on payments for admission to
any entertainment as respects which it
is proved to the satisfaction of the
Ministry of Finance that the entertainment consists solely of an exhibition
of all or any of the following games or
sports, that is to say:-
(i) Any games or sports which are
ordinarily played or contested indoors by two or more persons or two
or more groups of persons, and at or
in connection with which no money
is awarded or paid to any of the
contestants whether as prizes, remuneration or otherwise;
(ii) Any games or sports which are
ordinarily played or contested outof-doors by two or more persons or
by two or more groups of persons,
and do not involve the use or participation of horses, dogs, or other
animals, or the use of mechanicallypropelled vehicles.
(2) Paragraph (b) of Sub-section
(1) of Section One of the Finance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923, as amended
by Section Two of the Finance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1924 (which gives
relief from entertainments duty in the
case of certain entertainments) shall be
amended by the addition at the end
of that paragraph of the words
consists solely of such exhibitions or
displays of skill, together with an exhibition of any of the games or sports
which are exempt from entertainments
duty by virtue of Section Two of the
Finance Act Northern Ireland), 1927."

possibility for football clubs in Belfast
and throughout the North of Ireland endeavouring to install a similar equipment.

This is a thing that should be encouraged.
To express the personal point of view,
think it would be much better if the
Government would agree not to levy any
entertainment tax on this form of sport
at the present time. Probably at a later
stage, when the sport is properly on its
feet, we might agree to the Chancellor
levying the tax on this form of sport.
Possibly the Chancellor would agree to
that? I do not desire to detain the Committee, but I think I have made my point
clear, and with that I am satisfied.

Inland Revenue or from the Commissioners of Customs and Excise (as the

any such powers on behalf of that
Ministry by virtue of an arrangement
under section sixty-three of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920.

Finance Act (Northern Ireland), 1927.

Yesterday the Chancellor of the Exchequer told me that I take a considerable
amount of interest in the cinema proprietors. I am very pleased to tell him
I also take a considerable amount of interest in everything
that concerns my constituency and the Six
Counties. I think this matter of the
Entertainment Tax is one that must be
more carefully looked into. We have
something like £400,000 or £500,000 invested in this industry, and there are
something like 350 people employed. The
Minister told us yesterday that some of
the houses in the centre of the city have
been making money. From inquiries I
made to-day I find that with the exception of the published balance sheet of
Wardens, Ltd., practically no
house in
the cinema business is making money, but
that many are losing money.
There has been a large cinema erected
at a cost of £150,000, and the Minister
knows that when the deputation went to
him two or three of the directors who
erected that building informed him that
they were very glad to sell it to an
English syndicate and get rid of their
liability, and they ascribed the whole of
that to the incidence of this tax. Why
this particular industry should be singled
out and made to pay much more than
the people who have a similar industry
in England passes my comprehension.
It is all very well for the Chancellor
to tell us that he requires the money,
but he should not single out one particular
industry when that industry is practically
going to be killed. Take a place such as
the Hippodrome. The Hippodrome, I
understand, is a paying concern.
Hippodrome passes on to its patrons this
tax. I heard the manager of the Hippo-
The
Finance, Bill-

drome say the very moment this tax was

The cinema proprietors paid that tax

Mr. BLACK: I wonder have the
Government fully considered the effect of
Clause 9. The provisions in this Clause
are to the effect that when any seaman
receives an injury he is entitled to bring
proceedings in our court to get the compensation which he would be entitled to
recover in an English Court under the
1925 Act. I think that is very proper
and that should be the law, but my question is whether we have the power to
enact that by law at all, or whether we
do not require an Act of the Imperial
Parliament. Take a concrete case under
the existing Rules in Northern Ireland.
Suppose a man had signed on any ship in
Glasgow. The ship is registered in the
port of Glasgow. He sailed from Glasgow and got to Yokohama and was
drowned there under circumstances which
would give his dependants a claim under
the 1906 Act. According to our Rules,
if these dependants chanced to live in
Belfast they brought proceedings in the
Recorder's Court in Belfast against the
owners of the ship, whose place of business is in Glasgow and the ship registered
in Glasgow, to recover compensation in
respect of the accident which occurred at
Yokohama.
What this Clause intends to do is to
give, in the same circumstances and to
the same people, in our County Court
the same right of recovery. In that case
I have put before the Committee the
case of a ship registered in the port of
Glasgow, with owners resident in Glasgow,
and a seaman signing on in Glasgow, and
an accident happening at Yokohama,
that accident had nothing to do with
Northern Ireland. The contract which
the man entered into had nothing to do
with Northern Ireland. The case had
nothing whatever to do with Northern
Ireland except that the man's dependants, being resident in Northern Ireland,
were entitled to bring proceedings in a
Northern Ireland Court.
Under Section 4 of the Government of
Ireland Act it is provided that we shall
not have power to make any laws except
in respect of matters exclusively relating
to the portion of Ireland within our jurisdiction. How can the compensation payable in respect of the death of a seaman
who was drowned in the harbour at Yokohama, whose contract for employment was
made with employers in Glasgow, who served
on a ship registered at Glasgow, and
whose employers lived and had their place
of business in Glasgow-how can that be
said to be a matter exclusively relating to
the portion of Ireland within our jurisdiction? When one examines it in the
light of a concrete case such as this it
seems to me that there are circumstances
such as I have given which are outside
the competence of this Legislature to deal
with.
I would again impress upon the
Minister of Labour that we cannot adequately deal with the matter by a Section
in our Act, and that he will have to press
upon the Imperial Government to bring
in a corresponding Act providing for this
payment of compensation so that people
in our courts can recover compensation
under such circumstances, a provision
which I think a very proper one, but
which I fear we have not power to
make here. This is not entirely an academic matter, because it oftens turns up.
In the past we have had many cases here
where a man serving in a ship registered
elsewhere than in Ireland was drowned
upon the high seas or in some foreign
port and proceedings were brought here,
and I am aware of my own knowledge that
at the present time there are one or two
cases pending in the Courts of Northern
Ireland in which the very difficulty has
arisen.

The CHAIRMAN: Having given

Railways Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Chairman]
and not to a particular undertaking. On

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1,
page 2, line 32, at end ("or any such
railway company ") to add:
(4) Any railway company working a
service under this Act shall maintain a
regular system of omnibuses, coaches, or
other vehicles during the winter and
summer running to scheduled times and
places.
I am sorry I could not move the other
Amendment, but I cannot do other than
accept the ruling of the Chair. In regard
to this particular Amendment, I want the
Committee to visualize what might take
place in certain circumstances. A railway company, for instance, might get a
fleet of buses and put them on to, let us
say, Bangor, and after a few months they
night put those people who control the
Bangor buses off the road. Then at the
end of six months they themselves could
take their buses off and revert to the
railway, which is their own particular line
of business. It is to avoid such a set of
circumstances that I think the Committee
should pass this Amendment. It will
ensure that the railway company can get
power to own a number of buses and not
only run according to Schedule but maintain the service in the winter as well as
in the summer.
a
They may do what many bus owners
do at the present time, namely, run
very limited service at a given period in
the year; but we ought at least to have
it made clear that a railway company will
not do as I have suggested-start a fleet
of buses, and when they drive the small
bus owner off the road take away their
service and compel us to pay high fares
on the railway. It is from that point of
view I desire to put this Amendment
before the Committee.
Mr. BARBOUR: I am rather in a
difficulty to understand this Amendment.
As far as I can see, the hon. Member
contemplates a condition where a railway
company and an omnibus company are
competing one against the other on
certain route. The effect of that competition is that it is a non-paying proposition. Apparently the hon. Member
for North Belfast thinks it is a perfectly
legitimate thing for the bus owner to
discontinue, but he is not going to allow
the railway company to discontinue. Why
should an obligation be put on one that
is not going to be put on another? Or
if a service is going to be continued how
is one to select who is going to continue
the service?
This would not be in the spirit of the
Bill, because the spirit of the Bill is
merely to put a railway company in the
same position as any other user of motor
traction. As I have said before, I think
the question of omnibus traffic and motor
vehicular traffic is still more or less in its
infancy, and I cannot help thinking that
a time will come when far more regulation
of motor traffic will be necessary, not only
in our cities but also on our country routes
throughout the Six Counties. At that
time those regulations should be such
that they will affect buses run by the railway companies equally with buses run
by private individuals, but that, I think,
is a matter of general application to motor
vehicular traffic. It does not seem to me
that it should be made in a particular instance which applies to one class of owner,
as this Bill does. Therefore we cannot
accept this Amendment.
Question put: "That the words proposed be there added."

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I feel that it is
due to the House and especially to those
in Opposition that I should make a short
statement in explanation of the Vote
under discussion. An agreement was
arrived at on Friday that the Vote should
be taken and the debate resumed to-day;
that agreement was honourably kept by
those opposite in allowing the Vote to
pass so that what I left unsaid on Friday
I feel, in justice to those who will take
part in the discussion, I should now state
in opening the debate to-day The whole.
field of the Ministry of Labour has been so
widely covered in discussing the Estimates
passed recently that I feel it is un-

necessary for me to do more than make

brief, will, I hope, be so informative that

The gross amount asked for is £231,942,
being a decrease of £44,626 on last year's
amount. The receipts Appropriated in
Aid are £102,055, about which hon.
Members can read for themselves at the
end of this Estimate. This shows an
increase of £13,450 on last year's amount.

Mr. W. McMULLEN: Of which you
robbed the poor.
Mr. GORDON: Hon. Members can rest
assured that the Estimate I am submitting
to the House is not to rob the poor, but
to make grants towards the poor and to
keep them after struggling probably for
a long time in the industries of the
country. We are now making some provision for them that will tend to keep
them in their old age. I was referring to
the receipts appropriated in aid. These
represent £13,450 more than last year's
amount. The net total, therefore, required for the current year is £129,887a decrease of £58,076 on last year's
amount. At first glance this seems a
tremendous reduction and requires some
explanation. It is largely due to two
contributing factors: First of all, the disappearance of certain non-recurrent expenditure, such as the cost of the new
Belfast Employment Exchange - Item
D.4.-which represented £20,350; and,
secondly, last year's Estimate for expenses
connected with the apportionment of the
Irish National Health Insurance Fund,
shown under Item S, which was £23,628.
If, as now appears probable, the actual
figure for 1927-28 is lower than the figure
taken, the resulting surplus will be surrendered to the Exchequer.
Hon. Members are aware of the increasing work resulting from pensions payable
to insured persons between the ages of 65
and 70 years commencing in January,
1928, and the transfer to the Department
of about 12,000 old-age pensioners over 70
years who possess insurance qualifications
rendering further investigation as to
means unnecessary. This requires additional staff. The ordinary yearly increments to those in the Service mean
increased expenditure. After giving this
preliminary explanation I propose to deal
with the Vote under five heads, i.e.,
Headquarters, Employment Department,
Insurance Department, Inspection Department, and Finance Department, without
making reference to the more minor matters of expenditure. Any question arising
on these minor or bigger matters will be
dealt with during the course of the
debate.

Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Gordon]
An indication of this more stringent
administration will be obvious when it is
mentioned that during the first four
months of the present year 32 successful
proceedings have been instituted against
47 employers for the year 1926.
The publicity which these prosecution
proceedings receive in the Press ought to
bring to the notice of all employers their
duties under the Insurance Acts, but the
Department has gone even further in this
direction and published in the Press
during the months of August and
September of last year a notice expressly
designed to let employers know their
duties in this matter and the
precise
penalties to which they render themselves
liable for failure to carry out these
duties. Further, posters have been distributed to all post offices and police
barracks in Northern Ireland. I would
appeal to employers to co-operate fully
with the Department in this matter.
Apart from the fact that compliance
with the Acts is a duty laid upon them
by our Parliament, default in this duty is
unfair to those employers who loyally
comply, and to those employees whose
homes are jeopardized by non-compliance
when unemployment, sickness or old age
comes upon them, and when death removes the father of the house.
I have dealt specially with the question
of non-compliance to show that the
Department is fully alive to the necessity
for enforcing the law, and, as a warning
to those employers who refuse to comply,
but who are, of course, in the minority.
I would like to say to the hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Beattie) with regard to the textile
firms about which he talked to me, that
we have exhaustive inspections in our
spinning mills and in our textile works
to see that the terms of the Factory Acts
are carried out. My right hon Friend
(Mr. Andrews) and myself periodically
have conferences with those who represent
the head of the Inspection Department,
as we are most anxious to see that the
Factory Act legislation is carried out by
employers without unnecessarily imposing a hardship on the employers, but
to make it possible that those employees
engaged in textile firms will, at least, be
engaged under good, healthy and wholesome conditions.
Mr. BEATTIE: Safe conditions.
Mr. GORDON: I can give this assurance to the hon. Gentleman and any
other Member of this House that if he
knows where the conditions of the
Factory Acts are not carried out to the
letter of the law and, and if he brings the
matter before my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) or myself, we will take the
necessary steps to see that the law is fully
complied with. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

Mr. KYLE: Yes. I beg to move the
reduction of this Estimate by £100. I do
so to call the attention of the Department
to a state of affairs which exists in Belfast
and in certain country districts in regard
to the findings of the Local Employment
Committees being upset by the Headquarters of the Ministry of Labour.
Belfast a very considerable number of
applications for benefit have been made.
When the applicant appears before the
Local Employment Committee, the Local
Employment Committee asks the applicant where he has been seeking employment, and on the applicant giving
satisfactory answers the Committee recommends the payment of benefit for
a number of weeks. The claim then
reaches the Labour Exchange and goes to
Headquarters, and in too many instances
Headquarters turns down the recommendations of the Local Employment
Committees, makes the grant a final grant

sometimes of four weeks or six weeks, and
sometimes turns down the decision of the

It is not fair to the Local Employment
Committees that the Ministry should act
in this high-handed fashion in turning
down these claims.
In that connection it is well also to
remember that applicants are turned down
who have been out of employment for a
certain length of time and when the
applicant endeavours to be restored to
benefit again he is told that in consequence
of the fact that he has not had a sufficient
period of insurable employment during
the past two years he is not entitled to
benefit. The applicant strengthened by
that goes to another Department of the
Ministry of Labour to seek employment
on relief work. And when the applicant
appears the gentleman in charge of that
Department informs him that he is not long
enough out of work to be entitled to take
his turn on relief work. I have known
cases of men who have been out of employment for over three years and who
have been told by the gentleman in charge
of the Relief Work Department that they
are not long enough out of work to be
qualified for relief employment. And yet
they are turned down because they have
not had a sufficient period of employment
during the past two years. That seems
to me to be a very contradictory state of
affairs and it does involve a considerable
amount of hardship.
The hon. Gentleman who proposed this
Vote laid stress on the Inspectors' Department. I want to ask him or the right
hon. Gentleman the Minister of Labour
is he satisfied that the Inspectors' Department that he has can reasonably be expected to carry out all the inspections
necessary under the various Acts of
Parliament in Northern Ireland. These
inspectors apparently are expected to know
the Trade Boards Act, the Factory Acts,
and the laws relating to National Health
Insurance. Now, it seems to me to be
almost an impossibility for any persons,
however qualified they may be, to be
sufficiently expert in all these subjects I
have mentioned to warrant them to act as
inspectors.
I do find what I have gathered from my
họn. Friend the Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Beattie) he has found, because the
Parliamentary Secretary in making his
speech to-day has stated that there have
been some comments or conversation with
him about the state of affairs in textile
concerns. I have found, for example, in
some spinning mills in the North of Ireland that there is an absolute lack of dressing rooms and cloak rooms for the girls
who work in the spinning mills to have
their clothes kept in anything like decent
state. in some cases girls have got to
hang their shawls or coats in the room
they are actually working in. Anybody
who knows what the spinning rooms are
and the atmosphere there knows that for
a girl or boy to put on clothes that have
been hanging up in that humid atmosphere for 4 hours is not conducive to
health. As a matter of fact, I think the
present law if carried out would ensure
that in spinning mills there should be
sufficient cloakroom accommodation for
the people to hang up their clothes, so
that when they put them on again at the
end of 4 hours there should be some
reasonable expectation of their being dry.
I want the right hon. Gentleman to try
to do something if he can to remedy that
particular state of affairs that exists in
some particular mills. I do not want to
give names of mills. I do not think it is
very good to do that here. I think if
he will instruct his Inspectors' Departments to pay particular attention to the
spinning mills of the North of Ireland it
would be a good thing.
There is another question in regard to
mills, and that is the lack of fans in the
hackle shops. There has been a tremendous improvement during the past ten years
in the atmosphere both of the hackle shop
and the roughing shop in spinning mills.
Yet there is a good deal to be done particularly in regard to the country mills
in regard to the fans necessary in these
two departments I have mentioned. We
have a standing joke in the textile trade
about hacklers which I am not going to
repeat here. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I am not going to repeat it, except
to say that hackling and roughing by the
very nature of the employment tends to a
short life, because of the atmosphere the
workers have got to breathe and because
of the dust generated when the hacklers
are hackling flax and the roughers are
roughing it. A good deal remains to be
done in regard to accommodation and in
regard to fans so far as these two departments are concerned.

There is another matter the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Gordon) did not refer to except
in a subsidiary way and quite apart from
the main head. That is in regard to the
Court of Referees, the Board of Umpires,
and the Local Employment Committees. I
have referred to the hardship that exists.
at present in Belfast and in certain
country districts, particularly Lisburn,
about the L.E.C.s' decision. I do want, if
I can, to stress the hardships inflicted on
applicants in Belfast and country districts,
also the Courts of Referees. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). You have not
one chance in 50 to get through the Court
of Referees. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). And the action of the chairmen
of the Courts of Referees in my opinion,
after having a good many years' experience
of it, is very harsh, indeed. When the
applicant appears before the Court of
Referees he or she is asked where they
were looking for work yesterday. The
applicant replies and states where he
or she was looking for work. So
it goes on for a period of a fortnight.
The applicants are searchingly asked
where they have been seeking employment. Then at the end of a long
interrogation the chairman will suddenly
switch round and ask the applicant again
where he was looking for work say two
days ago.
Now as a matter of fact it is
extremely difficult to remember what one
states in a court, and to the average
worker when his very life depends on
whether he or she will get benefit or not
their state of mind does not conduce to
their being able to give satisfactory

With regard to Courts of Referees, I

think the Unemployment Insurance Act.
travelled quite so far in the legal sense as

Mr. GORDON: Would you be just?

is all very well for the Minister of

the case of a widow, who had been

I want to suggest to the Minister that
every contributor should have an opportunity, once every month or two months,
of inspecting his or her card, because by
that means you could prevent the possibility of employers neglecting to stamp
workers' cards. I was insured for six

saw my insurance card. I took it for

suggest to the Minister that in addition

months. That would give the workers

to be held to have refused work because

not his original occupation? I understood from this man's story that he had
been in a country spinning mill. Said I,
"You are a strong, healthy, vigorous
man, and there are plenty of people wanting strong, vigorous men like you to work.
Why do you not take any job that is
offered to you? Do you expect that the
country is going to pay you your wages,
year in year out, while you do no work?"
I really think that that was an unreasonable man. There was no remedy open to
the Committee but to strike him off the
unemployment roll.
With regard to the second question

They are insured under the Act. When

under the Workmen's Compensation Act.
I think he should only be asked to send

send a doctor to have the man examined
"
With regard to this question of
National Health Insurance, I am entirely
in sympathy with these organizations and
societies that are for the benefit of the
worker. I think they could not be done
without. I hope they will not be injured
or crippled in any way. It is not with
the Acts that I find fault; it is with the
administration. I think, perhaps, we
could reconcile the viewpoints of the men
on the opposite side with that of the men
on this side, because I thing that both
sides want to get at what is fair and
just. One thing that strikes me is this.
There are far too many societies, and a
good deal of the money that should go to
the worker is eaten up in the cost of
running unnecessary societies.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: I do not know the
number of these societies that you have
working in Northern Ireland. I know
there is a Committee looking after them,
and that there is a distinguished Member
of this House associated with it. I think
it does its work remarkably well. But,
at the same time, I heard a medical friend
of mine in Dublin say that the secretary
of a society had a salary equal to that of
a Cabinet Minister. I think he earns it,
but if you give large salaries to the secretaries of all these societies the money
comes from the contributions of the
workers, or the State, or the firm, and the
result is that there is less for the workers.
Regarding medical health insurance,
there has always been a question in my
mind that the man insured has difficulty
in getting his benefit. The Minister has
adopted a method by which he sends a
doctor to inspect a case in which he has
any doubt.
I think on the whole that is
a satisfactory method, because if the
Society complains or the patient complains
there is an independent court provided
apart from the doctor who is in attendance. There is only one objection that I
know of to that system, and it is this,
that in making these appointments, you
allow this regional officer to appoint a
deputy who lives too close to the district
concerned, so that there is sometimes
going into a patient a doctor who is more
or less in competition with the inspector
himself.

There is another point, industrial assurance, on which I wish to say a few words.
I think the House understands fairly
well that many of these great insurance
societies that are working in England and
all over the world have their fingers in
this pie of National Health Insurance in
Northern Ireland. A committee sat on
this question, and it showed that for every
shilling contributed by the worker he
got only sevenpence, I am not just sure
of the figure. A huge number of these
policies lapse, and the companies profit
thereby. We passed an Act in this House
with the object of remedying that grievance, but I am afraid it has not done it.
There has been a report submitted to
the Members of the House as to the working of the new Act, but I do not think
the information contained in it is of a
satisfactory character. The companies
once raised the point that they could not
make a separate return as between Northarn Ireland and England and Scotland.
They have their agencies here-the Pearl
and the Refuge. All these societies are
working in our midst. They have their
books and their returns, and until we
know the number of policies that lapse,
the income that they have, and the
amount of money that they are dealing
out, I am afraid this injustice will continue. I think, therefore, that further
information should be given to the House
on this matter. That is all I have to say
on this subject, and I hope that anything
I have said will be taken in a kindly
spirit. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

I do not believe that five per cent. of the

There is just one other thing. I heard

the inspector taking those costs is doing

whoever takes that 10s is liable to be
prosecuted.
I saw where in County Tyrone 10s was
awarded to an inspector in each case, and
according to the law he is entitled to
nothing more than his bare outlay and the
mere cost of the summons. In my own
constituency people are not a bit fond of
these cards and these stamps-they think
they have far too many of them-but even
if a man is summoned there is no reason

which often the employer is not entitled
to pay. I think if the Minister looks this
up he will find the Ministry have on many
occasions committed offences themselves
by taking these costs.

that the application of these rules should
be
less rigid now when the burden

At the time I was preaching the
Utopian doctrine now incorporated in
many Acts of Parliament, I always
started off in the belief that the function
of the State was to give maintenance to
all persons who are not able to secure
work. It was the function of the State
to secure work for them or to maintain
them. I have always held that, and
without any rules or regulations whatever. I remember the time when to
make a statement of that character would
have called forth the hilarious laughter
of nearly all responsible politicians and
business men.
I remember the time when
if you preached that doctrine you would
have been told you were preaching the
doctrine of Utopia. I remember the
time when it would have caused screams
of laughter amongst what is known as the
respectable class to lay down a doctrine
of that character, but that is accepted
now in principle. Therefore, I say that
unless a man is a sheer wastrel, unless a
man does not want to work at all, and
notoriously does not want to work, I think
he ought to get the unemployment allowance. This was the humane spirit which
inspired the State to pass all this social
legislation. I think it is not Christian
citizenship to allow any decent man
woman anxious to work but unable to get
it to starve. I do not think it is consistent
with modern Christianity even to
compel these people to starve, because
or
they cannot come up to the very acme of

I would like to say a word about the

will not have a duplication of the forms
we get from the income-tax people, for

Mr. DEVLIN: The right hon. Gentleman was not the Minister of Labour then,
but I had time in those days to detach

to them, and take up the work of the
conditions under which women worked in

got Trade Boards Acts put into operation
in Northern Ireland. I drew attention

Gentleman has referred, namely, to
women working from six o'clock in the
morning to six o'clock at night in these
heated spinning rooms and with their
shawls hung up in these rooms. When
they put on these shawls in the evening
they had to go out in the cold winter
nights. They had to sit on stone steps
with the steam flowing down and take
their food there because there was no
dining room. I raised these things in
Parliament and outside, and I understood it was all changed. Is it changed?
Mr. GORDON: Yes.
Mr. DEVLIN: I understand from the
hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) that it still
exists to some extent. I hope it does not.
Mr. KYLE: It does to some extent.
Mr. DEVLIN: I hope that this
barbarous system will be abolished entirely since the State has found it its duty
from an economic standpoint to reduce the
hours of labour of these women.
I was
able, I am glad to say, to secure the
appointment of an additional female inspector in the mills and factories. All
these things were done. And I will tell
you why they were done. They were done
because it dawned on the Government and
on society which seemed ignorant of it
that the average life of these women was
37 years, and that in these mills and
factories there worked little children of
from nine to twelve years of age-halftimers, who worked a day one day and
went to school another day-that the bulk
of these children had half-a-crown a week;
that they were children of migrated agricultural labourers who came in from
Monaghan, Tyrone, Fermanagh and all
the Ulster counties; and that these
children, with the flush, and the bloom,
and the beauty on their faces, at the end,
when they were thirteen years of age and
had passed into the whole-time system,
were old before they knew what it was to
be young, with the roses gone from their
cheeks and the bloom disappeared from
their faces. I remember that I tried to
change all that and was stigmatized as an
enemy to Belfast, a danger to society, a
potential Socialist, an unsuccessful, and
perhaps successful, revolutionary in some
other sphere of activity. That is what we
all got then. I do not want to quote these
things except as reminders of what
progress has been made by a common
agitator, although that agitator at that
time stood alone. I hope, therefore, that
if there are any factories or mills against
which a complaint of the character referred to by my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle)
can be levelled the Minister of Labour will
see to it that that complaint will not be
justified after his interference has taken
place.
With regard to these cards to which

In

say these

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I am very gratified at the way
this Vote has been received and for the
way hon. Members on both sides of the
House have approached the matter. The
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) spoke about claims being turned
down by headquarters when they had been
passed by the Local Employment Committee. As a matter of fact, only between three and four per cent. of the
claims recommended by Local Employment Committees have been turned down
by headquarters, and I would point out
to the House that these Local Employment Committees are advisory bodies.
It is their duty to advise the Ministry on
the evidence which is placed before them,
but sometimes the Ministry has other evidence as to the statutory qualifications,
for instance, of the claimants, and in
addition to that it is the duty of the
Ministry to ensure equality of administration throughout the whole of Northern
Ireland.
If Local Employment Committees were
left absolutely free to grant claims or refuse them as they thought right without
any central control, what you would find
would be this: that one Local Employment
Committee in one part of our area would
be particularly sympathetic and another
Committee might be quite the reverse.
It is the duty of the Ministry to endeavour to see that if a Local Employment
Committee is acting too harshly it is
pointed out to them, and if, on the other
hand, they are acting too leniently and
contrary to the law of the land, it is
equally the duty of the Department to
have that brought to the notice of the
Committee in question.
My hon. Friend referred to the fact
that some poor fellows who have been out
of work for a long time and sought to
obtain work on relief schemes have been
told that they have not been out long
enough to qualify for relief work. That
may be quite true because all relief work
is given on a priority list, and that priority
list has met with the approval of Trade
Union representatives, Local Employment
Committees and other Committees, and
the way it is arranged is this: Those
longest out of employment and with the
largest families and consequently the
greatest responsibilities get the preference. It is really a question of degree.
The more schemes that are put forward,
the more men can get work, but all that
my Department can do in that direction
is to see that such work as there is is as
fairly distributed as is possible.
The hon. Member also referred to the
Inspection Department and to the position
in mills and factories throughout our area.
I have no hesitation in assuring the House
that the Inspection Department is par
ticularly active and has been for some
years. I am in a position to say that I
do not think there is a roughing shop,
or hackling or sorting shop in the trade
now which is not very efficiently ventilated
by exhaust ventilation, removing the dust
from as near as practicable the place at
which it is generated so as to take it away
before it gets into the general air of the
There is a diffidepartment concerned.
culty in some of the older mills, I quite
admit, in connection with the provision
of waiting rooms for the workers and for
cloakrooms to keep their clothes in while
they are engaged at their employment.
Some of the older mills are a good deal
congested, and probably it is very difficult to arrange for cloakroom accommodation because of the fact that there are
probably a hundred or more workers
altogether at a particular time in a crush
trying to get their clothes and get away
from their work within a reasonable time.
Many of us who have gone to entertainments from time to time know the difficulty there is in getting our hats and coats
when we are coming away, and you can
imagine that in a mill that is probably
the difficulty. But I am in a position to
say that where cloakrooms are not avail
able waterproof boxes are provided
in which the workers can keep their
clothes, and I do feel that in this respect,
as well as in every other respect, the
workers' interests are being carefully
looked after.
The Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) referred to the danger to workers
from accidents due to machinery being
badly fenced. I may say the most careful inspection is taking place regularly of
all our firms, including saw mills and
works of that kind, and employers have
shown a great desire to comply with the
law in this respect. As regards the
Courts of Referees, I do think a rather
unfair attack has been levelled at these
Courts by several hon. Members to-day.
Mr. KYLE: It could not be too
unfair.

Nothing has taken place since

Mr. DEVLIN: I do not like to occupy

recognize because I am sure that like

organizations such as that to which I have
referred is absolutely inevitable if the
financial burden they have to bear to the
extent they do at present continues-that
it is quite desirable in the interests of
the city and of the community that we
should do our best to preserve and protect,
and if possible foster an organization of
the character of the Belfast Philharmonic
Society. The whole spirit of the age is
manifested in the nature of our entertainments and amusements. Jazz, revues, picture houses, a light order of.
entertainment all these things now constitute the amusements of the people, and
it is impossible for the greater musical
organizations like the Belfast Philharmonic Society to compete successfully or
effectively with the other forms of entertainment to which I have just referred.
The charges of admission into the concerts organised by the Philharmonic Society
are very high, and naturally the tax is a
bigger tax than that on any of the other
places of amusement. The cost of bringing artists, of paying musicians, and of
generally bringing together such a musical combination as will attract an everdecreasing section of the community,
namely, those whose interest in music is

As long as I am here, sent by eighteen
thousand sensible solid men, I shall claim
my right to use this Parliament for the
purpose that at all events I suppose it
was created for, namely, first of all, for
well-considered legislation; secondly, for
due criticism of that legislation in the
public interest; thirdly, for a clear and
logical analysis of those Measures, and,
finally, for complete discussion and dissection of all the outlay upon administration. Those are the functions for which
this Parliament was created, and those
functions cannot be adequately discharged
as long as the Government limit us to the
time which they have placed at our
disposal.

Now there is another matter. Speaking in this House but a few weeks ago the
Prime Minister made this statement:
I hope hon. Members on all sides of
the House realize that a scrutiny takes
place of all our Acts. After
our
Attorney-General has certified that in

powers of this Parliament under the
Act of 1920 the authorities on the other
side also take every care to see that we
are not infringing in any way either
the spirit or the letter of the 1920 Act.
-(Official Report, 30th March, Vol.
8, Col. 565.)
In other words, that there is a Board or
Government organization set up on the
other side of the water to watch our legislation, forgetful of the fact that our
legislation is their legislation. They
examine every Act we pass here to see
that anything we do does not impinge
in the slightest degree upon their authority
or upon their right. And yet, they
and pass Measures over there affecting
go
us.
I am not aware that the Attorney-
General here, or any body set up by the
Government here, meticulously examines
in our interests legislation that passes in
regard to Northern Ireland. The whole
thing so far as I am concerned is most
unjustifiable. I am not hopeful that any
protest I may make here in the House will
have any immediate effect. But I do put
it to hon. Members in this House, and
especially in view of the future, whether
it is consonant with such dignity as we
possess, that we should permit these
transactions to take place.
The other day in a sudden burst of
curiosity I visited Stormont. I heard
repeated complaints here that the progress
in the work of building that Parliament
was very slow. I went to see what was
being done for my own information.
There I saw the foundations of a structure
which, if I could imagine what that
structure would be like by its foundations, will be a wonderful building. After
you travel out there five miles and walk
about a mile then you reach a series of
majestic steps. Then step by step you
walk up these steps to the top, and I saw
this Parliament. I can imagine that
when this work has been completed there
will be a Parliament there in appearance
as a structure and in surroundings that
will equal the Parliament in the Capitol,
at Washington. Does it ever strike you
how absurd the whole thing is? And it
would strike you more if you were told
that this institution, which is to stand for
all time as an example of British
generosity, is to house the Parliament of
this Northern Ireland. How absurd and
grotesque it is when you are building a
structure or institution of that sort you
are quietly allowing yourselves to be
robbed of whatever privileges you possess
as a legislative assembly.
I cannot conceive the consistency of
that attitude at all and, therefore, I protest against it on the ground of undue
interference with the rights and privileges
of this House, on the ground that I think
it is wrong in principle and in operation
for the Parliament of another country to
pass legislation affecting our domestic

it is necessary that that Bill should be referred to in greater detail in order that
the circumstances may be explained. It
was found after long experience and investigation in Great Britain that the Act
of 1906 dealing with fertilizers and feeding stuffs rather more important perhaps
than the name implies--had become obsolete and was inefficient for the purposes
for which it was intended, namely, to
prevent fraudulent dealers imposing on
farmers and others to whom produce of
this kind was sold. A Committee sat and
investigated this matter, and finally it was
decided that an Amending Act should be
passed of a most important character, an
important character not only to Great
Britain but equally important to Northern Ireland from the point of view of
agricultural interests.
When in the form of a Bill this was
submitted it was considered here, and as
necessarily the two interests are interwoven in this matter almost before everything else that is the question of the
provision of fertilizers and feeding stuffs
for the farmers of this Province and Great
Britain-the Government decided at a
Cabinet meeting, when, unfortunately,
Parliament was not sitting, that it was
necessary that effect should be given to the
conditions of this Bill in Northern Ireland
before it was possible to legislate here.
That was the conclusion come to then, and
I think it was a right, a proper, and a
valuable conclusion. Let me indicate
what are the conditions under which this
Act will be carried out and what it set
out to do. It set out to protect the
farmers of Great Britain, and in the result
equally the farmers of Northern Ireland,
from the adulteration and mixture of im-

year
in the inspectorship, and that the inspector
retiring was a member of the Catholic
faith. I met the Minister, Lord Charlemont, on the matter, and I asked him if
an appointment was to be made would the
Government consider the question of appointing a Catholic. What he said to me
was that it was the opinion of the Government that it was desirable that one member of that faith should follow another on
condition that he was qualified for the
position, but that in every instance the
Government would select the best man.
That, in my opinion, was a fair line of
policy, and one to which I certainly took
no exception. I mentioned the case of
one particular applicant, whom I then
knew only for the first time. He was
then a teacher, and is to-day a teacher,
in a small elementary school in County
Down. He was appointed to that school
-his first school-in 1919. A year or
two afterwards this Government, when it
came into power, gave him facilities to
attend the University as he had shown a
desire to do so. He attended there, and
in the first year he obtained his diploma
in education. The Ministry still facilitated him and he attended the University,
being still in charge of his school, and he
obtained his B.A. degree. After that he
obtained the degree of Bachelor of Science
and then that of Master of Science in the
same year. He still attended the
University, obtaining his higher diploma
in education, and, ultimately, his M.A.
degree.
This was the man I spoke to Lord
Charlemont about, and I certainly have
no regrets for asking that he should be
appointed to this position, because I
think he was in every way fitted for it.
Indeed, I would have thought the
Ministry would have been delighted to have
a man who had been a teacher in one of
their own schools, and who, in the short
period of three years at a University
while still following his occupation as
teacher, had obtained all his degrees.
That is the only individual I asked should
be appointed, and Lord Charlemont was
the only man I asked should appoint him.
Any statement made to the contrary is
not right.
When I found he was not appointed I
did speak to the hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb), and I told him exactly

every opportunity I will still disapprove
of the action of the Ministry. I still
think this man has been most unfairly.
dealt with, and that it is the duty

not know where you can charge me
there with importuning the Government, or with wire-pulling, as was suggested in this question. If so, I certainly
take very grave exception to it.

There is another point I want to mention in connection with the administration of extended benefit. Grievances in
connection with this matter come before
me almost every hour of the day. The
Minister of Labour recognizes the colour
of the documents I have before me, and
when I was coming to this House to-day
his Parliamentary Secretary, who was in
the tram, knew what the Bill was that I
had in my hands. The administration of
extended benefit has been repeatedly
criticised by the
Opposition in this House.
Some of the decisions that are given are
very unfair. I will quote one case, and
I know that decisions of a similar nature
are given every week. Here we have a
man who was a joiner from 1912 to 1926.
After being nine months unemployed he
meets a pawnbroker who wants a little
structural alteration done to his shop.
The joiner takes the job at a price, which,
I presume, would be against the rules of
his trade union, and the pawnbroker supplied the materials and everything else.
The job lasted three months, and then
the man was put on another period of
benefit, and at the end of that period he
came before the Committee, and here is
the decision of the Committee:-
The Committee consider you have
failed to prove that you are normally
employed in insurable employment, and
that you normally seek to obtain your
livelihood by means of insurable employment.
That is very unfair, because it tends to
prevent an individual endeavouring to
get a job either by contract or at so much
per day. In order to qualify for extended benefit he must have a job under
an employer. That is the interpretation
of the clause in the Act. It would have
been to the benefit of this man if he i
arranged that the pawnbroker shou
have taken the part of the employer for
the three months, and that the joiner
himself should have paid for the insurance
stamps. That would have been a way of
getting over the clause, but he would not
have been an honest or conscientious man
if he had put stamps on his own card
when he knew it was illegal, and the
Ministry of Labour could have prosecuted him for putting stamps on his card
when he was not in an insurable occupation. The worst point about the whole
thing is that this man has a wife and five
children depending upon him, and for the
past fortnight there has not been a cent
coming into the house. That is one of
many points I could bring before the
notice of the Minister regarding extended
benefit. I will hand the particulars of
this case over to the Minister, and ask
him to look into it, and if possible restore
to that man the benefit he is justly entitled to.

not know whether it has escaped his attention or not, but I refer to a speech that
was delivered in the Carnmoney Orange
Hall and reported in the Belfast News-
Letter" on Friday, 13th May. You probably do not know the history of this
matter, and it might be as well if I gave
it very briefly.
Mr. SPEAKER: Would the hon.
Member tell me what he is referring to?
I did not catch it.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Rifles.
I made a speech in Tipperary a couple of
weeks ago, and the gentleman who is the
Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
Grand Master of the County Antrim
Grand Orange Lodge thought it advisable
to comment on that speech. Where he
criticizes myself, I have no complaint to
make. He uses fairly strong language,
but as a person who uses strong language
at times I have not the slightest
objection to it when it is applied to myself.
That is not the burden of my complaint.
I complain about the peroration, in
which he says:
There will never be a united Ireland
so long as one of you is living, and
whilst there is a rifle left in County
Antrim.
""
I want to know whether the right hon.
Gentleman is a reader of the "News-
Letter," whether his Parliamentary Secretary is a reader of the "News-Letter,
and whether this matter has received Departmental or Cabinet attention. Why
is this gentleman immune from prosecution? Is it because he is an Orangeman,
a County Grand Master, or because he
is a constituent of the Parliamentary
Secretary's?
I want an explanation of this matter,
because it appears to me to be a remarkably peculiar thing. I do not intend
it to be humorous in the slightest degree.
I recall that a few months ago a person
who made a no more drastic statement than
that at Carlisle Circus was prosecuted at
the instance of the right hon. Gentleman,
and that that young and somewhat unlettered man was incarcerated in the
Crumlin Road Jail for six months. I
want to know whether there is going to
be one law for the Socialist agitator and
another for the Orange agitator.
I want to know, so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned, if the law is be administered impartially. I cannot come
to the conclusion that the law is being
administered impartially if this gentleman is allowed to make a revolutionary
and inciting speech to young men to
utilize rifles and revolvers. Surely we
have had enough of that within our recent
history in Northern Ireland not to be
desirous of a recrudescence of that unsatisfactory state of affairs. I want to
repeat: Why is this gentleman immune
from prosecution? Is it for any of the
reasons I have indicated? I would like
a declaration from the Head of the Department concerned as to whether he
approves of this language or not and
whether I and others, who may believe
in a united Ireland, are going to be
allowed to agitate for that in a
constitutional fashion, without being
threatened with the use of rifles for indulging in a lawful pursuit.
I have the right to advocate constitutionally anything I like. What may be
my position, supposing I go to speak in
Carnmoney or any other part of County
Antrim, and some young man who may
have a rifle in his possession, and who is
influenced by the speech of that County
Grand Master, comes out and takes my
life, or the lives of those associated with
me at that meeting?
Mr. HANNA: The law would deal
with him.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Prevention is better than cure. That would
be a tremendous loss, because at least one
great life would be lost. I do not know
whether the life of the young man who
used the rifle would be of terrible importance, but I would suggest that it would
be a very tragic thing from the point of
view of Northern Ireland if my life were
lost, and I hope tne right hon. Gentleman will take cognisance of that statement. That is all I have to say in that
connection. I hope it is sufficient.
I want to refer to the Department of
the Minister of Labour. We had a discussion yesterday afternoon regarding the
treatment of provincial applicants for unemployment benefit. I got swift and
rapid confirmation of what I stated regarding provincial applicants when, this
morning, quite unexpectedly, and without
any solicitation on my part, a young man
from Enniskillen entered my office and
gave me his history. It is a tragic one
from his point of view, and I propose to
give it to the right hon. Gentleman after
I have referred to it very briefly for the
purpose of examination. I went into his
case as thoroughly as I could with the information he gave me. I understand that
he worked from 1906 until 1925. He
drew benefit approximately twelve months
up to May, 1926. Subsequent to that he
worked sixteen weeks.
I want at this stage to emphasize the
point made yesterday by the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Thomas Henderson). This young man, to whom I am referring, appears to have been attracted to
AD
1909 Appropriation Bill-

24 MAY 1927
Second Reading
to
Belfast by the glowing reports of our industrial conditions that are made by the
Gentlemen who occupy the Government
Front Benches when they get on to platforms outside and indulge in perfervid
perorations as to the industrial prosperity
of Belfast and the Six Counties. This
young man, attracted by the glowing reports of the conditions here, came
Belfast with five children, and found himself stranded. His unemployment benefit
was stopped in Enniskillen. He was unable to obtain employment in Enniskillen,
and he thought he was sure to get it in
Belfast, so he came here with his five
children. He discovered when he got to
Belfast that he could get neither employment nor unemployment benefit. I understand that the Grosvenor Hall people have
taken charge of three of the children, and
have very kindly and generously sent them
to some home until this young man can
get either employment or unemployment
benefit. He is left to the tender mercies
of the world, and I understand that a man
who has seven of a family, and a very
small income, is befriending this man, his
wife, and two of the children at the
present time.
I went as minutely as I possibly could
into the circumstances and I have come to
the conclusion that this young man,
notwithstanding his long and honourable
industrial life, has only been allowed an
overdraft of 70 days, as he said himself,
or, as I counted it on the information he
gave me, 100 days. If that statement is
true, and I have no reason at the moment
to doubt it, it proves that this man has
not got the same consideration as he very
probably would have got had he been an
applicant in the city of Belfast. If the
Minister can confirm the statement I
make, and I have no reason to doubt the
truth of it, I would ask that something
be done immediately to relieve this man
and his family from the unfortunate plight
in which they are placed at the present
time.
I have no doubt that, when I pass
this
statement to the right hon. Gentleman
he will give the matter immediate and
sympathetic consideration. If, from the
facts at his disposal my statement is borne
out, I hope he will very favourably reconsider this case, and either give the man
unemployment benefit or perhaps take
some steps in conjunction with the
Minister of Agriculture to place this man
in employment, because he holds out some
hope of getting employment in the Department of Agriculture. I understand
that he has been sitting on the door step
for some weeks. I hope that between the
two right hon. Gentlemen it will be possible to get this young man unemployment
benefit, or, what we would all prefer,
employment rather than benefit.
My main point was in connection with
the first matter that I raised, and I hope
it will receive the attention of the right
hon. Gentleman and of his Parliamentary
Secretary.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I rise to make a
very small point, of which I have already
given notice to the Minister of Finance.
I am sure this House has been delighted
at the fact that he has been able to show
a balance on the right side in connection
with the Appropriation Bill. I would
appeal to him once again—he has already
been appealed to this Session-to give a
few crumbs from that balance to secondary teachers' pensions. I refer to the
secondary teachers who have already obtained pensions. I know all the arguments which the Minister of Finance can
offer against these people getting any
further increase of pension; but I would
on this occasion-the last occasion we will
have of appealing on their behalf during
these sittings-appeal to the Minister of
Finance to see if he could make some
small concession to these people.
I think every one of us who saw the
particulars published in the daily papers,
particulars which we all have reason to
believe are accurate, was appalled when
he saw the very small sum which these
people were asked to accept as pensions.
I know that these people have no legal
right to pensions-that is admitted. They
have not paid contributions in order to
gain pensions, and some of them have not
done all their service in Northern Ireland.
But, while they have no legal right to
pensions, it is admitted that they have a
moral right by the mere fact that they
are now under a pension scheme.
Even if they have not spent the whole
of their service in Northern Ireland they
have at least spent the last years of it
here. They have been good enough to
have been accepted here as secondary
teachers. If they have come to us perhaps not at the very beginning of their

service, they have come to us with the

but these people are in a very unfortunate

There is one other point. I understand
that even the small pensions which these

for a pension. I think that is really a

been deducted receives the munificent sum

thing the Government of Northern Ireland should not do, and that they should
give to these people a sufficient pension
to enable them to live.
