Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard
to the matters raised by my hon. Friend
the Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie)
I would point out that the Regulations,
when made, will come into effect at once.
I hope that these Regulations will be
brought into effect on the 1st of July. I
think my hon. Friend is confusing two
matters. He refers to the Regulations
made by the Belfast Corporation.
think what he really means is that under
the Act the Belfast Corporation will have
power to make by-laws to control the
traffic inside the city. In future, when
those draft by-laws are made by the
Corporation, they will have to be submitted to the Home Office; an advertisement will then be issued, and anyone can
come in and object to the form of those
particular by-laws. If any objection is
lodged against the form of the proposed
by-laws, a public inquiry will be held, and
all the people interested will be heard at
it before the by-laws are finally settled.
Regarding the very important point
that he has raised of owners insisting upon
their drivers breaking the law, I would
like to assure him that we are bearing
that matter in mind in framing certain of
our Regulations, and if it is shown in the
future that an owner is forcing his driver,
at the risk of being dismissed, to break
the law, we will be in a position to deal
with him by taking away or suspending
his owner's licence. Apart altogether
from that, even at the present time, it is
a breach of the law for anyone to aid and
abet and assist his servant-worse still,
to force his servant-to break the law.
and he can be prosecuted under the common law at the present time.
With regard to the point raised by the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen), I would like to thank
him very much indeed for drawing my
attention to the very eloquent speech
which the Grand Master of County
Antrim delivered at Carnmoney. I very
often read the "News-Letter,
but I am
sorry that on this occasion I missed that,
and I am very grateful to my hon. Friend
for drawing my attention to it. He might
possibly also let me have a copy of the
speech which he delivered down in
Tipperary for I am certain it would
be equally eloquent. If my hon. Friend
knew the Grand Master of County Antrim
as well as I know him, or as well as a
great many Members of this House know
him, he would realize that he is a most
peaceful and law-abiding citizen of this
Province.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: He has
a peculiar way of showing it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: However, I
hope my hon. Friend will let me have the
benefit of his speech. With regard to the
point raised by the hon. Member for
Down (Mr. Patrick O'Neill) in regard to
an inspector, that is only a temporary
appointment. He was appointed so far
back as 1923. Hon. Members will
realize that at one time we had equipment for no less a number than 48,000
men. This comprised uniform and
general equipment that really applied to
an army, and amounted to a very large
amount in cash. My hon. Friend suggested that he thought all was not well
with these stores. I can only say that I
will be personally very grateful to my
hon. Friend if he, or any other hon.
Member, will come to me and tell me

Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Babington): This Bill is in exactly the
same form as the corresponding Bill that
passed last year, and which is
s now law.
It provided, as this Bill provides, for the
continuance of certain Acts of Parliament which, but for the passing of the
Expiring Laws Continuance Act, would
come to an end. The House will see
that the Bills are divided into two classes
-those which are Acts of the Parliament
of the United Kingdom, but still apply
to Northern Ireland; they are contained
in the first part of the Schedule of the
Bill. The second class are enactments
of the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
which also require to be continued.
As you, sir, ruled upon the occasion
when this Bill came before the House

3P
Expiring Laws Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
this time last year, that the only matter
for discussion was as to whether the
principle was to be accepted or not that
certain temporary provision should be
made permanent for another twelve
months, I need not enter at this stage
into a detailed account of the various
Acts which are to be continued by this
Bill, because, as I understand the rulings
that you gave last year, the discussion
upon these Statutes will arise in Committee.
The House will see the class of Acts
which have to be continued. The most of
them, I think, are matters about which
there will be very little controversy, and
the only two matters, so far as I recollect,
about which there was any serious controversy this time last year were the continuance of the Local Government (Emergency
Powers) Act, 1921, and the Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act, 1922. I assume
that there will be a certain amount of
discussion with reference to those two
Acts when this Bill reaches the Committee. It is enough for me to say at
the present moment that the Government
consider that those two Acts must still
be continued. Having nothing else to
add to what has been said in previous
years, I beg to move.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: One
would naturally have thought that the
Attorney-General would have given the
reason why the two Acts referred to are
included within the scope of this Measure. He has pointed out that considerable controversy raged round one
or two of the Acts that are included in
this Bill on the last occasion on which
it was before the House, and one would
naturally have expected that the Attorney-General would have given some reason as to why it is proposed to retain
these. In view of the fact that no reason
has been assigned, one is left to use one's
judgment in the best way possible as to
the reason why these Acts are retained.
I refer to one in particular-one that
has been enacted by the Parliament of
Northern Ireland-the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act, 1922. We have
pointed out on more than one occasion
that this Act was brought into operation
during an emergency in the history of
this Province, and we believe that that
emergency has now passed. There is,
therefore, no further justification for the
retention of this Act upon the Statute
Book. I think, therefore, that some
reason should have been given by the
Attorney-General, or some spokesman on
behalf of the Government, as to why it is
intended to retain this Act in the present.
Bill. If it has got anything to do with
the political situation in Southern Ireland-
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid I must
interrupt the hon. Member. As the
Attorney-General pointed out, in moving
the Second Reading of this Bill, we must
confine ourselves, by long-established
practice, merely to the question as to
whether or not it is desirable to extend
any Bills, but not to go into the merits
of particular Bills. That can be done in

Bill which he desires to leave out. But

Reading.

would appear then, from your ruling,

Mr. DEVLIN: I think some explanation ought to be given to the House as
to why this Bill has been put down at this
stage of our Parliamentary proceedings.
As far as my recollection goes, based upon
whatever experience I have, this Bill is
always put down at the end of the Session. We are in the middle of the Session, and why it should be put down now

hon. Gentleman, the Prime Minister,
will be glad to enlighten the House as to
why it has been put down at this stage.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): There is no great secret
about that. We thought it would suit
the convenience of the House to have a
certain amount of business to go on with
when we met in the Autumn, and as these
are the only Bills to be continued this
year there was really no necessity to postpone the Measure any longer. Whether
it is taken at present or later on makes
very little difference, and we thought it
would suit the convenience of the Members to take it now.

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard
to the Bill of which I have now the
honour to move the Second Reading, J
think it will require very few words on
my part, because it is largely selfexplanatory and follows on the lines of
the Act which was recently passed by the
British House of Commons. As the
House is aware, there is already on the
Statute Book legislation designed to ensure the production of milk under sanitary conditions. The law provides for
the inspection of dairies and cowsheds by
officers of local authorities, and, while
it cannot be disputed that this provision
has had a beneficial effect, it must be
admitted that in some districts these laws
are not enforced as rigorously as they
might be.
One of the most important elements
in the fight against tuberculosis is the
supply of pure milk, and the object of
this Measure is to ensure, as farras
possible, that the milk itself should be
free from tubercular bacilli. Abbeginning in this direction has already
been made by the Ministry of Agriculture,
who supervise the production of milk
from certain herds, and this Bill is introduced for the purpose of putting this
matter on a more compulsory basis. The
.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Bill has been prepared after consultation
between the Ministry of Home Affairs
and the Ministry of Agriculture.
""
I would like to point out to the House
that this Measure is of purely a voluntary
character. The scheme is to enable milk
producers to sell their milk under special
designations such as "Grade A-Tuberculin tested, or T.T., or some other designation to that effect, but before the
producer is allowed to use any of these
designations, or any other designation
signifying that his milk is free from
tubercular bacilli, the producer must
apply for and obtain a licence from the
Ministry to use these designations; and
before the licence is granted the producer
must satisfy the Ministry as a result of
a report from the Ministry of Agriculture, first of all, that the herd has
been tested and found clear, and,
secondly, that the milk is being produced
and sold under such conditions as will
ensure that the supply is pure and
free from tubercular bacilli.
The herds and the premises of the producer or the vendor of the milk will be
subject to inspection from time to time.
by these inspectors, and it will be open
to the inspectors to take samples of
the milk and have them tested. If the
regulations which are laid down by the
Ministry are not carried out by the
vendor or by the milk producer the certificate or licence can be revoked by the
Ministry. After this Bill becomes law it
will be an offence for any individual who
does not hold the licence, to which I have
referred, to use any of the prescribed designations or to make any statement to
the effect that the milk he is producing
or selling is free from tubercular bacilli.
I am sure hon. Members will appreciate
the enormous advantages that will
accrue to the producer because he will be
able, if he has a licence, to sell his milk
under a designation which will practically mean a Government guarantee as
to the purity of the milk, and I do not
think it is necessary to emphasize the
enormous advantage it will be to the
public to know that when they buy milk
which is sold under this designation to
which I have referred they are really
getting the article for which they are paying, and that the milk is free from tubercular bacilli. I do not think it is
necessary to say anything more to commend this Measure to the House. It is
a Measure that will commend itself to
the honest milk producer as much as it
will to the public who desire to get a pure
milk supply. I beg to move.

There is no doubt that the health of
the community here suffers very considerably, as we have seen from the

has not been properly handled and
prepared for consumption. In this connection, of course, there is a tremendous
amount of controversy as to which milk
is best, whether it is Grade A, or T.T.,
or any other designation which may be
put on it by the purveyor of the milk.
I think the House ought to know that the
Belfast Co-operative Society have gone to
very great pains in ensuring a very good
milk supply for the citizens of Belfast.
This has been so much appreciated by
the citizens of Belfast, as a matter of fact,
that from one-fifth to one-sixth of the
entire population is supplied by the
Belfast Co-operative Society.
The method which the Co-operative
have adopted in Belfast for ensuring a
clean milk supply is something well
worthy of emulation by other traders, or
even by the Government in insisting that
the milk supplied to the homes of the
people should be enclosed in bottles and
that the bottles should be sealed to prevent dirt from the streets getting in.

milk taken from the ordinary milk carts

Mr. SPEAKER: May I explain to the

of introducing Bills at the option of the
Government or the private Member who
introduces those Bills? One is as has
just been done by the Attorney-General,
and is the usual course to hand the Bill
in at the Table when it is automatically
read a First time. The other course is
very rarely adopted, and was adopted in
this House on only one occasion, I think,
that was when the Education Bill was
presented. A Motion is made asking
leave to present the Bill, and then a First
Reading debate can take place on that
Motion, and does take place, and a
division is taken if desired. It is at the
option of the Member who introduces the
Bill, and any Member who wishes to introduce a Bill, as the Attorney-General
has now introduced this one, has a perfect right to do so and nobody can
challenge it.

I come to the question which has been

Acts in any shape or form, but I think
the meanest form of coercion is to pass
what is called a temporary Measure, to

down, the occasion which called forth the
passing of this Measure having disappeared, to continue to make this coercive
Act a permanent one.
Why do you not bring forward, as they

Everyone agrees that peace exists in

I do not want to discuss these things,

ments, decisions, and conclusions, you

law?

The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.

we are dealing with now which is in any

We have heard no allegation that it

caused under this Act during the time of
emergency was as little as it possibly

could be.
When you look back to the time
when this Statute was enacted
as law

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
it is impossible not to realize that
but for that Act in all probability
hon. Members opposite would not be
sitting in their seats to-day, and very
possibly Members of the Government
would not now be in this House. In
six months in 1922 we had 159 murders
and 350 people wounded. We had
millions of pounds' worth of property
destroyed by fire and arson, and the compensation that had to be paid to the public
in respect of that damage has not been
paid for yet and will not be paid for for
many a long year. If it had not been
for this Statute the Government cannot
say how far the disintegration of society
would have proceeded. But in any event
it was put down, and I say it was
put down under the powers conferred
by this Act, and that without the
powers conferred by this Act disorder
could never have been put down. Special
powers were required.
The law, which for centuries in Great
Britain had proved adequate for any
ordinary case of crime, or even in an
ordinary emergency, was inadequate, and
it is no argument to say to this Committee
that because Parliament in England and
those responsible for the administration
of the law in England have not had to
have recourse to special legislation of this
kind that, therefore, this special legislation should be immediately taken off our
Statute Book. The conditions which
obtained here and the conditions which
obtain here at present have no parallel
in Great Britain, and I think it is obvious
to most Members of the Committee that
as special legislation was necessary this
special legislation which was passed by
this Parliament was in fact successful in
restoring law and order in Northern
Ireland.
Having succeeded in restoring law and
order, what the Government is now asked
to do is to throw away the weapon with
which law and order was restored. I
would invite the Committee to ask themselves this question. Have we, not only
in Northern Ireland, but across
Border in the Free State, reached that
stage of constitutional and social security
which the citizens of Great Britain have
attained and enjoyed for so many years?
I hope it may be so. Time will prove it,

CLAUSE 1 (Licences for Sale of Milk
under special designations)-
(1) A person shall not, either by himself or by any servant or agent, except
under and in accordance with a licence
granted by the Ministry of Home
Affairs-
""
(a) sell or offer or expose for sale any
milk as "certified,' "Grade A,"
"tuberculin tested" or ""T.T.," or
under such other designation as may
be from time to time prescribed by
regulations made under this Act; or
(b) on or in connection with any
sale or offer for sale or proposed sale
of any milk or in any advertisement,
circular or notice relating to any
milk, describe or refer to the same
" "tuberas "certified," "Grade A.,"
culin tested" or "T.T." or by any
other designation prescribed as aforesaid, or use any description or designation including or resembling
any such description or designation.
(2) A licence may be granted for the
purposes of this section for such period,
and subject to such terms and conditions (including conditions as to the
A
payment of fees), as may be prescribed
by regulations made under this Act;
and a licence so granted may be at any
time suspended or revoked by the Ministry of Home Affairs by reason of the
non-compliance of the holder thereof
with any conditions prescribed as aforesaid, or for any other reason which the
said Ministry may deem to be sufficient.
(3) If any person is guilty of a
contravention of the foregoing provisions of this section he shall be liable,
on summary conviction, for the first
offence, to a fine of two pounds or any
greater sum not exceeding ten pounds,
and for the second or any subsequent
offence to a fine of five pounds or any
greater sum not exceeding twenty
pounds, and, if the offence is a continuing offence, to a further fine not
exceeding two pounds for each day
during which the offence continues.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg
to move, in Clause 1, page 2 line 16, to
leave out the word "or" (to a fine of),
and to insert instead thereof the words,
not exceeding." I move this Amendment as a protest against the habit of the
Government of fixing minimum fines.
The fixing of minimum fines gives some
justification to the suggestion put forward by the Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) that the Government are trying
to make a paying proposition out of these
fines. As the Member for County Antrim
said yesterday, why cannot you trust the
magistrates who adjudicate on these
cases to fix a suitable fine according to the
nature of the offence. I very seldom
raise any Party question in this House,
but I think the Government show very
little respect to their friends by not trusting them to impose a penalty adequate to
the offence. I could understand a maximum fine, but I must protest against
these minimum fines, and I hope the Committee will agree to the substitution of the
words "not exceeding" for the word "of."
I therefore beg to move.

I think it was the intention of the hon.
Member who asked this question that the
Government should go further and press
them to do still more than they have done

at the present moment. Now that winter
is coming in, and the Poor Law Guardians are refusing outdoor relief, where
are they to go? They may go into the
body of the house, but that will only
increase the rates of the city of Belfast
still more, because do not forget that out
of every shilling we pay in poor rate in
Belfast 9d goes for the upkeep of buildings and the salaries of officials. Only 3d
out of every shilling is expended in relieving the poor, so that it would be much
cheaper for us to give these people some
relief through the Government than it
would be to have it administered by the
Poor Law Guardians. That fact has been
demonstrated in some parts of Great
Britain, that it is cheaper to administer
some form of relief by the Government
than it has been to do it through the Poor
Law Guardians.
I do earnestly beg of the Government
to exercise still further their authority,
to exercise their rights and all the privileges they have as the Government of this

number of people in Belfast, be it 20,000,

these people who are unemployed. I
would like to know if the Government
are considering in any way these people
who are hit so badly at the present time.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I propose to take this question.

NORTHERN IRELAND CIVIL SER-
VICE-MALE CLERKSHIPS.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister
of Finance whether an examination was
recently held for male clerkships in the
Northern Ireland Civil Service; how
many candidates sat; how many passed
the test, and what number of marks did
each candidate receive; how many of the
successful candidates were interviewed by
Selection Boards; how many were appointed to positions in the Civil Service;
and whether he will give the name and
address and the number of marks received
by each of the candidates so appointed.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I am replying to this question
as Financial Secretary.
An examination in connection with a
competition for Male Clerkships in the
Civil Service of Northern Ireland was held
on the 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th July last,
at which 117 candidates sat. Interviews
which formed part of the competition were
accorded on the 26th, 27th September and
3rd October to the 36 candidates who were
placed first in order of merit in the examination. One of these candidates did not
present himself for interview. The eight
candidates who obtained the highest
aggregate marks were declared successful
and will receive appointments in due
course, provided they furnish the Civil
Service Commissioners with satisfactory
evidence respecting age, physical fitness
and character.
A table showing in detail the marks
awarded to all candidates, indicating the
successful by name and the unsuccessful
by examination number, was issued to
candidates on the 6th instant and will be
published in due course in pamphlet form
together with the regulations, etc.,

SILENT VALLEY SCHEME-
RECENT PROSECUTION.
13. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that in a
recent. prosecution brought by the
Ministry against a man who refused (for
health reasons) a job at the Silent Valley
scheme, the magistrates decided that the
case should be dismissed; whether he could
state under what section of the Unemployment Insurance Acts this man was
prosecuted, as it is commonly believed
that an insured person has the right to
refuse an offer of unsuitable employment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The prosecution to which the
hon. Member probably refers was taken
under Section 22 of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, 1920, on the ground that
the workman had knowingly made a false
representation for the purpose of obtaining unemployment benefit. The workman had, in fact, refused an offer
of work which had been made to
him and, without notifying the Department, had continued to claim unemployment benefit. On the facts before
the Department, it appeared that there
had been an attempt to get benefit fraudulently. The Justices, however, took the
view that the workman was not actuated
by motives of fraud. As regards the suitability of the work offered, a medical
examination made beforehand by the employer's doctor showed that the man was
physically quite fit for the employment,
and the Department's view that the work
was suitable has since been upheld by a
Court of Referees to which the claimant
appealed.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman prepared to compensate this man for
the wrongful prosecution his Department
instituted against him?
Mr. ANDREWS: No.

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill has
for its object the amending of the exist
ing Housing Acts, by altering, and in
cases increasing, the Government
Grants, and otherwise continuing the
operation of the Acts for another year.
As the law now stands, the existing Acts
come to an end on the 31st March, 1928.
Hon. Members are aware that under these
Acts grants are made in respect of houses
coming within a fixed minimum and a
fixed maximum, viz., 500 superficial feet
as a minimum and 950 superficial feet
as a maximum, and in these cases a free
grant is given by the Government of £80
where the house is erected within 6
months, and £60 where a longer period is
taken to build. In addition to that, local
authorities have power to increase these
grants either by giving £100 loan free of
interest for a period of 25 years and remitting the rates for a period not exceeding 5 years, or by giving a free grant of
£40 and remitting the rates for 5 years.
Before dealing with the Bill which
embodies the Government's future policy
in regard to the housing question I would
like to give the House a few figures show-

ing the number of houses that have either

will show that the Government can claim

Hear, hear.) I find that from the commencement of the Housing Acts in 1924
up to date no less than 8,217 houses have
either been built or commenced or under
consideration, and that includes houses
for which plans have been lodged. Of
these 1,669 have been erected by local
authorities, and up to date no less than
5,314 of these houses have been built and
the subsidy paid. But an interesting
analysis of the figures I have given goes
to show that of the 5,314 houses already
built, 4,317 houses had an area of over
650 superficial feet, and 997 houses were
under 650 superficial feet.
If a further analysis of the figures was
taken it would go to show that the vast
majority of the figure of 4,317 houses
were of an area approaching the maximum
size, namely 950 superficial feet, and after
very careful consideration the Government have come to the conclusion that
while the present arrangement has done
much to relieve the house shortage, and
while the building of the larger type of
houses has done much to lessen the
pressure for the small houses, a great
deal needs still to be done to provide the
houses of the type which are within the
means of the working man. The Government feel that the present need of the
larger type of house has been met, and
they should now cease to give subsidies in
respect of the larger type of house, and
increase the subsidy for the smaller type.
Accordingly, the Government in this
Measure propose that as from the 31st
March, 1928, no further subsidies should
be paid in respect of the larger type of
house, and that payment in the future of
subsidies should be limited to houses of
an area of not more than 650 superficial
feet.
They also propose that the subsidy
should be increased from £80 to £100,
provided the house is completed within
6 months from the period when the
foundations are put down, and where
a house takes a longer period to build,
the subsidy will only be £80. They also
propose to continue to the local authorities
the right, if they so desire-and I certainly trust that they will continue to
help as they have done in the past-

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I have listened

by. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Until 1910 there was no city in the kingdom where houses were so cheap as were
to be found in the City of Belfast. I

Under Secretary for Home Affairs will

rent of houses in Belfast was something

was to be found in the cities of Manchester and Birmingham and other large
cities in Great Britain. How was that?
Because private enterprise was able to

cheaper than they can get by modern
methods.
I hope the hon. Member the Leader of

against Governments and Corporations

get over this difficult period. I hope it

Colonel WOODS: I have just a few
points to bring up on this Bill. Of one
of them I think the Ministry of Home
Affairs is aware. The local authority is
really the building authority for Belfast,
and the Ministry of Home Affairs approve
generally of any plans the local authority
pass as correct. I find that sometimes
delay of months has been caused in the
offices of the local authority, in Belfast,
the Corporation, in passing plans. The
delay does not occur in the Ministry of
Home Affairs. I have found that out.
The average time is about ten days for
the plans to be approved and everything
to be inspected by the Ministry of Home
Affairs, but the local authority do not
act with the celerity they should. They
take mouths to pass the plans and they
have rules and regulations of their own
which they break very gaily themselves,
but of course do not allow any outside
builder or any one coming in to break.
That is one point. Another thing that
strikes me as extraordinary is that
Government money, or the subsidy, should
be given without some restriction as to the
materials supplied. We find that French
and Belgian cement, Continental doors
and windows, German baths and lavatory
fittings, Belgian lead of all descriptions,
German and Belgian steel beams and rods,
glass, electric cables, wiring, and lamps,
and all kinds of nails and screws are used
in the construction of houses in Belfast.
These things are all foreign, so that we
are subsidizing foreign trade. Of course,
I know there is a considerable amount of
difference between Continental prices and
home prices, but could not something be
done under this Bill to restrict this use
of foreign materials in some degree?
There is very little difference in baths and
lavatory fittings and plumbing work.
Could not there be some restriction on the
Government subsidy to see that British
goods are supplied? That is a point I
wish to bring to the notice of the Government.

Now, after having disposed to my own

houses will be erected, say, for the City of
Belfast. As some one has pointed out

supremely important question, but in

the working classes, particularly in

their places of business. In other words,
there seems to have been no intelligent
direction so far as house building is concerned in Belfast. Houses have been built
in practically the whole of the suburbs of
Belfast. The rents of those houses from
the workers' point of view have been fairly
high if not exorbitant, and, in addition
to that the worker has been compelled to
pay away a considerable amount of his
wages each week on car fare.
With some intelligent direction the
probability is that this could be obviated
to a considerable extent. I understand
that there are plans in the much-maligned
City Hall at the present time showing the
industrial areas of this city where it is
highly desirable in a way that houses
should be built. I am quite conscious of
the drawbacks of this idea, because,
speaking personally, I would much rather
live in the suburbs of the city than in
the heart of an industrial area. I want
to say that quite frankly. But many of
the houses the dilapidated houses-that
have fallen into disuse in many parts of
the industrial areas could be profitably
knocked down and a lesser number of
houses to the acre erected on those sites.
How many houses to the acre are going
to be built of this smaller type of house?
Has that question received the consideration of the Ministry of Home Affairs, or
does it mean that for thirty or forty years
we are going to have a continuation of a
state of affairs that I regret to say exists
very extensively in the constituency I
represent? Does the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) never take a walk
through the slums of the Shankill Road,

of Belfast are housed at the present time,

Now there is another very important

believe that if the builders are left to
themselves they will satisfactorily solve

knowledge of house building that in every
type of house building there are rings
existing. I do not care what portion of
the house you take, whether it be bricks,
whether it be timber, whether it be light
castings, or any other commodity necessary for the erection of a house, you will
find that there are rings which are maintaining the prices. It is my opinion for
what it is worth that the question of
house building if left to public enterprise
is never going to be solved.
It is easy
to point out that we had sufficient houses
prior to the war. Yes, but most people
have learned a good deal since then, and
one of the lessons which, in my opinion,
the estate agents of Belfast have learned
is to keep a scarcity value on houses in
Belfast, or in other words never to allow
again a surplus of houses to obtain in
Belfast, so that they may get a scarcity
rent for those houses when decontrol
comes, particularly for the smaller type
of dwelling. That being so, it is necessary that the whole of the public bodies

No Member of the House has really

Rent Restrictions Bill—
Second Reading.
13 OCTOBER 1927


Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions
(Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill is
introduced for the purpose of removing
two abuses which have arisen under the
existing Rent Restrictions Acts. The first
abuse is in connection with the letting of
furnished houses. As hon. Members are
aware, a house let as a furnished one is
in some respects, i.e., as regards the rent
to be received, exempt from the provisions
of the Rent Restrictions Acts, and as a
result of this an abuse has grown up
whereby unscrupulous landlords-and
may I say, however, that I do not think
that the vast majority of the landlords
come within this category-are in the
habit of putting a few sticks of furniture,
sometimes one bed and a table or even less,
and letting the house as a furnished one.
This is such an obvious evasion of the provisions of the Act that it is clearly one that
should be made right, and accordingly it
is proposed to enact that the house shall
not be regarded as a furnished one unless
the house is let with all such furniture,
other than "plate," cutlery, and linen
and culinary utensils, as is reasonably required, having regard to the character of
the house which is proposed to be let as a
furnished one. In other words, a house
let as a furnished one must be a bona fide
furnished house. I think hon. Members
will agree as to the desirability of curbing
such an abuse, and I do not think it is
necessary to elaborate that part of the
Bill further.
The second abuse is one dealing with
the one-house owner. As hon. Members
are aware, section 5 of the Act of 1920,
as amended by the Act of 1925, provides
that a landlord may obtain possession of
a house where it is required as a residence
for himself or his wife, or for his relatives
as specified by the Act, and in order to
avoid possible abuse and misrepresentation in regard to obtaining houses on the
ground that the owner wants it for himself or his wife or his relatives, it is expressly provided that where a landlord has
by an Order of the Court obtained possession by representing that he required the
house for himself or his wife or his relatives, and subsequently it transpires that
these representations were fraudulent, the
Court can subsequently order the landlord
to pay compensation to the tenant for the
loss that such tenant has suffered. It will
be apparent to hon. Members that this
remedy is only available to tenants whose
landlord has obtained an Order of the
Court as a result of an action brought by
the landlord. That Act makes no provision for the case where the landlord has
served a notice to quit, and the tenant,
on the facts represented to him, has come
to the conclusion that it is useless to
resist giving up possession, as an Order
would be made against him if the case
came into Court. It may, however, subsequently appear that the representations
which induced the tenant to give up possession were fraudulent, and as the Act
now stands it makes no provision to make
the landlord amenable.
Hon. Members will agree with me that
it is illogical that the tenant who forces
his landlord into Court before giving up
possession should have a remedy, whereas
a tenant who does not force his landlord
into Court should have none, and accordingly we propose to remedy this state
of affairs by providing that where possession of a dwelling which is within the
provisions of the Act is obtained by
fraudulent representation, the tenant
shall have his remedy against the landlord, whether an Order has been made
for possession or not. I do not think there
is anything further for me to say.
I
think everybody will agree that these two
abuses should be remedied as soon as
possible. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE:
I agree that the

not

BELFAST BOARD OF GUARDIANS
-SPECIAL OUTDOOR RELIEF.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has seen the report of the Belfast Poor Law Guardians'
meeting, held on Tuesday, 11th October,
at which it was decided that special outdoor relief would be discontinued after a
certain period; what steps is he prepared
to take to prevent the Guardians from
executing such a drastic resolution;
whether he is aware that even under Commissioners appointed in certain places by
the Government of Great Britain a more
adequate scale of relief is given to the
destitute unemployed than is now given
by the Belfast Guardians, and will he
state whether he is prepared to lay down
Regulations to govern the granting of outdoor relief, and the amount of such relief,
to be given through the Belfast Poor-Law
Guardians.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A copy of the
Minutes of Proceedings of the meeting
of the Belfast Board of Guardians, held
on the 11th instant, containing the resolution referred to, has been brought to my
notice. The Ministry of Home Affairs
is not empowered to interfere with the
Board of Guardians in the exercise of their
discretion in connection with the granting
of special outdoor relief, full discretion in
this respect being vested in the Guardians,
who are responsible to the ratepayers for
their policy and action.
It is possible that in certain areas of
local government in Great Britain the
scales of outdoor relief may be somewhat
higher than those generally granted in
Belfast, but the scales adopted in Great
Britain vary very considerably from place
to place and, even in particular areas,
from case to case. Accordingly, no useful
purpose would be served by making a
comparison between the arrangements in
force in Belfast and those in operation in
any other part of the United Kingdom.
The Belfast Board of Guardians carefully consider every case that comes before
them, and in the exercise of their statutory
powers grant such relief as the individual
claims appear to warrant.
The powers of the Ministry of Home
Affairs are limited to prescribing the
general conditions under which special outdoor relief may be granted, and once
these conditions have been prescribed the
Ministry has no power to interfere with
the Guardians in connection with dealing
with individual applications or to prescribing the amounts to be granted.
At the same time I should add that I
have communicated with the Board of
Guardians in connection with a miscon-
Oral Answers

regard to the financial restrictions imposed

FREE WIRELESS LICENCES FOR
BLIND PERSONS.
a
4. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is
possible for blind persons in Northern
Ireland to obtain free wireless licences, as
they can in Great Britain; whether
difficulty has arisen through certain
county councils in Northern Ireland having no register of blind persons; and if
so, has he taken any action to ensure that
such registers are compiled, so as to enable
blinded soldiers and other blind persons
in Northern Ireland to obtain free wireless licences in future.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Wireless
Telegraphy (Blind Persons Facilities)
Act, 1922, authorises the issues of a free
wireless licence to
any blind
person in
Northern Ireland.
A blind person is defined for this
purpose as a person who produces a certificate issued by the Council of the County
County Borough in which he is
ordinarily resident that he is registered as
a blind person.
or
The Ministry brought the provisions of
the Act to the notice of the local authorities in a circular letter, dated the 7th of
March, and the local authorities were
requested to take steps to compile registers
of blind persons so that they might be in
a position to take advantage of the concessions offered.
It is the case, as suggested by the hon.
Member, that difficulties have arisen by
reason of the fact that certain county
councils have no registers of blind persons,
but it is not considered desirable to press
the county councils further in this matter
pending the publication of the census,
containing particulars of the numbers of
blind persons in each county in Northern
Ireland.
Major SHILLINGTON: Might I ask
the right hon. Gentleman if a Register
could not be compiled by enrolling on it
the names of those in receipt of blind
pensions, and soldiers and sailors who
have become blind and whose names could
be got from the Ministry of Pensions and
St. Dunstan's?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid
such a Register would not be complete,
but I am just as anxious as my hon.
Friend is that provision, such as he suggests, should be made for these blind
persons, and if he has any suggestions to
make and will confer with me later, I will
see if I can do anything in the matter.

UNEMPLOYMENT IN QUARRYING
INDUSTRY.
11. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the comparative figures for 1925, 1926, and 1927
showing the extent of unemployment in
the quarrying industry in Northern Ireland; whether the industry has suffered
and is suffering acutely from lack of orders,
and whether he will consult with the
Minister of Commerce as to what action it
is proposed to take to assist the industry.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The average extent of unemployment among persons engaged in
quarrying in Northern Ireland was 23 per
cent. in 1925, 33.2 per cent. in 1926, and
18.4 per cent. for the first nine months of
1927.
I am glad to say that there has been a
steady improvement in this industry since
January, and that to-day, out of 1,600
persons attached to it, only 175, or 10.9
per cent. are registered at the Employment Exchanges as unemployed. This
shows, I think, that the industry as a
whole is not in the position that the hon.
Member suggests.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce and I are at all times most
anxious to encourage the use, to as great
an extent as posible, of the products of
Northern Ireland quarries.

BILL PRESENTED.
Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing
Bill,
"to amend the law relating to the Sale
and Supply of Intoxicating Liquor (including Methlyated Spirits and Methlyated
Ether), the Registration of Clubs, and
the Licensing of Theatres and Music
Halls; and for purposes connected therewith," presented by Sir Dawson Bates,
supported by the Attorney-General (Mr.
Babington) and the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs
(Mr. Hanna).
Mr. DEVLIN: Would I be in order in
raising again this question of the procedure by which Bills are introduced into
this Parliament ? I understood, Mr.
Speaker, from your ruling on the last day
that it was quite within the province of
the Prime Minister or any Member to present a Bill in the form in which it is
proposed to present this Bill to-day, but
I may point out that in my judgment this
method of procedure is narrowing the
powers of this Parliament. We are denied
the right of discussing these Measures on
the First Reading, and I do not think,
considering the time that is given by this
Parliament to parliamentary work, that
those Members of the House who are quite
willing to give their time and attention
to all the legislative proposals submitted
to the House should have their rights and
liberties taken from them in this manner
by the Government simply placing the Bill
upon the Table instead of having it introduced for a First Reading, thereby
enabling the Members of the House to
discuss it.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): First of ail, I should like to
say that this House is making no departure from the Imperial Parliament in the
custom of its presentation of Bills. The
object of handing the Bill in at the Table
to-day is, as is well known to all Members
of the House, to enable the Bill to be
printed in order that it might get into
the hands of individual Members so that
they could study it before the real discussion takes place upon the Second
Reading. In other words, if we were to
adopt the other principle, which is sometimes taken in the Imperial Parliament
on very important Bills, Members would
really have nothing whatever before them
to indicate the nature of the Bill about
to be introduced. I can only repeat that
the Government would adopt any system
which would help the Opposition if it
was within the ordinary rules of parliamentary procedure. I can think of none
which is more simple than having the Bill
printed and circulated, as this will allow
about a week before we come to the Second
Reading. During this time Members of
all parts of the House will be able to
familiarise themselves with its contents
and will be in a fit position to discuss it.
There never has been in my recollection
or knowledge any other procedure in the
Imperial Parliament than the one we are
carrying out here.
Mr. SPEAKER: Bill read a First
time. Second Reading?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Tuesday.
Mr. GYLE: I think one week is much
too short to enable us to go into all the
various matters in connection with this
Bill, and I would respectfully suggest to
the Government that we get at least one
fortnight to consider it before the Second
Reading.

Clause 2 of the Bill deals with the protection of persons refusing to take part in
an illegal strike or lock-out, and is designed to render Clause 1 effective in
practice. No member of a trade union or

Now I come to Clause 3, which deals
with the question of intimidation, and in
order to make the effect of this Clause
plain I must go back to the law as it
stood before 1906. Prior to the Trade
Disputes Act of 1906 the law regulating
the right of persuasion was regulated by
the Conspiracy and Protection of Property
Act of 1875. Under Section 7 of that
Act every person who, with a view to compelling any other person to abstain from
doing or to do any act which such other
person had a legal right to do or abstain
from doing, wrongfully or without legal
authority used violence or intimidation
towards such person or his wife,
children, or watched or beset the house or
other place where such other person resided, or worked, or carried on business,
or happened to be, was liable to certain
penalities, or to be indicted; but if such a
person attended at such a place in order
merely to obtain or communicate information he was not deemed to be watching or
besetting the house within that Section.
or
Under this Section no one had a right
to watch or beset the house of a person
for the purpose of compelling him to work
or abstain from working, but Section 2
of the Trade Disputes Act, 1906, made
it lawful for one or more persons acting
on their own behalf, or on behalf of a
trade union, or of an individual employer
or firm, in contemplation or furtherance of
a trade dispute to attend at or near a
house or place where a person resided, or
worked or carried on business, or happened to be, if they attended merely for
the purpose of peacefully obtaining or
communicating information or of peacefully persuading any person to work or
abstain from working.
The House will appreciate the change
that this effected in the law. The Act of
1906 did not make intimidation legal but
permitted persons to attend in numbers
for the purpose of peacefully persuading
workers to abstain from work, and, unfortunately, many abuses have arisen
under this section. During the general
strike of last year in Great Britain there
were between 7,000 and 8,000 prosecutions
chiefly for intimidation, and the defence
put forward in most of these cases was
that the defendant was justified because
he was a member of a picket. Moreover,
the Courts had decided that intimidation

under the Act of 1885 meant threat of

between peaceful persuasion and intimidation is very narrow, there have been innumerable cases where, without actual

a large picket at a man's house has raised
apprehension in the minds of himself and
of his wife and children far more coercive

his own person. We all know that mental
and moral intimidation is often more

we do.

Clause 3 is designed to prevent intimidation of any kind, whether accompanied
by actual violence or not. Sub-clause (1)
of this Clause is merely declaratory, and

Clause (2) defines intimidation to cover
mental and moral intimidation arising in
the mind of any person from apprehension
of injury to himself or any member
of his family. This, I may state for the
information of the House, follows a recommendation made by a Royal Commission, presided over by Lord Dunedin, in
1905, clarifies the construction of the
Act of 1906, and makes it clear that under
the protection of that Act intimidation
cannot be practised in a way in which it
was never intended it should be practised
by the framers of the Statute.
Sub-Clause (4) makes it unlawful to

to persons engaged in à trades dispute,
because, apart from the protection afforded

or beset any man's house, and "watching"
and "besetting, " which are the words
taken from the Conspiracy Act of 1875,
are terms well known in law, and cover

comfort as would at law amount to what
is called an actionable nuisance.
Clause 4 contains new provisions as to

it stood prior to 1913 had certain

those statutory objects, and the collecting
of funds for political purposes was not one

trade unions, subject to the provisions of
the Act, to apply the funds of the Union
for certain political objects.
Before putting the powers given by this
Act into force, every trade union was

Sir ROBERT LYNN: No Member of
this House can as a rule put his point

speech, his mind has become somewhat

made a speech made up of confusion and
misrepresentation. He reminds me somewhat of the Irishman who addressed a
friend on the road, and said: When 1
saw you in the distance I thought it was
yourself. When you came near me I
thought it was your brother Mick, but
now, begorrah, it is neither one nor the
other." (Laughter.) Listening to his
speech, I was beginning to wonder where

hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) would step into

in the year with regard to the Trade
Disputes Bill in England. In those

Every branch should get all its inbrief
dividual members to write a
letterthank goodness for thatat once to the Member of Parliament
representating the division in which
they reside asking him to oppose the
new Trade Disputes Bill and Trade
Unions Bill.
And then he proceeded :--
Our members should also get their
wives and friends to write similarly,
and in every instance the letter should
be written as from a voter in the
division. This is by far the most
effective method of impressing a
Member of Parliament and making
him feel that it would be a very
dangerous thing for him to act in
opposition to the requests of such a
large number of constituents.
Not only was this sent out but he gives
them eight very strong adjectives all of

that I hope the House will not be too much
put out of its stride by any resolutions
that are sent along.

My hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) asked at

Northern Ireland? It is a fair
in
enough question. I say the answer

suffered just as much from the general
strike as any part of Great Britain.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Therefore, it is of the utmost importance that
we
should have the same legislation
against general strikes that Great Britain
has had since July last. My hon. Friend
also asked who desired us to introduce
this legislation. Well, I can say quite
truthfully that personally I was never
spoken to by an employer, but I have
been asked to support legislation such as
is before the House this day by scores of
trade unionists-
Mr. BEATTIE: Mention the unions.
Sir ROBERT LYNN-active persons
who are not-
Mr. BEATTIE: Mention the organizations.
Sir ROBERT LYNN-out for revo-
Jutionary or political purposes but who
are out to do the best they can
for the trade union movement, a
thing that revolutionary trade unionists
certainly are not out for. I say
to my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) that,
so far as the Act in Great Britain or the
Bill here is concerned, it has not been
introduced with the object of doing
injury to the trade union movement, and
it has not been introduced through fear
-neither the one nor the other. It has
been introduced for the purpose of protecting the State. Public memory is not
so short that it forgets what happened in
May last. An attempt was then made to
coerce the Government by inflicting hardship on the community as a whole. A
handful of revolutionary Socialists made
an attack not only on Parliamentary
institutions that have been in existence
for nearly a thousand years but also on
the people themselves, and I would point
out to my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) that
the last attacks of the sort that were made
were by two Stuart Kings, one of whom
lost his head and the other lost his
kingdom. It is not a very wise thing to
attack a Parliamentary institution that
is as broadly based as the Parliamentary
institution in Great Britain is and has
been. I say that that conspiracy was
defeated not so much by the Government
of Great Britain but by the people themselves (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and I say these people have a right to
look to us either in Westminster or in
Belfast to see that they are protected
from similar attacks in the future.
The learned Attorney-General (Mr.
Babington) in his lucid speech referred to
the right hon. John R. Clynes. Mr. Clynes,
writing in October last, says thisand I hope my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle)
will subscribe to what Mr. Clynes says
if he will not subscribe to what Members
of the Government or I say—
No Government, Labour, or Conservative, or any other, could permit its
responsibility to the country as a whole
to be torn from its grasp by a section
of the community, however large, engaged in conflict with another section,
however powerful.”
That is exactly what Mr. Clynes and his
friends did earlier in the year. They
allowed one section of the community to
get into loggerheads with another and
try to overthrow the constituted Government of the country. If the Trade Unions
Act had been on the Statute Book then
we would have been saved all the loss and
all the misery of the general strike, and
not only that but the trade union leaders
would have been saved from the folly of
their own weakness.

workers in our shipyards, the workers in

be anxious that this Bill should be placed
on the Statute Book.

Mr. Bridgeman to violate habeas corpus

permitted free invasion of private houses

Yet all the time he never ceased to protest his affection for the deserving poor,
and his voice shook with sobs as he described the villainy of his opponents.

Then we have the most vital part of the
Bill, that dealing with political funds.
I asked the Attorney-General how many
trade unionists in the North of Ireland
contributed to the political fund of the

He did not tell us how many people had

right to contract out. Every trade
unionist in the North of Ireland who is

party opposite took very good care to instruct their followers that this was a levy
for the upkeep of the Socialists. Certain
instructions, either verbal or otherwise,
were given to them to contract out.
The Political Levy Clause is about the
only clear Section of the Bill. If this
Section is passed only those members of a
union which has a political fund will be
liable to contribute to that fund, who
send a notice in the form set out in the
Schedule to the Bill. At present a member has to claim exemption from the
political fund. In future all those who
do not volunteer to subscribe will be
exempt. A voluntary contributor can
withdraw his consent and in that event
will cease to be liable after the following
January 1st. Rules of unions with political funds will have to be altered within
six months of the passing of the Act to
make the rules comply with the new provisions. All contributions to the political fund are to be levied and made
separately from other contributions.
Then we come to that part of the Bill
dealing with Civil Servants. We are
told that Civil Servants should be outside
political parties, and that they should be
subservient to the Government in office.
Has any case been proved where they have
failed to do their duty to any Government that was in office? I think that as
the British Government failed to prove
that the Civil Service was a menace to any
political party in office, they had no
justification for including this Clause in
the Bill. These provisions are complicated, but their effect appears to me to be
as follows. The Regulations governing the
Civil Service are in future to contain provisions which will prohibit established
Civil Servants from being members, delegates, or representatives to any organization, the first object of which is concerned
with wages or conditions of employment
that is, of course, a trade union-unless
the membership of such an organization
is limited to employees of the Crown.
Such an organization must not affiliate
with and must be independent of any outside organization, and it must not have
political objects or be associated in any
way with any political party.
That is a pretty drastic thing for any
employer to say to his employee that he
cannot vote or do as he likes, but must
do as his employer tells him outside his regular working hours. That is what the
Clause means. He has his full citizen rights,
but he cannot contribute to the funds of
the Labour party even if he wants to
do so. That is a high-handed way for
any employer to deal with his employee.
If a Civil Servant has been a member of a
forbidden union for six months before the
Bill is passed he may remain a member
if he is, or may become, entitled to certain
friendly benefits. If a Civil Servant knowingly commits a breach of these provisions
he is to be disqualified from membership
of the Civil Service. That provision is,
of course, devised for the purpose of
creating a Civil Service which will keep
clear of the Labour party and trade union
movement. It is based on the same principle as prevents the Army and Navy and
the Police from having a trade union.
It is not difficult to see the reasons for
this restriction.
The Bill contains another Clause for
giving freedom to trade unionists. No
public authority will be allowed to compel
an employee or a prospective employee to
join a trade union or to impose any kind
of disability upon a person who refuses
to be a trade unionist. This Section in
practice is only likely to apply to
Labour local authorities. Apparently
the Government is not only anxious
to
create a blackleg Civil Service,
but is doing all it can to have
blackleg service for public authorities.
This is another example of the faith which
the Tories have in democracy when it does
not work their way. This is not all, however. Any employee of a public authority who leaves without notice, on strike
or otherwise, will be liable to a fine not
exceeding £10 or three months in gaol if
he knew or had reasonable cause to believe
that his conduct would hinder or prevent
the authority from discharging its funca

The Bill as a whole is not wanted.
Nobody has asked for it. Repeatedly
Government members have declared
against a Bill of this kind. One Member
to-day made the statement that all the
people in Northern Ireland were lawabiding citizens and constitutionists.
This Bill is designed, in the words of
members of the Conservative party, to
prevent extremists from coercing the
Government or the community. If there
is any place in the world this Bill is unsuited to, according to statements from
the Government Benches, it is Northern
Ireland. I hope the Government will
take it away and disabuse their minds of
the idea that a Bill of this kind is required
in our area. I believe it is an insult to
the methods that have been employed by
decent trade unionists in the North of
Ireland for the past number of years.
I will conclude by making one or two
general comments. Up to the present
where the rights of a member of a trade
union were infringed only the member
could take proceedings, but in future the
Attorney-General may apply to the courts
if there is an application of the funds of
a union contrary to this Bill. In addition
to interfering busybodies of the past we
are now to have the Attorney-General
protecting the rights of the poor trade
unionist. All unregistered unions will in
future have to send to the Registrar their
accounts in the same way as registered
trade unions.
This is my opinion of this complicated
Bill: The right to strike is being taken
away; the sympathetic strike of any widespread or effective character is illegal;
Civil Servants are barred from organizing
with their fellows in the working-class;
the political funds of the Labour movement-this is the aim and object of the
party opposite are to be taken away;
public employees are in peril. There is
not a word about lock-outs, not a word
about employers' organizations, not a word
about victimization, and not a word about
Tory funds. This indeed, is a blackleg's
charter, and I have the greatest pleasure
in supporting my colleague in this most
damning indictment of the Tory party
who have now introduced it.

There was also a reference made to the
44-hours strike. Before I deal with my
association with that strike I want to
point out that the majority of these fulltime trade union officials secured these
jobs by deluding the poor members of the
trade unions, and making them believe
that it was necessary to have a full-time
official to look after their interests.
do not say that in regard to every case,
but it refers to many cases. After
they have got these positions as full-time.
officials they have discovered they have
quite a lot of spare time and that it is
not necessary to look during full time.
after the interests of trade unionists in
Northern Ireland and Great Britain.
They want to become politicians and
Members of Parliament, and they want
the trade unionists to pay them for
Occupying that position. That is the
reason why these people are opposing this
particular Bill.
In connection with the 44-hours strike,
the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) yesterday tried to make a point
of my association with that strike, and the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin), who does not know a great deal
about trade unions, but is very anxious
to pick up some scraps as the discussion
goes along, thought he had caught a point
when the hon. Member for East Belfast
stated that I was going up Cromac
Street to the gasworks, but he
covered in time, and corrected that statement. I just want to state fairly how
this 44-hours strike arose, and how I
became associated with it. For a considerable time the workers of this country had
been trying to secure shorter hours. Their
hours previous to that strike were 54 hours
per week.
The employers offered them
47 hours without any strike or without
any trouble at all in the industry. Then
resome of these enterprising trade union
leaders thought they would have a 44hours week instead of 47 hours. The
result was that a ballot vote was taken.
As a member of a trade union I was entitled to vote, and I voted in favour of
accepting the employers' offer of 47 hours,
but the majority of the members voted
for the 44 hours. The result was that I
had to go out of work along with the other
members. The members of my trade
union were of the opinion that I was a fit
and proper person to represent them on
the Negotiation Committee in connection
with the strike, and although I was defeated on the ballot vote yet I did not
sulk in my corner. I made up my mind
I would go on the Strike Committee and
represent the interests of the members of
the union that I am associated with.
I am very glad for many reasonssome of which I hope to put before the
House this afternoon-that I did take
an official part in the 44 hours' strike.
Some of the lessons I learned during
that strike convinced me that it was time
that legislation was passed to prevent
strikes of this sort ever recurring in any
industry. During the time that strike
was in operation-somewhere I think
from January, 1919, until some date in
February, 1919-most, if not all, of the
Members of this House are aware of the
state of chaos that existed in the city of
Belfast. Attempts were made to destroy
a good many of our public services.
Suggestions were even made at that
Strike Committee and I make this statement and I accept full responsibility for
it-that some of our larger power stations
in the city should be blown into the air,
and that tramcars should be tumbled in
the streets. We all know that the heat
and light in most of the places in the city
were cut off. On many occasions we had very
urgent messages from leading surgeons
and local hospitals asking that the light
might not be cut off in the hospitals as
they had some very urgent and important
operations to perform. Yet amongst
these so-called friends of the workers
suggestions were made that the light and
heat should be cut off the local hospitals.
I am very glad to say that with the assistance of some people who had some selfrespect at any rate, we were able to prevent these extremists carrying their plans
into operation.
I also want to point out to the House
that during the period of negotiations in
the Midland Railway Hotel when the late

Mr. GRANT: I am convinced that
until such times as all full-time officials
are put upon strike pay there is always
the danger that in strikes the real issue
will be very often lost sight of, and trade
unions themselves are beginning to realize
that. One of the largest trade unions in
the country at the present time is going
to amend and revise its rules.
I was
looking up to-day some of the suggested
amendments, and one of their amendments
put forward for consideration by this
union is as follows:
When a strike takes place all officials,
full-time or otherwise, are to be paid
dispute benefit only.
If that was in the rules of all trade unions
in this country I do not believe we would
have a single strike. It is all very well
for men of £4, £5 and £6 a week to talk

who are on the streets that hardly ever

of the strike. I am very glad to say that
the trade unions themselves are beginning
to take this matter up.

Then there is the question of intimidation. We all know how this peaceful
persuasion is carried on. The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) stated
yesterday in this House that I
panied him on this peaceful persuasion.
I certainly did go down to the Belfast
shipyards, but I never spoke to a single
man about not going to work, because the
men who had decided to go on strike were
so loyal to each other that they never
made any attempt to go to work. There
was no necessity for peaceful persuasion.
Mr. BEATTIE: Then why the necessity for this Bill?
Mr. GRANT: Another question in connection with this Bill is the contribution
tc the political fund of the trade union.
The peculiar thing about the political
fund is this: Only people of one particular
party can get money out of this political
fund. A Unionist or a Liberal or a
Nationalist contributes to this fund, but
they never get anything out of it. No
one can get any money out of the political
fund except the Socialists. If the
Socialists are so anxious to have a political
fund let them pay into the fund themselves
and use the money for their own purpose.
They have no right to expect people who
have other views on the matter to contribute to their party funds. Just let me
give an illustration of what will take
place. If the Leader of the Opposition
(Mr. Kyle) and myself were fighting a
seat in North Belfast, the consequence
would be that under present circumstances while he is a trade union representative and I am a trade union representative, actually at the end of the
election I would have to contribute towards his expenses for my fighting the
seat against him. That is a ridiculous
position and I think it is time it was
remedied.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) in his speech yesterday stated there
were roughly about one hundred thousand

people affected by the question of contracting out I think I am correct in making

were to be put to great inconvenience by

I do not accept
If
those figures at all. I am not going to

But I do not believe those figures.
there are only one hundred thousand

Surely it is only fair and reasonable

would make this suggestion to the hon.
Members opposite. I believe that if those

that party would fail to send their subscriptions back if the members did not
send in their contracting-in notices. I am

and they do not care where they get it
from.
This Clause further provides that
political contributions should be levied
separately from any contributions to the
Labour union funds, and that the ordinary
funds of the union shall not be used for
furthering political purposes.
In my
opinion this is the part of the Bill that is
touching the Labour party very sorely.
It is not the contributions paid in by the
political levy they are worrying about.
They are worried because the Government
are going to take care that the ordinary
funds of a trade union are not going to
be tampered with for political purposes.
That is the goose that lays the golden egg
for the Socialist and Labour party, and
they see it drifting out of their sight. I am
very glad this Clause has been put into
the Bill for those reasons.
The next Clause deals with the Civil
Servants of the State.. This Clause does
not interefere with the right of any Civil
Servant to vote for the Unionist,
Socialist, or any other party he pleases.
He has that right under the Bill. I believe this Clause is put into the Bill for
the protection of Civil Servants.
We
may have a Civil Servant who would be
injudicious enough to take a very prominent part in connection with the party
that is in power in the country at the
moment. If that party was turned out
that Civil Servant would be placed in a
very awkward position. If the Socialist
party, or any other party, got into power
the first thing they would do would be to
make some excuse to remove that person
from his position. Sometimes it is
necessary to legislate to protect people
even from themselves, and so I think this
Clause deserves the support of every Civil
Servant under the Northern Ireland and
Imperial Parliaments.
There is one particular Clause in this
Bill that I do not like, that is the Clause
dealing with the employees of municipal
bodies. It has been admitted publicly on
many occasions by the largest employers
of labour in the country that they prefer
to deal with their employees through the
accredited trade union representatives. I
think this Clause has left a loophole for
bringing in people who are not members
of a trade union, and who would offer
themselves for employment at a lower rate
of wages than the rate prevailing in the
district. As a result of that there would
always be the danger that the standard
rate of wages would be considerably
lowered. If so, it would become very low
then. This would also encourage the return of sweated labour. I certainly
would like the Government to do something to improve this Clause and not to
encourage non-union labour.
Clause 7 prevents the illegal use of
trade union funds. I do not see how the
Opposition could oppose that Clause.
Trade union funds are gathered together
for a definite purpose, and it is very regrettable to hear members and officials of
trade unions say their members were
entitled to superannuation and other
benefits, but owing to the misuse of the
funds they could not get those benefits.
We see in the reports of the Trades Union
Congress and of the Labour party where
they can spend large sums of money on
political propaganda, and yet they cannot
pay their poor, old superannuated members the benefits they are entitled to.
This Clause is a very worthy Clause and
one that ought to get the support of all
really genuine trade unionists.

Now I pass from the hon. Gentleman,

Government in introducing a Trade
Union and Trades Disputes Bill which
we believe is designed to cripple the
activities of trade unions, and further
we are of opinion that nothing of an
untoward nature has happened in the
Six Counties to justify the introduction
of the Bill
I cannot see in what way this Bill is
going to cripple the legitimate activities
of trade unions. The resolution says that
nothing of an untoward nature has happened in the Six Counties to justify the
introduction of this Bill. I think we are
too sensible to fall into the trap so easily,
but at the same time, if there is a reason
for passing this Bill it is this that it is
better to be forewarned than forearmed.
There is no harm in having this Bill on
the Statute Book. Those who are afraid
of it must presumably anticipate that
something will happen, otherwise they
would not object to it.
When the Leader of the Opposition got
up to oppose this Bill he said that no employer in Northern Ireland had asked for
it. Well, I propose now to make good
that omission by pleading for this Bill,
and when I do so I would like to make it
perfectly clear that as an employer I give
way to nobody in the whole of the Six
Counties in the high opinion I hold of the
genuine trade unionist who is working in
our midst. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Any employer who is against the
legitimate trade unionist is a detriment,
a drag, and a curse to the country. I
speak of the legitimate trade unionist, the
trade unionist who carries out his function as a go-between between the workers
and the employers, helping the employer
to regulate the terms and hours of employment. In this connection I think J
can honestly say that the Leader of the
Opposition has done as much as any trade
union leader in the country to promote
good feeling between employer and worker
in Northern Ireland.
But when a trade union begins to
dabble in politics and insists that trade
unionists shall subscribe to a political
faith in which they do not believe, then I
say they are going outside their proper
and legitimate functions. The Leader of
the Opposition said this legislation was
simply class war. He knows just as well
as I do that class warfare is the very last
thing that will do any country any good,
and thank God we see daily across the
water speeches by Labour leaders which
show that class warfare is becoming a
thing of the past. Mr. Thomas pointed
this out only last Sunday. The hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in
his speech said that if we are to do any
good it will only be by Labour Leaders
and employers coming together and examining together the problems of our
daily life in a spirit of peace and harmony,
and not by bickering and biting at each
other. I believe there is to-day a real
desire on both sides to come together and
work together and when that has been
accomplished, and not until then, will
Great Britain again attain the place in
the world's markets that she held in the
past. As soon as that day arrives we will
get back to our own position in the world
and we will live in a more peaceful and a
more contented country.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
Independent Members of this Parliament
have been described by the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) as cooing
doves. I do not know that I raise any
serious objection to that name because one
of the wisest men who ever lived penned
these words long years ago:
:-
A soft answer turneth away wrath,
but a grievous word stirreth up anger.
If my conduct in this House has been
in the nature of soft answers I am more
proud than if it had been in the nature of
grievous words, because I think we have
had too many grievous words in this
country. We have been inclined far too
much to accentuate our differences, and it
is because I feel that this Bill is of the
nature of grievous words that I will
oppose the Second Reading. It is fairly
generally recognized at the present time on
all hands, both by leaders of industry,
leaders of the Labour movement, and by
the community generally, that the great
essential for our industrial situation at
the present time is peace, and it is because
I believe that this Bill will not bring peace
but a sword that I will vote against the
Second Reading of it to-day.
The Government here and the Government in the Imperial Parliament missed
one of the finest opportunities ever presented to a Government in this country
to help forward the only thing that is
going to produce the peace that is so
essential in our industrial prosperity, to
help forward the feelings of goodwill and
co-operation between the different industrial arms in this country. As I said
before, I believe that this Bill is likely not
to produce peace but irritation. Just
take, for instance, the reasons given by the
right hon. and learned Attorney-General
(Mr. Babington) when introducing the
Bill. He said that the Bill was born,
conceived, and passed into law because of
what? Not because of anything that has
occurred in this area, but because of the
general strike and prolonged coal stoppage
that had occurred in another country.
Just let me quote here the testimony
paid to this community with regard to
their behaviour on this and other occasions
-I mean our industrial community in
Northern Ireland. Let me quote the
words of the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews). He is reported as having
said at Downpatrick that he was thankful
to be able to state that there was no
country in the world so peaceful as Northern Ireland, no land where crime was
less and where the will to maintain law
and order was stronger or so generally
held by all classes and creeds. They read
of war in some lands, of rebellion in
others, of rioting in several capitals, of
industrial strife on an extended scale in
many countries, but there in Northern
Ireland they remained free from all these
curses and impediments to national and
social progress.
He looked, therefore, to
the future of Northern Ireland
confidence.

war. The

Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I feel

and after the prolonged coal stoppage
there was in this country a similar feeling,

may be a blessing in disguise to this

both sides to see the absolute stupidity of

disputes.
I feel that if the Government, instead

we have in this Bill, which I think is
likely to produce irritation, which is likely
to produce suspicion, had only helped to
consolidate and strengthen the machinery
that is in existence at the present time
for negotiations and arbitration they
would have being doing this country a

possible, in the first instance, to travel in

that, with the awakened national conscience we have at the present time in
regard to these matters, if Labour would

as a means of settling industrial disputes

of this country would see that Labour got
a fair do.

general strike from an ordiary strike is
this: it is a strike not of employees against
employers, in order that their industrial
