The hon. Member for North Belfast, the
Leader of the Opposition, said yesterday
that this Bill made all strikes illegal.
"Every strike were the words he used.
It does nothing of the kind. A strike
carried on for ordinary industrial purposes
can take place in the future just in the
same way as it has taken place in the past;
and, further, a sympathetic strike can take
place in future, provided that it is conducted within reasonable limits, and is not
an attempt to hold up the entire community. Hon. Members may say that
there is no danger of a recurrence of the
general strike in Great Britain, and no
danger of a general strike taking place
here. Well, it is quite true that many
leading trade unionists in Great Britain,
both before and since the general strike,
have condemned it in no uncertain terms,
but other leading trade unionists have expressed approval of it, and have gone so
far as to talk about the next general strike.
For instance, Mr. Hicks, who is, I think,
president of the Building Trade Operatives, and a past president and member of
the executive of the Trades Union Council,
stated a short time ago that it would
appear that general strikes of a more intense and formidable character than the
one recently experienced are inevitable,
and many other Socialist leaders have said
exactly the same thing. Therefore, my
colleagues and I feel that it is the duty
of the Government to protect the community from a catastrophe of the kind.

depression in agriculture, to put any
additional burden on the rates to warrant
the appointment of a drainage officer.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

of the hon. Member, he is desirous that
the Government should give a grant to
County Councils to
to enable them to
appoint an engineer for the purpose of

expenditure on the schemes themselves, I

utility of such a grant; and, in any event,
to make such a grant for such a purpose
would strike at the whole basis of the
Drainage Act of 1925, which is to place.

P.E.S. TEACHERS' SUPERANNUA-
TION.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he proposes to amend
the Public Elementary School Teachers'
Superannuation Scheme, so that service
rendered by a public elementary school
teacher in a poor-law union or public
elementary school shall be deemed pensionable service; and, if so, will existing
pensioned teachers be included in the
scope of the amendment.
Mr. POLLOCK: I regret that I am
unable to adopt the suggestion of the
hon. Member. The Teachers' Superannuation Scheme is a contributory one,
and the proposal would involve the recognition, for pension purposes, of service under a local authority, in respect of
which no pension contributions have been
paid.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
FUND.
3. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state how much
was contributed during the year ended
31st July, 1927, by the secondary teachers
to the Pensions Fund, and how much was

£2,000.
SCHOOL BOOKS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether his attention has been
called to the complaints made by
Regional Education Committees and the
poorer parents of school children, that
owing to the policy of publishing new
class and story readers every year, and
using one set of readers in one school and
another set in another school, that poor
parents are put to unnecessary expense,
especially when they move from one part
of the country to another, the time of
moving not coinciding with the time
when new classes are formed and new
readers are prescribed, and the books
which the children bring with them having to be set aside and others purchased;
and will he consider the propriety of
adopting the policy which was pursued
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 OCTOBER 1927

by the Commissioners of National Education of preparing and publishing a set of
readers and obliging teachers to use them
to the exclusion of all others.
Mr. HANNA: In the absence of my
hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Robb), I
have been asked to answer this question.
The Ministry is not aware that the
present system of issuing a list of recommended books and leaving the choice of
the books to the managers. and teachers
has been the subject of any serious
complaint.
As stated by the hon. Member, the
Commissioners of National Education at
one time prepared and published sets of
reading books, the use of which was made
obligatory, but this policy was subsequently abandoned by them, as, on
educational grounds, it was considered
desirable to allow as wide a choice of
books as possible.
Experience has shown that it is most
important that pupils should have access
to a large variety of reading matter, and
could not be restricted to a single set of
readers without injurious effects on their
progress.
I may add that, under the Education
Act, it is within the discretion of Education Authorities to provide or assist in
the provision of books, stationery and
other school requisites for pupils attending public elementary schools in their
area.
JUNIOR CERTIFICATE
EXAMINATION.
5. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he can explain the seemingly incredible result that only 26 per cent. of
the girls taking the 1927 Junior Certificate Examination passed in geography,
although 92.6 per cent. of them passed
in English.
Mr. HANNA: English and geography
are quite distinct subjects, and there is
no reason to expect that a high standard
in English will be accompanied by a correspondingly high standard in geography
or in any other particular subject.
I would remind the hon. Member that
the teaching of geography upon modern
lines is only a very recent introduction
into the secondary curriculum, and that
the Ministry, while satisfied that progress
is being made, is not surprised if examination results in geography are inferior
to those in subjects whose teaching has
been established on sound lines for a
considerably longer period.
Mr. GYLE: What I wish to know from
the Parliamentary Secretary is this, is the
education authority not surprised that
only 26 per cent. passed in geography as
compared with 92.6 per cent. in English?
Mr. HANNA: I am not in a position
to answer that question.
Mr. DEVLIN: Could the hon. Gentleman tell the House why the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
is not here?
Mr. HANNA: I understand he is
unwell.

TOOME EEL FISHERY COMPANY.
12. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether the Toome Eel
Fishery Company, who claim not only the
eel fishing rights of Lough Neagh (an expanse of some 150 square miles), but also
the bed soil of the lough, contribute any
revenue to the Government, or in any way
contribute towards the services to which
they claim full rights, such as law enforcement, police, etc., and, if not, will he
consider the introduction of legislation to
provide that all property of the company
shall contribute by rates and taxes its fair
quota towards the State and local authorities for these services.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The poor-law valuation
of the property of the Toome Eel Fishery
Company is £1,280. The company is, of
course, rated in the ordinary way on this
amount by the local authorities in the
counties of Antrim and Londonderry in
respect of the portions of their property
situated in those counties respectively.
They are also liable for income tax in the
same way as any other business concern.
Over and above these rates and taxes the
company is under statutory obligation to
contribute annually to the Coleraine
Board of Conservators either 10 per cent.
of the total poor-law valuation of their
property or the aggregate amount of the
statutory licence duty payable on the
engines used by them, whichever of these
sums shall be the greater. It will thus be
seen that on a poor-law valuation of £1,280
the company is obliged to contribute at
least £128 every year to the Coleraine
Board. From information furnished to me
I understand that excluding income tax the
total payments made by the company
amounted in all to £725 in respect of the
year 1926. The hon. Member is, of course,
aware that these payments, in part at
least, are applied to the services mentioned
in the question. Having regard to the
information which I have given the last
part of the question does not arise.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Could the right
hon. Gentleman say what was the date
of the last valuation of the interests of
this company?
Mr. BARBOUR: I would require notice of that question.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Might I ask the Minister of Commerce if he has noticed from
the newspaper reports of the sittings of
the Commission, which started to inquire
into this matter during the past week,
that it was stated that the Lough Neagh
Eel Fishing Company produced an annual

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
that the Clause be now read a Second
Time. This is somewhat of a technical
matter, and I will endeavour to explain
the real meaning of the Clause. As the
Committee is aware, under Section 1 of
the Housing Act of 1924 local authorities are empowered when selling their
houses to tenants to accord to them the
benefits first of all of the Government
grants which the local authority has received and of their own subsidy which
they are empowered to make. In other
words where in the past the Government
made a grant of £80 to a local authority
in respect of each house and where the
local authority passed the general reso
lution agreeing to give £40 in respect of
a similar class of house built it is open
under the Act referred to for the local
authority to sell that house to the tenant
at the actual cost of the house, less the
sum of £80 and less the sum of £40.
That is to say in other words, if a house
cost £360 it is open to the local authority
to sell the house to the tenant for the sum
of £240.
Of course, as hon. Members are aware,
those figures are varied now because we
propose under this Bill to increase the
figures from £80 to £100. Hon.
Members are also aware that under the
Act it is open to the local authority in
lieu of making a free grant out of the
rates up to £40 in respect of a house to
give a free loan, that is to say, to give a
loan of £100 free of interest for a period
of 25 years. Now it has been represented
to the Government, and I am sorry that

Hon. Members will notice that these
words we propose should be inserted
mean that in future there will be no such
thing as letting as furnished a house with
a valuation of £8 and under. That is
the principle of the Amendment. I have
found during my experience, and I am
sure it has been the experience of all the
Members of this Committee, that when a
house with a valuation under £8 becomes
vacant a large number of very poor
people are unable to pay the exorbitant
rent charged through what we call certain
pieces of furniture being put in. I
believe this is a fair and reasonable
Amendment, and is going to protect the
very poorest of the poor.
The Amendment also prevents a tenant
who through economic circumstances cannot pay the full rent, if there are two
vacant rooms upstairs, sub-letting an
empty house that he cannot let as a
furnished house. Our Amendments also
go on to set up a system whereby adjudication can take place where these cases
arise as to what is really a fair rent
under that condition of affairs. In the
meantime the principle of our first
Amendment is to prohibit the letting of
furnished houses with a valuation of £8
downwards. Other Amendments will
follow, but I think the most important
is this one.
When the 1926 Act was before the
House I made a speech, and I think I
would not be justified if I did not make
an explanation. I got certain information and answers from the Minister of
Home Affairs, and as a result of my remarks and the replies of the Minister we
have had hundreds of cases that were
subject to court proceedings withdrawn.
The landlords have settled up and have
made arrangements for the tenants
according to the retrospective payments
they would have been entitled to if they
had been taken before the courts.
The landlords who are guilty of the
infringements which we exposed on the
last occasion in this House are, in consequence of the answers given by the
Minister, afraid to go to the courts. We find
it difficult to get them to go to the court.
Here is a point we are going to make.
We are going to secure that every house
entered under that valuation is going to
be let at an economic rent, or the rent
allowed by the Act, and we are going to

Mr. CRAWFORD: I wish to move
the resolution which is on the Paper in
my name. I understand that a very few
minutes can be devoted to this purpose.
Stated in ordinary every-day language,
this Antrim Electricity Supply Bill has
received a First and Second Reading, and
I propose that the Committee stage and
Third Reading be adjourned till 1928.
The promoters of this Bill find that there
are some difficulties in the way of getting the Committee stage carried
through; they ascertained that if the
Bill did not reach the final stages
before the prorogation all proceedings
would be discontinued. They were exceedingly anxious to get the Drainage
Bill through, as the idea was to have the
two things run concurrently and thus
save a great deal of money in carrying
out both schemes. The schemes are
closely interwoven, and it would be an
imprudent thing to proceed with the
one without the other. This Parliament
has power to carry over the scheme, and
it will be for the public interest, and
no hardship will be inflicted upon any
person by asking that this matter be
adjourned till 1928. The promoters of
this scheme will receive no benefit and,
in addition, those people who think it
their duty to oppose the scheme will have
no disadvantage imposed upon them. It
is in the public interest. I beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PENSIONS OF MODEL SCHOOL
TEACHERS.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education whether he can
state the number of years which have been
added, for pension purposes, to the actual
service of the teachers of the Public
Elementary Schools, designated
"Model
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
25 OCTOBER 1927
Schools," which have been transferred to
the Regional Education Committee and
Education Committees; by what Statute
or Statutory Order this has been done;
and from what service the expenses involved have been provided; and, further,
whether he proposes to add years to the
services of teachers of small schools scheduled for closing, or which have been
closed, with a view to providing these
teachers with sufficient pensions.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to reply to
this question. On the transfer of Model
Schools to the local education authorities,
an addition of years to their actual service
for purposes of compensation has been
made in the case of those Model School
teachers who were serving as such on 1st
February, 1922, and who therefore come
under the protection of the Government
of Ireland Act. The number of years
added varies according to the age of the
teacher and length of service; the maximum period added in any case is eleven
years and ten months. This addition of
years has been granted by the Civil Service
Committee acting under the powers conferred upon them by Sub-Sections (4) and
(5) of Section 55 and the Eighth Schedule
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
The expenditure is defrayed in the first
instance from moneys voted by the Imperial Parliament, but is finally borne by
Northern Ireland by deduction from the
residuary share of Reserved Taxes.
In regard to the last part of the question, there is no power to award additional
years for the purposes of pension to the
actual service of any other class of teacher.
I may add that I am informed by the
Ministry of Education that in the case of
the closing down or amalgamation of
schools, every possible facility is provided
for teachers to transfer to new schools and
in those cases where it is not possible, to
retain them on the staff of the amalgamated
school as privileged assistants. As far as
the Ministry of Education is aware, there
is no instance of a teacher having been
compelled to retire prematurely on pension
owing to the closing down of the school
in which he or she was serving.
FEES OF MODEL SCHOOL PUPILS.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether he can state how
the fees paid by the pupils in model
schools before they were transferred were
distributed; the number of fee-paying
pupils on the rolls of these schools on the
31st March, 1927; the aggregate amount
of fees paid by these pupils; and the number of teachers receiving aid from the
funds so created.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): As the answer is
long and complicated I propose to hand
it to the hon. Member and have it circulated.
The following is the reply:
Up to the date of the transfer of model
schools to the education authorities the
method of distributing the school fees was
as follows:
1. Teachers appointed to model schools
on or before 31st December, 1917, constituted a privileged class, each being entitled to receive from the general school
fee fund the amount which he would have
received had the method of distribution
in operation prior to that date remained
in force, viz:-
(a) If a Principal and appointed to a
model school between 1st April, 1900,
and 31st December, 1917, £10 in lieu
of local aid.
(b) Whether Principal or Assistant,
a share of the residue of school fees
-a Principal's share being twice
an Assistant's share.
(c) A share under (b) was arrived at
on the basis of including all model
school teachers, but was paid only
to the privileged teachers. The
residue on which the shares were
calculated was reduced by excluding
therefrom the sum of £20 per annum
for each headmistress appointed
between 1st April, 1900, and 31st
December, 1917, which was formerly paid from the school fee
fund, but is now a charge on the
Education Vote.
2. The sum remaining in hands after
the claims under (a) and (b) had been
met was allocated amongst the schools
in the proportion that the fees collected
in each school bore to the total fees collected
4B

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
from all the model schools, subject to the
condition that the amount allocated in
the case of any particular model school
should not be greater than the excess
(if any), of the amount of fees collected
in that school over the amount of the
payment to the privileged teachers serving in the school.
The sum allocated under (2) to a
model school was distributed amongst
the teaching staff in the proportion of
two shares to a head teacher and one
share to an assistant teacher.
The Ministry has no record of the
number of fee-paying pupils on the rolls
of model schools.
The fees collected from pupils in the
calendar year ended 31st December,
1926, amounted to £1,086 9s 5d, which
amount was paid to 109 teachers.

Proportional Representation 2254
Proportional Representation
25 OCTOBER 1927
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Proportional Representation.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House is of opinion that
before the principle of Proportional
Representation embodied in the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, is abolished,
a Select Committee of this House be set
up to consider and determine whether the
Government have legal authority to set
aside the provisions of the said Act, and,
if so, to define the boundaries of the new
constituencies."
Mr. KYLE: I rise to move the Motion
standing in my name, and I would beg
Members of the House to read carefully
the terms of the Motion. They will see,
if they do me the honour to read it, that
the Motion is not, as has been hinted by
more than one Member opposite, a defence
of Proportional Representation as such,
but simply have the Government the right
to abolish Proportional Representation,
and, if they have the right, that a Committee of the House should be set up to
determine the boundaries of the
stituencies in the Six Counties. Of course
Section 14, Clause 5, of the 1920 Act gives
this Parliament the legal right to change
the method of election. Perhaps I had
better read the Section itself:
con-
After three years from the day of the
first meeting of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland that Parliament may
alter the qualification and registration
of the electors, the law relating to elections and the questioning of elections,
the constituencies, and the distribution
of the members among the constituencies, provided that in any new distribution the number of the members shall
not be altered, and due regard shall be
had to the population of the constituencies other than University constituencies.
It will, therefore, be seen by this Section
that the Parliament has the legal right,
but what I really think is the more important aspect of the case, has it the moral
right? This Parliament was established
on the principle laid down in Section 3
of Clause 14. It is as follows:
The members shall be elected by the
same electors and in the same manner
as members returned by constituencies
in Ireland to serve in the Parliament of
the United Kingdom, except that at any
contested election of the full number
of members the election shall be according to the principle of Proportional
Representation, each elector having one
transferable vote, as defined by the
Representation of the People Act, 1918.
I contend that if the Government
abrogate this Section of the Act that the
whole Act of 1920 might very well be
superseded. I would warn those sections
of the citizens whose rights are protected
and governed by the Act of 1920 that a
change of the character enunciated by the
Prime Minister to the Orangemen on the
Twelfth of July-a very strange method
and strange way of announcing to the
country an important change of this character-is very dangerous to their rights.
Already some sections have suffered by
Government action in setting aside the
protection given by this Act in consequence of what the Government allege to
be changed conditions. The right hon.
Gentleman the Minister of Finance referred to model school teachers who contend that they lost something by the
changed conditions, and by the setting
aside of what they conceived to be their
due. What I am suggesting is the condition laid down by the 1920 Act. In
fact, if the change adumbrated by the
Prime Minister is made there is no reason
why the 1920 Act may not go altogether.
It was stated at the time of the passing
of the 1920 Act that Proportional Representation afforded protection and re-
Sir Worthpresentation to minorities.
ington Evans in the Parliamentary
debate in the House of Commons in 1920
when this Bill was being considered said
that
Proportional Representation was introduced into the Act as one of the safeguards by which it was intended to
protect minorities.
I think that was the reason for the passing of this and other Clauses. The Local
Government (Ireland) Act, 1917, had the
same idea of protection and representation of minorities. There again the
principle of Proportional Representation
was laid down. It will be recalled by the
Belfast Members of the House at least
that as a result of that Measure the Belfast election for local government pur-
2255 Proportional Representation.
Proportional Representation. 2256
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Kyle]
poses in 1920 resulted in the return of
ten Labour men, ten Nationalists, several
Unionist Labour nominees and a few Independents. Immediately after these
elections which were held under Proportional Representation-and I would
like to tell the Government they followed
immediately after the 1919 big strike
which was referred to the other day in
the House the Unionist Party in the
Corporation and outside it got thoroughly
scared about what was happening to their
-as they alleged-people in the city
of Belfast, and their leaders in the Corporation declared that this fair and equitable representation of minorities would
have to cease and they would see
that the Government-their friendswould abolish Proportional Representation in local elections. This was stated
by Sir Crawford McCullagh who at that
time was a Member of the House for
South Belfast.
It was a terrible state of affairs that
anybody save Unionists should be returned at the head of the poll in Belfast,
and that Independents were returned
who would not answer to the crack of the
Parliamentary Whip. Some people say
that as a direct result of these elections in
Belfast, which had for the first time
secured the return of representatives in direct proportion to the number
of electors who voted for individuals representing their point of view, the
Unionist Party got so alarmed that they
decided to abolish this system of elections
which ensured this perfectly fair representation for the people. As to those
people who do not think that Proportional Representation can work out
fairly I would recommend them to read
the 1920 report for the city of Belfast so
far as Local Government Elections were
concerned, and they will find that every
vote cast for a particular type of candidate
was used in the final results which is
entirely different to the system that the
Government intend to inflict again on the
people.
The Unionist Party did a much worse
thing than even abolishing Proportional
Representation in Local Government
Elections. It was they who instituted a
campaign for the driving out of employment of all those who did not see eye to
eye with them. This campaign was
started by a meeting held-without protest
from the Harbour Commissioners, itself
an entirely Unionist body elected on a
fancy franchise-on Harbour Commissioners property, where meetings have
been and are forbidden unless by special
sanction of that body. This meeting was
called under the auspices of that body of
whom the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) is the
chairman and of which Lord Carson is

2261 Proportional Representation

Proportional Representation

These editors also tell the country that
France tried Proportional Representation,
and that it failed there. These gentlemen
must be aware that they are misleading
the public, because they surely know that
the system that was in force in France
was not Proportional Representation as we
know it at all, but a system which could
be more properly described as the
majority-bonus system. Let me read the
House an excerpt from the Report of the
Commission on Universal Suffrage in the
French Chamber of Deputies. It is in
the Official Report of that body, No. 4625,
for 1927, page 25. The Report states:
""
The law of 12th July, 1919, is in
reality essentially a majority-election
law. An examination of Article 10
clearly shows this. If one party possesses an absolute majority of the votes
polled, that party secures all the seats
for the constituency. It is only in a
subsidiary degree, and where an absolute majority has not been obtained,
that the electoral quotient becomes
operative as a second method of distribution. Further, in respect of seats
not allotted by the electoral quotient the
majority principle is again invoked.
All the remaining seats are awarded to
the largest of the contesting parties,
that is to the list which has a relative
majority over the others.
"" 'An examination of the other
articles of the law makes it equally clear
that whenever the majority principle
came into conflict with the proportional
principle, the legislature solved the
difficulty by sacrificing the proportional
to the majority principle.
It will be seen by this report that the
editors of the papers in Belfast and outside Belfast who talk about France as having a Proportional Representation system
either do not know what they are talking about or, as I rather suggest, they
are wilfully misleading the public on this
question and endeavouring to prejudice
the minds of those who have not got
access to the facts of the case.

constitute forty per cent. of the population
of the Province rule four of the councils
out of 84. And we are asked to sit here
and to listen to the platitudinous statements of the Prime Minister about how
happily things will go along if we sit down
and submit without being outraged at this
attempt to constitute in a Parliamentary
sense the very system, which is a scandal
in any democratic age, and which I have
ventured to describe with the figures I
have quoted to the House in relation to the
rural councils. The result is that in
Ulster we do not exist. It would not be
known that there were Catholics and
Nationalists in Ulster if it were not that
I come here three times a week and say so.
So far as power is concerned, or the right
to exercize our power, or influence in the
State, or partnership in the welfare of the
community, or being allowed to say or do
anything that can in the least degree
prove that we are Ulster people, we might
as well be black as white citizens in our
own community. I am not, without a
most firm and vigorous protest, going to
stand here in this House and allow you to
do in Parliamentary affairs what you have
done in local affairs.
I am not a revolutionist and I never
was, and I may say in passing that-the
right hon. Gentleman (The Prime
Minister) did not state it out frankly; he
might have done it frankly, because I
understand that his chief boast is that
he is an outspoken and frank exponent
of what principles he holds-he charges
us with being enemies of the British
Empire. That was the innuendo that
lay in his suggestion, that on one side
you have the Empire and on the
other side the disruptionists of the
the Empire. I resent a charge of that
sort. The worst thing that ever happened to the Empire was to innoculate it
with revolutionary ideas, and that was done
by the party with which the right hon.
Gentleman the Prime Minister was associated. The first time we ever heard of
rebellion or revolution we heard it here
in Ulster, and it was not against the
Nationalists but against the authority of
Parliament which you now regard as so
sacrosanct. If the British Parliament,
about whose glory we have heard so
much, and whose prestige is so essential
to the stability of our institutions, if this
Parliament had dared to pass an Act of
Parliament, put it on the Statute Book.
and put it into operation, you threatened
to rebel. You organized rebellion, and
you have no right to charge me, who
never threatened to rebel, and, what is
more, never did rebel, and, what is further, never will rebel.
If I were less of a believer in constitutionalism; if I did not see the misery and
disaster that revolution bring to humanity, I confess and in this respect,
though I am not perhaps regarded,
simply because I am a constitutionist,
as the fitting exponent of the views of
many of my co-religionists in Ulster--
this I do say that in the position of things
which I have ventured to describe in this
recital I have given of how the Catholics
of Ulster have been treated, if ever we
got as near provocation for rebellion in
anything we got it there. To tell people
that they must obey the law and yet
have nothing to do with the administration of the law; to tell them that by
counting numbers, or heads, or
questions can be decided; to say that by
a policy of electoral manipulation by
scientific gerrymandering you can
them of every inherent right of citizenship, even down to the management of a
rural council, is quite enough in my
judgment to have justified many of these
men who refused to recognize your
Parliament or to take any responsibility
for or any part whatever in the government of Ulster. I read a speech the
other day I do not like to refer to these
things, though I may say in passing that
it is a great pity that some of the greatest orators in this House do not make
their speeches in this House.

English Government saw the necessity for

The Prime Minister stated that when the
1920 Act was introduced the present
Government of Northern Ireland would
never have accepted the principle of Proportional Representation but for the fact
that he thought the Free State Parliament was going to operate and have the
principle introduced into that Parliament.
I think that admission amounts to this,
that the Prime Minister for the sake of
protecting the minority in the Free State
was willing to have the system of Proportional Representation introduced into
Northern Ireland. Now he has no concern and no interest in the protection of
the minority in Northern Ireland when
he is not concerned with the Free State.
I would like to draw the attention of
the Prime Minister to the fact that in the
Senate of Northern Ireland, with Proportional Representation here, there is not
a single Catholic representative. The
Senate of the Free State, where election
is by nomination, consists of one-third of
his co-religionists. The judiciary of the
Free State, which is nominated by the
Free State Government, consists of nine
judges, five of whom are co-religionists of
the Prime Minister. In the Northern
Ireland High Court Judiciary there is not
a single representative of the minority.
One of the causes for the introduction of
this Bill-I think the Prime Minister's
speech was a clear admission of it—is the
fact that the present Government have
lost so much ground that they are not in
a position, under a fair, just and equitable
system of election, to face a disappointed,
exasperated and highly dissatisfied people.
It is a demonstration of their acute
realization, at this moment of the day,
that they have lost so much ground, so
much of the confidence of their own followers of their hopeless failure to deal
with the vital and material affairs that
affect the people who have been so long
neglected, of their failure to stabilise industry and to re-establish business and
industry in Northern Ireland. It is the
throwing of the ascendancy bomb and
throwing the match on the slumbering
forces of bigotry, the obscuring of the
issue, and mismanagement, inefficiency
and incompetence by the Government
which have brought about the present
state of affairs in Northern Ireland.

suffer for the sins and inefficiency of the

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 26th October, 1927.

The House met. at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
MEMBER SWORN.
Thomas James Stanilaus Harbison,

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Proportional Representation.
Order read for resumption of adjourned
debate on Question (25th October):
That this House is of opinion that before
the principle of Proportional Representation embodied in the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, is abolished, a Select
Committee of this House be set up to consider and determine whether the Government have legal authority to set aside the
provisions of the said Act, and, if so, to
define the boundaries of the new constituencies. (Mr. Kyle.)
Question again proposed.

Babington): Before I say anything with
reference to the Motion before the House
may I be allowed to congratulate the hon.
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Harbison) who has taken his seat here today for the first time-(Hon. Members:

to voice their sentments and feelings, the
2363 Proportional Representation
Proportional Representation 2364

[Mr. Babington]
people of those two great counties of Fermanagh and Tyrone, who have returned
the hon. Member to this House, will
never lack for adequate expression of
their views and opinions. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
This debate has wandered over practically the whole field of politics, and it
would be impossible for me at this hour to
do more than make one or two very cursory remarks upon the debate and its
conclusions. The first point that was
made, and, indeed, it is taken in the
Notice of Motion itself, was that there was
in some way or other a bond or contract
by which this system of election that is
known as Proportional Representation
was to continue in the interests of minorities, and that the intention of this Government to do away with Proportional Representation would be a breach of that
bond or contract. I have been asking
myself as to who was referred to when
this bond or covenant was alleged to have
been given. What minority was it intended to protect? I do not think it can
have been intended to protect the minority
which is now represented by the official
Opposition, because at that time they
were not in existence. I do not think it
can have been intended to protect the
somewhat heterogeneous party that is represented under the head of Independents, because they were not in existence.
Therefore, if it were intended to protect
any minority it was intended to protect
the minority referred to by the Prime
Minister, the minority which is represented by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) and the new hon.
Member (Mr. Harbison) who has just
spoken to this Motion.
But was it intended that it should protect them-if it were so intended, and I
think it is very doubtful whether that was
the intention-was it intended to protect
them indefinitely? It is quite plain from
the Statute itself, which says that this
Parliament is to have power to alter its
electoral system after three years. It is
quite obvious that Parliament contemplated that it should be altered or might
be altered. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Therefore, what we are considering now is whether it is proper for this
Government to use the power that was expressly given to it to alter this system of
election, and, as the House has clearly
got power to alter this system of Proportional Representation, the matter really
resolves itself into a debate, or should so
resolve itself, upon the merits of this form
of representation.
We have heard a lot upon the merits of
Proportional Representation. I really need
not refer to it at any length. It is perfectly
obvious that every Member of this House
has studied the matter with great care.
We have had a speech from every single
Member of the Opposition, whether he be
a Member of the official Opposition or one
of the Independents. They have all
spoken upon this Motion. Therefore, I
take it that they have all made up their
minds upon this question of Proportional
Representation. The hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) quoted, as
against the array of figures and statistics
given by the Prime Minister, two or three
of what he was pleased to describe as intellectual Tories. Well, I do not know
what the hon. Member would describe as
an intellectual Tory. I have listened to
him in this House for a considerable time
now, and I have gathered that no Tory
ever had an intellect according to his
view. At any rate he quoted these intellectual Tories, and suggested that we
should follow their opinions.
But why should we follow their opinions
when their own party in Great Britain
does not follow them? When, instead of
putting this form of electoral reform into
force in England, they wait until they get
a convenient opportunity in a Statute
which is applying to Ireland, they put it
in there in order to see how it would work,
and, being suspicious as to whether it is
going to work or not, they say that at the
end of three years this Parliament shall
have power to get rid of it. I think the
House-certainly Members on this side of
the House-will agree after this debate
that this particular form of representation is one which should be got rid of.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We have
heard all the arguments for it and against
it. We find that it is not in use in any
other part of the United Kingdom.
not treated, as I understand, with very
great favour even in the Free State, and
in a great many countries, as has been
referred to already, where it has been
tried, it has also been found wanting.

This protracted debate is now drawing
Division No 59]
to a conclusion. The Government ask the

AYES
Question put,
"That this House is of opinion that before the principle of Proportional Representation embodied in the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920, is abolished, a Select
Committee of this House be set up to consider and determine whether the Government have legal authority to set aside the
provisions of the said Act, and, if so, to
define the boundaries of the new constituencies."
The House divided: Ayes, 11; Noes, 24.

NEWTOWNSTEWART PETTY
SESSIONS CLERK'S SALARY.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the salary of the
Clerk of Petty Sessions in Newtownstewart is £60 per annum, and whether he
can state on what basis that salary is
fixed; whether, if this officer resigned
and a salary were fixed for the new
appointment, such salary would be about
£90 per annum; and whether any increment attaches to the salary as experience
and work increase; and whether the Ministry will appoint a small Committee to
consider the salaries of these officers.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The emoluments of
the Clerk of Petty Sessions in Newtownstewart, including War Bonus, amount,
approximately to £83 per annum.
The salary was fixed in conformity with
the order of the Lords Justices, dated 12th
November, 1921, under the Petty Sessions
Acts.
If this officer resigned, the salary for
the new appointment would be fixed under
the order of the Governor of Northern
Ireland, dated 13th March, 1924, and the
total emoluments would amount approximately to £99 on the assumption that the
district was not amalgamated with another one.
Petty Sessions Clerks become entitled
to an increment of 7 per cent after five
years' approved service, and a further
annual increment of 1 per cent for the
next five years; thereafter an annual increment at the rate of 1 per cent for a
further 30 years' service.
Having regard to the fact that the
AFFAIRS OF DONAGHADEE
URBAN COUNCIL.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of the
alleged illegal action of the Chairman and
Vice-Chairman of the Donaghadee Urban
District Council, in refusing to allow an
elected representative of the people to sit
and vote on their affairs from June to
October of this year, he is prepared to
order an inquiry into the affairs of this
local authority; whether he is aware that
the Surveyor under this Board is alleged
to have diverted a contaminated stream
into the public well, and that subsequently this matter was discussed at the
Board, and a vote of confidence in the
Surveyor was passed; whether he is satisfied that the health of this community is
being properly safeguarded; and whether
the Minister will print and circulate the
correspondence which took place between
his Department and the Council.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The action of
the Chairman and Vice-Chairman which
was taken in pursuance of a Resolution
of the Council, was to exclude from the
deliberation of that body a member who
was alleged to be guilty of disorderly conduct at a meeting of the Council. This is
not a matter in which I have any power
to interfere, nor would it justify the
exercise of my powers under the Local
Government (Emergency Powers) Act,
1921.
If the member concerned has been
illegally treated his appropriate remedy
would appear to be in the Courts.
I have already intimated to the Coun
cil in reply to a Resolution from that
body that if they so desire, I am ready
to direct one of my Inspectors to hold an
Inquiry into the administration of the
Urban District to ascertain whether the
Council has refused or failed or is unable
to perform all or any of the duties
imposed on it. I have not received any
reply to that offer, and I have no
authority to hold such an Inquiry without such a request.

Mr. ANDREWS: The position to

those which the Irish Free State created

Kingdom scheme of Health Insurance.
It is a consequence of that severance that
insured persons then resident in the Irish
Free State had to become members of separate societies within that area. No person is now compelled to transfer from an
Irish Free State Approved Society to one
witihn the United Kingdom, unless he
comes to reside permanently within the
United Kingdom. If he does so, however, it is only possible to mitigate the

benefits.

fee of £22-10s Od.
A large majority of the candidates
admitted to training have served as pupilteachers or monitors, and as such have

In
the case of senior pupil-teachers an additional gratuity of £18 is also paid or
the candidate's admission to the College.
I regret that the Ministry is not in
possession of the other information sought
by the hon. Member.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agriculture.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I beg to move:
That, in the opinion of this House,
the agricultural needs of Northern Ireland have been severely imperilled by
the failure of the Government to take
adequate steps to deal with the
grievances suffered by the farmers.
I think that Members on both sides of
the House will agree that in tabling this
Motion which stands in my name I have
selected an industry which is more vital,
and more far-reaching, and more comprehensive in its possibilities for good or
evil than any other industry in Northern
Ireland. It is beyond all question the
most important industry in Northern
Ireland. It
embraces the greatest
quantity of labour. It is the greatest
source of wealth in addition to being the
oldest industry. Whilst I do not profess
to be able to contribute any constructive
criticism by way of highly technical or
scientific suggestions, I do suggest that I
am in a position through daily and
hourly association in rural areas with the
farmers in this community to interpret
the position in which they find themselves
and to convey to this House something

which they are passing at the present
time.

to-day of the Chairman of the Ballymena

With regard to bulls, there is a universal condemnation of the Department.
It is common ground that under the

Society and our exhibit at Balmoral;
miscellaneous agricultural services, £170;
and the Weeds Act, £600. There is also
a grant of £5,000 given to the Ministry
by the Minister of Finance, and we hope
that this will last for a period of years.

When we came into office in 1921
had to establish Research Stations which
are in being in various parts of the country. In addition to the Agricultural
Research Divisions already established,
viz.-
1. The Chemical Research and Animal
Nutrition Division.
2. The Seed Testing and Plant Diseases Division.
3. The Plant Breeding Division.
4. The Poultry Division.
5. The Animal Diseases Division.
a further Division to deal with Crop and
Animal Husbandry Research commenced
to function in 1926, and just recently the
Dairying Division was introduced-we
have not begun work yet. The work of
the Husbandry Division will be, in the
main, carried out at the farm at Hillsborough, County Down, which has recently been acquired. The acquisition
of the farm will also make available in
future greater facilities for investigations
in connection with animal nutrition problems which have hitherto had to be undertaken on local farms.
Most valuable research work relating
to fertilizers, soils and crops, seeds, the
economic feeding of farm animals,
diseases in plants, the production of improved strains of agricultural plants, the
economic feeding of poultry and diseases
of farm animals, is being carried out by
the Ministry's research staff. The largely
increased number of inquiries which are
being received from persons desirous of
obtaining advice under the foregoing
heads is clear evidence that the value of
research work is gradually being appreciated by the farming community.
The importance of research work in
connection with problems underlying the
poultry industry cannot be over-estimated. A considerable amount of investigation work in regard to the gradingup of flocks by egg-laying trials and the
distribution of pedigree birds has already
been carried out by the Ministry, but it
was felt that further research work in
connection with feeding, diseases, and
marketing problems was essential to the
continued development of the poultry industry. With a view to the attainment
of this object a scheme for the carrying
out of investigations into poultry nutrition and marketing problems at the
Hillsborough Experimental Station,
County Down, in conjunction with the
Rowet Research Institute, Aberdeen,
was submitted to the Empire Marketing
Board by the Ministry and the Board of
Agriculture for Scotland. The Empire
Marketing Board has sanctioned a maximum grant from its funds of £5,000 for
capital expenditure, and of £2,000 per
annum for five years for recurrent expenditure in connection with the poultry
research work to be undertaken at the
Hillsborough Experimental Station,
which will be the centre for the work in
the British Empire.
During the past year 29 Instructors
in Agriculture, Horticulture and Poultrykeeping and Butter-making were
employed in Northern Ireland by the
County Committees of Agriculture. In

were actively engaged in the poor and

Following the transfer of Agricultural
Services in Northern Ireland to the
Ministry of Agriculture, steps
immediatey taken to make provision.
whereby extended courses of training in
agriculture and horticulture would be
available for Northern Ireland students
generally, and it was decided to utilize
the Greenmount Agricultural School,
Muckamore, County Antrim.
An extensive reconstruction scheme, including
the erection of new buildings and the
provision of laboratories and equipment,
was carried through, and it can be claimed
that. as
result, the facilities for
advanced scientific training now available
at the college are equal to those at the
leading agricultural colleges in Great
Britain. In January, 1922, only six
students were undergoing instruction at
the Greenmount School, but since then
a steady increase in the number of
students in training has taken place and
there are at present thirty-six boys taking
out the course.
a
There are two residential schools of
training for girls, viz.-the Ulster Dairy
School, Cookstown, and the North-West
Agricultural School, Strabane, equipped
on the most modern lines for the teaching
of poultry-keeping, butter-making and
rural domestic economy, at which there
is accommodation respectively for 50 and
24 students. Prior to the taking over of
control by the Ministry of Agriculture of
the Ulster Dairy School, the majority of
girls taking out training were drawn
from outside the area now constituting
Northern Ireland. This condition of
affairs has, however, undergone a complete change and for a number of sessions
past all the students in training at the
school have been Northern Ireland girls.
The demand for training from Northern
Ireland girls is now sufficient to fill all the
places available at both the Ulster Dairy
School and North-West Agricultural
School, and, in fact, there is in the case
of each school a list of girls awaiting
admission.
The question of the provision of facilities for obtaining the most advanced University training in Agricultural Science,
leading to a degree in agriculture was one
that, from the inception of the Ministry
of Agriculture, received the closest attention, as in the absence of such facilities the programme of Agricultural Education was necessarily incomplete. The
efforts of the Ministry culminated in the
establishment of an Agricultural Faculty
at the Queen's University of Belfast.
The foundation stone of the new buildings
for the Agricultural Faculty, which will
possess the most modern laboratories and
equipment, was laid in May last. Valuable scholarships, tenable at the Faculty,
are offered each year by the Ministry of
Agriculture, and it is made possible by
this means for any Northern Ireland student, who possesses the requisite capacity,
to proceed to a degree in agriculture at a
comparatively trifling cost. Pending the
erection of the new buildings for the
Faculty, the work of the Faculty is being
carried on in the existing buildings of
the University. Twenty-two students
are at present in training in the Faculty.
The sum of approximately £28,000 was
provided out of public funds to augment
the amounts contributed from local rates,
for the purposes of agricultural schemes
under local statutory Commitees of Agriculture. The titles of these schemes indicate their scope:-Horse breeding,
cattle breeding, swine breeding, subsidies to agricultural societies, in aid of
shows, ploughing matches, et cetera ;
prizes for cottages and small farms, instruction in agriculture, winter agricultural classes, instruction in poultry keeping, poultry stations, instruction
butter making and home cheese making,
instruction horticulture and
management of bees and sheep breeding.

Hon. Members are aware of the work
undertaken by my Department in connection with the marketing of eggs, and
I do not propose to pursue the matter
further than to direct attention to some
current happenings.
It is not so many years since we
took Danish prices on the British markets
as something to work up to. The position
to-day is very different as can be seen
from any of the trade papers that give
regular price quotations. For instance,
in "
The Grocer of the 15th instant,
the quotation on the London market for
Danish, 15-161b. eggs for the long 100
(i.e., per 120) is 17s 6d to 18s 6d; while
Agriculture
Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Archdale]
our figure for 15lb. is 23s 9d., i.e.,
roughly 5s 9d per long hundred in our
favour or over 3d an egg more. For the
same paper in its issue, dated 22nd instant, the quotations for the Glasgow
market show Danish 15lb. at 19s 6d and
Ulster 15 lb. at 21s 6d. This is the
position as revealed by the public Press,
and it is more than confirmed by the
private reports obtained by the Ministy.
Last week the Managing Director of
an important firm in Leith wrote as
follows:-
"The principal point is the high
price the North of Ireland is getting
for their eggs compared with Denmark.
For instance, on the 11th October an
important Northern firm
the correspondent gives the namewere quoting for 15lb. graded Northern Ireland eggs, 23s. Ireland, and on
that date Denmark was consigning into
Leith and had to sell at a price equal
to 17s Denmark.
"The position that the North of Ireland has now reached
continues the correspondenthas been remarkable in three short
years, and has only been attained by
carrying out fearlessly your Regulations. It is clear that to deviate
from these in the slightest degree
would be fatal."
Such is the opinion of an outside trader,
one of the largest egg merchants in Leith.
Personally, I do not claim that in the
marketing of eggs we have by any means
reached our final objective, but I can
say with confidence that thanks to the
goodwill and cordial co-operation of the
vast majority of poultry-keepers and egg
merchants we have made very considerable
progress indeed. It will be recollected
that last year there was the extraordinary
increase of one million in our poultry
population, compared with 1925. This
year the increased figure has been so well
maintained that the poultry population
is now over eight millions.
It will be recollected that two years
ago many farmers were severely hit by the
heavy mortality in live stock. To meet
this emergency the Ministry, in 1925,
granted 982 loans to farmers, amounting
to a total of £45,500. As it appeared
early this year that there were still some
cases which had not been dealt with
under the original arrangements, the
Ministry revived the scheme last Spring
and, as a result, a further sum of £23,700
was advanced in 483 loans for live stock
replacements, making a total of £69,000
advanced at the low rate of 2 per cent.
The Ministry has also granted loans and
subsidies to farmers for the purchase of
high-class stallions, bulls and rams, and
help on these lines will be offered next
year on a still larger scale. Loans and
subsidies amounting to a total of £9,430
already have been granted. This is apart
from the special assistance rendered to
Milk Recording Associations to enable
them to procure suitable bulls. Furthermore, arrangements have been made
whereby farmers can obtain loans for the
purchase of agricultural machinery and
for the erection of fencing in mountainous
districts. In addition the procedure for
the granting of loans for minor farm
improvements-out offices, poultry houses
etc., etc. has been simplified and
cheapened.
In order to preserve, and if possible
expand, the important potato trade of
Northern Ireland, the Ministry has been
devoting continuous attention to this
crop. Assistance has been given in three
main directions, namely:-
(a) to encourage the introduction of
varieties immune from the Black Scab
disease and at the same time suitable
for the export markets;
(b) to provide good seed in necessitous times for the poorer districts;
(c) to stimulate a demand for
Northern Ireland potatoes on British
and foreign markets.
As regards the introduction of varieties
immune from disease, it may be
mentioned that about 1,800 tons were
introduced by the Ministry and distributed on special terms in districts
where required. £5,300 has been
expended in this connection.

May I remind the hon. Member for
Derry (Mr. Leeke), that the distribution
of good new varieties of potatoes is helping tillage.
Mr. LEEKE: No, it is not.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I think potatoes
are most necessary in the tillage of the
country.

Mr. LEEKE: Will the right hon.

We sent over for distribution through

Mr. LEEKE: I agree.
Mr. ARCHDALE: We also, in addition

potatoes, are getting an opening in

grade their potatoes properly so that
when a man buys a ton of potatoes he will
know he is getting a ton of potatoes of
the sort he bid for.
That would alter
the trade enormously. There is no
greater handicap to our trade in potatoes
than the bad way they are graded and
the bad way they are packed. We have
had complaints from over the water from
dozens of merchants who are taking our
potatoes. They tell us that unless farmers grade potatoes better and do not
put an amount of clay in the bag, and
send potatoes of the right sort, and not
diseased potatoes, and pack them in bags
that will not get broken and thrown about
on the steamer, they will have to give up
taking them. It is causing a tremendous
lot of difficulty and bother in arranging
for the selling of potatoes on the other
side of the water.

We have to pay for agricultural education, £16,800; for cow-testing associations, £29,000; that is, during the five
years, I think it is; poultry, £2,000; improvement of pastures, £2,800; improvement of mountain sheep, £2,800. Agricultural education is the vital need of
farming at the present time. It is important that research work should be
brought to the notice of farmers.
Therefore, we are appointing 10 additional agricultural overseers and two
additional agricultural instructors to go
to the poorer districts in order that
education should be brought home to
them.
Milk recording associations require
notice. They offer a very wide field for
progress. As evidence of progress I may
say that in 1921 there were six associations with 199 members and 1,244 cows
under test. In 1927, this year, there
were 60 associations, 2,408 members and
12,165 cows. But the important thing
is that the average yield per cow in 1921
was 541 gallons and the average yield per
cow in 1926, the last year, for which we
have the full figures, was 680 gallons;
140 gallons per cow more on the average.

poultry and eggs in Northern Ireland.
The Ministry, therefore, made arrange-

In Northern Ireland we have 1,400,000
acres of pasture, disregarding mountain
grazing, the greater portion of which

supervision of the instructors and overseers. In the four years, 1924-1927,
approximately 4,000 of these plots were
laid down.

who said mountain sheep were no good

that
it is the small man they affect.

In the distribution of these funds my
Ministry has carefully considered the
needs of each county, taking into account
all the relevant factors. In the coming
Spring it is hoped to supply 85 bulls up
to premium standard on easy terms to

kept the bulls properly and have complied
with the conditions laid down, they will
have received as much in premiums as

price of the animals. In other words

Dairy bulls supplied on easy terms to

number of subsidized bulls supplied by

A sum of £400 has been allocated for

May I say, in conclusion, that while we
appreciate the hard times the farmer has
gone through it is not only by looking
to the Government for assistance the
Government, as I have shown, are perfectly willing to give to the utmost extent in their power. Both the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Finance are

that most vital necessity-a cycle of good
seasons. I certainly think that with a

things will improve. It is no good being

Let us take next the growing of
potatoes. That is one of the principal
industries here in Northern Ireland, but
it is an industry which I think must be
admitted has also been in a bad way for
a long time. The farmers find there is
no market for the varieties they are recommended to grow after they have gone
to the trouble of procuring the new seed,
at considerable expense in many cases.
The following year they are told to procure another variety and that they would
probably have a market for it, but the
results are practically similar.
The
greatest difficulty in very large districts
of the Six Counties is with regard to the
areas scheduled under the Black Scab
Order. There is no doubt it is a very
desirable thing that this disease should be
eradicated if that is at all possible, and
to a large extent it has been, but I believe the Ministry have gone to extremes
which were not necessary in connection
with this matter.
They will schedule an area which, in
my opinion, is quite too large. If they
find that black scab has occurred in one
farm in one townland, or in one field
in one farm in one townland,
they will schedule something like a
rural district or many townlands.
I think the Ministry are quite
right to take every precaution when
they have found black scab, but I really
do not think it is necessary to schedule
such large areas in order to combat this
is
is
disease. Even allowing they schedule
quite large areas, they prevent the farmers from growing any varieties of
potatoes but the varieties they recommend, that is, immune varieties, in those
areas. The fields in those areas are inspected regularly by numerous inspectors,
and when the crop
grown-this
where I think the Ministry make
will
mistake-they
not allow these
potatoes to go outside those areas. Therefore, in all instances of that nature, farmers are obliged to take less than the
ordinary market price for their potatoes,
often £1 and sometimes more than £1
a ton under the ordinary market value,
because they come from what is known
as a scheduled or black scab area.
I myself have had complaints-indeed I
have
papers in connection with the matter
here that even the people outside those

than a paying proposition to grow and sell
potatoes. The result is that the people
inside those areas who are obliged to take,
as I have said, sometimes 50 per cent. less
than the market value find growing them
a dead loss. I understand, I do not know
whether it will be denied or not, that the
growing of an Irish acre of potatoes costs
something like £30 apart from rent and
taxes, and that the average yield is something like ten tons. Anyone can see that
unless the farmer gets over £3 a ton for
his potatoes they are a loss.
In many
cases in those districts of which I am
speaking they have to take a reduced
price on account of the area they come
from, and anyone can see the loss is then
still more serious. What I would suggest
to the Ministry is in those areas when they
are satisfied they have been properly inspected and that immune varieties have
been grown the farmers should be allowed
to sell their potatoes in any market as
long as there has been no trace of the
disease.

Agriculture is an important factor.
Until recently agriculturists were not
thought much of. Remarks were made
about them as if they were of no account.
It is now realised that farmers are a most
important people. On three occasions
in this House and elsewhere I said they
are the only people who produce anything, the remainder of the people are
what you would call manipulators and
distributors, and get good profit in their
transactions. I do not think even yet
their difficulties are understood properly.
I know what farmers are. I am a farmer's son and was reared in a farmhouse.
There are
no harder worked class of
people on the face of the earth. They
are working from dewy morn to shady
eve. Their wives are perfect slaves in a
great many places owing to the amount
of work they have to do-milking cows.
and making butter. I remember when
they used to churn with the old churn
staff, when the work was never done,
when midnight did not see the farmer's
wife able to go to bed. In face of all
this, they have reared as well as they possibly could their families in honesty
throughout the country, and have tried
to do their best. They are the backbone
of the Northern area.

In my opinion the thing most necessary

reduced to some extent. Rates certainly
constitute the heaviest burden the

being spent by the different local

grants that are being given by the

In my own county of Armagh I know there

from the seaport of Belfast. Of course,

the grazier against the tillage farmer.
Take, again, the Government's policy at

There is just one other point I want to

the cost of our present Ministry of Agriculture as compared with the cost of the
entire Department for Ireland before the

that there is the danger of a growing

small community. What have been the

Parliament very elaborate research
stations. All their information is available for the agriculturists in this area.
I do feel that one of the difficulties in this
small area of ours was having to set up a

ing of farmers' produce is even more

I have no objection to-and, in fact,
have encouraged-subsidies to industries

to the farmers of Northern Ireland

could have given the use of free pedigree

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'
""
Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving
the Second Reading of this Measure, I
would plead for the indulgence of hon.
Members if I appear to take up the time
of the House unduly. Hon. Members
will, I think, agree with me at the conclusion of this discussion when I say
that of all the legal codes, the
code which governs the sale of intoxicating liquor is, not alone the most
intricate, but the most complex. As
someone has described it, the code is a
legal jungle full of pitfalls and dangers
for the unwary travellers," and just as
the deplacement of a stone in an ancient
building is likely to bring down a mass of
masonry, so the simplest licensing provision
may be followed, not alone by unexpected,
but also by disconcerting, results. As an
illustration of what I mean, I would
point out to the House that there are no
less than 24 different kinds of liquor
licences, and so a provision that is
appropriate to one may be quite inappropriate to another." Consequently,
to ensure that you are actually doing
what you intend to do, the closest possible
scrutiny of each Clause is necessary, and
therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like, in
moving this Second Reading to render
such help to hon. Members that they may
fully understand the Measure which is
now before the House.
(Hon.
I do not, however, wish it to be understood that it is my intention to apologize
for the necessity of any of the provisions
of the present Measure. This Bill is, as it
were, the finishing touch to a Measure,
the benefits of which are too little understood. I refer to the Act of 1923. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I claim that
that Measure is one of the most far-reaching steps ever taken by any Government,
either here or in Great Britain, in the
way of true temperance reform.
Members: Hear, hear). That Measure
could only have been passed by a Government the members of which were desirous
of bringing about temperance reform, and
as the years go on the beneficial results
which have accrued become more apparent, and personally I believe that the
real beneficial results from that far-reaching Measure will only be felt in the years
that lie ahead of us. It is a melancholy
fact that that Act, which has had such
beneficial and far-reaching results, has so
far received little recognition from those
who are intent upon the introduction of
ill-considered and impracticable Measures.
Certain well-meaning citizens arrogate to
Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Sir Dawson Bates]
themselves the claim that they, and they
alone, are true temperance reformers, but
the Government prefer to base their claim
to that title not on what they say, but on
what they have done, and what they are
doing. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
In framing a temperance Bill, amidst
the constant clamour of two opposing and
extreme views, it is only too easy to ignore
the view of the man in the street. That
his voice was not ignored when the Act of
1923 was drawn up is, to my mind, the
reason for the conspicuous success of that
Measure. Those who are in favour of
drastic and revolutionary changes are apt
to forget the simple fact that no rigid line
can be drawn between those who have got
to obey the law and those who have got to
enforce it. An Act which does not commend itself to the main body of good-living
citizens is bound, sooner or later, to
become a dead letter, and the nonobservance of a particular law can only
have a disastrous effect upon the observance of the law in general. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). There are some
who believe that the passage of a Bill in
Parliament is all that is necessary to make
men sober, but, believe me, you can no
more make a nation sober by Act of Parliament than you can make a nation religious
-both have been tried and both have
failed. The only method by which true
and lasting temperance reform can be
effected is by slow, sure and steadfast
steps.
When the Act of 1923 was introduced the Prime Minister expressed the
hope that, unless by general agreement between all the parties, no further temperance legislation of any importance would
be necessary in his time. That was the
Government's considered opinion then,
and that is our opinion now, fortified by
the results of the 1923 Act. Temperance
reformers had for many years hoped and
prayed for a Measure of temperance reform, but up to the establishment of the
Northern Government they were voices
crying in the wilderness. One of the first
Measures which the Northern Government
introduced was the Intoxicating Liquor
Act, 1923, an Act which far exceeded the
most extravagant hopes of temperance enthusiasts. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
This law was enacted at a time when the
State was fighting for its very existence,
and it is to me a signal instance of the
ingratitude of a certain section of temperance advocates that they should now vilify
this Government for refusing to introduce
a Measure which could only redound disastrously as well against the cause of temperance, which we all have at heart, as
against the community generally.
I propose to recapitulate very briefly
some of the provisions of the Act of 1923,
partly because the effects of that Measure have, of late, been ignored, and partly
because the present Measure is incomprehensible without a reference to the
1923 Act which it proposes to amend.
That Act prohibited the carrying on of
other businesses in licensed premises, and
the result of the operation of the Act was
this:-
No less than 335 spirit grocers' licences,
225 wine licences, and 28 public-house
licences were extinguished.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Making a
total of 588 licences put out of existence
since 1923, and I would ask hon. Members
to remember that most of these licences
were precisely those which had led to
serious abuses. Hon. Members are only
too well aware that it was formerly a
widespread practice for women to obtain
drink from spirit grocers by getting it
charged up as "groceries."
Mr. GYLE: Nonsense.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will have ample opportunity to
reply to me later on. As a result of the
Act spirit grocers are no more, and a stop
has been put to a course of action which
so often led to dishonesty and drunkenness.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is partly
due to this fact that the statistics of
female drunkenness have shown a marked
tendency to decline. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Again, chemists are no
longer allowed to sell wine, except upon
the written prescription of a doctor, and
these two factors have had the result of
decreasing drinking amongst the class of
person who would object to go into a
public-house but had no objection to
going to a place of a more respectable
character.
2453 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
