Second Reading

I

As hon. Members are aware, one of the
most important features of the 1923 Act
was the limitation of the hours during
which intoxicating liquor could be sold.
Prior to the Act of 1923 the ordinary
hours for a licensed house were from 7
a.m. to 11 p.m. in a town for 5,000 of a
population, and from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.
where the population was less than 5,000.
Undoubtedly the limitation of the hours
for drinking must account for the substantial decrease in the number of convictions for drunkenness, for I find that
in 1923 convictions numbered 5,747,
while last year they were reduced to
4,280. Another effect of the Act was
the abolition of the bona-fide traveller.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Prior to the
Act of 1923 coming into force it was a
comparatively easy thing to purchase
drink on Sunday. You got into your
motor-car or on to your bicycle, or if you
had not either of these means of conveyance you walked, and once you had
covered a distance of 3 miles you could
get as much drink as you could afford to
pay for. The whole system was, of
course, ridiculous, and it opened a door
to many abuses. The Act of 1923 swept
these away, and the result has been extremely satisfactory, and now a drunk
man on a Sunday is seldom to be seen.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The statistics
show that in regard to the offence of
drunkenness on a Sunday during the
first half of 1923-that is, prior to the Act
coming into force the number of cases
was 234, while the corresponding period
following the passing of the Act shows a
figure of 76, a drop of something like 67
per cent., and each year since there has
heen a steady decrease in these figures.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
And now let me say a few words about
the thorny subject of endorsement of
licences. Prior to the Act of 1923 if a
licence holder was convicted of certain
serious offences, the court which tried the
case had power not only to fine the delinquent but also to record the conviction
on his licence, a process commonly known
as endorsement, and, generally speaking,
two endorsements followed by a conviction
had the following effect: -(1)
effect:-(1) The
licensee was disqualified from holding a
licence for a period of 5 years, and (2)
the premises themselves were disqualified
from having a licence attached to them
for a period of two years. There was,
however, one great weakness in the law
prior to the 1923 Act. It enabled the
licensee who had two endorsements and
was frightened of getting a third endorseable conviction to sell his licensed
premises to a newcomer who could start
with a clean sheet.
The effect of the 1923 Act was this:
It provided that two endorsements, followed by what is known as an endorseable
conviction, cancelled the licence once and
for all. It left, however, a serious loophole which has only recently come to our
knowledge. This shows the extraordinarily complicated nature of the liquor
laws. The loophole was that an individual could, after his licence had been
twice endorsed, sell his licence to a new
man with the following result:-The
licence would continue in force until the
purchaser had two further endorsements
recorded on the licence. If the four endorsements recorded came within a period
of five years, the licence went and was
cancelled, but if, on the other hand, the
last of the four endorsements took place,
say, six years after the first endorsement,
then the licencee had another chance, and
the licence would not be extinguished until
four endorsements had been recorded
within a period of five years. It will thus
be seen that a bad house could pass from
hand to hand, the owner just keeping
clear of the penal clause, and this, to a
large extent, nullified the effect of the Act
of 1923. I propose to introduce an
Amendment on this subject during the
Committee stage, and I propose to say
nothing further in regard to it now.
There can be no doubt whatever that the
results of these provisions have acted as a
strong deterrent against illegitimate trading. Turning again to statistics I find
that in 1922 there were 495 convictions
of licensed persons for breaches of the
Licensing Laws, while the corresponding
figure for 1926 was 162.
A further important provision of the
1923 Act was that the adjudication in
licensing cases was placed entirely in the
hands of Resident Magistrates. The result has proved most beneficial, and it is
rarely that any exception can be taken to
the decisions in licensing cases, a very
marked contrast to the state of affairs
2455 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading

[Sir Dawson Bates]
which prevailed in the old days when
ordinary Justices of the Peace sat on the
beuch and tried these cases.
Another very important and very beneficial provision of this 1923 Act was that
it provided that no intoxicating liquor was
to be sold to any person under the age
of 18, and that no female under the age
of 18 was to be employed in a licensed
house.
Hon. Members will no doubt remember
that it was proposed to insert provisions
in the 1923 Bill in regard to illicit distillation. It was, however, ascertained that
is was not within the competence of the
Northern Government to legislate on this
subject, but subsequently, and at the instance of the Government of Northern
Ireland, a Section was inserted by the Imperial Government in the 1923 Finance
Act substantially increasing the penalties
for breaches of the Illicit Distillation Acts,
also providing for increased powers to the
police and Excise officials by placing the
entire jurisdiction for hearing this class of
case in the hands of the Resident Magistrate. The penalties were formerly a fine
of £100 or three months' imprisonment,
which were increased to a fine of £500,
plus imprisonment up to a period of 12
months. This section in the Finance Act
has had most beneficial results, and there
can be no doubt that the manufacture of
illicit spirits has fallen very considerably,
but I would not be doing my duty if I
said that the result of this Act has been
to kill the poteen trade.
I find that the statistics show that of
the 133 persons convicted in 1922, only
seven were sent to prison, but of the 51
offenders last year, 24 were given an
opportuity of reflecting upon their sins in
His Majesty's prison. There is no doubt
that the increased penalties have had a
very deterrent effect on the manufacture
of illicit spirits, but I cannot conceal the
fact that poteen is still being made in
substantial quantities in Northern Ireland. One has only to see the terrible
effect of poteen drinking to come to the
conclusion that really no punishment is too
severe for a man who indulges in this
terrible traffic. What strikes me from
time to time as a peculiar thing is the
number of friends that some of these
offenders have. I have often been approached on behalf of these offenders
asking that the term of imprisonment
might be terminated. I know only too
well that imprisonment often inflicts a
very great hardship on the wives and the
families of offenders, but, I would ask
those who come to me on behalf of these
poteen makers who have been caught in
the meshes of the law, not to make my
task heavier by having to refuse their
request for remission of their sentences.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The Government intend to do all they
can to stamp out what is a terrible
menace to the community, and in doing
so, they welcome any suggestions which
hon. Members have as to how better to
enforce the law. I have endeavoured to
sum up some of the effects of the operation of the Act of 1923, and I ask any
reasonable man or woman to say, when
they consider these facts, how it can be
alleged by anyone that the Government
is unsympathetic or indifferent to temperance reform.
Coming now to the present Measure,
what its general effect would be is already
known. It has been framed to carry
more fully into effect the general intention of the 1923 Act, and to remedy
certain technical defects in that Act
which have only become apparent since
the Act was passed. Dealing with the
first Clause of the Bill, this is mainly
concerned with certain technical defects
as regards the general prohibition of
"mixed businesses." Speaking generally,
the 1923 Act forbade the carrying on in
licensed premises of any business other
than the sale of tobacco, table waters
and food for immediate consumption.
The object of this, hon. Members will
appreciate, was to do away with the
spirit grocer.
It was never intended to prohibit
publicans from carrying on a wholesale
liquor business in conjunction with their
retail trade, but unfortunately the particular words in which the prohibition is
couched made the question highly doubtful. The first Clause of this Bill sets the
matter at rest by allowing a wholesale
liquor business to be carried on on
licensed premises. This Clause has also
the following practical effects:-First of
all it clarifies the law as regards the carrying on of what might be described as "subsidary businesses in hotels." It will be
remembered that a place
"uesd
clusively as a hotel " was expressly excluded from the Section prohibiting

ex-

mixed businesses, but a difficulty arose as to
the definition of the word "exclusively."
If a hotel contained, say, a hairdresser's
shop, a billiard room, or a stock-room,
could it be said that that hotel was "used

a hotel." It was never
intended to cast doubt upon the legality
of such very necessary adjuncts to an
ordinary hotel. The omission of the word
exclusively in the re-draft of the
Section will, we are advised, place the

think it is necessary for me to dilate on
this Amendment further. It seems to
me that it is only common sense.
The first Clause has two further effects
to which I desire to refer. It prohibits the
sale of non-intoxicants in public-houses
during closing hours. As the law now
stands, there is nothing to prevent a publican opening his house on Sunday for the
sale of non-intoxicating drinks, but when
7 this is done, I think hon. Members will
appreciate that police supervision becomes
absolutely impossible.

Finally, the Clause allows publicans to
provide temporary stabling or similar accommodation for vehicles or animals, not
only during the opening hours but also
during the closing hours. I think hon.
Members, especially those who have come
from the country, will see the reasonableness of such a concession. From time immemorial the country inn has provided
stabling for animals, and there is no valid
reason why farmers coming into country
towns early in the morning should not be
allowed to stable their horses on licensed
premises.
Hon. Members will appreciate that it
frequently happens that in these country
towns there is no place in which a farmer
can put up his horse other than in a local
publican's yard.
I come to the second Clause. When the
present Measure was being prepared the
whole of the Liquor Laws were explored,
particularly the 1923 Act, and amongst
other things it came to light that no
specific limits had been imposed as to the
hours during which liquor might be sup
plied to residents in a hotel on Sunday in
conjunction with a substantial meal.
Hotel keepers are, I think, under the impression that subject to the conditions laid
down in Section 1 of the 1923 Act, they
are entitled to supply liquor at any time
on a Sunday.
While I believe that this is an erroneous
impression there is undoubtedly some uncertainty on the point, and it is manifestly desirable that all ambiguity should
be removed.
Accordingly, the proposed Amendment
merely declares what was intended all
along, namely, that the permitted hours
on Sunday or Christmas Day are the
ordinary week-day hours.
I come to a Clause which will, I feel
sure, until it is explained, create a certain
amount of misunderstanding.
From time immemorial the consumption.
(as distinct from the sale) of intoxicating
liquor has been permitted in hotels and
restaurants after closing hours.
There can be, I think, few hon. Members who have not at any rate attended a
public dinner in a licensed hotel or licensed
restaurant at which drink was consumed
after the hours permitted for sale.
As to whether such consumption is legal
or illegal, the Licensing Laws afford us
very little assistance.
Not long ago I obtained the opinion of
eminent Counsel, and I was advised that
the question was one on which no decided
opinion could be expressed.
But I think hon. Members will agree
with me when I say it is not only unfair
to the hotel keepers but it is also unfair to
the police to leave the law on this matter
in a state of uncertainty, and consequently
Clause 2 of the Bill declares it to be unlawful for the proprietor of a hotel or
restaurant to allow the consumption of
liquor after closing hours unless
(a) a dinner or other entertainment
is being held; and
(b) a permit has been obtained from
the District-Inspector of Police authorising such consumption. The permit is
to specify not only the hours during
which, but also the rooms in which consumption may take place.
Hon. Members will, of course, appreciate that this does not in any way authorize the sale of intoxicating liquor after the
ordinary closing hours.

I would like to say a few words in respect

present time certain districts in Northern
Ireland where this stuff is sold in very
large quantities as substitute for
whisky.
a
At the present time, so long as the
chemist or druggist who sells the stuff
keeps a correct record of every sale, no
legal exception can be taken to his conduct, but I think Clause 9 of the Bill
will prevent any further abuse arising
in connection with the use of methylated.
ether. The Clause prohibits the sale of
methylated ether to anyone except:-
(a) a Doctor or Dentist;
(b) a Hospital or Infirmary;
(c) a Wholesale Dealer:
(d) a Licensed Chemist or Druggist;
or
(e) a person holding
a special
authorisation from the Minister of
Home Affairs.
Now, as regards methylated spirits,
here again the present restrictions, in the
opinion of the Government, do not go far
enough. At the present time a retailer
must keep a careful record of all sales up
to one gallon. Now a retailer has the
right to sell methylated spirits up to four
gallons to any one person, and under the
existing law there is no necessity for a
retailer to keep a record of his sales of
methylated spirits which fall between one
gallon and four gallons. This loophole
in the law has resulted in widespread
abuse.
Clause 9 provides that a record of all
sales must be kept up to and including
the maximum quantity that any retailer
can sell, that is, four gallons, but the Clause
goes further, because we provide that not
alone must a record of the sales be kept,
but also a record of the purchases made
by that retailer. I think it will be
obvious to hon. Members that this provision will have a salutary effect upon
the illicit sale of methylated spirits.
We come now to Clause 10, which places
restrictions on the sale of certain kinds of
alcohol. Most hon. Members are acquainted in some way or another with only
one type of alcohol, but it may be of
interest to hon. Members to know that
there are many other types. For instance
there are methyl, ethyl, propyl, and isopropyl. Methyl alcohol is controlled
under the popular name of methylated
spirits. Ethyl alcohol is the technical
name for the alcohol that is found in
whisky, wine and beer and so forth.
Some time ago it came to the knowledge
of the Government that iso-propyl alcohol
was being used by certain publicans to
adulterate, or as the phrase goes, “add a
kick to" low quality wines. This particular type of alcohol is a by-product of
petroleum. It is subject only to a very
small key-industry duty and can be obtained for 13s a gallon. Its toxic effects
are certainly treble that of methyl alcohol.
Up to a comparatively recent date it has
been used solely in the manufacture of
perfumes and essences, and it is only quite
recently that it has been found possible to
purify it to such an extent that it could be
used for adulterating wine. I am satisfied that the disastrous effects which follow
the consumption of what is known as "Red
Biddy" or "toney wine" are largely due to
its adulteration with iso-propyl alcohol.
Under Clause 10 we prohibit the sale or
supply in any licensed premises of any
kind of alcohol other than that of ethyl
alcohol, and we also provide that any
licensed person who sells or keeps for sale
Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
or supplies any liquor whatever which
consists of or contains or is mixed with
any alcohol other than ethyl alcohol will
be subject to the same penalties as a publican or a licensee who is convicted of selling poteen. In other words, on a conviction for this offence, the licence will
be cancelled. (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear).
I now come to the question of club
licences. In Clause 11 will be found
some very important provisions relating
to registered clubs, but before dealing
with the effect of this Clause may I draw
the attention of hon. Members to certain
statistics. Prior to the Act of 1923,
there were 53 registered clubs in existence
in Northern Ireland, and, at the present
time. that number has been increased
until there are 70. They increased in
Belfast by only 2. Prior to 1923 the
total membership was 13,986, while the
present membership is 17,855. The
amount of money spent by clubs in purchasing liquor has increased from
£38,426 to £76,202, and, therefore, when
one draws a comparison between the comparatively small increase in club members
and the very large increase in the consumption of liquor, one is confirmed in
the opinion that certain of these clubs are
mala fide, and I believe this applies particularly to certain of the new clubs that
have been formed since the Act of 1923
was passed. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I venture to suggest that very few, if
any, of the clubs of the type I have mentioned would have obtained licences if
the magistrates had been armed with the
powers which we propose to give them
under this Bill. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We propose under Clause 11 to
put the onus upon the applicant of proving certain specified matters set out in
the Clause such as: (1) that the premises of the club are suitable; (2) that
the club is intended to be conducted as
such, and not mainly for the sale of intoxicating liquor; (3) that the rules are
complied with; (4) that the club has conducted itself properly during the past
year; (5) that there is not sufficient club
accommodation of a similar character in
the neighbourhood. Hon. Members will
find the other conditions in the Bill. I do
not propose to weary the House going
further into them. These powers are so
wide that they will enable the Court to
be satisfied that the rules of the club are
suitable, having regard to all the circumstances. For example, I can conceive
the magistrates refusing a licence unless
the rules provide that the sale of liquor
was confined to reasonable hours, having
regard to the needs of the club members.
Hon. Members will observe that under
this Clause it is quite open to the magistrates and to the police to send for the
books of the club and for the applicant,
so that they may satisfy themselves that
the club is not mainly for the sale of
drink.
But there is a further very important
provision regarding the clubs. It enables
an officer with rank of not less than a
District-Inspector to enter a club at any
time and, if necessary, accompanied by
other police officers. The old method
whereby a police officer could not enter
or search a club except under a warrant
issued by the Bench has been found to be
most unsatisfactory.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Therefore, I
Sir DAWSON BATES:
am satisfied that if these provisions are
passed, they will strengthen the hands of
the magistrates, and strengthen the hands
of the police, and result in ne abolition
of what I think every right-thinking individual detests-a drinking club. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Now we come to the provision relating
to the licensing of theatres and music
halls.
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
I know my
Sir DAWSON BATES:
hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin) is very strong
on that point. At the present time the

and uncertainty, but one thing, however.
which does seem certain, is that any place
of public entertainment, by obtaining a
theatre or music hall licence, can, under
the existing law, obtain a liquor licence
by simply applying to the Excise authorities I think most hon. Members will
agree with me that it is very undesirable
that any place of public entertainment,
no matter of what character or class,
should be permitted to obtain, more or less
automatically, a liquor licence, and if we
allow the law to remain as it now is, it
is possible that at no very distant date we

shall see licences attached to the smallest

propose to stop. Accordingly, Clause 13,

licensed as such, and in future a place of
public entertainment which is not either
a theatre or a music hall, will no longer be

This licence, I would ask hon. Members

The Clause then goes on to provide that

licence, he must then apply to the Licen
ing Court for a liquor licence, and objections may be urged by the police, or indeed by the public, against his application
just as if it were an application for an

only to persons who are bona fide attending the performances, and then only during the performance or during thirty
minutes before or thirty minutes after
such performance. No sale is, of course,
allowed outside the ordinary hours applicable to licensed premises.
I am sorry I have had to occupy the
time of the House at such length, but I
feel that the importance of this Measure

Act, and will do all that is possible by

This is the third time that our licensing
laws are being discussed in this House,
and it is nothing out of the ordinary. In
1552 this matter commenced, and all

trying by making laws to muzzle this

Prohibition is not a new thing. Away

the people were prohibited from selling
liquor, and even now very few people
""
"""
in Northern Ireland, with a population

Prohibition.' Prohibition applies to
nearly the whole community of Northern
Ireland, and the keeping and selling of
liquor is prohibited to them, because it is

harmful. A person licensed to sell liquor
is licensed because what he is doing is
harmful to the community, and it is absolutely necessary to restrict it.
Mr. Gladstone said that drink was the

granted to privileged people, not to encourage drinking habits but to try to

In 1853 there was a declaration of

The history and results of all past legislation in regard to the liquor traffic
abundantly prove that it is impossible

tendencies.

Now I come to the Bill itself. I listened to the speech of the right hon.
Gentleman, the Home Secretary, and as

his only purpose in introducing this Bill

made in 1923. When the right hon.

it is a very remarkable statement, that
the 1923 Act exceeded the most extravagant hopes of the most extreme temperance orators and propagandists.
I confess that is a remarkable statement for a
Minister to make in regard to legislation
which deals with the private conduct, the
tastes, the appetites, and the lives of the
people of this Northern Province-that
all these questions were determined, not
by the public needs, but in order to satisfy
the extravagant hopes of the most extreme temperance orator. I have never
in my life heard such a strange interpretation by a Minister of the purpose that
should inspire him in dealing with a great
social problem of this character.
In connection with the question of the
bona-fide traveller, the Minister of Home
Affairs said no one could defend the bonafide traveller. I am here to defend the
bona-fide traveller if the right hon. Gentleman wants to hear someone who will defend him. The abuse of bona-fide travelling was quite recognized. It was realized
that if people deliberately walked out of
their homes and went a certain distance
entirely for the purpose of getting a drink,
that constituted not bona-fide travelling,
but mala-fide travelling. To put the
bona-fide traveller in the same position as
the mala-fide traveller is a thing that
could only be defended by the Home
Secretary, but he has not dared to defend
it.
What is a bona-fide traveller? If I
go out on Sunday for a day's pleasure,
if I walk ten miles or drive twenty miles,
and if at the end of that time I want a
meal, and go into a hotel and ask for one,
and with the meal I ask for a drink, I am
a bona-fide traveller, and am entitled to
be treated as a bona-fide traveller if my
purpose is not to secure intoxicating drink
as intoxicating drink or to set myself
drunk. I am entitled to a drink if I go
out on a Sunday as much as if I go out
on a Monday. If you make the assumption that drink is inherently bad in itself,
and that people should not be allowed to
consume it, if you take up the position
of the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Crawford)
that you ought to prohibit drink altogether, and that no one ought to be allowed
to consume it on Sunday or Monday, I

My real object in rising, apart from any
criticism of the Measure before the House,
is to draw attention to a scheme of temperance reform which has been most
successful in Great Britain. That reform is necessary, I think, is admitted on
all sides. No one, not even the brewers,

for the year ended 31st March, 1927,

Districts (Licensing Act, 1921.)" In it
it will be seen that from the point of view
of the financial position the scheme is absolutely sound. The financial position of
the State Management Districts on 31st
March, 1927, according to the official
report, is that the capital employed was
£1,107,314 14s 5d, and the trade profits
for the year ended on the 31st March,
1927, amounted to £98,916 9s 1d. This
year the licences have been bought out
and control taken of the public houses in
the Carlisle district, and £12,000 has reverted to the Treasury. I think from the
financial point of view the Carlisle
system is an absolutely sound one. The
temperance or prohibition people may say
that the financial aspect of the case is not
the only one, nor may it be in dealing
with the question of drink the most im
portant side to be considered. Take it
from the sane temperance point of view
and you will find that the number of
licensed premises and businesses acquired.
since the inception of the scheme in 1916
was 321, and that number has been
gradually reduced to 197; in Gretna from
29 to 15, and in Cromarty from 39 to 19.
Compensation was paid to the owners and
licensees of all premises acquired and in
respect of all interests concerned in 95
per cent. of the cases the claims were
settled by negotiation, while in 5 per cent.
of the cases only was it found necessary
to proceed by arbitration
In addition to this desirable state of
affairs there is also the fact of disinterested management taking the place of
the sort of management that exists in the
North of Ireland, which pays a manager
in proportion to the amount of intoxicating drink sold. The publicans in the
Carlisle scheme are salaried managers
who have had impressed upon them that
their first consideration is the sobriety of
their houses, and that instead of increased
sale of intoxicants being a ground for increased salary or commendation exactly
the opposite is the case. The managers
are given a commission solely on food and
non-alcoholic drinks. In addition to the
sale of drink, meals are provided at a
reasonable price, and the sordid and very
often degraded atmosphere of the publichouse has been changed into the pleasant
and wholesome feeling of a decent and respectable place of refreshment.

urging the Government to have State
control of public-houses. In addition to
the fact that you get food at a reasonable
price there is the removal of all advertisements of alcoholic liquors

town where I was living was in the State

Take the case of towns where there are

I know this is a case of tremendous

Every Clause has been debated, but on

Sunday travellers might as well be travelling in the Sahara as far as securing

may be travelling from Cork or anywhere

Even if a traveller is overcome with

has been dealt with very comprehensively

They should be reinstated. The present

There is another point not dealt with
in the Bill, and it is a point aimed against
one class of licence holders. I speak of
the early closing licences. Somewhere
about 1874 some licence holders
wished to close earlier than the normal
time, which I understand was then somewhere about twelve o'clock. They were
temperate men, the best class of licence
holders, and they wished to close an hour
earlier. They applied for and got permission to do so. I see the Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Hanna) smiling at the idea
of their obtaining permission, but that is
quite true, because in those days it was a
matter of public-houses having inn licences
or something of that kind, and they were
compelled to stay open during the hours
marked on their licences. They were
allowed also the concession of six-day
licences along with the early closing, which
brought their licences eventually to ten
o'clock. In the 1923 Act they were compelled to close an hour earlier still, which
brings them down to nine o'clock. Supposing the temperance party manage to
dictate to the Government they have
done so so far and there should be a
further shortening of the hours I can see
these early closing licences being wiped out
altogether. That would be quite consistent with the idea as it has been carried
out so far. Might I point out that these
early closing licences pay the same levy
for the compensation of spirit grocers as
do full-time licence holders who can open
from ten till ten for seven days in the
week? That is not right or fair, because
the last hour of the day, as every hon.
Member of this House knows, no matter
what he may say about it, is the best hour
of the day in a licensed house.

I object to the introduction of a Bill
of this kind, limiting, as it does, the liberties of the subject. I say it is a libel and
a slander on the respectable people of
Northern Ireland. It is an insinuation
that they are a degraded people, with no
self-will, no self-control, and that they
have not the power to distinguish between
right and wrong. I do not think that
that is a clear interpretation of the character and minds of the people of Northern
Ireland.
I look upon the possibilities of the development of the tourist traffic of Northern
Ireland as second only to the possibilities
of a successful farming industry. Surely
if that industry is to develop, one of the
greatest responsibilities must fall on
the shoulders of the hotel proprietors
of Northern Ireland, and if they
are to have an opportunity of attracting people to this country, with all
its natural facilities for the development of the traffic, they must have equal
facilities and be in the position to compete on equal terms with the hotels in
England. On that ground I suggest that
the Government should make provision
that a man living in an hotel should be
in the same position as if he were in his
own house, and that he should be at
liberty, while resident in the hotel, to
get all the liquor that he may legitimately
require.
I myself have met Englishmen who
have come over here to stop in Irish hotels
and when they heard the nature of the
legislation here, that after nine o'clock
on a summer evening in a first-class
hotel, it was impossible for them to get
the slightest refreshment, they could not
possibly understand it. They resented
the fact that they were treated as men
who did not know how to observe the
ordinary decencies of life that tend to
propriety of conduct. I think this is a
perfectly unjustifiable and indefensible
position.
With regard to the bona-fide traffic, I
think the Act of 1923 has had the most
degrading effect on the people of Northern
Ireland. The ordinary, normal man
might have one drink or two drinks after
nine o'clock, but on Saturday night he
is driven to the alternative of bringing a
bottle into his own room in the hotel.
If he wants to entertain a friend, he has
to go through the degrading and humiliating form of turning his bedroom into
a smokeroom, and of entertaining him
behind closed doors. If that is a method
of promoting temperance and of uplifting
the people of Northern Ireland, I do not
see the logic of it.
I also associate myself with the demand
that has been made on behalf of the
farmers who have to leave their homes at
three or four o'clock in the morning, and
who cannot get a refreshment until ten
o'clock. I suggest that the Government
should reinstate, with qualifications, the
bona-fide travellers' qualifications, extend
the limit to ten, twelve, or whatever number of miles they think sufficient, and
make sure that the bona-fide traveller is
a real bona-fide traveller and not a
mala fide traveller.

I do not propose to deal with the question of the theatres to-night, or rather I
am not going to analyze the Clause. I
only want to say that the reason for that
Clause being included in this Bill is that
it was felt that it would be competent, in
a certain set of circumstances, for a person having a theatre licence to go and
apply for an Excise licence to sell liquor
in his theatre without having any magisterial investigation. It was felt that,
as the burden of compensation in respect
of premises closed under the 1923 Act
falls upon the members of the trade who
continue to carry on, it would be very unfair that any person, whether he had a
theatre licence or not, could walk down
to the Excise without the matter being
tested and say, Give me the right to sell
intoxicating liquor." That was the
original reason that operated in the minds
of the Government in introducing this
Clause at this time, and advantage was
taken of it, or we hope to take advantage
of it, to settle and make clear a law that is
exceedingly involved and doubtful. Hon.
Members will perhaps accept that in the

come to examine it analytically on the

not to prohibit a use, but to regulate

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 3rd November, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
EXTENDED BENEFIT IN ANTRIM
AREA.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is a fact that his
Department has reduced the scale laid
down by the Antrim Local Employment
Committee governing the payment of extended benefit to certain insured persons
in that area.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The family income scale applied by the Antrim Local Employment.
Committee in the beginning of this year
was higher than that in operation in any
comparable area and, in the case of an
average family, was in excess of the
standard rates of wages in the district.
The Department, therefore, asked the
Committee to apply a scale that was in
operation in the adjoining area with the
object of securing greater equality of administration. I may add that with the
same object the Department has had to
ask other Committees to increase the
scales they proposed to adopt.
Mr. KYLE: Can the right hon.
Gentleman state what the scale was that
was too high according to his Department,
and is he prepared to authorize Coleraine
Local Employment Committee to pay on
the basis of the same rate as in the Ballymena area?
Mr. ANDREWS: The scale is 50s for
a wife and three children, and I am not
prepared to interfere with the Coleraine
Committee in connection with this matter.
Mr. KYLE: Can the right hon.
Gentleman state, or is he prepared to lay
down from his Department, the scales
which would meet the requirements of his
Department for all areas?
Mr. ANDREWS: No, Sir, because
conditions vary in different areas.
Mr. KYLE: Seeing that the Antrim
Local Employment Committee has declared no fewer than three times that the
rate they laid down was inadequate in
their opinion can he state why he is not
prepared to issue from his Department
a scale such as I have referred to?
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes. It is necessary for the Department to see that
equality of administration is observed
throughout the whole of Northern Ireland
Mr. KYLE: Can the right hon.
Gentleman say if it is not a fact that no
fewer than four workers' representatives,
I think, on the Committee have refused to
act owing to the arbitrary action of the
Department?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not admit the
action was arbitrary, but I believe some
worker members of the Committee
resigned.
Mr. KYLE: Can the right hon.
Gentleman state whether it was because
the rate was so high they resigned? Does
he think that 50s is too much for a man
and his wife to live on?
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
COOKSTOWN DISTRICT.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labourer whether any labourers' cottages are being erected in the Cookstown
District; whether he could state what firm
has obtained the contract; and whether
he will take steps to ensure that adequate
wages will be paid to workmen engaged
in the erection of these houses.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Cookstown
Rural District Council have in operation
a scheme for the erection of 86 labourers'
cottages. Contracts have been entered
into for the building of 74 cottages, of
which Mr. Samuel Cummings is the contractor for 61, Mr. Francis Quinn 6, and
Mr. John McCartan for 7.
In November, 1911, a circular was
issued to all local authorities recommend-

ing the insertion of a Fair Wages Clause

NEWRY CHILDREN'S DENTAL
TROUBLES.
3. Mr. McMULLEN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether it is a fact that 1,700
children are suffering from dental troubles
in the Newry Urban area, as a result of
Section 47 of the Education Act not
being put into operation; whether it is
a fact that, having regard to the impaired health of the children in question,
the Newry Urban Council have made
repeated requests to the Down Regional
Committee to give effect to this section
of the Education Act; and whether le
will make representations to the Committee in order to expedite the consideration of this question in the interests of
the children of that district.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply to this Question.
According to the report of the Health
Visitor in Newry, the teeth of about 70
per cent. of the children examined require treatment, and I understand that
the Urban District Council of Newry
have made representations to the Regional
Committee on the subject.
The Regional Committee will have these
representations before them at their next
meeting, and I am sure that they will
receive full consideration from the Committee.
TAXATION OF MOTOR CARS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that 'he
present system of taxing motor cars is
held to be unsatisfactory and excessive by
users of motor cars, and whether he could
introduce some modification of the existing regulations.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am taking
this Question for the Minister of Finance.
I am not aware that the tax on motor
cars can be regarded as unsatisfactory or
excessive.
Mr. BEATTIE: I may say that the
answer is very unsatisfactory from the
point of view of how the question was put
down. I would like to ask the Minister
is he prepared to re-establish in Northern
Ireland the old system of taxation? Is

[Mr. Beattie]
he prepared to drop the present system of
taxation on horse power and adopt the
system of taxation on petrol, which is the
most satisfactory system for all motor

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend has put a very big question to me
in reply to a very small answer, but I do
not think it would be possible to consider
the advisability of changing over to

petrol. There are many difficulties, but

not be practicable.

Parliament imposes taxation on motor
vehicles.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think that the
question of taxation on petrol is an
Excise matter, and outside the jurisdiction of this House.
WHITLEY COUNCILS IN THE CIVIL
SERVICE.
Mr.
5.
KYLE asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware of the feeling of dissatisfaction existing in the Civil
Service (Northern Ireland), owing to the
fact that a Whitley Council has not been
established in the Service; whether the
Northern Ireland Civil Service has by
ballot of its members rejected the proposed establishment of House Committees
for each Department; and whether he is
prepared to establish a Whitley Council
for Civil Servants in Northern Ireland,
and accord them the same rights and
privileges that Civil Servants in Great
Britain possess.
The PRIME MINISTER: In reply to
the first and second parts of the hon.
Member's question, I am not aware of any
general feeling of dissatisfaction existing
in the Civil Service in consequence of the
non-establishment of Whitley Councils,
nor have I any knowledge of any ballot
having been taken throughout the Service
on the question of the existence or otherwise of House Committees other than the
statement to that effect which recently
appeared in the Press.
In reply to the last part of the question
I may say that there is no intention of establishing Whitley Councils for the Civil
Service in Northern Ireland.
Mr. KYLE: Can the right hon. Gentleman state why this difference should be
enforced on the civil servants of Northern
Ireland to worsen their position, as compared with civil servants in Great
Britain?
The PRIME MINISTER: There is no
worsening of conditions in Northern
Ireland. The Government are opposed
to the establishment of Whitley Councils
in a small Civil Service like ours. We
consider it would not be for the benefit of
the Civil Service itself or of the Government.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman state whether or not he, in
common with the rest of his colleagues,
received a resolution from the Civil
Servants of Northern Ireland, asking that
a Whitley Council should be established?
The PRIME MINISTER: That circular may possibly have been a circular
sent out to Members on both sides of the
House, but it does not alter the decision
of the Government. We do not propose
to have Whitley Councils in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. KYLE: Is this in keeping with the
policy or tactics of the Government declared by the Prime Minister, of following
on parallel lines with Great Britain?
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I want to ask
the Prime Minister can he state specifically the Government's objection to Whitley Councils?
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think that
can be given in answer to a question.
That would have to be debated.

We start these colleges; we train these
young men, and we send them out; and
according to official information placed at
my disposal, more than these trained emigrants are going out. What do you give
to Australia and to Canada? You give
the life, the vigour, the health and the

years of age, who has had to be reared
in the country at a cost of something like
one thousand pounds. You take him into
a college, you train him up scientifically
for a few months, and you pay out of the
ratepayers' money a sum to enable him to
become an efficient agriculturist abroad.
Then you send him out to one of those

cannot altogether leave out of the picture
that during this time 5,000 "Specials"
were disbanded as well as a similar number
of those in the Free State Army and
Republican Army, while there are 3,000
less engaged on relief works. Therefore,
13,000 additional persons have been made
available for employment of the ordinary
kind.
Further, there is an improvement, I
maintain, in all our industries in Northern
Ireland. The unemployment percentage
in shipbuilding at the beginning of this
year was 35.5 per cent.; in September
last it was 16.4. In the linen trade it
was 14.5; it is now 7. In the building
trade it was 36.4; it is now 19.1. In dress
goods, including the shirt and collar industry at Londonderry, it was 15.3; it is
now 10.3. In the distributing trades, notwithstanding the tariffs which the Free
State Government imposed against the
goods of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, an improvement has taken place
from 12.8 to 9.9. As regards food and
drink, there is an improvement from 14.9
to 10.1.

Let us see how we have been getting on
as compared with Great Britain. In
January, 1926, the percentage of unemployment in Great Britain was 11.1; here
it was 24.7, a difference of 13.6.
January of this year it was 12.1 in Great
Britain, here 19.2, a difference of 7.1.
In August of this year it was 9.4, and in
Northern Ireland 12, a difference of 2.6.
In September last it was 9.4 in Great
Britain, and here it was 10.7, a difference
of only 1.3. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) This shows clearly that our progress has been quicker than in Great
Britain. To listen to the hon. Member

The PRIME MINISTER: I will not
detain the House for more than a few
moments. The hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) referred in his speech
to the decision arrived at by the Government in making a grant out of the Road
Board Fund towards the erection of a new
bridge at Derry. I am only too pleased
to confine my remarks to that one episode,
and to give the hon. Member as well as the
House the fullest possible information on
the subject. I think everyone is aware
that the old bridge in the City of Derry
has become dangerous, and that it has become necessary to replace it at the earliest
possible opportunity as it is quite
unsafe for traffic.
The authorities in the city have
have approached
the Government for some considerable
time with a view to securing from us as
large a contribution as is possible to have
that bridge rebuilt and made fit for traffic.
The Government have had to take into
consideration several important factors.
First of all, the bridge is really not a city
bridge, it is an Ulster bridge. It is practically the only way of communication
between the southern part of Northern
Ireland and the northern part of Northern
Ireland. If that bridge broke down the
only way that one could maintain through
traffic between this part of Ulster and the
north would be by diverting it from Derry
right down to Strabane where there is a
bridge, but it is of a totally inadequate
character for carrying the traffic that
passes between the northern and southern
parts of our territory.
In the ordinary way the grants that
are made from the Road Fund are made
by my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates) in consultation with the Minister
of Finance, and there is never another
word about it, that is to say, adjustments
are made by the local authorities approaching my right hon. Friend. Then he and
the Minister of Finance get together and
the proper allocation from the Road Fund
is made in order to assist the whole of the
area under our control. This became a very
big question, and as this was by far the
largest single grant that has been made
out of the Road Fund my colleagues and
myself came to the conclusion that the
more open and honourable way to take
would be to announce the fact that we are
willingly going to bear upon that Fund
the cost of the Derry Bridge. It would
have undoubtedly leaked out in time and
there might have been something said
about underhand methods, or that the
country should have been informed at an
earlier date.
Now, supposing that the Government
did not help to build the bridge it would
cast upon the city of Derry rates which
the people really could not bear. It
would mean, taking an ordinary loan to
expire or pay itself out in some twentyfive years, that it would impose an additional rate upon Derry city of something
between 2s 4d and 2s 6d in the pound
straight away. The consequence would
be that, with unemployment rather severe
in Derry at the moment owing to the unfortunate closing down of the local shipyard, the people there, with the burden
of the new waterworks they are undertaking at the moment and other improvements in the city, would be really unable
to afford the cost of such an enormous
undertaking as the new bridge.
In the ordinary way a very large grant
would have been given out of the Road
Fund, but we must take into consideration the fact that the Corporation of
Derry have been made custodians of
the bridge and the only custodians
for the future-so that by aiding
the whole of Ulster in securing
proper through traffic Derry will be
saddled with the upkeep of that bridge
for all time to come, and that will be a
considerable expense on the city outside
the question of the extra 2s. 4d. or 2s. 6d.
on the rates to which I have referred. As
this will impose no taxation whatever
upon Ulster, as the Road Fund is in
a healthy condition and will be able to
afford the money, and as all money from
the Road Fund is spent actually upon
roads and bridges, we think it is only
right that this work should be carried out,
and carried out at the earliest possible
date, and I do not believe there is anyone in the House or outside it will grudge
this little extra generosity to the Maiden
City in making good the difference between
what they would have got in the ordinary
way out of the Road Fund and what the
Government have undertaken to pay for
the whole of the work.
There is just one other point in connection with this to which I would refer.
Those of us who have been in close touch
with that city realize the very high capabilities of the authorities in Derry. I

Mr. COLLINS: I rise to support this
Motion which has been proposed by the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) and which I think is most opportune. The Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) made it easy for me when he
used what I would call almost a threat,
if I did not know his own good nature.
He said that if anyone had any remedies,
or knew of any remedies for the state of
affairs which exists in Northern Ireland
at the present moment it was criminal on
their part not to bring them forward. He
also spoke of original remedies. I will
now disclose to the Minister of Labour a
few remedies which I think would help
matters, and I think he will find that
they are original. I do not propose to
deal at length with the figures dealing
with the registered unemployed which the
Minister gave at such length. I leave
that to my Friends on the Labour
Benches, but one thing I would like them
to remember when they are discussing
this matter is the enormous number of
unemployed who have passed through our
ports within the last few years, many of
whom could not have come under the
notice of the Minister of Labour.
Though I am a new comer to this
House I have carefully followed in the
Press its activities, and was surprised
to observe that the House instead of
attacking the existing appalling conditions
expended its efforts in bringing forward
Bills of the type of the Trade Unions
Bill. Had I been here earlier I would
have opposed this Bill strongly, because
there was no general strike in the Six
Counties nor in any part of Ireland, and
I would have objected to the time being
taken up discussing the terms of the Bill
framed to meet a hypothetical situation
that had no appearance of arising and
that may never arise.
We are faced in these Six Counties
with situations that are not hypothetical,
that are very real, vital situations which
demand immediate attention. I refer in
particular to the desperate plight in which
our farmers find themselves, and to the
very depressed condition of commerce.
These conditions bring in their train
sufferings for a large number of the inhabitants of all classes, some of whom are
registered unemployed, but many of whom
are workless and draw no unemployment
benefit.
Before developing my argument and
suggesting the remedies which should be
adopted by this House to ease these situations, I crave your indulgence for a short
time to make a personal explanation regarding the position of my constituents
and myself now that I have appeared in
this arena. I represent people who believed that they had specific rights reserved for them in Article 12 of the Irish
Treaty. They believed these rights were
sacred and inviolable, but, alas, these
rights were violated, notwithstanding the
solemn declarations of the chief English
statesmen who signed the Treaty-Lord
Birkenhead and Mr. Lloyd George.
I was elected before the finding of the
Boundary Commission on the express
understanding that I would not prejudice
the rights of my constituents by entering
this House at any time, but existing circumstances being what they are, I have
been requested by many of those who
elected me to take my seat and to do what
I can in their interests, without prejudicing in the slightest way the ultimate recognition of their inherent rights to full Irish
citizenship.
Now that I am here I wish to tell the
House that, while the people whom I
represent protest through me, and will
continue to protest against the injustice
and unfairness of condemning them to live
under a constitution with such limitations
as the 1920 Act has imposed on this House,
yet I will give while I remain here my unstinted support to legislation introduced
by any party, Government or otherwise,
which will alleviate and improve the lot

of the people amongst whom we move. It

Many people are suffering in this area,

these tenants in a most unfair position.
They compete in the same market with the
Free State unbought tenants, who have
the advantage of a double reduction on
their rents. A Louth farmer whose rent
was £20 now pays £12 10s, while a neighbour across the Border in County Armagh
continues to pay £20, which will be
reduced to £16 11s 8d only when the

on their rents, such payment to take effect
from the day the Free State Act came into
operation. The necessary money can be
reserved from the annual Imperial contribution which we are told goes to London.

propose
This Parliament is in a difficulty about
doing anything big for commerce, for its
hands are tied. Section 4 of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, prohibits it
from making any laws regarding the external trade of the area and from granting
bounties on the export of goods, and
Section 21 prohibits it from taxing any
article manufactured and produced, so it
is useless to talk about a subsidy for beet
here, because you have no power to put a
tax on any sugar that may come into the
port of Belfast from Liverpool or elsewhere. While I personally believe that
the condition of the commerce and trade
of this area will never be fully righted
until the three million customers on the
other side of the Border are restored to
the distributors and manufacturers on
this side of it, there seems to be a consensus of opinion that if the crushing
taxation could be reduced commerce and
trade might improve to an extent, and
unemployment in a corresponding ratio
would tend to disappear.
You have Section 25 of the Government
of Ireland Act, and I would like to refer
the House to that section. It states that
the Parliament of Northern Ireland
shall have power to grant relief from
income tax and super tax, or either of
those taxes, to individuals resident and
domiciled in Southern and Northern
Ireland respectively, and such relief may
be given either generally to all such
individuals whose total income is less
than such amount as may be determined
by the Act granting the relief.
There you have a power which you have
not exercised in any way. Since the year
1921 no Bill has been brought into this
House to reduce the crushing income-tax
that is keeping down industry to a great
extent. Subject to the recommendation
of the Prime Minister, or whoever is the
responsible and proper person from whom
to obtain leave, it is my proposal to introduce a Bill which will wipe out this
income-tax altogether. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I told you my remedies
would be original. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I request the Prime
Minister then to get that permission for
me so that I may introduce the Bill.
On this my maiden speech in this House
I regret to have to make a personal ex-

The policy pursued by the Ministry of
Labour is something to be deplored. It is
not only brutal; it is outrageous. What is
the policy of the Ministry in regard to
claims for benefit? His servants appear
at the counter, and they put the question
very abruptly, "Where were you looking
for work this morning"? If the claimant
has not got the name of a firm on the tip
of his tongue, a bad mark goes down
against him. On the next signing day the
same query is put to him. Perhaps the
individual is taken unawares.
He may
give only three firms where he has been
looking for employment. The next thing
he receives is a notice to attend the Court
of Referees. as he has failed to prove that
he is genuinely seeking work. That is
done by the clerk; that is done by the
servants of the Minister.
I say that that is unfair, and that a
gross injustice is being inflicted on men
who are not prepared for the questions
put to them. 1 protest strongly against
such action at the Labour Exchange.
The Labour Exchange is a standing disgrace to the Government of Northern
Ireland. It is a monument to the continuous unemployment that has prevailed
in our day and generation. We would not

farmers farming their holdings profitably
and many labourers employed on these
holdings who would not be employed
if this scheme had not been adopted. It
is all very well for the Minister of Agriculture to prophesy that when the subsidy
is withdrawn the scheme and the industry
will collapse. But we
are shown that
very often schemes of this kind succeed
despite the advice and prophesy of experts.
I read in Hansard recently the reply of
one of the Ministers, in which he admitted there were 6,000 children in Belfast schools and 6,000 children in the
other primary schools in the Six Counties.
Have you thought seriously of what is
going to happen to those young people
when they are discharged, as they must
be discharged, some of these days on the
labour market? Is your only reply to
say,
"We have set up an Emigration
Department in Armagh "? The duty of
the Government is to provide a living
wage, or at all events to provide employment, for the young citizens, but the only
practical way in which I think you have
tried to grapple with the situation is by
teaching these people shorthand and typewriting. How are you going to improve
the position of the children of the farmers
and the labourers who ought to be employed on the land by teaching them
two such useless subjects from the point
of view of either wage-earning or utility?
What you ought to do is to fit those
people for carrying out the primary objects for which they were created, namely,
to earn their living on the land. I have
recently come across two instances of the
appalling conditions that obtain in the
rural areas which would, I think, put to
shame anything in the cities. But because these people have not trade unions,
because they are not directly represented
in this House, the possibilities are they
will go on suffering in silence. I read of
a man in County Tyrone who had been
prosecuted for not making his children
attend school, and he went to the court
and told the magistrates that they had
had no food in the place for some days.
The school attendance officer and the sergeant of police confirmed that statement.
That happened in what may be regarded
as the comparatively prosperous County
of Tyrone
Then in the town of Enniskillen,
which has certain historical values that
the Minister of Agriculture would appreciate, at all events about the twelfth
of July, I know to my own knowledge
two able-bodied labourers who went two
days without food. These people are too
proud to beg. I suppose they are too
honest to steal, and they are not courageous enough to go into the streets and kick
up a row, as they would do if they lived
in Belfast. There is reason for the Government dealing with this problem, inasmuch
as in the Colwyn Report the amount of
the Imperial contribution is the surplus
of income over revenue. If you spend an
adequate sum in the development of the
rural areas you will have a smaller contribution to pay, and surely it is far more
essential that you should attend to the
needs of your own people than that you
should be in a position to boast one of
these days of having sent an enormous
sum of money across to Great Britain.
I know some of the Members on the
Government Benches will tell me
they have as much sympathy with the
workers as I have. I will tell them that
if I were sitting on the Front Bench I
should attempt to do something for the
agricultural labourers. There is no use
in a Minister shedding metaphorical
crocodile tears over the fate of the
labourers. There is no use in his telling
how much he feels for their sufferings if
he sits down there and does practically
nothing for them. All that has been
done for labour in the Six Counties has

LICENSING SESSIONS.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state how many Petty Sessions Courts
are held annually in Northern Ireland
for the renewal of publicans' licences;
what number of miles is travelled by resident magistrates for the purpose of holding these Courts; what was the amount
of their travelling expenses for September, 1926; and what number of licences,
if any,
were refused renewal in
month.
that

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): There are
Courts held each year in the month of
September for the renewal publicans'
licences.
The total distance travelled by resident
magistrates during the month of Septemher, 1926, for the purpose of holding such
Courts was approximately 10,000 miles,
and the travelling expenses in respect of
that month amounted to £336 15s 6d.
No licences were refused renewal in
September, 1926.
RAILWAYMEN'S WAGES IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he has received any notification from the railway companies operating in Northern Ireland as to their
alleged intention to reduce the wages of
the employees; and whether he is aware
that negotiating machinery exists in this
trade for settling differences and disputes;
and would he take steps to compel these
companies to submit their claims to the
proper authority for settlement.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The answer to the first part
of the question is in the negative and to
the second in the affirmitive. As regards
the last part, I am quite satisfied that the
railway managements in Northern Ireland, as well as the railway employees,
will honourably adhere to any agreement
they have entered into, and are most
anxious that no industrial trouble should
arise.
REORGANIZATION OF NORTHERN
IRELAND RAILWAYS.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister whether any steps have been taken to
carry out the reorganization of the railways in Northern Ireland, as suggested
in his statement on this subject in April
låst.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply.
Following upon the statement referred
to by the hon. Member, my colleagues
and I took steps to call together, in conference, the Chairmen and General Managers of the various railway undertakings
operating in Northern Ireland.
of
From the discussion which took place
at that meeting it was evident that there
would be serious difficulties in the way
reorganization by grouping on the lines
adopted in Great Britain and the Irish
Free State, and also that the economies
which might normally be expected from
such a course would not be readily obtainable here.
As the hon. Member is aware, one of
our most important Railway systems
already forms part of one of the principal
groups operating in Great Britain, while
a number of the other undertakings
operate only partly in Northern Ireland.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that
the right hon. Gentleman has told us that
one of the systems operating in Northern

smaller houses, and they used some hard
words in connection with my Amendment

of the house is going to reap the benefit
of the Government's subsidy. There is no
guarantee in this Bill as it now is that
the tenant will reap the benefit of the
subsidy of £100 Parliament is making.
If, for example, a private contractor
builds three houses he gets the Government subsidy of £100 and he may get a
local subsidy of £40. There is no
guarantee that the advantage of that
£140 will be given to the tenant, none in
the world. It is possible the tenant may
get the advantage of it, but there is nothing in this Bill to ensure that he will.
There is another point in connection with
this Bill. I think it is
I think it is a reactionary
policy to bring down the number of
superficial feet in a house from 950 to
650. One can quite understand the
hon. Member (Mrs. Chichester) feeling
annoyed at people calling that a reactionary policy. I think it is a reactionary
policy when the working people have to
live in those houses. I would say this
much, that so far as any Member of this
House is concerned I do not know that
he or she would care particularly to live
in a house of 650 superficial feet or less.
I think we on these benches are quite
justified in calling it a reactionary
Measure in so far as it has reduced the
number of superficial feet for which the
subsidy will be granted.
A grant of £140 is equal to 2s 10d a
week. Like my hon. Friend the Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) I was not
at all clear as the result of the Second
Reading speeches and the subsequent
Second Reading speech of the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
regarding this particular Clause in the
Bill, that is Clause 2, that a loan repayable in twenty-five years works out at
5s 8d a week. It seems to me it works
out at something like 2s 7d, whereas the
grant of £140 works out at 2s 10d a week.
I understand this Clause is purely a permissive Clause, and that it is put in at the
instance of the local authorities to enable
them to sell the houses they build because
private enterprise failed to build houses.
Private enterprise has not succeeded in
building sufficient houses with the result
that the Government have had to step in
and subsidize both the private builders
and the local authorities so that the community may be properly housed.
There has been a tremendous lot of
criticism of this and other Measures from
the point of view of subsidies. I wonder
do hon. Members ever realize the extent
to which subsidies are paid in the modern
State, in the Six Counties, for example.
I have a long list here which I do not intend to weary the House by going through,
but if hon. Members would think for a
moment or two before they complain about
subsidies from the point of view of the
State and the desirability of getting back
to private enterprise they would realize
how absurd their particular contention is.
We are glad the Government have thought
fit to subsidize the building of houses,
because otherwise it would be impossible,
and we can prove to the hilt if necessary
that private enterprize has failed.
One of the greatest complaints we have
made on the Second Reading and during
the Committee stage of this Bill is that
the Government even now apparently are
not prepared to submit plans to local
authorities for the erection of decent
houses to be let at decent rents. That
this has been done in Great Britain some
of us at least know, and I would entreat
the Government, because, after all, this
will not be the final word so far as housing
is concerned, to produce plans for the local
authorities to enable them still further
to erect houses for the working class
people. It will mean an extension of subsidies, but so far as we on these benches
are concerned, we are quite prepared to
face up to the subsidising of housing or
anything else that requires it.

interest.
In this Bill as it stands at present the
authorities advancing the money in a rural
district have no security whatever, and
the reason they have no security is this:
If a small farmer applies for money to
build a house the Act says that the plot
on which the house is to be built is to be
taken out of the farm and is to be separately registered on a separate register in
the local Registration of Title Office.
The effect of that is that if a man wants
to build a house in the middle of his farm
you must take the plot on which the
house is out of the farm, leave the house
standing there with the farm all round it;
and if it is necessary to realize that house
if, for instance, the man does not pay his

one

CLAUSE 1 (Illegal strikes and lockouts).
1. (1) It is hereby declared—
(a) that any strike is illegal if it-
(i) has any object other than or in
addition to the furtherance of a
trade dispute within the trade
or industry in which the
strikers are engaged; and
(ii) is a strike designed or calculated to coerce the Government
either directly or by inflicting
hardship upon the community;
and
(b) that any lock-out is illegal if it-
(i) has any object other than or in
addition to the furtherance of a
trade dispute within the trade or
industry in which the employers
locking-out are engaged; and
(ii) is a lock-out designed or calculated to coerce the Government
either directly or by inflicting
hardship upon the community;
and it is further declared that it is illegal
to commence, or continue, or to apply any
sums in furtherance or support of, any
such illegal strike or lock-out.
For the purposes of the foregoing provisions-
(a) a trade dispute shall not be
deemed to be within a trade or
industry unless it is a dispute between employers and workmen,
or between workmen and workmen, in that trade or industry,
which is connected with the employment or non-employment or
the terms of the employment, or
with the conditions of labour, of
persons in that trade or industry;
and
(b) without prejudice to the generality of the expression "trade or
industry" workmen. shall be
deemed to be within the same
trade or industry if their wages
or conditions of employment are
determined in accordance with
the conclusions of the same joint
industrial council, conciliation
board or other similar body, or
in accordance with agreements
made with the same employer or
group of employers.
(2) If any person declares, instigates,
incites others to take part in or otherwise
acts in furtherance of a strike or lock-out,
declared by this Act to be illegal, he shall
be liable on summary conviction to a fine
not exceeding ten pounds or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three
months, or on conviction on indictment to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding
two years:

of view before the Committee. In the

strike the alleged general strike-was
the biggest strike that ever took place,

not only to declare strikes illegal, however, that this Bill is brought in. It is
brought in because of the growing
strength of the trade union movement as

growing strength of the trade union movement as a whole. As my colleague says,
all the laws in the land will not stop the
workers from striking if the workers think

some hope for the trade unionists in

We know that there is a certain class
in the community which is opposed to
strikes. I believe the general opinion
amongst trade union officials and the
majority of trade union representatives,
is that a strike is not a desirable thing.
But there comes a time when the workers
have to resort to strikes, that is, when
they meet the type of person who will not
consider their claims in a sensible way.
That is an awkward time for the workers,
because they have, in their wisdom, to
consider three things. First and foremost, is the strike to be undertaken with
the object of improving their conditions?
Second, is it designed and calculated to
injure the Government? Third, what
part will the strike play in so far as the
community is concerned? When they
have made up their minds as to whether
the strike is legal or illegal, perhaps the
iron rod has gone, and they are left in
the hopeless position that a strike would
be of no use to them.
I want to ask the Attorney-General if
he has ever heard of a lightning strike.
I was working in an industry in which
lightning strikes took place. We had,
perhaps, three or four strikes in one week.
These struggles take place periodically
within an industry, and they have the
effect in an indirect way of injuring the
community. I would like to hear how
the right hon. and learned Gentleman
proposes to deal with a strike of that

feel that if an end is going to be put to

in grave danger of being subjected to the
last word of the employers every time.
That is to say, take it or leave it. Trade
unionists should have the right, if the

get their grievances settled in the shortest
possible time.

suggest is we are mentally in a ramshackle

It is quite a common part of the propaganda of the party opposite and their
associates in England always to represent
the working classes as if they were dull,
stupid, silent creatures who would never
revolt against the conditions imposed upon
them by their masters if cunning and
selfish leaders did not lure them away from

by the classes represented by hon. Gentlemen opposite both in England and in Ireland. But in the working out of it there
could be nothing so foreign to the real
condition of affairs. I have rarely known
a strike that was inspired or ordered by

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in Clause 1,
page 2, line 3, to leave out from "illegal"
(lock-out is illegal") to end of line 12
(upon the community").
The object of this Amendment is perfectly obvious to every member of the
Committee. It is to obviate all the
"other thans, "the "in addition to's,"
and the "buts" and the "whens" of this
Clause. The object of the Amendment
is to make all lock-outs illegal. Anybody
who has any experience of, or who has
taken advantage of the experience gained
by, a big lock-out, say, the engineers'
lock-out in 1898, or any of the other great
lock-outs that have taken place in industry, cannot but agree that these lockouts have been instrumental in causing the
greatest suffering to hundreds of
thousands, if not millions, of the population. The biggest illustration, of course,
is that of the lock-out which preceded the
general strike, the lock-out by the coalowners of the miners.
That lock-out had such serious consequences that it made this Government
as well as the British Government introduce legislation. Therefore we are perfectly entitled as a Parliament to say to
employers and associations of employers
that they are going to be prohibited by
law from declaring a lock-out. Lockouts are generally indulged in by associations of employers to compel the working
people to accept conditions which the
employers cannot justify through negotiations or argument. That is generally the
case, I do not care what lock-out is taken
in history. Take the 1898 lock-out in the
engineering trade. No doubt the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Labour will be able to give us his
experience of the lock-out in the engineering trade in 1898, when the men were
McMullen, William
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattle.
prepared to carry on at their original
rates of pay, but the employers worsened
their position and lowered their rates of
pay.
Those men were locked out in consequence of the fact that the employers
could not justify this reduction in wages
before any responsible body of men, or
even before the British Government of
that time. The whole aim of lock-outs is
to starve the workers to submission. If
the weapon of the lock-out is not for that
purpose, what is it for? I defy the
learned Attorney-General or any Member
on the other side of the Committee to say
any lock-out engaged in by any employers
or association of employers is not engaged
in in order to starve the women and the
children of the people they lock out and
compel them through sheer hunger and
starvation to accept the terms laid down
by the employers. I think it is a perfectly desirable thing to declare any lockout illegal.
The fairness of the Amendment I move
will be obvious to anyone, particularly to
those on the opposite side who have been
unfortunate enough to have been locked
out. They are very few, I agree. But
those others who have never been locked
out by employers, and those who have the
advantage of higher education than some
of us here have got, will remember when
they were being taught history in the
colleges of Northern Ireland, what the
results of lock-outs in the past have been.
Surely it is up to them to do something
for their less fortunate fellow-creatures
in Northern Ireland and to help us to
declare that any lock-out is illegal.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I think
the Committee can very well appreciate
the position which this Amendment
2697 Trade Disputes Bill-

8 NOVEMBER 1927
Committee
stands in when it is contrasted with the
Amendment they have already dealt with.
The first Amendment proposed that any
strike should be legal if it was authorized
in writing by a trade union, that means
to say, the legality or illegality of a strike
was to be entirely in the judgment of a
trade union. This Amendment is designed from an entirely opposite point of
view. Instead of allowing the legality
or illegality of a lock-out to be decided as
the Bill says the legality of a strike shall
be decided, namely, by a competent court,
it is declared if this Amendment is carried that it is illegal in all events. The
merits of the Amendment can easily be
grasped by contrasting it with the Amendment which has been already defeated.
I submit it is perfectly fair to put strikes
and lock-outs on precisely the same footing. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). In
this Bill they are put on precisely the
same footing, and the hon. Member who
has just sat down put it to this Committee as if there was something entirely
distinct between the strike and the lockout. He says to the Committee that
lock-outs cause suffering. Admittedly
they do, in a great many instances, but I
would point out to the Committee that
strikes also cause suffering. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). We are all aware of
strikes which have caused an immense
amount of suffering. Our memories need
not go further back than the strike of
May of last year of which this Bill is the
outcome.
He says also that a lock-out is at the
whim of an employer. There is no doubt
that employers from time to time have
whims, but I would ask the Committee
to consider whether trades unions have
not got whims, and whether it is not just
as possible that a trade union should call
their people out for a mere whim, which
has no real foundation in justice, as it is
that an employer should lock his people.
out for a similar reason. Therefore, the
Government have to stand impartially between the employers on the one hand and
the employed on the other.
He says
It
again that lock-outs are done to compel
people to starve. Well, I do not knowthere may have been lock-outs which were
designed to compel people to stave.
may be that that is only an incident in

Therefore whatever is alleged on the

cases can be alleged equally against the
employed, and the Government have to
stand clear between the two. It is erroneous to assume that an employer is
always unreasonable, and that the employed are always reasonable. I do
not think any Member of this Committee,
or any member of the community, could
draw a line as to where the reasonableness or unreasonableness of either employer or employed begins or ends. In
matters of this description the Government have got to stand impartially between both parties, and for that object
this Clause has been included in the Bill,
to put both on precisely similar footing,
and to ensure that before a strike or lockout is declared to be illegal it must involve certain conditons which are explicitly laid down in the Clause now under
consideration.
