The reason why I support this Amendment is that it eliminates all those qualifications. It frankly asserts that a lockout is illegal. I would even much prefer
that that was done as far as a strike is
concerned, because then we would know
what our position was, and the people
would know what their position was. The
Minister of Labour and the other spokes
men of the Government want Members on
these benches and the trades unionists of
Northern Ireland to believe that their
powers are not being curtailed in any way
at all, whereas the liberties of the people
are actually being filched away from
them.
It would remove all that vague
ness and would let the people actually see
what the situation was. I am sure it is
not the intention of the Government that
the trades unions and the men should be
involved in costly litigation to find out
extactly what is a legal strike and what is
a legal lock-out.

I would suggest that the old methods
are much preferable to these. They have.
brought some hardship in their train undoubtedly. Anybody who has read anything at all about industrial disputes is
quite conversant with the fact that lockouts have brought a tremendous amount
of hardship, and there is far more reason
why a lock-out should be made illegal
than there is why a strike should be made
illegal. Strikes are not indulged in by
a number of irresponsible people.
withstanding what the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant) on the Government benches may say, a person must give
some evidence of reliability and common
sense before he is put into the positiona very responsible position-of being the
leader of a trade union branch or a trade
union movement, and those people very
acutely realize that when engaging in industrial disputes they have in their hands
the lives and destinies not only of their
own members, but also of their wives and
dependants.
Those circumstances are always
weighed very fully and very carefully
before anybody contemplates launching out on an industrial dispute.
That is sufficient deterrent to prevent
any wild attempt on the part of any.
industrial leader to employ his forces in a
futile industrial dispute. That has
always been a deterrent, and I suggest
that if an analysis were undertaken of
industrial disputes in Northern Ireland
and in Great Britain it would be found
that those that have been unjustified were
infinitesimal, that fundamentally there

grievance for which any particular dispute was undertaken, and that it was only
undertaken as a last resort. The same
thing cannot be said as far as lock-outs
are concerned. I was reading quite recently a novel by Upton Sinclair, which

it was scandalous and shameful the open
victimization that took place there
amongst the American coal owners.

SAFEGUARDING OF THE LINEN
TRADE.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Prime
Minister whether any action has been
taken, and, if so, of what nature, to have
the linen trade of Northern Ireland
scheduled under the Safeguarding of Industries Act, and assisted against unfair
competition.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply. The hon. and
gallant Member will, doubtless, appreciate
that it would not be possible for the linen
trade of Northern Ireland to take any
independent action in this matter as apart
from the linen trade in Great Britain.
An application for safeguarding has been
made by those interested in this trade in
Northern Ireland, acting in conjunction
with those similarly interested in Great
Britain. The position is that so far the
applicants have been unable to satisfy the
Board of Trade that a prima facie case
exists for the appointment of a Committee
of Inquiry in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Rules which have
been prescribed in connection with the
Safeguarding of Industries Scheme.
Mr. KYLE: Is it a fact that the
Government have made a mess of the
application of the linen trade? Is it not
a fact that the linen trade is practically
solely in the North of Ireland and the
application for the safeguarding of the industry is more important for the North of
Ireland than it is for Great Britain? Is
it not a fact that the Government have
made a mess of the negotiations between
the British Government and ourselves?
Mr. BARBOUR: I am much indebted
to the hon. Member for affording me the
opportunity to correct the statement
which appeared in the public papers, I
think, of yesterday, and if the hon.
Member had read a little further down
in the same column he would have seen
that a prominent member of the trade had
stated that the Government had not been
responsible in any way for the case submitted to the Department in London.
Mr. KYLE: Would the Minister say
the leaders of the linen trade made a mess
of the application?
Colonel WOODS: I would just like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman does he not
think this would be essentially a case for
the Government of Northern Ireland,
affecting as it does the most vital interests
in the country?
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether on an important
matter of this character it was not desirable to get all the thirteen Members from
Northern Ireland and have a conference
with them, have a proper case prepared
for them, have a proper presentation of
that case in the Imperial Parliament, and
whether that was done?
Mr. BARBOUR: Of course we are
very proud of the position we enjoy as an
integral part of the United Kingdom, so
that we have direct representation in the
Imperial Parliament, but after all, it is
a matter for the members of the trade
themselves to take up and present their
case where they consider they are suffering
from unfair competition from abroad.
They are more intimately acquainted
with the details of their trade than a
Government Department can be. I may
say my Department is in entire sympathy
with them and anxious at all times to
render such assistance as they can to those
industries which may be desirous of submitting a case for consideration. I believe

RECONSTRUCTION OF CARLISLE
BRIDGE, DERRY.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether the grant promised by the Prime
Minister to Derry Corporation in connection with the construction of Carlisle
Bridge will in any way affect the ordinary
grants made out of the Road Fund to
Derry County or to any of the other local
authorities.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This proposal will
not affect the grants payable out of the
Road Fund to road authorities in Northern Ireland.
It must be borne in mind that the reconstruction of the bridge, which forms
part of a Class 1 road, would in the
normal way be equitably entitled to rank
for grant in the same way as other approved reconstruction works on Class 1
roads and, therefore, qualify for a 72 per
cent. grant, leaving the Londonderry
Corporation to find the remaining. 28 per
cent.
In the present case, however, owing to
the importance of the bridge from a
national point of view, the Government
have taken a broad view of the situation
and have agreed to bear the remaining
28 per cent., which will involve a yearly
additional charge on the fund of, approximately, £4,000 during the loan period,
an amount which will not affect the payment of the normal grants to road authorities.
It must be also remembered that under
the Acts under which the bridge was
originally constructed, portions of the
counties of Londonderry and Tyrone were
charged with the cost of construction and
maintenance, thus showing that the bridge
was one of more than local importance.
The counties in question have been since
the passing of the Act of 1924 relieved of
these charges on the ground that the
bridge would qualify for a substantial
grant from the Road Fund.
BELFAST GUARDIANS AND OUT-
DOOR RELIEF.
Mr. McMULLEN (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware that the Belfast
Board of Guardians have carried into
effect their Resolution of the 11th October,
1927, terminating outdoor relief to all
those who have been in receipt of same
continuously for 12 months; whether as
a result of this action relief has been discontinued in 235 cases, affecting 1,097
persons, and whether he will state what
action the Government intends to take to
prevent starvation and famine entering
the houses of the people.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It has been
brought to my notice that the Belfast
Board of Guardians at their meeting held
yesterday have decided to adhere to the
policy formulated by them on the 11th
October last, and that 235 cases affecting
1,097 persons have, apparently, been
struck off the outdoor relief list.
.
At the same time it is
open to the persons affected to renew their applications to
the Board of Guardians, upon whom it
will then devolve to reconsider the cases
on their merits.
I find it difficult to believe that if any
cases of starvation or famine come under
the notice of the Board of Guardians that
Board would be capable of incurring the
very serious responsibility of refusing to
deal with them equitably and adequately.
As I have frequently stated in this
House, Parliament has placed on the
Guardians, and on them alone, the responsibility for relieving cases of distress
and destitution, and the Government has
no jurisdiction to interfere with the
Guardians in their discretion in dealing
with individual cases.
My Ministry is keeping in close touch
with the situation, and I am still not
without hope that the Guardians will not
decline to relieve any cases of real hardship or destitution.

for a term not exceeding two years:

under this section or at common law by

or refused to continue to work or to
accept employment.

this section, no further proceedings in

Mr. KYLE: I beg to propose the
Amendment you have read to the Committee. The reasons for doing so are that
the sub-sections (a) and (b) of this Clause
are so vague, and so indeterminate in
character that it is impossible for an
ordinary person, be he lawyer or trade
union official or a member of a trade
union, to understand when a lock-out or
trade dispute is legal. It seems that paragraph (a) of this Clause I means that if a
shop was composed of 90 per cent. of trade
unionists and the other 10 per cent. were
either non-unionists or members of some
blackleg organisation like the Unionist
Labour Association, the 10 per cent. of the
employees could hold up and determine
what conditions the whole shop were going
to work under, and that if a dispute took
place in consequence of the fact that some
90 per cent. of the men ceased work then
the strike might be declared illegal, and
the trade union resposible for that strike
might be held liable for damages or the
members taking part in the strike might
be liable to imprisonment.
Paragraph (b) of this Clause states:
without prejudice to the generality of
the expression "trade or industry"
workmen shall be deemed to be within
the same trade or industry if their
wages or conditions of employment are
determined in accordance with the conclusions of the same joint industrial
council, conciliation board or other
similar body, or in accordance with
agreements made with the same employer or group of employers.
Now when discussing this Blll on the

(Mr. Andrews), declared that engineering
was an industry. He is the first man in
Great Britain or Ireland who has been
bold enough to make such a statement.

Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman
jumps in where obviously the difficulty
was so great to define this industry,
and he says that engineering is an industry. What we want to know is: will
the right hon. Gentleman's opinion hold
in a court of law, or will it be the Bill as
it is now before us? Will we be entitled
to quote the right hon. Gentleman when
we have a dispute, for example, in a
section of the linen trade where engineers
may be effected? As engineering is an
industry, according to the right hon.
Gentleman, their trade union should not
be held liable for damages in a strike held
A to be illegal under the Act. The
engineering trade is a complicated one.
For example, the negotiations that take
place in the shipyard trades govern the
wages and conditions of the engineers.
An entirely different set of employers decide the wages of men in what are called
the up-town shops. The employers in the
linen trade determine what wages they
are going to pay the engineers engaged in
that trade. The employers in the motor
trade, or the employers in, perhaps, half

a dozen other trades, determine what
wages their engineers are going to get.
We suggest to leave out all these
ambiguous things and put in something
definite. That something definite is on
the Order Paper, where it states that
where no negotiating machinery exists as
between employers and employees, every
employer shall be compelled to ask that
a tribunal of employers selected by the
Government and an equal number of
workers' representatives selected by the
trade unions shall be established to determine the claims either of the employers
for a reduction of working conditions or
of the employees for an increase of wages
or a betterment of conditions. Surely it
is a much more sensible proposition to ask
that that form of machinery should be
introduced than it is to put in Sections
(a) and (b) of this Clause.
There is also another very important
point about the Amendment we propose,
and it is that we, as trade union representatives and as Members of this House interested in the conditions of the working
people, are desirous of obviating strikes
and lock-outs. It is with that intention
that we propose this Amendment, and if
the Government and the Government's
supporters fight against this Amendment
are we to take it that those gentlemen
do not want to obviate strikes and lockouts in industry?
This Amendment will prevent what
takes place at the present time. You will
get, in country towns particularly, employers whose workpeople are not in a
trade union and have got no trade union
machinery to govern their conditions. Or
you will get in the country a great many
agricultural labourers employed by little.
farmers, who may or may not be members
of the Farmers' Union, and these gentlemen arrogate to themselves the right to
determine the hours, wages and conditions
under which their workpeople are going to
work. Because these people have been so
poorly paid in the past that they cannot
be members of a trade union, or because
they are so indifferent to their own conditions that they have no trade union to
argue for them, the employers adopt the
high hand, reduce their wages, increase
their hours or worsen their working conditions, and the workpeople have no option
but to strike. That has happened in many
cases not only in the country but in Belfast
in the mills particularly in Belfastwhere, although there are quite a number
of those people in trades unions, yet when
an alteration is made in their conditions
whole mills have been deserted by their
workpeople for days, and sometimes weeks
on end, because they felt that an injustice
was being perpetrated on them by their
employers. This is to obviate any stoppage of work of that character. It is also
to obviate lock-outs by employers and to
establish negotiating machinery where
people have got no trade union to
negotiate for them. Surely that is an
eminently fair proposition to put before
this Committee.
There is another matter, which appears
on line 14 of page 2, where it is further
declared that it is illegal
"to apply any sums in furtherance or
support of any such illegal strike or
lock-out."
What exactly is meant by the words
"to apply any sums in furtherance of"
a strike or a lock-out? Does it mean that
I as an individual am not going to be allowed to contribute money to persons who
are out on strike to enable them to keep
their wives or children, or to see that
those wives and children are fed during
the course of a strike which may be determined by the Courts to be illegal?
And what sort of machinery is it that is
going to determine the legality of the dispute? All these questions have not yet
been answered by the Government. They
have not been answered by the Government in Great Britain. They have not
been answered by the Government here,
and really before one could say that there
was any sense at all in the Measure we
would have to get much clearer definitions
than we have had up to now of the various
titles that are in this Bill.
You get an industry mentioned and a
trade mentioned, and it is not defined
what is a trade or what is an industry.
There is a very good reason for that ambiguity in the Bill, and it is because it
is impossible to define exactly what a
trade or what an industry is. But there
is one thing that is absolutely true, no
matter what else may be false, and that
is that engineering is not an industry.
Neither under this Bill nor by any stretch
of any person's imagination could engineering be called an industry. Different.
sets of employers determine the rates of

a Bill intended to regulate the relations

We have been asked a further question
with reference to the first portion of the
Clause with which we are dealing. It is
further declared that it is illegal
"to commence, or continue, or to apply
any sums in furtherance or support of,
any such illegal strike or lock-out."
I should have thought that on the face of
that sentence it was fairly clear what the
meaning of it is. It is quite plain that
under that it will not be an offence for
any citizen to apply money to persons who
are in distress as a result of a strike even
although that strike be illegal.
On the other hand, it will be illegal
for persons, whether they be members of
organised trade unions or otherwise, to
apply funds for the support of the strike.
That is to say, if the trade unions themselves apply their funds towards the
furtherance of an illegal strike the employment of those funds in that way will
be illegal. I think there can be no doubt
that if it is illegal, and if the House shall
so determine as a result of this Bill, under
the circumstances set out in Clause 1, it
is perfectly obvious that the corollary
should be included in the Bill that any
person who applies money towards the
furtherance of an illegality should not be
protected by the law. Consequently, it
is quite obvious that the Government
could not accept this Amendment, which,
as the hon. Member for North Belfast has
frankly admitted, is introduced entirely
in favour of the workers without reference whatever to the employers.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The
first point that has been made by the
hon. Member is this, that apparently
there might be great delay in obtaining
a declaration of the court in reference to
the legality or illegality of a strike. In
a matter of this sort, that could not take
place, because as many Members of the
Committee know there is always at least
one Judge of the High Court ready to hear
pressing applications during all the vacations throughout the whole year, and
there is never any difficulty in getting a
Judge of the High Court to deal with a
matter of this description.
The hon. Member further suggests that
what he calls a temporary injunction
might be granted without argument.
There again, according to the practice of
our courts that could not happen, because
no injunction, even what we call an interlocutory injunction, which is one made
by a judge in the first instance to continue until the hearing of the action, is
never made without hearing both sides.
fully, and giving them an opportunity of
putting their evidence before the Court,
either by affidavit or viva voce; and one
of the conditions which a court always imposes upon a litigant who is asking for an
interlocutory injunction is that he should
give an undertaking for damages towards
the defendant in the event of it being
ultimately decided that he was not entitled to his interim injunction.
Therefore I think that on those legal
points there is nothing that hon. Members opposite need fear, though I can
quite understand they object very much.
to having these questions decided by the
courts. But so far as the machinery of
the courts is concerned, I suggest that
there is no reason to anticipate any of
those difficulties that have been suggested.

served by the introduction of this Bill,

the people of Northern Ireland, that
those of us who are really interested in

Gentleman, the Attorney-General, a declaration of policy and an explanation of

British Parliament, and how any layman,

and Lord Halsbury, in the Lords; and
eminent lawyers like the late Attorney-
General in the Labour Government, and
the Attorney-General in Mr. Baldwin's
Government. One would have imagined
that this Measure was introduced for the

ought to be dealt with from a purely
human and industrial point of view.

difficult, but it would be almost impossible. But if the feeling of the Government, and of the hon. Gentleman opposite

I should have thought that the Government would have accepted that Amendment, subject to such changes as they
themselves might believe were essential

preferable, to starting prolonged litigation, a series of trials and all the irritation that spring from trials, fines, if it

people engaged in it were illegally engaged in it; imprisonment, and all the
heart-burnings and irritations that are

We hear a great deal nowadays of peace
in industry, of international peace, and
these trite sentiments are expressed upon
nearly every occasion by prominent politicians on public platforms. I very often
find that the official peace-maker or rhetorical peace-make, is a gentleman who,
in international affairs, believes in the
maintenance of the policy of large armaments. In industrial affairs it means that
when he talks about peace he introduces
some Measure of this sort that really provokes war. I think that men of sense,

would have expected that some Member

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: This
Amendment contains the germ of a principle that I would like very much to support, and that is the adoption of conciliation and arbitration as a means of settling
industrial disputes rather than that either
side should resort to warfare. I feel
strongly that war, as a means of settling
industrial disputes, is just as foolish and
wasteful and futile as is war in the international sphere as a means of settling
international disputes. I am sorry that
this Amendment is not drawn up in such
a way that I can support it, because I
am entirely in favour of that principle.
There is not a person who is interested in
the prosperity of his country who does not
rejoice to see the new spirit that is growing up in industry, the spirit of peace that
is asserting itself at the present time, and
we rejoice to see that, instead of resorting
to warfare in the industrial realm, both
labour and capital are more disposed to
settle their disputes by means of arbitration.
If this Amendment had been couched
in a different form I would have been
very glad to have supported it. If it
had made it illegal for either a strike or
a lock-out to take place until some conciliatory machinery had been set up by
the Government to deal with the merits
of that dispute, and until that tribunal
had given its decision, I would have supported it whole-heartedly. As the
Amendment has been drawn up, I do not
think it can be worked in practice because
it only goes in one direction. If the
amendment had introduced the thin end
of the wedge and had substituted, to some
extent, even compulsory arbitration and
made it illegal for either strikes or lockouts to take place until the merits of the
dispute had been dealt with by some
conciliatory Board set up by the Government, it would have had my wholehearted support. As it is I think it is
an Amendment that deserves the careful
consideration of the Committee and of
every man who has the prosperity of his
country at heart.

ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
number of concrete cases have been suggested here, and hon. Gentlemen have
asked whether under those circumstances
strikes would be legal or illegal. The
hon. Member who has just sat down has
put two. There was at least one put
yesterday by the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) when he asked
whether a lightning strike would be legal
or illegal. I think the case of the sympathetic strike has already been put by
the hon. Member who has just sat down,
and was also put yesterday by some Member on the other side of the Committee.
I am not going to direct, as we lawyers
say, the hon. Members' proofs for them.
but I can tell them this, that in the case
of the strikes they have mentioned,
whether they are lightning strikes, or
sympathetic strikes, or ordinary strikes
in the case of the men of one individual
employer, they can put the matter to a
very simple test.
They have only got to take Clause 1
of the Bill and ask themselves, first of all,
when ordering that strike if they have got
any object other than, or in addition to,
the furthering of a trade dispute, that is
the furthering of the interests of those
workers for whom they are acting, and if
they have not, then according to this Bill
it is not an illegal strike. If, having
made up their minds they have got some
ulterior motive, that is, if in the case of a
sympathetic strike they have got some
ulterior motive not connected with a trade
dispute at all, something connected with
some general social scheme, then having
made up their minds that they have got
this ulterior motive they have to go a step
further and propound a second question
for themselves. That is, whether that
ulterior motive is an attempt or a design
that is calculated to coerce the Government, either directly or indirectly, by inflicting hardship on the community. I
think hon. Members will really have no
difficulty whatever when they have to make
up their minds whether to call a
strike or not, in propounding these two
questions and seeing at once whether or
not the strike is illegal.
A great deal of criticism has been
passed with reference to this Bill upon
the score that it is going to lead to a
great deal of litigation. I think that,
so far from being so, it is very unlikely
there will ever be any litigation as the
result of this Bill, because once the declaration in this Bill becomes law, everybody will know with reasonable certainty
whether a strike is legal or whether it is
not legal, and the only effect of the Bill
will be to stop illegal strikes without requiring any declaration of the court, and,
as the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour, reminds me, also illegal
lock-outs. Therefore, I think the criticisms that have been passed upon this
Clause really do not go to the root of the
Clause itself, and that the great difficulties which have been professed by hon.
Members on the other side will not
mature when it finally becomes law.

The ATTORNEY GENERAL: This
proposed Amendment is first of all unnecessary, and secondly, it would
entirely out of place in a Clause of this
description. The Clause declares:
If any person declares, instigates, incites others to take part in, or otherwise
.
acts in furtherance of a strike or lockout, declared by this Act to be illegal,
he shall be liable
•
"
to certain penalties. It is one of the rules
of our law that with a penal Clause like
this, what we lawyers know as mens rea,
which means guilty intention, is always
of the essence of the offence. Therefore,
the use of the word deliberately is
quite unnecessary, because the declaration, instigation or incitement must be
done with the intention of furthering an
illegal lock-out in order to bring the delinquent or the accused within the scope
of the Act. Therefore the penalty which
the hon. Member (Mr. W. McMullen)
appears to think may follow from the Act,
namely, that an innocent person who had
unwittingly engaged in the declaration or
instigation of the illegal strike would be
penalized under the Section, does not
arise, because our law, which is framed
for the protection of people who commit
crimes unwittingly would protect him
from that penalty. Consequently, this
Amendment is quite unnecessary, and it
would be inappropriate too, to put "deliberately" before the word "declares" in
the Clause.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The following Amendment stood on
the Order Paper in the names of Mr.
Kyle, Mr. William McMullen, and Mr.
Beattie :-
Page 2, line 36, leave out sub-section (2)
and insert "if any employer of labour
shall combine with other employers for
the purpose of reducing wages, lenghtening the working week, worsening the
working conditions, or lowering the social
status of their employees, by lockout or
otherwise, they shall be liable for a first
offence, individually and collectively, on
summary conviction, to a fine of £10 or
to imprisonment for a term not exceeding
three months, and for a second offence
they shall be liable to suffer the confiscation of their undertakings."
The CHAIRMAN: I propose to take
this Amendment together with the three
following amendments, which are all part
and parcel of the same general question,
and they can be discussed together.
Mr. KYLE: This Amendment puts
from our point of view what the Government have put from their point of view
as regards the penalties that are to be imposed on persons who declare a strike or
incite others to take part in a strike. In
this Amendment we state:
—
"If any employer of labour shall
combine with other employers for the
purpose of reducing wages, lengthening
the working week, worsening the working conditions, or lowering the social
status of their employees, by lockout or
otherwise, they shall be liable for a first
offence, individually and collectively,
on summary conviction, to a fine of £10
or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, and for a second
offence they shall be liable to suffer the
confiscation of their undertakings."
This is a very revolutionary proposal
to put forward in a respectable Parliament of this nature, but it is not a bit
more revolutionary than the proposals the
Government have included in their Bill,
and it is because hon. Members opposite
and some hon. Members on this side of
the Committee are not accustomed to
hearing things put from the workers'
point of view that this proposal sounds rerevolutionary. It sounds just as revolutionary to me to be told that I am liable
to get two years' imprisonment for doing
what I conceive to be my duty as it does
to hon. Members opposite when we propose that an employer should suffer the
confiscation of his undertakings if he
offends twice against the law, or that an
employer should not be allowed to combine with other employers to worsen the
conditions of their workers. That is what
combinations of employers do in many
instances. You have got the historic
example of the mine-owners in Great
Britain. They combined and conspired
together to reduce the wages and worsen
the conditions of their workpeople, just
as the employers in Northern Ireland
have combined together in their respective associations to worsen the conditions
and reduce the wages of the working
people.
It is not more right for them to do that
than it is for trade unions to insist that
men should come out on strike if their
conditions of employment are such that
they have determined they are no longer
prepared to put up with those bad conditions. What is sauce for the goose should
be sauce for the gander. If you say that
workpeople, who take certain action
through their trade unions, are to be compelled to suffer penalities, it is equally
right that employers should be made
to suffer the same penalties. The fines
and terms of imprisonment I propose in
this Amendment are exactly the same as
are prescribed for workpeople in the
event of a strike in which they take part
being held to be illegal. If it is fair
from the point of view of the Government
to put these pains and penaities on trade
unionists, then I hold that it is equally
or even more fair to give to the employers
the same sauce that the Government intend to give to those of us who are in the
trade union movement. That is the sole
aim and object of this Amendment. I
beg to move.

Mr. ANDREWS: The Government
cannot accept this Amendment because,
obviously it is a one-sided one. It would
really make it impossible for employers
to combine and that would mean that collective bargaining and conciliation as between the representatives of the trade
unions and the representatives of the employers would be impossible. The penalties set out under this Bill are exactly the
same for employers and workers.
Bill does not really deal with legal strikes
at all. It only deals with those strikes
which are held by the courts to be illegal.

I employed an argument which I be
lieve is perfectly germane to this Clause.
that the general strike was not a cause it.
self, it was an effect, and we are asked to
believe that this legislation was introduced to deal with an effect and not with
the original cause. Now the Prime

The mineowners who did the locking out
were expecting employees to go down some

During the time the fratricidal

Outdoor Relief in Belfast.
MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed :
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Mr. Mulholland.)
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I want
very briefly to refer to a question I asked
to-day, and I regret very much, in connection with this matter, that I was not
able to extract a satisfactory answer from
the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates). I do not want to speak at very
great length because my throat is very
sore, but I would like to try to impress
upon the Government the gravity of this
whole situation. I understand that by a
resolution of the Belfast Board of Guardians of the 11th October, they have decided that a person who has been continously in receipt of outdoor relief
for twelve months will not receive
any more outdoor relief, and that
in the case of a person who has been
drawing continuously for six months outdoor relief will be discontinued on the expiration of three months.
In order that we might try to realize
the position in which these poor, unfortunate people are going to be placed, I
mentioned the fact that one of my constituents, the night before last, was compelled to take his wife and nine children
into the workhouse as a result of the
action of the Guardians in refusing to
give him outdoor relief. In circumstances like these it means a man has got
to sell up the home that he may have
gathered up during a lifetime of sacrifice.
That man has had to break up his home
in order to go into the workhouse to get
the necessaries of life, which have been
denied him by this most reactionary
Board-perhaps the most reactionary
Board to be found in any part of Northern Ireland, or, indeed, in the whole of
Ireland.
I would urge upon the Government
that they should take this matter seriously
into consideration. People are unable to
get employment. They cannot get unemployment benefit, and now, after they
have been drawing outdoor relief for a
time, it cannot be got either. Now we
want to see things conducted in a constitutional fashion so far as this Province
is concerned. I have been talking to a
number of men who have been driven to
a state of desperation as a result of this
action of the Board of Guardians, and I
want to say to the Prime Minister, that I
would not be responsible for the action
some of these people might take, being
deprived, as they are, of the necessaries
of life. I would not like to visualize a
state of affairs where my wife and family
were going to be subjected to starvation
as an alternative to going into the workhouse. It meant that the husband had to
go to one part of the institution, his
wife to another, and the children possibly
to another.
I hold that there is no justification for
this state of affairs at all. The Guardians
argue that the amount of their estimate is
exhausted, but the Minister of Home
Affairs points out that there is no limit
to the expenditure of the Guardians, so
far as providing outdoor relief is concerned, and this appears to be the conflict
between the Guardians and the Government. The Guardians, I understand,
contend that this should be 8 national
responsibility, and I observe from the
answer I have had to my question to-day
that the Government. take the point of
view that it is the duty of the Belfast
Board of Guardians to do this thing.
There is the conflict, and while that conflict is raging the people are starivng.

There has been a suggestion that, in
view of the fact that this burden would be
exceptionally heavy upon the ratepayers of
Belfast, the Government should come to
the assistance of the Guardians to enable
them to carry on the work they have been
doing up to the moment. I am indifferent as to where the money comes
from, but what I do not want to see, particularly in severe weather like this, and
with the early approach of Christmas, is
thousand of families in Belfast absolutely
destitute and not able to get the necessaries of life. This is one of the gravest
situations that has arisen during my lifetime, so far as Northern Ireland is concerned, and having briefly stated the
case I want to make an urgent and an
earnest appeal to the Prime Minister and
the Minister of Home Affairs to set to
and to do something in this situation to
ensure that these peoples' homes will not
be broken up through starvation, and
they themselves compelled to go into the
workhouse in order to get the necessaries
of life.

May I explain very shortly the legal
position of the Board of Guardians? The
general principle on which Boards of
Guardians were established was that indoor relief alone could be provided. It
was found in the old days that there were
certain exceptions in which outdoor relief
could be given. One was in the case of
old age and another was in the case of
infirmity. But an entirely new principle
was established under the Local Government Act of 1898. By virtue of Section
13 of that Act a Board of Guardians,
where they came to the conclusion that
exceptional distress existed, could apply
to the local authority-which in the case
of Belfast would be the Belfast Corporation-and the two combined could apply
to the old Local Government Board-now
the Home Office for authority to spend
money in relief of destitute cases without
bringing those people into the house.
The first application was made in 1924
ny the Board of Guardians themselves,
and the Corporation who realised then,
as they realise now, that there was and is
exceptional distress. The Government
at once acceded to the application, and an
Order was put into force. Since that
time Orders have been in force. My hon.
Friend has referred to the fact that conflict has arisen between the Board of
Guardians and the Government in regard
to a certain legal point.
on
I think the point is, roughly, the Board
of Guardians take the view that they are
limited to a threepenny rate in regard to
the expenditure
outdoor relief.
That is not so. It is perfectly true that
they are limited to a threepenny rate, so
far as the ratepayers under the Belfast
Corporation are concerned, but they are
not limited in regard to the area of the
Union of Belfast. The jurisdiction of the
Home Office is roughly this, they have the
right to question the advisability of putting these Orders into force, but up to the
present they have never questioned the
advisability of doing so, because they
admit that such distress does exist. On
the other hand, they have not the right
to interfere with or question the dis
cretion of the Board of Guardians in the

with individual cases.
I would remind my hon. Friend that

ESTABLISHMENT OF SUGAR BEET
INDUSTRY IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether the Commission on
the Natural and Industrial Resources of
Northern Ireland in their report on the
practicability of establishing the Sugar
Beet Industry in Northern Ireland, recommended that the question of a subsidy
be postponed for two years; whether these
two years will expire in April, 1928; and
whether he has considered the question;
and, if so, what decision has he arrived at
in view of the fact that farmers are now
preparing their land for next year's crops,
and should know whether or not the subsidy is to be given.
.
The MINISTER
OF AGRICUL
TURE (Mr. Archdale): The Commission on the Natural and Industrial
Resources of Northern Ireland recommended that the question of providing a
State subsidy for the establishment of a
Sugar Beet Industry in Northern Ireland
should be postponed for two years and
that during this two years' interval my
Ministry should arrange for the experimental growing of a limited area of
sugar beet in various districts. These
experiments, which are being carried out
at eleven centres in co-operation with
every County Committee of Agriculture
except Fermanagh, which declined to
undertake the work, were begun in the
present year and will be continued for a
second season in 1928. The two years'
period will not terminate until the 1928
crop has been saved and tested-which
will be at the end of 1928 or the beginning of 1929.
Until the results of the two years'
experiments in the growing of sugar beet
LOANS TO FERMANAGH
FARMERS.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has received any
representations from farmers in the
County of Fermanagh in favour of the
extension of the repayment period for the
Live Stock Replacement Loan, and representing the urgent need for a new longterm loan, to tide farmers over the losses
they have sustained in the past two years;
and if he will give sympathetic consider.
ation to such representations.
The following question also stood upon
the Order Paper.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT to ask the Minister
of Agriculture whether the Government
propose to extend the time for repayment
of loans which have been given to farmers
for replacement of live stock.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I shall take
questions 2 and 4 together. Before
answering them I propose to give the hon.
Members a brief history of operations
under the Live Stock Replacement Loans
Scheme. This scheme was first put into
operation in 1925, when 982 loans, representing a total of £45,509 were advanced.
These loans were repayable in full at the
end of 1925, but as it appeared to the
Ministry that it might in some cases be a
hardship to recall the loans as originally
intended, the period for repayment was
extended to the end of December 1926.
Towards the end of last year the Ministry
went into the position again and agreed
to grant a still further concession by
making the loans repayable in three
annual instalments at the end of each
of the years 1926, 1927 and 1928.
The scheme was re-opened in 1927 and
483 further loans, representing £23,753
were advanced. These 1927 Ionas are repayable by three annual instalments on the
31st March, 1928, 31st March, 1929, and
31st March, 1930. Thus a total sum of
£69,262 has been advanced to farmers for
live stock replacement at the low rate of
21 per cent. per annum.

I have received representations from

instalments, which fall due at the end of
December next, should be deferred for
another 12 months. I regret, however,

further extensions of time can be given
for the repayment of these loans.
The question of reviving this scheme for
a limited period for the benefit of any
farmers who have sustained losses of live
stock and who have not already received
loans is under consideration.
FREIGHT RATES ON POTATOES.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware of the
failure of the potato crop in England and
Scotland, whereas there is an abundant
crop in Ireland; whether the prevailing
rate per single ton is 21s from Belfast to
Manchester, whilst the cost per ton would
be only 69 6d if a small steamer were
chartered; and whether his Department
is willing to organize transit and supplies
on behalf of the farmers from Northern
Ireland.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The official forecast of the yields of the potato crop in
England and Wales at the beginning of
October was 2,985,000 tons as compared
with a total production of 2,763,000 in
1926. Although the average yield is
estimated at nearly one-third of a ton per
acre below the average of the preceeding
ten years it is yet slightly above that of
1926. In Scotland reports regarding the
condition of the crop at the beginning of
October were varied, but it was stated that
speaking generally, the crop prospects
were far from satisfactory, and the gross
yield will probably prove to be below normal. In Northern Ireland the crop has
not turned out so well as was anticipated
earlier in the season and the yield is not
expected to be above average.
I understand that the charge for the
conveyance of potatoes, in five ton lots,
from Belfast via Liverpool to Manchester
is 21s 2d per ton, and that a rate of
18s 7d per ton is in operation for similar
quantities between the points by direct
steamer.
The chartering of special steamers
would not, of course, be a feasible proposition unless large quantities, say 300 tons
and upwards were available for a single
shipment. Chartering charges ordinarily cover only the actual conveyance,
and, even so, I am advised that at present
they would be appreciably higher than the
figure mentioned. Besides very substantial additions would have to be made for
such services as loading at Belfast and
unloading at Manchester and for harbour
dues and insurance. For such shiploads
the tonnage charge that would be comparable with the rates I have already
mentioned would, so far as I can ascertain, be between 13s and 14s.
The work of organizing special transit
services is primarily a matter for the
interests concerned, and I cannot go
further than to promise the advice of the
Ministry in any case where such a course
is contemplated by an association of
farmers or other organized body.
Mr. HEALY: Did the right hon.
Gentleman not organize the transport of
potatoes from South Derry last year to
the great advantage of the farmers, and
would he see if he cannot inaugurate
something on similar lines this year?
Mr. ARCHDALE: That was done by
special arrangement with the railway.
company, the L.M.S., which had been
very considerate. With regard to the
charge of 13s to 14s, we have been to the
railway companies about the charge and I
do not think we can get any lower rates
at the present time. Of course we keep
continually pressing them about the
charge.
Mr. HEALY: Will the right hon.
Gentleman not promise, in view of the
importance of this question, to see the
railway company again on this matter.
My information is that lower rates
obtain.

Mr. ARCHDALE: I will certainly
be glad to see the railway company and
try if anything can be done.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry
of Home Affairs has not refused to sanction a loan to the Urban District Council
of Enniskillen for the purchase of a Fire
Engine. The facts of the case are:-
In September last the Council applied
to the Ministry for sanction for a
loan of £550 for the purchase of
a fire engine and appliances. The
specification of the engine which it
was proposed to buy was examined and,
after obtaining advice from a practical
expert in these matters, the Ministry came
to the conclusion that the proposed engine
was entirely inadequate for a town like
Enniskillen, and that the purchase of such
an engine would be to a large extent waste
of money. The Ministry suggested to the
Council on the 6th October last that they
should consider the provision of a more
suitable engine and fire escape, but up to
the present no reply has yet been received
from the Council.
I am aware that a fire involving loss of
life and a considerable damage to property occurred in Enniskillen last week, and
I am of opinion that it is essential that a
proper engine and fire appliances should
be acquired by the Council.

naked tragedy was brought into five homes.

The CHAIRMAN: The next Amendment which I ask attention to is page 3,
line 8, to leave out "further" ("no further
proceedings"). That Amendment appears
to me to be out of order. The Committee
will observe that certain proceedings are
authorized and certain penalties provided
by the earlier portions of Clause 1, with
which we have dealt. The effect of leaving
out the word "further" would be that
under this Clause no proceedings could be
taken without the authority of the
Attorney-General, but the Committee
has already approved of provisions in
the Clause which entitle proceedings to
be taken without reference to the
Attorney-General at all. It is clear,
therefore, that the word is out of order and
that the Amendment cannot be moved.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I beg
to move in Clause 1, page 3, line 17, to
leave out from the first "shall" ("Trades
Disputes Act, 1906, shall") to "apply"
("Emergency Powers Act [Northern
Ireland], 1926, apply').
This appears to me to be one of the
most important Amendments put on the
Order Paper, because the object of the
Clause as it stands at present is to undo
all trade union legislation passed in the
British Parliament extending over the
course of a quarter of a century. I presume the Committee is conversant with the
fact that the Trades Dispute Act, 1906,
was passed after what was known as the
Taff Vale decision. That decision held the
trade unions responsible for any loss that
might accrue to an employer in consequence of a trades dispute.
Even a
quarter of a century ago that outraged
public opinion to such an extent that the
Trades Disputes Act of 1906 was passed.
We hold that no Government, either here
or in Great Britain, should attempt to
undo what the electors and the citizens
thought was right to do approximately
21 years ago.
I think it is the intention of this Clause
to render nugatory all the advantages
even under the Trade Unions Act, 1913.
The intention of the Amendment is to
keep the law in its present form, because
it is quite obvious that if a trade dispute
takes place there may be as much responsibility on the part of the employer as there
would be on the part of the employees. Is
a trade union going to be left in this
position that for any losses that might
result in consequence of a trades dispute it might be held responsible, and possibly its funds seized
for the purpose of paying compensation to the employer? We think this
is one of the most reactionary Clauses in
the Bill, and therefore I move this Amendment with the object of allowing the trade
union movement to have the benefit of
the Trades Disputes Act, 1906, because for
the functioning of the trade union movement we believe it necessary that we should
have the protection of that Act.
I want to be quite frank with the Committee. In connection with this Emergency Powers Act that I am proposing to
delete, I have not taken the trouble to examine that Act any way closely in order to
find out exactly what it proposed to do,
but I bracket it with the intention of the
Government in relation to the Trades Disputes Act, 1906, and I come to the conclusion that inasmuch as it is contained in
that portion of the Bill that intends no
good to the trade unionists of Northern
Ireland I believe I am right in my argument. I have pleasure in moving the
Amendment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I wish to say that this does
not take away from the trade unions any
rights which they acquired under the
Trades Unions Act, 1906, so far as a legal
strike is concerned. All it does is to deal
with an illegal strike. And, further, I
think I am correct in saying it would be
a great disadvantage to trade unionists
here if these words were omitted, because
obviously it would bring the Emergency
Powers Act of Northern Ireland into force
in Northern Ireland in a case of this kind,
which it is not the intention of the Government to do.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman has not explained at all why it is
necessary to suspend the provisions of the
Trades Disputes Act of 1906. It is the
intention of the British Government as
well as of the Northern Government to
make trade unions liable for the offences
of members of the society as is contemplated by the taking away of the privileges the trades unions got under the 1906
Act. The right hon. Gentleman has not
explained, except in a very loose way,
what the intention of the Government is
in this regard. He says it is only to take
away the provisions of the Trades Disputes

Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to move the
rejection of this Clause, because I think
that if the Clause is accepted, it will be
the beginning of what we have always
tried to avoid in Northern Ireland at
any rate the thing we call a class war.
I believe that this Section in the Bill is
a challenge of war by the employing
class to the working classes of the country
--a war which we all tried to prevent
taking place. It is a deliberate attack
inspired by motives of partisanship upon
the workers' organizations, and designed
to deprive them of protective powers of
resistance when their standards of living
and conditions of employment are assailed
by the organized employers.
What does the Section do? The Section
takes away the only weapon of defence
the working classes have. It takes away
the right to strike. The right to strike
is the only valuable thing the workers
have. The only protection they have is
in the right to strike when labour is in
danger of being undervalued by the employing class. The Clause is taking away
that right. I am determined to resist
this Clause being put on the Statute Book
of Northern Ireland without due course
being shown for its inclusion there.
Why is this Clause being imposed on the
workers of Northern Ireland? It is not
for any crime they have committed. The
workers of Northern Ireland never committed a crime, for in their negotiations
with the employing class they used constitutional ways and means. No, they
are going to be penalized because of the
fact that in Great Britain trades unionism
is growing in strength, and is reaching
such a height of perfection that the employing class are in danger of being replaced in power by the true representatives of the masses of the people. They feel
their power slipping out of their grasp,
and posing as friends of the workers they
are telling trades unionists that this will
be an Act of protection for them. Is it an
act of protection to take away from them
the liberties they have gained, not by
means of legislation, but by suffering, by
being deported from their own country, by
being imprisoned for periods of from one
to ten years? These were the men who
fought for the position which we now
preserve. This is now being filched from
us by a Tory Government which never did
anything else except endeavour to keep
the working classes in the position they
now occupy. The working classes are
now in a state of semi-starvation. It is
a crying out shame and disgrace to put
this clause in an Act.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: The representatives of
the Government sit on the other side.
Pardon me saying that they sit there.
The majority of them have been sitting
in the smokeroom during the debates on
this Bill. It is a crying out shame and
scandal for the Government and its
followers to put a Clause of this kind in
the Bill. It seems to me that under it
strikes will be subject to so many interpretations that as one who has been
sixteen years in the movement I would
be very loath, if I were timid of imprisonment, to speak to, or counsel anyone.
When I have a just cause and when I feel
I am on the side of right it matters not
to me where they incarcerate my body.
I feel when I am on the side of right I
have the side of might with me. I feel
I am justified in standing here in
defence of the rejection of this Clause.
What do we find? We find from the
Clause that the workmen's right to combine for the maintenance and improvement of their standards which have been
established for more than a century
is going to be taken away. The
Clause imposes on trade unions outrageous conditions of a kind hitherto
unknown in any Act of Parliament. We
have had tyrannous things placed on the
Statute Book as far as trade unions are
concerned, but nothing so outrageous as
the tyranny embodied in this section. I

HOUSE OF COMMONS

certainly feel that it is my duty here

to be the senior member of that constituency-to make this protest on behalf
of the trade unions and to go into the

The Clause not only takes away the
right to strike, but we find the financial
position of the unions is going to be in
danger. All the protection given under

Statute Book for
Book for protection of the
workers owing to the action taken by Forrester, is to be taken away.
That case
cost the union £35,000 and they won it.
This Bill is going to rob the trade unions.
It is going to rob them in two waysmorally and financially. The Government
are going to support what I would call
the blackleg. They are going to give him
all the protection of the law in order to
scab on his fellow workers. Will you support a Clause which robs the unions of
all they ever possessed? The Clause is
going to have a far-reaching effect.
Though the Opposition placed Amendments to the first Clause on the Order
paper not one letter or word of any of
those Amendments has been accepted by
the Government. The majority of the Opposition remained here during the debates, but the same cannot be said of the
other side.
I feel we are in danger of having an
upheaval that I hoped and always wished
would never come. When the first strike
takes place in the city of Belfast, we will
then learn the lesson of the far-reaching
effect of your Bill. If the bakers went
out on strike after the operation of this,
owing to the employing classes lengthening their hours and reducing their wages,
would that be a legal or an illegal strike?
If the N.U.R. went out on strike owing
to the reduction of wages and lengthening
of hours, would that be a legal or illegal
strike? If the municipal workers went
out on strike would the courts declare it
to be legal? I am prepared to say that
if the transport workers or any section.
of that kind went out on strike it would
be interpreted as coercing or intimidating
the community. The Attorney-General
would apply for an injunction and he
would have the strike declared illegal,
and any person inciting or instigating or
doing any act contrary to the Clause
would be the guest of the Minister of
Home Affairs.
I hope that the Minister of Labour, if
it is his intention to father this Clause
along with the Attorney-General, will,
at the next meeting of his association,
fully explain the far-reaching extent of
this Clause. I do not object to him as
a Minister defending the Bill, because in
his position as an employer he knows that
under this Bill he is being protected.
From that point of view he is justified in
looking after the interests of his class.
I feel I am also justified in looking after
the interests of the class I belong to. I
have been in receipt of declarations from
20,000 trade unionists in Northern Ireland.
Those were not hole-in-corner meetings.
I am also in receipt of further declarations
from 10,000 workers in Northern Ireland
instructing me to oppose this Clause very
strenously and to endeavour to maintain
the rights and liberties which it had
taken the trade unions over a generation
to establish. For that reason I want to
move the rejection of Clause 1, and I hope
I will have the support not alone of the
front bench of the Government, but also
of some of its followers.

to

I say then, in supporting the rejection

does not indicate a healthy state of

bring about simply by the manifestation

think this House whatever our views
may be in regard to strikes, their virtues
or their limitations, or their utility as
weapons for the defence of the working
classes-whatever hon. Member's opinions
may be, they will agree that a Bill of this
character, introduced into a normal community where there is industrial peace,
where there has been neither a general
strike nor any other form of strike, not only
from a strategic point of view on the part
of the Government but from the point of
view of every interest, is a fatal blunder
made by the Government and can find no
justification-and no justification has
been offered from the benches opposite.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 15th November, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
FUND.
1. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if it is a
fact that almost £10,000 was paid by
secondary teachers into their pension fund
for the year ended 31st July, 1927, and
only £2,000 paid out for the same period,
and whether he stated on 19th May, 1927,
that this fund was completely insolvent.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock) The hon. Member quotes from
replies given by me to questions put by
him on 20th October, and 19th May of
this year.
His quotations and my statements are essentially correct in all particulars.
TEACHING OF GEOGRAPHY IN
SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether there was a large decrease in the
percentages of passes in geography for
both senior boys and girls and junior boys
and girls, at the 1927 certificate examinations as compared with 1926; whether the
Ministry's official report states that there
was a "marked improvement" in the
teaching of this subject; can he explain
the reason of the decrease of 44.9 per
cent. in the junior girls' section; and
whether the Ministry attributes the very
low percentage of passes (25.6, 26.0) to
the unsuitability of the examination
papers; and, if not, can he state to what
cause this result is attributed.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative, but if the hon. Member will again
refer to the Ministry's Report for 1926-
27 he will observe that the statement as
to the improvement in the teaching of
Geography is immediately qualified by
the endorsement by the Ministry of the
view expressed by its inspector, that
"there is still too little practical work and
too great a tendency to rely on textbooks."'
A scrutiny of the scripts of candidates
at the recent certificate examinations
shows that there was a deplorable weakness in answering the questions involving
just this practical knowledge of geography to which the Ministry's inspector
refers.
The question on contour maps was the
most highly marked question in each
paper. The number of failures may be
largely set down to the general inability
of the candidates to score marks in this
part of the paper.
In the opinion of the Ministry the
papers set at the examinations were suitable papers.
It is not uncommon for the standard
of attainment of candidates for examinations to vary from year to year, and it is
to this circumstance that the hon. Member must look for an explanation of the
particular decrease in the percentage of
passes to which he refers.

Suspension of Standing Orders 2858
Business of the House.
SUSPENSION OF STANDING
ORDERS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That for the remainder of the Session
Government business be not interrupted
under the provisions of any Standing
Order regulating the Sittings of the
House, may be entered upon at any hour
though opposed, and after the conclusion
of this day's sitting shall have precedence
at every sitting. (The Prime Minister.)
Mr. KYLE: I want to enter a very
strong protest against the proposed action of the Government in this particular
Motion. This House, as everybody
knows, is not sitting for a considerable
portion of the year. Then immediately
we start to sit Bills are flung at us with
the result that these Bills do not get the
public discussion that is absolutely essential in the public interest. The result
has been in the past that Measures have
passed this House of Commons, and have
received the assent of the Governor, and
in a few months the Minister responsible
for the introduction of that Bill or other
Bills is bringing in amending Bills to
amend the mistakes that were made in the
original drafting of the first Bill. That
is in consequence of the lack of public
discussion in this House on the matters
affecting the interests of the entire community. And to have a Motion put
down on the Order Paper and the Prime
Minister to get up and formally move
that Motion without giving any reason
whatsoever is a thing, I think, that no
public body such as this House of Commons should tolerate as long as they can
avoid tolerating any such action. Is it
the Government's intention to introduce
Bills and put them through without
giving the public, as well as the Members
behind them, and the Opposition an
opportunity for mature consideration of
the Measures proposed? I believe that
the Measures in this House do not get
the consideration which they are entitled
to and which the public expects from the
House. Very often members of the
public will write to you regarding the
Rent Restrictions Act or the Housing
Acts, because they see this matter mentioned in the public Press as being dealt
with in this House of Commons, and before an opportunity is given of ventilating the undoubted grievances many of the
people of the Six Counties have the Bill
is on the Statute Book-and
no redress
can be expected from the Government,
with the result that at the end of a very
few months the Government themselves
have got to introduce amending legislation.
The Government propose to take up the
remainder of the time after to-day of the
sittings of this House, despite the fact that
there may be, and probably will be, some
very big questions which ought to be
settled by the Government in consultation
with the rest of us in this House, notably
the question of the Guardians' action in
refusing out-door relief to the people of
Belfast. That is a matter which, if the
Guardians do not take another line, will
have to be debated in view of the Home
Secretary's statement that the Guardians
could do more than they are doing in the
matter. I think it is nothing short of
scandalous that the noble lord, the Prime
Minister, should get up and in such a
cursory manner move this motion without
giving any adequate reason for it at all.
It shows the amount of respect he has for
this House and for public opinion. I
want to enter as strong a protest as I can
against the action of the Government in
proposing to take the remainder of the
time of the House from to-day.
With your

permission, Sir, and that of the House,

Suspension of Standing Orders HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
The other matter to which the hon.
Member referred is the question of taking
the remainder of the time hitherto available for private Members. That is a
very customary Motion in the Imperial
Parliament. Towards the end of the
Session the Motion is always put down.
The Government claims all the time in
order to get through the concluding business of the Session. There is nothing untoward about that part of the Resolution.
All we desire is that this House should in
a businesslike way discuss to the full all
Measures placed before it, but we are
bound in the interests of the public to
protect the Government against undue
discussion, and that there is undue discussion hon. Members will realize when
it takes much more time to get a Bill
through than otherwise would be the
case. Everybody is agreed that it is
necessary to get on with these useful
Measures. We will not, of course,
necessarily sit after 6-30 o'clock on some
days if we get through what we consider
a fair day's work, but on the other hand
my colleagues and those behind me are
quite prepared to sit on to see that Bills
are put through in a resaonable time.

understood when he last delivered a speech

2885 Representation Bill---

15 NOVEMBER 1927
Second Reading

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Representation of the People Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'
Mr. DEVLIN: I have ventured into an
entirely new domain. This is my maiden
effort in regard to legislation, and it is
the first time I have been privileged to
introduce a Bill. I shall therefore require
-and I am sure it will be extended to
me the sympathy of the House in this
undertaking. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) If I succeed, as I believe I will,
in carrying this Measure through it will
be an encouragement to me to embark
further upon what would be for the community the successful task of carrying
other great and important Measures.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But if I
am defeated it will mean that I have been
robbed, and what is more important, the
community will be robbed of many of
those legislative Measures which I think
if I were permitted to introduce into the
House would solve many of the problems
that affect us to-day.
I was charged by the Minister of
Labour in a speech the other day-and
that charge of his was emphasised in the
local Press-that I had brought forward
no practical solution of the unemployment
. problem. Well, if I carry this Measure
to-day, as I believe I will, as I am making
this a test case, I believe it will be possible
for me to satisfy the insensate desire of
the Minister of Labour for the production
of such wisdom as I have at my disposal
which would constitute a contribution to
the solution of the problem we then discussed. Now, I have never been, as the
House knows, greatly enamoured with the
establishment of a Parliament for the Six
Counties. It has involved the maximum
of irritation and the minimum of good,
but seeing that we have a Parliament I
have sufficient respect for it and sufficient
regard for the suffrages of those who
enacted it to desire that even with its
humiliating limitations it shall be something of a reality and not wholly a sham.
Up to the present time we have been engaged, as I said in the earlier part of the
day, in little better work than merely
This
sanctioning British legislation.
Parliament has been nothing more than
a rubber stamp for Measures passed by
Britain. I think myself that that is
neither a desirable nor a dignified position.
The Gentlemen on the Government
benches are never tired of impressing on
others the respect that is due to this
assembly. Well, I am going to put their
confessions to the test. The cry of "keep
step by step' with Westminster is in my
judgment a confession of impotence, a
surrender of our status to be in any sense
a legislature. I want in introducing this
Measure to show that we can legislate for
the needs of Northern Ireland and that
we refuse for ever to be at the apron
strings of the Mother of Parliaments,
always toddling laboriously in the rear.
I am happy to say that in the proposals I
venture to submit to the House I shall
have almost universal sympathy.
In asking the House to give a Second
Reading to the Representation of the
People Bill I am giving this Parliament a
chance of showing that we can do something off our own bat, and prove that we
are not so hopelessly impossible that we
can do nothing but say ditto to everything
that the British Parliament does. In asking for the assimilation of the Parliamentary franchise for men and women
I am only asking that the Northern Legislature shall for once, in a
small way, show some capacity for
initiative. If this Parliament cannot act
of its own accord it ceases in my judginent
to have any reason for its existence. The
reform which I am introducing if not
passed by the Northern Parliament now
as its own enactment will have to be
adopted very soon as part of the step-bystep policy, and I object to this further
humiliation being placed upon this Legislature.
The provisions of this Bill, which I have
the honour to introduce, are few and
simple. Broadly speaking, it aims at
doing away with sex inequality and placing men and women on a level as regards
the vote, thus giving legislative effect to
a claim to which serious or effective opposition on any ground is no longer offered.
I was reading during the recess some of
the speeches made by Ministers, and I
am happy to say that the entire Cabinet
-if I am wrong those who dissent can
contradict me-are in favour of the principle of equality of franchise for men and
women. There was only one Member I
thought might dissent, and that was the
Representation Bill--

surprise you the possibilities are that before long the thing will happen. Therefore, I hope before I am much longer in
this House to be able to see one of those
chairs in front of me that are so constantly
vacant filled by the lady who represents

I said, of the most stable and conservative

I do not know what the mentality of

The provisions in this Bill which I introduce aim at the creation of the condition which I ventured to describe, and
I shall just briefly refer to them, because
the Bill is so simple that it does not require any meticulous examination or very
close analysis. The Bill is so simple that
it will be clear to every Member, even
those in the smokeroom. Sub-clause 2 of
Clause 1 sets out the requisites for a residential or business qualification. The
third Sub-clause defines the words
"Business premises and the fourth
Sub-clause deals with
essentials as
to the length of time that entitle a
woman to vote in a particular constituency. Clause 2 is a mere consequential Amendment of the provisions of
the principal Act. Clause 3 defines the
right of persons registered to vote, while
Clause 4 provides for the repeal of certain
provisions of the principal Act. By
Clause 5 it is proposed that the Bill shall
become law as soon as it passes, and the
Governor of Northern Ireland is given
power by Order in Council to alter the
registration dates in connection with the
register under the new Act.
I have been trying to find out if there
can be any possible excuse for rejecting
this Bill or for shelving it. I never could
find any reason for anything in this
House, and I generally go to the Unionist Press in order to know what is in the
Unionist mind. I found that some objection to this Bill had been raised on the
ground of expense and multiplicity of
registers. Each year only one Parliamentary and Local Government voters' list
is published, usually in the month of
December, and the last date, December
15th, would remain in operation until
December 14th, 1928. A supplemental
register could be issued, showing the
names of women entitled to vote under
the provisions of this Bill, that is supplemental to the register of December, 1927.
This would not involve much time or
much expense.
Now if this Bill is rejected it will mean
that the unfair denial of civic rights to a
large section of women would be maintained for two or three years to come.
Is
it just to continue a wrong so that the
Northern Parliament may always march
wherever and at whatever pace the Westminster Parliament directs? I need
hardly worry the House with any detailed
exposition of the Measure unless in so far
as I have done it. It is so simple in its
purpose and its provisions that I feel sure
I need not labour the claims of women to
be entitled to the same constitutional
privileges as men. After a period of
agitation and excitement enlivened by
picturesque historical episodes,
women have successfully stormed the barricades of male privilege and monopoly.
I heard a man say the other day that one
of his chief objections to our present democratic system is that he has only equal
rights with his gardener. "Why should
my gardener," he said, "who has 35s a
week have the same civic and electoral
rights as myself who own the house and
gardens and have larger interests?''
some
I never could understand that argument
myself. It is not the rich or carefully entrenched who should have electoral power.
They can look after themselves. It is the
poor who cannot look after themselves
individually and can only exercise power
through collective activity on the part of
the whole number, and it is for that
reason I advocate the giving of votes to
women. You do give votes to women as
it is, and you give votes to men at 21. In
the Free State they give votes to women
at 21. Why should you not give it here,
where there is a larger reason even than in
the Free State? Female employment is
practically unknown in Southern Ireland.
Here female employment constitutes to a
large extent the most powerful part of
our industrial life in our mills and
factories. Was it not a scandal when
factory legislation was being passed that
women, who are so deeply and so profoundly concerned with that legislation,
had no right to interfere and had no
direct power to influence such legislation.
Women work in our mills and factories.
They are the least vocal of all those who
suffer wrong.
Therefore I say if we give
votes at 21 to men, who can fight for
their rights much more powerfully than
women, we are entitled also to give
women votes at 21.

But, apart altogether from the industrial sphere, women have established
their right in another and wider and
larger domain of our national life.
Women are to-day invading all the old
preserves from which for many centuries
they have been excluded. We have the
lady doctor, the lady surgeon, the lady
solicitor, the lady barrister, and, if I
may say so without apparent disrespect,
the new occupations that women have assumed, and in my judgment effectively
assumed, have become mere
places. Ladies have swum the Channel,
an achievement that for so long had defied
the efforts of mere man.
They have
scaled the air, they have ascended almost
inaccessible mountain heights. Physical
and intellectual, social and professional
barriers have disappeared. They have
successfully challenged man in many
arenas where man had imagined himself
so secure as to be beyond the possibility
of interference.

wonder will that policy continue when the

Mr. KYLE: I beg to second the

support the hon. Member for West
Belfast in his effort to extend the
franchise to women on the same terms as
men.
The efforts that have been made by
women in the past to obtain enfranchisement have met with a great deal of success, but it was not until 1918 that the
actions of women in the country-the
work that they performed in the country,
the services that they rendered to the
country, particularly during the years
1914-1919-made the claim so overwhelming that even leaders of reactionary
thought in Great Britain, such as Mr.
Asquith, who up to that time had
posed the enfranchisement of women,
were converted.
It is not for that reason that I desire
to support this Measure The policy of
the enfranchisement of women has been
consistently and presistently advocated by
the members of the party of which I
have had the honour for a great many
years to be a member. In fact, they have
been the pioneers of votes for women.
Right from the time that the idea was first
promulgated until to-day they have held
that if men are entitled to the vote at
21 years of age, the women are too. I
do not think there is anybody bold
enough to-day to say that men who are
entitled to fight for their country from 18
years of age are not entitled to vote to
ensure better conditions for themselves
and their comrades. If it is just and
right and proper, as the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Finance, said, that
men of 21 should have the franchise, then
it is equally just and right and proper
that women of the same age should have
the same rights.
