I think that this is strengthened very considerably by the fact that in Parliament
during the last twenty years woman has
been, rightly I think, interfering to a very
considerable extent with the conditions
under which the common people carry on
their lives. With the advent of National
Health Insurance, and Unemployment
Insurance, with the advent of other social
and ameliorative Measures that have been
introduced in Great Britain and here, it
is all the more necessary that women,
whose conditions are governed by the
actions of Parliament, should have a say,
an effective say, in seeing that their representatives are in the House of Commons to voice their particular ideas in
regard to these social changes that I have
mentioned.
The Bill itself, as the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) said, is a simple
one, and does not require a great deal of
explanation. It attempts-I think successfully-in Clause 3, to embody the
acceptance of the principle of one person,
one vote. Though we are not attempting
to curb the Universities, which I think
have the right to exercise two votes, this
Bill does attempt to lay down, and to have
accepted that fundamental principle of
one person, one vote.
I cannot for the life of me think that
the right hon. and hon. Gentlemen opposite, who have given lip-service to the
women's cause, can now refuse to vote in
favour of this Measure.
You may say
that it is going to add a very considerable
number of voters to the register. You
may say that it is an attempt to extend
the franchise to women of 21 when it was
not been done in Great Britain. We have
the assurance of the three political parties

of the acceptance of this principle, and
we are driven to the conclusion that it is
largely in consequence of a multiplicity.
of work that has got to be got through in
the Imperial House of Commons, that a

However, we are strengthened by the

that at long last, after twenty or thirty

They have been converted, I say, as a

have passed Trade Board legislation to

to make is that there is no urgency in this
matter. The hon. Member stayed out of
the House a long time. Then he comes
into the House and he thinks everything
must be done in a minute. We must
hurry legislation. The hon. Member got
up and made a most fervid speech in
favour of the unbought tenants after remaining out of the House for some five
or six years.
This must be done in a
moment. I do not think there is any
great hurry about this. After all, we do
not require to go to the country until
April of 1930. By that time I think Mr.
Baldwin's pledge to the country in England will have been fulfilled. By that
time it will be possible for us to take up
this whole subject embodied in the hon.
Member's Bill and Proportional Representation, coupled with votes for young
people of 21, will be dealt with by the
Government, whose responsibility is the
proper responsibility and not that of any
private Member. I beg to move that
this Bill be read a Second time this day
six months.

Mrs. CHICHESTER: I am convinced
that as the only woman Member in this
House hon. Members will have expected

a Measure of this character. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Therefore, I rise

support it but to express surprise that the
hon. Gentleman should have considered
this an opportune moment to introduce it.
I cannot really see how he was able logically to support its introduction at this
time. lt seems, as the Prime Minister
has, of course, already very fully pointed
out-it seems to me that were
this
Measure to be passed a very curious, very
difficult, and very complicated position
would arise, especially in connection with
the register. There would be a different

what the situation might be. I am not
going to touch upon the question of expense, because, again the Prime Minister
has dealt with that question, but the expense of the revision would be enormous
and quite unjustifiable expense I consider
at the present moment.
I cannot help wondering in spite of
what the hon. Member has said-I must
remind the House that he said-I took
particular note of his words-he was very
anxious-in fact, he is always telling us
he is very anxious-to show his independence and to cut us off from the apron
strings that bind us to the Imperial
Parliament. That was what he gave as
his reason. I cannot quite believe that
he was not actuated by other motives in
the introduction of this Measure at this
particular stage. I wonder if he had in

that always catches the worm. I also
wonder whether he possibly had been indulging in visions of the future, whether
he had visualised himself in the rôle of
the Pied Piper of Hamelin, and whether

pleading so persuasively as we know he

and Tyrone flocking behind him on the

must say flashed across my mind. I also
thought that possibly he might see himself in the rôle of the great benefactor,
crowned with laurels, by the youth and

that he would be looked upon with such

I consider and I believe that every Member of this House considers that the position of denying equality of suffrage is
logically indefensible. I believe that

I go still further, and I would say that

Many excuses have been given in the

It is quite a commonplace to find women

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in page 2,
line 2, at end ("in respect of those premises') to add "or as debarring the
holder of an off-licence from selling tobacco or matches on those premises.
This is merely restoring a right that
the licence holders had up to the passing
of the Act of 1923. I think it was not
the intention of the legislature in 1923
to debar this lawful business of the sale
of tobacco and matches on off-licensed
premises. That being the case, and with
this Amending Bill now introduced,
surely it is a reasonable request to make
that the Government should accept this
Amendment. It is obviously correcting
something that was done inadvertently in
the 1923 Act. Hon. and right hon.
Gentlemen opposite may say that this prohibition of the sale of tobacco and
matches on off-licence premises was done
deliberately to prevent mixed trading. I
think most people are agreed that the
abolition of the spirit grocer was a good
thing. Certainly, so far as I am concerned, I have not a word to say against
the Government for doing away with the
spirit grocery, because it undoubtedly did
give an opportunity for people to get
put down to them grocery goods, when in
reality they were getting intoxicants.
This Amendment which I have proposed, limits the off-licence holder to the
sale of tobacco and matches, and that
being the case I think the Government
would be well advised to accept the
Amendment. The sale of tobacco,
especially in the form of cigarettes,
has always been recognized as part
of the licensed trader's stock, and
the sale of tobacco is allowed by their present licences, with the exception of the
off-licence holder. It is to remedy that
that we propose this Amendment. The
off-licence holders in the Six Counties
only number about 120, and I cannot see
at all any valid reason that the Government may have for resisting this Amendment and debarring this perfectly legitimate class of trader from the right to
sell tobacco and matches. It seems to
me that by no stretch of imagination
could you hold that because an off-licence
holder would have the right to sell tobacco
and matches it would prejudice in any way
at all the good conduct of that business. I
have mentioned that the object of the
amendment is not to allow the off-licence
holder to carry on mixed trading to any
extent except for the sale of tobacco. If
this mixed trading is a legitimate trade
so far as other sections of the same trade
are concerned then we should be very
pleased to learn of any legitimate reasons
the Government may have for opposing
this Amendment. I stated at the beginning that it was not the intention, so far
as I can read, of the Government when
they were proposing the 1923 Act, to debar off-licence holders from selling tobacco
or matches. That being the case I have
great pleasure in moving the amendment
standing in my name.

Mr MCALLISTER: With regard to this
particular Amendment, there is one aspect
would like to draw attention to.
In refusing this Amendment the Committee
is differentiating between the off-licence
holders and every other class of trader
in Northern Ireland. Every other class
of trader is permitted to take out a licence
to sell tobacco and permitted without a
licence to sell matches. The Minister of
Home Affairs has given no justification
and absolutely no explanation whatever
why this particular trade should be differently treated to every other class of
trader. I suggest to the Committee that
they have all the requirements and requisites to suitably carry on this particular
business. In the first place there are
houses of a good and sufficient valuation,
and in the second place, the owners of
these houses have received, and must receive annually, a certificate of good
character. Further, no traders in Northern Ireland are so closely supervised
both from the matter of revenue, which is
important, and the sale of tobacco and
otherwise, than the licensed traders.
Therefore, I think the Minister should explain to the House why this particular
trade is singled out as being the only trade
deprived of the right to sell matches and
to take out a tobacco licence.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in page 2, line 2, at end ("In respect of

that the sale of intoxicating liquor by
wholesale in premises in respect of which
a retailers' off-licence is in force shall be
carried on only at the times during which
such off-licence business may lawfully be
carried on."
This Amendment speaks for itself.
Under the Bill, as it stands at the present time, the sale of liquor under a
wholesale licence on premises to which
are attached a retail ordinary licence is
limited to the ordinary opening hours,
and we desire by this Amendment to put
all licences exactly on the same lines as
an on-licence.

Mr. GYLE: Since the passing of the
1923 Act, which, it is acknowledged by
most people, was rushed through in
rather a hurry, I have read over all the
debates on the introduction of the Bill
and during the Committee stage, with
special reference to mixed trading. I
can find no reference of any kind to the
use of a billiard table or a bagatelle tablo
for hire on licensed premises. We all
know that the police are very fond of
acting as amateur lawyers, and after the
Bill has been put on the Statute Book
a police officer discovered something regarding a billiard table, and he decided
to put it to the test He went to the
Home Office, and he found that there
was a decision making the use of a
billiard table or a bagatelle table a mixed
business.
2955 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee

[Mr. Gyle]
The case was not taken on the question
of hiring; it was taken on the question
of whether the billiard room could be
kept open after hours. It was an un.
defended case. It was made out that the
hiring of a billiard table or a bagatelle
table was a mixed business. I respectfully submit to the Committee it was not
in the ordinary sense of the term considered a mixed business at the time of
the passing of the 1923 Act. It is entirely different from the question of selling tobacco or matches, which this Committee has determined is a mixed business. You cannot have tobacco or
matches for sale on the premises of a
licence holder, but there is nothing in
this Act to prevent an on-licence holder
from having on his premises a billiard
table or a bagatelle table.
If my Amendment is ruled out by this
Committee, the only thing that can
happen is that it will prevent the licensee
of a public-house hiring out his billiard
table or bagatelle table, over which he
has gone to considerable expense. To
put in a billiard table costs about £160,
and it also takes up considerable room.
They cannot prevent the publican from
having the billiard table or the bagatelle
table in use on his premises, but he must
not charge anything for the use of it. He
can have it on the premises, and allow
billiards or bagatelle to be played.
If we rule out this Amendment, we are
penalizing the publican. We are taking
from him the right to hire out that which
he otherwise has the legal right to have
on his premises. I suggest that you
should not deal with this as mixed trading
in the ordinary sense of the term, but that
a publican should be allowed to hire out
a billiard table or bagatelle table. In
some part of the Six Counties-I cannot
say where at the moment-it was decided
by a resident magistrate that a billiard
table was properly used if it was used in
an hotel, although I cannot find anything
in the Act dealing with an hotel in that
way. Still, I believe the resident magistrate ruled that it was necessary for the
convenience and the comfort of the people
staying in the hotel.
I shall read an extract from the Report
of a Committee that was recently set up
in England. The Report of the Committee on the Disinterested Management
of Public Houses, recently published,
states in Paragraph 40:-
It is claimed by the management that
the provision of recreational facilities
tends to decrease excessive drinking;
the public-house customer has something in addition to his drink to
occupy the time he spends in the house,
and he drinks less or takes longer over
his drink in cousequence. This is
stated to apply not only to the
customer who actually plays the game,
but to the customer who merely watches
the players on the bowling or quoiting
green, or watches the billiard players
in the public bar.
That is in the report of a recent Commission, and I think it should make this
Committee feel that if a billiard table or
bagatelle table were allowed on licensed
premises it really would encourage
temperance. Seeing that they cannot
do away with the use of a billiard table as
long as it is not for hire I think this Committee would be well advised to accept my
Amendment, and so I beg to move.
Mr. LEEKE: In supporting this

are aware that in country districts the

or two and play a game of billiards. But
following on the action of the police in
taking out prosecutions in these districts
it was discovered that it was not legal to
keep these billiard tables, and, consequently a great hardship was inflicted
upon the agricultural people of Ulster in
the country and small market towns. Not
only did it handicap them but it also
handicapped a large section in the watering places. In places like Portrush the
public-houses and off-licence premises all
had billiard tables, but they
allowed to retain them.

Member (Mr. Gyle) will know, in reference to the paragraph he himself quoted,

merchants and sales including auctions,
and so on. These businesses are not in
any way connected with the licensed premises. At certain seasons of the year

up and they cannot get in. There are
large warehouses and stores round some
of these houses, and to my own knowledge
I know it is a tremendous hardship on
these people that they cannot get into the
yard before the regulation hours.
There is one item which I think is a
reductio ad absurdum. I know one or two
auctioneers who have had to sacrifice their
premises in order to keep their auction
business separate. What an auction business has to do with drinking whisky I do
not know. I have known a case where an
auctioneer had an office in which to keep
his books and it was held to be a business.
It is carrying the thing a long way beyond
the bounds of common-sense and reason to
say that because an auctioneer keeps his
books in the same premises as the liquor
is sold it is a breach of the laws of temperance. As I said on the Second Reading

time to enable these people to carry

(Mr. McAllister) and the hon. Member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Harbison) will again be that this is a mixed
business, and as the Government had
decided in 1923 to put an end to this sort
of business they cannot depart from that

departed from that decision owing to persuasion on the part of some people I do
not know whom-and I suggest that
under the circumstances that have been
brought forward by the Amendment the
Government should now depart from that
policy. This Amendment would restore
to the farming community generally the
great convenience which had been taken
from them by the Act of 1923. Many
people know that in the country districts
the publican's was the store that provided
the farmer with many things he required
in connection with his farm, such as
farming implements, manures, feeding
stuffs, and things of that character. By
the action of the Government under the
Act of 1923 the publican has now been
deprived of the privilege of supplying the
farmer. Therefore I think the Govern
ment should accept this Amendment in
all fairness not alone to all engaged in
this business but to the farming community. This dealing was a real accommodation to the farmers. In some districts of the country opportunities for
providing farmers with these things are
not many.
Often we find that in a dis.
trict some three or four miles from a
market town or village, as the case may
be, there is only a small licensed house
which has been established probably for
fifty years or even longer than that.
Those people, in addition to the licensed
premises, have established the business of
providing farmers with feeding stuffs,
farmers' implements, manure, seeds, and
various other things of that character.
In that Act you have deprived the farmer
of the opportunity of obtaining those
things, and you have put him to the
inconvenience of travelling three or four
miles to obtain his supplies. I believe
that the Government should take a
reasonable view of the situation, and
should accept the Amendment which has
been proposed. For those reasons I have
very much pleasure in supporting the
Amendment.

businesses

so for several reasons. In the first place,

discussing the question

not give these matches away for nothing?"
Imagine this Government suggesting that
anybody should give anything for nothing.
What would it mean? It would mean
that the people engaged in the trade would
attract people into their licensed premises
on the pretence they were going to get
free matches, and when they got them in
on that pretence they would consume intoxicating liquor. That would involve a

people to go into these premises instead
of openly and boldly allowing them to sell
matches and tobacco, which are commodities usually bought or consumed on
premises of this sort.
Take the next case, the use of billiard
and bagatelle tables. The suggestion was
that the publicans should allow people to
play billiards or bagatelle without charg
ing them for it. In other words, it would
he illegal to charge persons who go into
licensed premises to play billiards or bagatelle, but it would not be illegal to allow
them to do it free. What is the meaning
of it? That again is a hypocritical position
taken up by the Government. The meaning is the publican is to lure these people
in on the pretence of playing billiards and
when they get them in they are to buy
drink. In my opinion the Amendment is
more directly in favour of temperance than
the Clause as it stands at the moment.
I am not arguing this question from the
point of view of the publican or licensee
at all; I am discussing this from the
public point of view, and the contention
deliberately put forward by the Members
of the Government is that you can go
into this house, you can play billiards or
bagatelle if the publican lets you play
free that they can allow you to play
billiards but they are not to charge you
for it, thus offering an attraction to
persons to go into public-houses on the
pretence of having free billiards and free
bagatelle and then consuming liquor.
That is a position which seems to me absolutely inexplicable and is incapable of
defence.
Then there is the other questionwarehouses, carriage and transport of
goods, posting, funeral undertaking,
coal merchants-these are things that
are carried on in the yards of licensed
premises. They are the only places in
country towns and districts where business of this character could be carried on,
and you have refused to accept these
Amendments. All I think is this that
the more I listened to the discussion and
the closer I watched the proceedings in
connection with this Bill the more I am
convinced that the Government have
been guilty of a gross departure from
what they conveyed to the public when
they stated this was to be a non-contentious Measure conceding nothing to
any of the conflicting interests involved.
It was to be of no advantage to the
licensed trade and of no advantage to the
Temperance party. If it is not a Bill in
favour of
of the so-called Temperance
party then how is it that none of them
have put down any Amendments whatever? On the contrary they have all
gone away. There is not a single one of
them in the House. It is an attempt in
my judgment on the part of the Government to try to conciliate the Local
Option party, to silence them, to render
them less critical than they have been,
and to prevent them constituting themselves the great obstacle to be used against
the Government at the next election. For
what purpose this Bill is introduced I do
not know. The noble Lord declared again
and again that if it were found that there
was any inconvenience, if anything was
done that was not legitimate, if it were
found in the working of the Act dissatisfaction existed, he would do what he
could and bring in an Amending Bill to
improve it. He has done none of those
things.
Now we have spent the whole night
and whole day discussing this one Clause,
and the noble Lord is determined to force
this Clause upon the House of Commons.
It is tired and incapable of discussing it.

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I
should explain to the Committee that this
Bill is a Bill introduced by the Government in consequence of a pledge given on
many occasions both by my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs and
myself to clear up those administrative
difficulties and also those legal difficulties
that were found to exist in the Act of
1923. If I may say it, I think it is remarkable how well the Act of 1923 was
drafted, because it was a very large Act,
indeed, and far-reaching in its effects. It
has stood from then to now without having any Amendment till this day. As time
went on the Government felt there were
difficulties of interpretation and difficulties of administration which it would be
only sensible to clear up. This Bill is in
order to smooth over those difficulties, to
round off the rough edges, and to make it
easier for the people as a whole. Yet
when the Amending Bill is introduced the
discussion centres not upon those Amendments which are intended to help the
administration of the Act, but upon reopening the main questions that were all
settled in 1923. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Mr. DEVLIN: When there was no
Opposition.
The PRIME MINISTER: And whose
fault was that?
Mr. BEATTIE: The gunmen's.
The PRIME MINISTER: We on these
Benches certainly cannot have it thrown
up in our teeth all the time that we are
in any way to blame because the hon.
Members did not come and represent their
constituencies. I really and honestly
think that the Government have perhaps
shown too long-suffering an attitude towards the criticisms that have taken
place. We want to help, and we want to
get on. Hon. Members opposite do not
want to get on. They want to block this
Bill, and they have already said they are
going to do all they can to obstruct the
other Bill. Any self-respecting Government should stand up to that challenge.
and certainly I am not a person to be

of the thing, and realize that this Amending Bill is a helpful Bill, designed to assist
everybody concerned in the trade and in
the country, and give us reasonable progress as time goes on.

Wednesday, 16th November, 1927.

Oral Answers to Questions.
INDUSTRIAL RESOURCES OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
Prime
on
Mr. DEVLIN asked the
Minister whether the Commission on the
Natural and Industrial Resources of
Northern Ireland, in a report.
the Mineral Resources of Northern
Ireland, dated 20th March, 1925, recommended that two bore holes should
be made to prove coal measures,
provide further geoglogical information
and to encourage early exploitation; that
the Government should ascertain the
extent of certain iron ore resources with
a
to
view to encouraging the erection by
private enterprise of a smelting plant in
a locality contiguous to coal and lime deposits and transport facilities; and
whether further recommendations were
made regarding rock-salt and potash,
other minerals and lead; and what steps,
if any, the Government has taken to carry
out these recommendations.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply.
Upon the publication of the report the
Government considered it desirable to defer action for a certain period in order to
ascertain whether the information con
tained in the report was such as to attract
private enterprise to the mineral field,
suitable, as in the case of coal, for
Government support, as it has always
been prepared to afford financial
assistance to such propositions on their
merits. Unfortunately the experience
gained from further coal-mining operations since the issue of the report has
'been such as to suggest that no useful
purpose would be served by expenditure
of public funds upon speculative borings
for coal. Moreover, it is well known
that, for the time being, the output of
coal in Great Britain exceeds the demand, and wages are down to the minimum in all districts. Under these circumstances the Government do not consider
it desirable to embark upon an undertaking which has not been, and is not
likely to be in the near future, attempted
by private enterprise.
With regard to rock salt and potash,
the recommendations in favour of boring
for these minerals were made as corollaries to the main recommendation in
favour of boring for coal, and it was not
suggested that separate boring operations
should be undertaken.
The Commission were of opinion that
expenditure on boring for lead could only
be justified by an increase in the market
price for lead. That price has decreased
from £26 per ton, the figure given in the
report for 1923, to the neighbourhood of
£20 per ton at the present time.

these recommendations.

AFFORESTATION SCHEMES AND
EMPLOYMENT.
owners
Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister whether the Commission on the
Natural and Industrial Resources of
Northern Ireland, in a report dated the
3rd of December, 1924, on Afforestation
in Northern Ireland, stressed the urgent
necessity for action by the State, both in
extending its own scheme of afforestation and granting assistance to
willing to replant old woods; whether the
report states that if the Government of
Northern Ireland gave prompt effect to
these recommendations, it would, while
affording much-needed employment to
labour in rural districts, have taken a
distinctly practical step forward in the
developement of the rural resources of the
Province; and what steps, if any, the
Government has taken to carry out these
recommendations.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): I have been asked to
reply to this question. The reply to the
first part of the question is in the
affirmative. In accordance with its previous policy and in pursuance of the
recommendations contained in the report
referred to in the question the Ministry
has had the lands on 27 estates inspected
with a view to the acquisition of areas
suitable for afforestation. The
comprised in the lands so inspected was
approximately 18,000 acres.
area
The chief difficulty experienced in the
acquisition of land has been to secure
suitable areas, either by purchase or on
lease at a figure which, for forestry purposes, would be economic. Nevertheless,
in eight instances, negotiations have
been concluded, or practically concluded,
for the purchase or leasing of areas comprising altogether about 6,176 acres.
Negotiations are proceeding in five other
cases, where lands in the aggregate con
tain an area of over 2,660 acres. The
Ministry is also keeping in touch with
the Land Purchase Commissioners, who
have been asked to inform the Ministry
regarding any lands suitable for afforestation which may come under their
notice.
Apart from the efforts, as aforesaid, to
acquire additional lands for planting by
the Ministry, a scheme has been adopted
and has been in force since the beginning
of this year, under which grants are made
to owners of lands, who undertake to plant
trees on a commercial scale on their holdings.
A scheme is also in operation under
which farmers will be supplied at reduced
prices, with various trees grown in the
Ministry's nurseries.

Mr. BEATTIE: There is contentious
matter in this Clause, which we on this
side of the Committee would like if it
were possible for the Government, before
they take the Third Reading, to delete
or to alter.
At the risk of repeating
myself I would draw the attention of the
Committee once again to the position of
hotel proprietors and the sale of intoxicating liquor. We on this side of the
Committee have moved, and rightly so,
that residents in an hotel should have the
same liberty as a person has in his own
household. A resident in an hotel is restricted to certain hours for consumption,
and we feel that if the words "at any
time" had been added to the Clause it
would have removed a very grave injustice which is being inflicted under the
1923 Act, and which the Clause as it
stands does not remedy.
Now arguments may be put forward
as to whether the 1923 Act has been an
incentive to tourists or whether it has
been a barrier against tourists coming
here, but one thing I can say is that the
1923 Act has taken away the liberty of
a resident in an hotel as far as the consumption of drink is concerned. I would
have liked the Minister to have conceded
the Amendment proposed by the hon.
Member for Down (Mr. Patrick O'Neill)
so as to allow consumption at the times
stated in that Amendment. He also referred to the regulation of the hours for
consumption in various towns. There is
no earthly reason why a man selling
drink in a place with a population
of less than 5,000 and paying the
same licence fees should not have
the same conditions for the sale of
that drink as those obtaining in
town or city that has over 5,000 of a
population. None of the Members on the
front Government Bench told the Committee why this inequality of hours was
imposed upon the licensed trade. We are
told that it was in operation before the
1923 Act. We were all aware, of course,
that the lesser hours operated in the rural
areas, as compared with the cities, and we
a
knew that it was regulated by population,
but we were not told the reason why it was
regulated according to population. I
think the conditions under which that
provision was placed upon the Statute
Book have now passed, and in our rural
areas and seaside places, the people are
just as much advanced and as interested
in the welfare of themselves and their
families as are the people in the cities.
No great hardship would be imposed upon
the Government, or on the city traders,
if the Government could see their way to
extend that uniform hour regulation, to
abolish the old system, and to institute
the more modern system of equal rights
for all classes of traders within our area.
While I am speaking on the question of
hours there is another point that I might
mention. I do not know whether it has
been mentioned during the Committee
Stage, but I take the privilege now of
mentioning it. In the city here we have
also nine o'clock closing in some cases.
Seventeen houses come under that ban.
I hope the Government will deal fairly
with that matter, explain it fully, and
give us reasons why that state of affairs
exists in our own city. Hon. Members
sitting behind me are more capable than
I of dealing with this Clause from the
point of view of the hotels and seaside resorts, and of our rural areas, and I am
sure they will have something to say on it.
But those two omissions to which I have
referred are not going to straighten out
the anomalies that I, in my own individual capacity, have come across during
the period of the operation of the Act.
The last request made was, I think, a
reasonable one. We did not press for a
division, and we hope that when this
Clause comes up on the Third reading we
will have a concession also in line 23. I
am sure that if the Government take the
advice given them in the course of the
debate on this Clause, they will see the
wisdom of altering the items which came
under their notice during the discussion.
To me, the Clause as it stands is not satisfactory, from the points of view I have
expressed. I do not think it is going to
meet the desired aims and objects of the
people who are really endeavouring to
bring about the straightening-out process.
I will allow some of the hon. Members
who, as I say, spoke very truly, and gave
great information on the Clause, to support me in my suggestions, and we will

HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 17th November, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PUBLICATION OF PORK PRICES.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to several public meetings
of Fermanagh farmers, asking the Government to bring pressure on the pork buyers
of Northern Ireland to publish their
prices a week in advance, following the
precedent of the Free State and Great
Britain, so that producers may know the
price they are likely to receive before
killing their animals; and will he take
the necessary action.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): I am aware that meetings of Fermanagh farmers have been
held at which resolutions have been
passed requesting the Government to take
up the question of the advance publication of pork prices. I am not aware,
however, that Great Britain and the Free
State afford legislative precedents in this
matter. In the Free State and in Great
Britain certain firms do publish an advance indication of prices, but this action
is purely voluntary.
The present desire for the publication
in advance of pork prices arises out of the
problem of stabilization. Fluctuations
in the price of pork have from time to
time been acute and sometimes unexpected. At conferences summoned by
my Ministry, the whole question of stabilization was explored by representatives
of all the interests concerned, but unhappily no tangible result accrued.
It is scarcely necessary to say that I
would welcome whole-heartedly an arrangement whereby an advance indication
of probable prices would be available for
the farming community, but in any efforts
that have been made in this direction
serious difficulties have been encountered.
In several districts in Northern Ireland
there has been a tendency to sell fat pigs
by live weight and to cater for the fresh
pork market in Great Britain. There
can be no doubt that the
the development of
this tendency and of the pork trade in the
cross-Channel markets will make an important contribution to the solution of the
problem.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
answer, is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that at the present moment pork
is being sold at 58s per cwt. and is being
retailed in this city at 146s a cwt. showing
a net profit of 150 per cent. ? In these
circumstances, if the pork buyers are not
willing to voluntarily publish prices a
week in advance, will the right hon.
Gentleman not promise to seek legislative
powers in this House to compel them to
do so?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am afraid that
legislation for that purpose would not be
possible.
Mr. HEALY: But it would be popular
on both sides of the House.
NEW VARIETY OF POTATO.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware of the
remarkable productivity of the new
potato, the "Arran Banner," which multiplies its own weight 168 times; and
whether he is going to make this seed
available to Northern Ireland growers at
the earliest possible moment.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The reply to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is in the affirmative. The new potato,
Arran Banner," has been tested at the
Ministry's farms, and has given a very
high yield per acre. The figure quoted
by the hon. Member, however, could only
he reached by intensive scientific culture
or by cutting up the sets to the smallest
possible size and growing these sets in
boxes for the first stage of growth.
"Arran Banner" seed is at present on
the market in limited quantities, and was
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
17 NOVEMBER 1927
quoted very recently at £500 per ton.
The potato is round in shape, and it is
questionable whether it would be suitable
for the export trade of Northern Ireland,
which favours an oval-shaped potato.
MOTOR BUSES ON LIGHT
RAILWAYS.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has considered the
feasibility of running motor buses on certain light railway tracks in Northern
Ireland, where the services have been suspended or may be suspended owing to
lack of traffic and competition.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The hon. Member will
appreciate that the question of the feasibility of running motor buses on light
railways is primarily one for the management of the respective railways. I can,
however, assure the hon. Member that I
am watching attentively any transport developments which may assist and improve
the position of light railways in Northern
Ireland, and in this connection
may inform him that I am given to understand
that a petrol-driven car is being operated
successfully on the Donegal Railway.
Mr. HEALY: The Donegal Railway, if
my geography is correct, is not in Northern
Ireland at all. Is the right hon
Gentleman aware of the fact that on the
Victoria Bridge Tramway, which is in
Northern Ireland, such a scheme has been
in operation for some time, and is he also
aware of the fact that a recommendation
for transport of that character has been
made with regard to the Cloghher Valley
Light Railway?
Mr. BARBOUR: I am not aware that
there is a petrol-driven car on the Castlederg Railway, but I am quite aware of
the suggestion that has been made as to
the Clogher Valley Railway. The whole
question of transport on that railway is
under consideration at the present time.
Mr. HEALY: I am sorry that the right
hon. Gentleman is much worse informed
in this matter than I am or the
public is.

this statue in the public interest.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

question.
I have no official cognizance of the proceedings of the Libraries, Museums and
Arts Committee of the Belfast Corporation, and am, therefore, without information on the matters dealt with in the

Monuments Act gives me no power to
purchase a modern work of art.

What this Clause proposes to do is to
take away two licences. I understand
there are only two in the whole of the Six
Counties. These licences were properly
and legally granted at the time they were
granted. The people who applied for and
got those licences were acting legally and
constitutionally and quite within their
rights. What does this Clause propose
to do now? In its present form it is
retrospective and it proposes to deprive
these people of the rights which they
legally had. I do not think the Government intend to do a thing like that. It
is quite right that they should prevent it
in the future. If that is their intention
they could do that by stating that it
should have effect from the passing of
this Act, instead of from the passing of
the Act of 1923, and then they would be
doing no harm to these people. These two
men took out their licences, as I have

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
in page 7, line 30, to leave out the words
"spirits in retail quantities' and to
insert "
at any one time spirits in the
quantities prescribed in the sub-section."
As I explained in my Second Reading
speech, the law is that wholesale dealers
McMullen, William
O'Neill, Patrick
Woods, Lt.-Col. Philip James
TELLER FOR THE NOES
Mr. Beattie.
could not sell more than two gallons of
spirits, and when I say "spirits" I include spirits, rum and so forth, at one
particular time. But there was a mixed
parcel. That is to say, rum, whisky,
etc. The effect was that a wholesale
dealer could sell only two gallons of each
particular drink, that is to say, two
gallons of rum, two gallons of whisky, or
two gallons of any other spirits. It was
considered that this imposed a hardship on
the retailer, as it meant locking up a great
deal of money. Therefore, we propose to
amend the clause so as to enable a composite, a mixed, bag of drink to be made
up, amounting to not less than two
gallons.
A question was raised in the House
during the Second Reading to the effect
that the Bill did not clearly define what
was intended, and I think there is no
doubt about it that, as the Bill stood, it
would have enabled a wholesaler to sell a
total quantity of less than two gallons.
This Amendment will make it perfectly
clear that a wholesaler can sell a mixed
bag of two gallons, and not less.
Mr. GYLE: I wish to say, speaking for
the retail trade, that we are quite satisfied
with the Amendment as it is now proposed.
Amendment agreed to.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in Clause 5, page 7, line 36, at the end
to add, "the quantities prescribed by this
sub-section are quantities of not less than
two gallons consisting of spirits of different denominations.

This is a formal matter and the Amendment is really to bring the existing prac
tice in the Courts into line with the Act
of 1923. The law as it existed before the
passing of the Act of 1923 required any
publican, when making application for a
transfer or confirmation, or for a new
licence, to serve, amongst other people,
the two Justices residing nearest to the
premises. It always gave some trouble
to find out who the two nearest Justices
were, because with the modern idea of
Justices having business in one place and
residing in another place we never knew
really where we were. However, the 1923
Act withdrew from the ordinary justices
all duty as regards the licensing laws, and
I introduce this Amendment to bring the
law up-to-date, and to say that, in place
of serving the two nearest Justices, the resident magistrate should be served with a
copy of the application through the Clerk
of Petty Sessions.

CLAUSE 10 (Restrictions on sale of
certain kinds of alcohol)-
(1) It shall not be lawful for any
person in any premises licensed for the
sale of intoxicating liquor by retail to
sell, expose for sale, keep for sale, or
supply any liquor which consists of or
contains or is mixed with any alcohol
of a kind other than ethyl alcohol:
Provided that this sub-section shall
not apply to a person holding any such
licence as is mentioned in section
twelve of the Act of 1923.
(2) The Ministry of Home Affairs
shall have power to make regulations
prescribing the conditions under which
the sale, keeping, supply and consump
tion of alcohol, other than ethyl alcohol
may be permitted, in cases other than
those to which sub-section (1) of this
section applies; and, as from the making of such regulations, it shall not be
lawful to sell, keep, supply or consume
alcohol, other than ethyl alcohol,
except as permitted thereby.
(3) Any person who acts in contravention of the provisions of this section,
or of regulations made thereunder, shall
be guilty of an offence under the Act
of 1923, and the provisions of section
eight of that Act with respect to forfeiture of licences and recording of
convictions shall apply where any person
licensed for the sale of intoxicating
liquor by retail is convicted of any such
offence, as if such offence was an
offence specified in sub-section (1) of
the said section eight.

of a similar character already in

rules of the club which have been

This is an entirely new departure from
the policy that has existed up to now in
regard to clubs. For my part I desire to

in any name, against the right of any district-inspector or any policeman to go into
a club without warning. As far as I can
see--I do not say it is the purpose-this

the rights of members by districtinspectors going into them in order to find
if illegalities are taking place within the

the Union Club and other clubs will really
be exempt from interference of that character altogether. I always understood
that a club was a man's home while he was
in that club, and any police interference,
in my opinion, is as reprehensible as if
it was his private house. I have my own
views with regard to clubs and the sale
of drink in clubs. I have always been of
the opinion that the sale of drink in clubs
should be approximately on the same lines
as in public-houses.

CLAUSE 12.-(Licensing of theatres
and music halls).
(1) As from the commencement of
this section, a building, hall, room or
other premises shall not be used as a
theatre or music hall without a licence
for such purpose first obtained from
the licensing court under the provisions
of the Second Schedule to this Act; and
for the registration of such licence a fee
of five shillings shall be paid by the
person applying therefor.
Such fee shall be paid to the clerk of
petty sessions of the petty sessions district in which the premises are situated
and shall be deemed to be a fee to which
the provisions of section nineteen of the
Licensing Act (Ireland), 1874, apply:
Provided that, where the application
is for a new licence, the fee shall be paid
in the first instance to the clerk of the
crown and peace and by him transmitted
to the clerk of petty sessions.
(2) A theatre or music hall shall not
be deemed to be a place of public entertainment within the meaning of section
fifty-one of the Public Health Acts
Amendment Act, 1890.
(3) It shall not be lawful for any
officer of excise to grant, under the
authority of section seven of the Excise
Act, 1835, a licence for the sale of intoxicating liquor (in this section referred
to as a "retail licence") to the proprietor of any place of public entertainment, except a theatre or music
hall for which a licence has been obtained under the provisions of the
Second Schedule to this Act; and no
retail licence shall be granted, transferred or renewed except upon production of a certificate given by the licensing court, in like manner and subject
to the like provisions as are applicable
to the grant of a licence under subsection (1) of this section, and being to
the following effect, that is to say :-

in reply to the case I made. He stated
that if this Amendment were passed
theatres would spring up like mushrooms
all over Northern Ireland, that the citizens of the Six Counties were so grotesquely foolish, that they had so much
money to spend that they would proceed
to build colossal theatres, not in order to
have the theatres, but in order to turn
them into public-houses where they could
sell drink for half-an-hour before and an
hour after the regulation time. Does the
noble Lord put that forward seriously!
Does he really think there is any possibility of anything of the sort?
What are the facts? A bar in a
theatre opens at a quarter to eight. No
one enters the bar when the performance
is being carried on. At the end of an
hour there is an interval, which lasts about
ten minutes. Then there is an interval
after the second or third act. Here is a
Government introducing what they call
a temperance Measure, and they. prevent
the citizens who go up for five minutes
to the bar, between one act and another,
from enjoying the benefits of a refreshment. If I had thought, or if any reasonable or sensible person had thought, that
it was the intention of the Act of 1923 to
rob the patrons of these theatres and
music halls of this simple right which is
enjoyed by citizens in every normal community in these islands, I believe there
would have been a howl of execration.
As I said before, is this an attempt
to make the people sober, is it the
suggestion that people go to theatres in
order to get drunk? The noble Lord put
forward also the argument that these are
places of entertainment, and that people
ought to go to theatres to see plays, to
music halls to watch the performances, to
picture houses to enjoy the pictures, and
that they ought not to drink. But, as
my
hon. Friend has pointed out, you
have a bar at horse races, and people
not go to horse races to drink at the bar.
It is there as a convenience, and in the

normal course of affairs people may have
a drink. Take clubs; they were never
intended to be drinking institutions but
places of social resort, and in the course
of your pleasant evening if you want a

a club is for, and there are numbers of

If it is a good play he feels well and the

play that he has not enjoyed he gets exhilarated and consoled for the money he
spends, and so a public service is rendered.
I appeal again to the noble Lord and
ask him to divorce himself from prejudice,
to consider this Amendment as if it came
from the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) or the hon. Gentleman who
spoke so eloquently in its favour from
those benches, to forget that I have fostered this Amendment, that it is my
Amendment-because, since I have come
into this House, and notably during this
Session, the noble Lord has insisted,
rightly or wrongly, defensibly or indefensibly, in rejecting every proposal I have
put forward. There never was a saner
proposal than this. This is merely to
continue the arrangements for public convenience in theatres and music halls that
have been in existence for 100 years. By
a subterfuge you robbed them of that
right. You never mentioned theatres in
your Bill of 1923. The Prime Minister
quoted the preamble of the Bill. I do
not know why he quoted the preamble,
because there was not a word about
theatres or music halls in the preamble.
These people who own the theatres,
music halls, and picture houses-if there
are any bars in picture houses, I do not
know whether there are or not-got no
warning of what was happening. The
retail traders got warning, our clubs more
or less got warning, but these people in
the theatres got no warning at all. The
first thing they knew about it was when
they were prosecuted, and when the prosecution was brought before the local
magistrates I am very sorry I have not
got here with me the report of the proceedings that took place in court, but
after the hearing of this case, the two
magistrates postponed their decision for
nearly a fortnight. They were so impressed with the fact that the Government
was ignorant, the draftsman was ignorant,
Parliament was ignorant, everybody was
ignorant of any intention whatever to include theatres or music halls in this Act,
that they merely imposed a nominal fine,
and did not record the conviction.

NEW CLAUSE (Summer time extension of hours)-
"Notwithstanding anything in any
enactment it shall be lawful, during
the periods of statutory summer time
to keep open, sell, and consume intoxicating liquor in any premises licensed
for such purpose between the hours 10
a.m. and 10 p.m. on week days in the
following holiday resorts-Antrim,
Ballycastle, Portrush, Portstewart,
Newcastle, Rostrevor, Whitehead,
Warrenpoint, Holywood, Groomsport,
Millisle, Ballywalter, Portaferry, Ardglass, Killough, Kilkeel, Carnlough,
Glenarm, Cushendall, Giant's Causeway, Donaghadee, and Cushendun."

to our holiday resorts in Northern Ireland those facilities which they expect to
get, and my suggestion is that during

Great Britain, and indeed from various

now is different from what it was before

should be adopted.

of people over a big area. Many of these
people are farmers and labourers who
have to come a long way into the towns
to get drink, and the consequence is
that they cannot be there at nine o'clock,
whereas, in Belfast, there is no man living
at any street but practically has a publichouse at his corner. He can get to a
public-house in five minutes. If the

NEW CLAUSE: (Opening on Sunday
and Christmas Day).
"It is hereby declared that Part 2 of
the Second Schedule to the Act of 1923
shall be amended, and that the sale or
exposing for sale and the opening and
keeping open of any premises licensed for
the sale of intoxicating liquors on the
premises, shall be lawful on Sundays and
Christmas Day between the hours of 2
p.m. and 5 p.m., provided that no person
shall be employed to work on licensed premises during such hours on Sunday or
Christmas Day unless he has made a clear
day of 24 hours holiday during the preceding week."

Mr. GYLE: That is the answer to the
question as to whether this Act has been
a failure or not. I will pass on from that,
and I will give you some facts as to what
Sunday closing in Northern Ireland has
done. It has been maintained that the
public-houses in Northern Ireland, with
the exception of Belfast, have been closed
for many years on Sunday. Anyone who
knows anything about it is aware that
the public-houses were not closed, because
all you have got to do was to go a distance of five miles and you could receive
any alcoholic refreshment that you desired. In the country it was a distance
of three miles.
We all know that that was practically
Sunday opening in Northern Ireland.
Our friends the teetotal party are always
complaining about the ills of bona fide
travelling which they constantly call
mala fide travelling. In my Amendment
I am going to get over their difficulty.
I am going to ask the Government to open
the public-houses throughout the Six
Counties from 2 o'clock to 5 o'clock on
Sundays. That is a matter of three hours
and will enable anyone who so desires to
get reasonable liquid refreshments on
Sunday. The Parliamentary Secretary
spoke about the five wise and the five
foolish virgins. After the passing of the
1923 Act, there were some people who considered themselves very wise virgins indeed. Many working men are fond of a
glass of porter and are used to what we
in the trade call draught porter. On the
first Saturay night they thought they
would get a glass of porter in to drink on
Sunday, but they found it was "flat."
Mr. ELLIOTT: Bad.
Mr. GYLE: That is the result of its
remaining overnight in a vessel that is
not properly corked.

this House were violent temperance supporters, or supporters of liquor legislation. Some Members of the House were
in favour of the unfettered freedom of
the people to act as their consciences distated in regard to the consumption of intoxicating liquor. The present Liquor
Act was passed in 1923. Two years
elapsed from 1923 to 1925, and the
judgment of the people was taken in
many cases upon the liquor legislation of
the Government.

I quite agree with my hon. Friend, the
Leader of the Opposition, that now that
these houses are closed it would not be
desirable to re-open them. I will tell
you why. I think the whole case was
put in a nutshell by a friend of mine who
went to work in Glasgow. He was very
fond of a glass of whisky. This was many
years ago, when Sunday closing was put
into operation in Glasgow. He said,
"When I was in Belfast I used to work
with some friends and I was satisfied with
one or two half 'uns for the day, but
when I went to Glasgow I found the
public-houses closed on Sunday. I went
to live in a lodging-house and everybody
in the lodging-house bought a bottle of
whisky on the Saturday night. I was compelled to drink practically a bottle of
whisky which I brought into the house
the night before, whereas if the publichouses had been open for a couple of
hours on the Sunday, as I was not drinking for the love of drinking, one or two
half 'uns would have satisfied me."
I believe there is a good deal in that,
but since the change has been made, and
people have become accustomed to it, I
am not inclined to alter it now.
I am
rather inclined to give it a chance,
whether it is for good or evil, and, therefore, I appeal to my hon. Friend, the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Gyle), to

NEW CLAUSE (Bona fide travellers).
Nothing in this Act or in the Act
of 1923 shall be construed to preclude
the sale at any time at a railway station of intoxicating liquors to travellers
by railroad on arrival or departure of
trains or the sale of intoxicating liquors
to bona-fide travellers within the
meaning of the Licensing (Ireland)
Acts, 1833 to 1906, with this amendment, that the words ten miles shall be
substituted for three miles in Section
28 of the Act of 1874, and for five
miles in the Act of 1906 respectively,
and section 2 of Part 1 of the Second
Schedule to the Act of 1923 shall be
repealed accordingly."
Brought up and read a First time.

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
22 NOVEMBER 1927
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 22nd November, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
APPOINTMENT OF BELFAST
MAGISTRATES.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
cause of the delay in the appointment of
magistrates in the County Borough of
Belfast whose names have been recommended to him, and whether it would not
be possible to expedite these appointments.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The question of the
appointment of magistrates is one dependent on the administrative requirements
of the particular area affected, and the
determination of the suitability or otherwise of the persons recommended for such
appointment.
A very large number of names have
been brought under my notice with a
view to appointment to the Magistracy,
and the hon. and gallant Member will
understand that very careful consideration has to be given to these recommendations before appointments are made, and
that it would not be in the public interest, in an important matter of this
character, to act in a hasty and ill-considered manner.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if there is any
reason why the counties should have had
three periods of appointments since the
last appointment was made in Belfast?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The interests
in the one area may be entirely different
from the interests in the other area.
HOSPITAL FOR MENTALLY
DEFECTIVE CHILDREN.
2. Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
would consider applying to the Joint Law
and Improvement Committee of the Belfast Corporation for a building site at
Asylum grounds, Grosvenor Road, Belfast, for the purpose of the erection of
a hospital for mentally deficient children,
which, he stated, was under consideration.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Minister
of Home Affairs has no power or authority to establish institutions of the
character indicated in the hon. Member's
question.
At the same time I would refer the
hon. Member to the powers vested in Local
Education Authorities in regard to
making provision for mentally afflicted
children, and I would, at the same time,
remind the hon. Member that the Local
Government Commission which has recently submitted its Report to the Government, formulated certain recommendations in regard to making provision for
afflicted children, which proposals will
be carefully considered in connection
with any proposed legislation dealing
with the various matters referred to in
the Report.

THE NEW PARLIAMENT HOUSE.
5. Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the approximate date of the completion
of the new Parliament House
Stormont.
at
The MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As the hon. Member has
doubtless observed, a contract for the
superstructure of the building has now
been advertised. The Imperial Office
of Works, who are the responsible authorities, have adopted special measures to
avoid any suspension of the work at
present being carried on, and are prepared to prosecute with all possible expedition the work yet to be completed,
and to place no obstacle in the way of
the successful contractor as regards its
acceleration, but in an undertaking of
this magnitude it would be unwise to
indulge in any forecast of definite or even
approximate dates. The Government has
lost no opportunity of stressing the importance of the new Parliament House
being available at the earliest possible
moment.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing Bill.
As amended, considered.
NEW CLAUSE (Bona-fide travellers).
"Nothing in this Act or in the Act of
1923 shall be construed to preclude the
sale at a railway station of intoxicating
liquors to travellers by railroad on arrival
or departure of trains, or the sale of intoxicating liquors to bona-fide travellers
within the meaning of the Licensing
(Ireland) Acts, 1833 to 1906, with this
Amendment, that the words ten miles
shall be substituted for three miles in
section 28 of the Act of 1874, and for five
miles in the Act of 1906 respectively, and
section 2 of Part 1 of the Second Schedule
to the Act of 1923 shall be repealed
accordingly."
I beg to
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL :
move this new Clause in order to induce
the House, if I can, to consider whether
the time has not arrived for the Government to give way to the wishes of very
many of the people of Northern Ireland. I do not move this Clause in the
interests of those engaged in the liquor
business-not solely in their interests
as might be reasonably assumed, but
I do it on account of the number of
travellers who frequent seaside resorts,
and who have made representations to
me that they think the Government
should in justice to them restore to them
in a somewhat different form the right
which they so long enjoyed.
Many complaints, as the House know,
had been made with regard to abuses of
the bona-fide traveller Clause in the previous Acts, but in my opinion these complaints were largely exaggerated. There
is no Act of Parliament that I know of
but is occasionally broken in some way,
and in my opinion-and I think you
will find that it is the opinion of a very
large number of people in the Six
Counties the bona-fide Clause of the
previous Acts was not broken to such an
extent as to warrant the elimination of
the Clause altogether. Everyone knows
the number of people who frequent the
seaside and health resorts during the
summer months-people who come from
a distance in our own Six Counties, and
many people indeed owing to the advent
of motor traffic who come from a much
greater distance. These people complain
bitterly that while they are able anywhere else outside the Six Counties to
get what reasonable refreshment they
are entitled to, here they are totally deharred. That is not fair to those people
who do not abuse any of the conditions of
the Acts and who never did abuse them:
and they consider that because of a few
in number who did take undue advantage
of those conditions they should not be
penalized.
-3335 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

22 NOVEMBER 1927
Report Stage
I do not think it can be held by any
sense of reasoning that because one or
two or any small number of people did
break the law in regard to a matter of
this sort the whole community should be
penalized for it. And it is because of
the demand, and I may state to the
House that there is a very large demand,
that these facilities should be restored to
the general public that I have put down.
this new Clause. The House will know, I
am sure, that this right was eliminated in
the 1923 Act, and not alone were the
public, whom I speak for now, greatly
inconvenienced by it but those engaged
in the business particularly in seaside
towns were very severely hit in this
matter. Their business to a large extent
was taken away. Indeed I think I
might state as a matter of fact that the
licensed houses in the seaside places are
just getting as much as they can do to
live at all. But I do not expect from
what I know of the dealings of the
Government with regard to liquor
licensing legislation that they have ever
taken into consideration those engaged
in the business. I mention that merely
as a fact knowing that in all probability
the House will assume that it is solely
from their point of view I am speaking.
It is not solely from their point of view;
it is from the point of view of the
general public I am speaking who have
been immensely inconvenienced because
of the abolition of this right they formerly
had.
In addition to those who frequent seaside places the public who travelled by
rail always had this right of being able
to get liquor refreshment at any of the
railway saloons. It is on their behalf as
much as for the people who do not travel
by rail I have put down this new Clause.
I hope the House will give it greater
consideration than they have given
already to any of the Amendments which
Members of the Opposition have put
down. I therefore wish to move the
Clause standing in my name.
Mr. GYLE: In seconding the Amendment that has been put down by the hon.
Member I wish to draw the attention of
the House to the grave inconvenience
that many people labour under through
the abolition by the Act of 1923 of the
facilities afforded to the bona-fide
travellers. During the election of 1921
it was never thought that such drastic
changes would be brought about by that
Act. As I said in this House before,
there is no doubt that the Prime Minister
mentioned that there would be licensing reform, but I do not think that anyone in the Six Counties, whether on the
side of the Teetotal party or on the side
of the Liquor party, as they are called,
ever thought that there would be such
drastic changes in the licensing law. At
one fell swoop not only were publichouses closed in Belfast but all facilities
were taken away from the public of the
Six Counties in regard to reasonable refreshment on Sundays.
We found that for some reason or other
-I do not know exactly what it was the
Prime Minister was coerced from the position he took up to set up a Royal Commission. If that Royal Commission had
been set up and facts and figures had been
produced before them I am perfectly sure
that no such recommendations would have
been made as were carried out in this
House. We all know--and I do not think
anyone can controvert the statement that
I am now making-that it is an enormous
inconvenience to the travelling public on
Sunday. A great many of the working
classes have not been able to get as much
work in recent years as we would like them
to have, but those who are working and
have money to spend visit seaside resorts
on a Sunday, being accompanied in many
cases by their wives and families, but they
are now debarred from going into licensed
places. They may carry with them alcoholic beverages which can be consumed in
unlicensed places, which pay nothing towards the revenue. The people who pay
licence duty are debarred from supplying
those people on Sunday. Those who are
in the habit of having alcoholic drink on
other days of the week are debarred from
participating on Sunday in that which
they enjoy during the remainder of the
week.
It has been stated by the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Finance,
and it is generally agreed that Ulster is
one of the most sober places in the United
Kingdom. It was stated here that the
people of Ulster were able to take care of
themselves, and yet they are debarred
from enjoying themselves in the same way
as the people in any other part of the
United Kingdom are allowed to enjoy
themselves. Although there is no bonafide traveller in England still the publichouses, hotels and restaurants are open at
certain hours of the day. People are
Intoxicating Liquor Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Report Stage

[Mr. Gyle]
allowed to go in and get what they desire
in the way of alcoholic refreshments. In
Scotland, although the bona-fide traveller
is done away with, from 12 o'clock on
Saturday to 12 o'clock on Sunday night anyone travelling a distance of three miles can, if he so desires,
have alcoholic refreshment. Why should
we in Northern Ireland, acknowledged to
be the most sober part of the British
Empire, be penalised in such a manner?
The Prime Minister referred to the Isle
of Man. It is about the only place where
one finds Sunday closing in the sense that
the public-houses are not open to residents. Most of the people in the Isle of
Man are there as visitors, and the people
usually resident there have hotels and
boarding houses where sleeping accommodation and meals are provided for the
visitors. There is no difficulty in the
world for anyone, either a visitor or resident, getting anything he requires in the
shape of intoxicating liquor on Sunday. I
do not think it is fair to put the Isle of
Man in comparison with a place like
Northern Ireland which is an industrial
community and where conditions are
altogether different.
After all is said and done those who
do not desire intoxicating liquor are not
asked to go into public-houses, and why
a small minority of people should debar
others who desire to have their refreshments on Sunday passes my understanding. It is simply that a little clique
desire to interfere with the rights and
liberties of the people. They are always
at it. If it is not
one thing it
is another. Now that they have
got rid of Sunday opening they are
attempting to bring forward other
things-
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. GYLE -SO as to prevent the
people retaining the rights and liberties
they have. It goes on from day to day.
I want to ask the House to think
sensibly of the rights of the people of
Northern Ireland. Think over it and do
not say they are to be debarred, because it happens to be Sunday, from
having alcoholic refreshment. After
they have gone to their place of worship
on Sunday they may desire to go to the
seaside or the country. Some people
prefer the country to the seaside, and I
see no reason why those who go to the
country or seaside should be debarred in
this way.
I want to put before the
House one thing. Think over it, and
think it over very seriously, because you
are not stopping one half-glass of
whisky or one bottle of stout from being
consumed in Northern Ireland by this
Bill. You are simply driving the people
to get it by other channels. That is the
most important part of the whole thing.
Since the passing of the 1923 Act clubs
have sprung up all over the place. In
this Amending Bill you have tightened
up, and rightly tightened up that matter,
I believe, although I do not believe in allowing a police officer to enter clubs. In
other respects you have rightly tightened
up matters regarding the non-bona-fide
clubs.
I believe you will close quite a number
of clubs, but you are going to drive
people who had the right to go into those
clubs back on to the streets, and where are
they going? Remember this that a man
who wishes to have a drink will always
get it.
You are going to drive them
into shebeens and perhaps into even
worse places. That is a point I want the
House to take into consideration. During
the summer I saw many excursions for
Sundays advertised. I will not mention
any names. Most of you are aware of
the large excursion parties that leave
Northern Ireland, and where do they
go?
Mr. ELLIOTT: Warrenpoint.
Mr. GYLE: They
State.
go to the Free
Mr. GRANT: What for?
Mr. DEVLIN: For pleasure.
Mr. GYLE: The reason they go to
the Free State is because they get more
enjoyment, more freedom and more rights
than they get in Northern Ireland. I am
sure those who organise these excursions
know perfectly well that if they organised

This is the first proposal in the nature
of an Amendment to the Bill which I
have made, and perhaps it is an ex-
It is a proposal
ceptional proposal too.
in which I think there are very good

It is a proposal that deals practically
with the country districts outside Belfast,
and in a small way it may affect Belfast
also. It has been a puzzle to me that in
the passing of all the other liquor legislation in the past nothing was put into
any of the Bills in order to solve the

meet.
It is not an extraordinary proposal,
because in England, where people have
to travel long distances into the markets
in Covent Garden and elsewhere, the difficulty has been met by the Legislature.
They passed special legislation to meet it.
As I know, people come from outside districts in the winter night or early in the
winter morning at two, three, four or five
o'clock. They come from their homes and
travel fifteen or twenty miles with their
horses and carts carrying loads of agricultural produce. They come into the
towns, and by reason of the railway
arrangements they have to be in the towns
at a very early hour in order to get their
produce away to be shipped.
I make this proposal with all sincerity,
and in the interests of common humanity.
I have witnessed what I have described
in the town where I live myself. I have
seen it for years and years. I have seen
men, some of them old men, and women
coming into the town, either drenched to
the skin with the rain, or practically
frozen through coming across the mountains in the snow. A slight concession has
been given in this Bill to meet the difficulties of those people. The Government
have graciously deigned to allow the
horse to be put in the stable, but the
man, the human being, is not to have a

kind. He can go into the yard with his

cannot go.
a

on the

The
The law as it stands is this.
Government was good enough to provide
the other night in one of the Amendments
to this Bill that a farmer coming into a
market or a fair in the morning may
stable his horse in the yard of licensed
premises. They would not grant me the
favour of putting in a simple thing to
save the publican from prosecution. All
that can be done is that a horse may be
stabled in the yard. If it were a teeming
wet or snowy morning, such as we are
accustomed to in the country, in the
winter, the farmer could not safely go
into the kitchen of the public-house to
get warmed at the fire, because his

This legislation is to deal with one

You can teach them to have contempt for

is not attributable in any way to the Act

Mr. HANNA: I beg to move, in page
3, lines 14 and 15, to leave out the words
in such hotel for the succeeding night,"
and to insert instead thereof the words
"for the succeeding night in such hotel."
This Amendment, which stands in my
name, is purely a drafting Amendment,
and it is designed to make clear that both
the person who has lodged the night before in the hotel, and also the person who
has engaged the room for the succeeding
night must be living in the same hotel.
If we allow the words to remain exactly
as they are some difficulty or doubt
might arise as to whether the person
must have lodged the night before in that
hotel. It is with a view to avoiding that
that this drafting Amendment has been
put down. I therefore beg to move.
Amendment agreed to.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I beg to
move, in page 3, line 15, to leave out
from the word "night" ("for the succeeding night") to the end of Sub-section
(1).
•
This Amendment which I have put
down has already been debated for a considerable length of time. As a matter
of fact I am very much surprised that
this Sub-section still appears in the Bill,
because I understood from the arguments
which were put forward before that the
Government were prepared, at least, to
look favourably at my proposal. But in

still included in this Clause, I find it
necessary to propose the Amendment,
which provides that a resident in an
hotel, or a guest staying in an hotel,
should have the right to consume intoxicating liquor at any hour in the hotel.
That, I suggest, is reasonable. What
the Bill contains at the present time is,
I think, most unreasonable.
Take an extreme case, the owner of an
hotel. If this Bill passes as it is, and I
arrive home in my own house, as I usually
do, at nine o'clock to-night, I will not be
entitled to consume a drink if I want one.
That, I suggest, is a quite unreasonable
and quite indefensible thing for any
Government to enact in any Act of Parliament. But apart from the individual
himself, I think a still greater hardship
is imposed on the guest or the traveller
who frequents the hotel, or is staying in
the hotel. Commercial men particularly
have very late hours in their business.
They change from one town to another.
Some of them work quite late. Often
they do not arrive in a town until after
9 or 10 o'clock. As the House knows,
there is a difference between a town with
a population of under 5,000, and a town
with a population of over 5,000. In
towns of under 5,000 the guest or traveller
will not be entitled to be supplied with,
or to consume, intoxicating liquor after 9
o'clock at night. In towns of over 5,000
he will not be allowed to do either of those
things after 10 o'clock at night.

I cannot, for the life of me, see why this

proposes that if I am staying in an hotel
where I have the right to a drink during

a drink after these hours. In other
words, if after the clock strikes ten I

guest I cannot get it. I cannot get it

so reasonable an Amendment. Up to the

(a) A district-inspector of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, alone or accompanied by one or more constables,
shall have power to examine and to
search for liquor upon any premises
licensed for the sale of intoxicating
liquor by retail, which such districtinspector is entitled to enter under
any enactments of the Licensing
(Ireland) Acts, 1833 to 1900;
(b) such inspector shall be entitled to
obtain for analysis samples of any
liquor found upon such premises, on
tendering the price for the quantity
which he may require for that purpose, not being more than may be
reasonably requisite ;
(c) Where the sale of such liquor to
him is refused, or the price demanded is unreasonable, such districtinspector shall have power to seize
and remove any liquor found by him
upon the premises, if he has reasonable ground for suspecting that it
is upon the premises for any purpose in contravention of sub-section
(1) of this section."
The House will recollect that with
a view to dealing with an abuse, namely,
introduction of toxic alcohol other than
ethyl alcohol into liquor, we had occasion
to introduce into this Bill a Clause making
it an offence to indulge in that practice.
If we are successfully to carry out the
intention of all hon. Members in this
House, that this evil and abuse should be
dealt with and dealt with urgently and
efficiently, it becomes necessary that we
should introduce this new Clause so that
we will have machinery by which we can
bring those who indulge in this practice.
to a court to be dealt with. I need
scarcely address the House on this point.
We propose to empower a district-inspector of the R.U.C., alone or accompanied
by one or more constables, to go to a
place where he has reason to believe this
practice is indulged in and there to buy,
if he can buy, a portion of the liquor he
suspects, or if he has any difficulty in regard to purchase, he may be able to seize
it for the purpose of analysis and examination. I am perfectly confident that
every Member of this House will afford
us this Clause, to give us the machinery.
we want for the purpose.

to suit English needs. They were flung
at us, and we had no course but to take

Orders of the Day-"Lisburn Electric
Supply Company (Agreement) Bill."
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. BARBOUR: I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not going to explain anything? I thought we were to have an
explanation of the Bill.
Mr. SPEAKER: That may have been
