Mr. BARBOUR: I feel it will be
necessary for me to say only a very few
words as to the introduction of this Bill.
The Government is at all times anxious
to use every means at its disposal to secure cheap electrical power for industrial
enterprises throughout Northern Ireland.
There is little doubt that the most valuable
prospective field for electricity development lies in the Lagan Valley in its extension southwards from Belfast.
field properly lies within the supply radius
of the Belfast Electricity Station. Some
time ago a company was registered for
the purpose of obtaining statutory powers
to supply electricity within the Urban
District of Lisburn. This company proposes to purchase its current from the
Belfast Corporation and to carry it to
Lisburn by an overhead line.
This
The Company's programme did not
contemplate the sale of current to large
power users en route, and the overhead
line was accordingly designed to transmit electrical energy at a pressure of only
6,600 volts, sufficient copper only being
provided in the lines to furnish about
1,000 kilowatts, which is the maximum
estimated requirement of the power and
lighting consumers in the Lisburn area.
It appeared to the Government, however,
desirable that this main transmission line
should be so constructed as to be capable
of use at a much higher pressure, so that
it might not only provide current for
large power users between Belfast and
Lisburn but also be capable of forming
the first link of a main transmission line
extending further into the Province by
way of Lurgan and Portadown. Negotiations were accordingly entered into with
the representatives of the company and
finally an agreement was reached in the
terms of the Schedule to this Bill.
The details of the arrangement are
that the Government is to advance to the
company a sum of £1,450, which will be
secured by a debenture. In consideration of this advance, the company undertakes to construct an overhead line capable of carrying electrical energy at a
pressure of 33,000 volts, instead of 6,600
volts. Interest is not to be paid upon
the £1,450 so advanced until the maximum load delivered to the company exceeds 1,000 kilowatts, or until power is
transmitted over the line for the company's own purposes at a pressure in excess of 6,600 volts. Further, the right
is secured to the Ministry of Commerce
to transmit energy over the line at any
time and also to purchase the line at any
time on giving six months' notice.
I need hardly explain to hon. Members
that the effect of the improved construction of the line will be to increase its capacity for the transmission of electrical energy
five-fold, that is to say that at 6,600
volts which the company originally proposed for their own requirements they
could only
only have transmitted 1,000
kilowatts, whereas under the arrangement
now proposed by raising the pressure to
33,000 volts it will provide for an ultimate load of 6,000 kilowatts. I beg to
move.

ter the conditions of the workpeople by

-
a general strike, nor is one desirable from anybody's point of view.

takes part in an illegal strike. If the

CLAUSE 2 (Protection of Persons
refusing to take part in illegal strikes and
lock-outs).
2.-(1) No person refusing to take
part or to continue to take part in any
strike or lock-out which is by this Act
declared to be illegal, shall be, by
reason of such refusal or by reason of
any action taken by him under this
section, subject to expulsion from any
trade union or society, or to any fine
or penalty, or to deprivation of any
right or benefit to which he or his legal
personal representatives would otherwise be entitled, or liable to be placed
in any respect either directly or
indirectly under any disability or at
any disadvantage as compared with
other members of the union or society,
anything to the contrary in the rules
of a trade union or society, notwithstanding.
(2) No provisions of the Trade Union
Acts, 1871 to 1917, limiting the proceedings which may be entertained by
any court, and nothing in the rules of
a trade union or society requiring the
settlement of disputes in any manner
shall apply to any proceeding for enforcing any right or exemption secured
by this section, and in any such proceeding the court may, in lieu of ordering a person who has been expelled
from membership of a trade union or
society to be restored to membership,
order that he be paid out of the funds
of the trade union or society such sum
by way of compensation or damages as
the court thinks just.

I am absolutely opposed to the Government aiding and abetting anyone prepared to sell his fellow-workers. You
have that in black and white. Not only.
are you going to make it almost impossible
for trade unions to take action, but the
hon. Member for North Belfast has made

at work, if he is prepared to do a thing
contrary to trade union principles, he is
protected. Every man of this House is
satisfied that the question of a legal or
illegal strike is only a matter of bluff pure
and simple. We are all quite satisfied
that the right hon. Gentleman opposite,
or someone acting on his behalf, will soon
declare a strike illegal. The result is that
the individual who is prepared to sell his
principles, the principles for which
thousands of trade unionists have suffered,
and by which they have the right to defend
themselves against the attacks of the employers, is to be compensated.
I was always very proud of the fact
that since I became an employer 15 years
ago there was no necessity for the employees going out, because immediately
a demand was made I accepted it right
away, and I believe other employers could
do the same thing. I believe that is
the only weapon the workers have got.
Right hon. and hon. Gentlemen opposite
are trying to take that weapon away from
them. What would have happened to
the people if they had not had the trade
unions behind them? The Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Labour (Mr.
Gordon) knows what would have happened.

CLAUSE 3 (Prevention of Intimidation).
3.-(1) It is hereby declared that it
is unlawful for one or more persons
(whether acting on their own behalf or
on behalf of a trade union or of an
individual employer or firm, and notwithstanding that they may be acting
in contemplation or furtherance of a
trade dispute) to attend at or near a
house or place where a person resides
or works or carries on business or happens to be, for the purpose of obtaining or communicating information or of
persuading or inducing any person to
work or to abstain from working, if
they so attend in such numbers or
otherwise in such manner as to be calculated to intimidate any person in that
house or place, or to obstruct the approach thereto or egress therefrom, or
to lead to a breach of the peace; and
attending at or near any house or place
in such numbers or in such manner as
is by this Sub-section declared to be unlawful shall be deemed to be a watching
or besetting of that house or place
within the meaning of Section seven of
the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act, 1875.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
regard to the word "intimidate," under
the provisions of the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act of 1875, it had
been ruled by the Courts on numerous
occasions that something in the nature of
physical violence was necessary in order to
constitute intimidation. A Commission
sat in England some years ago on this
very question, and they came to the conclusion that that interpretation of the
word intimidate" was too narrow, because a great number of acts may be
done which, though they do not appear as
physical violence, may be much more intimidatory, so far as the individual against
whom they are directed is concerned,
than if they were accompanied by physical
violence. For instance, it is quite easy
to understand that a large crowd of persons attending at a man's residence,
when he is not there on the scene and
where his wife and family are residing,
might have a much more coercive effect
upon his mentality than mere physical
violence offered to himself. Consequently,
the Government thought it better to give
a wider interpretation to the word "intimidate than was given in this Act of
1875, and anybody who has had experience of this class of case in the Courts
will realize that that is a just provision
and one inserted in the interests of the
liberty of the subject.

CLAUSE 4 (Provisions as to Political
Fund).
(1) It shall not be lawful to require
any member of a trade union to make
any contribution to the political fund
of a trade union unless he has at some
time after the commencement of this
Act and before he is first after the
thirty-first day of December, nineteen.
hundred and twenty-seven, required to
make such a contribution delivered at
the head office or some branch office of
the trade union, notice in writing in
the form set out in the First Schedule
to this Act of his willingness to contribute to that fund and has not withdrawn the notice in manner hereinafter
provided; and every member of a trade
union who has not delivered such a
notice, as aforesaid, or who, having delivered such a notice,
has withdrawn it in manner hereinafter provided, shall be deemed
for the purposes of the Trade Union
Act, 1913, to be a member who is
exempt from the obligation to contribute to the political fund of the union,
and references in that Act to a member
who is so exempt shall be construed
accordingly :
Provided that, if at any time a member of a trade union who has delivered
such a notice as aforesaid gives notice of
withdrawal thereof, delivered at the
head office or at any branch office of
the trade union, he shall be deemed for
the purposes of this sub-section to have
withdrawn the notice as from the first
day of January next after the delivery
of the notice of withdrawal.
For the purposes of this sub-section,
a notice may be delivered personally or
by any authorized agent and any notice
shall be deemed to have been delivered
at the head or branch office of a trade
union if it has been sent by post properly addressed to that office.
(2) All contributions to the political
fund of a trade union from members of
the trade union who are liable to contribute to that fund shall be levied and
made separately from any contributions
to the other funds of the trade union
and no assets of the trade union, other
than the amount raised by such
separate levy as aforesaid, shall be
carried to that fund, and no assets of
a trade union other than those forming
part of the political fund shall be
a

in furtherance of any political object to
which Section three of the Trade Union
Act, 1913, applies; and any charge in

Thursday, 24th November, 1927.

Oral Answers to Questions.
CATTLE REPLACEMENT LOANS.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether an official of his
Department recently issued a circular,
quoted at a meeting in Enniskillen, intimating that if the current instalment of
the Cattle Replacement Loan was not
paid forthwith the whole amount would
be demanded; and whether he approved
of that circular.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): If, as I assume to be
the case, the hon. Member refers to the
instalments which become repayable at the
end of December next, the answer is in
the negative. Possibly, however, the
following circumstances gave rise to the
suggestion in the hon. Member's question:
In 1925 loans were advanced by the
Ministry under the Live Stock Replacement Scheme. As originally arranged,
these loans were repayable in full at the
end of December, 1926. It appeared,
however, to the Ministry that to recall
the loans at that date would, in many
cases, be a hardship and, accordingly, it
was arranged that the advances should be
repayable by three equal annual instalments on the 31st December, 1926, the
31st December, 1927, and the 31st December, 1928. This concession was conditional on one-third being paid, and on the
execution of new promissory notes by
borrowers and their sureties. In certain
cases, where borrowers had taken no steps
to comply with the conditions, the Minis
try considered it necessary to warn them
that further delay in the matter would
render payable, immediately, the full
amount of the loan.
In the Spring of this year it was found
that there were a small number of borrowers who had not paid the instalments
due in December, 1926, and who, at the
time, could only pay with considerable
difficulty. An extension to the 30th June
was, therefore, given to these parties for
the payment of the December instalments. This extension was also conditional on the execution of new Promissory
Notes. As in the case of the previous
concession, parties who had not complied
with the conditions were warned that unless the new Promissory Notes were completed at once the full amount of the
loan would become payable. I was, of
course, aware that such communications
were being issued.
Mr. HEALY: I was quoting from a
newspaper report of a meeting at which a
letter from the right hon. Gentleman
himself was read, and it was considered
at that particular meeting that the issue
of such a circular in the peculiar circumstances of the times was pretty harsh. We
were also surprised that the right hon.
Gentleman would authorize the issue
of it.
Mr. ARCHDALE:
It was necessary
when the banks were coming to the
Minister for the money to warn borrowers that they were obliged to take out
new promissory notes, which was the
reason they issued the notice. Some did
not seem to know it.
Mr. HEALY: To ask a man to pay
three instalments when only one instalment was due does seem rather harsh.
Mr. ARCHDALE:
that.
We did not do

Ministry at first refused its sanction, but
later as the result of representations gave

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): The Armagh
Regional Education Committee has
proposed, subject to the sanction of the
Ministry, to acquire certain vacant premises in Lurgan for the purposes of a

When the proposal was first submitted

asked the Minister to receive a deputation in relation to the proposal. In
consequence of the representations made

to
Regarding the situation of the premises,

RATING OF TOOME EEL FISHERY.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
method by which the rateable valuation
of the property of the Toome Eel Fishery
Company, including an exclusive eel
fishery in Lough Neagh and the Lower
Bann, has been arrived at; and whether
he is satisfied that such valuation is adequate.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The valuation of the Toome Eel
Fishery is arrived at in accordance with
Section 11 of the Valuation (Ireland)
Act, 1852. This Section provides that
the valuation shall be made upon an estimate of the net annual value, that is to
say, the rent for which one year with
another the same might, in its actual
state, be reasonably expected to let from
year to year, the probable annual average
cost of repairs, insurance and other expenses, if any, necessary to maintain the
hereditament in its actual state, and all
rates, taxes, and public charges, if any,
except tithe rent charge, being paid by
the tenant.
I cannot express any opinion as to
whether the present valuation, which was
made, as to part, in the year 1915 and,
as to part, in 1902, is adequate, having
regard to the fact that an application for
its revision is at present before the Commissioner of Valuation.
CIVIL SERVICE ARBITRATION
COURT.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether the awards made by the
Civil Service Arbitration Court to Civil
Servants in the service of the Imperial
Government will be applied to the corresponding classes now in the employment
of the Northern Ireland Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Civil Service
Arbitration Court has no jurisdiction in
regard to the Civil Service of Northern
Ireland, which is an entirely distinct
organization from the Civil Service of the
United Kingdom. Neither the Government of Northern Ireland, nor members
of the Northern Ireland Civil Service are
represented on or before that Court. In
many cases, the circumstances in relation
to which an award is made by the Court
differ materially from those affecting
Northern Ireland Civil Servants of classes
or grades corresponding to the Imperial
classes or grades concerned in such award.
Consequently, while my Ministry might
feel justified in following the lines laid
down in a particular award of this Court,
its decisions have no direct or general
application to the Civil Service
Northern Ireland.

COOKSTOWN RURAL COUNCIL
AND HOUSING.
10. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, in view of the
fact that the Government, by increasing
their grant for the building of houses,
increased the liability of the Cookstown
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
Rural District Council by about £1,000,
he will consider the propriety of recouping the Council by that amount, and thus
avoid an unforeseen burden being placed
upon the ratepayers of that rural district.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is no
doubt that the Bill recently before
this House has had the result of
stimulating the activities of builders of
small houses throughout the country.
In the case of the Cookstown Rural
District Council, building operations have
steadily increased during the last four
years, and development has been during
the current year most marked, as may
be seen from the following figures:-
In the year 1924 the Council granted
certificates for seven subsidy houses. For
the year 1925 the number was nine. The
number increased to 19 during the year
1926, while during the current year no
less than 64 certificates have been issued.
While, no doubt, this rapid development of building has imposed an additional financial burden on the ratepayers
of the district, it must be remembered
that this Parliament has undertaken a
much heavier financial responsibility in
connection with the houses with the object
of reducing the housing shortage and providing houses suitable for the working
classes.
It should also be remembered that
every house built in a particular district
increases the valuation of that district
and thereby tends to reduce the rates.
This aspect of the case is fully realized
by all the local authorities in Northern
Ireland who have studied the needs of
their respective districts, and who have
willingly co-operated with the Government by supplementing the Government
grants in aid of housing.
As the Council in this particular inis merely supplementing the
Government financial provision there can
be no question of making any recommendation.

THE ARREST OF A BUS DRIVER.
12. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs, whether Victor Stanex,
an omnibus driver, employed by Messrs.
Bell & Paisley, on the Belfast to Whitehead route, was at Carrickfergus Petty
Sessions, on the 28th October, fined one
pound with three shillings costs for speeding; whether the fine was not paid, and
Stanex was arrested at Carrickfergus on
the 14th November while driving an
3487 Sittings of the House

24 NOVEMBER 1927
Trade Disputes Bill
omnibus on the regular service, which
was thus disorganized; whether Messrs.
Bell & Paisley did not know that the fine
had not been paid; whether they wrote
to the Minister protesting against the
action of the police and received no reply;
and what explanation he can give of the
action of the police in thus dislocating
the service and causing inconvenience to
the public.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Victor
Stanex, an omnibus driver, was fined
£1 and 38 costs at Carrickfergus on the
28th October last, but did not pay the
fine. On the 11th November Stanex
was warned by the police that a warrant
had been issued and would have to be
executed unless payment was made, but
he stated to the police that he had no
intention of paying the fine. On the
14th November the police again asked
Stanex to pay; he refused, and in these
circumstances the police had no alternative but to execute the warrant. I
understand that a second driver was
available in a very short time to take
the bus to its destination.
I have no information beyond their
own statement as to whether Messrs.
Bell & Paisley knew that the fine had
not been paid. On the 14th November
I received a personal letter from this
firm stating that they proposed to have
the matter raised in this House.
With regard to the last part of the
question, as already indicated, the man
had been given ample time to pay, and
was twice warned that if he did not pay
the warrant would be executed. The
police had, therefore, no alternative but
to execute the warrant of the court,
which this man was defying.
I understand that the bus was delayed
for a very short time only, and the
public suffered practically no
venience.

I will give the Committee an illustration of a ballot taken in a trade union.
We will take the Amalgamated Society
of Dyers and Bleachers. The first ballot resulted in 3,013 members voting in
favour of a political fund, and 3,670
against. That was a union whose members turned up en masse and voted
against a political fund. They thus
failed to have their interests represented
in the British House of Commons, owing
to their failure to pay a shilling per year
to the political fund. A second ballot
was called for in 1919, with the result
that 11,004 members voted for a political
fund and 3,135 against.

member enjoys such liberties and privileges so far as a political levy is concerned.
What you have got to understand is
this, that a trade union is a democratic

disagree with the forms of procedure of

I do not get the consideration in this

the grievances of the workers, of improving their condition, of raising their standard of livelihood, of giving them power
to exalt themselves, to render their conditions happier and safer what more
effective method can you apply to carry
out that purpose than through political
agitation and Parliamentary representation?
For-
Everybody knows, as I told the House
the other day in that tragic and appalling
passage which I read from the life of
Lord Beaconsfield, the conditions under
which workers lived in Great Britain before the trade union organization was
started or assumed the powerful proportions it has assumed to-day. Men were
working in the mines for 16 hours, women
compelled to draw carts with ropes round
them some of them about to give birth
to children. These were the conditions
in those days, and even in my own
memory, without going back to 1813, I
remember conditions here that were almost as appalling though less picturesquely cruel than the conditions I
described in that quotation-women work-

we won for them. They were glad to get

I am of the opinion that this legislation
is brought in simply and purely for the
purpose of destroying trade unions that
have been built up by men for a generation. Men have rendered great service
and have undergone great hardships to
build up this great organization, and why
the Government should bring forward a
Clause that will cripple it is more than
I can understand. There is absolutely
no necessity for this Clause, which will
simply compel the trade unions to reorganize their departments and have
thousands of new forms printed which,
I consider, is very unfair. This Clause
will allow a member of a trade union to
stay at home and disregard the rules of
his trade union and take no active part
in any step that is taken to better the
condition of his fellow-workers. That is
wrong. I would have introduced a Bill
to compel every man to attend his trade
union.

attend and to take a lesser interest in the
affairs of their union. I am certain the

has to-day the same rights that this

Mr. KYLE: I want to oppose this
Motion. In September, 1921, the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland, speaking
on the establishment of the Government
of the Northern Province, stated that he
intended to model the Northern Ireland
Civil Service upon the Imperial Service.
The Northern Ireland Civil Service has
been modelled to some extent on the
Imperial Civil Service, but the Northern
Government left out one very important
factor in regard to the Civil Service.
A good many years ago the present
Speaker of the Imperial House of
Commons was appointed Chairman of a
Committee that was set up by the
Imperial Government to consider the best
ways and means of establishing some
form of negotiating machinery to obviate
the possibility of either strikes or lockouts. As a result of the careful examination which Mr. Whitley gave to this
problem, certain councils were established
in Great Britain governing the conditions of workpeople in a very large
number of trades. Amongst those councils was a Whitley Council which was
established to govern the conditions of
the Civil Servants. The Association of
. Civil Servants had that applied to the
Imperial Civil Service.
I want to contend here that it was
never the intention of the Imperial
Government, when they established this
Parliament under the Act of 1920, that
there ought to be a variation in the conditions appertaining to the Civil Service.
Therefore, I want to contend that if this
Clause is retained in the Bill the Civil
Servants of Northern Ireland are going to
be merely the lap dogs of the party that
is in power. They are going to be merely
the kept servants of the Unionist party
while the Unionist party is in power.
We are reverting to a very dangerous
principle indeed, the principle that has
been laid down in America, that to the
victors go the spoils. I want to say here
that unless some Regulations are issued
by the Government to take them out of
the ambit of being mere political hacks,
and to put them on a proper basis with
an association to look after their interests,
the ultimate result so far as the Civil
Servants are concerned will be that to the
victors go the spoils.
It means that if ever there is a change
of Government in Northern Ireland the
present Civil Servants will not be happy
in their positions. There is no doubt
about that. I think that it is a most reprehensible principle, a principle that was
exploded long ago so far as Great Britain
is concerned, and that a Whitley Council
should be established here in order that
the Civil Servants of Northern Ireland
might have the same conditions as the
Civil Servants of Great Britain.
Speaking the other day on another Bill
that was before this House-the Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing Bill-the
Prime Minister referred to the Isle of
Man. I would point out to the Committee
that even in a small place like the Isle
of Man there is a Whitley Council governing the conditions of the Civil Servants.
In reply to a question that I put to the
Government the argument was used in
this House that Northern Ireland was so
small that there was no reason for the
establishment of a Whitley Council, and
that a certain form of machinery had been
adopted here.
Mr. POLLOCK: Is this argument
directed to the Amendment?

certain that he would desire the members

to have the same liberties as the members

CLAUSE 6 (Provisions as to persons
employed by local and other public
authorities).
(1) It shall not be lawful for any
local or other public authority to make
it a condition of the employment or
continuance in employment of any
person that he shall or shall not be a
member of a trade union, or to impose
any condition upon persons employed
by the authority whereby employees
who are or who are not members of a
trade union are liable to be placed in
any respect either directly or indirectly
under any disability or disadvantage as
compared with other employees.
local

or other public' authority to make it a
condition of any contract made or proposed to be made with the authority, or
of the consideration or acceptance of
any tender in connection with such a
contract, that any person to be employed by any party to the contract
shall or shall not be a member of a
trade union
(3) Any condition imposed in contravention of this section shall be void.
(4) There shall be added to section
five of the Conspiracy and Protection
of Property Act, 1875, the following
provision, that is to say:-

or other public authority wilfully

conviction, to a fine not exceeding
ten pounds or to imprisonment for
a term not exceeding three months."

In doing so I wish to state that it is
apparently the intention of the Government to prevent local authorities from
retaining the right conferred upon them

In this Amendment of mine I propose to
limit somewhat the power the Government is now taking from the local autho
rities. Up to now we have always been
told that all we had to do was to convert

and, as a result of conversion to our particular way of thinking, everything would
be done constitutionally and in order.
Well, certain towns in England have

the employees should belong to a trade

I say this Clause is unnecessary and unwanted. I do not think this Clause is
really aimed at Tory Councils at all. The
growing strength of the Labour Councils
throughout Great Britain-and we hope
in the near future in Northern Irelandis something that has had the serious
consideration of the Tory party. To try
to retard and keep back the advancement
of the Labour Councils the Tory party has
thought fit to put this Clause into a Bill
of this character. It is going to place
public bodies in a totally different position
from all other employers. Ordinary employers are at liberty and are still to
continue to be at liberty to discharge or
to refuse to employ men who belong to
a union. They often do so as we on this
side well know, and as the whole Committee well knows. Following the recent
alleged general strike in Great Britain,
to-day men are suffering because they
exercised a right, which the law had made
legal for them, namely, the right to strike.
The right to strike is being taken away
by this Bill. Many ways are taken by
employers to mark men out as victims for
dismissal. I know many ways which I could
repeat. If a man takes an active part,
say, in his trade union movement, if he
is a branch secretary or shop steward,
or perhaps is treasurer or some other
officer in his union, and he is in
a workshop and finds that the position
of the workers is being attacked
and he thinks he could assist in retarding
the onslaught; he speaks his mind; the
employers will not dismiss that man instantly he is an officer of a trade union
-but they take an indirect way of dismissing him, and on the first opportunity
when a slackness comes along he is on
the list for dismissal. That has been
done repeatedly. I have known men who
were officers in trades unions where their
work was more than they could contend
with and they were paid off for slackness
of work. It was for their activities as
members of trade unions for which they
were dismissed. We have that now
amongst private employers, and now we
are going to have amongst municipal employers a different state of affairs to what
we have had previously. This Clause is
aiming at the municipal worker, to take
away any little liberty he has had in
regard to standing by his conditions of
employment and of declaring when he

not be. The real object of the Government is the deunionizing of the public
services. That is the real object. They

Here is a very important portion of the

A penalty is imposed by this Clause

We oppose it strenuously. This Clause
is aimed at trade unionists in public employment, and it penalizes them.
I want to give an illustration that I
refrained from giving on the last Amendment that was before the Committee. In
practice this Clause works out in this way.
If a local authority is building houses by
direct labour, and its employees cease
work without notice, those workers become criminals. But the same authority
may have a building scheme let out to a
contractor, and if his men cease work
without notice they are not exposed to the
penalties of this Clause. That is my interpretation of this Clause. Private employees may go on strike, although they
are employed on the same class of work as
those engaged in the direct labour scheme.
One is classed as a criminal; the other
fellow gets off scot-free.
There is no
liberty about that at all. Under this
Clause you are compelling the municipal
employee to accept conditions which he
knows perfectly well are unfair.
I always understood that the great
local authorities realized, if the Government did not, that trade unionism is an
asset to them instead of a hindrance.
Here is a quotation from the "Municipal
Journal and Public Works Engineer,"
issued on April 8, 1927. This represents
the opinion of all the municipal authorities in regard to trade unionism. This
journal says:-
Trade unionism is an advantage to
local authorities. Collective bargaining and negotiations with representatives more or less skilled in the management of those by whom they are.
elected save time and inconvenience.
No borough surveyor desires to haggle
with each employee about the rate of
wages. Large scale production and
broad administration require the trade
union as a factor in work.
I think that is recognized by all concerned, but if you are going to curtail

It
What I say is this, and I say it in the
presence of the Chief Whip (Captain
Dixon) that this is the most horrible
place to be found in all Europe, if not in
the world. Considering that we Ulster
people are the greatest people in the
world. and that this Parliament is supposed to be the greatest Parliament in
the world, really, if we have to sit here
for twelve hours, we ought to have some
place where we could go and have a cup
of tea, without having the memories of
it clinging round us like a nightmare for
weeks. I am not alone speaking for the
Members of Parliament. Take the Pressmen here. Look what these gentlemen
suffer. If it were not for the intellectual
delight of listening to the Opposition they
would all droop and die. Take the other
members of the Press and also take the
officials of this House. I understand
they have no means of getting refreshment at all.
For my part I detest talking about
these purely materialistic things in an ideal
Parliament of this character, but we have
to look at things in a spirit of commonsense. Is it fair? I know myself that
one Member of the Committee whom I saw
sitting here as one of the sentinels on the
watch tower of Parliamentarianism, went
out three times. (Laughter). No doubt
he has been here since ten o'clock-
(laughter) but before that this Gentleman went out and he came back bursting
with speech, and, but for the intervention
of the Leader of the Opposition, the Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie), and
myself, he would have made three
speeches. But he was not allowed to
make them. I say, therefore, that the
treatment of the officials, the treatment
of the Press, the treatment of the Members
of this House, and the whole arrangement
and organization of this place, is terrible.
I was going to say something else, but I
will satisfy myself with using the milder
word. This is a terrible place in which
to have to spend your time.

TEACHERS AND SCHOOL ATTEN-
DANCE WORK.
1. Mr. HEALY (for Mr. Donnelly)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education whether Clogher
(Co. Tyrone) Regional Committee requires all principal teachers in that area
to furnish each month lists of all pupils
absent on any day or days during the
previous month, giving in each case the
name, address, standard, age, and number of days absent; whether this Regional
Committee allows any remuneration to
teachers for this work, which was, until
recently, the duty of the school attendance
officer; whether any such payment would
be sanctioned by the Ministry of Education; and whether the Education Act
obliges teachers to furnish particulars of
attendances only in those cases in which a
prosecution has been decided upon.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb):
I regret
that I am unable at the moment to give
the hon. Member the information he
seeks. I am in communication with the
Clogher Regional Education Committee
on the subject of his inquiry, and if he
will repeat his question early next week
I hope to be in a position to give him a
reply..
NEW SCHOOL AT LISFEARTY.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Educa
tion whether his attention has been
drawn to a public meeting of ratepayers
held in Dungannon, on Tuesday last, to
protest against the expenditure of £2,500
in building a new school at Lisfearty;
and whether he would not consider instead the repair of the existing schools.
Mr. ROBB: I am aware of the holding
of the meeting of ratepayers referred to
by the hon. Member, and the Ministry
has received from a local solicitor, acting
on behalf of a number of ratepayers, an
objection to the proposal of the Education Authority to borrow £2,500 for the
purpose of erecting a new school at Lisfearty. In consequence of the objection
the Ministry will hold a public inquiry on
the subject of the raising of the loan.
Information before the Ministry, from
its inspectors, is to the effect that the
existing schoolhouses which it is intended
to supersede by the new building are so
old and unsuitable that their repair would
not meet satisfactorily the need for improved school accommodation in the district.
Mr. HEALY: Is the hon. Gentleman aware that the local public, who
ought to know the circumstances best,
think repairing the school should be sufficient, and that the hon. Gentleman
and his Department are engaged in a
policy of squandermania which is very
undesirable at this moment?
Mr. ROBB: Without admitting any of
the charges the hon. Member has made.
I may say the object of holding the local
inquiry is that those persons who object
to the scheme may put their objections
before the inspector.

INLAND REVENUE APPEALS.
4. Mr HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has been in communication with the Board of Inland
Revenue in the matter of appointing
local Commissioners to deal with appeals
and disputes.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer is in the negative.
The administration of the Income Tax
Acts is a Reserved Service, and interests
which desire to make representations concerning any matter arising out of those
Acts should communicate direct with the
Board of Inland Revenue. My Department has no control whatever over
such matters and cannot assume the role
of intermediary.

LICENSING PROSECUTIONS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
5. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of prosecutions instituted against licensed traders in Northern
Ireland for breaches of the Licensing Laws
for the twelve months ended 31st October,
1927; the number of convictions, and the
number of cases in which licences were
endorsed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number
of prosecutions instituted against licensed
traders for breaches of the Licensing Laws
for the year ended 31st October, 1927,

COST OF FIRST-CLASS ROADS.
7. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
be able to grant the County Councils of
Northern Ireland the full cost of reconstruction and maintenance of first-class
roads for the coming financial year.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It would not
be possible with the limited funds available to grant any further assistance from
the Road Fund to road authorities than
that already indicated in the recent
circular issued by the Ministry to the
various authorities in Northern Ireland.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I ask the
right hon. Gentleman is he aware that 75
per cent. of the cost of works on roads has
been granted to about 80 per cent. of the
Road Authorities in Scotland? Is he
further aware that the Trunk Roads in
Scotland are being reconstructed on a
100 per cent. grant to authorities, and
that in addition 33-1/3rd per cent. is
granted for 2nd class roads and 35 per
cent. for unclassified roads, and will he
consult with the Minister of Finance and
make such arrangements that the ratepayers of this area will receive equal
treatment with those in Scotland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not prepared to give a negative answer to the
supplementary question of my hon.
Friend, but I would tell him this, that
the Road Authorities are treated in a
very much more generous way in
Northern Ireland than they are in either
Scotland or England.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to
ask whether the allocation of £250,000 to
Carlisle Bridge is responsible for the depletion of the Road Fund?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.

I think that justifies us on this side,

of

1916 in South Wales. The South Wales

That action of the Government in taking

Attorney-General on a previous occasion
gave us an assurance that that was not
likely to take place so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned, but supposing the
funds of an organization are prevented
from being disbursed, and the Law
Courts later determine that a strike is
legal, then an obvious hardship and injustice would be inflicted upon the organization or upon the workers who could not
share in the strike fund to which they
had contributed.
We cannot lose sight of the fact that
the probability is that when a strike takes
place some of the employers are likely to
suggest to the Attorney-General and to
the Government that the strike is illegal,
and under those circumstances the Government might be inclined to give a great
deal of credence to the arguments put
forward by the employers. In that way
I can quite visualise that the workers
might not get the justice to which they
are entitled. Therefore, it seems to me
to be perfectly fair and reasonable to ask
that an Amendment of this kind should
be accepted, and that if an injunction is
going to be taken out it should be taken
at the instance of a member of the organization and nct left either for the Government or for the Attorney-General to
take it out. Neither should the
employers be allowed to prompt or
suggest to the Government when
injunction should be sought.
an
I have noticed in connection with the
working of the Act in Great Britain
that there is a very marked tendency on
the part of employers to take all disputes.
that have occurred in Great Britain
since the passing of the Act to the Law
Courts. I noticed quite recently in connection with the strike that took place
amongst the tailors in some parts of
England that it was the intention of the
employers to refer that case to the Law
Courts. That course was obviated because an arrangement was made in the
meantime and an amicable settlement
arrived at. There will be a tendency on
the part of employers when they are
being inconvenienced to do this. If the
community was being inconvenienced or
intimidated to a very slight degree there
would be a tendency on the part of the
Attorney-General or of the Government
to lend a very ready ear toany
representations that might come from
the employers on this point, and I
can see many injustices taking place and
great hardships being inflicted upon the
people who happen to be on strike.
Therefore, I respectfully suggest to the
Government that this matter should be
reconsidered, unless it is their intention
to try to outlaw the trade union organization altogether. If the Government
are not prepared to accept these eminently sane and reasonable Amendments
which have been put on the Paper by my
colleagues and myself then we are forced
to the conclusion that it is the intention
of the Government to ostracise and outlaw the trade union organization
altogether.

Mr. BEATTIE: I get up to support
the leaving out of a Clause of this kind.
Reading over the Clause, which is composed of eight and a half lines, I find out
that the sting of the Clause is in the tail.
In the last three lines of the Clause we
find the powers, and the persons to whom
those powers are going to be granted can
use them to great disadvantage as far as
the trades unions and their legitimate
rights are concerned. This Clause, in my
opinion, is very contentious. It is a deliberate attempt to tie up any funds that
a trade union may desire to use for the
establishment of their legitimate rightsthat their standard of life shall not be
reduced.
The Clause gives extensive powers to
those who are not members of trade
unions. I am sure there is no business
man or business concern would think it
just if a law allowed an outsider to come
in and take action to restrain him or it
from carrying out legitimate business.
This Clause introduces new principles into
trade unionism. It is a settled principle
of English law that only a person having
a proprietary interest in the funds-that
is a member of the society-can complain
to the courts against the wrongful use of
the funds. That principle is completely
overthrown by this Clause, because it
gives the right to people, other than members of a trade union, to take action to
tie up the funds which have been subscribed for a particular purpose.
Under Clause 7 a injunction may be

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This is
a very usual form of clause in dealing
with matters of this description. The
hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) who has just
moved this Amendment has pointed out
the difficulty that might arise if the individual who is named as having authority
to accept service on behalf of a trade
union happened to have left the country.
I think the Committee will see that in
reality there is no difficulty in that respect
because, if the address that is given for
service together with the name of the
person to whom service is to be addressed
are correct, that document will no doubt
be seen and opened by some other servant
of the trade union. On the other hand,
if service were to be confined to service
in person upon the named representative
of the trade union, if that named representative of the trade union, either accidently or on purpose, happened to be out
of the jurisdiction, it would be impossible
to effect service at all.
Therefore, it is necessary in cases of
this sort where the registered address of
the trade union is outside Northern
Ireland, that there should be some person
inside the jurisdiction to represent that
trade union for the purpose of serving
notices and other documents upon them.
The Committee will notice that it only
refers to those trades unions which are not
trades unions registered in Northern
Ireland. A trade union registered in
Northern Ireland, of course, has a
registered address at which it can be
served in the ordinary course, and it is
only to provide for those trades unions
which carry on their operations outside
Northern Ireland and have registered

Paragraph (a) itself is very contentious,

being taken by the workers if they think
them reasonable. As I have said, many
times in my own history lightning strikes
have taken place, and there is no law in
the land can prevent those strikes from
taking place in the future. It matters
not what Clauses of this nature the
Government pass, they will continue to
take place where you have big industries
such as shipbuilding or engineering.
Say a trade dispute takes place. According to the definition of the Attorney-

the Courts, when we have gentlemen adjudicating who do not understand the
economic conditions of the workers, who
do not understand the working of trade
unions, and who do not understand the
ways and means that the workers resort to
in order to establish their claims. I think
that those means are reasonable.
I am
afraid that the misinterpretations of the
word "reasonableness" in the future will
lead to serious conflicts with the workers
in the various industries in which they are
engaged. I do not think that any strike
will be legal in the future. That is my
own impression. The trade unions will
not know what position they occupy.

CLAUSE. (Circulation
-
of
"It is hereby declared unlawful for
any employer or association of employers to circulate a list of workers'
names with the object of influencing
and preventing other employers from
employing these workers. It is further
declared illegal for any employer to
dismiss other members of the family of
any person discharged without giving
satisfactory evidence of the unsuitability of the persons discharged. Any
employer found guilty of such practices
to be find £10 for a first offence, and
for a second offence three months without the option of a fine."
Brought up, and read a First time.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move, "That the
Clause be read a Second time."
purpose
of
This is a Clause for the
giving the same treatment to employers
as the Government are compelling the
work people to submit to. It is to prevent employers or associations of employers from circulating lists of workers
with the object of inducing other employers from giving employment to those
people. In other words, it is to prevent
the circulation of black lists, a practice
which is in operation in Northern Ireland. It goes further than that, it
attempts to put a stop to a very reprehensible practice in certain country districts of employers dismissing the
members of the family of a person who
has transgressed against the rules of the
firm, or who has done something that the
foreman considers worthy of dismissal.
Not only do some employers dismiss the
person who commits the offence, but they
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattle.
dismiss everybody connected with that
person, the boys and girls, and sometimes
the women-folk who are employed in the
same mill or factory.
I know that hon. Members opposite will
find it difficult to believe that this practice is carried on to any extent, but I
want to assure hon. Members opposite
that it is in existence to-day. It is not
six months since my attention, as a
trade union official, was drawn to the
case of a family who were dismissed from
the employment of a certain mill in Northern Ireland because the father had been
dismissed.
If
This Clause, therefore, makes an attempt, not only to prevent employers
from blacklisting workpeople but to prevent their dismissing other members of
the family of any person who is discharged, without giving satisfactory evidence of the unsuitability of the persons
discharged. It also proposes to put a
fine of £10 upon any employer who is
found guilty of any of these offences.
there is any fair-mindedness in the hon.
Members opposite, they will agree that
if it is good business to fine a trade union
£10 for breaking rules and regulations it
is equally good business to fine employers
who either blacklist workpeople or dismiss persons without just cause. I think
that if there are any fair-minded men
opposite, they will see the justice of this
Clause. It is just the same principle as
is embodied in Clause 3 of the Bill, where
it is declared unlawful for members of a
trade union "to attend at or near a house
or place where a person resides or works
or carries on business or happens to be."
In other words, it prevents employers
from picketing in their own particular
way, just as you have in Clause 3 prevented the workpeople from picketing.
Trade Disputes Bill-

29 NOVEMBER 1927
We are endeavouring to impress upon
the minds of the Committee the importance of preventing employers from doing
the same thing. I do not know whether
the hon. Members opposite will agree that
this is a practice that should be stopped
--the circulation amongst other firms of
black lists of people who have been employed in a firm, to the end that the other
employers shall not give employment to
those people because they are notorious
trade unionists or take a line of action in
the firm that the management do not
agree with. This has been done, not only
in the country districts but in the city of
Belfast. If it is a good thing to prevent
workpeople from picketing, it is surely
equally good to restrain employers from
circulating black lists. If it is a good
thing to fine workpeople for any offence
that they may commit under Clause 3,
it is equally good to fine employers for the
same thing. If it is a good thing to imprison a workman for three months because he breaks this law, it is equally
good, it is equally fair, it is equally
reasonable to ask the Government to
agree to the principle contained in this
Clause, and to penalize the employers in
the same way. I beg to move.

Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Bill.
Considered in Committee (Sixth Day).
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
NEW CLAUSE (Breach of contract
by local authorities).
If any public authority or employer
break their contract with any employee,
knowing or having reasonable cause to
believe that the consequence of this
action will be to cause injury, danger,
or grave inconvenience to the employee
or employees concerned, the employer
so acting, or the chairman or mayor of
the public authority, shall be liable,
on summary conviction, to a fine not
exceeding ten pounds, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three
months.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I beg
to move, That the Clause be read a
Second time." For the information of
the Committee it is desirable that I should
read the Clause before proceeding to
speak to it. The Clause is as follows:
McMullan, Thomas Wallace
Miller, William Thomas
Morrison, Hugh Smith
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Shillington, Major David Graham
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Captain Dixon.
If any public authority or employer
break their contract with any employee,
knowing or having reasonable cause to
believe that the consequence of this
action will be to cause injury, danger,
or grave inconvenience to the employee
or employees concerned, the employer
so acting, or the chairman or mayor of
the public authority, shall be liable, on
summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding ten pounds, or to imprisonment
for a term not exceeding three months.
We have found it necessary to move
this new Clause owing to the fact that
the Government's legislation is hopelessly
lop-sided and one sided. If there had
been any attempt on the part of the
Government to deal in a fair or impartial
manner it would not have been necessary
to have introduced a new Clause of this
kind. However, owing to their biased
and partial attitude, it is incumbent upon
myself and others to move this Clause. I
think the logic of this Clause will be absolutely irresistible, and I cannot see how
the Government can refuse to accept it.
I take it the Government have not shown
their hand or declared their intentions as
far as this new Clause is concerned. It
might shorten our proceedings a great
deal if the Government were prepared to
accept this new Clause. I do not know
whether any of the Government representatives would be prepared to give an
undertaking now as to whether they would
accept it or not. It would appear to me
to be perfectly fair and reasonable, when
an attempt is made to penalize the employees of a municipal body, that a similar penalty should be attached to the
municipal body itself in the event of its
breaking its contract.
The Bill puts the employee of a public
authority in a very unenviable position,
because up to the moment it has been
Trade Disputes Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. W. McMullen]
possible for an employee of a public
authority to terminate his employment
without any reason almost at a moment's
notice. Though it has been possible to
do that I do not think that has been the
practice because the employees of a public
authority are perfectly reasonable, individually and collectively. From my
knowledge of the city of Belfast and the
scanty knowledge I have of undertakings
in different parts of Northern Ireland, I
scarcely think a case can be cited where
the employees of these municipal bodies
have attempted to act in an unconstitutional manner. That being so I am at a
loss to understand why a Clause of the
character of that contained in the Bill
should be put into the Bill, because, as I
have pointed out, these people have acted
in a perfectly reasonable and legitimate
way in any dispute they have had.
When an attempt is being made to
penalize the employees we think it only
fair and reasonable that we should ask
the Government also to penalize the
municipal bodies in the event of their
breaking their contracts with the men.
I attempted to show when we were discussing this matter previously that you
can never tell what thought or idea
might guide the majority in reactionary
assemblies. I should not be surprised if
on some occasion that hopelessly reactionary body which the hon. Member
for Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) does not like
should decide substantially to reduce the
wages of their employees without giving
anything like a week's notice. We have
got to legislate for contingencies that
might arise, and that body might decide
on some occasion to terminate the existing agreement and very drastically to
reduce the wages of their employees, or
alternatively to increase their hours inordinately. If either of these two things
was done without the necessary notice
being given, is it not fair that the public
body should be penalized if the men are
going to be prevented from indulging in
lightning strikes or if they are not going
to be permitted to withdraw their services
without giving at least a week's notice?
Is it not only fair and reasonable that the
same conditions should attach to the
municipal body? I believe the fairness.
of it is absolutely irresistible and I cannot see any reason why the Government
should not accept it. In view of the
alterations that took place in this Bill
when its defects were pointed out it
was made clear on the other side that the
Government were legislating to deal with
a general strike and were making no attempt to deal with a general lock-out.

possibly refuse to accept this most emiuently reasonable Clause. I observe the

(Mr. Elliott) has come somewhat nearer,
and that to me indicates he perceives the
reasonableness of my argument.

Mr. HEALY: I have taken almost no
part in the discussion on this Trade Disputes Bill up to now. What has been
occurring to me as the debate has been
going along, particularly on this new
Clause, has been the utter want of sympathy on the Government benches with
the trade union point of view. I think
it is absolutely deplorable because the
trade union representatives stand for the
workers in a particular way that Members
on the Government benches do not pretend to. Amendment after amendment
has been proposed in this Committee only
to be turned down. Do the Government
really think that Members on this side
of the Committee do not represent any
public opinion outside? I do not think
there has been a single comma altered in
any of the sections or sub-sections as a
result of the representations put forward
by this side from the beginning of these
discussions up to this very hour.
It seems to me that what is sauce for
the goose is sauce for the gander, and if
it be an offence for an employee to do
something it should also be an offence for
an employer. In the Six Counties I am
perfectly satisfied a majority of the public
boards will not represent democratic
opinion, and, therefore, this Clause is
all the more necessary as regards the
rights of the workers. I have in mind a
particular urban council in the Six
Counties who changed their whole employees as a result of a strike. Men who
had served that particular municipality
for twenty or thirty years were thrown
out into the streets, and obliged to seek
their living otherwise at a time when
they could not find suitable employment.
If the Government would accept this
Clause they would prevent an occurrence
of that kind. It is deplorable to find
men in the position of municipal employees, who, after long experience, have
become specialists in a particular class of
work, thrown out of their employment in
their old age when no other employment
offers, just because of some dispute in
which they had been engaged, and as to
the origin of which, very often, they
have practically no responsibility. Even
though I were satisfied that a particular
urban council or corporation were more
representative of the workers than they
are to-day I should still be of opinion that
a Clause of this kind was necessary The
whole tendency of this unwanted Bill is
to penalize the workers and to put them
in an unfair position. If by accepting
this particular Clause you will be doing
nothing more than placing the worker in
the same position as his employer I hope
the Government will see their way, par
ticularly at this late hour, to do the decent
thing towards the men and accept this
Clause.

This Bill was conceived in England and
here in the interests of the employing
class. I am not an enemy of the employing class. They occupy a rightful
position in the life of the community,

They are entitled, in the ordinary adjustment of our public affairs, to equality

proposed.

NEW CLAUSE.-(Restraint of application of funds of employers in contravention of S.1 of the Act.)
Without prejudice to the right of any
person having a sufficient interest in the
relief sought to sue or apply for an injunction to restrain any application of the
funds of any employers association in
contravention of the provisions of this
Act, an injunction restraining any application of the funds of any employers
association in contravention of the provisions of section one of this Act may be
granted at the suit or upon the application of the Attorney-General for Northern Ireland.
Brought up and read a first time.

A trade union holds a meeting of its members and decides on pursuing a certain attitude, call it politics if
you like, by which they will secure Parliamentary representation. It is a very
legitimate thing in my judgment for a
trade union to want Parliamentary representation. It is the only way in
which their ideals can be fashioned into
material operation through an Act of
Parliament, and the only way in which
they can do the work for which a trade
union exists outside the purely benevolent
aspect of their work is in Parliament.
Supposing they determined in their judg
ment to contest a Parliamentary seat,
that is a purpose for which these political
funds are used. They hold a meeting and
decide upon a certain course. After this
course is adopted, probably unanimously,
by all the members who have been notified
that this question would be brought before
the trade union, they are compelled
to go to the expense of machinery to ask
their members to contract in. I cannot
see any defence of that attitude. I can
see the force of contracting out if a decision has been come to that I do not
agree with.
Supposing I am a Tory
trade unionist, or a member of the association that has been so much discussed,

Since 1919 no fewer than eleven Bills
have been introduced into the House of
Commons by Tories anxious to reform
the unions. In 1920 we had two Bills
introduced for reform when we had the
Trade Union Ballot Bill and the Trade
Union Emancipation Bill. In 1921 we
had the Trade Union Act amended, and
in 1922 we had another Amendment to
the 1913 Trade Union Act. Then we
had also another Act in 1924-an
Amendment Act-and in 1925 we had
the Trade Unions Political Fund Bill.
You can see from the number of Bills
the activities of the governing classes of
the time, and how anxious they were to
place Bills on the Statute to guard the
interests of the poor trade unionists.
The Title of this Bill conveys the idea
that those Tories above all things are
anxious to assist the poor, down-trodden
trades unionists. They have shown their
anxiety by placing on the Statute Book
the number of Bills which I have
quoted. The last of those Bills is now
before the House, and on behalf of the
Opposition I am moving the rejection of
it. While we have these benevolent

why this Bill has been introduced.
would say deliberately that the Bill nas

I can safely say, from the point of view

simply at the dictation of their masters
on the other side of the Channel, and
the alleged general strike on the other
side of the Channel has been the surface

the surface excuse for the introduction

position in Northern Ireland for the past
number of years has been one of settled
policy, so far as the settling of disputes
is concerned. I cannot remember one
case of where anything in the nature of
a general strike ever took place, with one
exception. That one exception was in
the year 1912 when on the 28th September, at the dictation of an English Lord,
the whole of the industrial concerns of
Northern Ireland downed tools for that
day and solemnly declared that they
would not have Home Rule. But we
have Home Rule to-day, and the No
Home Rulers of that time are the
strongest Home Rulers of to-day.

I have several of the other influences
that were at work before the introduction of this Bill which I would like to
quote. As I have said, the surface excuse was the alleged general strike, but
the real influence behind it has been the
magnates of the classes which I have already stated. In June, 1926, the
Central Journal of the National Union
of Conservative and Unionist Associations was vigorously demanding the
repeal of the Trade Disputes Act of
1906. In July, 1926, it was the turn of
the National Union of Manufacturers,
who wanted to cut down the right of
picketing, to make the unions liable for
damages and to hamper the operation of
the political levy. In October of the
same year we have the National Conference of the Conservatives at Scarborough
demanding secret ballots before strikes,
the abolition of massed picketing, the
abolition of the picketing of houses and
the compulsory auditing of trade union.
funds.

In the same year-in Novemberdeclaration on the same lines came
from their Grand Council of the Primrose League. Last, but not least, in
November of the same year, a special
meeting of the Association of British
Chambers of Commerce reported in
favour of the compulsory regulation of
trade unions, the separation of benefit
from strike funds, the liability of unions
for damages, contracting in to the
political levy instead of contracting out,
and the abolition of the right to picket
at houses. In the same month, in the
same year-1926-the Scottish Unionist
Association passed a resolution demanding a change in trade union law. Then
we had one of our widely circulated daily
papers-the "Daily Mail"-coming out
in December screaming for a law to declare general strikes illegal. In the same
Trade Disputes Bill-

month Colonel Allbrook, M.P., presented
a petition in the House of Commons
claiming to have 10,000 signatures from
43 branches of the National Citizens'

We had in this present year-in
January--the other great influence of the
Conservative ranks, and one that Mr.
Baldwin finds it very difficult to keep
quiet. They came out in January, 1927,
and they dictated to the Government that
a Bill should be introduced immediately
declaring strikes in transport and
sanitary services impossible, prohibiting
strikes in cases where the dispute was referred to an industrial court until the
report of the court was issued, endorsing
a ballot before all strikes, and substituting contracting in to the political levy for
contracting out, prohibiting mass pickets
and picketing at houses, and making
unions liable for damages.
The Engineering and Allied Employers
having got such a magnificent lead from
these other associations from June, 1926,
until January, 1927, came out in
February, 1927, and declared to the
Government what their opinion was in regard to the present position of the unions
of the country. The Engineering and
Allied Employers, thinking the pressure
was not strong enough, declared in favour
of making the unions liable for damages,
making breach of contract actionable,
substituting contracting in to the political
levy for contracting out, enforcing the
separation of benefit from strike funds,
and prohibiting mass picketing and
picketing at houses.
That is the real position. That is why
the Bill was introduced in Great Britain.
The alleged general strike was only a sort
of an
excuse for the introduction of a
Bill of this kind. The reactionary crowd
of the Tories for a number of years past
have been crying out about the liberties
of the trade unionists in Great Britain
and Ireland. Although the Tories were
opposed to the Act of 1906 they could not
object to it, because the electorate was
sufficiently intelligent to know not to
tolerate the laws that existed prior to
that date. The Government were therefore compelled to place the 1906 Bill on
the Statute Book.

Mr. BEATTIE: These are the forces
which are always up against the trade
unions in their attempts to raise the
standard of living of the workers, and the
forces that are up against the Labour
movement politically. No wonder the
Bill is one-sided. So far from the unions
having a privileged position, the entire
history of the laws affecting trade unions
is a record of bias and prejudice in favour
of the employers against the workers.
In view of the ferocious proposals of
the Bill, and the well-known anti-Labour
bias of the courts, we may easily find ourselves in a few years in the same position
as the workers occupied in the beginning
of the nineteenth century. The workers
at that period occupied a position that no
one in our day and generation would desire to see restored. This Bill, when it
becomes operative, is going to apply in
the same way, and in the same manner,
and we will be in the same position as the
people of the nineteenth century, when
laws were unknown so far as liberties for
trade unions were concerned.
In 1812 there were 40,000 Scottish
cotton weavers on strike because the employers refused to accept a table of piecework rates declared by the magistrates to
be reasonable, and obtained by the
parties at the cost of £3,000. The word
"reasonable" is very extensively used in
this Bill. As I said in Committee, what
may be reasonable to me may not be
reasonable to the Attorney-General or to
the courts deciding whether a strike is
legal or illegal. In the case of the
40,000 Scottish weavers, the law of the
time was brought into operation against
them, and the whole of the members of
the Strike Committee were arrested by
the police. Five of the leaders were
sentenced to periods of imprisonment
varying from four to eighteen months.
I am sure there is no one in this House
or outside of it who would desire to see a
return to the condition of affairs, in
which 40,000 people declared a strike in
order to raise their standard of living,
and because of that strike the committee
who had been conducting it were imprisoned. This Bill, in my humble
opinion, is going to restore those conditions in the near future, so far as the
right to strike is concerned.

concerned in regard to the settlement of

The whole Bill is guided by judges and
magistrates. The Bill is framed for the
purpose of putting us once more under
the heel of the law. It is taking away
all the liberties that we have won, and we
are going to be subject to the definitions.
of judges, and in some cases of magistrates, who are ignorant of trade
unionism. Under Section 1 the court
has to say if a strike has any object other
than the furtherance of a trade dispute.
They are to define the trade or industry.
They are to say whether a strike is likely
to coerce the Government or intimidate
the community. They are to say what is
a substantial portion of the community.
All these baffling points may be decided

we have Section 3 of the Bill where magistrates will have to say whether a blackleg

the word itself throughout the whole Bill

amending Bill to the present Bill. We
may find that the legitimate activities of

From that point of view this Bill is not
required. Another thing the Bill may
do is that it may very effectively put out
of operation strikes of a legal kind, also
strikes of a sympathetic nature that have
not for their object any intimidation of
the Government or coercion of anybody
other than the employer. The strike is

The other portions of the Bill make one
believe that the unions in future are going
to be strangled by the law, We are
going to have the iron hand brought down
upon us and its grip is going to be felt
before anything of an illegal nature is
committed. When you are going to bring
about that position of affairs I think the
Government is in the position of intimidators, because they are going to intimidate the trade unions, who will not
be able to strike only in the way set apart
by the Government, otherwise they will
be made the guests of His Majesty for a
period of months and perhaps years.
The Bill also makes one feel that no
union will know how it stands.
No worker will know how he stands. They will
not know whether a strike or a contribution to a strike fund or a peaceful conversation with a blackleg is going to land
them in jail as a criminal, and fear of
this may prevent persons from striking,
although, later on, that strike may be
declared legal when it is all over. The
fear of this Bill itself may be such intimidation to timid trade unionists as to
prevent them coming out for legitimate
purposes and taking their stand on the
side of a legitimate cause. The Bill
will thus keep them at work scabbing on
their fellow-workers.
•
Another thing is that the law as it is
is now being brought into operation in
Great Britain is not a new law by any
means. It is new in the British Isles, but
its origin is outside Great Britain. It is
the copyright of the employing class in
another country-a country that has the
greatest number of millionaires in the
world. I find that this law has been
operating in America for a number of
years, and they have been operating it so
successfully that it is nearly impossible
for one trade unionist to consult with
another whether they should do this or do
that so far as organization is concerned.
I have a list of instances of where the
law is in operation, and how it is applied,
but I might be boring the House if I
quoted how they have really put trade
unionists out of being. I will just give
two or three illustrations to show you what
we are likely to have in future in Northern Ireland if this Bill becomes law. It
may convert some of the Government followers, who are sympathetic, and inclined
to reject this Bill only they have to do
the bidding of the political whip.
In America we find that the employees
of the telegraph companies were prevented
from refusing to work with non-unionists.
No man or trade union that is working
in a trade or industry and fighting to get
the standard of life in that trade kept
to the level of the cost of living desires a
man to be allowed to work at his calling
who refuses to contribute to the upkeep
of the union that has kept the standard
at the level it is. But we are going to
have that by the introduction of this
Bill. We had waitresses who struck in
America and these waitresses were forbidden to picket outside the restaurant by
a law similar to this. Peaceful picketing
has been conducted in Northern Ireland
on many occasions, and I cannot see that
peaceful picketing has ever been turned
into anything other than the term implies.
But we are to have that right taken away,
and we are going to be subject to the law
if we go near a place of business or in any
way interfere for the purpose of showing
our dissent from the position taken up by
the blackleg. I think that is rather farfetched. We have had many liberties in
the past, and I feel that this Bill is aimed
at taking them away, and taking away
the position of the worker as it was during
my term as a trade union official.
Now, in 1906, in announcing that the
Conservatives were not going to oppose
the Trades' Disputes Bill, which is the
Bill that this Bill is going to whittle
away, Lord Lonsdale said they objected
to it, but there was no doubt about the
feeling of the electorate and he thought
the House would have to pass it. That
is taken from the British Hansard,
December 4th, 1906. Now, the feelings
of the electorate on this Government's
Bill are equally clear, because, as I said
before, the Government have no mandate
for this Bill. They have received no
authority from the electors to make these
drastic alterations in the trade union law
that are inspired by inveterate hostility to the working classes. Speaking in
the House of Commons on March 6th,
1925, on the latest of several Bills for reforming trade unions, that is, Trade
Union Political Fund Bill, the Prime
Minister said: "We find ourselves after
two years in Parliament in possession of,
perhaps, the greatest majority we ever
had. How did we get there. It was
not by promising to bring this Bill in."
Of course the Prime Minister is a wise
man so far as this Bill is concerned, because the Prime Minister never wanted to

I will have of passing my comments on the

would ask the Government-even at this

classes if they have nothing else but contempt for the Government. I want to
assure the Government that I am not now
an active trade union official, but I am a
member of a trade union; I take a deep

offering the advice and counsel which I

should not be worsened.
I will now take my seat. I am as

that things will arise out of this Bill

there will be the question of repealing the

English Bill is inserted in this one with

unions will have to name a person who

If the Labour party get into office in
Great Britain at the next general election,

out the policy step by step irrespective
of what class of Government operates in
England. Custom, I believe, can be
made a law. Judges have often decided
on what has been a custom. I believe
that you will be compelled by custom to
follow the step-by-step policy
policy and
repeal this Act. I satisfy myself by

The Clause itself does not prevent the

from attending at a man's house and endeavouring peacefully to persuade him as
to the proper course to take in any trade
dispute, but the Clause in this Bill is
an endeavour to prevent the law from
being overstepped, and to prevent what

Members opposite who are Members of
the legal profession know perfectly well
that in our courts no injunction is ever
granted except upon proper evidence,
either upon affidavit or orally, and that
no judge ever grants an injunction upon
the ex-parte statement of one side without having given the other party to the
application, or the defendant, ample
opportunity to be heard. It is one of
the fundamental rules of our jurisprudence that no man shall be condemned without being heard, and if for
a moment a judge was to be led away by
any statements that were made either by
the Attorney-General or by any other
applicant into departing from that strict
rule of law it would not be very long before the decision was reversed.

Northern Ireland and to the workers of

people wanted it I was prepared to accept

allowed England to take away from you

Excise, the power to impose taxes and
