you that power, and I do not blame you
for not having it. She gave you the
power to legislate in your own domestic
affairs and your right to fashion out your
own life and conditions as they suit the
desires and needs of the people of
Northern Ireland, but you do not do
it. You go across to London to your
masters for direction and you come over
here. The masters' voice is sounded to
the Opposition, because the rest go into
the smoke-room to hear what the masters'
voice is.
I protest against this, and that is why
I am opposed to the Third Reading of
this Bill. Finally, in order to get this
Measure through this Parliament you
have made a departure, namely, you have
introduced a new method of all-night
sittings and have prolonged Sessions.
You compel Members to come here at the
greatest inconvenience and at hours
which are not suitable for lucid thought
and still less lucid expression. You have
upset the whole convenience of our former
Parliamentary arrangements, and to do
what? Was it to deal with the question
of unemployment? No, that was a pressing question. Was it to deal with the
condition of our gradually decreasing industries? No, that would have called
forth all that was best in sound statesmanship. Was it to deal with the question of poverty that is widespread, the
tragedy of which is constantly ringing in
our ears? No, nothing of the sort. It
was to pass this wretched Measure that
can never possibly be of any use, because
I do not believe that this Bill can even be
effectively put into operation. That part
of the first Clause which deals with
general strikes will never be put into
operation because I do not believe there
will be a general strike. That part that
strives to cripple the trade unions will not
do so, because conduct of this sort does
not cripple organizations made up of men.
It vitalizes them just as coercion over
fifty years ago in Ireland gave strength
and passion to the people's movement for
reform. So with these things here.
Measures of this character which are introduced here can only be effective in
irritating the working classes and cannot
possibly carry out any purpose, even your
purpose, even the purpose you have in
view. Now that is my protest against
this Bill. It has been wasted effort.
has been an indefensible transaction.
has occupied uselessly our time. I would
advise you to get to real business as soon
as possible.

The MINISTER OF
(Mr. Barbour): I think the explanation
I am able to give will meet quite satisfactorily what has been said by the hon.
Member, the leader of the Opposition.
In the first place, I would like to clear
away any impression that we are giving
away any money under this Bill. The
money is advanced in a debenture by
means of which we are secured by a
charge on the undertaking. I am sure
hon. Members have often heard the criticism that is levelled against public authorities that they do not look forward into
the future, and how it often happens, for
instance, in the case of a new road being
laid down that when it is completed it is
almost immediately opened for the purpose of laying down sewer pipes or gas
pipes or for providing other public
facilities which the ordinary man thinks
3789 Lisburn Electric Supply Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Mr. Barbour]
might have been foreseen and provided for
before the road was laid down. We have
tried to provide for the future in this present Bill.
The Lisburn Electric Supply Company
entered into an arrangement with the
urban authority of Lisburn, by which
provision was made for a supply of
electricity, the area of supply being
limited to the urban area of Lisburn.
After canvassing likely users of current
in that area it was thought that the provision of 1,000 kilowatts would probably
meet the requirements for some time to
come. When the matter was brought before the Ministry of Commerce we hoped
that with the development in the use of
electricity that supply of current would be
taken up in the comparatively near
future. We had before us the recommendation of the Development Commissioners,
who stated that the most probable area of
development would be the valley leading
from Belfast in the direction of Portadown, where we have the important town
of Lurgan, and to a lesser degree Waringstown and Moira in that direction.
The Ministry of Commerce thought it
would be well while the poles and wires
were being erected to make them capable
of transmitting a much larger voltage and
a larger load than that which would be
sufficient for the Lisburn area. Between
Belfast and Lisburn there is an area of
distribution of electricity, namely, Dunmurry, which is working with an inadequate plant which is loaded up to its maximum, and it is hoped the supply from the
Belfast Corporation may be made available for Dunmurry should they wish to
take advantage of it once the transmission line is provided. So far as this company is concerned, it has been registered
with a merely nominal capital of £100,
and the directors, as hon. Members will
see in the Schedule, consist of local people
with the exception of one name, namely,
that of Mr. Salmon, who comes from
England.
I understand it is the intention of the
company, as soon as this Bill passes, to
go ahead with the raising of the extra
capital that will be required, and which,
1 believe, will amount to a sum of round
about £30,000. I am sure every opportunity will be afforded to any member
of the public who desires to subscribe to
the capital of the undertaking. I think
that the interests of the general public are
amply provided for in the Schedule and
the Clauses which enable the Ministry of
Commerce to take over the undertaking
at any time on giving six months' notice.

fact that they are all anxious to hear

men it is a non-contentious Measure.
feel certain, after I have submitted the

Mr. BEATTIE: Question.
Mr. GORDON: Let me say, that since
the administration of old-age pensions at
70 years was taken over by this Government the investigation of claims to pensions were made on an agency basis; that
is, they were made by Customs and Excise

regulation-making authority and the appeals tribunal. Now we propose to put
it on a proper basis, and the scheme, in

pensions are first of all to be investigated
by pensions officers, who will be appointed

That has been brought into operation for

I am
rather inclined to think that a magistrate

that take place?

POLLOCK: When I took up
office I found the Imperial Government
worked the old-age pensions scheme
through the machinery of the Customs
and Excise. From that there developed
the present method. I began to exercise
a scrutiny into the whole subject very
shortly after I became Minister of
Finance, because I was under the impression that it was very expensively administered. Hon. Members will realise that it
was my duty to see that economy was
exercised in the working of all the Departments. The Customs and Excise Departments was no doubt a very admirable
system for the work, but it was a very
expensive system. It was expensive in
this respect that the men are all highly
trained technical men and were paid
proportionately. Men with such high
technical qualifications were not required
for a scheme such as the old-age pensions.
Therefore I was desirous of effecting some
change, but the weight of business that
devolved upon me and my Department
in establishing a new federal system and
in carrying out the financial arrangements, very involved and very complex,
rather overshadowed this work, and consequently it was allowed to remain over
until quite recently.
The hon. Member for Derry (Mr.
Leeke) asked me very pointedly in regard
to the relative cost of the old system as
compared with the new. It is not easy,
I admit, to be meticulously accurate as to
what the new system under the Bill will
cost, but we can tell it very approximately.
If hon. Members will consult the Estim
ates they will see under the head of the
Ministry of Home Affairs that the Customs and Excise Department, which we
continued to employ, because, as I said.
it had been in existence, cost a sum of
£45,000, becoming slightly lower in the
present year. But the cost of the Customs
and Excise and the machinery which
existed in the Ministry of Home Affairs,
roughly a total of £40,000, I considered
was a very expensive method of carrying
out the old-age pensions scheme. Besides

I am sure the passengers were highly entertained. I am sorry that both my hon.
Friends adopt a flippant tone in regard to
these bus prosecutions. I think this is a
most serious matter for the welfare of the
community as a whole. I would have
thought that hon. Members, who profess
to represent the democracy, would have
tried to ensure that the steps taken by the
Government to protect life in Northern
Ireland would be supported.
To show the seriousness of the whole
situation, may I point out that between
January and October there were no fewer
than 1,198 accidents, involving injuries to
1,293 persons, while 75 persons were
killed. It is all very well for hon. Members to get up here and talk-
Mr. DEVLIN: We want all the facts.

you all the facts.

Gentleman must really be allowed to make

What were the offences for which these
men were prosecuted? I think one of the
friends of the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) was prosecuted for
permitting overcrowding in a vehicle. Can
anybody imagine a more serious offence
than overcrowding a bus? I myself have
seen a bus on fire, with the passengers
scrambling out to save their lives, and
any of the hon. Gentlemen opposite who
have seen anything like that would agree
with me that one of the worst offences
that could be committed by a bus conductor would be overcrowding. That law
was brought in with the consent of this
House. It was brought in not for the
purpose of paralysing the development of
the bus industry, but for the protection
of the ordinary man in the street, not the
individual who can afford his own car, but
the ordinary man who uses the bus.
Speeding is another offence, which the
hon. Member for East Belfast referred to.
One has only to take the
up newspapers
in the morning to see the number of accidents that take place. I know that my
hon. Friend, the Member for East
Belfast is a motorist himself.
He is one
of the most careful drivers that one could
imagine, and I do not believe that he
countenances vehicles driving through
crowded throughfares at 28, 30, 40, and
even 50 miles an hour. The speed limit
was fixed at 20 miles an hour, and I would
remind the House that the speed limit in
England is only 12 miles. The speed
limit of 20 miles was fixed after consultation with the bus owners.
What do we
find? Deliberate attempts to break the
law. Not only is the law broken, but the
individuals who break the law turn round
and say "We will not pay." Does the
hon. Member suggest that the Government
should simply lie down and refuse to administer the law? The whole thing is
perfectly ridiculous. Up to the present
time I have not heard a single argument
put forward that would justify the Government in altering the law in regard to
these buses.

Mr. BEATTIE: What is the smallest
amount that would be taken weekly when

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government have no desire to act harshly. I
am perfectly well aware of cases where
the bus drivers were induced by the
owners to break the law, and in those
cases the Government have prosecuted the
bus owners. But that is not the point in
this case. In any case where it is suggested that a man who has been fined is
not in a position to pay, but is willing to
pay, the Government are perfectly willing to allow the amount to be paid by instalments. If my hon. Friend will bring
any case of hardship to my notice, I will
look into it. I think, however, he
will agree with me that when the
penalty is one of £1, when a period of six
weeks is allowed to elapse, and on top of
that there is a deliberate refusal to pay,
the Government have no option but to
take action.

11. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
representations with regard to the establishment of a home for inebriates in
Northern Ireland; whether it is the fact
that prior to the passing of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, there was a
home for inebriates for the whole country;
whether this home is still available, and,
if not, whether he would consider the
advisability of establishing such a home
for Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No general
representations have been made to me in
this matter, but I have received a communication from one gentleman on the
subject.
It is a fact that there was formerly a
State Inebriate Reformatory at Ennis for
the reception of inebriates from Ireland
generally. That institution was closed in
1921 owing to the lack of inmates, and it
is apparent that this method of dealing
with inebriates has not met with any real
measure of success in Ireland.
In these circumstances, the Government
would not be justified in considering the
establishment of a similar institution for
Northern Ireland alone.

The primary object, therefore, of the
present Measure is to bring within the
compass of one Bill the various statutory
provisions relating to quarries. Certain
Amendments of the law which experience
has shown to be desirable are also incorporated, the general principle aimed at
being to provide reasonable protection
for the workers engaged in the quarrying
industry, and at the same time to impose
the minimum burden on owners and
occupiers of quarries.
I have already alluded to difficulties
which arise through the fact that
different provisions apply to quarries
according as they are less than, or exceed,
20 feet in depth and according as they
have mechanical power installed or otherwise. The consequence of this is that
there is a dual code and a divided jurisdiction, the factory inspectors receiving
their powers by virtue of the provisions
of the Factory and Workshop Acts, and
the Inspector of Mines and Quarries
having powers under the Quarries Acts.
As a result of the present Measure all
these powers will, it is proposed, reside
in my Ministry, whose inspector will
undertake the duties hitherto imposed by
the various Statutes I have mentioned.
Workmen's Compensation Bill 3868
Quarries Bill
1 DECEMBER 1927
On this point of inspection I should.
like to draw the attention of hon. Members to Clause 13 which provides for the
appointment of Inspectors of Quarries.
This Clause is 8 re-enactment, with
adaptations, of Section 15 of the
Metalliferous Mines (Regulation) Act,
1872.
In order to allay any fears that
hon. Members may have as to appointments of numerous inspectors, I should
like to explain at this stage that the work
of quarry inspection is now undertaken
by a part-time officer of my Ministry.
Furthermore there is no intention of
appointing additional inspectors as a
result of the present Measure.
I should just like to add that the
principal Amendments of the law which
have been incorporated in the Bill now
before the House may be summarized as
follows: .--
(a) The definition of "quarries" to
which the code is made applicable is
altered so as to include all quarries.
(b) A definition of the term
"occupier" has been introduced so as
to attach responsibility to persons
working the quarries who hitherto
could not definitely be held accountable.
This change experience has shown to
be necessary.
(c) Certain further provisions have
been introduced for safeguarding the
use of steam boilers and machinery.
(d) As I have already indicated
there have now been incorporated as a
Schedule to the Bill the rules of general
application to quarries. The object in
so doing is to enable those interested in
quarry administration to have readily
available all Statutory Regulations
governing such matters.
I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I am glad that this Bill
is now getting a Second Reading. I am
glad also that the Government are apparently paying some attention to the protests that have been made from the
Opposition benches against legislation by
reference. I think that this Bill is a very
good example for the Government to set
themselves in future as regards consolidating the law relating to the various
matters they have administration over. I
am particularly pleased that the Government have taken some cognisance of the
criticisms from these Benches as to legislation by reference, and are consolidating
the law relating to quarries. I have carefully examined the Clauses in this Bill
and so far as the Opposition is concerned
we welcome a Measure of this character.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). In consolidating the law it makes it practicable
for quarry owners and workers' officials
to know their position without having to
go to numerous Acts of Parliament to find
out the position.

The first three Amendments relate to
Clause 1, Sub-clause 3. The effect of
these Amendments is this-that the provision as to the minimum penalty will only
apply to persons who are convicted of
having sold or offered for sale milk described as Grades A or tuberculin tested,
and who have not a licence from the
Ministry of Home Affairs. Under the
Clause as it originally stood, any dealer
who was guilty of a technical offence
would be liable to the minimum penalty,
and the effect of these Amendments is to
ensure that the only person liable to the
minimum penalty will be one who deliberately commits an offence.

remember very well that, when this Bill

grounds I wish to say that I am glad the

SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to answer this question.
There are 15 female nurses employed in
Male Wards at Belfast Mental Hospital,
Purdysburn, at the present time.
Female nurses are only employed to
look after certain categories of male
patients who have been selected by the
medical staff of the Institution as suitable for supervision by female nurses.
Before taking up duty with male
patients nurses must have acquired experience in the female department.
I should mention that in addition to
the female nurses referred to, there are
male nurses on duty in each of the Male
Villas and in the Male Hospital.
The system has been in operation for
a number of years and has been found
extremely satisfactory both at Purdysburn and in Institutions in England and
Scotland, and I am glad to be able to
tell my hon. Friend that in regard to the
last part of his question, no such cases as
those indicated by him have occurred.

CLAUSE 2.-(Functions of pension
officers, local pension courts and umpire).
(1) Every pension officer shall take
into consideration any claim or question
submitted for his determination under
the provisions of this Act, and shall
give a decision thereon within the
prescribed time after the date on which
the claim or question was so submitted.
(2) In any case where a claim for
pension is refused, or the rate of a
pension is reduced, or the payment of
a pension is discontinued, the person
claiming the pension or in respect of
whose pension the decision is given, as
the case may be, may, within such time
and in such manner as may be pre-

Miller, William Thomas

Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham

Mr. Beattle.
scribed, require the pension officer to
refer the matter to a local pension
court constituted as hereinafter provided, and the local pension court
after considering the circumstance, shall
make to the pension officer such recommendations on the case as they may
think proper, and the pension officer
shall, unless he disagrees, give a decision in accordance with these recommendations.


(3) If the pension officer disagrees
with any recommendation made by a
local pension court as aforesaid, he shall
refer the matter in the prescribed manner, to the umpire appointed as hereinafter provided.

(4) The pension officer, in any case
in which he considers it expedient to
do so, may, instead of himself determining the claim or question, refer it to
a local pension court, and if the pension
officer so refers any matter the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of this
section shall apply as if he had referred
the matter to a local pension court.
(5) Where a recommendation has
been made as aforesaid in the case of
any person by a local pension court,
that person may, with the leave of the
court, require the pension officer to
refer the matter to the umpire, and the
pension officer, if so required, shall refer the matter to the umpire accordingly:
Provided that the local pension court
shall give leave under this article in
any case in which it appears to the
court reasonable so to do, having regard to the importance of the principle
involved in the case or any other
special cirsumstances.
(6) Where, in pursuance of this Act,
any recommendation made by a local
pension court is referred by the pension
officer to the umpire, the decision of the
umpire in the matter shall be final and
conclusive and not subject to appeal to
any court.
(7) Nothing in this Act, or in the
Old Age Pensions Acts (Northern Ireland), 1908 to 1925, shall be construed
as preventing a pension officer or
umpire or a local pension court, on
new facts being brought to his or their
knowledge, from revising a decision or
recommendation given in any particular case, but, where any such revision is made, the revised decision or
recommendation shall have effect as it
it had been an original decision or
recommendation, and the foregoing
provisions of this section, and the provisions of the said Acts, shall apply
accordingly:
Provided that where by a later decision a former decision is reversed, and
a person has received any sums on account of a pension in accordance with
the former decision, that person shall,
notwithstanding anything in sub-section
(2) of section nine of the Old Age
Pensions Act, 1908, in the absence of
any fraud on his part, be entitled to
retain any sum so received up to the
date of the later decision which he
would have been entitled to retain but
for the reversal of the former decision.

The real purpose of the Amendment is
that the Court of Referees appointed by
the Minister shall have the power to give
a decision in the case of a person claiming an old-age pension. We have had
very good examples of the things we have
been complaining about this afternoon in
regard to the administration of Unemployment Insurance. In connection with
that Act there are what we call Courts of
Referees. Sometimes, strange as it may
seem, they give a decision in favour of
an applicant. In one case, or perhaps
two cases, out of ten an applicant gets
the benefit of the courts decision, but
under the Clause now before the Committee the court's decision is not to be
final, and the case may be sent to the
umpire. In other words, a person who
never sees the applicant has the right to
determine whether or not that person is
entitled to an old-age pension.
We hold that the court which has
heard the evidence and seen the applicant
should have the right to finally determine
whether or not the person is entitled to
the old-age pension. You will observe
that the pensions officer need not submit
any evidence at all. He can just disagree
with the award of a pension. As my
colleague, the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) has pointed out, the
pension officer has disagreed with the
claim in the first instance. Let us assume
that the Committee recommend the applicant for a pension. The pension officer
who disagreed in the first instance
obviously can do nothing else but disagree in the second instance.

within the competence of the pension

It appears to me that the importance of
this whole thing would be in doubtful
cases. Those who are in charge of oldage pensions administration at the moment
would agree that the most difficult case
with which they have to deal is one where
there is no authoritative evidence of age.
There they have to depend upon circumstantial evidence together with the appearance of the applicant. Under those
circumstances should not the court be the
authority to decide whether a person
should get the pension or should not? So
far as my experience of pension officers
goes-and I do not suggest for a moment
that they are less considerate or less
humane than anyone else in connection
with the administration of this whole Act
-you have got to bring complete and
satisfactory proof to the pension officer
that the person is the right age, and in
the absence of that satisfactory proof the
tendency is to hold up the claim of the
applicant.
Under those circumstances, particularly
in the case I have cited, it would appear
to me to be a reasonable proposal, bearing in mind, as I understand from the
argument of the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie), that the pension
officer has already disagreed to the person
getting the pension, and that then the
matter is referred to the local court. In the
event of the local court giving a favourable decision why should the pension
officer have the right to object? If you
intend the pension officer to have that
power in my judgment you should cut out
the intervening step, that is the court. It
appears to be perfectly ridiculous, if you
are going to constitute a court, and
possibly pay the chairman two guineas
per sitting, as the chairmen are paid at
the present time on the Courts of Referees,
that the decision of that chairman, or of
that court, should be treated lightly.
Because I believe that the decisions of
these courts are going to be to a large
extent flouted is the reason I am in
favour of this Amendment. I would like
to hear some really convincing reason why
the Amendment which stands in our
names should not be accepted.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in page 2,
line 25, to leave out paragraph (3). The
real purport of leaving out paragraph (3)
is that the pensions officer shall not have
the powers that are conferred
him
by that paragraph. We have heard the
position of the pension officer discussed at
some length on the previous Amendment
and no argument we might possibly
adduce will convince the Government of
the desirability of this change. Certainly the change is essential, if we are
going to have anything like pure administration, and going to make members of
committees feel their personal responsibility in dealing with claims. I was a
member of the Belfast Corporation for
three years, and during those three years
I served on the old-age pensions committee
for some of the divisions in Belfast, and
the feeling that was expressed often at
those committees was: "seeing we are
not the final body responsible for the
granting or withholding of pensions the
claim might be considered in that light,
and that the pensions officer would then
exercise his discretion untrammelled,"
and therefore the committee did not act
as considerately perhaps as they might
have acted in this connection. So that if
this Clause or if this paragraph (3) is
taken out every member who may be
appointed to this court of referees will
feel that the responsibility rests with
him or her as to whether or not the claim
O'Neill, Patrick

Mr. Beattle.
of the old-age pensioner is to be allowed.
And from that point of view and the desirability of getting more and more
members of the community acting in this
public way with a full sense of their responsibility on the committee it seems to
be a much more desirable thing to have
this responsibility thrust on members of
the committee rather than to allow them
to get out of their responsibility by
saying "It does not matter what we say,
the pensions officer will come along after
us and he will give his decision on the
subject."
I do not think the intention of the
Government is to make these persons feel
their irresponsibility. Rather I take it
the intention of the Government is that
the members of the courts should feel
their responsibility. How are they to
feel as much responsibility as they would
feel if the power to grant the pension is
taken out of their hands? It is from that
point of view that we desire to leave out
paragraph (3).
In regard to the other Amendments
that are being discussed in this connection
it seems to me that more is required than
is contained in paragraph (3), but as I am
only responsible for leaving out paragraph (3) I will leave these other Amendments to the Members responsible for
them. But it does seem to me that more
is required in the Clause than presently
exists if it is going to remain part and
parcel of the Bill.

ANDREWS: I really do not

ap is most extraordinary. I was asked

I made that concession to the Opposition,

He suggests, I take it, that the umpire
should be really left out of it and that
these local courts should be the only
body dealing with appeals of the pension
officer. The Government cannot agree
to that because they do not think it
would be fair to the claimants in some
instances, perhaps, and in other instances it would be unfair to the fund.
What we want in this Measure is to
make certain that all persons who are entitled to pensions shall get them, and
those who are not entitled will not get
them. Therefore, we have set up not
only these local courts but also we have
set up an umpire so as to give the right
of appeal to both parties. May I say
that in this connection we are going
further than we went in connection with
the contributory old-age pensions, because there is no local court at all.
Here we have established a local court
just for the purpose of keeping in touch
with local opinion and for the purpose of
making doubly sure that those old-age
pensioners shall get the pensions to
which they are entitled.

entitled to a pension or not. The committee and the pension officer go into the
figures, and as a rule they do carefully go
into them.
I have had some experience of these
pension committees myself. I found that
the committee were quite anxious to do
what was fair not only to the claimant
but to the Government. In nearly all
cases very satisfactory decisions were come
to.
When the committees and the pension officer disagreed and it was necessary
to refer the case to the Ministry we found
the results were just as fair as could be
expected under the circumstances. In
my judgment there will not be any more
difficulty dealing with cases under this
Bill than there was under the old one.
I repeat that the appointment of an
umpire under this Bill is altogether unnecessary. It is really only making an
unnecessary job and adding to the many
officials the Government have. There are
quite too many officials in my opinion.
It is quite unnecessary to add an umpire
as well as a number of pension officers
who will be appointed under the Bill, and
it is for that reason that I have moved the
Amendment which stands in my name.
Mr. COLLINS: I rise to support
strongly this Amendment on account of
the expense. Really if you can save the
salary of one man, even if he is paid on
piece work, it should be saved. There is
no necessity for this umpire. There is no
provision in this Bill that this umpire is
going to travel round the local courts. As
far as I can see from reading the Bill the
machinery will be the same. After the
local court has done its work the appeal
will go to the umpire and it will be done
by correspondence with the head office.
Is that the intention? There is no provision that he will be a travelling umpire.
I think this part of the work could be
done as formerly in the office of the
Ministry without the extra expense of
appointing another official.

CLAUSE 4 (Constitution of local pensions court).
4. (1) A local pension court for the
purposes of this Act shall consist of two
or more members chosen from a panel to
be established by the Ministry of Labour, and a chairman appointed by the
Ministry of Labour.
(2) Regulations to be made under section ten of the Old-Age Pensions Act,
1908, may provide that any claim or
question which is referred to a local pension court may, with the consent of the
claimant but not otherwise, be proceeded
with in the absence of any member or
members of the court other than the
chairman, and in any such case the court
shall, notwithstanding anything in this
Act, be deemed to be properly constituted, and the chairman shall, if the
number of the members of the court is
an even number, have a second or casting
vote.
(3) Panels of persons chosen to act on
local pension courts shall be constituted
by the Ministry of Labour for such districts as the Ministry of Labour may
think fit, and the members of a local pension court shall be selected from those
panels in such manner as may be prescribed.

The object of this Amendment is not

(2) The Ministry of Labour with the

It seems to me that those are very wide
powers, indeed, for any Ministry to obtain, and I think we ought not to agree
to this Sub-section without some definite
limitations other than the proviso contained in the last portion of the Clause.
This proposal would have effect until the
31st December, 1928, and a great deal
might be done in the meantime by a
Minister in connection with the administration of old-age pensions that would
not meet with the approval of even his
friends in the country. Therefore, I
think that this Clause should be deleted,
and that on the Report stage the Minister
should bring in an amended Clause seeking lesser powers than this sub-section
proposes to give him.
Just fancy, at
this time of the day, a Government
coming along and asking for power to "do
anything which appears to be necessary
for giving full effect to this Act."
No matter how fantastic it may seem,
the Governmeent propose to do that fantastic thing, and then come along and
say, if they are challenged in the Courts,
that they were empowered by the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland to do
it. This Sub-section gives them the
power to do anything up to 31st December, 1928, and I think it is a power we
ought not to confer upon the Ministry of
Labour or the Government of Northern
Ireland without a definitiion of what
they want power to do. It is specified
to some extent that the power they are
to get is to give effect to this Bill. The
Minister may do something between now
and 31st December, 1928, which he
might think would be giving full effect
to some portion of the Bill, but which
might not be held by the Courts to be
something that would be giving effect to
the Bill. Therefore, I beg to move that
this Sub-section be deleted from the Bill.

Old Age Pensions Bill-
Report Stage
7 DECEMBER 1927
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 7th December, 1927.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Old Age Pensions (Administration) Bill.
As amended, considered.
Clause 3 (Appointment of umpire).
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I beg to
move the deletion of this Clause. This
Amendment is in relation to the Clause
that empowers the Government to appoint
umpires in connection with the administration of the old-age pensions scheme,
and proposes to leave that Clause out,
because I think in the administration of
that scheme there is no necessity for the
officers which the Government now ask
for. I think that the Ministry, under
whose charge this Act is to be administered, have got sufficient officers in their
establishment without creating any additional ones. As a matter of fact I think
they have at the present time, though it
may not be in connection with this, an
arbitrator, or umpire, rather, an office
which, under the estimates passed by the
House last year, costs the sum £4,000
odd. Now, in my judgment, that office
could be made use of, if required, for the
purpose of this Act. Even if that officer
is not available for that purpose in my
opinion the Ministry itself can amply
deal with any cases that might arise, and
that would require the jurisdiction of an
appeal court or umpire to deal with.
Therefore, I think that the Government
is not justified in asking the House to
give them leave to appoint a new officer
or more than one officer in connection
with this matter.
There are something like 800 officers in
connection with the Ministry of Labour
-in round figures something in the
neighbourhood of 800, and I think the
House would not be justified in adding
anything to that. I cannot understand,
if the Old Age Pensions Act has been
carried out since its establisment in this
county without an office, such as this one
they now ask for, why it cannot be done
now. Up to now the Ministry of Home
Affairs have been dealing with this matter
of old-age pensions, and I think, on the
whole, they have been doing that very
satisfactorily. I had occasional complaints myself with regard to some of
the decisions of the Ministry, but I venture to say on the deepest consideration
of the question that probably the Ministry
were right in all instances. And I say
if that Ministry was able to deal with
these questions without the establishment
of an umpire I do not see any reason why
the Ministry of Labour should not be able
to do likewise. I have not heard any
arguments in support of the establishment of this office which, to me at any
rate, are convincing. Indeed I do not
think there are any arguments further

The decision in this Amendment, I suppose, will guide that in the next Amendment on the Paper. The object of this
Amendment is to preserve what has
hitherto been in force, namely, the right
of a county council or county borough
council to appoint the committees or, as
they are now called in the Bill, the courts,
which will consider claims for old-age
pensions. I think the Government should
give way on this point, because since the
Act was first introduced the local authorities have had the right of appointing
pension committees. These committees
have carried out their work up to now
very efficiently, and no complaints have
been made in that respect. No complaints
have been put forward in any of the arguments by those supporting this Bill, and
no suggestion was made that the committees did not do their work satisfactorily to
all concerned. We have only to consider
this thing as ordinary individuals should

to know that the elected representatives
of the people on the county councils and
the county borough councils are at least
in as good, and I think a better, position

administration of this Act.
The Minister told us when we were discussing the last Amendment that one of
the principal reasons for the introduction
of this Bill was the question of economy,
that something in the neighbourhood of
£10,000 would be saved by the adoption of

so far in connection with this economy it
has not been shown where this economy is

opinion it cannot take place more readily
than by leaving the appointment of the

charge up to the present for any of the
committees they have appointed. It is
not contended that that will be the case
in regard to the courts.
There will be some officials in connection with them who will be paid, and
consequently in that respect there will be

I hold that these bodies who have carried

In addition the county councils and the

accept it.

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I cannot
agree to the Third Reading of this Bill,
because I have never seen the necessity
for the Measure at all, and none of the
arguments that have been put forward
here has convinced me in that respect.
The Old-Age Pension Act, since it came
into operation nearly twenty years ago,
has been carried out very successfully by
the various authorities entrusted with its
administration. When this Government
was established in Northern Ireland, the
business in connection with old-age pensions was given over to the Ministry of
Home Affairs, and during their time no
complaints that I am aware of have been
made as to the methods by which they
carried out their duties.
4019 Old Age Pensions Bill-

7 DECEMBER 1927
Third Reading.
It is my opinion that the principal
reason for the introduction of this Bill is
the desire to create new jobs for friends
of the Government, because until the
present time the Old Age Pensions Act
has been carried out by an agency, as it
is called; that is, the principal officers in
connection with it are civil servants of the
British Government. I understand that
the cost in that connection was something
over £40,000, and it is now proposed to
discontinue paying those officers of the
British Government, and new officials of
course, will have to be appointed by the
Ministry of Labour for these purposes.
The Minister of Finance has stated in
this House that the principal reason for
the introduction of this Bill is economy.
It has not been made clear to me in any
case where there is going to be any great
economy in the working of this Bill when
it becomes an Act, because the officers
who will be appointed to take the place
of the British civil servants-the Excise
men-who presently carry out the work,
will be appointed at a certain salary.
That is not mentioned. We have no information at all in respect of what the
salaries of those officers will be; but there
is hardly any doubt that they will be
appointed at a salary fixed on a graduated
scale, and as the years go on those
salaries will increase, as the salaries of
nearly all the 2,000 officials which the
Government have in their employment
are increased. Therefore, I hold that in
years to come there will not
be any
saving, and, indeed, I shall not be surprised to know that before many years
pass the administration of this Bill
will be just as costly as the system of
to-day.
There was one thing stated by the
Minister of Finance, on the Second Reading of this Bill, which seemed rather
strange in face of all the arguments and
all the statements we have heard regarding this Measure. It was this:
use in

We do know--there is no

was necessary that there should be close

with the object of ruling out those entitled to it, but in order to prevent

Have there been abuses? From that
statement you would infer naturally that
some abuses had taken place, but the
Government would not admit that, because one of the Ministries had charge of
the administration, and if abuses were
taking place then that Ministry was the
guilty party. If no abuses were taking
place, then why this statement from the
Minister of Finance? In my opinion no
abuses did take place, and this was
simply put in as an argument to show
that abuses might take place, and that
the Government would be much safer
under the Bill now before the House than
under the system at present in force. On
every ground, I think there is no necessity for this Bill. Everything in connection with the administration of old-age
pensions was satisfactory. We have
never had any complaints in this House,
or at any rate no complaints of such a
nature as to warrant the introduction of
a new Bill and the alteration of the

I have already stated that I thoughtand I still think-that this Bill to a large
extent was introduced for the purpose of
satisfying some aspirants for jobs in connection with the Government. I have
endeavoured to point out to the House
that there was no necessity for the appointment of an umpire in connection
with this Bill. Already the Ministry of
Labour, who will have charge of this Bill,
have a branch of that Department costing
some £4,000 a year, and in my judgment
the umpires-there are more than onecannot be so busily engaged in a small
area like ours that they could not deal
with the few claims that are likely to go
their length in connection with old-age
pensions. I think the cases that are not
decided by the local pension committees
and the pension officers are very few, indeed. Cases that would go the length of
the umpire would be very rare, so rare,
indeed, that I hardly think there is any
necessity for an umpire at all. I believe
that if the Government made an endeavour to carry out what they state is
their intention, to have some regard for
economy in these matters, they would not
appoint an umpire, but they have done
that. As the House knows, I divided the
Committee on that subject. For this
reason, and for the various other reasons
which I have mentioned, I am sorry to
say that I cannot agree with the Third
Reading of this Bill.

two
Ministries dealing with old-age

wish I was absolutely convinced that that

reason, if new facts arise which would
warrant that case being re-examined, and
the hon. Member interested would bring
those new facts before the Minister of
Labour or myself, or the pensions officer,
or the court, or the umpire, there will be
a new investigation of the claim. That
will mean that in the event of the claim
being admitted on the second application,
the pension will be paid from the time the
claim was first made.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: To what authority would I have to go with new facts,
before a claim is finally turned down?
Mr. GORDON: Suppose a case first
comes before the pensions officer, and on
the facts before him he turns the claim
down, the applicant would then have
the right to appeal to the court, and the
court might also turn the claim down.
Then if the hon. Member had any new
facts that she could submit, she could
send them to the Ministry of Labour, and
we would see that those new facts were
placed before the umpire for his consideration. Another question asked in
the course of the debate was whether
there will still be inspection and investigation. We propose that there shall be
inspection. It may be different, in some
respects, to the inspection that has been
carried out under the Imperial Government, but we propose that inspection and
investigation shall be carried out. The
hon. Member for Derry said she had some
misgivings, but, I want to assure her, and
every Member of the House, that it is the
intention of the Government that the
same sympathy and the same human
touch that has characterized the administration of the Act under the Ministry of
Home Affairs, will be manifested in the
administration of the Act by the Ministry
of Labour.
The Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Healy) admitted that the
coalition of the contributory and noncontributory pension services was a good
business proposal, and he agreed with it.
He did not agree with the fact that we
proposed to appoint as chairmen of the
courts gentlemen who would be representative of the legal profession.
We are
going to appoint as chairmen of those
courts men of administrative ability and
legal capacity. I do not say that they
will necessarily be legal gentlemen, but
they will be men of administrative ability
and, to some extent, of legal standing.
I agree with hon. Members opposite when
they say that very often a man, by virtue
of his wide public and administrative experience, is capable of discharging the
duties of an important administrative
post. We have not definitely decided
that all the chairmen of these courts will
be members of the legal profession, although I am sure no Member on the
opposite, or this side of the House, would
condemn a lawyer as not being competent
to carry out the duties that would devolve
upon him as chairman of the Court of
Referees.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: They are not
all competent.
Mr. GORDON: I will give this assurance to the hon. Member; that if we appoint lawyers to the position of chairmen
of Courts of Referees, we will see that we
select only competent lawyers. I think
that should satisfy the hon. Gentleman.
I give that undertaking. I come to the
hon. Gentleman who represents the
County of Antrim (Mr. George Henderson). I want to say this regarding him.
that I never heard him speak in this
House without illuminating the debate.

Labour. If the hon. Gentleman was not

this evening.
Mr. LEEKE: You are instructing us
all.

if they are able to perform any work.
I am going to make no observations.

Now I come to the hon. Gentleman
who represents North Belfast. I think

elected members of the Belfast City

those committees, that they did perform

I thank hon. Gentlemen for the criticism they have offered-offered in an

paid my right hon. Friend and myselfwell deserved tributes no doubt (Laughter), and I want to say, in conclusion,
that we have endeavoured to meet, as far

look at Clause 2, at the end of Sub-clause
8, they will see we have put an addendum

shall be afforded an opportunity of submitting his evidence to the local pension
court or to the umpire as the case may
be." So that it is not a case of the

being heard. He will have every opportunity of having his case examined, but
it lies with him to make the case. It

feel certain he will agree to be compromised--I say on his behalf, and on my
own, that it is our intention that this
Act shall be carried out considerately and
sympathetically so far as he is concerned,
and so far as I am concerned.
We will
see that it is carried out sympathetically,
and the pensions officers will give every
help to those claimants who are anxious
to make their claim for a pension
and anxious to get help when they come
before the local courts and before the
umpire. We will see that our pensions
officer gives them every assistance and
every help, so that their claim may be
formulated in a proper and regular
manner, and that they will receive the
utmost sympathy from every officer who
operates these claims in the Labour
Ministry.

Oral Answers to Questions.
AGRICULTURAL PRODUCE COM-
MITTEE REFUSAL TO GIVE
EVIDENCE.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
the Belfast and
Agriculture whether
North of Ireland Grocers' Association
and the Belfast Chamber of Trade, as
well as certain road transport companies,
have given any reason for their refusal
to come before the Agricultural Produce
Committee; and if, in view of the striking difference between the price received
by the farmer and the cost to the purchaser of certain commodities, the Government will introduce legislation on the
subject.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): With regard to the
first part of the question, the answer I
understand is in the negative.
In regard to the second part of the
question, I have to refer the hon. Member to the reply given on the 24th ultimo
on behalf of the Prime Minister to the
hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Elliott), in which the
policy of the Government in reference to
the control of prices was outlined.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the difference between the buying and selling price of
pork is at present 300 per cent., and does
he not think some step should be taken
by legislation to bring these profiteers to
justice?
Mr. ARCHDALE: The policy of the
Government is given in the answer of the
Minister of Commerce on 24th November.
Mr. KYLE: As the right hon. Gentleman in his reply to this question has
stated no action has been taken by the
Government, what action is the Government prepared to take to compel these
road transport companies and those other
associations to give reasons why they
would not give evidence before the Committee set up by the Government? Is the
Government prepared to allow this state
of things to continue?
Mr. ARCHDALE: The hon. Member
will have to put down a question.
IMPORTATION OF TUBERCULAR
COWS.
are
2. Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether it is a
fact that large numbers of tubercular and
emaciated cows, which
unfit for
human consumption, are being imported
into Northern Ireland; and, if so, what
steps he proposes to take to prevent this
undesirable state of affairs.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative. Steps have already been taken to
terminate this undesirable traffic.

KILLEN.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether his attention has been
called to a resolution of the Enniskillen
Urban Council objecting to his Ministry
sanctioning a further continuance of a

by the Enniskillen Gas Company, Ltd.,
in view of the present cost of coal; and
if so, what steps he proposes to take in
the matter.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
The Resolution referred to by the hon.
Member has not, so far, been brought to
the notice of my Ministry.
The Company's application for the continuance of the charge in question was
advertised in the local press on 1st
instant, and it is open to any person to

instant. Any such representations will,

DEATH AFTER CHILD-BIRTH AT
POMEROY.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been drawn to the death, following
child-birth, of Mrs. Mates, Pomeroy, in
November, 1925; whether it is a fact that
this woman was left unattended by the
nurse under direction of the doctor;
whether it is a fact that the incidents of
this tragedy were placed before the
Tyrone County Council, and that no explanation of the doctor's action
was
given; and whether the Minister is prepared to order a sworn inquiry into the
death of every woman who dies in childbirth to the end that mothers may feel
more secure in the future.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have
been asked by the right hon. Gentleman
to reply.
My attention was drawn to this case.
Mrs. Mates was attended by a doctor
holding a dispensary appointment in a
district other than that in which she
resided. She was a private patient of
the doctor's, and there is no suggestion
that he was in any way acting in his
capacity as a dispensary doctor. The
Ministry have, therefore, no jurisdiction.
to inquire into the circumstances of the
case, nor can I express any opinion as
to the accuracy of the allegations in the
question.
It is a fact that the matter was reported to the Tyrone County Council as
the authority responsible under Statute
for the supervision of midwives in the
county, but no suggestion of negligence
was made against the nurse who attended
the case, and, therefore, there was no
case for inquiry by the Council. The
Council have no jurisdiction to inquire
into the action of the doctor in the matter, nor to call for any explanation from
him.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the Ministry has no power to
take the course suggested.
HOURS WORKED BY CO. DOWN
SURFACEMEN.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the employees of the County Down
Council employed as surfacemen work 56
hours per week, or 9 hours per week
longer than similar workers in County
Dublin, and six hours per week longer
than in other counties throughout
Ireland; and whether, in view of the fact
that the County Down roads are as well
kept, if not better, than those of any
other county in Ireland, he can state
why these employees of the Council
should not have equal conditions of hours
and
pay with the employees of other
counties.
Mr. HANNA: The wages paidasto
surfacemen and the hours which they
are required to work, are matters entirely within the province of the county
and rural district councils, the Ministry
having no jurisdiction to interfere.
From information which I have received from the county council, it appears
that the nominal working hours for
surfacemen in Down County are 56
hours per week, but that during the
winter months the actual working hours
are only from daylight to dark, although
the same wages are paid as if full-time
had been worked.
I have no information as to the time
worked in County Dublin, or any other
county in the Irish Free State, but can
say that the nominal working hours in
County Down are only two hours per
week longer than in the adjoining counties, and that the hours worked in the
winter are the same.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
8 DECEMBER 1927
As already mentioned the conditions
under which surfacemen work both as
regards pay and working hours are not
matters in which I can interfere. They
are entirely within the jurisdiction of the
local authorities, and must be determined
in accordance with local conditions as to
labour.
Mr. KYLE: Would the hon. and
learned Gentleman say whether or not the
Government are prepared to make representations to the Down County Council
in order that these men should get better
treatment than apparently the Down
County Council are prepared to give
them?
Mr. HANNA: I can only say, as I
pointed out in the answer, that the
Ministry have no power to interfere.
Mr. KYLE: Have they any jurisdiction over anything?
Mr. HANNA: Oh, yes.
COUNTY DOWN SURVEYORS
CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT.
6. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
conditions of employment of the County
Surveyor and his assistants employed by
the Down County Council; and whether
it is a fact that this Council have twice
reduced the wages and increased the
working hours per week of the surface
men in recent years.
Mr. HANNA: Down County Council
employ one County Surveyor, two special
Assistant Surveyors and 10 ordinary
Assistant Surveyors.
Except in the cases of four Assistant
Surveyors, all these officers are required.
to devote their whole time to the County
Council's services.
The four Assistant Surveyors who are
not whole-time officers were appointed on
the part-time basis before the passing of
the Local Government (Ireland) Act
1898, and are consequently entitled under the Act to continue in office as parttime officers.
As regards the wages and working
hours of surface men the matter is one
wholly within the province of the County
and Rural District Councils.
During the war the wages paid to surface men in County Down increased considerably, and during the years 1921
and 1922 were reduced, but since the latter year no further reduction has taken
place, the present rates being in most
cases more than twice the pre-war rates.
I have no information as to whether
the working hours have been altered in
any way.
Mr. KYLE: Is the hon. and learned
Gentleman aware that- the wages which
he says are a hundred per cent. increase
are at present 25s? Does the Government think that is an adequate wage.
Further, the hon. and learned Gentleman
has not answered the first part of my
question about the conditions of employment of the County Surveyor. He has
referred to other surveyors.
Mr. HANNA: I imagine from the
question that what the hon. Gentleman
was anxious to know was what the remuneration was. There would be no
difficulty in getting that from the returns.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Did the hon.
Member not ask in this question for the
conditions of employment of the county
surveyor.
Mr. HANNA: They are not wages.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: That is a peculiar attitude to take up.

Mr. HANNA: On the 30th September,
1927, the Newtownards Rural District
Council had 700 cottages in the occupation
of tenants, 641 of which were let at 9s per
month, or approximately 29 a week, and
59 at 14s per month, or approximately
3s 3d a week.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
The total rent receipts for the half

BELFAST GUARDIANS AND
LABOUR TEST.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can say if the
Belfast Board of Guardians are legally
entitled to make payment in kind under
a labour test, and whether he can state
under what Act of Parliament such a test
is allowed.
Mr. HANNA: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the labour test is allowed under
the provisions of Section 13 of the Local
Government (Ireland) Act, 1898.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to
ask the hon. and learned Member whether
he thinks it a desirable practice that
people who are employed on a test scheme
should be paid in kind instead of in wages.
Mr. HANNA: I am afraid my own

TING FOR POLITICAL MEETING.
Mr. KYLE (by private notice) asked

reply he received from the Secretary of
the School Committee in regard to the

is to be held under the auspices of the
Shankill Unionist Association on Friday,
9th, and Saturday 10th, in aid of the

state how he can justify these meetings in
view of his reply of Tuesday, 6th December.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): No reply
has yet been received to the Ministry's letter to the Secretary of
the Committee of Tennent Street School
which was sent on the 30th November,
1927.
On receiving notice yesterday afternoon that this question would be asked I
sent a letter to the Secretary asking him
to communicate with me before this
House sat to-day, but I have not had any
communication from him.
It is a fact that a Sale of Work is
advertised to be held in Tennent Street
Hall, which I believe to be the school, on
Friday and Saturday, 9th and 10th December, in aid of the Building Fund of
the Shankill Unionist Association.
In the view of the Ministry the holding of a Sale of Work for that purpose
is a breach of the Ministry's Regulations,
and I do not justify it.
Mr. KYLE: Is the hon. and learned
Gentleman prepared to get the Government to stop this practice, which he says
is irregular in the view of the Ministry?

The only action which my Ministry can
take for breach of the regulations is to

a case such as this involves the immediate
closing of the school. This school is attended by over 300 children and employing eight teachers. The result of taking
immediate action by stopping grants for
such a breach of Regulations would involve 300 children, for whom there is no
accommodation in the adjoining school,
being thrown out of school without any
provision being made for their teaching.
If they do not attend school their parents
are liable to be prosecuted. It is not the
intention of the Ministry to suffer a continuance of the breach of the Regulations, but the House will understand, I
hope, that immediate drastic action can-

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Yote of Censure.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move :
That in the opinion of this House
the Government no longer represents
the views of the great majority of the
people, owing to its neglect of the vital
needs of each section of the community,
and especially on account of its failure
to deal with the widespread poverty
which exists in Northern Ireland.
I rise to propose the Vote of Censure
standing in the names of a singularly
united Opposition. We say that the
vital needs of the community have been
neglected and that the Government are
not worthy of continued respect in consequence of this neglect.
are
We
supported in this Motion by the resolutions which have been passed by various
bodies in Ulster for the last two or three
years. We are supported, for example,
by the Motor Association which has described the recent legislation of the
Government as legislation that is calculated to harm that particular industry.
We are supported in this Motion by the
county councils which have protested
against the Government's interference
with their legitimate business and against
the raiding of the Road Fund by the
Government, and the application of a
peculiarly large sum to one particular area
of the Six Counties, and which some of
the county councils at least feel will have
the effect of lessening the amount of
money that should be available from that
fund for the roads of the other counties
in the Province. We are supported in
this Motion by resolutions of the farmers'
organizations in the Six Counties, and by
meetings of farmers who have declared
that the Government have not taken
sufficient steps to see that the farming
interests were protected during the particular period of depression that they have
been and are going through.
We are supported in this Motion by
resolutions of women's organizations
which have protested against the inaction
of the Government and the refusal of the
Government to introduce legislation which
would ensure the guardianship of infants
in the Six Counties equally with Great
Britain. We have had resolutions from

We have asked the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour, repeatedly
in this House, and outside this House, when
he was prepared to have printed a cost-ofliving index figure for Northern Ireland,
the same as they have in Great Britain.
He has refused to do that. We have
always contended that the cost of living
in Northern Ireland is round about 5 per
cent. higher than it is in Great Britain.
We have got the actual facts of the cost
of living in the Irish Free State, which is
considerably higher than the figure for
Great Britain, and we know that the
figures for Northern Ireland bear a nearer
relation to those higher figures that obtain
in the Free State. Yet the right hon.
Gentleman hides himself behind the fact
that there is no absolute information, no
correct data to go on, and so he leaves us
in the position that we can state that in

the cost of living is higher in Northern
Ireland than it is in Great Britain.
The Government themselves have admitted on more than one occasion that
the cost of food is one of the most urgent

various Unionist Association meetings.
They go to the Women's Unionist Assocition meetings, when they can get, and they
say all sorts of nice things to them, but

for the women and for the men of this

the issue of guarantees up to the aggregate amount of £8,690,000 the Government have thus secured the continuous

(3) The Government of Northern Ireland are fully alive to the difficulties

of the Government of Northern Ireland,

reasonably claim place for two Irelands

the King, Parliament and people of the
Six Counties, and only those, shall make

Minister here by his own letter shows
what his earlier meaning was, and the
fact that he has kept quiet, and has made
no move to get greater control over Ulster
taxation is enough to condemn him on its
own.
Certain remarks have been made here
by other Members in reference to the Free
State. The hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) has pointed out certain disadvantages in the Free State. I am not
here arguing the Free State case. The
Free State has got rid of us and does not
want us at all. They are getting on with
their manufactures, and laughing at us,
but en passant I do not think it is any
harm to remind the hon. Lady that the
old-age pensioners there have advantages
that the old-age pensioners have not got
here. For instance, the old-age pensioners in the Free State can get their tea
and sugar more cheaply than the old-age
pensioners in Northern Ireland. As I
said, we have nothing to do with them
good, bad, or indifferent, but I was sorry
indeed to hear the note struck by the hon.
Lady-whose utterances in this House I
usually enjoy so much-in reference to
recent happenings. On consideration, I
think she herself will see that her words
had better been left unsaid. Many good
men have given their lives and suffered
for their convictions, and I suppose will
continue to do till the end of time. I believe hon. Members on both sides of the
House would agree that it would be a
poor day for this country when her men
were afraid to stand for their convictions
and principles. I have great pleasure in
supporting the Motion.

pushed upon them and accepted by them.
for the express purpose of settling the

Then I want to tell the Opposition that
if they think the Government do not deserve the support of the people in the
country, at least the people in the country
think the Government do deserve their
support, and perhaps the best way to find
that out is to see whether the people trust
them with their money or not. People
may go to a street corner or the Custom
House steps and clap their hands and
shout "Hear, hear, to any political
speech that might be delivered from a
soap box, but when you ask them to put
their hands in their pockets and trust you
with their money you will find what side
they are on. In connection with the
Ulster Saving Certificates, the total
number sold since 1st April, 1922, was
4,611,749, representing a round sum in
cash of £2,882,344, or an average saving
of £2 5s 11d per head of the population.
That shows that the people who put their
money in Ulster Savings Certificates at
any rate trust the Government and realize
that the Government represent their
opinions and their point of view.
In my opinion the Government has magnificently weathered the storm and
emerged with laurels. To-day they

Amendment made for the betterment of

Lord Carson said in the House of Lords

may well ask that every day. I do not

They must all be scrapped. We, the unfortunate nobodies in this House-the

Colonel WOODS": These men are

a local hospital on the lines of Chelsea,
for Ulster. I have asked him at intervals

It will be something the people of
Northern Ireland will never forget in the
same way as they will forget the Carlisle
Bridge. Some of them never heard of
the Carlisle Bridge until they heard of
this money being granted. I never did.

persons were cut off benefit, I always felt

SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION IN
CONNOR DISTRICT.DAN

1. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether he received
a memorial
signed by at least 95 per cent. of the
residents in the neighbourhood of Connor,
County Antrim, requesting that a new
school be erected in that neighbourhood;
whether he will state what steps he proposes to take to ensure that this request
is acceded to; whether he considers that
the present scheme at Connor is suitable
for the children in that area, in view of
the fact that the out-offices of that school
are very unsatisfactory to teachers and
pupils; and whether a considerable saving
could not be effected on principal teachers'
salaries if the schools within a two miles
radius were amalgamated and this proposed new school erected; and whether
the Government is prepared to grant the
prayer of the memorial.
SECREa
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): I have not received
the memorial referred to by the hon.
Member, but I understand
that
memorial asking for the erection of a
new school to accommodate the children
attending Connor and Lower Tannybrake
Schools was addressed to the Antrim
Regional Education Committee and to the
Ballymena Regional Education Committee, which are responsible for school
accommodation and school provision in
their respective areas.

While I cannot say that the Ministry
regards the present scheme as satisfactory,
it is, nevertheless, of opinion that it may
suffice until other more urgent cases have
been dealt with by the Committees concerned. The Ministry is causing inquiry
to be made into the present condition of
the out-offices.
A considerable saving in the salaries
of teachers is usually effected by the
amalgamation of schools. Since July,
1925, two other schools, namely, "Lislunan
""
and Connor and Kells," have
been amalgamated with Connor School,
and other schemes of amalgamation in the
neighbourhood are in contemplation, but
the possibility of amalgamating in one
building all schools within a two miles
radius of Connor would depend to a great
extent upon the accommodation provided
outside that radius.

HARBOURS-Mr. GORDON NICOL'S
REPORT.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Devlin)
asked the Minister of Commerce whether
he has now received the report of the
expert who examined the harbours of
Northern Ireland, and, if so, when he
proposes to issue it.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) to reply. I
would refer the hon. Member to the reply
given to him by my colleague in answer
to a similar question on the 25th October
last. I have to add, however, that the
report on Ballycastle Harbour has since
come to hand, and that it will be issued,
together with the report on Ardglass and
Killough, as an appendix to the report of
the Inter-Departmental Fishery Harbour
Committee, which is now in the course of
preparation.
IRISH SOLDIERS' AND SAILORS'
LAND TRUST-RENTS IN CO.
ANTRIM.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Finance whether it
is a fact that the rents of three cottages
in connection with the Irish Soldiers and
Sailors Land Trust at Townhead, Co.
Antrim, are charged at five shillings per
week, while the rent of cottages on the
other side of the road are charged at four
shillings per week; and whether cottages
at Muckamore had their rents reduced to
four shillings per week in October; and,
if this is so, will he make representations
to the proper authority to have the rents
of these cottages reduced to the level of
the others connected with the Trust in the
same neighbourhood.
Mr. POLLOCK: As the hon. Member
is doubtless aware the Irish Sailors' and
Soldiers' Land Trust is an Imperial Service, and questions relative to
to its
activities should be asked in the Imperial
House of Commons. I have, however, as
a matter of courtesy to the hon. Member,
obtained the following information:--
The Land Trust recently revised the
rents of all their cottages in Northern
Ireland, and as a result of such revision
the rents of the three cottages referred to
in the question remained at 5s per week.
The rents of the cottages on the other side
of the road were fixed at 58 per week,
instead of the existing rent of 4s, but the
Trust decided not to apply the increased
rent until vacancies occurred in the existing tenancies. The rents of the cottages
at Muckamore were reduced to 4s per
week.
The question of the appropriate rents
payable for the Trust cottages is one
entirely within the discretion of the
Trustees, and as I am aware that most
careful consideration was given to the
whole matter, it would not be proper for
me to make any representations with a
view to further reductions being effected.

whether, in view of the fact that the
action of this employer, approved by the
Rural Council, is having the effect of
making it impossible for other contractors
to get contracts, he will exercise his
authority and compel this contractor to
pay the agreed rate of wages to his
employees.

Conlig, but I understand that representations have been made to the Newtownards Rural District Council to the effect

DTS
LABOURERS' COTTAGES-REGU-
LATIONS FOR LETTING.
5. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his Department has issued any
Regulations to Rural District Councils to
ensure, in cases of the letting of labourers'
cottages, that agricultural labourers and
applicants with families living in unsanitary houses should have preference
for these cottages, and whether he can
inform the House as to the nature of
these Regulations.
Mr. HANNA: Section 29 of the
Labourers' (Ireland) Act, 1906, provides
that the District Council shall make regulations with respect to the letting of
cottages under the Labourers Acts, and
for preventing any undue preference in
the letting thereof. The Regulations
made by the Council are subject to confirmation by the Ministry. T
Model Regulations have been prepared
for the guidance of the Councils, and
these have been closely followed in all
cases.
The Model Regulations provide that
preference is to be given to families residing in unsanitary houses, but make no
special distinction between the classes of
rural workers coming within the definition of agricultural labourer under the
Labourers' Acts.
I am sending the hon. Member a copy
of the Model Regulations referred to.
