PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
acquaint the House that the House has
this day attended in the Senate, where
his Grace the Governor, on behalf of his
Majesty the King, delivered his Speech
to both Houses of Parliament as follows:
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I congratulate you upon the result
of your labours during the session now
concluded.
I regret that it cannot be said that
Agriculture has yet emerged from that
period of depression which has for so
long affected conditions in the primary
industry of Northern Ireland. Fortunately the spell of fine weather which
marked the late autumn was of great
benefit to the farmers in enabling the
harvest to be saved. It is to be deplored, however, that owing to the low
prices prevailing in respect of certain
commodities, farmers have not secured
proportionate remuneration for their
laborious work. It is hoped that the
steps taken by the Ministry of Agriculture, particularly in the matter of
granting a further sum of £40,000
towards the extension of the Live Stock
Improvement Schemes, ably adminis
tered by the County Committees, will
promote beneficial results.
I am very gratified to observe that the
improvement in trade continues, the
number of persons registered for employment at the Exchanges having been
on the 31st October the lowest since the
Great War, and on the 5th December,
26,710, a reduction of 22,697 since the
beginning of this year. Most of the
staple industries have shared in the
better state of trade, and in the linen
industry, in particular, the percentage
of persons registered as unemployed has
fallen from 14.5 per cent. in January,
1927, to 6.8 per cent. My Government
has continued to develop trade and
foster employment through the facilities
afforded by the Loans Guarantee Acts,
loans to the extent of £2,700,000 having
been guaranteed during the year ended
30th September, while the maximum
limit under these Acts has been increased from £9,000,000 to £10,500,000.
In addition since 1st January, 1927,
133 schemes of public utility, giving
employment to a considerable number
of people, have been initiated by Local
Authorities with the assistance of
Government grants amounting to
£208,205.
I note with satisfaction that measures
of great social value have been passed.
The Acts that have amended and consolidated the law relating to Workmen's
Compensation, that have provided
precautions against the danger of lead
poisoning, and that have safeguarded
those employed in the quarrying industry, mark important steps in the
development of my Government's policy
of improving the industrial conditions
of the people. The Trade Disputes and
Trade Unions Act, while providing
King's Speech.
King's Speech.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
additional safeguards for the liberty of
the individual and the vital interests
of the community, preserves to employers and employed their right to
combine for the furtherance of their
own legitimate interests.
I am glad to learn that preparations
have been completed for bringing into
operation on the 2nd January next the
final portion of the Contributory Pensions Act, under which pensions will be
provided for insured persons and their
wives at the age of 65. It is estimated
that the number of persons who will at
once benefit will be over 8,000. The
passing of the Old Age Pensions Act
also will serve to co-ordinate the administration of the Contributory and Noncontributory Pension Schemes.
The steps which have been taken to
remove the difficulties and anomalies
which have arisen in connection with
the interpretation and administration
of the Intoxicating Liquor Act of 1923,
will prove beneficial.
I am gratified to find that my Government's subsidy arrangements in connection with housing have produced such
satisfactory results that in so far as the
larger types of houses governed by
various statutes are concerned it is now
considered unnecessary to accord further
assistance from public funds.
It has
been decided, horvever, to augment
grants for the purpose of encouraging
the building of the smaller types of
houses more suitable for the requirements of the industrial wage earner,
and I hope that in due time by these
means the housing difficulty will have
been completely removed.
I am also glad to note that a special
grant of £30,000 to assist in the provision of Ex-Servicemen's houses has
been made.
Steps have been taken which will, it
is hoped, tend to develop and safeguard
the supply of Tuberculin Tested Milk,
and I trust that full advantage will be
taken of this Measure and that a pure
and clean milk supply may be ensured
for Northern Ireland.
I note with satisfaction that it has
been possible to afford some relief from
taxation by the exemption from Enteroutdoor
tainment duty of certain
sports, and in the case of other entertainments the remission of duty on the
charge for admission to the cheaper
seats.
Members of the House of Commons.
+
I thank you for the provision of
supplies for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am gratified to learn that the conditions in Northern Ireland still continue to be peaceful, and that cases of
serious crime are now happily rare.
It is my earnest prayer that the
blessing of the Almighty may rest upon
all your past and coming labours.
After which the Proclamation proroguing Parliament was read as followeth :
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall in His Majesty's name
summon, prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern Ireland should be prorogued to the sixth day
of March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Tewnty-eight:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation
do publish and declare His Majesty's
Pleasure that the said Parliament be,
as from the reading of this Proclamation
in the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
prorogued to Tuesday, the sixth day of
March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Twenty-eight.
Proclamation.
End of Session.
21 DECEMBER 1927
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
sixth day of March, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twently-eight, assemble
and be holden for the dispatch of divers
urgent and important affairs, and the
Senators and Members of the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland are
hereby required to give their attendance
accordingly.
Given at Government House, Hillsborough, this twentieth day of December,
One
Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-seven.
Signed by his own hand,
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.

Public Accounts Committee.
Resolved: That, notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Orders Nos.
50 and 70, the Committee shall consist of
seven members.
That Mr. T. W. McMullan, Mr.

Lloyd Campbell, Mr. Patrick O'Neill,
and Major Shillington be members of the
Committee.
That the Committee have power to send
for persons, papers, and records.
That three be the quorum of the
Committee. (Captain Dixon).
House of Commons (Kitchen and
Refreshment Rooms) Joint Committee.
Resolved: That a Select Committee be
appointed, with such Members as may be
added thereto by the Senate, to control
the arrangements of the Kitchen and Refreshment Rooms for both Houses.
That the Committee do consist of five
Members of this House, with an equal
number of Members of the Senate.
That Dr. Morrison, Mr. R. J. Johnstone, Mr. McAllister, Mr. W. McMullen,
nd Mr. Mulholland be members of the
Committee.
That the Committe have power to send
for persons, papers, and records.
That the Committee have leave to sit
notwithstanding the Adjournment of the
House. (Captain Dixon).
Local Bills Standing Orders (Joint
Committee).
Resolved: That a Select Committee be
appointed, with such Members as may be
appointed thereto by the Senate, to consider how far the Standing Orders of
Parliament relating to Local Bills have
been complied with on such Bills, and to
report to the House.
That Mrs. Chichester, Mr. Collins, Mr.
Elliott, and Mr. Lavery be members of
the said Committee.
That all petitions relaing to the compliance with the Standing Orders or Local
Bills which shall be presented during the
present Session be referred to the
Committee unless otherwise ordered.-
(Captain Dixon).

McBride be members of the Committee.
That the Committee have power to send
for persons, papers, and records.

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
7 MARCH 1928
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I do
not intend to take up the time of the
House to-day. I am quite satisfied that
statement will be satisfactory to the hon.
lady Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester).
Mr. SPEAKER: I suppose the hon.
Member understands the position. If
he had not finished his speech yesterday,
he is entitled to continue, but if he had
finished he is not entitled to make another
speech.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I will
just take a few minutes. I am altogether
disappointed with the contents of the
King's Speech. In order that the Prime
Minister and the Government should
know exactly the position that exists in
relation to the condition of the unemployed workers of Ulster, I made it my
business this morning to visit the Whitewell site. The weather conditions were
not altogether so bad to-day as I have
seen them on former occasions. The
people at this site are very dissatisfied,
and are blaming the Government for
allowing this condition of affairs to exist.
There is one gentleman there, he is
named Morgan, and lives at 64 Avon
Street, which I am sure the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) knows.
He has eight children and his wife and
himself to keep. He has to do four days
work and he receives for four days work
He does not even get
a pound note.
the money.
He gets four dockets entitling him to £1 worth of goods. I want to
ask the Government do they stand for
such a condition of affairs as that.
is a case from the Ballymacarrett side.
That
There is a gentleman called Given, 17
Clementine Street, which is in Sandy Row.
He is very dissatisfied. I may tell you
he was very indignant, and blamed the
Government entirely for it. The Government are not entirely to blame, but
they are partly to blame. He has a
family of six; he works for four days.
and receives 15s. He does not even get
the money.
Then there is is the case of
Hugh Morgan, who is a young man I
have known for a considerable time. I
was with the clerk of works, and this
young man came over to me. He did
not wait to be invited to come over. He
came running over and said, "Hello,
Tommy," and held up his boot to me.
The upper was torn from the sole.
could not tell you if he had any socks on,
but I know the toes were protruding
I
from the boots. That is the condition of
affairs that exists. I have the names of
twelve men here. Some come from
Ballymacarrett, some from Sandy Row,
some from the Shankill Road, and some
from other parts of the city.
The clerk of works there is well known
to Members of the Government. He is
a Mr. Geddis, a very staunch standardbearer of the Unionist cause, and a great
friend of my own. While I was talking
to Mr. Geddis another man who lives in
Gibson Street came over to me. He did
not know who I was. He showed me this
piece of bread, and asked me how a man
could be expected to do a day's work on
that. The Parliamentary Secretary to
the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon)
knows Mr. Geddis, who will bear me out.
The bread was not in this bit of paper
which was lifted off the field. He
showed me that piece of bread, and I felt
very sore about it. There is what that
man was doing eight hours work cn.
That was his dinner. I purposely
brought this piece of bread to the House,
in order to create an impression, and get
the Prime Minister to take action in this
inatter. The man felt very indignant.
I feel this is a system of slavery that the
noble Lord, the Prime Minister, would
not be a party to.

"Is
I have seen these men with hardly a
boot on their feet, and hardly a rag on
their backs, and yet a particular body in
this city ask these men to do eight hours'
manual labour. This is the piece of
bread that a man out of Gibson Street
had to exist on. I do not think the
noble Lord (the Prime Minister) could
stand for that. Any Member can get in
touch with Mr. Geddis and have
my statement confirmed. I asked the man:
that all you have to eat?" He said:
"This is all the piece I have; if I had
taken any more my children would have
been left without anything at all."
had very few coppers in my pocket, but
I gave them to Mr. Geddes, and asked
him to provide a dinner for the man.
As the Government are being blamed for
this condition of affairs, I suggest that
the Prime Minister should take a deep interest in this matter. Many of these
people I came in contact with to-day are
great supporters of the Government.
While it may be a very distasteful thing
to do, it is my duty to tell the Prime
Minister that the people are entirely dissatisfied. Had he been there this morn-
I
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr T. Henderson]
ing he would have got the same information as I received. I went there to see
exactly what was taking place. I got up
a little earlier than usual. I was there
at nine o'clock, and the men had already
started work. I am quite satisfied that
there is not a Member of the House, irrespective of what side he sits on, would
be a party to such a condition of affairs.
Apart from the exploitation of these
men we realize the blunder that took place
in regard to the purchase of this site.
Surely to goodness the Government or the
Poor-law Guardians are not going to get
anybody out of a hole by getting labour
for nothing. Without taking up the time
of the House I would appeal to the
Government to see if something could be
done to give these men a few more
shillings. These men get four coupons
from the Poor-law Guardians, and I
would suggest that they get money instead. One of the men on that site put
the case very lucidly before me, and as
an Ulsterman I felt ashamed.
I want to be quite serious. I want the
Members of this House to realize that this
is not an attempt to play to the gallery.
We very seldom have a gallery here, so
that cannot be imputed on this occasion.
And it cannot be said that we on this
side of the House are doing it for Press
purposes. Whether the speeches we make
are good or bad, we very seldom get a
Press. In fact, I would take it as a
favour if it was kept out of the Press.
plead with the Prime Minister to try to
get a few more shillings for these men.
They have to work for four days-it is
hard work, I have seen them digging clay
and wheeling barrows-and they work as
well as the Corporation labourers who receive 50s and 3s tram fares.
I
I believe the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Labour do not know the conditions of affairs. I suggest they pay this
place a visit, hear the complaints of the
men, and try to do something to help
those poor men who are suffering so much
at the present time. My particular reason
for appealing to the Prime Minister is
that one of the men pointed out to me
that he gets two or three coupons, but if
one of the "kiddies" wants a pair of
boots or if he wants a couple of shillings
for the rent he has not the money. John
Anderson, a personal friend of my own,
and a personal friend of many Members
on the other side of the House, was put
out of his house in Huss Street, off Agnes
Street, and is living in rooms in Enniskillen Street. He said, "The rent of the
house in Huss Street was about 3s a week,
and had I any money I would have been
able to pay the rent, but owing to the fact
that the Board of Guardians gave me
coupons instead of money I was put out
of my home." None of us wants to see
Ulster people dissatisfied, and for that
reason I appeal to the Government to try
to induce the Poor-law Guardians to increase the amount given to these people
and also to give money instead of coupons.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: The hon.
Member (Mr. Thomas Henderson) who
has just sat down has spoken at very
considerable length both yesterday and today, I think altogether very nearly 55
minutes. I propose to detain the House
for only a few minutes. During the course
of his speech he touched on every conceivable subject, on matters which possibly
were in some instances germane to the
King's Speech, and in other instances certainly were not germane. He covered a
very wide range. I am not going to follow
him, but I would just like to say in regard
to all the matters he brought up I did not
think I was in sympathy with any until
his remarks to-day. With a certain
amount of what he said to-day on the
subject of this labour test I certainly am
in agreement.
As far as his remarks yesterday on the
same subject were concerned I am afraid
I cannot agree with them. I do not think
it is in any way degrading to these men,
who for some reason or other are unable
to receive unemployment benefit and are
in dire distress, to give of their best in
the way of labour in return for what I
suppose is really outdoor relief from the
Guardians. But I do agree with him
when he speaks of the degradation of receiving dockets instead of money, and I
would like to join with him in appealing
to the Government to use any influence
they can with the Belfast Guardians to
revise to this extent their method of dealing with these unfortunate men.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I think the
labour test is only right and I cannot
see that any genuine advocate of Labour
can possibly see anything in it calculated to degrade the men concerned. I
81 Debate on the Address

7 MARCH 1928
Debate on the Address
do, however, think the giving of
dockets, especially where the men are
giving a quid pro quo in the way of
labour, is an uncalled-for hardship, and
I hope the Government will be able to
use their influence with the Belfast
Guardians in respect of this matter.
I have always thought the Opposition must have a very easy task, and I
have often envied them. I have often
thought that if it were not for the wreck
and ruin which I am confident the hon.
Gentleman if put in power would leave
in their wake, I would have wished that
we on this side of the House could have
been in opposition so as to give them a
little chance to make good the promises
they make. It would be very much more
amusing for us at times, and it would
certainly be pleasanter to be able to
promise and never be called upon to perform, and to be able to destroy and never
be called upon to construct. But in
spite of the fact that I do think their
task is the easier one, I could not help
feeling a little sympathy with them
yesterday because it seemed on this
occasion particularly that their task was
not quite so easy, as was manifest from
some of the
the speeches to which
listened.
we
The King's Speech and the speech of
the Prime Minister I think have completely cut the ground from beneath the
feet of the Opposition. From the remarks which they made, lengthy though
they may have been, the position of the
Opposition is obviously a difficult one.
Some of the criticisms which they endeavoured to make were already
answered in the speech of the Prime
Minister, though I must confess I found
it exceedingly difficult to follow in some
instances the speech of the hon. Member
(Mr. Thomas Henderson) who has just
sat down. He criticized the fact that
the Government were bringing in no
legislation with regard to slaughterhouses. He talked about tuberculosis in
cows, and, as I say, he covered a very wide
range mostly connected, it seems to me,
with local government.
I suppose that really what he was endeavouring to point out was that the
Government had lamentably failed in
their duty by not bringing in legislation
on the lines recommended by the Local
Government Commission which has just
finished its labours. All I can say is that
it appears to me, and to every right-thinking person, that if the Government had
brought in legislation on that Report at
this early date it would clearly have
proved that they were not giving it the
consideration due to a subject of such
vital importance to the whole of the Six
Counties. I hope very much that before
legislation is brought in the Government
will give their lengthiest and soundest
consideration to all the recommendations
we thought fit to put forward.
Then another subject was dealt with by
several speakers, and that was one mentioned by the Prime Minister and not
mentioned in the King's Speech, the question of the drainage of the Bann. I feel
I would like to say a few words on that
subject as it is one which has always lain
particularly close to my heart, and in
which I feel most deeply.interested. The
hon. Member who has just sat down suggested that during the course of my parliamentary life I have put forward many
Amendments, and perhaps he had in his
mind the Motion which I put forward in
regard to the drainage of the Bann. He
said I always withdrew my Amendments,
and that I might fool some of the people
some of the time, but I would not be able
to fool all the people all the time. That was
an instance not perhaps of the way I carry
out my duties, but of the in which the
way
Government are endeavouring to carry
out their duties to the country, and the
way in which they carry out the promises
made in this House.
I
I put forward a Motion calling upon the
Government to carry out the drainage of
the Bann, and they put forward an
Amendment to insert the words "to take
initial steps to deal with the matter.
accepted that Amendment against the
vote of the Opposition, and I explained
that I was satisfied to trust the Government on that occasion. I think I have
shown the people that, perhaps in a small
way, I have been able to put forward my
views effectively before the Government,
and I think the Government have shown
that if they give a promise they keep to
their promise. They have gone further in
the Report, which we have seen issued,
than the people had a right to expect from
them, and I know that the people in the
devastated areas concerned are very grateful indeed. When the time
comes,
whether they are political followers of
mine or of the Opposition-in many cases

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Chichester]
that I know they are the latter-the
Government will receive their support
because of their gratitude.
I ought to take this opportunity of
saying that the Government have done
their part, and it now lies with the people
of Ulster, and if I may add my words to
those spoken by the Prime Minister
yesterday I would hope from the bottom
of my
heart that those representatives
chosen directly by the people to look
after their interests should deliberate
well and carefully before they reject a
scheme such as I have reason to believe
the Government are going to put forward.
As I say, even if they think that these
terms are not as generous as they might
be, I trust they will think very carefully, at any rate, before rejecting them,
and will consult with the Government on
the matter. I cannot see how it is
possible for hon. Members opposite to
say that the Government are not attempting, in the first place, to deal with the
vital question of the drainage of the Bann
and, in the second place, to give employment to the large number of unemployed
throughout the Six Counties.
I would like to take this opportunity of
thanking the Government for the additional assistance which has been promised
to agriculture. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We do not know what may be
still in the minds of the Government. We
do know that yesterday the Prime
Minister, in giving us some details as to
what they proposed to do, said that he
could also give us some little hope that
there might be more. I would like to say
that the additional grant in aid of agricultural rates will be received with gratitude throughout the Six Counties by those
sorely depressed, sorely taxed, and sorely
rated people. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) At the same time I would like to
say that we are looking forward with
great anxiety and great hope to any other
help which may be forthcoming. I
believe that the Government realize that
the farmers are almost on their beam
ends, and certainly unless some assistance.
had been forthcoming I hardly care to
visualize the possibilities and prospects in
the country this year.
I notice that mention is made in the
King's Speech of a proposal for the registration of Nursing and Maternity
Homes. I can only say I am more than
glad that the Government are going to take
this matter up. I do not propose to say
anything further until I see the Bill dealing with this subject. I am also very
glad to see that they are going to introduce Measures dealing with the adoption.
of children and legitimacy. I hope that
in this way we will keep in step with
England, for up to the present moment
we have lagged somewhat behind in this
direction.
I will not detain the House any longer,
but if I may just go back to the one point
I have raised I would say that I do thank
the Government for having taken steps,
at any rate, to give the people of Ulster
an opportunity of dealing with the evil
of flooding which has lain so heavily on
them for generations. If the people of
Ulster will only rise to the occasion-and
I believe they will then we will have
accomplished something that will redound
to the credit not only of the Government,
but of the citizens of the whole Six
Counties.
Mr. HARBISON: I wish I could
speak in as optimistic a tone as the hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) who
has just sat down. Before this Session
opened I had hoped that there would be
something tangible done or proposed
by the Ministry. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I have searched through the
Gracious Speech and I can find nothing
except one or two little doles that, placed
on the surface on the plane of the difficulties that the people have to meet, could
hardly be seen by a powerful microscope.
I come from an agricultural district
and also a semi-industrial district. We
are suffering now on the agricultural side
for the sins of this Government. The
farmers have burdens laid upon them
that, as far as I can see and I yield to
no man in this House as to my knowledge
of the conditions of the people; I have
lived my lifetime amongst them, and in
the part of the country where I live I
know the greater part at least of their
personal affairs. I know the difficulties
from which the farmer at present
is suffering. I would venture to
estimate that there are not more
than twenty or thirty per cent. of
the farmers of Northern Ireland at
the present time solvent. The noble Lord
(Viscount Craigavon) stated that they
had information especially from the banks
as to the condition of the farming classes
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
7 MARCH 1928

in the North, or the community at large.
I know their condition, and there is
hardly a farmer at the present time who
would be granted £1 of an advance from
the bank without at least £10 of security.
I know also that the banks which did
heretofore advance money have lost very
heavily in their advances to the farming
community.
I say that the farmers are suffering
for the sins of this Government. In
the first place they carried a Land Purchase Act that laid upon the farmer a
burden that he should not bear, at least
twenty to thirty per cent. higher than he
should have to bear. Contrast that with
the situation in that country which we
despise here in the North-in Southern
Ireland. Contrast the conditions of purchase there and the conditions of purchase
here and it will be seen that there is an
unjust burden placed upon the farmer.
Then take the rates-the local ratesand the taxes. Why, if there were no
rent whatever, or no instalment to a
Land Commission, these are impossible.
The tenant cannot meet them. The right
hon, and noble Lord, when he was making
that speech praising what the Government
had done no doubt they have done some
good things; anything good they have
done I candidly admit-did not touch, and
nobody from the Government side has
yet touched the real difficulties of this
question. He said that what annoyed the
Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle) was
that there was nothing expressed in the
Speech that could irritate him.
But a
far more scientific way of irritating a man
is by remaining silent and saying nothing
to the clamant cries of those who are
seeking some redress for the evils under
which they are suffering. What was
irritating in that Speech in my judgment
were the things that were not expressed
in it, and which should have been expressed. There is nothing about the
difficulties that the farming community
are at
present suffering under, and
there is no hope held out of any remedy.
This increase in the agricultural grant
-I believe it is somewhere about
£30,000-what is that per farm in
Northern Ireland? Why an ordinary
hen would lay as many eggs in a fortnight as would equal the benefit it would
do any farmer.
Hon Members on the other side of the
House remind me very much of a mutual
admiration society. Everything they do
is perfection, and anything we ask them
to do-well, a plague upon it, it is nonsense, and will not be done. On that
question of the Bann drainage, to which
the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.,
Chichester) has just referred so sympathetically, I would like to bring to the
memory of the Government a remedy
which would not cost anything like the
money that it is suggested it might cost
-hundreds of thousands, I think
£600,000. There are somewhere in the
pigeon holes either here or in Dublin
reports of scientific commissions, reports
of competent surveyors who suggested
some sixty or seventy years ago a means
of draining the Bann area.
The suggestion in those reports was that the Bann
is being dammed up somewhere about
Kilrea up there, that there is a rock
there in the bed which if blown away
would lower Lough Neagh at least two
feet, and the estimate at that time-
I speak subject to correction-would be
somewhere about £20,000 or £30,000.
But the answer to that I know will be
"Oh we cannot touch that Lower Bann
because there are vested rights there."
Some one or two people have a right to
cast a rod over that river, but the
hundreds and hundreds of people along
the shores of Lough Neagh and the
banks of the Bann are to be flooded out,
their property destroyed, and no effort.
made to save them. I would put it up
to the consideration of the noble Lord to
find in the pigeon holes the reports of
those inquiries that were made away
back in the middle of the last century,
and find out if something more economic
could not be done and far bigger benefit
done to the farmers surrounding the
Bann and Lough Neagh.

Now, there is another question, and I
am glad to see it mentioned in the forecast
of legislation, and that is that a Fishery
Bill is to be brought in. But I regret to
have read this morning a speech by the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Finance, in another place, in which he
refers to the fishing in Lough Neagh. I
had hoped yesterday when I saw the
speech that the adumbrated Fishery Act
that was going to be passed was going to
bring the charter of freedom to the
Lough Neagh fishermen who reap their
little harvest in the Lough. But from all
I can gather from what the right hon.
Gentleman said last night it is merely an
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Harbison]
Act of Parliament to put in force rules
that have already been drawn up to deprive-it means absolute deprivationthe fishermen of the right to reap a living
out of the waters of Lough Neagh.
I need hardly tell the House-I am sure
every Member of this House remembers
the history of the right of the fishermen
to fish in Lough Neagh and what
happened. An appeal was taken by
these lessees, these vested owners, against
a certain decision in the Irish Courts.
It went to the House of Lords, and there
was not a man living at the time that
decision was given that did not look upon
it-I say this with all due respect and
deference to the House of Lords-with
suspicion. The court consisted of seven
judges, and the decision of the court was
four to three against the fishermen, and
amongst the three was the highest legal
authority in the land. The Lord
Chancellor of England decided with the
fishermen that they had from time
immemorial the immemorial right to fish
there. And the boon this Government is
going to give these fishermen is practically
to deprive them of fishing in the Lough
for ever. Well, I would like the Government to reconsider it before bringing in
their Bill. They have the power to fix
he rates, and to fix them in such a way
that the fishermen will not be penalized
by the putting on of prohibitive tariffs
upon these poor men who have had the
right for countless generations,
centuries until this decision of the House
of Lords robbed them of their natural
rights. These are questions I think that
should have been included in this Speech
to the House.
for
Then I do not know whether we have
any hope of asking the Government to
do anything more for agriculture. A good
tree, they say, can only bring forth good
fruit (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and
a bad tree nothing but evil fruit. Well, I
am speaking now after a good many years'
experience in politics, and my mind goes
back to the time when we were fighting
for the emancipation of the farmer, when
the farmers were just rising from slavery,
and when all the forces of landlordism
were against them. I do not want to say
it in any offensive way, but the Members
of the Government and their followers
are the lineal descendants of the men who
fought the farmers, and fought them to
the death. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
And I am sorry the farmers themselves
supported them when we were fighting for
them. Poor men, we forgave them because they did not know what they did.
They were carried away by the false cry
of another issue, and were blinded to their
own interests. It is the same here to-day.
They are being blinded by promises that
mean nothing. The people to-day are
crying for bread---
Mr. BEATTIE: And they give them a
stone.
Mr. HARBISON: Well, it is a piece
of paper, not a stone. There is nothing
in it. Now I have only one more thing
to say, and I have very intimate knowledge of this.
Where I live, in my home
town, there is a state of affairs that I
venture to say is nowhere amongst white
races. At the present moment we are
making an effort and making some sacrifices to keep the children there 500 to 700
children-alive. We are feeding them at
the schools. We are getting no grants
except what we do by individual effort,
and I must say the committee, who represent all classes and creeds, are working
morning and night-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-working the skin off their
fingers preparing food to feed these people.
There is no hand extended out by the
Government. Myself and my brother
Member for Tyrone have done our best
to try to get the wheels of industry
running. We have so far failed, but I
hope yet with some assistance from the
Government to get that grievance remedied. There is hunger and famine
staring them in the face every day.
With reference to the terms of unemployment, I do not know how the Government make up the figures. I presume
the way they make up the figures is this:
if the men go off unemployment benefit
they are no longer unemployed.
Mr. ANDREWS: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes.
Mr. HARBISON: I understand in
Cookstown it is a small number, and I
know there are three times that number
in starvation and unemployment. I do
not know how the statistics are made
up. I do not know how it is done in
general, but I am talking about my own
particular case. I know there are at
least 300 per cent. more starving and

he was not in the House yesterday when

He probably would have seen what morning dress meant. Because he is in a

Coming to the King's Speech, I, with
every
Member on both sides of the House,
rejoice that there is still peace in industry. During the last Session of this
House we were told that if certain legislation went on the Statute Book there
'would be trouble in Belfast and the North
of Ireland. It is just like all the threats
handed out by the Opposition. There is
really no substance in it. There is still
peace in industry. There is just one thing
I regret is not mentioned in the King's
Speech, and I hope the Minister responsible will give the House some assurance
about this particular matter that I want
to draw the Government's attention to.
That is the question of rent restriction.
In May of this year the restrictions on
all houses above £26 and under £52 in
valuation come off. Now, some people
may say that these are houses that people
who have plenty of money can afford to
live in. The trouble about that is this
that rents are becoming exorbitant for
this class of house, and the people living
in them cannot afford to pay the increased
rent that will become due at that particular time-not due, but which the
landlords and agents will be charging for
them. The result will be these people
will be compelled to leave their houses
and go into houses of a lower valuation,
and will by inducements of money and
other things deprive the people in poorer
circumstances of having the opportunity
of living in this class of house.
I hope the Government will give some
assurance that they are going to take this
question of rent restriction into consideration and give the tenants of these houses
some further protection. I only want to
call the Government's attention to this
fact. Then I would like to join the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. T.
Henderson) on the other side of the House
in appealing to the Government to do
something in connection with this very
vital question he dealt with to-day, that
is, the men who are in receipt of outdoor
relief being paid not in money but in
dockets. I know this documentary system
is a vicious system. It means that people
who cannot get money by any other
methods sell these dockets for less than
their face value, and it defeats the very
end the Government are trying to carry
out. Of course, we all know that while a
man's wife and family require food they
also need to pay their rent or they will be
evicted from their houses. They require
clothes. They cannot get that if they

Mr. LEEKE: I heard the Prime
Minister speak yesterday about the conditions of agriculture in the Six Counties.
He dwelt very much on the great wealth
represented by the numbers of poultry
that had been exported from Ulster.
After listening to the speeches of yesterday and to-day, I think it would be very
hard to convince anyone that agriculture
in the Six Counties is in even a fair
condition. In fact, I think it must be
admitted by all that agriculture was
never in a more depressed condition.
The only thing on which I can congratulate the Prime Minister-and upon
which I do congratulate him--is the fact
that he is raising the grant for local loans
in agricultural areas. I have only one
objection to his proposal, and that is that
the amount is far too small. If he had
made it £300,000, an average of £50,000
a county, he would have helped the situation. One of the greatest handicaps
under which the agricultural industry is
suffering at the present time is the high
rate of taxation. We as Members are
constantly listening to the complaints of
the farmers, and we know that a lot of
the blame that is put on the local authorities should fall on the Government, who
have passed over to the local authorities
a great many services which were formerly
maintained out of the National Treasury.
I should also like to call the attention
of the House to the condition of unemployment still existing in Derry City. It
is very bad, and the numbers affected are
no less, despite the figures that I have been
produced. I was reading the other day
a report of the proceedings of the Derry
Chamber of Commerce, in which it was
suggested that there was a fine opportunity of taking over the distilleries that
have been abandoned and of utilizing
them for the purpose of manufacturing
artificial silk. I understand that the
artificial silk factory in Ballymena is a
very promising concern, and is likely to
be a success. The Member for West
Belfast who sits on the Benches opposite
(Sir Robert Lynn) said yesterday that
he was
sure there were other sites as
good as the Ballymena one, and that if
the Government encouraged this industry
the state of Ulster might be revolutionized. I think there are possibilities
in this connection which the Minister of
Labour might explore. After all, the
members of Derry Chamber of Commerce are shrewd, successful business
men, and they are not making statements of that kind for the purpose of
establishing a reputation for themselves.
They make those statements with the
object of seeing if there is any possibility of the industry being established
in Derry city and carried to a success.
We have been told by some Members,
by the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester), for instance, that the
Opposition have a very easy task; they
have nothing to do but get up and
criticize. But if we made suggestions
they would not be undertaken.
She suggested that the people who defend the
farmers should be hanged from the
highest tree, and that no grave deep
enough could be got in which to bury
them. That is her panacea for the evils
under which the farmers of the Six
Counties are suffering, and I hope they
I will take note of her views.
Then I think no branch of industry
has been more neglected than our
fisheries. They are in charge of the

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Leeke]
Minister of Commerce. Several attempts
have been made by the fishermen around
the coast to get an inquiry held into the
fisheries problem, but they have met
only with repeated refusals. No
sufficient grounds have been put forward
for the refusal; there was simply the
statement that no good purpose would
be served by an inquiry. All that these
people want is an inquiry, and, after
they have given their evidence, they are
prepared to accept the findings of an
impartial tribunal. I fail to see why
the Government should refuse an honest
demand like that. Rights were taken
from these people forty years ago; they
are only asking for the restoration of
those rights, and they are not even
granted the right of an inquiry at which
they can state their case. An inquiry
would cost very little, and if the Act
were repealed the Fisheries Board would
have an increased revenue. There is no
question about that. I appeal to the
Minister of Commerce to look into this
matter again, and to give these people
an opportunity of stating their case before an impartial tribunal.
I hope that in the near future the
Government will do something for the
fishermen of Portstewart. The County
Council have agreed to put up their
.share, but for some reason or other the
Government have refused to carry out
their part of the bargain, and the result
is that the fishermen are left with very
bad harbour accommodation. There is
nothing in the nature of propaganda in
my putting this case forward. I do not
suppose I would get four votes amongst
those men; they are absolute supporters
of the Government. They are hardworking and industrious fishermen, and
I hope the Government will reward their
loyalty by helping them to develop their
industry. It would be only fair for the
Government to keep their promise, and
to give the grant that was asked.
The development of agriculture and
the fisheries would absorb many men who
are unemployed in the rural areas, and
I think that in that direction lies the
only hope for the reduction of the
number of unemployed in the country.
I think the Government would be well
advised to go into the fisheries question.
An inquiry, as I have said, would not
cost very much. I know that Commissions do not usually end in tangible
results, but that is the fault of the
Government. I had the honour of
sitting upon a Government Commission,
but none of the recommendations of that
body were carried into effect. We made
recommendations they may have been
bad recommendations-but that could
have been found out only by time and
practical experience. The Government
are very slow about carrying out those
recommendations. They should put
them into operation so as to test them,
and see if any effective method can be
devised for reducing the present distress
that exists in agricultural areas. I
understand there is some constitutional
hitch, and that the Northern Government would be committing a breach of
the Treaty by putting them into operation, but if that is so then they cannot
carry out inspection. If they cannot do
the one they cannot do the other.

particularly glaring case is that of the
Derry motor-car owners who have to pay
the Free State duty as well as the taxation imposed by the Northern Government on their cars. As most of their
traffic goes into the Free State they must
either pay the double tax or give up their
business. This means a great blow to
the holiday and tourist traffic. If you
impose such big restrictions on these
people how can you expect them to give
cheap and attractive fares sufficient to
bring tourists here. The tourists complain that the prices of hackney cars and
buses are high, but if the Government
will condemn cars which are known to be
perfectly sound and these men have to
borrow money to buy new cars it is impossible for them to give cheap and
reasonable fares.
I was expecting to see foreshadowed in
the King's Speech an Amending Bill to
relieve the persecution which is at present
going on against the bus and hackney
car owners and against the motor trade
generally, but it appears that the Government is confident of its position.
would not be so confident if there was a
by-election. There is general discontent
all over the Six Counties, in both agricultural and industrial areas, and the
Government should at once take steps to
have these grievances remedied. If they

do not the responsibility will fall on them.

Mr COOPER: I should like to congratulate the Government on the programme outlined in the King's Speech.
It is not a very showy programme but
there is quite a lot in it. I would like
particularly to congratulate the Government on that part of the King's Speech
which deals with agriculture.
Mr. KYLE:
More doles.
Mr. COOPER: You have got a good
many at any rate, and you want a good
many more. As regards agriculture, I
agree with the hon. Member for Derry
(Mrs. Chichester) when she says the position of the farmer is really worse to-day
than the Government thinks. I agree
that the farmers are in a bad state, and
that no section of the community is more
in need of assistance. There is no section
of the community that has carried its
I know
burden with less complaint.
perfectly well that the Government is
anxious to assist, and that the Minister
of Agriculture is anxious to assist. At
the same time it is very difficult for the
Government to formulate schemes to deal
with all sections of the farming community, because various sections of it
require different forms of assistance.
I want to refer for one moment to the
loan which was granted to the farmers
for the purpose of re-stocking their lands
when their cattle died from fluke and
other diseases. The Minister of Agriculture came to the assistance of the
farmers very generously and provided
money for them to re-stock their lands.
But in my opinion the loan has to be
too quickly repaid. A farmer gets a loan
of £100 at the beginning of the season,
perhaps in the month of May, to buy
stock. Unfortunately, during the last
couple of years, when October, November
or December came round, he had to sell
those cattle at the same price he paid
for them, and in some cases he had to
sell them at a loss. When he had to
raise one-third of the loan to repay the
Ministry he found himself in exactly the
same position he was in before, namely,
without stock.
He had only two ways of getting the
money. One was to sell the stock he
bought with the money and the other was
to borrow money at a higher rate of
interest. I have heard what a lot of the
farmers have had to say about this, and
I would appeal to the Government to extend that loan to a period of at least ten
years and to allow the farmers to repay
both principal and interest in half-yearly
instalments. If the Government would
do that I think it would be of real assistance to those farmers, and I do not think
the Government would lose very much
by doing it.
I would also like to congratulate the
Government on the increase in the agricultural grant. My Friend from County
Tyrone said that that was a very small
thing. I do not regard it as a small
thing at all. In my county it represents
4d in the £ off the rates, and it is 4d
in the £ which is spread over the whole
agricultural community. Every farmer
in the county gets the benefit of it.
There is nothing I know of that the
farmer appreciates more than a reduction
in the rates. I know it has been said
that this money could have been more
usefully spent in buying all sorts of
things, and in research, but there is
nothing that farmers want more at the
present time than a reduction in what
they have got to pay.
There is one thing that is not mentioned in the King's Speech, and I hope
it is one of the things the hon. Member
for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) referred to
when she said that the Prime Minister
had said there might be something more
to come. I received a promise from the
Minister of Home Affairs that he would
try to remedy an Act of Parliament
which I on various occasions have told
him was defective. This is the Small
Dwellings Acquisition Act. So far as
the rural districts are concerned that
Act is practically useless, and it is useless
for this reason. If a farmer wants to
take advantage of it to get a better house
the first thing he has to do is to have the
little piece of land on which he is going
to build a house taken out of the middle
of his farm. That piece of land has
then to be registered on a separate folio,
and it is often a very much more expensive thing to take that one piece of
land out than to convey the whole farm.
It causes very considerable delay, and
gives very much diminished security to

I

managh was the only county left without military, and we felt it very much

Mr. COLLINS: I have listened, I

on now as outlined in the King's Speech.
I think it would be a fair deduction to

cannot agree with that, and I am sorry
I cannot agree with it, because I am an
Ulsterman bred and born and all my

Members: Hear, hear.) The first note

referred to figures as regards his town of

were employed 500 and 600 hands since
I was a boy, and I was horrified at night

Debate on the Address

While the Prime Minister was in the
south of Europe the news reached us in
Newry that Marsh's biscuit factory in
this city was closed up. I understand
that prior to closing 300 workers were
engaged there, but that the number
of workers before the boundary was
set up between the Six Counties and
the Irish Free State was 600. I would
like to know where they are going to be
absorbed, and how in face of these
figures there is going to be a general
decrease in unemployment. My colleague on the Government side (Mr.
Davison) who joins with me in representing Armagh, made a very interesting
speech yesterday. I noted it particularly because it dealt with the vital
question of agriculture. Did the
Minister of Agriculture hear him say
that there was a bad falling off in the
fruit crop? Lamb's jam factory in consequence of the tariff caused by the
boundary has been removed to Inchicore
in Dublin. That is the position, and
that is why the fruit crop has fallen off.
The Prime Minister gave us figures
dealing with poultry which if prepared
on a proper basis are undoubtedly something encouraging to us in the North.
He told us that almost £4,000,000 was
realized by the export of poultry and
eggs. We who live in the North and in
the border towns and whose existence is
at stake know something about the working of this. I want the Minister of
Agriculture to tell us whether the figures
he submitted to the Prime Minister were
simply figures showing the exports from
the ports in Ulster.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): It was not so much as
that. I think it was three million
pounds. They were exports from Ulster
ports.
Mr. COLLINS: I know as regards the
export of poultry from Newry that they
are brought in over the Free State
border from Dundalk, and from Carrickmacross and other towns in County
Monaghan by the largest firm of poultry
exporters in the North of Ireland-
Messrs. Murphy-and part of the three
million pounds is going into the pockets
of Free State farmers, although the
poultry are going out of the North of
Ireland. I know myself that Donegal
eggs that come across the border into
Derry to be shipped are treated as imports into Northern Ireland, and you are
taking credit for that as exports going
out. Before I can be satisfied that all
is well with the poultry and egg position
I would like to know how much of the
stuff that went out of Northern ports was
created in the Irish Free State the
money for which has gone into the
pockets of Free State farmers.
The noble Lord (the Prime Minister)
has done us a good turn according to
what he said yesterday regarding the
working of the existing Land Purchase
Act for the unbought tenants. He has
told us that he is putting on the screw
and getting the Imperial people to fix the
1st May, 1929, as the "appointed day."
That is so far so good. If that promise
be carried out, on that day every tenant
who was an unbought tenant at the passing of the Act will get a reduction of
3s 8d in the £. I represent farmers
alongside the Border who are buying in
the same markets, selling the fowl in the
same markets as the County Louth
farmers who are getting a permanent reduction of 7s in the £, and these farmers
will only get 3s 8d as from the 1st May,
1929. Since the passing of the Free State
Act, 1923-I know this as I have clients
interested in it-all the Free State
tenants got an immediate reduction of
5s. Our tenants get none of that. We
feel that keenly. We feel that this differentiation is most unfair.
After all, it is right for me to tell you
that most of the people I represent desire
to be in the Free State. We are coerced
to be here, and when we are coerced into
coming here you should do something not
to worsen our position, but put us nearly
in as good a position as regards land
purchase as we would have been had the
Border not been created. We handed in
a Bill on the last occasion. The King's
Speech promises that the agricultural
position will get consideration. I hope
that the Government will give fair consideration to that. The figures of the
Minister of Finance, I understand, show
that this year we sent £1,400,000 to
England. England reserved the land
question herself. She did not entrust it
to you who represent the majority of the
people in the Six Counties. When she
did that you should reserve sufficient out
of the Imperial grant to compensate the
tenants here.

Mr. ARCHDALE: I do not intend to
occupy the time of the House very much.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
McAllister) was very much down on agriculture yesterday, and I had no chance of
correcting some of his figures.
He certainly is correct when he said that the
farmers have been down and out during
the last few years. He put it all down to
the Ministry of Agriculture, but he entirely forgot the clerk of the weather. I
have a note of the hon. Member's remark;
it was that when we took over agriculture
was in a prosperous condition.
I suppose opinions differ about that. He said
that we in the Ministry had done nothing
during the last six years to improve the
position of agriculture, and had let everything go on. Everyone knows that three
of the years we have had have been as
bad as could, I think, be experienced.
There was heavy rain from end to end;
all the crops were nearly destroyed, and
then there was an outbreak of fluke,
through which we lost an enormous number of cattle. That was during the years
1923-24 and also part of 1925.
What are the facts? During the past
few years there has been a tremendous increase in cattle. I think we will soon
have as many as ever we had. In 1927
there was an increase in cattle in Northern
Ireland of 30,000. The best thing of all
about our increase in cattle is that our
breeding stock are increasing more than
ever. In 1926 the in-calf heifer increase
was 10,000. In 1927 the increase in
breeding cattle- -cows and in-calf heifers
-was 11,500. In the last two years there
has been a greater increase in breeding
cattle than ever before. I think the
number of breeding cattle in Northern
Ireland in the last two years is almost
a record. The hon. Member (Mr.
McAllister) also charged us and the old
Ministry in Dublin with having ruined
the milk industry. What are the facts?
By milk recording and supplying dairy
bulls the milk supplies increased in 1926
by three million gallons over the year before. In 1927 the increase was 1,400,000
gallons over 1926. If you take the value
of milk at, say, sevenpence per gallon,
that would leave £44,000 more in the
pockets of farmers in 1927 than in 1925.
I think that is a considerable sum.
We know the farmers are in a bad
way, but anything that tends to increase
the money going into their pockets is
good. Certainly that is what has been
going on in the last year, and I hope it
will continue. The export of eggs,
which my hon. Friend the Member for
Armagh (Mr. Collins) spoke about, is
only through the Northern ports.
Mr. BEATTIE: And not produced in
Ulster.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The great majority
are produced in Ulster.
Mr. BEATTIE: What percentage is
produced in Ulster?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am afraid I did
not ask the mothers.

we
assist
Mr. ARCHDALE:
them in every possible way. (Laughter).

Then with the money which we were given

we placed bulls and boars. Now we are

year almost doubled the value of the
good black-faced lambs in the mountainous districts of County Antrim. The
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister)
can bear witness to that because he has

During the past year or so there has
been considerable talk about our bulls
being placed in places where they were
too well bred to stand the climate. Our
bulls are not all extra well bred and it
is the County Agricultural Committees
that place the bulls. During the present

for nothing at all. The farmer gets

state. In regard to land purchase, which
the hon. Member spoke about, I think
our system of land purchase is a great
deal better than that in the Free State.
Mr. COLLINS: Explain.
Mr. ARCHDALE: In Northern Ireland when a man buys his land it is his
own, but in the Free State it belongs to
the Government. The Government cau
come in at any time and take any portion
of that land it likes and let him do with
the rest.
Mr. COLLINS: Are you not going to
do that with the roads this year? Do I
understand the Minister of Agriculture is

nothing?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am not going to
try to say that two and four make eight,
but I do say it is a great advantage to a

Cooper) reminds me that a great many

Mr. COLLINS. Good gracious!
Mr. ARCHDALE: In Belcoo and

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Do
you not mark them?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I hope, and the

Mr. COLLINS: Would I be in order

in this area. Since he has got to the
of
other side of the House his ardour has

In trying to justify the programme in

long as I am top dog and there is no

"As
The hon. and learned Member for
Armagh (Mr. Davison) said the first step
necessary for the Government was to
realize the state of affairs in the agricultural industry. That has really been the
great trouble. The Government have
seemed so much out of touch with agricultural opinion and agricultural conditions that they have failed to realize the
seriousness of the state of affairs. Take
the reference to agriculture in the King's
Speech. What is there definite in it?
What does it mean? It may mean something or it may mean nothing. In other
directions definite promises are made by
the Government as to what they intend
to do, but the reference to agriculture is
an entirely indefinite matter and ends up
with a pious, Micawber-like hope that
something will turn up. That is the
extent of the reference to agriculture
made in the King's Speech.
There should have been a serious attempt on the part of the Government to
get to the root causes and to give real
assistance to our basic industry.
A great
effort should be made to develop our
dairying industry. We are all glad to
hear the figures the Minister of Agriculture has put before the House with regard
to the increase in the quantity of milk.
I do not know whether those are general
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
7 MARCH 1928

figures or whether they apply only to
milk-recording societies, but we are glad
of them. Still we have got to face the
fact that the exports of butter from
Northern Ireland are only about onethird what they were twelve years ago.
There is some cause for that, and I think
the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
McAllister) was justified to some extent
in blaming the policy of the old Department of Agriculture, and that of the present Ministry of Agriculture, in insisting
on pure-bred shorthorn bulls being the
only bulls that could get premiums in this
area.
These bulls were almost entirely bred
for beef, and I feel that to some extent
the decrease in our dairying industry is
due to that fact. I am, however, pleased
the Minister of Agriculture has said they
have to some extent modified this policy,
and that this year they are adopting
another policy. The campaign carried on
with regard to supplying suitable bulls
has had some effect. I hope the Ministry
will keep before them the desirability
that these bulls should if possible have a
good milk record. Our dairying industry
really needs to be reorganized, and I have
a feeling that in the success of our dairying industry lies the key to tillage farming.
There must be some determined effort
made to put an end to the decline in tillage farming. If we could successfully reorganize our dairying industry it would
probably prove the key.
Could there not have been something
done on a big way with regard to supplying cheap credits to farmers? It is admitted on all hands that at the present
time the farmers have been suffering from
a lack of capital owing to four or five bad
seasons and owing to falling prices and the
high cost of production. They have done.
something, but they have done it in a
way that, to my mind, encourages grazing
farming more than tillage farming. They
have given cheap loans to replace stock
that these men lost during the very wet
years, but these loans are confined to men
who have lost stock. Could the Government not do something in a bigger way,
in a general way along the lines of cheap
credit, to enable the farmers to meet
the present difficult times and to develop
their holdings? And could they not devise some scheme whereby the poorer farmers could get cheap loans for the improvement of their dwellings? A great
many of our small farmers are really the
worst housed people in our area.
This is
a question that has been raised time and
again in this House by the hon. Member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh, and I do
hope that something will be done to meet
what I believe is a very crying need.
Could not something be done along the
line of utilizing some of the money that
is being spent on unproductive purposes
for the relief of unemployment at the
present time for providing cheap lime for
our farmers? There is no more useful
manure than lime at the present time.
On the small farm on which I was reared,
I remember, as a boy, we used to put 10
or 12 tons of lime on the land every year.
Now I do not suppose that land has seen
lime for the past ten or twelve years.
There is no better fertilizer than lime,
but the price at present is beyond what
the farmer can pay. Could the Government not utilize some of the money that
is at present being spent in unproductive
ways for unemployment to provide lime
and to give it a reasonable and cheap rate
to the farmers?
There is another question I want to
bring before the Government. I do not
see why the Government should not extend the period for the repayment of advances under the Land Purchase Act,
and so reduce the present charges. This
was done in the case of the Ashbourne
Act. Under the Ashbourne Act the
period was 49 years. It was extended to
79 years, and that extension enabled the
Government of the day to give the
tenants three seperate reductions of ten
per cent.
What has been done surely
could be done. Surely it would be possible
for the Government to devise a scheme,
because I understand that the Government have in their hands the collection
of these annuities. Surely it would not
be beyond the ability and capacity of our
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) to devise a scheme whereby the period of repayment could be extended, and so give.
these men much needed relief at the present critical time.

The next important question that the

was going along very nicely. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) stated here

I am glad that the Government have

guidance to the Government of Northern
Ireland, and I have asked the Government here again and again to come down

this Government might have been frank

hiin. What I understood the Prime

Then with regard to the Bann drainage, the Prime Minister said that no loss
had occurred by the delay. I think
there is a loss occurring every year that
this question is deferred. Will the farmers who lost their crops this past season
say there was no loss by delay? The
Minister of Finance said they were very
anxious to make sure before they would
spend this money that it would accomplish
what they intended it for. He said
£200,000 had been spent before without doing any good. I wonder if one
of the reasons for that was that the
former Drainage Act was coupled with a
Navigation Act that has never benefited
anybody and never helped any industry.
It was always a drag on the ratepayers
and no help. I know that the farmers
along the Bann edge are largely of
opinion that this Navigation Act should
be scrapped, and if the Lower Bann were
given free flow and the weirs taken off,
it would obviate to a great extent the
flooding of the Lower Bann.
This other scheme that is now before
us is to be coupled, I understand, with
a hydro-electric scheme. I must say
that I am really afraid of coupling a
Government scheme with a scheme promoted by a private company for producing electricity. I have no objection to
the Bann being harnessed to produce |
cheap power. It is one of the things that
industry needs most at the present time.
But I do think it is a dangerous thing
to couple a Government scheme for draining the Bann with a scheme promoted by
a private company for producing electricity. I do not know how you will couple
the two schemes together. It seems to
me that the man in the street does not
think a river can be drained by putting
a barrage across it. With regard to the
cost I would like to say there was a
scheme for the drainage of the Bann put
before this country by an eminent
engineer appointed by the Imperial Parliament in 1906, Sir Alexander Binnie.
His estimate for draining the Bann was,
I think, £76,000. I do not know what
objection can be taken to that scheme.
I think that probably one of the reasons
it was not carried out was this: When
the scheme was put before the Government of the day they sent a valuer to
value the land that was flooded and to
say what would be the increased letting
value after drainage. That report of
Mr. Bell was published in 1908 and the
total amount that he valued the benefit
in the flooded lands was somewhere about
£900. That was one of the reasons the
Imperial Parliament did not carry out
that scheme.
The Minister of Finance suggested yesterday that this was largely a National
affair. I agree with him, because the
Bann drains to a great extent the whole
catchment area. Of course, I think the
Minister of Finance rather exaggerated,
because there is a great deal of flat land
down the Lough, then it rises abruptly.
However, I think he said enough to prove
that this was a National thing, and I do
not see why the Government should not
take this as a National charge. Take
these farmers along the Bann. They
have been paying for I do not know how
many years a very heavy drainage rate
for works that do not drain at all.
these farmers get another rate on top of
that? Are they going to bear another
rate at the present time?

thing I feel is this: If our financial relations are such that any savings that are

So that the only charge made was in regard to the difference between the Land
Purchase Bill applicable to Northern

State Land Purchase Bill that we hear

Free State and the value of land in Northern Ireland is obtained from comparative auctions held on one side of the
Border and the other. It may be information to the hon. Member opposite
to know that a farm of land in Northern
Ireland will, perhaps, bring twice as
much as a farm of similar size and area in
the Irish Free State.
Mr. HARBISON: No, no.
Mr. ELLIOTT: That can be proved by
figures. He did not tell us that the
Irish Free State Land Bill, which may
be a good one as far as the Irish Free
State is concerned, gives the Government,
not the opportunity but the right to go
on to a farm, any man's farm, and distribute it, cut it up, as they think right,
and that the owner gets compensation
only according to the amount at which he
purchased his farm. His improvements
go by the board. I do not think our
Northern Ireland farmers to-day would
want a Land Purchase Bill like that. I
have asked several of them whether they
preferred the Land Purchase Bill of the
Irish Free State to the Land Purchase
Bill that applies to Northern Ireland, and
they certainly preferred the Northern
Ireland Land Purchase Bill. In spite
of the fact that the Land Purchase Bill in
the South is such a benefit to the agricultural community, I find that far more
inquiries come to the auctioneers in
Northern Ireland as to the sale of land
in Northern Ireland than as to the sale
of land in the Irish Free State. I think
that speaks for itself.

Now, dealing with the question of the

of the bulls, because if you confine them

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 15th March, 1927.
The Third Session of the Second Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 15th March, 1927, in the Seventeenth
year in the reign of King George V, was
opened by the Governor (His Grace the
Duke of Abercorn, K.P.) in person.
The House met at Five minutes before
Twelve of the clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Most hon. the Marquess of Dufferin and
Ava, D.S.O., D.L.) in the Chair.
KING'S SPEECH.
His Grace the Governor being seated
on the Throne, commanded the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod to let the
Commons know "It is His Grace's
pleasure that they attend him immediately
in this House."
The Commons being at the Bar with
their Speaker, His Grace delivered the
following Speech from the Throne:-
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
It is a matter of profound gratification that such a considerable improvement has taken place in regard to
Unemployment. To-day the number
registered at the Employment Exchanges as out of work is 37,125 as
compared with 64,000 a little over a
year ago. This improvement has been
most marked in the Linen Industry,
and has been reflected in the important
shirt and collar manufacturing trade
in Londonderry. A year ago I referred to the financial assistance which
my Government was rendering to the
advertising of Ulster linen in the
United States of America and I am
glad to know that this effort is bearing
fruit. Further contributory causes
towards the improvement have been the
stabilization of foreign exchanges and a
widespread recognition of the fact that
prices have now fallen to a firm level.
I am also glad to observe that the
Shipbuilding Industry is sharing in the
revival in trade. My Government
is continuing the Loans Guarantee
King's Speech
Papers Presented
THE SENATE
facilities to foster further trade whereever possible.
I earnestly pray that those engaged
in the various industries of Northern
Ireland will use their utmost endeavours
to ensure that the improvement in
the volume of employment will be
maintained.
Proposals will be laid before you with
Road
the object of according to
Authorities further powers in connection with the improvement of the roads
generally and particularly in relation
to widening and rounding-off corners,
with the object of reducing risks of
road accidents to the lowest possible
dimensions.
As it was not found possible to
complete the necessary arrangements
to admit of legislation being introduced
during last Session in regard to the
minor difficulties which have arisen in
the interpretation and administration
of the intoxicating Liquor Act, I
trust that the Bill which is now to be
laid before you will receive your earnest
consideration.
A Bill will be submitted to you to
deal with the evil of the worrying of
sheep and cattle by dogs.
It is also proposed to bring the
existing arrangements for the provision
of funds for the erection of labourers'
cottages by Rural District Councils
more into harmony with the system
which is already in operation in
connection with the provision of capital
funds for Urban housing and Local
Government services generally.
Other Bills will be laid before you
dealing with the following matters: ---
To make provision regarding Unemployment Insurance.
To protect persons engaged on
painting work against the
dangers of Lead Poisoning.
To amend and consolidate the law
relating to Workmen's Compensation.
To extend the powers of Railway Companies with regard to
the owning and running of
omnibuses.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
My Government has caused an expert
investigation of the potentialities of
Coastal Harbours to be undertaken
with a view to the development of the
Fishery Industry of Northern Ireland,
and has set up a Departmental Committee to inquire into the marketing of
Agricultural Produce.
I
pray that your
deliberations may,
under the Divine blessing, result in the
happiness and contentment of the
people of Northern Ireland.
Then His Grace was pleased to retire,
and the Commons withdrew.
The House adjourned during pleasure.
The House resumed.

THE SENATE

NEW MEMBER SWORN..
Mr. James Hamilton, sworn, and took

ADDRESS IN REPLY TO
HIS MAJESTY'S MOST GRACIOUS
SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER having read the King's
Speech,
Mr. BARBOUR (in morning dress):
I beg to move: That a humble Address
be presented to his Grace in the following
words:
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Senate of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, beg
leave to offer our humble thanks to
your Grace for the Speech which your
Grace has addressed to both Houses of
Parliament.
With that touch of human sympathy
and that deep interest in his subjects'
welfare, His Majesty opens his Speech by
calling our attention to the somewhat
brighter business outlook which at long
last seems to be opening up.
The linen industry seems to be beginning to come back to its own, and the
Government are to be congratulated on
the measure of support which it gave to
the advertising campaign which was initiated in the United States, which is the
most important market for our linens.
This, in conjunction with the increased.
activities in the shipyards, goes a long
way to dispel the cloud of pessimism which
has for so long been overshadowing our
two main urban industries.
The public generally will welcome the
giving of further facilities to our road
authorities whereby the use of our roads
may be rendered less dangerous.
This may seem to some an unimportant
Measure, but one has only to read the

Press with a little care to realize what a
serious question it is. Local Authorities
up to now may possibly not have done all
that a critical public might think they
should, but while it is easy for anyone to
point out a danger, it is not always easy
to gain the consent of a reluctant owner
for the land necessary to remedy the evil.
Any Measure which will facilitate procedure, without undue hardship on
private ownership, will be generally
welcomed.
In a piece of major legislation such as
our Intoxicating Liquor Act, it is only
reasonable that with the lapse of time
and experience gained in the working of
the Act some minor anomalies should
come to light and need rectification.
The sheep and cattle raisers of the
country will be glad to know that an
effort is to be made to cope with the
hardship to which they are subjected
in the matter of dogs molesting their
animals.
I am sure that this House will give its
cordial support to any Measure which
will provide the means of facilitating the
economical erection of cottages in rural
areas.
The other Bills mentioned in the Royal
Speech speak for themselves, with the
exception of the proposal to allow railways
to add to the existing number of omnibuses plying on our roads. Being of a
somewhat bucolic mentality I confess I
regard this proposal with some anxiety.
I confess that I had noticed no lack of this
means of transit in any part of Northern
Ireland in which I had been. In fact it
has occurred to me that some of our roads
were rather overworked in this respect,
and that the lives of His Majesty's loyal
subjects in some localities might be likely
to last longer if the number of omnibuses
could be reduced rather than increased.

Though late in the day, perhaps, I

My second reference is to the dissatisfaction of Secondary School teachers with
the present provision for superannuation.
I would appeal to the Government to
grant such increase in the pension scale
as would place them more on a par with
the teachers in England, and remove what
I regard as their most reasonable claim on
the administration.
I cannot speak concerning agriculture
with the authority of Senator Barbour,
but I think the entire community will
welcome the decision of the Government
to appoint a Committee to inquire into
prices, transport, and the marketing of
agricultural produce. This is another
illustration of the anxiety of the Government to advance the interests of the leading industry of the Province.
With regard to the King's Speech, it is
certainly encouraging to note the great
diminution in the number of the unemployed. Everyone must long for the time
when our industries will have absorbed
those who are really willing to work, but
for whom there is no work. The evils of
the existing state of affairs are too well
known and too rightly deplored to need
any comment from me.
