Reference has been made to the shirt
and collar manufacturing trade
Londonderry. Our new colleague, the
Mayor of Derry, will be a better exponent
of that than I, but I myself have visited
some of the manufacturers, and they tell
me what I am sure will be pleasant information; that although many of the
advantages which Derry once possessed in
competition with other centres have disappeared, notwithstanding this the conditions during the strike, and at the
present time were and are much better
than might have been expected, and it is
hoped that with better times in Great
Britain those healthy conditions may be
prolonged if not improved upon.
The revival in the shipbuilding trade
must prove of great benefit to the City
of Belfast. Would that there were any
prospect of the Derry yard resuming, but
it is at least hopeful that the company
and plant are still in existence and ready
to start should circumstances make it
possible.
I was interested to read in the Press
of the discovery of a new material woven
from flax and artificial silk which is said
to promise well for the weaving industry
of Northern Ireland, and which may still
further diminish the number now seeking
employment.
As regards the forecast of legislation,
compared with the previous Speech from
the Throne, we are all, I believe, gratified

practical kind, and designed to further
the best interests of the Province. The
Prime Minister of what is henceforth
to be termed the Parliament and Government of the United Kingdom of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland, in defending the modest programme submitted at
the beginning of a new Session, said it
was chought well not to attempt too much,
but rather to submit a programme which
it was possible to carry into effect.
other words, it was considered better to
set before Parliament a programme with
which it could comfortably deal rather
than one so over-loaded that most of it
had in the end to be jettisoned, while that
which was attempted was because of the
rush and crush, often crude and ill
digested.

will be given sufficient matter to engage

Mr. DORMAN: I wish in the first
place to express my appreciation of the
very able manner in which the Address
to His Grace the Governor has been moved
and seconded. I am sure that the reduction in the number of unemployed is,
as the Speech from the Throne states, a
matter of profound satisfaction to us all.
I recognise that the Government of
Northern Ireland has probably had to
face a more gigantic problem in this respect than has had to be faced in any of
the States constituting the great British
Empire or the Commonwealth of Nations,
inasmuch as our industry was in pre-war
times largely for a world market, and,
therefore, an old-established Government
would have had a very great advantage
in meeting the post-war difficulties that
arose in consequence of the dislocation of
the markets of the world which were
largely the customers of this particular
area of Northern Ireland.
I think the figures are still lamentable

I
from the point of view of the loss that
we are sustaining in potential wealth by
the enforced unemployment of men and
women who are prepared to enter industry and produce something in return.
for that which they are consuming.
think it would be a low estimate to
calculate that probably over £5,000,000
will be lost in production to the State
during next year if the present number
of unemployed are necessarily kept in enforced unemployment during that particular period. The effects upon many of
the young men who are in the early stage
of their journeymenship is certainly
disastrous. Large numbers of them who
have completed their time as skilled
artisans have been unemployed for one,
two, or three years, and while unemployed
they will be losing the adaptability they

We are also, I am sure, gratified that
the Government is taking steps to safeguard the public and motorists from the
dangers to which they are exposed by
corners in the various roads which obscure
vehicles at an angle in the roads on which
motorists are travelling from day to day.
Any legislation to reduce the number of
accidents due to that cause will be
welcome.
I do not like to have to strike a note
of anything like discord. I would
personally wish to be able to give my full
support to the Address, but circumstances
exist in our midst to-day of such a
character that I feel I must necessarily
voice an expression of regret in the
following Amendment, which I move to
be added to the Address:
but regret that in the Gracious Speech
from the Throne no mention has been
made of any intention of the Government to amend the Rent Restriction
Act so as to provide adequate protection
for the tenants of the Six Counties.
This is a very pressing question indeed
so far as the most helpless part of the
community is concerned. Since the prewar period there has been an increase of
approximately 700 per cent. of one-room
dwellers in the City of Belfast. When
first looked at these figures do not seem
to convey very much, but when one
examines them it is found that the
number of one-room dwellers, which include from three to six persons per room,
has increased to an enormous extent in
comparison with the general increase in
one-room dwellers. The number of rooms
in which are resident three, four, five,
and six persons has increased by from 700
to 1,200 per cent. compared with the prewar period, the result of that being that
owing to the congestion the bread-winners
suffer more from sickness and the children
suffer from overcrowding.
The large increase in the death rate
amongst the citizens of Belfast is due to
the ever increasing number of the workingclass population who are forced to resort
to one-room dwellings. It may surprise
some of the Members of the Senate when
I tell them that the one-room dwellers
to-day in Belfast are actually paying more
rent for their single apartments than
would have enabled them in pre-war times
to have maintained a residence with four,
five, six, seven and eight apartments. There
are numerous portions of the city in which
one-room dwellers are paying from 8s to
15s per week for a single apartment in
which to house their families from week
to week.
Everyone who has studied the vital
statistics of any community knows that
the death rate amongst one-room dwellers
is more than double the death rate
amongst those who are more fortunately
circumstanced. I therefore wish to express the hope that the Government will
see its way to amend the Rent Restriction
Act so as to protect the tenant from the
evils that prevail to-day. If some step is
not taken to protect the tenants in this
matter the result will inevitably be that
the conditions will become more intense,
the sickness amongst these one-room
dwellers will be increased, the death
rate will be increased, and charges
will be heaped upon the local Boards that
would be obviated if proper housing
accommodation was within the reach of
the people.

Another matter which I note
Government are to deal with is the worrying of sheep and cattle by dogs. I have
no idea what the proposals of the Government are, but it is a matter in which
legislation is long overdue. In the
County of Londonderry the County
Council has made a Regulation that dogs
must be under control from sunset to
sunrise, but for some reason or other that
regulation seems to be ignored, and very
few dogs are under control during those
hours. The fault is not altogether that
of the Constabulary, because it is very
difficult to detect a dog in a country place
on a dark night, and also discover who
the owner is. However, I hope and trust
that the Government have found a way
to deal effectively with this pressing
matter.
The other matter on which I am pleased
to note the Government are going to bring
in legislation is in regard to the provision
of funds for the erection of labourers'
cottages. The Rural District Councils
are in a difficulty with regard to the provision of cottages. They find it is almost
impossible to provide cottages under the
present Regulations at a rent which the
agricultural labourer can pay, and
although cottages are very much needed
in many districts the Rural District
Councils are reluctant to put on the rates
the sum that would be necessary if these
cottages were erected.
I should like to join the mover and
seconder of the Address in expressing the

received the visit of the Prime Minister
and the Minister of Home Affairs in the

Without fee or rethe
ward, and often exposed to unfriendly

naturally enough, to the fall in unemployment which is disclosed in the Gracious
Speech. It is a matter indeed for profound
gratification that, although unemployment does press heavily upon us still, the
percentage of unemployed amongst us
appears to be now only three per cent.
This time last year it was almost double
that figure. I think that percentage is

and we hope that in time there may be

a
The hon. Senator who moved the
Amendment to the Address gave us
harrowing picture of the number of
people in Belfast who are condemned to
pass their family life in single-roomed
houses, and he suggested, if I understood
him correctly, that something could be
done to mitigate the evil by the amendment of the Rent Restriction Acts. I
am afraid that I do not quite follow the
chain of reasoning by which he arrived.
at that conclusion. It seems to me that
if you want to prevent whole families
living in one-roomed houses the first requirement is that there should be an
adequate supply of houses of more than
one room for them to resort to. It does
not seem to me that any alteration in the
rents of existing houses has any bearing
on the question, unless it can be shown
that there is a substantial number of unoccupied houses at present in the area
under discussion. The hon. Senator did
not give us any figures pointing to the
fact that houses in Belfast generally were
unoccupied, and I think that we should
require definite and reliable information
on that point before we start off in chase
of what I am afraid I must regard as a
will-o'-the-wisp. But I am not, of
course, to be understood as in any way
decrying the evil of insufficient housing
accommodation, nor the evil of overcrowding. It is an evil which is not
entirely of modern days. It has been
dealt with by reformers for certainly the
better part of a century.
Now, passing to the actual Gracious
Speech itself, and the Measures the production of which it forecasts, to some
extent I think it will be found that the
majority of the Measures mentioned will
be based on legislation recently introduced in England. For instance there is
the proposal to legislate in the matter of
lead poisoning. A Measure for the
protection of our workers against the illeffects of dangerous trades has occupied
the attention of Parliament across the
water for many years past. There are
several Measures dealing with that. We
have ourselves already followed to some
extent in the footsteps of those who have
been working in that way in England,
and I am sure we will be quite ready
to adopt any well-thought-out proposal
for following on the same lines. That
matter of dangerous trades is one of
those on which it is absolutely imperative
we should keep strictly on all fours lest
we should allow Northern Ireland to become an experimenting ground for proceedings forbidden across the water and
which might be permissible here.
I observe that something is to be done
in the way of amending and consolidating
the law of Workmen's Compensation. I
am sure we shall welcome that Measure.
It is, if I may say so, due to us. The
House, I think, will share my recollection
that it is now some three years since it
was necessary for us to pass a Measure,
with a celerity which occasioned some
remark at the time-not criticism. But
when some three years ago we were confronted with a Workmen's Compensation
Act, it was clearly understood that the
Bill was not to remain for any length of
time on the Statute Book, but that a consolidating Measure should be introduced
at the earliest practicable moment. That
moment it seems has now very nearly
arrived, and I am sure we shall be prepared to deal with a Measure that is
likely to be somewhat lengthy and possibly of some complexity, though not in
any way controversial. We shall be prepared to give that Measure the consideration which it will demand.
As regards dogs, I am sure that our
farmers and all those interested in
sheep raising-and with sheep may be
included other forms of animal lifewill welcome the assurance that that
matter is to be dealt with. Those of
us who live in the country, and who
endeavour to keep sheep, and particularly
those of us who endeavour to breed sheep,
are aware from bitter personal experience
of the heavy losses which are occasioned
by the ravages of dogs. These dogs do
not, unhappily, limit their operations to
night time. They worry sheep just as
much sometimes in the day as at night.
I am afraid that nothing-no further
Debate on Address

THE SENATE
Debate on Address
[Mr. Leslie]
restrictions, as regards licence duty or as
regards collars with name and address
attached will be of any use. I am afraid
that what we require is something that
will practically ensure, so far as we can
ensure, the destruction of dogs wandering
at will about the country where there are
sheep and other attractive forms of animal
life to damage, and will require that
those dogs should practically be treated
as wild beasts and be destroyed as such.
Nothing less than that, I am afraid,
would meet the evil which has grown
to enormous size. Nothing less than
that would protect our strictly
domestic animals, such as sheep from
sufferings which it is impossible
to contemplate with a calm mind.
One has seen sheep so worried and torn
as to be unable to move. One has seen
sheep with legs practically raw while the
sheep were alive, and it has been found
necessary to bestow on the sheep an end
to its life which might have been more
happily bestowed on the particular dog
which was the author of the evil. The
evil has grown to immense proportions,
and we are gratified to hear that it is
about to be dealt with.
Taking the Speech as a whole I am sure
we shall be happy-all of us, on reconsideration to join in the Address of this
House, and that we shall feel that the
opening of our work of this Session has
been auspiciously begun.

travelling to the country I can get a return ticket from Belfast to Magherafelt
or Ballymoney almost one hundred per
cent. cheaper than a railway ticket, but
by going by bus I am only employing two
men, and these men are in a great many
cases paid a very small wage. When I
travel by rail I am employing a large
number of men, and although I benefit by
travelling by bus I do not want to be selfish. I want to sacrifice something for
the benefit of my fellowmen. I have
great pleasure in congratulating the mover
and seconder of the Address upon their
speeches, and I hope that before this
Session is over some very useful legisla.
tion will be passed for the benefit of the
whole community.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
THE SENATE
Mr. SAMUEL CUNNINGHAM: In
rising to speak to this Motion I would
like first of all to congratulate the mover
of the Address on the very full and interesting speech he gave us, and might
I say how pleased we all were to see his
brother, the Minister of Commerce, sitting beside him on that auspicious occasion. I would also like to say how much
I appreciate the very able speech of Senator Glendinning in seconding the Address
in Reply.
In looking through the Gracious
Speech, there is one point I would like
to draw attention to. The Government
refer to the financial assistance they rendered to the linen trade in advertising
linen, and they rightly take credit for it.
I think we all know that if advertising is
not followed up the money spent is
not of much service. If we go to
London or to America to buy linen
goods we do not know whether
or
not we are getting linen. We may get
cotton goods made locally and finished
with a linen finish. This may be bought
by a lady, and when she gets it home she
may discover it is only cotton that she
could have bought as cotton. This gives
a bad name to the linen trade, and it
would be of great benefit if the Government would follow up what they have
already done by adopting some system of
inspection with the object of ensuring
that material which is labelled as Enen in
London or anywhere else is really linen,
and that the buyer is getting honest value
for his or her money, and that he is getting flax when he is paying for flax.
If the Government took some such step
as I suggest we should have our tables
covered with white linen tablecloths
sooner than by any other means. I am sorry
the Minister of Commerce is not present
to tell us whether anything can be done
in this connect on, but I wish to draw the
attention of the Government to the matter. In conclusion, I think the speech
from the Throne is short and to the point,
and we have every reason to hope that the
Measures forecasted in it will be of great
benefit to the community. I therefore
most heartily support the Motion.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT (Leader
of the House): I should like to be permitted, at the outset of my speech, to
make a brief reference to the high honour
which His Gracious Majesty the King was
pleased to bestow upon our Prime Minister
at the beginning of the year, mention of
which has already been made by the hon.
Senators who have moved and seconded
the Humble Address. I believe that
every hon. Member of this House, no
matter what his political creed and convictions may be, will join with us in
congratulations to the man who, through
stress and strain, has laboured unceasingly to bring peace and tranquillity to
Northern Ireland.

When His Majesty came in person,
almost six years ago, to open our First
Parliament, he expressed himself as
'confident that the important matters
entrusted to the control and guidance of
the Northern Parliament would be
managed with wisdom and with moderation, with fairness and due regard to
every faith and interest and with no
abatement of patriotic devotion to the
Empire." The signal distinction which
he has now seen fit to confer upon the
Head of our Government may be accepted,
I think, as a clear indication that that
confidence was well founded, and that to
our Prime Minister, above all, is due the
greatest praise for the sane and successful administration of the affairs of
Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
I am only echoing the feelings of every
Member of this House when I offer my
congratulations to the mover and
seconder of the Humble Address upon
the felicitous manner in which they delivered their speeches. The hon. Senator
who moved the Address bears a name
which is known, I am sure, to every
citizen of Northern Ireland and which is
recognized by them as connoting public
service in the highest and truest sense,
love of one's fellow-men, and zeal for the
well-being of the State. As you are all
aware, Mr. Barbour has been for the past
twenty years an untiring worker in the
cause of agriculture, seeking especially
to promote amongst the farmers of this
country those methods of co-operation
which are admitted to be essential to the
success of our chief industry.
For almost an equal length of time he
has been prominently identified with the
local government of his own county, and
more recently he has added to the
obligations which the State already owes
him by assuming the Chairmanship of the
Education Committee, which is engaged
in his own part of County Antrim in
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
15 MARCH 1927
carrying out the duties imposed upon
local authorities by the Education Act of
1923. But it is unnecessary for me to
recount at length the various claims
which the hon. Senator has upon the
gratitude of Northern Ireland. We in
this House welcome him, not only for his
good works, but for his charm of personality, and we shall be forgiven, I trust,
if we express a regret that the responsibilities which he has lately undertaken in
a distant part of our Empire deprive us
oftener than we would wish of his counsel
and assistance in this Chamber.
The hon. Senator who seconded the
Motion is also very well known throughout Northern Ireland, and particularly
SO in his own city of Londonderry.
where he has always stood as the embodiment of those loyalist principles which we
in this part of Ireland are proud to
cherish so fervently. A constant worker
for the welfare of his own native city,
he has not been unmindful of the duty
which every good citizen must owe to the
State as a whole, and the Members of
this House have always listened with
pleasure and benefit to the contributions
which he makes from time to time to our
debates.
The legislative programme which is
outlined in the Gracious Speech from the
Throne is not as ambitious or as varied
in aspect as that which was presented to
us a year ago, but, nevertheless, Bills
will be introduced which are of great importance. You will be asked to consider,
amongst others, a Bill under which local
road authorities will be accorded increased powers in regard to the improvement and the widening of public roads.
Danger to the travelling public arises
from two main causes. Under the first
head come either defects in the vehicle,
defects in the driver, or carelessness and
negligence; while under the second head
may be grouped such factors as narrow
roads, blind corners, obstructions, etc.
Steps have already been taken by Parliament to remove or remedy the first class
of factors, and it is now considered, as a
natural corollary, that every possible
effort should be taken to remove any defects in our road system which might be
conducive to the danger of the person or
property.
The improvement of roads has been
well maintained during the year. Grants
have been made from the Road Fund in
aid of expenditure by local authorities.
amounting to over £50,000, an amount
which is nearly four times the grant paid
at the time of the transfer of services to
Northern Ireland.
An important step in connection with.
the improvement of road traffic conditions was taken by our Parliament last
year when it passed the Motor Vehicles
Act. This Act, introduced, as hon.
Senators are aware, the principle of
differentiation in regard to motoring
offences by specifying substantial penalties for those offences which are conducive
to the danger of those using the roads and
by applying a more modified scale of
penalties for simple technical offences.
The most important element in the Act,
however, is contained in Part II, which
establishes for the first time in Northern
Ireland-or, indeed, in any part of the
United Kingdom-the principle
central control and licensing of public
service vehicles. This portion of the Act.
will probably come into full operation in
the course of a few months.
of
The Gracious Speech referred to a Bill
which will be submitted to you and which
deals with the evil of the worrying of
cattle and sheep by dogs. Those of you
whose homes, like mine and Senator
Leslie's, are in the country, must often
have encountered instances where substantial loss has been caused to farmers
by reason of dogs worrying their stock,
and as Senator Leslie has said, that
worrying is not necessarily done by night.
I myself, it might be interesting to say,
lost four sheep in about a quarter of an
hour one afternoon between two, and
three. It has often been felt that existing legislation on the subject was to some
extent inadequate. The problem is an
extremely difficult one, but it is hoped
that a remedy may be found in the Bill
which will be laid before you during the
Session.
Hon. Senators will, I am sure, share to
the full the gratification expressed in the
Gracious Speech at the improvement
which has taken place in regard to
unemployment. Almost exactly a year
ago, when I made my first speech
leader of this House, I referred to the unhappy fact that more than 61,500 persons
were at that time unemployed. That
as

Debate on Address
THE SENATE
[Viscount Charlemont]
figure has now been decreased by over
24,000, and we shall all pray that the
corner has at last been turned and that
an era of prosperity is beginning to dawn
for the industries of Northern Ireland.
Every practicable opportunity of
fostering industry and creating additional
employment has been taken by the
Government, in conjunction with our
local authorities, who have continued to
bring forward relief schemes. Since the
prorogation of Parliament in November
last twenty-six schemes in different parts
of the Province have been approved, the
Government's contribution in respect of
the wages expended on unemployed men
specially engaged on these schemes being
estimated at more than £28,000. You
will be interested to learn that the total
number of relief schemes approved since
they were first initiated in May, 1922, is
783, while the estimated grant from the
Government has been £837,000. There
are at present over 1,400 men actually at
work on schemes of this nature.
The Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Contributory Pensions Scheme is gradually coming into fuller operation, the
number of widows benefiting having increased from 3,350 about a year ago to
4,283, while the figure for the dependant
children in receipt of allowances is now
9,890, as against 8,300. 1,123 orphans
are also in receipt of weekly payments.
In July of last year there came into
operation that part of the scheme which
enables Contributory Old-Age Pensions to
be paid to persons over 70 years of age on
an insurance qualification, and 4,495 pensions of this kind are now being paid,
bringing the total number of beneficiaries
under the new Act to 19,791 persons.
I may, perhaps mention here that there
has been an increase in the number of
firms enrolled on the King's National Roll
of Honour, and that there are 637 more
disabled ex-Servicemen employed to-day
than a year ago.
In other words, the
number of such men unemployed has
fallen by about one-third. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
The present position in the linen industry gives reasonable grounds for optimism as to the future. The difficulties
which were caused by the coal strike in
Great Britain last year have been overcome and a feeling of greater confidence
now obtains. Reports from Overseas
markets indicate that the demand for
linen goods is increasing, and you will be
glad to know that several local weaving
factories, which had been closed for a considerable time, have been reopened. The
unemployment figures for the industry are
at present lower than they have been at
any time during the past two years, and
while it is true that the export statistics
do not yet fully reflect the improvement
which has actually taken place, yet it may
be confidently anticipated that the values
of exports will increase during the next
few months. The linen publicity campaign which was recently launched in the
United States of America has already
proved productive of result, and sales of
damask goods are steadily increasing.
It is pleasing to be able to record that
the prospects for the shipbuilding industry
have also improved. The local firms have
secured substantial orders for both liner
and cargo vessels, which will give muchneeded employment to a sorely-tried
industry. Recent launches from the
Belfast shipyards have included some of
the finest motor-vessels in the world, and
it is very gratifying to find that we are
in the van in respect of the most modern
methods of shipbuilding.
I referred last year to the scheme of
loans which was brought into operation in
1925 by the Ministry of Agriculture,
whereby farmers, more particularly in the
poorer districts, were enabled to secure
money at a low rate of interest for the
purpose of replacing live stock which had
been lost in previous abnormal seasons.
The Government are aware that the repayment, at the present juncture, of the
first instalment of these loans would, in
certain exceptional cases, be a matter of
difficulty and hardship and it has been
decided that, so far as special cases are
concerned, an extension shall be granted
to the end of June of this year. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I may mention
that similar loans will be available again
this year and those farmers who are
des rous of obtaining the facilities which
they offer would be well advised to make
application to the Ministry of Agriculture
as soon as possible and, in any case, not
later than the end of next month.
Hon. Senators may, perhaps, remember
that a few years ago the Commission on
the Natural and Industrial Resources of
Northern Ireland, of which I had the

honour to be the Chairman, made an exhaustive investigation of the possibilities
of increasing the afforested areas of this
country. Certain recommendations were
submitted to the Government and I am
glad to be able to report that important
steps have now been taken in this direction. Arrangements have been completed
for the acquisition by the State of additional lands for forestry purposes, for the
supply to farmers, at cost price, of forest
plants grown in the nurseries of the
Ministry of Agriculture, and for the
making of grants to land-owners towards
the cost of preparing ground and planting
trees. A satisfactory feature of these extended forestry operations, and one which
will commend itself to this House, is that
they will provide an opportunity for
giving work to a certain amount of unskilled labour.
The Gracious Speech makes reference to
the setting up of a Departmental Committee to inquire into the Marketing of
Agricultural Produce. The Committee
will investigate the cost of transit of farm
produce and the reasons for the difference
which exists between the prices obtained
by producers and those paid by customers,
while the methods of marketing agricultural produce generally will be closely
scrutinised. No impartial and fairminded critic of the Government can
deny, I think, that every possible effort
is being made to place the agricultural
industry in a position to hold its own
against the increasingly severe competition which is being encountered at the
present day.
The administration of services in connection with jurisdiction, law and order
presented no unusual feature during the
year. You will have seen from the
Judges' Addresses to the various Grand
Juries at the Assizes that the state of the
country is, on the whole, very good and
compares favourably with previous years.
The alterations in the law relating to
juries, embodied in the Jury Laws
Amendment Act (Northern Ireland),
1926, and the Supreme Court of Judicature of Northern Ireland Act, 1926,
have come into operation generally and
are proving effective in equalising the
burden of jury services in Northern
Ireland.
Before I conclude I should like if I may
to say a few words about my own department, the Ministry of Education.
The hon. Senator who seconded the
Motion to the Address referred to the
recent agitation which has arisen in the
Press with regard to the salaries and
pensions of Secondary teachers. I can
assure the hon. Senator and all the other
Members of this House that the matters
of which complaint has been made have
been most carefully investigated by myself, and I am satisfied that, in all the circumstances, the Secondary Teachers of
Northern Ireland have been treated by
the State not only with justice but also
with generosity. I shall be happy if this
House desires it to give some more detailed statement on the whole subject at
a later period.
The year which has passed has been one
of normal progress, and the Education
Act is steadily being put into operation
throughout Northern Ireland. A great
deal of what may be called spade-work
has been done by the local education
authorities, the ground has been reviewed, and the task which lies before
them is now clearly appreciated.
Although this preliminary work must
from its very nature be comparatively
unobtrusive and to the onlooker unproductive of result, it is, nevertheless of
the greatest importance, for a sure
foundation is being laid upon which will
be built the educational system of the
future a system which I am confident
will prove to be worthy of the high hopes
which have been lavished upon it.

Lead Paint (Protection against Poisoning) Bill [S.]
Order for Second Reading read.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT (Leader
of the House): I beg to move, That this
Bill be now read a Second time. It is on
similar lines to an Act which was passed
by the Imperial Parliament last year, and
which came into operation in Great
Britain on the 1st of January of this year.
Lead poisoning amongst persons engaged in the manufacture and use of lead
paints is due principally to the use of
white lead which, on account of its marked
durability, is the principal lead compound
used in paints. A painful and distressing
disease, known as plumbism may be incurred, the results very often being fatal
to the unfortunate victims. The incidence of this form of poisoning has
occupied attention for many years,
and, with the permission of the House, I
shall give a short summary of the
negotiations and conferences which took
place in the past and which led up to the
passing of the Lead Paint Act by the
Imperial Parliament in 1926.
In 1911 the British Government
appointed two Departmental Committees
to investigate the danger attendant on
the use of lead paints in the painting of
buildings and vehicles. These Committees
satisfied themselves that lead poisoning
occurred to a serious extent in these two
trades, and that the main channel of lead
absorption was by the inhalation of dust
when surfaces which had previously been
painted with lead paint were being
rubbed down with dry sand-paper to produce the smoothness necessary for the
application of a fresh coat of paint.
These two Committees were of opinion
that efficient and non-poisonous substitutes
for white lead were available and that
their compulsory use would not lead to
financial loss, and they, therefore, recommended that the use of lead compounds
Lead Paint Bill-
Second Reading
24 MARCH 1927
and paints should be almost completely
prohibited. It should be borne in mind,
however, when considering the Reports
of these Committees, that at the time they
made their investigations dry rubbingdown was the only practicable method
in use, as waterproof sand-paper had not
been invented, and, furthermore, it had
not been ascertained definitely whether
the non-poisonous substitutes, which were
paints with a zinc base, would be as satisfactory under exposed weather conditions
as the lead paint which it was sought to
prohibit.
During the war, white lead available
for painting was reduced to a negligible
quantity, and paint manufacturers were
compelled to use a zinc base for paints to
a much greater extent than formerly. The
experience which was thus gained showed
that the zinc substitutes, when exposed to
humidity or hard wear, were much inferior to lead, unless they were protected
by enamel or varnish, thereby adding
materially to the cost of the work.
We come now to the First International
Labour Conference which was held at
Washington in 1919. At that Conference
a recommendation was passed which led
to the Women and Young Persons
(Employment in Lead Processes) Act of
1920, whereby regulations were imposed
in regard to the employment of women
and young persons under eighteen in any
process involving the use of lead compound if the process were such that dust
were produced from the compound, or
the persons employed were liable to be
splashed by it.
Two years later, in April, 1921, the
International Labour Conference, which
was held at Geneva, went a stage further
and considered the question of the prohibition of the use of white lead in painting.
Towards the end of the year, a draft Convention was agreed to
to prohibiting,
amongst other things, the use of white
lead and sulphate of lead in the internal
painting of buildings. It should be
noted that a Committee of Experts,
which had been set up to advise the
Conference was in favour, not of the
prohibition of lead paints, but of the
framing of Regulations as regards their
use, and the Chairman of this Committee
has stated that on the last day of the
Conference, when matters were rather
hurried, the Committee's recommendation was rejected, and the Convention
adopted upon arguments which were not
strictly scientific. I may add that this
draft Convention has never been adopted
by any part of the British Empire.
In the meantime, the Imperial Government had set up in the same year, 1921.
a Committee known as the Norman Committee, which was asked to re-examine
the ground explored by the two Departmental Committees in 1911 in the light of
the developments which had subsequently
taken place. The Norman Committee
examined a great number of witnesses,
who agreed generally that lead poisoning
among painters was due almost entirely
to the inhalation of lead dust, and that
this danger might be obviated by the use
of waterproof sand-paper and wet rubbing. As regards the durability of zinc
paints compared with lead paints, a series.
of practical tests was made which proved
conclusively that the lead paint was
greatly superior.
This Committee therefore reported that,
as there was no efficient substitute for
lead paint for outside painting and for
certain kinds of interior painting, and as
the danger arising from the inhalation
of dust could be obviated by the use of
waterproof sand-paper, it was of opinion
that the use of lead paint need not be
entirely prohibited for the painting of
buildings.
The next stage was the introduction,
in 1924, of a Bill in the Imperial Parliament, which was designed to give effect
to the Geneva Convention and to prohibit
the use of lead paint. The Measure,
however, was so strongly opposed that it
was withdrawn, and before the Government of the day was able to decide on
a new line of action a General Election
took place, which resulted in the return
of Mr. Baldwin's Ministry. In March
of last year that Government introduced
a Bill which provided for the regulation
of the use of lead paint, instead of prohibition, which the former Bill had
sought to secure. It received the Royal
Assent in December last, and came into
operation for Great Britain on the first
day of this year. During the passage
of the Bill in the Imperial Parliament
it was made quite clear that the Measure
was, to some extent, experimental, and
that if it were found that a system of
regulation was powerless to reduce the
number of workers smitten with the
Lead Paint Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Viscount Charlemont]
disease of plumbism, then the Government would not hesitate to bring in a
Bill for prohibition.
We come now to the position of
Northern Ireland with regard to this
difficult question; and I do not think
the Members of this House will require
an apology from me for having detained
them so long with a recital of the events
which led up to the Imperial Act of
last year. Our Government, that is the
Government of Northern Ireland, has
been moved by two main considerationsfirst, that every reasonable and possible
precaution should be taken to safeguard
workers in our painting industry from
falling victims to this terrible disease,
and, secondly, that the industry should
not be placed under any greater restriction or disadvantage than is absolutely
It
necessary to secure such safeguards.
is believed that the Bill now before the
House achieves these two objects.
It
asks that the Ministry of Labour be given
power to make Regulations for prohibiting, in connection with the painting of
buildings, the use of any lead compound
except in the form of paste or paint
ready for use; for the prevention of
danger arising from the application of
lead paint in the form of spray; for
prohibiting dry rubbing-down and scraping; for providing for the periodical
medical inspection of workers; for securing to the workers facilities for washing;
for the use of protective clothing; and
for the distribution of instructions regarding hygienic precautions.
The
If the Bill becomes law, every person
who employs other persons in painting
buildings, whether he uses lead paints in
his work or not, will be required to send
to the Ministry of Labour a written notice
stating his name and address, and he will
be obliged to keep at his office a register,
in the prescribed form, of the persons
employed by him in painting, and the
work on which they are employed.
Bill also provides for the notification by
employers of cases of lead poisoning
occurring to their employees, and gives
factory inspectors the same powers of
entry and inspection in any case where
persons are employed in painting buildings as they already have under the
Factory and Workshop Acts, in respect
of factories and workshops.
It is estimated that the Bill will bring
about 1,200 persons, comprising painters,
paper-hangers, and decorators within the
scope of the factory code for the first
time. It is, I think, a Bill which is
unlikely to provoke any controversial
criticism, for it is designed towards the
protection of our workers. I beg to
move.
Colonel SINCLAIR: After the admirable résumé of the object of this Bill
which has been furnished by the noble

been before not only the public but the
medical profession, and suggestions have
been made that it is high time that something was done. Members of the Senate
may not be aware that the mortality
of plumbism or lead poisoning is as high
as 22 per cent., and there has been in
the United Kingdom a matter of 500
cases a year of the more severe type,
not to mention persons who suffer from
the milder type of the disease and who
attend the extern department of the
hospitals.
I understand from the noble Viscount

if it is not sufficient for the purpose of
protecting the workers engaged in this
particular trade it will be followed by a
prohibitive Measure at some later date.
That is an uncertain period, and in the
case of a Bill such as this which may
not be, and in my judgment is not,
thorough enough to meet the case, there
is an inclination to let things drift for
a number of years and not follow what
I deem to be the better course of prohibiting the use of lead paint.

It is not my intention to divide the
Senate on a matter of this kind, because,
after all, the Bill is a step in the right
direction, and I think it would be unwise
to divide the House on it. But I cannot
allow the opportunity to pass without

that it is a step in the right direction,
but a very feeble step, and one which I
hope will ultimately be followed by a
more thorough Measure that will reduce
the incidence of this terrible disease and
the heavy mortality it entails.
The disease is one of insidious onset,
and it does not therefore attract so much
public attention as a more acute disease
with its tragic results. Nevertheless, it
is there, and in the more mild cases,
which are not so easily recognised, if
medical advice is not sought the amount
of misery and discomfort occasioned is
much greater than the statistics supplied
to the Home Office would indicate, as
these merely deal with the severe cases
and the mortality that takes place.

into account is the real ignorance of the

Year after year I have been working
with lead for jointing purposes on ships.
We use white lead to a considerable extent
for steam joints, and red lead is used to

for working with this material, and it is a

I am pleased to see that the Government are introducing this Bill, and I

would remove a great deal of the danger
to which workers are at present exposed,
because boys who are called upon to work
with this lead would appreciate its danger.

SECRECY OF THE BALLOT.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Dorman:
To ask the Leader of the House
whether, in view of the practise that
has become common in Belfast at Parliamentary and Local Government
elections of allowing persons who are
not appointed by the Returning Officer,
are not officers of the Law, and are not
sworn to secrecy to enter the polling
booths with the voters, the Government
will take steps to ensure that the secrecy
of the Ballot is preserved, by excluding
from the booths during the polling
hours all unauthorized and unsworn
persons.

Mr. DORMAN: I rise to draw the
attention of the Leader of the House to
the question I have put down on the
Order Paper. It has been my fortunate,
or unfortunate lot, to have contested elections in various parts of the country both
for Parliamentary and Local Government
bodies, and I have been struck by the
custom that has been allowed to grow up
at times of Parliamentary, Municipal,
and Poor Law elections in the City of
Belfast, of persons, as I have stated in
the question, other than persons appointed
by the Return ng Officer, persons who are
not officers of the law, and who are not
sworn to secrecy, entering the polling
booths. On many occasions these unauthorized persons have opportunities of
ascertaining how various electors cast
their votes, thus rendering the Ballot Act
inoperative so far as these elections are
concerned. It is well known that the
Ballot Act was placed on the Statute
Book to protect the elector from being
victimized in his means of living by others
discovering through the Ballot box his
political faith.
In justification for my putting down
this question, I would like to relate an
incident that took place at the last election. I have myself witnessed such incidents as this, having been a candidate in
several elections and having participated
in other elections as an official. At one
of the booths at which I was acting as a
tally clerk for a candidate at the last
election I happened to get out of the
tally room to observe what was going on
in the booth. I followed one man, who
was accompanying a woman, for about
thirty yards along a pathway, and he was
warning the woman to be very careful.
The man had in the lapel of his coat a
Party emblem, but I had no Party emblem in my coat.
The man entered the booth with the
lady voter and I attempted to follow
them, but immediately a representative
of the opposing candidate, who was wearing the colours of that candidate in the
lapel of his coat, peremptorily ordered me
out of the booth. I understood that I
had no legal right to be in the booth and
I immediately retired into the porch and
watched what took place. The man went
to the polling clerk with the woman, and
he also had the audacity to pass from the

secrecy of the Ballot is violated, as suggested in the hon. Member's question.
The returning officer is responsible for
the conduct of elections, and for the
appointment of presiding officers to preside at each polling station. The duty
of the presiding officer so appointed is to
keep order at his station, regulate the
number of electors to be admitted at a
time, and to exclude all other persons
except the clerks, the agents of the candidates, and constables on duty. The
duties of both the returning officer and
the presiding officer are prescribed by
statute, and they are each liable for any
wilful misfeasance or wilful act or omission in contravention of those duties.
The Under Sheriff of each county acts as
returning officer for Parliamentary Elections, and in the case of local government
elections, the principal officers of local
authorities act as returning officers.
Senator Dorman admitted that the
moment he drew the attention of the
presiding officer to the practice in the
particular case he mentioned it was immediately stopped, and therefore, I think
the case of the Government for non-interference is justified, on the ground that the
existing law is sufficient to deal with the
matter. At the same time I hope the
Kingstown Mail Route.

Agricultural Research Station Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT: I beg
to move, That this Bill be now read a
Second time. This is a Bill to give
effect to an agreement for the establishment of an Agricultural Research Station
for Northern Ireland, at Hillsborough,
Co. Down. A copy of the Agreement
appears in the schedule to the Bill.
In recent years both England and Scotland have increased and extended con-
57 Research Station Bill-

29 MARCH 1927
Second Reading
siderably their activities in the domain
of research, particularly in connection.
with the many perplexing problems which.
beset farmers in those countries. As,
however, the agricultural conditions
which prevail in our province are totally
distinct from those which obtain across
the Channel, our farmers have to contend with special problems for which there
is no analogy in either England or Scotland. Strong representations were made
to the Government by prominent agriculturists as to the need for investigating
these special problems, and when ultimately a carefully prepared scheme for
the institution of a Northern Ireland
Research Station for Agriculture was
submitted, it was supported by both the
Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry
of Finance.
The Station, as I have mentioned, will
be situated at Hillsborough, and will have
attached to it close on 500 acres of landportion of surplus lands acquired in connection with a residence for the Governor.
The Imperial Authorities have transferred these lands to our Government free
of charge. The principal, although not
the sole, purpose for which the
Station will utilize these lands will be
investigations on the nutrition of every
class of live stock-dairy cows, pigs,
poultry, etc.
There is no need to stress the importance of such work, particularly in view
of the lean years which farmers have
unfortunately experienced recently, but I
wish to utter a word of caution. From
remarks which I have observed from time
to time in the Press, some persons seem
to think of research as
a process for
mechanically turning out ready-made
solutions for agricultural troubles. This,
of course, is a complete misconception.
The word " research," as I need scarcely
remind the House connotes constant,
minute, and patient investigation, extending possibly over a series of seasons
before it could be definitely asserted that
a solution to the particular problem
under examination had been obtained.
The Station will be controlled and
managed by a Board of Trustees, whom it
is proposed in the Bill to incorporate as
"The Agricultural Research Institute of
Northern Ireland." The Board, which
is quite independent of any Government
Department, consists of nine members,
representing the Ministry of Agriculture,
the Agricultural Faculty of Queen's University, the Ulster Farmers' Union, and
the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society.
Under the agreement the Government,
in addition to handing over nearly 500
acres of land, will provide a capital sum
of £30,000 for buildings and for equipping and stocking the Station. The cost.
of maintaining and running the Station,
when completely organized, is estimated
at £3,000 per annum. This income will
be available from an Endowment Fund of
£60,000, which the Government will also
provide. All these sums will be paid
over to the Trustees by 31st March, 1932.
I beg to move.
Mr. PORTER PORTER: I would like
to make a few remarks on this Bill, and
to call the attention of the House to the
letters which are being written and the
speeches which are being made by certain
people in Ulster concerning the action of
the Ministry of Agriculture. Hon. Members have probably noticed that the people
who write these letters and make these
speeches are not really agriculturists. I
have read all the letters very carefully,
and I have tried to read the speeches, and
in no case have I found that the writer
or the speaker is a man with an agricultural training. I have not noticed that a
farmer from the district of the Ards,
which is perhaps the best farming district
in Ulster, has made any adverse criticism
of the Ministry of Agriculture. Perhaps
the Ministry have taken up the attitude
of treating the criticisms with the contempt they perhaps deserve, but I think
we, as a House, should show that we regard the work of the Ministry in a better
light than do those gentlemen who have
written and spoken on the subject.
Agriculture is now in a different state
from that which it was in fifty years ago.
It has to be carried on in a different way,
and in a more scientific way, and this
Research Station which it is proposed to
set up is, no doubt, greatly needed in
Northern Ireland. We badly require
something of that kind. Agriculture must
improve. The Ministry has been abused
a great deal for its past work, but I think
it has accomplished a great deal of good.
In fact, I think every Member of this
House will support me in saying that in
years gone by farmers sold their yearling
bulls for £10 or £12, and now they get
£100, which is entirely owing to the
Research Station Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Mr. Porter]
Ministry's foresight and wisdom, to their
action in promoting cow-testing associations, and to their policy in killing scrub
bulls. No matter what people say to the
contrary, stock in the North of Ireland
has greatly improved, and anyone who
has got an eye for a beast can walk into
a fair and see cattle of a quality he would
not have seen fifty years ago.
There have been many other steps
taken by the Ministry to improve agriculture, but I will not detain the House by
detailing them. I will only say that I
am not much of a believer in the quack
cry that the farmers are "stoney broke."
Farmers made a good deal of money
during the war. They quite forget that
now. It must be remembered that the
conditions of agriculture vary almost
every year. If one year is a good year
the next one is probably a bad one, and
you may lose some of the money you made
the previous year. That has to be taken
into consideration. You must remember
that you cannot make an omelette without breaking eggs, and I think the money
which the Ministry of Agriculture propose to spend upon this Research Station
is money that will be well spent.
I am
very glad to be able to support the Bill.
I
Mr. SAMUEL CUNNINGHAM:
would like to say how pleased I am to

With regard to the Ministry of Agriculture, I am of the opinion that there has
been no Department of the Government
that has done so much for the country
as that Ministry has done. In my young

for seed. The Ministry of Agriculture
have shown the farmers that if they do
not put in good seed they are not making
the most of their land. I am very pleased
to see this Bill introduced, and I think
the House will agree that it is a good
thing for the country that the Ministry
of Agriculture are providing these

cannot forget that agriculture is really
the mainstay of our Province. I have
great pleasure in supporting the Bill.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: I rise to support the Second Reading of this Bill, and
I have no doubt it will do a great deal

to conduct experiments and investigations
relating to animals and crops. I know
there are many stations in England,
Scotland, America, Italy and elsewhere,
and I am inclined to think the results of

area, and without overlapping these experiments. I freely admit that the conditions in this country are not like those
in America or Italy, or even in England
and Scotland, but the propagation of

present agricultural depression.
I do not suggest that the money which

only object in rising is to see that none of

of documentary evidence from
countries without going to the expense

Mr. DORMAN: I wish to express my
approval of this Measure. I think a
Government in its relation to the land,
and those who work on the land of any
country, hold an analogous position to
that of the rational father of a family.
The source of the people's life, happiness,
and prosperity is in the land, and it depends very largely on the use that is made
of the land and the development of its

I do not presume to speak with anything

having seen land from the crudest stage

this little island of ours, and I have observed for thirty-five years the advantages
that have come to the backward parts of

diverted the centre of that organization

I can assure hon. Members there are

This is another striking instance of the

necessary for the needs of the people from

the interests of the people.

FERRARD: I beg to move the Second
Reading of this very short Bill, the necessity for which I think will be apparent
to hon. Members of this House. As this
House is no doubt aware, when this
Government was set up one Minister was
in charge of the two Departments of
Agriculture and Commerce, and one Parliamentary Secretary was appointed to
the Ministries of Education and Commerce. The Act of 1921, therefore, in
its Schedule, speaks of the Minister of
Agriculture and Commerce and of the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministries.
of Education and Commerce, but owing
to the changes that have taken place
there is now a separate Minister for
Agriculture and Commerce and a Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministry of
Education alone. The Bill before the
House merely regularizes in Clause 1,
Sub-Section (1) the position as it now is,
and in Sub-Section (2) orders that the
sum of £2,500, which was devoted as to
be divided equally amongst the Members
of the Cabinet, should now be divided
amongst those Ministers who in fact
actually receive Cabinet salaries.
I beg
to move.

AND
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE
FERRARD: In rising to ask the House
to give the Bill a Second Reading I may
perhaps inform the House that this Bill
is more or less in the nature of a Money
Bill and, therefore, I do not think I need
detain the House at any great length.
The Bill makes reference to Subsection (2) of Section 1 of the
Labourers Act of 1923, under which
annual loan charges of rural district
councils in respect of Labourers Acts
schemes have hitherto been subsidised by
the Government to the extent of 36 per
cent., and it proposes to repeal that Subsection as regards future schemes from
1st April of this year up to 31st March,
1930, and to provide instead a subsidy
of 40 per cent of the annual loan charges
of rural district councils.
was
As hon. Members are probably aware,
the financial scheme under which the
Labourers Acts are administered
formulated over twenty years ago when
advances could be obtained much more
cheaply than at the present day, and so
owing to the rise in the value of money
the fixed percentage grant no longer
truly represents the real assistance
which is being given by the Government
to the construction of these houses.
In future, therefore, advances for the
erection of labourers' cottages will be
made from the Government Loans Fund,
thereby eliminating the anomalies which
arose as the result of issuing stock at the
low price necessitated by the low rate of
interest payable. This entails a readjustment of the fixed percentage grant which
has hitherto been paid, and it has been
decided that a Government grant of 40
per cent. of the loan charges will have
the result of fairly distributing the
financial responsibility as between the
local authorities and the Government.
I beg to move.
Mr. LONG: I have previously assured
the House of the anxiety of local
authorities to provide cottages for agricultural labourers, and I have also dealt
with their difficulties. They are mainly
to provide a suitable cottage for a
labourer at a rent which that labourer
can pay on the small wage he receives.
Labourers' Cottages Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Mr. Long]
Local authorities have been in a difficulty
because they found in the past that, for
the reasons stated by the noble Viscount
who moved the Second Reading of this
Bill, they could not provide a cottage at
what was considered an economic rent for
agricultural labourers. They were reluctant to subsidise these agricultural
labourers out of the rates, and, if I am
correct in my view, on a cursory reading
of this Bill, that the object and the
result of the Measure will be to enable
local authorities to bridge that difficulty,
and facilitate the building of labourers'
cottages, I shall certainly welcome the
Bill. My view, after a cursory reading
of the Bill, is that it will be a step in that
direction, and will contribute to that
result. Therefore, I support the Second
Reading.
Mr. DORMAN: I also wish to welcome
the introduction of this Measure, or any
Measure which is calculated to improve
the conditions of the working classes. I
especially welcome this Bill because I
know that for many years disparaging
comparisons have been made as to the
moral status of the people living in this
particular part of Ireland as compared
with the people living in other areas.
These statistics have had a more or less
world-wide dissemination, and have, no
doubt, lead to a misconception as to the
real moral status of the people in this
particular part of the country.
I believe that that has been mainly due
to the want of proper housing facilities
being brought within reach of the
agricultural labourers in the Province
of Ulster as compared with those in
Munster and Leinster. The labourers in
the other parts of Ireland, from the time
that the Labourers Act was placed upon
the Statute Book, have forced their representatives to make every provision for
the housing of the coming generation,
the young men
and women who are
entering into the bonds of holy
matrimony and setting up homes. Unfortunately that progress has not been
correspondingly made in the North of
Ireland, with the result that the disparaging comparisons I have already
referred to have been made, and
justifiably made, from the Government
statistics.
There is another aspect of this particular Measure I would like to refer to,
and it is this. Making a comparison of
the incidental expenses charged in connection with the erection of labourers'
cottages, I believe, speaking from
memory, that the legal and other expenses in regard to the erection of labourers
cottages in this part of the country have
been abnormally high in comparison with
the expenses in Munster and Leinster. If
my memory serves me right, I think that
in one district of Cork the average legal
expenses in connection with the erection
of each labourer's cottage are somewhat
over £7, and in some parts of County
Down they have amounted to £32.
That
is an aspect of the erection of labourers'
dwellings that ought to be given due consideration by public representatives on
local bodies to whom these facilities will
be extended. I have great pleasure in
welcoming the Bill, believing that it will
do good to those whom the Government
is anxious to assist.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: This being a
Money Bill I take it that we can have
very little to say to it. I understand,
however, from the Labourers Acts that
rural district councils in Northern Ireland were receiving a grant of 36 per
cent., but under this Bill we are to
receive 40 per cent. Therefore, in connection with those schemes that are at
present under consideration but have not
been completed, it would be in the
interest of rural district councils to hold
them up until after 1st April, when
they will get 40 per cent. instead of 36
per cent.
In the district I represent,
Newtownards, we have a big scheme coming on and we have done our level best
to force the Government's hands to get it
ready, but if this Bill becomes law I
should be inclined to tell the rural
council to hold back until 1st April and
get 4 per cent. additional grant.
Mr. LESLIE: I hope I need scarcely
say that on a Bill of this kind I can only
rise to support it. All of us who have
been concerned in any capacity during
the past few years in securing or promoting the erection of labourers'
cottages know what the difficulties have
been and what the necessities have been.
We must all agree with the hon. Member,
the Chairman of the Londonderry
County Council (Mr. Long) that the real
problem is to provide a cottage which
can be rented at such cost as the agricultural labourer can pay in the way of
rent. That is always our problem and
the only way we can meet it is, I think,

that expression "Land Act terms" frequently in the country districts. It has
been inappropriate for some years past,
and the objection to it of course is that
if people think you can get money for

It is sometimes thrown up both against the

money for labourers' cottages on Wyndham Land Act terms they are not doing
it. Of course, the charges are entirely

:-
I beg
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT:
to move the Second Reading of this very
short Bill, which seeks to enact that it
shall be a valid defence to an action for
damages for the shooting of a dog to prove
that the dog was shot when chasing or
worrying cattle. The Bill is very simple,
but it is hoped by the Government that,
if it receives the approval of Parliament
and is placed upon the Statute Book, it
will go some way towards mitigating an
evil from which almost every sheep-keeper
in the country districts has suffered.
The last legislation on this difficult
matter is contained in the Dogs Act of
1906, which provides that the owner of a
dog shall be liable in damages for injury
done to any cattle by that dog. It is
common knowledge, however, that the Act
has by no means proved as efficacious as
was hoped. First of all, the dog and its
owner must be identified. Hon. Members
know as well as I do that dogs that worry
sheep are generally dogs that come from
a distance. The reason for that is beyond the capacity of the Leader of the
House to give, but it is a fact, I believe.
Dogs Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Viscount Charlemont]
In the second place, when the owner of
the dog has actually been identified, and
an action brought against him by the
farmer whose sheep have been worried, it
frequently happens damages cannot be
obtained owing to the fact that the dog
is not
financial
of sufficient
Owner
standing.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, received a deputation
short time ago from the Ulster Farmers'
Union, who supplied details of fully
authenticated
cases of sheep-worrying
dogs. During 1926 there were 115 sheep
and lambs killed by dogs, 95 worried and
7 flocks chased; while, since the beginning of the present year, there have been
75 killed, 2 worried and 4 flocks chased.
Now, there is no doubt whatever that
these figures are not final. Indeed, I
could add to them myself from my own
personal experience, and I have no doubt
many other hon. Members of this House
could do so also.
I
There has recently been in Northern
Ireland an increase in the number of
sheep kept by our small farmers, who are
beginning to find it a profitable occupation, and this Bill is designed to help
them, so far as can be done without acting unfairly towards the dog owner.
do not think that I need say any more; I
do not anticipate that any Member of
this House will oppose the Bill, or try
to show that it is designed unfairly
against the dog owner. A very important safeguard towards that end is inserted in the Bill, by which it is required
that the person who shot the dog shall
notify the police within 48 hours. I beg
to move.
Mr. ARMSTRONG: This Bill will be
heartily welcomed by the farming community in every part of the Province,
and I think the statistics, which the
noble Leader of the House has given,
show the absolute necessity for it. The
present remedies in the case of sheep
worried or killed by dogs are quite ineffective, and people hesitate to let themselves in for a law suit with very doubtful results. The law being ineffective it
became necessary for some steps to be
taken. I think the Government is to be
congratulated on bringing forward a
Measure of this kind which, though
perhaps not remedying the evil to the
fullest extent, will nevertheless go far
to mitigate it. The difficulties of tracing
dogs that have worried or killed sheep are
very great, and the art of eluding the Act
by owners has been brought to a very
fine point.
I know myself where within the last
few months eight ewes have been killed
and the rest of the sheep so driven and
tormented that the lambs they had to
produce have been abortions. Unless
some Measure of this kind was introduced
the keeping of sheep would not only
diminish but would probably be terminated in the Province. Sheep are most
valuable animals. First of all, as we all
know, we have lambs and we have wool,
and the sheep themselves are beneficial to
the land, often bringing back land to a
state of productiveness when it has been
exhausted. They also have a very good
taste for noxious weeds, which is another
advantage. Therefore, it is essential
that the keeping of sheep should be
encouraged as much as possible, and,
consequently, I very cordially support
the Measure proposed.
Mr. LESLIE: Like the hon. Senator

our counsels, I welcome this Bill, and I

from the public standpoint, and partly,
as I must admit, from the private
standpoint, as one who endeavours
to mitigate the losses that agricultural property entails by rearing
sheep and lambs. The difficulty is one
which has already been alluded to.
noble Viscount, who moved the Second

the owner of the dog was a man of straw.
The
There is another very serious difficulty.
The heaviest loss is really not the worry
ing of a few incidental sheep, although

ewes that are in lamb. These ewes do, as

your loss.
This Measure will assist in

As regards the Bill itself, the thing that
I think ought to be noted particularly is
that it is an additional Measure, that is,
it affords additional protection. It does
not in any way take away from the
common law right of a man to protect his
property, but it does tend to protect him
from vexatious actions when he has acted
in defence of that property. It does that
provided he has taken the precaution of
notifying the police authorities.
I am
bound to say if this Bill had originated in
this House I should have felt obliged at a
later stage to draw the attention of the
House to the fact that notice had to be
given within 48 hours, because it seems to
me, perhaps, open to question whether in
the case of a shepherd on one of our
sheep mountains a period of 48 hours is
sufficient within which to give notice.
Shepherds' houses, as we know, are rarely
provided with a telephone, the pillar
box is invariably at the bottom of the
mountain, and the police barracks are
sometimes several miles distant.
It might be felt in isolated instances
that a shepherd on a mountain might find
some difficulty in giving notice. On the
other hand I think, as I believe is the
general impression amongst those who
have endeavoured to study the Bill and
work out its possible consequences, that
this giving of notice and so on will operate
probably not so much on the mountains
as on the smaller farms to which the
noble Viscount alluded and which
more or less contiguous to towns of some
size or places where there are police barracks or, at all events, post offices. On
the whole I do not believe that the 48
hours provision will be found to be of any
serious
are
detriment. It will certainly

The only other point it seems necessary to make is to suggest to the Government, if indeed a suggestion is necessary,
that some steps will have to be taken to

I do not think that in practice any

I am very pleased with the reception the

a
Many years ago I was struck with this
particular feature of the animal creation
by a cat I had. I was living in the neighbourhood of a nobleman's estate on which
there were a large number of rabbits, and
a large income was derived from the sale
of these rabbits. I happened to have
cat and every morning that cat got over a

rabbit. I ult.mately had to destroy the
cat because practically every morning,

found a rabbit in the yard. That was
the urge of the savage ancestry of that
young cat which influenced the animal to
go back to the habits of its savage
ancestors. I have no doubt that if I had
kept the cat, which was a great pet, it
would have succeeded in destroying a
large number of rabbits

Order for Second Reading read.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT (Leader
of the House): I beg to move the Second
Reading of this Bill, the object of which
is to regulate the sale on commission of
horticultural produce, that is, vegetables,
fruits, flowers and plants. The Bill has
received the whole-hearted support of the
fruit-growing interests, and the Ministry
of Agriculture are confident that it will
prove of great assistance in improving the
grading and packing of fruit. I may say
that an identical Bill was introduced into
the Imperial Parliament last year, and
became law for Great Britain in last
December,
By whom Deposited
Robert Wallace
French and French
James O'Brien
Tillie, McDermott and Munn
William Currie
Crookshank, Leech and Davies
W. A. Lane
White, McMillan and Wheeler
W. A. Lane
The Bill provides that the salesmen
of horticultural produce must keep
a record of the actual price paid
by every purchaser for the consignments which have been entrusted
to him for sale on commission and
must forward that information to the
owner, together with particulars of the
commission which he has charged, and
details of any amounts paid by him on
behalf of the owner in connection with
the sale.
The whole object of the Bill will be
quite clear to hon. Members of this House,
and I am sure that it will receive their
hearty support. It is designed to secure
that the grower who has taken pains in
grading and packing his produce will be
paid the extra price to which he is entitled, and that he will not be obliged
to content himself with a sum which has
been reached by averaging all the sales
on the same day, thereby giving the unprogressive grower exactly the same price.
for his produce as his more enterprising
neighbour. I beg to move.

Mr. LESLIE: I am sure we shall all
sympathize with the object of the
Measure, the Second Reading of which

I take it that the particular object of the
Bill is the prevention of fraud, because
something in the nature of fraud would

times. If a man does not really get the
fair selling value of his produce he is, I
think, defrauded, and we should all
naturally desire to protect him from
injury of that description, and we should
all be equally anxious to assist the ultimate consumer to obtain fruit and vegetables that have been properly graded
and packed and delivered to the salesman.
The Bill, as I understand it, is ultimately based on a Report of the Linlithgow Committee, which sat, I believe,
about 1921, and it follows word for word
the English Bill as it was last year, and
the English Act as it is now, to which
the noble Viscount has alluded. I think
there is scarcely a word of difference
between the two Measures, but I am
afraid that if we are going to introduce

which are absolutely clear.
