There are a larger number of people
and a larger number of cattle suffering
from tuberculosis than is generally supposed. I have been informed that one
out of every eleven persons who die have
been suffering from some of the numerous
forms of tuberculosis. The hon. and
gallant Member (Colonel Sinclair) is a
better authority on that question than I
am, but I know for a fact that a promising
family in my neighbourhood has been entirely wiped out and the doctor in attendance attributed their diseases to infection
received from contaminated milk. Any
steps taken to secure an improvement,
however slight, should be welcomed.
With regard to the number of cows
suffering from tuberculosis, I should like
to tell the House that the Londonderry
Asylum Committee supply milk to the
institution, and for many years they have
bought the very best cows to be obtained,

In this matter they

In a recent test, out of 48 cows-and they
are a picture to look at-eight
found to be suffering from tuberculosis.
If one-sixth of that herd is suffering from
tuberculosis-a carefully selected and
splendid looking herd-what is the proportion in the ordinary herd? I should
think that at least 50 per cent. of the

The expense entailed in keeping a
licensed dairy will be very considerable,
and not the least part of that expense
will be represented by the scrapping of
these unsound cows that have failed to
pass the test. It would be interesting if
we asked ourselves what is to become of
those cows that fail to pass the test. Suppose that a Mr. Brown has a licensed
dairy or is trying to establish a licensed
dairy. Fifty per cent. of his cows fail to
pass the test. What is done with those
cows? A few, no doubt, are used for
food, and the public at one fell swoop
consumes that infected meat, but the
great majority of those cows go to another
dairy. They will be sold to a Mr. Robinson, who has an ordinary dairy, or to
farmer Jones.
What is achieved by moving these cows
from Brown to Jones? I suggest that if
the Ministry of Agriculture are in real
earnest in this matter their logical duty
is to require the rejected cows in Brown's
dairy to be branded as suffering from
disease, thus letting all and sundry know
that these cows are unsound. That step
might be considered drastic and severe,
but I feel sure it would secure the approbation of all interested in the welfare of
society and the health of the community.
There is another matter I would like to
bring before the House with a view to
having some information given on the
Third Reading of the Bill. It is a well
known fact at least I have been informed it is well known that a cow
which has been subjected to a tuberculin
test and failed to pass will, if again submitted to the same test in a week's time
successfully pass it. I understand that
dealers who expose cows for sale readily
submit to their cows being tested. If
they fail they take the cows back that day
week and with equal readiness again submit them to the test, and the cows pass
on the second occasion.
I submit it is the duty of the Veterinary
Department of the Ministry of Agricul
ture-and they are a very competent body
-to make such provision for testing as to
secure absolute accuracy so that there shall
be no possible doubt about a cow being
free from disease when it has passed the
tuberculin test. In the ordinary course
of events a person purchasing a cow is unaware whether it is the first or second
occasion on which it has been tested, and
I submit it is the duty of the Veterinary
Department not only to devise a method
by which the object I mentioned can be
attained, but also to put into the hands
of every veterinary surgeon in Northern
Ireland the means of seeing that every
cow tested in the Province is really and
truly free from disease. On the whole I
support the Bill, but I want to reserve
the right to suggest some amendments in

Mr. DORMAN: This Bill is a step in
the right direction. The subject with
which it deals is one in which I have been
intensely interested for the last thirtyfive years, and during the course of my
lifetime extremely wide opportunities
have been afforded me of endeavouring,
as an unskilled man from the medical
point of view, to ascertain the sources of
illness and death of probably thousands
of members of the working classes who
became victims of tuberculosis. My interest in this question has gone sufficiently
far back to justify me in saying that,
before the inspection of milk was brought
under the control of the municipalities of
the country I had taken a personal interest in this particular question, because
of my occupation in life as manager or
inspector of an Industrial Assurance
Company. In that capacity I was brought
daily into contact with fellow-workers
who have passed over the border, many of
them prematurely, through this widespread cause of infection.
It seems to me that to make a Bill of
this kind optional is leaving it open for
that dread disease to continue in
the community from this particular
source of infection. Unless it is made
compulsory the real source of the spread
of the disease will be more or less left
uncontrolled. In my opinion the sources
of the supply of all milk ought to be
under inspection to ensure that they are

free from contamination. I do not wish
to occupy the time of the House by giving
numerous illustrations which have come
under my personal observation, but I
think I will utilize this opportunity of
giving at least one which will show that
it is not merely the congested areas and
the poor and needy that are subject to
contamination from this particular source
but those of the professional and upper
classes of society.
I remember the late Professor
McWeeney telling us some twenty years
ago of a medical colleague whose wife
died from this dread disease in early life,
and she left one child. After the death
of his wife he took upon himself the responsibility of personally examining every
particle of animal food before it was
handed to the cook to be cooked for the
use of the family. At the age of twentyone his only daughter showed indications
of having been infected with this disease.
For two years he was troubled in mind to
ascertain the source of the contamination.
He had a residence in the country to
which he used to go during the summer,
and it suddenly struck him that the contamination might have taken place there.
He consulted a maid, who attended his
child while she was resident in the
country, and inquired into her habits.
She incidentally told this doctor that the
child was very fond of going to an adjoining farm and asking the farmer for a
drink of hot milk as it came from the
cow. The Professor's friend immediately
despatched the maid to this country
residence and instructed her to bring back
to him a bottle of the hot milk as it came
from the cow. He passed it on to Professor McWeeney for bacteriological examination, and it was discovered to be
teeming with tubercle bacilli.
One illustration like that ought to be
sufficient to rouse us as to the importance
of this question and the dangers of leaving a Measure such as this optional. All
the sources of the supply of milk should
be under strict inspection in the interests
of the health and well-being of the community as a whole. The amount of unnecessary suffering and early death and
misery amongst the working classes in
Belfast is increasing according to the
report of the doctor in charge of that
particular department of our municipal
services. While I give whole-hearted
support to this first step I hope the day
is not far distant when the Government
will place on the Statute Book of Northern Ireland a Bill to enable local
authorities to inspect every source of milk
supply in order to preserve the health of
the public.

Although in one group the microbes

May I refer for a moment to Sir
Bernard Spilsbury. I know Sir Bernard
Spilsbury very well. He is a man of the
highest scientific attainment, he is a
trained jurist, and every word he utters
is uttered with a full sense of responsibility. The extract which has been read
of his recently expressed views is very interesting, but I am sure he would be the
last to suggest that a generalization of
that kind should be made of universal
application. If it were so, and the statement attributed to him of the indestructibility of microbes and their poisons were
accepted, then there would be no use in
the surgical profession making the elaborate sterilizations they have had to make
to secure the surgical triumphs that have
been so conspicuous during the last
twenty-five or thirty years. A generalization of that kind may be useful amongst
scientists and laboratory workers, but
when you come to deal with Measures
applied to the food of the people we may
have to be content with something short
of the ideal.
Scientists know that certain forms of
microbes are not capable of entire destruction by heat. Take, for example,
anthrax or splenic fever in cattle. There,
while the bacilli themselves can be destroyed, it seems almost impossible to
destroy their spores, the seeds by which
they propagate themselves. That, however, is no reason why efforts should not be
made in many directions to at least secure
attenuation of the virus ensuring that
even a residual potency in the toxins and
germs may be happily overcome, so that
the resisting power of the human body
might be able to successfully cope with
such mitigated toxins.

The following Report was made from
the Joint Committee on Consolidation
Bills:-
(i) The Committee have examined the
Workmen's Compensation Bill and have
made therein the Amendments specified
in the Appendix to this Report.
that
(ii) The Committee are satisfied
the Bill, as amended, reproduces the existing law without alteration and recommend that the Bill be proceeded with.
(iii) The Committee wish to draw
attention to a question which the trend
of their discussions leads them to fear
might conceivably be raised in relation to
Clause 35 of the Bill. Clause 35, which
provides for the application of the Bill,
and of the Workmen's Compensation Act,
1925, to persons employed in ships, is
based on the Act of 1906, as extended
by later legislation and reproduces
Section 9 of the Workmen's Compensation (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1927. When that
Section was before the House of Commons
of Northern Ireland as a Clause the limitations of the powers of the Parliament
of Northern Ireland as regards making
laws in respect of navigation, which were
enacted by the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920, were considered, and the
Attorney-General stated to the House:-
"The law as it stood, or rather as it
stands at present, is that under Section 7
of the Workmen's Compensation Act of
1906 these very proceedings can be
brought by a workman in the County
Court in Northern Ireland.
I conceive that this legislation is within
the powers of this Parliament.”—(Parliamentary Debates, House of Commons,
Vol 8, No. 27, col. 1765, 20th May,
1927).
The Clause was then accepted and the
Bill containing it received the Royal
Assent on 31st May, 1927.
Nevertheless, a possibility, however remote, may be thought to remain, that a
plea might be set up in a County Court.
in Northern Ireland, as against a person
employed in a ship who had suffered injury,
213 Workmen's Compensation Bill.

Adjournment.
or against some other person claiming in
respect of such injury, that Clause 35
(assuming that Clause to have been enacted) would be void as a contravention
of the Act of 1920.
The Committee feel that litigation as to
that, whatever the ultimate result, would
impose a hardship on the claimant from
which, or from the risk of which, both the
Parliament of the United Kingdom and
the Parliament of Northern Ireland would
desire to protect him.
The Committee, accordingly, submit
that it ought to be considered whether,
as a matter of precaution, His Majesty's
Government should be approached in
order that declaratory legislation may be
initiated in the Parliament of the United
Kingdom.

VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT (Leader
of the House): In moving the Second
Reading of this Bill perhaps I may explain the circumstances which have led to
its introduction. There are in Northern
Ireland some hundreds of quarries, in
many of which explosives and machinery
are used. The system of inspection and
regulation set up by the Quarries Act,
1894, is limited to quarries exceeding 20
feet in depth. Hon. Senators will
realise the extent of this industry when
I mention that there are 361 quarries of
this description on record, and of these no
less than 227 were worked during the year
1926.
All quarries, without reference to depth,
are either "workshops" or, where machinery is used, "non-textile factories"
within the meaning of the Factory and
Workshops Acts. Quarries are
are also
subject to other Statutes of general
application, including the Notice of
Accidents Act, 1906, the Check Weighing
in Various Industries Act, 1919, the Employment of Women, Young Persons and
Children Act, 1920, and the Workmen's
Compensation Act (Northern Ireland),
1923.
So far as quarries exceeding 20 feet in
depth are concerned, the administration in
Northern Ireland, both of the Quarries
Act and of the Factory and Workshop
Acts, is mainly in the hands of the
Inspector of Metalliferous Mines and
Quarries, who holds appointment both as
an Inspector of Quarries and an
Inspector of Factories, and is a part-time
officer of the Ministry of Commerce.
Quarries not exceeding 20 feet in depth
have not been subjected to regular inspection in Northern Ireland by the Factory
Inspectors, but in the event of a fatal
accident occurring it has been their
practice to visit the quarry and attend the
inquest.
I understand that the limitations of
regular inspection to quarries exceeding
20 feet in depth was originally intended
to be of temporary duration, and was
applied in order that the work to be done
should not exceed the capacity of the new
body of Inspectors set up in the United
Kingdom in the year 1894. Many
quarries not exceeding 20 feet in depth
use explosives and machinery and employ
a number of men, and experience has
shown that the depth of a quarry cannot
be held to be a true measure of the necessity and importance of inspection and
regulation. The existing difference in
status and treatment between quarries
above and below 20 feet in depth would
appear, accordingly, to have little to
commend it, and it would seem desirable to
grant to the workers of all quarries equal
protection under the law, so far as such
an end can be attained, by bringing all
quarries under a single jurisdiction and
system of inspection.
This Bill has, accordingly, been prepared in order to consolidate, and amend
where necessary, the law relating to
quarries so that the new Measure will form
Quarries Bill
Second Reading
27 OCTOBER 1927
a simple code suitable to the requirements
of the industry and readily available for
the information of employers and workers
alike.
The principal Amendments incorporated
in the Bill are as follows:-
(a) The definition of "quarries" to
which the code is made applicable is
altered so as to include all quarries;
(b) A definition of the term "occupier" is introduced so as to attach responsibility to persons working the
quarries who hitherto could not
definitely be held accountable;
(c) Provisions are introduced for
further safeguarding the use of steam
boilers and machinery;
The
(d) Rules of general application are
introduced approximating closely to the
Special Rules which heretofore were
applied only in individual cases.
justification for this course is that the
ordinary precautions and rule of conduct necessary to ensure the safety of
the workers thus imposed will be placed
on record and brought to the notice of
all concerned in the operation of a
quarry.
The Bill does not impinge upon the
Workmen's Compensation Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, except in the subject
matter embodied in Sections 25 and 26,
the general provisions whereof have been
re-enacted in Clause 6 in a form simpler
and more in consonance with quarry
conditions, or upon the Check Weighing
in Various Industries Act, 1919, or upon
the Employment of Women, Young Persons and Children Act, 1920.
It is not anticipated that the additional
work of inspection and administration
proposed by this Bill will call for the appointment of any additional staff. I beg
to move.

The following Question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Hill
Dickson: :-
To ask the Leader of the House if he
will state whether any convictions took
place as a result of the misleading circular
which was issued by the Ministry of Home
Affairs in respect of the Motor Vehicles
(Traffic and Regulation) Act, 1926; and,
if so, whether any steps are being taken
to remedy any injustice so done
It
Mr. HILL DICKSON: In putting the
question which appears in my name on the
Paper I desire to say that the word "conviction" should read "endorsement."
was not the question of convictions I was
so much interested in. I do not mind a
man being convicted for committing an
offence, but when a circular is issued to
magistrates by the Ministry of Home
Affairs which makes it appear to magistrates that when they have decided to convict they must endorse the person's licence,
and when the terms of that circular are
afterwards upset by the King's Bench
Division on appeal and the circular is
subsequently withdrawn by the Ministry
of Home Affairs, I think it is very unfair
to the persons who may have had their
licences endorsed in consequence of that
circular. If the magistrates had not received this circular and had not been
under the impression that they were bound
to endorse an offender's licence it might
not have been endorsed. When people
who have had their licences so endorsed
go to seek employment elsewhere the first
thing the prospective employer asks is to
see their licence, and when he sees a
licence has an endorsement on it, it militates against the man's chance of employ.
ment.
Colonel SHARMAN CRAWFORD:
And quite right, too.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT: The
hon. Member having made it clear that
the word "conviction" was wrongly used
in the question, and that he refers to endorsements, I will omit the first part of
the answer to the question, which was
based on the assumption that "conviction" was the word intended to be used.
From returns furnished to the Ministry it appears that between the dates on
which the two circulars were issued, 208
licences were endorsed. It is impossible
to say how many of these were endorsed
by the magistrates, by reason of the view
expressed by the Ministry that endorsement was compulsory. It may be admitted that in all probability a considerable proportion were so endorsed.
The question appears to suggest that
an injustice has been done, but this suggestion would seem to result from a misapprehension as to the effect of an endorsement of a licence under the Act.
Many people, no doubt, think that an
endorsement under this Act is analogous
to an endorsement under the Intoxicating
Liquor Acts, but this is quite fallacious.
Under the Intoxication Liquor Act it is
only convictions which are actually endorsed on the licence that entail consequences if the holder is subsequently
convicted. In other words if a
licence-holder upon whose licence
two convictions have been endorsed is convicted a third time, his licence is forfeited. An endorsement under the
Motor Vehicles (Traffic and Regulations)
Act has no such effect.
The increased penalties for second or
subsequent offences depend on previous
convictions whether they are endorsed or
whether they are not. If the previous
conviction is not endorsed it is the duty
of the police to inform the court thereof
at the proper time, and to offer proof of
it. Endorsement on the licence is merely
a convenient form of record, which enables the previous conviction to be easily
proved, but it does not in any way preclude proof of the previous conviction
which has not been endorsed.
Endorsement of Licences 224
Motor Vehicles Act-
THE SENATE
[Viscount Charlemont]
The convictions in these 208 cases did
not in any way depend upon the Ministry's
circular, and whether they were endorsed
or were not endorsed, the police, in the
case of subsequent conviction would be
bound to bring them to the notice of the
magistrates and to prove them in the
ordinary way.
Mr. LESLIE: Arising out of what has
just been said, I may perhaps remark
that I am very glad to find that a considerable interest is taken in this House
in the matter to which the question of
my hon. Friend refers. It has just been
admitted that in no less than 208 cases
something may have been done which
would not have been done but for a mistake made in the Ministry of Home
Affairs. We were told the day before
yesterday that the circular was issued on
the advice of the Ministry's legal advisers,
and I can only hope that those legal advisers, whoever they may be, will feel
something in the nature of repentance
when they learn of the consequences of
their mistaken action.
To suggest that there is a popular idea,
a popular mistake, of the effect of an
endorsement under the Motor Acts, and
that the situation is in any way comparable with that under the Intoxicating
Liquor Acts seems to me to be somewhat
absurd. The confusion, if any, does not
seem to be in the mind of the general
public. I am afraid 1 must say that I
think some confusion
as regards this
matter has been in the minds of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and the
Parliament of Northern Ireland. I venture to say, when speaking on the Second
Reading of the Bill of 1926, that I had
never been able to clearly appreciate with
what object licences under the 1903 Act
were endorsed, because however many
endorsements a man had on his licence
under that Act, it did not in the least
prevent his getting another driving
licence. County councils had no power
to refuse to issue another licence merely
because his previous licence was plastered
with endorsements.
But there is this effect. If a man is
seeking employment and his licence is
endorsed he is far less likely to get that
employment; in fact the endorsement of
a licence is, as I think the Lord Chief
Justice said, a penal provision. If
magistrates do become aware of the endorsement of a licence, a fact of which they
should be and are kept in the most complete ignorance until the question of conviction or acquittal is decided, they are
likely to consider, and I venture to say
I think they should consider, whether the
previous offence has been of so serious a
charcter that the bench who tried it felt
it right to endorse the licence, and we
should consider whether that does not lead
them to consider the imposition of a more
severe penalty than the minimum penalty
which happens to be provided in the Act
Certainly I, myself, would give effect to
that consideration.
The whole question of the production
of these licences in court seems to me to
be one of great difficulty. It is universally admitted that until a conviction has
been decided upon a licence cannot be
produced. It is equally universally held
that if a licence is produced to the court
it is the best possible evidence for satisfying the requirements of the Prevention of
Crimes Act, as being an abstract of the
proceedings of another court, and it
usually settles the question of identity.
But our 1926 Act does not provide any
satisfactory method of getting the licence
before the court. There is a provision
that the holder of a licence must produce the licence in court if required, and
the requirement can only be by the court
itself. I think, reading our Act of 1926
with its predecessor of 1903, we are driven
to the conclusion that the only purpose
for which a court can possibly call for the
production of the licence is so that it may
be endorsed, in which case the licence in
most cases would never get to the bench
at all, but would simply be handed to the
clerk, who would make the necessary endorsement.
If a court were to require a man whom
they had just convicted to produce his
licence, to see whether or not it was endorsed, it seems to me they would be requiring the man to give evidence against
himself. As an old writer said and I
am sure this will be familiar to the right
hon. and gallant Gentleman (Colonel
Sharman Crawford)-—
Magistrates must be very careful as
regards the common law lest it break
in upon them and level their proceedings.
I think that is one of the classics with
which magistrates ought to invest themselves. On the other hand it is obviously
225 Motor Vehicles Act
27 OCTOBER 1927
Workmen's Compensation Bill. 226
most convenient that the licence should
be produced and if, as I have heard, a
police officer asks a man in court for his
licence, although I do not think the man
is bound to give it to him, if he does in
fact give it to him, the court cannot interfere to prevent the police officer from using it. Therefore I hope those points
will attract the attention of the House or
the legislature, but in the meantime I
think we are satisfied that due care will
be taken in future to render, as far as
possible, absolutely impossible the recurrence of any mistake of this sort, which
has such far reaching consequences for so
many comparatively innocent people.
Colonel SHARMAN CRAWFORD: I
had not intended to intervene in this debate, but Senator Leslie always seems to
have the faculty of provoking me to get
up to say something. I cannot agree
with his views on this question at all.
The number of endorsements on licences
that has been quoted by the leader of the
House cannot be wholly ascribed to the
circular issued by the Ministry of Home
Affairs Speaking for the bench on
which I sit, I can say that 90 per cent.
of the endorsements put on licences are
put on solely by the desire of the bench,
and not in consequence of the circular
issued by the Ministry. I think it is
most desirable that in every case of a first
offence the licence should be endorsed.
In the end it is the quickest and easiest
way, because otherwise the police might
have to spend some considerable time
searching the records to ascertain whether
a man had been before the court before
or not.
I also think it is in the interests of the
motor driver himself, because if his
licence is not endorsed for a first offence
he might go and commit similar offences
in other parts of the country, where they
would be regarded as first offences.
hope all benches of magistrates will fol
low the example of my bench, and endorse
licences for all first offences.

VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT: I think
I can give the assurance Senator Leslie
asks for that as far as the Home Office
can preclude the possibility of anything
of the same nature happening again they
will do so.

PREAMBLE.
Whereas it is expedient to consolidate, as respects Northern Ireland, the
law relating to compensation to workmen for injuries suffered in the course
of their employment:
And whereas the enactments relating
to such compensation as aforesaid, so
far as they were enacted by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, contain,
in relation to Northern Ireland, certain
provisions as to matters in respect of
which the Parliament of Northern Ireland have not power to make laws (in
this Act referred to as "reserved provisions"):
And whereas it is expedient, for the
purpose of consolidating the law as
aforesaid, that the reserved provisions
should be set out in the Fourth Schedule to this Act in the manner in which
they are applicable to matters arising
under the provisions of this Act:
Be it therefore enacted by the King's
most Excellent Majesty, and the Senate
and the House of Commons of Northern
Ireland in this present Parliament
assembled, and by the authority of the
same, as follows:-
*
*
*
*
*

MOTION FOR ADDRESS.
The following Motion stood on the

Bangor :-
That an Humble Address be presented
to his Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland, praying that the Regulations,
dated 26th September, 1927, made by the
Ministry of Education, under Sections 73,
76 and 77 of the Education Act (Northern

VISCOUNT BANGOR: With regard
to the Motion on the Paper which stands
in my name, I should like, if I may be
allowed, to give this House a slight explanation of the events which led to my
giving notice of this Motion. The whole
matter has arisen owing to the placing on
the Table of both Houses of Parliament
of the Regulation to amend Article 3 of
the Parliamentary Grant to Education
Authorities Regulations, 1927-1928. The
Amendment or Proviso reads as follows:
Payments made in respect of capital
expenditure incurred on works or equipment, whether such payments are made
by way of interest on, or repayment of,
loans obtained to meet such expenditure
or otherwise, shall not rank as part of
the approved expenditure of an education authority unless the expenditure
on such works or equipment was incurred under the lowest tender received
therefor by the education authority or
unless the Ministry, in any case, authorizes such capital expenditure to be incurred otherwise than as aforesaid.
This proviso, however, shall not apply
to payments made in respect of capital
expenditure incurred under contract
entered into by education authorities
prior to 1st December, 1927.
The Regional Education Committee of
County Down, over which I have the
honour to preside, were very dissatisfied
with this procedure, and it was decided
that a representative deputation should
approach the Minister of Education to explain their views. This deputation was
as representative as possible, and was very
kindly and courteously received by the
noble Viscount, the Leader of the House,
on Wednesday, 19th October, and they
expressed to his lordship that they were
pressing the claims of those who were
empowered to speak for the whole county.
We represented that we had a concrete
case when the committee disagreed with
the Ministry of Education as regarded the
acceptance of a tender. I refer to the
tender for the enlargement of a certain
technical school.
In this case the lowest tender was not
taken by the Regional Committee, and for
very good reasons which I shall be quite
prepared to give if necessary. The difference between the lowest and next lowest
tender on a contract of between £3,000
and £4,000 was under £80, which was
subsequently reduced by an amendment
241 Expenses of Educ. Authorities

1 NOVEMBER 1927
Expenses of Educ. Authorities
of the lowest tender to a difference of
about £50. The matter was referred to
the Ministry of Education, who passed
it on to the Ministry of Finance, and the
latter said that it considered that the
lowest tender in this case should be
accepted. The Ministry of Education
concurred, but the Regional Committee
was not definitely ordered to accept the
lowest, or any tender at all. The next
lowest was accordingly accepted, and when
the item came before the Local Government Auditor he approved fully of the
reasons given by the Committee for the
acceptance of the next lowest tender, and
there was no question of any surcharge.
I merely quote this case because, on the
occasion of the deputation to the Ministry of Education, we were informed that
it was this case which gave rise to the
amendment of Article 3 of the Parliamentary grant. The deputation explained
to the noble Viscount, the Minister of
Education, that in their opinion the imposition of such a Regulation indicated
that the Ministry had little confidence in
the judgment of either Local Education
Authorities, or Local Government Auditors, that the members of the Education
Committees gave their energies, time, and
abilities, entirely gratuituously, and that
they used their best endeavours to safeguard the ratepayers in every way. They
further expressed the opinion that Regulations such as these, instead of fostering
local interest in matters educational,
would most successfully stifle it. They
also said the lowest tender is not, ipso
facto, the best, nor is it always the cheapest or most economical in the long run.
We
The deputation finally asked that the
Regulation might be withdrawn.
were most courteously and kindly received,
but I can only say that our efforts were not
successful. I do not wish to weary the
House with a long narrative, but I want
to give a perfectly straightforward account
of these events, and the reason for my
present action in the matter. Our
Director of Education was then instructed
to communicate with the Committee's
Solicitor, who advised that the matter
should be raised in this House. Accordingly, a sub-Committee, mainly composed of members of the deputation, was
formed, and this Committee was granted
an interview with the Prime Minister,
with the object of securing an amendment
to the Regulations which would be acceptable to the Regional Committee and to
the Ministers of Finance and Education,
and, in the event of such amendments
being favourable, the withdrawal of the
Motion now before the House.
The sub-Committee put their case before the Prime Minister, and were very
favourably and sympathetically received,
and they left under the impression that
the Regulations would be amended so as
to give the Local Education Authority
discretionary powers in respect of tenders
to cover cases of new constructions without limit as to amount, but with a
limit on the discretion of the Committee,
either in the shape of a fixed sum, or of
a sliding scale of percentages, according
to the amount of the contract.
I was in hopes that we should have
received Amendments which would have
enabled me to-day to have asked the leave
of the House to withdraw this Motion,
but I can only tell you that the text of
the amendments, when they reached us,
merely gave the Committee discretionary
power over contracts not exceeding £500,
which would only include ordinary maintenance or repair work. I am sorry to
say these amendments were wholly unacceptable, and therefore, I felt that my
only course was to submit the Motion
which stands in my name. Accordingly,
I beg to move.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: I rise to support the Motion of the noble Lord who has
just sat down. In the days before the
passing of the Education Act the Commissioners of National Education had charge
of the education in the country, and at
that time the repairs and other work in
connection with schools was usually done
by the managers in charge, except in the
case of those schools which the Commissioners themselves had charge of. In the
case of those schools the Commissioners
sent down an architect from the Board
of Works if a slate came off a roof.
specification was prepared and tenders
were invited, and perhaps in about six
months' time the slate was put on again
at about three or six times the cost at
which the work could have been done
locally.
A
The whole spirit and intention of the
Education Act passed by this Parliament
was to place this work in the hands of the
local Committees, and I do not 'think it
was ever the spirit or intention of the Act
that Regulations should be framed and

[Mr. Dickson]
passed through Parliament at the instance
of either the Ministry of Education, or the
Ministry of Finance, Regulations similar
to the circular we discussed in this House
last week, which was issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, directing magistrates to endorse licences under the Motor
Vehicles (Traffic and Regulation) Act,
and which was afterwards proved to be
altogether illegal. If the Regulations
which have been issued by the Ministry
of Education are enforced, it will give
the Ministry power to insist that the
lowest tender shall be accepted, irrespective of the knowledge which the local
people may possess.
Why should a Regional Committee be
treated in a different manner to a Board
of Guardians, a Rural District Council,
or any other local authority? They all
have power to use their own discretion in
these matters, and I do not think officials
have any right to treat people who are
giving their time to the work of education in this red tape manner.
Of course,
it may be said that the Government give
£66 out of every £100 that is spent, but
that comes from the taxpayer, and the
other £33 comes from the ratepayer. It
makes little difference, because all the
money comes from the people of Northern Ireland. I think that by their
superior knowledge of local conditions the
members of Regional Committees have
a right to be allowed to use their own
discretion in matters of this kind without
being harassed by Regulations such as
those which this Motion seeks to annul.
I have great pleasure in supporting the
Motion.

VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT (Leader
of the House): The noble Lord has given
an account of this matter from his point
of view, and I should like to give the
House a little precis from the point of
view of the Ministry of Education. The
County Down Regional Committee had
obtained the authority of the Ministry for
raising a loan for making these alterations to Banbridge Technical School, and
having considered the tenders submitted,
they decided to accept the second lowest
tender, and they requested the authority
of the Ministry for proceeding with the
work. The Ministry, after consultation,
did not see any reason why other than the
lowest tender should be accepted, and
they gave this opinion to the Committee
who, nevertheless, proceeded with the
work.
The Local Government Auditor, when
auditing the Committee accounts, was con
fronted with the fact that the Committee
had acted in opposition to the advice of
the Ministry, and he had an interview
with the Ministry to find out what their
views in the matter were. He pointed
out that in ordinary circumstances he had
no power to disallow expenditure incurred
under contracts, or approved, for
other than fraudulent or improper
conduct. That was rather news to the
Ministry, because they thought he had
far greater powers than that. It is
obvious that fraudulent reasons for
accepting a contract are at the present
time non-existent, and we hope they will
be in the future. The Ministry were
under the impression that the Auditor
had power to disallow expenditure on the
ground of indiscretion or extravagance in
accepting contracts, and their discovery
that this was not so was the reason for the
issue of this amending Regulation.
The
The object of this Regulation is that
expenditure incurred by a local authority
on buildings or equipment shall not rank
as approved expenditure unless the lowest
tender is accepted, or the Ministry is
satisfied that there is very good reason

draft of these Regulations was sent to

Chairman of this Association, Senator

discussed by that body, but I have received no official communication from it.
I should like to add also that this

but that did not apply to the representatives of other Regional Committees who

As the Members of this House know,
the Ministry pays out of public funds
two-thirds of all approved expenditure
of education authorities up to the produce of a shilling rate. If a contract

costs £9,000 the Ministry pays £6,000,

for its money, otherwise the Public
Accounts Committee might very possibly
arraign the Ministry of Education for

It is true the Auditor of the Ministry
of Home Affairs goes through the accounts
of education authorities, but his function
is confined, as I have explained already,
to ascertaining whether these tenders are

can only draw attention to the matter.
But the Comptroller and Auditor-General
will want to know why the Ministry paid
over public moneys to education authorities without satisfying itself that these
moneys were expended to the best advantage.
There is nothing at all in this Regulation directed against the County Down

not suggesting anything against other

Regional Committees elsewhere.
Regulation is a safeguard for the future.
Circumstances might arise where

a
draw the attention of the House to the

We did not feel that any unfair imposition had been placed upon us, nor were we

the members of the Down Regional Committee are concerned with the question

Mr. LESLIE: Speaking generally, I
find myself in agreement with the theory
propounded by the noble Viscount, the
Chairman of the County Down Regional
Education Committee, whose voice, if I
may venture to say so, is not heard as

Almost the first thing that occurs to me
in endeavouring to consider the matter
before us is the recognition of the fact
that the calling for tenders is almost universally insisted upon and adopted when
public money is in question, because it is
always thought that competition has the
effect of lowering prices. But competition, although an admirable servant, is, I
to think, an extremely bad
venture
master.
Almost every body who has had practical experience of tenders is aware that
unvarying adherence to the principle of
accepting the lowest tender is a policy
which is very often penny wise and pound
foolish, and I would venture to suggest
that if there is one form of contract more
than another to which that remark applies
it is contracts in relation to building. It
is, perhaps, in connection with contracts
for building that the hon. Senator, the
Chairman of the Londonderry County
Council (Senator Long), has just said
that local knowledge is of more importance
than anything. It is not, of course, possible to confine the acceptance of tenders
to tenders in the immediate locality, but
when it is possible to accept a local tender
properly possible, the result is, I think,
as a rule most satisfactory.
You will remember, as we all remember, that when the noble Marquess, the
first Leader of this House, laid before us
the Education Bill, which has since passed
into an Act, he laid great stress on the
intention of the Government to decentralize education and all matters connected therewith. I think that is a fairly
accurate summary of that part of his
Second Reading speech-decentralization
and popular control of what is, after all,
a popular matter. Then there arises the
obvious question of finance. At the present time the Government makes from
public funds a very liberal contribution,
up to two-thirds of the expenditure of a
Regional Committee. That contribution
is subject to review, I think, at any

comes from the rates in the area. It is,

ment of Sir Peter O'Brien's, which is

a rural district council is under obligation to accept the lowest tender.
no

It is obvious that those on whom the

possible to refer the question of accepting
or rejecting the lowest tender to the

arrived at.
Now, it seems incumbent upon us to

We have heard this afternoon, not only

Education Committees, and
especially the poorer members, when estimates are brought before them from time
to time. It states definitely that contracts other than the lowest contract shall
not rank as being entitled to two-thirds of

THE SENATE
[Mr. Dorman]
Ireland, and the large number of schools.
that must necessarily be erected, might
so specialize as to be able to reduce the

that is supposed to have been adopted
by all local bodies, and which I take it is

We have really revolutionized the educational system of Northern Ireland, and
we are merely building up on the Education Act certain Regulations which will
control those who administer the Act in
the future. In view of what Senator
Leslie has stated the Marquess of Londonderry said when moving the Second Reading of the Education Bill, I think it is
our duty to safeguard the interests of the
Regional Education Committees, and to
preserve their right to accept other than
the lowest tender.
My mind goes back to another great
change that took place in this country,
when for four or five years local governing
bodies continuously contested with the
Local Government Board this question of
their right to accept other than the lowest
tender. Numerous local bodies insisted
upon accepting not the lowest but the
highest tender submitted, on the ground
that the contractor who had the highest
tender was calculated to do the greatest
amount of good in the area over which
that particular local body had control.
At that period numerous contracts were
submitted to local governing bodies, although our own industries were languishing and our people were being sent to the
ends of the earth in order to obtain a
living. Circumstances similar to those
exist to-day. We are training our children to go out to the Colonies, and thousands of young men are leaving the
country because they cannot obtain employment here.
If this Regulation is enforced it will,
in my opinion, act as an intimation to
many members of Regional Committees
that they may be surcharged if they accept
any tender other than the lowest. For
these reasons I feel it my duty to vote for
the Motion.

The Civil

Ireland), 1922.
The whole
Act.
This Act was placed on the Statute
Book at a time of emergency when the
threat of what was practically Civil War
existed in Northern Ireland, and when
it was impossible for those who had no
means of living except by the sale of their
labour from day to day to exercize that
right of freely offering themselves in the
labour market of Northern Ireland, because of the influence of savagery and
barbarism and sectarian ill-will on the
part of a certain section of the community. This section was, to a certain
extent, the dominant party, and they deprived thousands of their fellow creatures
of the right to sell their labour because of
an accident of birth, they having been
born of parents of a different religion to
that which the other section professed.
Few hon. Members, except perhaps those
who sit behind me on this side of the
House, are aware of the true circumstances,
and those who are aware of the circumstances would be prepared to-morrow to
support the Government in bringing in a
similar Measure should the same circumstances arise again.
It is all very well for us to blame this
unfortunate event on one part of the community, but I happen to have gone
through it, and I know what it meant.
At the time these conditions existed I
was engaged in working as a labouring
man in the shipyard, and I incidentally
happened to be taking my food from day
to day with another man whose religious
beliefs I never inquired into. On the
day the violence broke out, which ultimately resulted in the Government finding
it necessary to place this legislation on
the Statute Book, I was called over and
commanded to put my hat and coat on
and home.
go
I asked why, and the
answer I got was that men were coming
from other parts of the works to hit me
on the head with a spanner. The only
reason I could find for such a threat was
that I happened to have been having my
meals with a man whose religion I did
not know, but at whose feet I was happy
to sit for half an hour or so every day to
gain a little knowledge.
Those conditions have all disappeared
and I hope they will never be renewed. I
would remind the Government that since
this emergency existed a new party has
arisen in the country whose policy it is to
bring the warring elements together, and
I would be almost bold enough to prophesy
that never again will circumstances arise in
this area as a result of which the working
classes will perpetrate on each other the
crimes that were committed during the
period I have referred to. The party to
which I belong, a constitutional party,
attempted to hold a public meeting in the
principal hall in Belfast. This constitutional party, on whose leader his Gracious
Majesty thought fit to confer the highest
office in the great British Empire, was deliberately deprived of the opportunity of introducing its opinions
to the public in order
to
obtain
its support at the then forthcoming election, and now the Members of this Government, who approved of the conduct of
breaking up public meetings and suppressing the civil liberties of their fellowcitizens, are asking us to continue to
confer upon them these extra legal powers.
I wish at least to express my disapproval
of the practice of carrying on year after
year powers such as this Act confers.
When King William and Mary ascended
the Throne they had to take an oath that
they would cease to suspend or dispense
with laws as a legal right, and the great
revolution we are actually commemorating
from 12th July to 12th July is based upon
the removal from the Statute Book of the
legal right to suspend all laws unless an
emergency had arisen. As one who has
some respect for the memory of that revolution I intend to divide the House on this
question.

After all, the dispensation of laws which

Crown. The Civil Authorities (Special

by the Crown and its being done deliberately by Parliament. I think that if the
Bill of Rights is to be brought into this

sight of.

(1) A person shall not, either by himself or by any servant or agent, except
under and in accordance with a licence

Affairs-
(a) sell or offer or expose for sale

or

other designation prescribed as aforesaid, or use any description or designation including or resembling any
such description or designation.
(2) A licence may be granted for the
purposes of this section for such period,

this section he shall be liable, on sum

mary conviction, for the first offence,

for each day during which the offence
continues.
(4) Any authorized officer shall have
power to take and submit for expert

or exposed for sale, by or on behalf of

(5) A prosecution for any contravention of or offence under the provisions of this Act shall not be instituted except by, or with the consent of,

Parliament as soon as may be.

The problem of the minimum
fine
has engaged the attention of this House,
either sitting as a House or as a Committee, on more than one occasion of late.
Since the Parliament of Northern Ireland
was established it has engaged the attention of both Chambers on more than one
occasion. Strong remarks are to be found
in the Reports of the proceedings in another place emanating from the Government Bench, and pointing out the impropriety of interfering with the discretion of magistrates by requiring minimum
fines to be inflicted. A statement made
by the noble Leader in this House is on
record that the Government are not
wedded to the principle of the minimum
fine, yet here we find in a Measure dealing with a perfectly new subject, a
matter which magistrates have had no
opportunity of dealing with, a proposal
for a minimum fine.
In speaking on this subject on a former
occasion I pointed out that one of the
difficulties of dealing with the matter was
that whenever a proposal of a minimum
fine was made you had to examine
it not alone on its own
particular
Sale of Milk Bill-
Committee
2 NOVEMBER 1927
merits. There is also the general
question of interfering with the discretion of magistrates, an interference
which anybody who moves about
the country or reads the newspapers
cannot fail to notice is greatly
resented by magistrates themselves. Expressions are to be found reported again
and again that magistrates feel they are
required to sit there, as I think one gentleman said, as the dummies of the Ministry
of Home Affairs. If that feeling grows
what will the effect be? It will be that
the class of man we most desire to have
as a magistrate will decline the honour,
or, if he accepts it, he will not go on the
Bench. If once you interfere with the
exercise of the discretion of a man in any
office you will find that the best men will
not take the office. I do not say you will
not have plenty of applicants for what is
very erroneously called "Appointment
to Justice of the Peace," but I do say
you are gravely risking the chance of
getting the best men.
mean.
Another thing I said when speaking
on this subject was that there were cases
to be found in the Statute Book where
ininimum fines were justified, even in my
opinion, and it so happens that with care
and good management the case to which
I am
now referring might have come
within that category. The standing case
is the case of what they call the Fishery
Act. I think it is under a different Act,
but everybody knows what I
Certain offences in connection with the
taking of fish are subject to a minimum.
fine of £4. That Act has been on the
Statute Book for some time and can be
defended, and I have always myself been
prepared to defend it on the ground that
that offence against the law, besides being
an offence against the Crown in the
ordinary way, was to some extent an
offence against private rights. That is,
there is a certain wrong done by the use
of illegal instruments in fishing to those
who have the legal right to take fish in a
legal way.
Similarly in this Measure if a man who
has not got a licence to sell T.T. milk
does purport to sell it he is not only offending against the Statute, but he is doing
something in the nature of wrong to the
man who is lawfully supplying T.T. milk.
If the minimum fine had been limited to
cases of that sort I should not have had
anything to say against it. Indeed, being
anxious to encourage the supply of this
super-excellent milk in every way that
would induce men to make a success of it
I think I would support it. Unfortunately
the provision does not relate only to that.
It will catch the person who contravenes
in any way the conditions of the licence.
That sort of contravention is purely a
matter for the discretion of the Court
which hears the evidence and tries the
case.
I am sorry that we have not in this
House a House which we endeavour to
model on the principles and practice of
another Second Chamber across the
water; I hope on the principles of that
Chamber as it was last century rather
than to-day-we have not copied that
Chamber by the introduction of what 1
understand is called a Protest Book. If
there was such a book I would long ago
have recorded my protest against the insertion of anything which impaired the
discretion of a legally constituted court.
Again and again I have suggested that
if you cannot trust your magistrates to
administer the laws faithfully and properly, or "indifferently" as in an ancient
expression which I think I noted the right
hon. and gallant Gentleman (Colonel
Sharman Crawford) using, if you cannot
trust them change them and make some
other arrangement, but as long as you
have a court to administer the King's
law do not impair its discretion, but leave
it to do the work for which it was appointed. Therefore, I am obliged to
oppose this proposal, although had it
been limited in the manner I have indicated I should certainly not have troubled
the Committee with this Amendment.

Colonel SHARMAN CRAWFORD:

Mr. LESLIE: But I cannot help feeling that some explanation ought to be

Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon.
Member is quite justified in giving an

reason for the Amendments.
Mr. LESLIE: The point here is that
this Sub-section, as we shall see in reading it, is only to come into operation if
something is going on in a quarry which
in the opinion of the inspector involves
imminent danger to life. Anything of
that sort must be dealt with immediately,
and it is therefore necessary, I think, that
the appropriate remedy should be found
at the earliest possible moment. Quarries,
as a rule, are situated in the country,
very often quite a long way from a town,
and Courts of Summary Jurisdiction in
the country usually sit only once a month.
It is therefore not very much use waiting
to apply to a Court of Summary Jurisdiction when you are dealing with a case
of imminent danger to life.
Resident Magistrates appointed under
the Act of 1836 are not usually to be
found in a spot immediately adjacent to
a
quarry. Therefore, I substitute for
"Resident Magistrate " the word
"Justice" in order that any Justice of
the Peace having jurisdiction in the
a
county concerned may, if necessary, make
this Order. He cannot do much harm.
The most he can do is to give an Interim
Order suspending operations until
Court of Summary Jurisdiction does sit,
and he has this advantage over a Resident
Magistrate, who may be residing in
Belfast or some other large town, that he
can himself go and see the quarry before
he makes the Order. I am advised that
the conferring of this power on ordinary
magistrates is more in accordance with the
Factories and Workshops Act than limiting it to Resident Magistrates. I think
the point in suggesting Resident Magistrates was to prevent any possibility of
local influence, but I do not think that
ought to weigh against the urgency of
imminent danger to life.
Mr. McDOWELL: I do not think the
argument of the hon. Senator is in conformity with the speech he delivered the
other day. We were then led to believe
that it very frequently occurred that
benches of magistrates were packed for a
specific purpose. If that is so I do not
see why the hon. Senator wants to do
away with Resident Magistrates. For
this reason I shall vote against the Amendment.
Mr. LESLIE: I cannot charge my
memory with the speech the hon. Senator
refers to, but I do not think I made any
suggestion against magistrates. My remarks have always been rather on the
other side, I ought perhaps to explain
that this is not a case for a bench of magistrates at all. This application will be
made ex parte to the selected magistrate
very much in the same way as an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus may
be made to a judge. It may be made
to a magistrate in his bedroom or diningroom. The only point is that it shall be
made as speedily as possible.

AND
the
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE
FERRARD: In rising to move
Second Reading of this Bill, I should like,
first of all, to inform the House that the
object of the Bill is firstly, to alter and
in some cases increase the Government
grants and otherwise continue the operation of the Housing Acts for another year,
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Viscount Massereene and Ferrard].
and secondly, to extend the powers of
local authorities in connection with the
sale of houses.

Hon. Members are aware that, as the
law now stands, the existing Housing Acts
come to an end in March of next year.
Under these Acts grants are made in respect of houses coming within a minimum
of 500 superficial feet and a maximum of
950, and a free grant of £80 is given by
the Government where the house
erected within six months from the date
of commencement, and £60 where a longer
period is taken. Further, local authorities are empowered either to give a loan of
£100 free of interest for twenty-five years
and to remit the rates up to a period of
ten years, or to give a free grant of £40
and to remit the rates for a like period.
The Government now feel that the need
for the larger type of house has been met
to a great extent, and that subsidies in
respect of this type shall cease. A great
deal, however, still remains to be done to
provide houses of the type which is
within the means of the working man and,
accordingly, it is proposed in this Measure
to subsidize houses of not more than 650
superficial feet. In addition, the subsidy
will be increased from £80 to £100 in the
case of those houses completed within six
months from the date of commencement,
and from £60 to £80 where the house
takes longer to build. This is contained
in Clause 1 of the Bill.
It will be noted that the grants will be
payable in respect of houses commenced
on or after 1st August, 1927, and completed before 1st April, 1929, and that
local authorities will retain the power to
make supplemental grants or loans free
of interest, and to exempt houses from
payment of rates for a period not exceeding ten years. The Bill also expressly
provides that the arrangements made
therein are not to affect in any way the
grants to the Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust for the erection of ex-Servicemen's
houses.
I come now to the second Section of
the Bill, which is rather technical and
somewhat difficult to follow. Hon.
Members will, I trust, bear with me if
I appear somewhat tedious in endeavouring to explain the purpose of its provisions in simple language. As I have said
before, local authorities may subsidize
the building of a house in alternative
ways; that is, they may give a loan of
£100 free of interest and repayable in
25 years, or they may give a free grant
of £40. The relationship which these
figures bear to each other will be apparent
when I explain that it costs the local
authority the same amount of money to
give the loan free of interest as it does
to give the free grant. It will also be
helpful if hon. Members will bear in
mind that the proportion of 100 to 40 is
as 5 is to 2.
Under Section 1 of the Housing Act of
1924 it was provided that local authorities
might sell houses erected by them at
the price which they actually cost to
build, less the amount of the Government
grant and the local authority grant, if
the house happened to be in an area
where the local authority had agreed to
give a subsidy. For example, if the cost
of a
house was £370, the Government
subsidy being £100 and the local
authority subsidy £40, the purchaser
would pay £370, less £140; that is £230.
The usual method by which this £230
was provided, the purchasers generally
being people without much capital, was
for the local authority to require the
payment in cash of a small sum, say £10,
the balance being advanced to the
purchaser, to be repaid by instalments
with interest over a period of 35 years.
Under this system, as hon. Members
will appreciate, the repayments made in
the early years of the period consisted
chiefly of the interest due, and the capital
sum outstanding was reduced very
slowly.
Thus a considerable number of
years had to elapse before the purchaser
could feel that he had paid off a substan
tial portion of his debt, and that his
payments for the rest of the period of
35 years were rapidly reducing his capital
liability.
The object of the Clause in the present
Bill is to enable local authorities, if they
so desire, to finance these purchasers by a
somewhat different method which, without
placing any additional burden on the
rates, will be more advantageous to the
purchaser and will have the further merits
of clearing off the mortgage in a shorter
period and of enabling the annual payments by the purchaser to be put in reduction of the capital outstanding, rather
than in repayment of interest.
Housing Bill—
Second Reading
10 NOVEMBER 1927
I mentioned earlier in my speech that
£40 in cash was equivalent to a free loan
of £100. The proportion of 5-2 being
observed, it follows that £140 in cash is
equivalent to a free loan of £350. The
local authority, with its Government
grant of £100 and its own subsidy of £40,
will be allowed under this Clause to give
the purchaser of a subsidy house a free
loan of £350, instead of, as in the past,
paying over a sum of £140 towards the
reduction of the gross price of the house.
a
I will, if I may, take a concrete example to show the effect of the new
proposal, as compared with the former
state of affairs. If the gross cost of a
house was £370, under the Housing Act
of 1924 the authority would deduct the
grant of £140 and would sell the house at
£230. The purchaser would pay £10 in
cash and would borrow the balance,
£220, under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, making himself liable for the
repayment of £15 3s. 7d.
7d. per year
for
of 35 years.
period of
Under
the new scheme, the £140 grant is
converted into an interest free loan of
£350. The price of the house, as before,
is £370 and the purchaser pays £10 cash,
being still liable for £360. But he is
given an interest free loan of £350, which
he pays back in twenty-five years at the
rate of £14 per year. He has also to
pay back the remaining £10, with interest, which involves him in a payment
of 15s 8d per year, making his total
annual repayments £14 15s 8d. Thus he
discharges his liability at a less cost, and
in twenty-five years instead of thirty-five
as formerly, and furthermore, he is able,
at any date during the twenty-five years,
to estimate his position with regard to repayments, instead of finding himself inextricably entangled in the difficulties of
Sinking Fund finance, as was the case
under the 1924 Act. I trust I have said
sufficient to indicate the general purport
of the Bill. I beg to move.
Mr. DORMAN: I want, in the first
place, to draw attention to the fact that
the Bill, which we are now considering,
only came into the possession of some
hon. Senators late last night, and I want
once again to protest against being called
here for the purpose of considering a Bill
that I have not had sufficient time to
read and digest. Those of us who have
to follow our daily work and return
home after a hard day's work the night
before this House sits are not in a position to give proper and careful consideration to even short Measures, such as this.
In the first place, we are not provided
with the Acts of Parliament that may
be referred to in the new Measures
brought before us, and we are debarred
of the right of taking advantage of the
facilities afforded us in the Parliamentary
Library. Therefore, I again desire to
appeal that more consideration be given
to those of us who have not had the advantage of a legal training, and, therefore, require longer time to study the
Bills that are brought before us.
With regard to this Bill, I welcome it,
and I welcome the fact that the Government have realised the necessity of increasing the subsidy and encouraging the
building of houses that are within the
reach of the working classes. I noticed that
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs, referring to the model

Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions
(Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT: I beg
to move the Second Reading of this Bill,
which is designed to cope with two
abuses which have arisen under the Rent
Restriction Acts. The Bill need not detain us very long, I think, and I shall
confine myself to a brief indication of the
remedies which it proposes to effect.
As this House is aware, a furnished
house is exempted in some respects from
the provisions of the Rent Restrictions
Act, a fact which has led to some landlords adopting a practice of putting in a
nominal amount of furniture and letting
their houses as furnished houses. This
practice is clearly against the spirit of the
Acts and, accordingly, it is proposed, in
Clause 1 of the Bill now before you, that
a dwelling-house, the rateable value of
which is greater than £8 and which is subject to control, shall not be deemed to be
bona-file let as a furnished house unless
it contains all such furniture as is reasonably required, having regard to the
character of the house. The same Clause
also provides that in future no house of
a valuation of £8 or under can,
in any
circumstances, be let as a furnished house,
the reason being that tenants of these
small houses seldom need a furnished
house, and the landlord's action in letting
them as furnished is simply a pretext for
evading the restrictions of the Acts.
I come now to Clause 2. Hon. Members are aware that it is possible for a
landlord under the former Rent Restriction Acts, to obtain possession of a house
when it is required for residence by himself or by certain specified relatives. It
is provided in the Act of 1920, as amended
by the Act of 1925, that where a landlord
has so obtained possession of a house and
it transpires subsequently that the order
was made on misrepresentation or concealment of facts, the court may order the
landlord to pay the tenant adequate compensation for loss or damage incurred by
him as the result of the order.
Now this remedy only applies to cases
where the tenant has compelled the landlord to take him to court, and no provision
is made for the tenant who has received a
notice to quit, and who has come to the
conclusion that it is useless for him to
fight the matter, but who may, in fact,
have been induced to give up the house
on fraudulent representations. It is not
right that the tenant who has acted thus
should have no remedy, while the tenant
who forced his landlord into court should
be protected, and, accordingly, it is proposed in Clause 2 that the tenant shall
have his remedy, whether there have been
proceedings for possession or not.
It is also provided that the landlord,
when giving notice in writing to the tenant, shall state that he requires possession
of the house for himself or some specified
relation. It is hoped by this provision to
make it easier to obtain proof of misrepresentation on the part of the landlord,
whenever such has occurred.
I may say that the drafting of Subclause 2 of the second Clause does not
appear at present to be perfect, and I
hope, when the Committee stage is
reached, to move a slight amendment
which will make it clear that its provisions are not retrospective. I beg to
move.
Mr. DORMAN: I rise to welcome this
Measure, because I think the conditions
that have been prevailing in Belfast
with regard to houses of the class dealt
with by this Bill have not been realised
as they should be. I, myself, know of
houses that in pre-war days were let at
3s 9d and 4s a week. The landlord has
placed in those houses furniture of the
value of 15s or £1 or 30s, and has then
charged the incoming tenant a rent of
from 15s to £1 a week on the pretence
that he was letting the house furnished.
The housing conditions in Belfast at
present are really very bad. I think
Belfast is probably the only large city
in Great Britain and Northern Ireland in
which one-room dwellers have increased
to the extent they have. For every oneroom dweller resident in Belfast before
the war there are to-day seven.
That is
a shocking state of affairs to exist in any
progressive community, and it points to
the necessity of the Government and local
authorities concentrating their attention
on this problem.
Anyone who knows the congested
working-class areas cannot but be convinced that if the laws at present on the

VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT: I beg
to move the following Amendment :-
Clause 2, page 3, line 10, at the end of

Provided that in the application of

principal Act to a case where the landlord has given to the tenant a notice to
quit before the passing of this Act such
landlord shall give to the tenant within
fourteen days after the passing of this
Act the notice in writing required by
paragraph (d) and sub-division (iii) of
paragraph (e) of the said sub-section.
I should like to point out that there is
a misprint in the Amendment as it appears
on the Order Paper. In the last line but
one, after paragraph (d) the word "of"
should read "and". It is a printer's
mistake. As the Members of the Senate
will recollect, I stated in moving the
Second reading of this Bill that the drafting of Sub-clause 2 of Clause 2 was not
entirely free from objection. The object
of that clause is to compel a landlord to
give to a tenant a written statement showing the purpose for which he requires the
house, and the Clause provided that this
notice shall be given at the time that the
notice to quit is being served. I think it
will be agreed that under ordinary circumstances, that is the proper and fairest
time for giving the notice. It was, however, pointed out at a later stage of the
proceedings in another place, that the
Clause so drafted would render all notices
to quit served before the passing of this
Act and now running invalid, in that it

and to show that he had served the notice
at the same time as the notice to quit.

after the passing of the Act, within which
the necessary notice may be served in
cases where the notice to quit was served

ingly, it seems fair to divide the available interval equally between the two

The Price of Pork.
QUESTION TO MINISTER.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Barclay :-
To ask the Leader of the House if he
can state the reason for the great dis-
The Price of Pork
The Price of Pork
15 NOVEMBER 1927
crepancy in the price of pork as sold
by the producer and bought by the
consumer; and whether the Government will take steps to stop profiteering
in this commodity.
Mr. BARCLAY: I beg to ask the
Leader of the House the question which
stands in my name on the Order Paper.
I do not intend to say very much, because
it is a subject that offers an opportunity
to every Member of the House to say
something if they so wish. It is a question that severely touches the pockets of
two sections of the community. The producer does not get sufficient for the
trouble and labour he expends to put the
article on the market, and the consumer
has to pay far too much for the article
when he comes to buy it. The reason
that prompted me to ask this question
was that I saw in the newspaper a few
nights ago a report of a farmers' meeting
that was held in the County of Fermanagh I think it was in the town of
Enniskillen-at which a number of farmers gave expression to their feelings as
to the injustice inflicted upon them,
owing to those engaged in the pork trade
not receiving the price they were entitled
to.
One farmer said that pork could be
bought in the market at Enniskillen at
from 48s to 52s a cwt. It is brought to
Belfast and sold there at a price 100 per
cent. higher. A lady from whom I made
inquiry to-day told me that of late she
had not bought so much ham or bacon as
she did some time ago, and the reason
she gave was that it was too dear and she
could not afford to pay the high price
that was charged for it. The result was
that she and her family had to deny themselves this very important article of food.
She informed me that a few weeks ago she
was paying 2s 3d per lb. for ham. Then
there was a reduction to 1s 10d per lb.,
and last week she paid 1s 3d a lb. for
ham. Therefore, you have the fact that
pork can be bought in the town of Enniskillen for 48s a cwt., and in the city of
Belfast it is retailed over the counter at
186s 8d a cwt.
I would like to know where the
difference between £2 8s Od and £9 6s 8d
goes to.
I think the Government should
interest itself in this question, because in
the past the Government has done a great
deal and has spent a considerable amount
of money to encourage the agricultural
The
industry in Northern Ireland.
Minister of Agriculture nas not spared
himself. He has spent both time and
energy in visiting the different parts of
Ulster encouraging the farmers to experiment in different ways. Some of those
experiments have not proved very profitable to the farmer, who has been put to
a loss in connection with them. I think
it was and is the intention of the Government that the farmers should have the
benefit of the money that was provided
for this purpose, but we find that instead
of the producer and the consumer benefiting, both are losing. The farmer is
not getting a fair price for his produce,
and the consumer has to pay too much for
the necessaries of life the farmer produces. Therefore I think the Government should inquire whether some step
cannot be taken to remedy this evil, so
that justice may be done to both producer
and consumer.
Mr. PORTER PORTER: 1 would like
to support the remarks of Senator Barclay on this subject. 1 am sure all the
Members of this House are aware that
this question has been the subject of considerable agitation in the country for
some time, and it is a very vital question with the people in the country, and
particularly the poorer people. There is
an old saying that a pig pays a tenant's
rent, and that is one of the reasons why
the Government should do something to
stabilise the price of pork. Two or three
counties have sent deputations either to
the Government or the Ministry of Agriculture on this subject. If pork can at
one period be sold in the market at 106s
or 120s a cwt, as it was eight or ten
months ago, and then drop down to what
Senator Barclay states is the present
price, namely, 48s a cwt, there must be
something radically wrong.
Senator Barclay mentioned as the price
of ham in the shops in Belfast, a sum
which I thought was rather high, but I
dare say he is correct. We do not find
the price of pork fluctuating in the shops
in the same way that it does in the country
markets. If the Government could help
the country in any way in this matter
it would be one of the most beneficial acts
they could perform. When the poor
farmer has to pay, as he is now paying,
20s a bag for yellow meal, and has to buy
his young sucker pigs for £2 or £3 and

keep them for six months, and then sell

Mr. DORMAN: This is another instance of the folly of producing things for
profit instead of for use. Farmers are not
producing pork for the purpose of feeding
the people of Northern Ireland. They
are producing pork for the purpose of
making a profit, and the larger the profit
the farmers get, the better they are satisfied with the result of their labour. The
man who buys from the farmer does not
buy to provide for the needs of the people,
but that he also may make a profit. The
man who cures the pork when it comes
to his factory does not cure it, and will
not cure it unless he knows there is a
certainty of his making a profit, and the
higher the profit he makes the more satisfied he is. I am very pleased to see the
hon. Senators behind me coming over to
the philosophy of the
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is

be
essay on a subject that may

Mr. DORMAN: I wish to express my

owing to the vast profits that are made

This
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT:
question of the discrepancy between the
price of pork received by the producer
and that paid by the consumer, is not, of
course, purely a local question. It was
considered inter alia in its wider range by
the Departmental Committee established
under the Chairmanship of the Marquess
of Linlithgow in 1923, I think, by the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, to
inquire into the distribution and prices
of agricultural produce. If the hon.
Member will refer to the report of that
committee he will find that the position
regarding the spread between consumers'
and producers' prices has been examined
at some length. While it cannot be
satisfactorily dealt with in a reply to a
Parliamentary question, I would draw
attention to the fact that the Linlithgow
Committee, after stating that “a marked
difference beween the position of primary
producers and that of distributors is a
common feature of every industrial depression in this and other countries," go
on to say that "apart from the special
circumstances arising out of the economic
conditions created by the war, a stage of
national development has been reached,
of such complexity and interdependence,
that the fundamental problem of the
cheap and efficient distribution of foodstuffs is one of the most pressing and important with which modern society is
faced. Primary producers, whose produce
is sold in the wholesale markets in competition with supplies from abroad, are
restricted in their returns by the prices
realized for the imported article.
prices they receive are largely fixed by
forces outside their individual or even
collective control."
