So far as the local aspect of this matter
is concerned, the immediate question
turns, perhaps, on the stabilisation
of prices. It is admitted that fluctuations in the price of pork have been
acute from time to time, and occasionally
At conferences summoned
unexpected.
by the Ministry of Agriculture the whole
question of stabilisation has been gone
into by representatives of the Ulster
Farmers' Union, the Ulster Agricultural
Organization Society and the bacon curing interest. While the Ministry would
welcome an arrangement whereby an advance indication of probable prices would
be available for the farming community,
it is clear that there would be serious
difficulties in putting such an arrangement into force as a voluntary measure.
Official machinery for the fixing of prices
is clearly out of the question.
I understand that in several districts
in Northern Ireland there has been a tendency to sell fat pigs by live weight, and
that in some quarters serious consideration has been given to the question of
catering for the British pork market in
Great Britain. These two factors will,
no doubt, tend towards the stabilisation
of prices.
I propose to circulate, in connection
with this matter, a lengthy tabular
statement showing the prices of Northern
Ireland pork and Irish bacon and hams
from the beginning of July to the end of
October of this year.

Mr. LONG: I beg to ask the Leader

progress is being made with regard to the
building of the new Parliament House at

temporary Parliament House is borne by

AND
The
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE
FERRARD: I have to inform the hon.
Gentleman that the basement work in
connection with the new Parliament
Buildings at Stormont has now practically been completed, and that, as explained in answer to a similar question
in another place on the 22nd instant, a
contract for the superstructure of the
building has now been advertised.
Imperial Office of Works, who are the responsible authorities, are prepared to
prosecute, with all possible expedition,
the work yet to be completed, but in an
undertaking of this magnitude it would
be unwise to indulge in any forecast of
definite or even approximate dates. The
Government has lost no opportunity of
stressing the importance of the new Parliament House being available at the
earliest possible moment. I suggest to
the hon. Member that he should avail himself of the kind invitation of the contractors to see, to-morrow morning, the progress that is being made with the work.
The reply to the latter part of the
question is in the affirmative.

Its
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE AND
FERRARD: In the regrettable absence,
through illness, of the noble Viscount,
the Leader of the House, I beg to move
the Second Reading of this Bill.
object, as hon. Members all know, is to
carry more fully into effect the general
intention of the Intoxicating Liquor Act
of 1923, and to remedy certain technical
defects of that Act which have been disclosed by actual practice and experience.
This House will recall that on the
Second Reading of the Intoxicating
Liquor Bill in 1923 we were favoured
with a visit from the Prime Minister,
who spoke eloquently in its support and
expressed high hopes that it would do
much to promote the cause of true temperance throughout Northern Ireland.
That those hopes have been realized will
be admitted by all here to-day, and there
must be very few people, I think, who
will deny that the Act of 1923 has justified its place on the Statute Book.
The Bill before us is an Amending
Bill and it will, therefore, be necessary,
in explaining its general effect, to keep
hefore us the main provisions of the
parent Act, which is being amended. The
title of that Act reads as follows:
"An Act to make provision for the
closing on Sunday and Christmas Day
of certain premises licensed for the sale
of intoxicating liquor, the abolition of
certain off-licences, and the settlement
of claims for compensation arising
thereout; to impose restrictions on the
sale of methylated spirits and to amend
the law relating to the sale and supply of
intoxicating liquor by retail, and for
purposes connected therewith.”
Clause 1 of the present Bill must
be read in conjunction with Section 2 of
the 1923 Act, It will be remembered
that that Section states that it shall not
be lawful for any person to carry on, in
any part of any premises licensed for the
sale of intoxicating liquor by retail for
consumption off the premises, any trade
other than that trade or the sale of table
waters. One of the effects of that Section has been that the legality of selling
liquor by wholesale, in off-licensed premises, has been rendered doubtful, and
as such a prohibition was never intended,
it is made clear in Clause 1, Sub-clause
(1), that henceforth it shall be lawful for
the holder of a retail off-licence to carry
on in the same premises the sale of liquor
by wholesale.
Sub-clause (2) of the first Clause, besides providing a more satisfactory wording for Section 6 (1) of the 1923 Act, has
also the following effect:

(1) It permits the inclusion in hotels
of legitimate subsidiary businesses as
hairdressers' shops, stock rooms, etc.;
(2) It definitely permits publicans to
carry on the sale of intoxicating liquor
by wholesale in the same premises as
are used for their on-licence business;
(3) It prohibits the sale of nonintoxicants in a public house during
closing hours. The necessity for such
a provision will, of course, be quite
clear;
(4) It permits publicans to provide
temporary stabling accommodation, not
only during opening but also during
closing hours. This concession, which
was not allowed by the 1923 Act, has
been made to convenience farmers who
arrive in country towns at the early
hours of the morning, especially on
Fair days;
331 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

THE SENATE
Second Reading
[Viscount Massereene and Ferrard]
(5) It prescribes a specific penalty
for mixed trading. This is necessary,
as it was doubtful whether any penalty
could be imposed under the 1923 Act,
for a breach of the statutory prohibition regarding mixed business.
Now I come to Clause 2. Clause 2 relates to the hours during which liquor
may be consumed in hotels. Sub-clause
(1) provides that the hours during which
it is legal to sell or consume drink in a
hotel on Sunday or Christmas Day are
ordinary week-day hours, that is, 10 a.m.
to 9 p.m. or 10 p.m., as the case may be,
and it will no longer be necessary for a
bona-fide resident in the hotel to have a
substantial meal in order to obtain a
drink. Sub-clause (2) makes it unlawful
for the proprietor of an hotel to allow the
consumption of liquor after closing hours,
unless a dinner or other entertainment is
being held and he has secured a permit
from the police authorities authorising
such consumption.
As
Clause 3 is a lengthy Clause, and will
require some detailed explanation.
regards the first Sub-clause, under Section 9 of the 1923 Act, new licences were
allowed to be issued for premises which
were licensed between 1920 and 1923, and
there was nothing in the law to prevent a
man from obtaining compensation and
then applying for a new licence in respect
of the same premises. It is now proposed
definitely to put an end to the possibility
of a compensated licensee obtaining a new
licence for the same premises on the
ground that he was licensed in 1920.
Sub-clause (2) provides that where a
new licence is substituted for a licence
previously in force, the new licence shall
be of the same quality as the old; that
is, if the old licence was an off-licence,
the new one shall also be an off-licence,
and so on. Sub-clause (3) provides that no
licence which was an early-closing licence
at the date of the passing of the 1923
Act can be extended to a full licence
under Section 9 (a) of the 1923 Act, and
every licence so extended shall revert to
an early-closing licence.
I will pass over Sub-clauses (4) and (5),
which are not very important, and I will
come to Sub-clause (6) Under Section
9 (c) of the Act of 1923, the issue of a
new licence is permitted in a ward or
electoral division where the population
has increased by 25 per cent. since the
last census and the applicant must surrender two licences of the same quality
in substitution for the new one. Under
the Sub-clause before us a new onlicence is permitted for the surrender of
one on-licence and one off-licence, but the
surrender of these two licences must involve the cessation of the sale of intoxicating liquor in two different sets of premises. It is also made clear that the
phrase "the last census" means the census
of 1911, that is, the last census before the
passing of the 1923 Act.
Clause 4 deals with the provisions as
to licences for the sale of wine and sweets,
and I may, perhaps, here remark that
the word "sweets" means, in this connection, fermented liquor made from
fruit and sugar. Under Sub-clause (1)
the future issue of a wine retailer's onlicence or a sweets retailer's on-licence is
absolutely prohibited, and the future
issue of sweets retailer's off-licences is restricted to premises where spirits or beer
off-licences are in force. These licences
have hitherto escaped the provisions of
the 1923 Act, and in view of the, what I
might call pernicious, concoctions which
are at present being sold, it has been
thought advisable to restrict their issue
in future.
The chief effect of Sub-clause (2) is to
provide that no future wine off-licences
shall be issued, except in respect of premises continuously licensed since before
the passing of the 1923 Act. Sub-clause
(3) provides that no person shall be entitled to take out or hold a wine retailer's
off-licence for any premises in respect of
which compensation was awarded under
the former Act, while Sub-clause (4) confers upon wine off-licensees the same
benefit as is conferred upon publicans and
beer or spirits off-licensees by Clause 3,
Sub-clause (4), of the present Bill. The
last Sub-clause of Clause 4 exempts from
all the foregoing provisions of the Clause
those wine licences which are issued to
chemists and which authorize the supply
of wine only on presentation of a doctor's
prescription.
Clause 5 allows the issue of a spirit
dealer's licence to wholesalers, which will
authorize the sale of quantities of not less
than 2 gallons consisting of different
denominations, such as whisky, brandy,
rum, etc., to holders of retailer's on- or
off-licences. Perhaps I might explain to
333 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

29 NOVEMBER 1927
Second Reading
the House that under the former Act a
man could sell two gallons of whisky
or
two gallons of brandy, not
less. Under this Clause, so long as the
total amount he sells is two gallons or
over, he can distribute the two gallons
among the different denominations of
spirits. Hitherto the wholesaler
has
been prohibited from selling in these
smaller quantities and inconvenience has
been caused to certain retailers which it
seemed unfair to impose upon them. It
will be observed that a somewhat similar
concession is also allowed to wholesale
cider dealers.
Clause 6 is administrative and will ensure that the description of the licensed
premises in the Excise licence and in the
magistrates' renewal certificate is always
the same, and does not vary from year
to year, except in accordance with a definite order of the court.
Clause 7 is fairly simple and calls
for little explanation, except, perhaps,
with regard to sub-Clause (4).
Hon,
Members are aware, of course, that under
the 1923 Act if a publican gets three endorsements on his licence that licence
automatically becomes null and void, but
where two or more persons consecutively
possess licensed premises, four, and not
three, endorsements are necessary to cancel the licence and they must all occur
within five years. It will be appreciated
that these provisions gave scope for
evasion and the present sub-Clause is designed to put an end to it. It provides
that in all cases three endorsements shall
annul the licence with, however, the further provision that where there has been
a period of five years with, so to speak, a
clean sheet, the licence shall be considered
to be free of all endorsements.
Clause 8 provides a definition for
the term "licence" as used in the 1923
Act, the chief practical result being that
by bringing wine licences within the provisions of Sections 2 and 3 of the former
Act the payment of compensation to
holders of extinguished wine licences is
legalised. It also brings wine licences
under Section 8 of the 1923 Act and renders them endorsable.
I come now to Clause 9, which deals
with methylated spirits and methylated
ether. It has been found necessary to
tighten up the restrictions imposed by the
1923 Act upon the sale of these products
and sub-Clause (1) will, it is hoped, go
far towards affecting that end. It gives
the Ministry of Home Affairs power to
make regulations prescribing the kinds of
accounts and records that are to be kept
by the retailers, and it will enable the
Ministry to provide for a record of all
purchases being kept, thus devising a
check on the retailer. It also provides that these regulations shall apply
to all retail sales and there will no longer
be a hiatus between the sales up to one
gallon and the sales over four gallons.
Hitherto, as the House is probably aware,
no record of sale was required for
quantities between these two figures and
the result, as one might expect, has been
abuse. The remaining sub-Clauses are
simple and do not require any explanation from me.
Clause 10 also is simple and is concerned with restrictions to be placed
upon the sale of alcohol other than ethyl
alcohol, which is, of course, the alcohol
of which wine, beer, whisky, etc., are
composed. The Clause has been inserted
in view of the increasing sale by
publicans of iso-propyl alcohol to fortify
cheap wines. This type of alcohol is
practically duty free and can be purchased very cheaply. It is a by-product
of petroleum and in its effect is much more
toxic than whisky.
Clause 11 amends the law with regard
to the registration of clubs. With regard
to the first Sub-clause, I may explain
that at present there are certain specified
grounds of objection to the grant or renewal of a club certificate, and if no objection is lodged, the certificate is granted
automatically. The Sub-clause now before us is designed to make it very difficult for any club, other than a bona-fide
club, to obtain a certificate, by placing
the clubs themselves the onus of
proving affirmatively certain specified
matters which, as hon. Members will see,
are set forth under the heading (a) of
the first Sub-clause. I' may mention
that the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister for Home Affairs, speaking on this
Clause in another place, recited some
figures with regard to clubs which were
certainly very striking and which will,
perhaps, bear repetition.
on
He said that registered clubs in Northern Ireland had increased, since the 1923

Clause 12 seeks to clarify the law relating to the issue of liquor licences to
theatres and music halls. It provides

ment in their effort to steer a fair and

I only intend, at this stage, to refer to

on persons resident in hotels. There has
been a lot said about the tourist traffic
but I do not want to refer to tourists in
general. It has always caused me a
certain amount of detestation to think
that a person coming here from England

something which makes him think that he
is in a different country. We should try to
preserve the same social conditions as
exist in England, and it is not pleasant
to think that a person coming over here
and staying in an hotel has reason to
believe that he is in a less pleasant and
sociable country than the one he is accustomed to live in.
A person resident
in an hotel, if he knows he cannot get
drink at a certain hour of the day, will
have that drink sent to his bedroom, and
I think that is a practice that would be
objected to by those who have very strong
temperance ideas. It leads to
pernicious habit of secret drinking. I
think that a person living in an hotel
should have all the comforts he would
have if he were residing in his own house.
In the course of their business commercial
travellers and other people are, unfortunately, obliged to live in hotels and I do
not see why they should be under any
restrictions whatever.

Complaints will no doubt be made-in
fact they have been made as to the
maintenance of complete Sunday closing
and as to the preservation of such an
antiquated absurdity as that which differentiated between the visitor to Portrush
and the visitor to Bangor. It is certainly
based on a somewhat out-of-date consideration relative to population. The distinction, as the House will remember, is
that a town with a population under
5,000 is to have its public houses closed
an hour earlier than a town that has a
population exceeding that figure. The
reason for that distinction and it is a
distinction that has endured for some
time; it was not the product of the Act
of 1923-the reason for the distinction has
been variously given. One suggestion is
that a complaint was made on behalf of
the publicans of the smaller towns that if
their hours were lengthened their duties
of supplying liquor were also lengthened.
That is that if they were licensed to be
open for so many hours, for that number
of hours were they bound to be open.
Owing, as they are reported to have said,
to the small size of their population that
lengthened opening was not necessary.
Another explanation is that in the
smaller towns the police force is so small
that the public houses could not be
effectively supervised. I hope that that.
is not the true explanation, because it
seems to suggest that the publicans exist
for the purpose of being supervised by
someone else rather than for the purpose
of meeting a public want. But in either
case it has to be considered that the
situation has wholly changed. In the
first place, the population is very much
less than it was in the early days I am
speaking of, and the number of public
houses is very much less also, but still
that distinction does remain and I am

what was said by the Minister of Home

An Act which does not commend itself

the law in general.-(Official Report,

1st November, 1927.)

It is more in reference to that part of

the Bill to control the sale of these materials. I do not think I fully endorse what
Senator Leslie has said, but no doubt
there are plenty of opportunities for the
supply of these methylated spirits in connection with the manufacture of scientific
instruments. I am more concerned with
their use as stimulants or fortifiers in connection with ordinary drinks as retailed
in public houses or in druggists. Perhaps
one reason why this drink came to be particularly favoured was because on market
days people could become riotously or
gloriously drunk four times in one day for
2d. or 3d.
It commended itself to a certain class
on that account, but the deleterious effects
of the use of this methylated spirit and
methylated ether are so pronounced and
so obvious to the members of the medical
profession that they are of the opinion
that the sale of these spirits cannot be too
I hope
strictly limited or supervised.
Senator Leslie's fear that in country districts the small number of inspectors
available will lead to an evasion of the
Act will not prove to be true, but surely
without multiplying the army of inspectors some provision should be made for
supervising the sale of methylated spirits.
With regard to Clause 10, I think one
might say that if alcohol is to be provided
it is of the utmost importance that pure
ethyl alcohol should be used. Much of
the evil effects of alcoholic beverages is
due to the adulteration of drinks by
petrid alcohol or wood spirit, and, apart
altogether from the use of these things by
themselves, when they are improperly employed either as stimulants or fortifiers a
great deal of harm is done. Therefore,
I hope that these provisions, which I welcome with great cordiality, will not only
be on the Statute Book but will be enforced, and that we may be freed from the
reproach which certain parts of the Six
Counties have been credited with of using

to an extraordinary and undue extent.
With reference to Senator Leslie's remark about the use of these materials for
anasthetics, pure ether is used occasionally in methylated form, but he is quite

anasthetic involving the use of spirits
methylated ether is perfectly harmless
and is quite a good anasthetic on account

it in this connection, I do not anticipate

body and anybody.

against me because this has only been

no idea what a country town was like.
know good country market towns where

VISCOUNT MASSEREENE AND
FERRARD: I beg to move the Second
Reading of the Trade Disputes and
Trade Unions Bill, and in doing so I do
not anticipate that this House will expect from me a lengthy defence of the
policy of the Government in introducing
the Bill to this country. I shall, therefore, content myself with saying that the
Bill is on the Statute Book of the Imperial Parliament, and our Government,
after mature consideration of the provisions which it contains, have come to the
conclusion that it is only proper that it
should be made law in Northern Ireland,
both from the point of view of uniformity
and also because its provisions appear to
be just and reasonable.
McDowell, Mr. W. J.
The purport of the Bill is clearly
shown in the Title on the first page.
seeks
It
"to declare and amend the law relating to trade disputes and trade
unions, to regulate the position of civil
servants and persons employed by public
authorities in respect of membership of
trade unions and similar organizations,
to extend Section 5 of the Conspiracy
and Protection of Property Act, 1875,
and for other purposes connected with
the purposes aforesaid."
I shall take the Clauses of the Bill one
by one, and endeavour to explain, clearly
and concisely, the effect of each.
The first Clause is, of course, the vital.
Clause, Sub-clause (1) is framed as being
declaratory and not as an amendment of
the existing law. It declares that a
strike or lock-out is illegal if it satisfies
two conditions: :-
1. If it has any object other than or
in addition to the furtherance of a
trade dispute within the industry in
which the strikers or employers lockingout are engaged, and
2. If it is a strike or lock-out designed or calculated to coerce the Government either directly or by inflicting
hardship upon the community.
I should like to emphasise the fact that
the "sympathetic" strike, so-called, is not
prohibited under the clause.
Such a
strike might well come under the provisions of the first condition laid down,
that is, its object would be "other than
the furtherance of a trade dispute," but
if it were purely "sympathetic," and if
there were no other ulterior motive it
would not be calculated to coerce the Gov-
Trade Disputes Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Viscount Massereene and Ferrard]
ernment. Thus the second condition
would not be satisfied and it is the fulfilling of both, and not one, of these
conditions that will render a strike illegal.
The Sub-clause then proceeds to define
"a trade dispute within an industry" and
in this connection I may point out that
it does not alter the existing definition
of "a trade dispute;" it merely copies the
definition from the Trade Disputes Act of
1906 in order to define the larger expression "a trade dispute within a trade or
industry." The general meaning is perfectly clear and does not call for any great
elaboration by me.
Sub-clause (2) lays down the penalties
for engaging in illegal strikes and lockouts, and provides a safeguard for the
ordinary workman who merely ceases to
work and takes no active part in the
furthering of an illegal strike.
Sub-clause (3) provides that where any
person is charged before any court with
an offence under Clause 1, no further proceedings shall be taken against him without the consent of the Attorney-General,
and Sub-clause (4) provides that any person taking part in an illegal strike or
lock-out will be denied the benefit of the
Trade Disputes Act, 1906, which gave
relief from actions for damages for conspiracy, allowed peaceful persuasion, and
relieved officials of a trade union from
any liability for any tort committed on
its behalf.
The first
I come now to Clause 2.
Sub-clause provides that no person refusing to take part in an illegal strike or
lock-out shall on that account be subject
to expulsion from any trade union or
society, or to any fine or penalty, or to
deprivation of any right or benefit, or be
liable to be placed at any disadvantage as
compared with his fellow-members. The
second Sub-clause deals with the same
matter, and gives to a person who has
been penalized by a trade union for refusing to take part in an illegal strike or
lock-out the right to apply to the Court
for redress. Sub-clause (3) is clear. It
provides that the enactment which prevents penalization for refusal to take part
in any illegal strike or lock-out shall be
retrospective to 1st May, 1926.
Clause 3 deals with intimidation, and
makes picketing unlawful if the pickets
attend at or near a house or place where
a person resides or works in such a manner
as to be calculated to intimidate any
person in that house or place. It lays
down the second main principle of the
Bill, which is that no person shall be compelled by threats to cease from work
against his will.
Sub-clause (2) alters the existing law
by giving a new meaning to the word
"intimidation." Under Section 7 of the
Conspiracy and Protection of Property
Act, 1895, intimidation is made an
offence, but there have been decisions
given that in order to come within the
meaning of that Act the intimidation
practised must include the threat of
personal violence. The new definition
given in this sub-clause is quite clear, and
I may incidentally point out that its
terms are in accordance with the recommendation made by the Royal Commission in 1905, whose chairman was
Lord Dunedin.
Sub-clause (4) amends the picketing
section of the Trade Disputes Act, 1906,
and is designed to prevent the recurrence
of such cases of coercion and undue interference with the liberty of the subject
as have happened in the past. Under
the new provision it will not be lawful for
one or more persons to watch or beset a
house where another person resides for
the purpose of inducing him to work, or
to abstain from working.
Clause 4 deals with provisions as to
political funds. In considering this
Clause it must be borne in mind that
prior to 1913 it was unlawful for a trade
union to have other than what are called
"statutory" objects, that is, objects consisting of the regulation of the relations
between workmen and masters, or the
imposing of restrictive conditions on the
conduct of any trade or business, or the
provision of benefits for members. Trade
unions, therefore, could not apply their
funds to political purposes.
The Trade Union Act of 1913 altered
the position and made it legal for a trade
union to raise political funds subject to
the approval by a secret ballot of the
members concerned, and subject to the
rights of any member to claim exemption
from contributing. There is evidence to
Trade Disputes Bill-
Second Reading.
1 DECEMBER 1927
show that the requirements of the Act
have been infringed in several instances,
and undue pressure has been brought to
bear upon workmen by exposing lists of
those claiming exemption, and by levying
political contributions with other contributions, so that a member has no fair
opportunity of objecting to contribute.
With this explanation the meaning of
Sub-clause (1) becomes simple. Briefly
put, it substitutes the method of "contracting in" for "contracting out" which
was provided by the 1913 Act. Subclause (2) also becomes clear.
It provides that all contributions to the political
fund must be levied and made separately
from any contributions to the other funds
of a trade union, and that the assets of
a political fund shall be kept strictly
separate from the assets of other funds
which are not to be applied in furtherance of a political object.
Sub-clause (3) is consequential and
follows upon the preceding Sub-clauses.
The remaining Sub-clauses are simple and
do not require any explanation at this
stage of the Bill's progress.
Clause 5 deals with the position of
established Civil Servants in the Civil
Service of Northern Ireland. In short,
it provides for the making of regulations
prohibiting established Civil Servants
from being members of an organzation of
the nature of a trade union, unless that
organization is confined to persons employed by or under the Crown, and is not
associated with any political party or
organization. I do not think there is any
hon. Member of this House who can
reasonably object to the provisions of this
Clause.
Clause 6 prohibits any local or other
public authority from making it a condition of employment or continuance in
employment, that a person shall or shall
not be a member of a trade union, or to
impose any condition upon employees,
whereby those who are or are not trade
unionists are liable to be placed under
any disability or any disadvantage as
compared with other employees. It also
provides that an employee of a local
authority who wilfully breaks his contract
of employment, knowing that the probable consequence of his action will be injury or grave inconvenience to the community, shall be liable, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding £10 or to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding
three months. The Clause is designed
to maintain essential services upon which
the public depends, and which clearly
must be maintained irrespective of trade
disputes.
Clause 7 gives power to the Attorney-
General to apply for an injunction to restrain the illegal application of trade
union funds in contravention of the provisions of Clause 1, and it is then a matter for the court to decide as to the
legality of the strike or lock-out, and as
to whether an injunction should issue to
restrain an application of the funds of
the union to an illegal purpose. It will
be observed that the Clause does not take
away the right of any person, who has
a sufficient interest, to apply for an injunction to restrain an illegal application
of trade union funds.
Clause 8 deals with the furnishing of
returns by trade unions. At present a
trade union registered in Northern Ireland files all its Rules and Returns with
the Register of Friendly Societies for
Northern Ireland, and complete information about these unions is available at
the Registrar's office on payment of the
usual fee. A union registered in Great
Britain and operating in Northern Irland
is, however, required only to lodge its
Rules with the Registrar in Northern Ireland, and it is not obliged by law to
furnish a financial return to the Registrar in Northern Ireland.
The first Sub-clause of the Clause before us proposes to equalise the position
as between Northern Ireland unions and
British unions, and it provides that certified copies of the returns made to the
Registrar in Great Britain shall be forwarded to the Northern Ireland Registrar
with an additional statement giving such
separate Northern Ireland figures as the
Registrar may require.
Sub-clause (2) provides that unions
operating in Northern Ireland from headquarters outside the United Kingdom
shall furnish to the Registrar a return
on the same lines as the returns made by
a Northern Ireland union. Sub-clause (3)
provides that every trade union which is
not registered in Northern Ireland, but
carries on business here shall furnish to
the Registrar the name and address of
some one resident in Northern Ireland
and authorised to accept on behalf of

Sub-clause (4) is incidental upon Subclause (3) and requires no explanation except that Section 15 of the 1876 Act provides that a trade union which fails to
give any notice or to send any document,

Mr. DORMAN: I appreciate the
lucid explanation the noble Viscount has
given us of this Measure. There never
has been a law promulgated in any
country, from the oldest law of which we
have a record, which was promulgated
four thousand years ago, of which it has
not been said by those who promoted
it that it was in the interests of the community, and for the welfare of the community as a whole. It does not require a
very extensive legal knowledge for any man
who examines the Statute Book of those
days, and concentrates thought upon the
consequences of the various Acts of Parliament which at that time were placed
upon the Statute Book to realize that at
the time they were placed upon the Statute Book they were declared by their
promoters to be in the interests of the
community as a whole, and for the establishment of just relations between the
various members of the community.
many of these Measures were afterwards
discovered to be of an intensely biassed
character in their application to the community as a whole. Whether the law
was promulgated by an absolute monarch
claiming the Divine right of ruling in

this claim has always been made for legislation that has been placed upon the
Statute Book.
But
I have closely followed the debate on
this Bill in another place, and I followed,
to some extent, the debates in the Imperial Parliament. I do not see that
many of the speakers-probably because
they might have been ruled out of order,
as I may be-examined the circumstances
leading up to the necessity of a Bill such
as this being placed on the Statute Book
either of Great Britain or Northern Ireland. We passed through a great war,
and the victors, glorying in the victory,
imposed upon the defeated enemy certain
indemnities and reparations. Individuals
pointed out that the consequences of these
reparations would be fatal to the interests
of various economic and commercial undertakings in the victorious countries.
One of the particular industries for which
reparation had to be made was the great
basic industry of coal.
It was pointed out even by the
economic advisers of the British Government that to pursue the policy they were
then pursuing would ultimately mean
chaos, disintegration, and the absolute
destruction of this great basic industry
of our great British Empire. These
prophets have unfortunately proved
correct, and the position of that particular
industry was due to the evil effects of these
reparations. It was in a state of absolute
chaos, and its world-markets were lost,
simply because those markets had been
captured by our late enemies owing to the
coal reparations. The position became
so serious that the Imperial Government
found it necessary to appoint a Royal
Commission to inquire into the position
of the industry. That Commission made
certain recommendations, which were
ignored by the Government. Two Departmental Committees were set up, and
they also made recommendations to the
Government, but their recommendations
were likewise ignored. A second Royal
Commission, known as the Samuels Commission, was set up to inquire into the
chaotic condition of this particular industry. The only remedy that
apparently present in the minds of the
coal owners was the remedy of reducing
the wages or extending the hours of
miners so as to overcome the difficulties
that confronted this basic industry in the
world's markets.
was

The result of that lock-out and that
appeal was that a large number of the
organized trades unionists of Great
Britain, in sympathy with their fellow
workers in the coal industry, withdrew
their labour from the market in which
they usually sold it, in order to manifest
their feeling against what they conceived to be the oppression imposed on
their fellow workers in another branch
of industry. There has always been a
state of fear and dread in the minds of
a certain class with regard to the actions
of the working classes when an industrial
conflict has taken place. I was struck
in reading in this connection from an
authority that I do not think any Member
of this House will object to have quoted.
Mr. Benjamin Disraeli wrote a book
called "Cybil, or The Two Nations,"
which I would commend to the Members
of this House. He was speaking of a
time when the country was passing
through a crisis something like the crisis
of last year when the general strike took
place. The governing class, and certainly
the upper classes whose opinions the
writer imaginatively tries to describe
were in a state of panic, and he directs
these words to them at that particular
time. We who are members of the great
Labour Party, the coming party in Great
Britain, and I hope in Northern Ireland,
were accused of creating class hatred and
ill-will, and of stirring up strife in the
community of which we are a part, but
under almost similar circumstances Benjamin Disraeli wrote the following words:
"Two nations between whom there is
no intercourse, and no sympathy, who
are as ignorant of each other's habits,
thoughts and feelings as if they were
dwellers in different zones, or inhabitants of different planets, who are
formed by a different breeding, are fed
by different food, are ordered by different manners, and are not governed
by the same laws, the Rich and the
Poor."
Then he goes on to say in another part
of his book--and this is almost prophetic
of the conditions that prevail in Great
Britain, if not in Northern Ireland, today :-
"Predominant opinions are generally
the opinions of the generation that is
vanishing. Let an accident, which
speculation could not foresee, the
balanced state at this moment of Par-

liamentary parties, cease, and in a few
years, more or less, cease it must, and
you will witness a development of the
mind of England, which will make up
by its rapid progress for its retarded
action. I live among these men; I
know their inmost souls; I watch their
instincts and their impulses; I know
the principles which they have imbibed,
and I know, however hindered by circumstances for the moment, those
principles must bear their fruit. It
will be a produce hostile to the oligarchical system. The future principles of
English politics will not be a levelling
principle; not a principle adverse to
privileges, but favourable to their extinction. It will seek to ensure equality,
not by levelling the few, but by elevating the many.
All that the people want is justice;
that labour should be as much respected
by law and society as property."
That is what I believe this Bill is calculated to retard. This Bill is distinctly
calculated to retard the combination of
Labour, not in the industrial field, but in
the political field. So long as the workers
were willing, as I have known they
were willing during the last quarter of
last century, through the Parliamentary
Committee of the Trade Union Congress,
to set a certain number of their members
apart and pay them for remaining in the
vicinity of the Parliament of Great
Britain and Ireland in London, for the
purpose of lobbying the Members of the
two great political parties in the State,
the Tories and the Liberals, no objection
was raised. There would be no objection
at all to their continuing to spend money
in that way, but there is objection to their
spending money for the purpose of getting
direct representation in Parliament, and
in my opinion one of the objects for which
this Bill is going to be placed upon the
Statute Book is to prevent the workers
obtaining that direct representation to
which they are entitled.
If we look back at the constitution of
Parliament in Great Britain and Ireland
as it existed 100 years ago, we find that
267 individuals had the right of nominating 487 Members of the Imperial Parliament out of a membership of 658.
Some people each had the right of nominating half a dozen Members. I hope I
will not be out of order when I state that
a nobleman of County Down had the right
of nominating three Members of the Irish
Parliament before it was abolished, and
he received considerable fees for relinquishing his privileged position of nominating those Members. I have gone into
the figures, and I have calculated that if
his ancestor had invested that money at
5 per cent., it would to-day amount to a
sum of £23,000,000. It was stated then
that 280 persons had the right of nominating 487 Members of Parliament, and
that there was an electorate of only
500,000 persons in Great Britain and
Ireland.
In other words, the Parliament of
100 years ago was elected by 100,000
odd less electors than we have on the Parliamentary franchise of this little State
of Northern Ireland to-day. The fran
chise has been widened, and widened on
foundations that constitute the aggregate
of sovereign power, and instead of one out
of twenty-eight having the right to exercise the Parliamentary franchise, one in
two has the right of exercising the Parliamentary franchise to-day. It is only
to be expected that when the vast majority
of people have the right of exercising the
Parliamentary franchise, they will seek
to obtain direct representation in Parliament.

This Bill has produced a lot of talk
about a general strike. There never has
been a general strike under what we call
free labour. There have been three great
strikes but no general strike under free
labour in any country. There was the
great strike of the Israelites in Egypt
when they went out of Egypt. Probably
had they remained behind they would
have found that the law was too powerful
for them, but they had to get out to get
free. There was the great strike of the
slaves in one of the states of Greece, and
there was also the great strike of slaves
in one of the West Indian Islands. There
have been other strikes in Western China
during recent years when all those engaged in that particular area ceased work.
What is a general strike? May I
presume to give a definition? I believe
a general strike may be said to have taken
place when those in any town, county,
province or country who have no means
of livelihood but the sale of their labour
power from day to day withdraw that
labour power from the control of those
to whom they are accustomed to sell it
As
in order to obtain their living.
Mr. Ramsay Macdonald has said, there
never has been a general strike under free
labour. He stated that it was the last
resort of a lunatic, and I think my colleague, Mr. William McMullen, M.P.,
improved upon that when he said it
would be the first resort of a lunatic and
the last resort of sensible men. A general
strike would mean the withdrawal of the
labour of the cook, the butler, the housemaid, the nurse, the keepers in
asylums, the warders in our prisons, and
by all those who have no means of living
except by the sale of their labour.
our
A general strike of that kind would.
bring us back to a state of barbarism and

ours there cannot be a general strike.
People talk vaguely of a general strike
without taking time to visualise what it
would mean to a civilized community as
a whole. A general strike would not be a
revolution. It would be a revelation;
it would reveal to those who control industry and command the credit
of the country that, after all, we are all
inter-dependent, and that the many are
not under a greater obligation to them
than they are to the many by reason of
the service the many give to them from
day to day.
As I have quoted an eminent Tory
statesman may I be permitted to also
quote an eminent Liberal statesman.
The words are taken from an essay by the
eminent Duke of Argyle on the subject of
Law and Politics. He said:
"What combination does for the
protection of labour, it does better,
and with better consequences, than
positive institutions. Men are driven
to excessive labour, because if they don't
work excessively, others will. But it
is the effect of combination that others
won't .. Under positive institutions they are not allowed. Under
combination they are determined not."
He goes on to say:-
"It tends to subordinate the present
to the future, and the temporary interests of self to the permanent welfare of the brotherhood of men. And
this it tends to do in classes otherwise
prone to follow only the impulses of
the moment.
I believe the Governments of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland are largely
following the impulses of the moment in
trying to place legislation such as this on
the Statute Books of both countries.
"and to consider only the apparent interests of the individual. These considerations should disabuse our minds

The Bill before us, as hon. Senators
will see, is to be construed and cited as
one with the Trade Union Acts, 1871 onwards. Now, the Trade Union Act of
1871, the first of the series, most clearly
provides for the hearing of cases by a
court of summary jurisdiction, which,
in Ireland, outside Dublin, was to consist of one resident magistrate. The expression used was the rather loose
expression "resident magistrate" and of
that I am rather glad. It further provided for appeal to the ordinary court of
quarter sessions. It, therefore, would
seem to follow that any summary jurisdiction proceedings under this Bill, when
it becomes an Act, will be taken before
a court consisting of a resident magistrate.
There is another Act referred to many
times in this Bill and closely connected
with it, and when this Bill is passed the
two Acts will be inextricably interwoven.
I am referring to the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act, 1875, to one of
the sections of which we are adding a
provision. Now, under the Conspiracy and
Protection of Property Act, provision is
made for the constitution of a court of
summary jurisdiction in Ireland, and it
is provided that that court of summary
jurisdiction shall consist of two magistrates sitting in petty sessions, and again
appeal is given to the ordinary court of
quarter sessions. It seems, therefore, that
if we pass this Bill as it is under one set
of contigencies which might conceivably
arise-I think it is in Clause 2-that
proceedings would have to be taken before one court and in another set of contingencies they would have to be taken
before another court.
What would happen as regards section 5

part would be tried by the ordinary

Let me now touch on the sympathetic
strike. I remember at one time there was
a trades council here. I was a member of
that council, and we carried on business
successfully as far as the interests of the
working men were concerned. Then it
commenced to take a political turn, and
a great many of the unions fell out of it.
After that a federation was started; it
was called the Shipbuilding and Federated
Trades Council. What did that stand
for? At that particular time one trade
was infringing on the work of the
other. Shipwrights were against the
joiners and joiners were against the
shipwrights; plumbers were against
engineers and engineers were against
plumbers, and this association was formed
for the purpose of settling the differences
between the different trades.
What is the upshot of it now? This
body has become a political organization.
It is composed of quite a number of
trades, the members of which are skilled,
semi-skilled and otherwise. If a man
does not belong to the same trade as I do
and he has no conception of what work I
have to perform, how can he be in
sympathy with me when he is receiving
10/- a week less than I am receiving?
He cannot be. It is unnatural to expect
him to do so when the question of a
sympathetic strike comes in. So far as

THE SENATE
[Mr. Barclay]
I intended. (Hon. Members: No, no.)
Looking at the Bill I naturally come to
the conclusion that it is a very harmless
document. I do not see anything that
any working man may be afraid of. In
the first place, it does not interfere in
any way with the rights of trade unionists
to organize themselves in trade unions
tor the purpose of collective bargaining
or for the purpose of improving their
working conditions. All the Bill does is
simply to safeguard trade unionists from
any political party. It sets a man practically free. I would not like the Unionist
party to have any kind of a grip upon me.
I have an independent spirit. Although
I might not be independent financially,
still I have something within me that is
independent. I would not like any
Unionist, even you, Mr. Speaker, to
come to me and tell me to do a certain
thing or try to coerce me to do a certain
thing. I would say, "No, I will not do
it." I take every working man to be of
the same temperament and of the same
spirit. Why should any working man be
compelled by any political party to act,
or vote or pay as that party thinks fit?
Therefore, this is a Bill that safeguards
the trade unionist and practically sets
him free.
Again we have been told that this Bill
interferes with and takes away from the
working man his strongest weapon, namely,
the strike weapon which has been referred to by Senator Cunningham. I
cannot see for the life of me how any man
can say that this Bill takes away that
particular weapon. It does not interfere
in any way with legitimate strikes.
Railwaymen, miners, bricklayers, carpenters, engineers, and transport workers
who have a disagreement with their employers are quite at liberty to test the
matter by a strike if saner methods cannot be used. I hope saner methods will
always be used, but they have a right
according to this Bill to test the matter
by a strike. But the Bill does prohibit
a general strike. Senator Dorman has
been trying to explain to us this afternoon what a general strike is, and I must
say that I am just as wise now as when
he began. He made reference to the
Israelites down in the land of Goshen. I
suppose there was a general strike on the
day they left there to go on their journey
to the Promised Land.
It may have
been, but at any rate I do not understand
the definition he has given. I understand that the Bill prohibits a general
strike, and it is very emphatic upon this
point, because it is so worded as not to
permit in any way a conspiracy against
the Government of the country. If we
look back upon past strikes that have
taken place, even apart from the general
strike, we find that sympathetic strikes in
many cases have done a great amount of
harm to the country as a whole. The
general strike in 1926 deprived the people
of their food in a great many cases.
Ships were held up; perishable food was
lost and destroyed. It deprived travellers
of transport. Instead of having buses,
trams, or trains by which to travel they
had to go on foot. It deprived the
people of light and heat, and threw
thousands of men and women who were
very much in need of money out of employment.
Then there is the political levy. There
has been a great deal said about the
political levy, and I do not suppose that
I could improve on anything that has
been said. But this I will say, that I
look upon the political levy as a sporting
Clause. The trade unionist is left a free
man, and if he has a shilling, or two
shillings, or a pound to spend he is quite
at liberty to put it on whatever political
party he fancies. If he fancies the
Socialist or the Labour party he is quite
at liberty to put his pound on the Labour
party. If he fancies the Liberal party
he is quite at liberty to put his pound
upon the Radical, and if he fancies the
Conservative party he is quite at liberty
to put his pound upon the Tory. He is
quite at liberty to do that. There is no
person to hinder him, and so I think this
Clause about which we have heard so
much, and over which there has been such
weeping, wailing and gnashing of teeth,
is a pretty fair Clause.
A lot has been said about the civil
servants. I am not going to say any
thing about the civil servants, only that
seeing they are the servants of the State
they have no right to combine with any
political party. There is one question
that arises in my mind, and that is that
if it is right for a trade union to use
pressure upon a group of men in the
interests of the union, is it wrong for the
Government to apply pressure to prevent
an injury being done to the whole country
by a group of trades unionists?
question has presented itself to me. If
it is right for the trades unions to bring

a
pressure upon a group of men in its own

group of trades unionists for the benefit

Looking over the Bill and taking the
Measure as a whole I naturally come to
the conclusion that it is a fair Measure.
There is nothing in the Bill to interfere
with the independence of the trades.
unions. There is nothing to prevent a
trade unionist from subscribing to any
political propaganda he wishes, and there
is nothing to debar him from voting as he
pleases. Therefore, I have great pleasure
in supporting the Second Reading of this

Lisburn Electric Supply Company
(Agreement) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE AND
FERRARD: I beg to move the Second
Reading of this Bill, the object of which
is to confirm and give effect to an agree
ment made between the Ministry of
Commerce and the Lisburn Electricity
Supply Company with respect to the
transmission line to be constructed by the
company for carrying electrical energy
from Belfast to Lisburn.
I will explain very briefly the circumstances which have given rise to the introduction of the Bill. Some time ago a
company was registered for the purpose
of obtaining statutory powers to supply
electricity within the Urban District of
Lisburn. It proposed to buy its current
from the Belfast City Council and to
carry it by overhead transmission to
Lisburn. The overhead line which the
Company intended to erect was designed
to transmit energy at a pressure of 6,600
volts only, sufficient copper being provided
in the line to furnish about 1,000
kilowatts, which is the maximum estimated requirement of the consumers in
the area covered by the company.
Government, however, looking to the
future, and knowing that the Lagan
Valley was a very favourable field for
electricity development, thought it would
be advisable that this proposed transmission line between Lisburn and Belfast
should be made capable of a much higher
pressure than would be necessary to supply
the electrical demand from Lisburn only,
so that it might be able to provide current
for large power users on the route between
Belfast and Lisburn, and possibly in the
future form the first link of a main transmission line extending further by way of
Lurgan and Portadown.
The
Accordingly an agreement in the
matter was reached with the company on
Trade Disputes Bill-
Committee.
8 DECEMBER 1927
The
the lines set forth in the Schedule.
Government will advance to the company
£1,450, which will be secured by a debenture, and the company, on its part, undertakes to construct a transmission line
capable of carrying energy at a pressure
of 33,000 volts instead of 6,600 volts,
which, as I have said, would have been
sufficient for its requirements in the
Lisburn area. It will be noticed that
interest will not be payable upon the debenture until the maximum load delivered
to the company at the Belfast terminus
of the transmission line exceeds 1,000
kilowatts or until power is transmitted
over the line for the company's own purposes at a pressure exceeding 6,600 volts.
I beg to move.
On Question, Motion agreed to.

Unfortunately, so far as I can make out,

rather different when I suggest to permit

I have one rather special reason for asking this. A practice has grown up of late

That is a small form of charitable collection. Therefore I beg to move to insert
the word "matches."
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE AND

seems to the Government, that if publicans are permitted to sell matches really

reason for departing from what was clearly
the intention of the Act of 1923. I

FERRARD: So many objections have

What would be the real effect of this
Amendment? The effect of it would be
to allow members of the general public
to be on licensed premises during closing
hours. That would mean that the supervision of the licensed premises by the
police would be extremely difficult, even
more difficult than it is at the moment.
The Amendment is in direct conflict with
the provision of the 1923 Act, and that
provision is an important one. It places
the onus upon the publican of proving
that persons found on licensed premises
during closing hours were there for no
illegal purpose. If a publican has got to
provide suitable accommodation for persons in charge of animals and vehicles
how is he going to do it? The accommodation must have no connection with the
public house. It must have a separate
entrance, and persons would have to con:e
out of the yard into the street in order to
get to the room provided. Otherwise the
publican would not be complying with
the Act of 1923. On those grounds the
Government cannot accept the Amendment.

being so, I withdraw the Amendment.

The object of. these Amendments is to
remove the restrictions on bona-fide
residents in hotels, and I ask hon.
Members to regard these Amendments in
the light of common sense, and to deal
with the matter as ordinary members of
the public. As I said on the Second
Reading, my reasons for moving these
Amendments are three in number.
first concerns people coming over from
Great Britain to Northern Ireland and
staying in hotels here. I am proud, and
The
I hope most of us are proud, to belong
to the United Kingdom. I have always
loved to regard our part of Northern
Ireland as if it were a county or shire on
the other side of the water where people
are of the same type and have the same
ideas. There is nothing calculated to do
more harm to our beloved Province than
the idea of a person coming over here
and finding himself in many respects in
a different country. When a traveller
from Great Britain comes over here and
takes up his residence in an hotel he goes
about his day's business, and when
he comes in again at night he goes
into the lounge of his hotel and calls for
a drink. He cannot get it. He probably
says to himself, "This is a funny place
I am in with all these petty restrictions.
1 hope I shall not have to come back
here.' Such a thing as that belittles
this country and does it a great deal of
harm.
My second reason is with regard to
residents in hotels in general. Broadly
speaking, residents in hotels may be regarded as of two distinct classes. The
first class comprises the business people,
and if owners and managers of hotels
were consulted I think they would say
that the travelling residents are really
the mainstay of the hotel trade. The
business-man staying in an hotel is
already subjected to a considerable
amount of discomfort. He is living in an
uncongenial atmosphere and he loses a
good many of the home comforts he is
accustomed to, and it is rather tantalizing
to him that he should be restricted from
so many of the comforts that he enjoys
in his own home or club. A business-man
does his business during the day and after
dinner he may go out to a place of amusement. He comes back into the lounge
of the hotel and probably wants the little
refreshment that he is accustomed to have,
but he finds that he cannot get it.
As a
bona-fide resident in an hotel I think he
should be able to get a drink at 10 or 11
o'clock at night if he wants it. That
applies to a very large class of hotel
residents.
Another class of residents in hotels are
those who are there on holiday. I would
like hon. Members to consider the life in
an hotel during the summer months, from
May until August. We are then under the
Summer Time Act and as a matter of fact
at the closing hour it is only 7-30 p.m.
by ordinary time. People are out play-
Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
Committee.
THE SENATE
[Mr. Glendinning]
ing golf or tennis or walking until dusk,
which is about 10 or 11 o'clock. When
those people come back to the hotel in
which they are staying they cannot get
a drink. I think that is another very
good reason why the Government should
accept these Amendments. Even those
who are not engaged in playing golf or
other games probably dine later in the
summer time than they usually do. They
may have their dinner at 8 o'clock. After
sitting chatting they may go into the
lounge to have a liqueur with their coffee,
only to be informed by the waiter that
they cannot have it because it is after 9
o'clock. I think that is a very irritating
restriction.
That brings me to the third reason I
have for proposing this Amendment.
People who are caught like that make up
their minds that they will not be caught
again, and they take good care that on
every other night of the week they will
have something upstairs. The result is that
they will order drink to be taken up to their
bedroom, and I venture to say they will
actually drink more in their bedroom
than they would if they had been able
to have a small whisky in the ordinary
course downstairs. I think that is only
a common sense way of looking at the
matter. The adoption of these Amendments would be in the interests of true
temperance, because I believe more harm
is done to true temperance by these petty
restrictions than in any other way. One
hon. Senator, speaking on the Second
Reading of this Bill, said he would object
to these Amendments because people
would engage rooms in an hotel on a

as many people as they liked on Sunday
to drink. I would ask hon. Senators not
to allow their imagination to run away
with them. I do not think anything like
that would occur.
a
I would ask hon. Members to remember
that hotel owners and managers are
respectable body of persons. There is in
existence a very strong hotel managers'

Government accepted these Amendments
and removed these restrictions, that

not abused. The Government have gone
a step in the right direction in this Bill

Act was
not infringed in any way.
And as a matter of fact could it be infringed? The really decently managed
hotel looks with considerable suspicion on
any person coming in without baggage
in the ordinary way. They want to know
why they want a room without any apparent evidence of travelling or anything
else. The probability is that unless the
man puts down a heavy deposit he would
have very great difficulty in getting a

the small hotel, which Senator Dickson
says might infringe the Act, my opinion is
if it were tried on in a small hotel the
police and everybody else would twig it
at once, and know that it was a bogus
business altogether. The hotel proprietor would be too much concerned about
his licence to permit it going on.
I have only one or two further things
to say. I am not asking the Government
to abandon any principle for the sake of
public popularity, but there certainly is
a feeling that the Government in this
Bill have shown some indifference to the
general views of the community. I think

reasonable request that people living in a
hotel temporarily should be able to regard
that hotel as their home, and there should
be no restrictions in regard to liquor or
anything else. I beg to move.

Old Age Pensions Bill-
Second Reading
9 DECEMBER 1927
THE SENATE.

Friday, 9th December, 1927.
The Senate met at Quarter after Three
of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the
Chair.
Old Age Pensions (Administration) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
VISCOUNT MASSEREENE AND
FERRARD: In rising to move the
Second Reading of the Old Age Pensions
(Administration) Bill, I should like to
say that my right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour, has come here to-day, in
order to answer any technical points that
may be raised during the course of the
debate, and to which I myself might find
As hon.
some difficulty in replying.
Members know, this is not the first time
the right hon. Gentleman has been in this
House. He was here twice in 1923 and
again in 1925, and I am sure we are all
pleased to see him here once again. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The purpose of this Bill is to transfer
to the Ministry of Labour the responsibility for the administration in Northern
Ireland of the public service in connection with non-contributory old-age pensions, and to make certain changes in the
method of determining claims and questions under the Old Age Pensions Acts.
It is, I think, desirable that I should, at
the outset, give to the House the reasons
which have led to the introduction of this
Bill. Non-contributory old-age pensions
are a transferred Service under the
Government of Ireland Act, and responsibility for their administration at the
moment rests with two Departments of
the Government, the Ministry of Finance
and the Ministry of Home Affairs, and,
as respects certain important functions,
with Local Pensions Committees.
An essential feature of the effective administration of the Service consists in a
preliminary investigation of claims, and
as the Ministry of Finance has not a staff
of its own officials at local centres in
Northern Ireland outside Belfast, that
Department in 1922 made an agreement
with an Imperial Department, the Commissioners of Customs and Excise, under
which the Customs and Excise officers,
who, as hon. Members know, have many
local duties to perform, would carry out
the necessary preliminary investigations
on claims to pensions. The Imperial
Department was, of course, recouped by
this Government the cost of the time of
Customs officers engaged on this work.
Hon. Members will remember that
when the Contributory Pensions Act of
1925 was passed, the Ministry of Labour
was made the Department responsible for
its administration. That Act made provision for pensions at 70 years of age.
without restriction as to means,
for per
sons insured under the National Health
Insurance Acts, who satisfied certain insurance tests, and it further provided that
from 2nd January, 1928, insured persons
will become entitled to pensions at 65
years of age.
It is obvious that a simpler and more
economical service could be secured by the
transfer to one Department of the administration of all the old-age pension
services, both contributory and non-contributory, certain of the tests, for instance,
the age test, being the same in each case.
Trouble would be saved to the claimant
who would only have one Government
Department to deal with instead of
several, as is the case at the moment.
Moreover, the Ministry of Labour has
already a network of local offices throughout Northern Ireland, and a staff experienced in investigation of similar questions arising under the Contributory
Pensions Act. For these reasons it has
been decided to propose the transfer of
the service to the Ministry of Labour.
Before alluding to the suggested
changes of machinery, I should like to
inform the House briefly what are the
existing arrangements. A person wishing to claim a pension obtains a form of
application from the post office, completes
it and sends it to the Pensions Officer who
Is, as I have mentioned, an officer of the
Customs and Excise Department.
The
Pension Officer makes investigations into
the circumstances of the claim, and, when
he has done so, forwards a Report with
his recommendation to a Local Pension
Committee. These Committees, as hon.
Old Age Pensions Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Viscount Massereene and Ferrard]
Members are probably aware, were established under the Old Age Pensions Act of
1908, and are appointed by County and
County Borough Councils and, in certain
circumstances, by Urban District Councils. Where necessary, Local Pension
Committees set up Sub-Committees to
act for districts within the Committees'
areas. The Local Pension Committee
considers the claim in the light of the
Report from the Pension Officer and gives
its decision
From this decision the claimant or the
Pension Officer may appeal to the Ministry of Home Affairs, which is the final
authority. It will be noted that there are
three different authorities concerned with
the determination of a claim, viz., the
Pension Officer, who is nominally an
Officer of the Ministry of Finance, but
actually an offcer of an Imperial Department; second, the Local Pension Committee, a body appointed by a local
authority, and third, the Ministry of
Home Affairs. In addition to these
authorities dealing with non-contributory
pensions there is the Ministry of Labour
which administers or will administer all
pensions payable to insured persons. In
these circumstances a certain amount of
confusion must inevitably arise in the
minds of applicants as to what authority
ought to be approached in order that they
may secure any benefits which they may
be entitled to claim.
I now come to the machinery proposed
by the Bill. As at present, a person
wishing to claim a pension will obtain a
form from the nearest Post Office: after
completing it he will send it to the nearest
Local Office of the Ministry of Labour.
An officer from the Ministry of Labour
will investigate the claim and will forward it with his report to the headquarters
of his Department. The claim will there
be considered by a Pension Officer, to be
appointed by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour. If the Pension
Officer, after an examination of all the
facts, considers that a pension should be
paid, he authorises the claim at once.
Hon. Members will see, therefore, that
in the case of what I might call straightforward claims there will be no delay in
authorisation. If, however, a Pension
Officer considers that a claim should not
be admitted, he informs the claimant accordingly. The claimant will then have
the right of appeal to a Local Pension
Court, which will be a body composed
ordinarily of three members, two of whom
will be drawn from panels appointed by
the Minister of Labour, and the third a
Chairman appointed by my right hon.
Friend.
The panels from which the personnel
of the Local Pension Court will be drawn
will be set up in various areas throughout
the country.
The Local Pension Court
will consider the appeal and will make
a recommendation to the Pension Officer.
The Pension Officer is required to
give effect to that recommendation
unless he disagrees with it, in which
event he must refer the matter to
the Umpire for a final determination.
The Umpire will be an independent person appointed by His Grace the Governor.
Again, should the Local Pension Court
recommend to the Pension Officer that a
claim for pension should be disallowed,
the claimant may appeal to the Umpire
with the leave of the Court, and a form
of words has been introduced in the Bill
in Sub-Cection 5 of Clause 2 with the
object of securing that a claimant should
be given the right of appeal to the Umpire
in any case where it seems to the Court
reasonable that he should have it.
Hon. Members will appreciate that an
unrestricted right of appeal would inevitably lead to frivolous appeals going forward, thus adding unnecessarily to the
cost of administration. It is anticipated
that the proposals in this Bill will result
not alone in the facilitating of applicants
for pensions but also in economies in the
cost of the administration of the Old-Age
Pensions Acts.
Before concluding, I should like to pay
a tribute on behalf of the Government to
the able and efficient service which has
been given to us by the officers of the
Customs and Excise Department, who
have assisted in the administration of this
Act since our Government took over responsibility for it, but I think a special
tribute is due to the members of the
Local Pensions Committees in every area
in Northern Ireland who have given loyal
and dutiful service without reward or
remuneraion, and often at considerable
personal inconvenience. My right hon.
Friend hopes to be able to avail himself
of the services of these ladies and gentlemen to assist in the administration of
the Act under the new procedure proposed in the Bill. I beg to move:

week I had occasion to call at the Ministry
of Home Affairs regarding an old-age
pensioner. The pension officer in that
case had found that the man was entitled
to free turbary-the right to cut turf--
and estimated forty loads of turf at 5s a
load, and a total income of £10 from that
right of free turbary. Everyone who is
familiar with the cutting of turf knows—
these were, I should say, for his own
use they would cost at least as much
as they would be worth. The man could
buy coal quite as reasonably. I must say
the Home Ministry agreed with me that
that was an unreasonable thing to charge
that man with.

With regard to the reported saving of

Mr. JOSEPH CUNNINGHAM:
would like to join with the noble Viscount in saying how pleased we are to
have the Minister of Labour attending in

to sit in this important House along with

As far as the Old-Age Pensions (Administration) Bill is concerned I have
really no particular objection to raise to
it, because if the intention is economy
and the simplifying of the system which
has been in existence I certainly think it
will serve a good purpose. The system
that has been in operation for some time
was not simple. It was very confusing.
I have many old-age applicants with me
from time to time wondering at the
delay. It had to pass through different
hands. So that if it is intended to simplify I believe it will have some good
effect. There is only one objection that
I have heard raised to it, and I have some
little feeling in this respect myself, and
that is the abolition of the committees
who were acting voluntarily. I would
like the Minister of Labour to say whether
he is perfectly satisfied that the Government officials will deal as sympathetically
with these poor applicants as the voluntary committees did. We know perfectly
well that among the applicants for old-age
pensions there are a number of very poor
individuals. Indeed, I am sure a considerable number are illiterate, and require a large amount of assistance. Now
I
it is not usual to find Government officials
very considerate for these dull people who
may apply to them for assistance.
always think those who are closely associated with them know them best and are
more likely to give the sympathy and
assistance they require. That is one of
the principal objections that the electors
have to this Bill.
With reference to the courts of referees
I do hope when these referee courts are
set up-and certainly when they are carried out properly they are quite satisfactory-I do hope that in connection with
the old-age pensions they will be a little
more satisfactory than the referee courts
which we know of in dealing with unemployment benefit. There was a time
when those courts were very satisfactory.
They could not have been better than
when they had on the bench a workman's
representative, an employers' representative, and a chairman. But seldom do we
find the three persons acting on it. It is
generally left to the Chairman to decide.
I feel that the applicants do not get decisions which the cases require. I do hope
care will be taken so far as the old-age
pensioners are concerned, because the

There is the other matter too. I know

scheme for a long time. Those who have
been acting as clerks on old-age pension

system and grown up with it, and more

those people who are dependent to a considerable extent on the little remuneration

I am sure, at any rate, we will be

I know the Minister of Labour himself

the Second Reading of the Bill.

Departments of State concerned in it, it

Then there remains the question of

to an Old Age Pension Committee was

transmitted to the pension officer. That

The hon, Senator (Mr. Long) who sits

tribute to
the pensions committees

evidently not been generally known up to

the basis from which committees will in

man and woman in Northern Ireland that

I have been asked as regards the question of economy. Well, of course, I can
only give estimates, because in establishing a new departure of this kind it is
obvious to everyone you cannot lay it

the Customs officials, and we see no reason

have in the first instance to be sent to the

one apart from any Government,

The difficulty in deciding these claims
in the past, I admit, has been one of age,
and I have no hesitation in saying the
Department will recognize the difficulty
which some claimants have in establishing
their age. When they cannot produce birth

will be accepted in lieu of birth certificates. And, may I add in passing,
this difficulty of age will in a very few
years disappear, because about 62 or 63
years ago there was compulsory registration, and so a great deal of this difficulty
of age will be got over and the work of
administration will be very much simplified. The only other test that has got
to be applied, of course, is one of means,
and there, I think, reasonableness has got
to be shown again, because many applicants for these old-age pensions in future
will be of the farming and shopkeeping
community, because, as hon. Members
know, in future almost all our industrial
classes will be entitled to contributory
pensions.
A great difficulty at the present time I
recognize is to establish the value of a
small holding. Well, amongst other
things I happen to farm a pretty large
holding, and I therefore have no exaggerated views (laughter) of the value of
either large holdings or small holdings at
the present time. Therefore, if I have
any influence in the matter I do not think
the interests of the claimants will be overlooked.
I think I have covered most of the

I would like the House to appreciate
that really the only reason that this
administrative change has been made
is because, obviously, there had
be a good deal of overlapping since our

now that making one Department the
responsible authority will again cheapen
administration, and not only do that, but
what I think is almost equally important,

reasons why I think this Bill, which is
purely an administrative one, should become the law of the land, but I will
conclude by thanking all the Members of

Mr. DORMAN : I rise to draw the
attention of the Government to a practice
which is growing up at present in order
to evade the provisions of an Act which
this Parliament has placed upon
Statute Book for the protection of
tenants of houses at a valuation of £8
and under. The Government have found
it necessary to place this Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions Act on the
Statute Book to prevent profiteering on
the part of landlords by the latter putting
into a house a few articles of furniture,
letting the house as a furnished house,
and charging the tenant an exorbitant
rent. What is taking place now is even
of a more heartless nature.
The agents
of landlords are asking for large sums,
varying from £5 to £16, from applicants
for vacant houses in the working class
districts of the city.
There came under my notice this morning the case of one woman who made
application for a vacant house in the
centre of a working class district in the
city. The controlled rent of that house
At the present time the city is in a
deplorable condition so far as the housing
of the working classes is concerned. As
I have mentioned before, Belfast is the
only large industrial centre in Great
Britain or Ireland that has increased its
one-room dwellers between the last two
census, and the physique of future
generations is going to be seriously
affected if this condition of affairs is
allowed to continue. I make a wholehearted appeal to the Government to see
if something cannot be done to stop this
method of profiteering at the expense of
the working classes. Words fail me in
attempting to give my opinion of the
character of any man who could prosecute
a system of this kind for the purpose of
exploiting the most poor and helpless part
of the community.
VISCOUNT MASSEERENE AND
FERRARD: The reprehensible practice
of which the hon. Member has given the
House such a glaring example is one which
I personally cannot too strongly condemn.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I cannot
carry in my mind the provisions of the
various Rent Restrictions Acts that have
been passed during the last four or five
years by this Parliament. My own
opinion is that what is taking place is
illegal, but I will at once bring the matter
to the notice of the proper authorities,
with the object of ensuring, if possible,
that this practice is not continued.
