Mr. DORMAN: I refrained from
exercising my right to propose any
Amendments to this Bill on the Committee stage, but I felt it my duty to
review this Measure in order to show the
disabilities that would be suffered by the
working classes who refused to sell their
labour power so as to resist any injustice
that may be attempted to be inflicted
upon them by their employers. I do not
now desire to occupy the time of the
Senate at any undue length, but I want
to refer to the difficulties that will confront the working classes if this Measure
becomes the law of Northern Ireland. I
notice that under the First Clause of the
Bill any working man or body of working men who participate in a strike
calculated to coerce the Government, or
to inflict hardship upon the community
will come within the provisions of the
Bill and will be liable to the penalties set
forth in the Act. If I were a magistrate
in Northern Ireland and had taken an
oath or made an affirmation to administer
this Bill when it becomes an Act of
Parliament justly as between the Crown
and the subject, I would feel compelled,
while these words remain in the Bill, to
convict any man or body of men brought
before me for participating in a strike of
any kind.
I cannot conceive of any strike that is
not calculated to inflict injury upon the
community. Suppose I
Suppose I was presiding
over a bench of magistrates, and the
learned Attorney-General brought a
number of individuals before that court
under this particular Clause. I do not see
how I could do otherwise than declare
them to be guilty. Suppose a baker was
brought before the court I would feel
compelled to address my fellow magistrates and say: "I cannot help believing
that this man is inflicting a hardship
upon the community. He is engaged in
an operation the continuance of which is
absolutely necessary for the life of the
community as a whole." Therefore, as
a magistrate I would be forced to come to
the conclusion that that man was guilty
and was subject to the penalties prescribed in the Bill. Suppose a tramwayman, a motorman or a conductor, was
brought before me for a similar offence.
Tramway-men cannot withdraw their
labour without in some measure inflicting
hardship upon the community inasmuch
as they would be depriving them of the
facilities for travelling from point to
point inside the city boundary. Therefore, magistrates would have no alternative but to find those men guilty. I
have no desire to go on giving a catalogue
of strikes that would come within the
purview of this particular Clause of the
Bill. Suffice it to say that I cannot
conceive of any body of men, in our
intricate and inter-dependent social
conditions coming out on strike without
inflicting hardship on the community.
There is another point I wish to direct
attention to. It is with reference to the
words in lines 13, 14, and 15 on page 2.
of the Bill, where it makes it illegal for
any person to apply sums of money in
furtherance of any such illegal strike or
lock-out. The circumstance which led to
the necessity for this Bill being intro-

stand by the majority vote of his union.
I approach that man with the obiect of

some small insect ran

foolish, but what is to prevent a man

such a threat. Suppose I unconsciously
clench my hand and raise it up my side,

with my clenched fist. The law is a
peculiar thing.
Hon. Members may laugh, but in this

men who had products to sell in the

than that he had asked, was hanged by

I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but I cannot conceive of any

them making that combination a success.
From the political point of view Labour
is marching on. We can hear their
footsteps-

a policeman to complain that a horse or
vehicle had been stabled for too long a
time. The word "temporary" does
not help us in the least, but if
the two suggestions I had intended
to make had been accepted, I think
the difficulty would have disappeared.
My idea was that it was not
necessary
say anything about
"temporary" or "similar" at all, but
simply leave it that a yard might be open
for the provision of accommodation for
vehicles or animals. Directly you get
over that it would at once be recognized
that a horse might stay there over-night.
If a horse stays there over-night the
farmer, who, as the right hon. Gentleman
says, does very often bring his fodder
with him, will have gone home. What
is going to happen to the horse? Surely
the Minister of Home Affairs does not
want to reproduce the horrors dilated on
by hon. Members on my left; those
horrors that took place on Dry Sunday,
the Sunday succeeding the date of the
coming into operation of the 1923 Act
when the poor animals were left unattended because it was thought that if the
yards were opened it would be alleged
that the public-houses were opened
during prohibited hours.
It appears to me that we have not got
much satisfaction out of these new words
which were put in in order to prevent a
misconstruction of the terms of the Act
of 1923. I am sure the House would be
only too pleased to give the right hon.
Gentleman the opportunity to speak
again, and then, perhaps, he would be
able to tell us what exactly he does mean
by the word "temporary." The whole
difficulty seems to me to be this. Certain
people seem to think the world will come
to an end if a cold and famished farmer
gets intoxicating liquor to drink at too
early an hour in the morning. That is
a view I do not share. It seems to me to
be much more likely that the unfortunate
farmer will come to an end if he does
not. That is an example of opposite
points of view. I say the licensing laws
were made for the public, not the public
for the licensing laws, and that is really
the main point of difference between
those who do not support the whole 1923
Act and the present Bill, which will be
part of it, and those who do. None of us
want to encourage the tippler, but we do
not like the suggestion that a balance has
got to be held between the mere tippler
and the person who wants to say that nobody shall have a drink at all, or at all
events only at the time somebody else
suggests.
Passing from that to the general question of the sale of drink, the right hon.
Gentleman rather accused me of having
moved an Amendment on that subject,
although I did not do so. There was an
Amendment to leave out the two words,
Sunday and Christmas day," and to
add or during the hours.' The effect
of that Amendment, if it had been
carried, and if nothing else had been done,
would have been that the resident in a
hotel could have got his drink at any
time, just as he could in his own house.
It has just been admitted that the effect
of the 1923 Act was to cut off an hour,
because before the passing of that Act
you could get a drink up to 11 p.m., and
now you cannot get one after 10 p.m.
There was a general feeling in my part
of the country-I do not say it was a
universal feeling, but there was a general
feeling of expectation that this Bill,
when it came, would, as somebody had
said, round off the corners of the 1923
Act and would take away some of the
restraint that was regarded as having
gone beyond legitimate interference with
personal liberties. The people who
thought that will, I think, entertain distinct feelings of disappointment.
However, what merit the Bill has-and
I do not for one moment say it has not
merits-I am not wishing to be unappreciative of the alteration as regards the
substantial meal, although I recognize
the difficulty of defining substantial "
just as I recognize the difliculty of defining "temporary." I think one may
consider whether in the future the proper
solution of that difficulty is not to permit
variation in the hours. In order to prevent undue tippling-and I use that
word advisedly it is probably necessary
to limit the hours of public-houses, but I
cannot see any reason why the old licensed hours, the hours at which hotels could

Leaving those matters which relate to

I still regret that clubs were not dealt

Sir DAWSON BATES: You will know

Mr. LESLIE: Then I am afraid the

The only other point to which the right

be the case, because although I cannot

apparently the wording of the Article
would preclude the tenant of the premises using those premises for any purpose connected with a theatre or music
hall, such as the admission of people
wanting to arrange scenery or to have
rehearsals, and rehearsals, I understand
from those who frequent stage doors and
other places, are held at most unholy
hours. They necessarily have to be held
when the stage is not being used for a
performance. I imagined that the explanation of the Article might be found
in the terms of the licence. I cannot say
that I think the wording of the Article
is very explanatory. On the other hand,
I do not suppose it will occasion any difficulty, the more so as the right hon.
Gentleman has said the intention is not
to interfere with what you may call the
more or less private portion of the theatre.
The intention is to prevent theatres and
music halls being open for performances
except during the hours mentioned in the
licence. That is the intention, and as
long as that information is conveyed to
those interested, I do not imagine there
will be any difficulty.
I do not think there is any other point
on which I should desire to detain the
House. I certainly shall not oppose the
Third Reading, because the Bill has certain merits, and although this House
cannot claim the honour or distinction of
having originated any of those merits,
neither can this House be fairly blamed
for the maintenance in the Bill of any
original sin with which it may have
entered this Chamber I shall certainly
not oppose the Third Reading.
Mr. DORMAN: Since the last meeting
of this House I have heard the Government accused of playing up to the publicans in introducing this Measure. I am
not going to express an opinion whether
that is true or not. I rise to express my
approval of at least two portions of this
Measure. The first is the determination
of the Government not to grant any new
licence where an off or on-licence is
abolished. I believe there are too many
licensed premises in working class areas
in all big centres of population. I believe that they are a class who, suffering
through depression and other things, have
a craving for some stimulant to enable
them to feel something like a normal condition. I whole-heartedly approve of that
action on the part of the Government.
I also wish to express my approval of
the action of the Government in giving
power to district-inspectors of the R.U.C.
in regard to the question of clubs. I be-

lieve when the right hon. Gentleman, the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I just want to
say a few words in reply to the remarks
that have fallen from hon. Senators with
regard to the question of stabling. My
hon. Friend (Mr. Leslie) objects to the
term "temporary." In this Bill we want
to draw a hard and fast distinction between the ordinary livery stable and
public-house. I absolutely see no reason
why a horse should not get shelter
in a yard overnight, in the event of the
owner being unable to leave the house.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Leslie) talks about
interference with the liberty of the subject, and used those words in connection
with the Section which deals with the
restriction of the sale of drink after ten
o'clock to a resident. In dealing with
the liquor laws, I do not believe in dealing
with them or any other laws in the way
of laws for the rich and laws for the poor.
1 could understand my hon. Friend being
logical on this subject, if he had advocated the opening of public-houses on
Sunday. I do not think any hon.
Senator in the House would advocate the
opening of public-houses on Sunday.
Those of us who can afford to live in a
hotel ought, I think, to suffer a certain
amount of inconvenience, having regard
to the good done to the community as a
whole by passing a restriction Act such
as this may be, even though it does interfere with the liberty of the subject.
After all, we have suffered inconvenience
by the Motor Act and other Acts.
Senator Dorman, a short time ago, spoke
about intemperance, but he himself, a
member of a trade union, has not free
liberty. Nobody has.
Mr. LESLIE: Yes.
Colonel SHARMAN CRAWFORD .
No.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think hon.
Members will agree that it is absolutely
essential, for the good of the community,
that there should be no further extension
in regard to the sale of intoxicating
liquors. Now, with regard to the club
question, I do not know whether my hon.
Friend would like the same conditions
to prevail here in regard
regard to club
licences as prevail in England. In England anybody can get a club licence, and
it is one of the greatest curses and
nuisances the police have in putting an
end to those clubs. They spring up like
mushrooms. In England the magistrates
cannot refuse to give a club licence. As
often as an application is granted the
police raid the house. We want to do
away with that. We want to put the
clubs on a reasonable basis. I really do
not see why a club that gets certain privileges should not submit to certain restrictions. I do not believe any decently
run club will suffer a modicum of harm
by the passing of this Bill. I do not believe that there are many drinking clubs.
I believe they exist to a small extent.
Mr. LESLIE: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: We do not
want to have a lot of clubs springing up
in Ulster that are going to give trouble
to anybody. My hon. Friend knows perfectly well that there is a tendency on
the part of a certain class of clubs to sell
liquor on Sundays to the members, who
retail that liquor at about three times the
price to individuals who are not members.
I mention that as one form of abuse.
Therefore, it is very necessary that there
should be some control. The Bill applies
to clubs, whether working-men's clubs or
other clubs. I think most of the clubs
that de exist in Northern Ireland are
working-men's clubs. The hon. Senator
referred to temperance hotels. I know
certain very undesirable practices exist,
but law, I suppose, will never make the
world pure.
By this Bill we are trying,
at all events, to make the North of Ireland a little more temperate, and we are
rounding off the corners. I hope that the
House will give this Measure the Third
Reading.

THE LONDON-BELFAST MAILS.
VISCOUNT CHARLEMONT: I have
here a reply to a question asked by
Senator Leslie the last time we met, in
which he asked me to get some information, on behalf of Senator Colonel Sharman Crawford. Here is the reply:
The reversion to the Holyhead-Kingstown route for the conveyance of mails
between London and Belfast in either
direction, has resulted in two distinct
advantages:-
(1) Letters posted in Belfast in time
for inclusion in the mails despatched
by the mail train to Dublin are included in the first delivery in London
on the day following. No other route
would permit of this connection;
(2) Correspondence passing from
London and district to Belfast posted
too late for despatch by the Fleetwood
route now reaches Belfast at or about
9-10 a.m. with almost unfailing regularity, and is thus included in the
second delivery in Belfast commencing
at 10-45 a.m.
According to information supplied by
the Post Office, deliveries in Belfast are
now much more punctual than when the
Stranraer-Larne route was utilized for
conveyance of London-Belfast correspondence. This improvement has been reflected in an almost entire absence of
complaints regarding incoming London
mails.
In addition to the letters posted in
London early enough to make the connection, a considerable volume of letters
from the North of England destined for
Belfast is carried via Fleetwood. Unfortunately the timekeeping of the Fleetwood steamers has been unusually irregular during the past few months, with the
result that the incoming letters frequently
fail to secure inclusion in the first delivery
in Belfast starting at 7.30 a.m. The
irregular timekeeping is attributable to
the fact that one of the steamers employed on the route is incapable of
making the passage in the scheduled
time. The matter has been called to
the notice of the Postmaster-General,
who in turn has brought it to the attention of the London, Midland and Scottish
Railway Company. The Company, while
unable to effect any immediate improvement in this respect, have directed attention to the fact that new and faster
steamers will be employed on the service
as from the date when the transfer from
Fleetwood to Heysham takes place, and
have intimated that an improvement in
the timekeeping will thereby result. The
Ministry is directing its effort to securing,
if possible, arrival of the new steamers
by not later than 6-15 a.m., so as to ensure of the mails being included in the
first delivery.
Colonel SHARMAN CRAWFORD: I
am much obliged for the statement made
by the Leader of the House, but I would
like to point out just one or two things
with regard to the Holyhead route.
There is really no advantage in it, because when the mails by the Holyhead
route come in they are detained in the

mails come in and are delivered with
them. As a matter of fact the mail has
been more irregular in its delivery in
Belfast lately. When the new 21-knot
boats are built the train will probably
leave London an hour later and arrive in
Belfast about 6 o'clock or 6-30. There
is no doubt that the Fleetwood route
always meant the earliest delivery in
Belfast. I suggest and it is only a
suggestion, because I believe the delay

PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT.
His Grace the Governor, being seated
on the Throne, commanded the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod to let the
Commons know, "It is his Grace's pleasure that they attend him in this House."
The Commons being at the Bar, with
their Speaker, his Grace delivered the
following Speech from the Throne:
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I congratulate you upon the result
of your labours during the session now
concluded.
I regret that it cannot be said that
Agriculture has yet emerged from that
period of depression which has for so
long affected conditions in the primary
industry of Northern Ireland. Fortunately the spell of fine weather which
marked the late autumn was of great
benefit to the farmers in enabling the
harvest to be saved. It is to be deplored, however, that owing to the low
prices prevailing in respect of certain
commodities, farmers have not secured
proportionate remuneration for their
laborious work. It is hoped that the
steps taken by the Ministry of Agriculture, particularly in the matter of
granting a further sum of £40,000
towards the extension of the Live Stock
Improvement Schemes, ably administered by the County Committees, will
promote beneficial results.
I am very gratified to observe that the
improvement in trade continues, the
number of persons registered for employment at the Exchanges having been
on the 31st October the lowest since the
Industrial depression which followed the
Great War, and on the 5th December,
26,710, a reduction of 22,697 since the
beginning of this year. Most of the
staple industries have shared in the
better state of trade, and in the linen
industry, in particular, the percentage
of persons registered as unemployed has
fallen from 14.5 per cent. in January,
1927, to 6.8 per cent. My Government
has continued to develop trade and
foster employment through the facilities
afforded by the Loans Guarantee Acts,
loans to the extent of £2,700,000 having
been guaranteed during the year ended
30th September, while the maximum
limit under these Acts has been increased from £9,000,000 to £10,500,000.
In addition since 1st January, 1927,
133 schemes of public utility, giving
employment to a considerable number
of people, have been initiated by Local
Authorities with the assistance of
Government grants amounting to
£208,205.
I note with satisfaction that measures
of great social value have been passed.
The Acts that have amended and consolidated the law relating to Workmen's
Compensation, that have provided
precautions against the danger of lead
poisoning, and that have safeguarded
those employed in the quarrying industry, mark important steps in the
development of my Government's policy
of improving the industrial conditions
of the people. The Trade Disputes and
Trade Unions Act, while providing
additional safeguards for the liberty of
the individual and the vital interests
of the community, preserves to employers and employed their right to
combine for the furtherance of their
o'vn legitimate interests.
I am glad to learn that preparations
have been completed for bringing into
operation on the 2nd January next the
final portion of the Contributory Pensions Act, under which pensions will be
provided for insured persons and their
wives at the age of 65. It is estimated
that the number of persons who will at
once benefit will be over 8,000. The
passing of the Old Age Pensions Act
also will serve to co-ordinate the administration of the Contributory and Noncontributory Pension Schemes.
The steps which have been taken to
remove the difficulties and anomalies

King's Speech.

End of Session.
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
which have arisen in connection with
the interpretation and administration
of the Intoxicating Liquor Act of 1923,
will prove beneficial.
I am gratified to find that my Government's subsidy arrangements in connection with housing have produced such
satisfactory results that in so far as the
larger types of houses governed by
various statutes are concerned it is now
considered unnecessary to accord further
assistance from public funds. It has
been decided, however, to augment
grants for the purpose of encouraging
the building of the smaller types of
houses more suitable for the requirements of the industrial wage earner,
and I hope that in due time by these
means the housing difficulty will have
been completely removed.
I am also glad to note that a special
grant of £30,000 to assist in the provision of Ex-Servicemen's houses has
been made.
Steps have been taken which will, it
is hoped, tend to develop and safeguard
the supply of Tuberculin Tested Milk,
and I trust that full advantage will be
taken of this Measure and that a pure
and clean milk supply may be ensured
for Northern Ireland.
I note with satisfaction that it has
been possible to afford some relief from
taxation by the exemption from Entertainment duty of certain outdoor
sports, and in the case of other entertainments the remission of duty on the
charge for admission to the cheaper
seats.
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank you for the provision of
supplies for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am gratified to learn that the conditions in Northern Ireland still continue to be peaceful, and that cases of
serious crime are now happily rare.
It is my earnest prayer that the
blessing of the Almighty may rest upon
all your past and coming labours.
Then the Proclamation Proroguing the
present Parliament of Northern Ireland
was read by the Speaker as followeth :
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall in His Majesty's name
summon, prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern Ireland should be prorogued to the sixth day
of March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Twenty-eight:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation
do publish and declare His Majesty's
Pleasure that the said Parliament be,
as from the reading of this Proclamation
in the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
prorogued to Tuesday, the sixth day of
March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Twenty-eight.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
sixth day of March, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twenty-eight, assemble
and be holden for the dispatch of divers
urgent and important affairs, and the
Senators and Members of the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland
hereby required to give their attendance.
accordingly.
are
Given at Government House, Hillsborough, this twentieth day of December,
One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-seven.
Signed by his own hand,
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
His Grace, the Governor, then retired.
End of the Third Session (opened 15th
March, 1927) of the Second Parliament
of Northern Ireland, in the Eighteenth
year of the Reign of His Majesty King
George the Fifth

7 MARCH 1928
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I do
not intend to take up the time of the
House to-day. I am quite satisfied that
statement will be satisfactory to the hon.
lady Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester).
Mr. SPEAKER: I suppose the hon.
Member understands the position.
If
he had not finished his speech yesterday,
he is entitled to continue, but if he had
finished he is not entitled to make another
speech.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I will
just take a few minutes. I am altogether
disappointed with the contents of the
King's Speech. In order that the Prime
Minister and the Government should
know exactly the position that exists in
relation to the condition of the unemployed workers of Ulster, I made it my
business this morning to visit the Whitewell site. The weather conditions were
not altogether so bad to-day as I have
seen them on former occasions. The
people at this site are very dissatisfied,
and are blaming the Government for
allowing this condition of affairs to exist.
There is one gentleman there, he is
named Morgan, and lives at 64 Avon
Street, which I am sure the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) knows.
He has eight children and his wife and
himself to keep. He has to do four days
work and he receives for four days work
a pound note. He does not even get
the money. He gets four dockets entitling him to £1 worth of goods. I want to
ask the Government do they stand for
such a condition of affairs as that. That
is a case from the Ballymacarrett side.
There is a gentleman called Given, 17
Clementine Street, which is in Sandy Row.
He is very dissatisfied. I may tell you
he was very indignant, and blamed the
Government entirely for it. The Government are not entirely to blame, but
they are partly to blame. He has a
family of six; he works for four days
and receives 15s. He does not even get
the money.
Then there is is the case of
Hugh Morgan, who is a young man I
have known for a considerable time. I
was with the clerk of works, and this
young man came over to me. He did
not wait to be invited to come over. He
came running over and said, "Hello,
Tommy," and held up his boot to me.
The upper was torn from the sole. I
could not tell you if he had any socks on,
but I know the toes were protruding
from the boots. That is the condition of
affairs that exists. I have the names of
twelve men here. Some come from
Ballymacarrett, some from Sandy Row,
some from the Shankill Road, and some
from other parts of the city.
The clerk of works there is well known
to Members of the Government. He is
a Mr. Geddis, a very staunch standardbearer of the Unionist cause, and a great
friend of my own. While I was talking
to Mr. Geddis another man who lives in
Gibson Street came over to me. He did
not know who I was. He showed me this
piece of bread, and asked me how a man
could be expected to do a day's work on
that. The Parliamentary Secretary to
the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon)
knows Mr. Geddis, who will bear me out.
The bread was not in this bit of paper
which was lifted off the field. He
showed me that piece of bread, and I felt
very sore about it. There is what that
man was doing eight hours work cn.
That was his dinner. I purposely
brought this piece of bread to the House,
in order to create an impression, and get
the Prime Minister to take action in this
inatter. The man felt very indignant.
I feel this is a system of slavery that the
noble Lord, the Prime Minister, would
not be a party to.
I have seen these men with hardly a
boot on their feet, and hardly a rag on
their backs, and yet a particular body in
this city ask these men to do eight hours'
manual labour. This is the piece of
bread that a man out of Gibson Street
had to exist on. I do not think the
noble Lord (the Prime Minister) could
stand for that. Any Member can get in
touch with Mr. Geddis and have my statement confirmed. I asked the man: "Is
that all you have to eat?" He said:
"This is all the piece I have; if I had
taken any more my children would have
been left without anything at all."
had very few coppers in my pocket, but
I gave them to Mr. Geddes, and asked
him to provide a dinner for the man.
As the Government are being blamed for
this condition of affairs, I suggest that
the Prime Minister should take a deep interest in this matter. Many of these
people I came in contact with to-day are
great supporters of the Government.
While it may be a very distasteful thing
to do, it is my duty to tell the Prime
Minister that the people are entirely dissatisfied. Had he been there this morn-
I
Debate on the Address

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr T. Henderson]
ing he would have got the same information as I received. I went there to see
exactly what was taking place. I got up
a little earlier than usual. I was there
at nine o'clock, and the men had already
started work. I am quite satisfied that
there is not a Member of the House, irrespective of what side he sits on, would
be a party to such a condition of affairs.
Apart from the exploitation of these
men we realize the blunder that took place
in regard to the purchase of this site.
Surely to goodness the Government or the
Poor-law Guardians are not going to get
anybody out of a hole by getting labour
for nothing. Without taking up the time
of the House I would appeal to the
Government to see if something could be
done to give these men a few more
shillings. These men get four coupons
from the Poor-law Guardians, and I
would suggest that they get money instead. One of the men on that site put
the case very lucidly before me, and as
an Ulsterman I felt ashamed.
I want to be quite serious. I want the
Members of this House to realize that this
is not an attempt to play to the gallery.
We very seldom have a gallery here, so
that cannot be imputed on this occasion.
And it cannot be said that we on this
side of the House are doing it for Press
purposes. Whether the speeches we make
are good or bad, we very seldom get a
Press. In fact, I would take it as a
favour if it was kept out of the Press. I
plead with the Prime Minister to try to
get a few more shillings for these men.
They have to work for four days-it is
hard work, I have seen them digging clay
and wheeling barrows-and they work as
well as the Corporation labourers who receive 50s and 3s tram fares.
I believe the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Labour do not know the conditions of affairs. I suggest they pay this
place a visit, hear the complaints of the
men, and try to do something to help
those poor men who are suffering so much
at the present time. My particular reason
for appealing to the Prime Minister is
that one of the men pointed out to me
that he gets two or three coupons, but if
one of the "kiddies" wants a pair of
boots or if he wants a couple of shillings
for the rent he has not the money. John
Anderson, a personal friend of my own,
and a personal friend of many Members
on the other side of the House, was put
out of his house in Huss Street, off Agnes
Street, and is living in rooms in Enniskillen Street. He said, "The rent of the
house in Huss Street was about 3s a week,
and had I any money I would have been
able to pay the rent, but owing to the fact
that the Board of Guardians gave me
coupons instead of money I was put out
of my home." None of us wants to see
Ulster people dissatisfied, and for that
reason I appeal to the Government to try
to induce the Poor-law Guardians to increase the amount given to these people
and also to give money instead of coupons.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: The hon.
Member (Mr. Thomas Henderson) who
has just sat down has spoken at very
considerable length both yesterday and today, I think altogether very nearly 55
minutes. I propose to detain the House
for only a few minutes. During the course
of his speech he touched on every conceivable subject, on matters which possibly
were in some instances germane to the
King's Speech, and in other instances certainly were not germane. He covered a
very wide range. I am not going to follow
him, but I would just like to say in regard
to all the matters he brought up I did not
think I was in sympathy with any until
his remarks to-day. With a certain
amount of what he said to-day on the
subject of this labour test I certainly am
in agreement.
As far as his remarks yesterday on the
same subject were concerned I am afraid
I cannot agree with them. I do not think
it is in any way degrading to these men,
who for some reason or other are unable
to receive unemployment benefit and are
in dire distress, to give of their best in
the way of labour in return for what I
suppose is really outdoor relief from the
Guardians. But I do agree with him
when he speaks of the degradation of receiving dockets instead of money, and I
would like to join with him in appealing
to the Government to use any influence
they can with the Belfast Guardians to
revise to this extent their method of dealing with these unfortunate men.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I think the
labour test is only right and I cannot
see that any genuine advocate of Labour
can possibly see anything in it calculated to degrade the men concerned. I
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
7 MARCH 1928
are
do, however, think the giving of
dockets, especially where the men
giving a quid pro quo in the way of
labour, is an uncalled-for hardship, and
I hope the Government will be able to
use their influence with the Belfast
Guardians in respect of this matter.
I have always thought the Opposition must have a very easy task, and I
have often envied them. I have often
thought that if it were not for the wreck
and ruin which I am confident the hon.
Gentleman if put in power would leave
in their wake, I would have wished that
we on this side of the House could have
been in opposition so as to give them a
little chance to make good the promises
they make. It would be very much more
amusing for us at times, and it would
certainly be pleasanter to be able to
promise and never be called upon to perform, and to be able to destroy and never
be called upon to construct. But in
spite of the fact that I do think their
task is the easier one, I could not help
feeling a little sympathy with them
yesterday because it seemed on this
occasion particularly that their task was
not quite so easy, as was manifest from
some of the speeches to which we
listened.
The King's Speech and the speech of
the Prime Minister I think have completely cut the ground from beneath the
feet of the Opposition. From the remarks which they made, lengthy though
they may have been, the position of the
Opposition is obviously a difficult one.
Some of the criticisms which they endeavoured to make were already
answered in the speech of the Prime
Minister, though I must confess I found
it exceedingly difficult to follow in some
instances the speech of the hon. Member
(Mr. Thomas Henderson) who has just
sat down. He criticized the fact that
the Government were bringing in no
legislation with regard to slaughterhouses. He talked about tuberculosis in
cows, and, as I say, he covered a very wide
range mostly connected, it seems to me,
with local government.
it appears to me, and to every right-thinking person, that if the Government had
brought in legislation on that Report at
this early date it would clearly have
proved that they were not giving it the
consideration due to a subject of such
vital importance to the whole of the Six
Counties. I hope very much that before
legislation is brought in the Government
will give their lengthiest and soundest
consideration to all the recommendations
we thought fit to put forward.
I suppose that really what he was endeavouring to point out was that the
Government had lamentably failed in
their duty by not bringing in legislation
on the lines recommended by the Local
Government Commission which has just
finished its labours. All I can say is that
Then another subject was dealt with by
several speakers, and that was one mentioned by the Prime Minister and not
mentioned in the King's Speech, the question of the drainage of the Bann. I feel
I would like to say a few words on that
subject as it is one which has always lain
particularly close to my heart, and in
which I feel most deeply interested. The
hon. Member who has just sat down suggested that during the course of my parliamentary life I have put forward many
Amendments, and perhaps he had in his
mind the Motion which I put forward in
regard to the drainage of the Bann. He
said I always withdrew my Amendments,
and that I might fool some of the people
some of the time, but I would not be able
to fool all the people all the time. That was
an instance not perhaps of the way I carry
out my duties, but of the way in which the
Government are endeavouring to carry
out their duties to the country, and the
way in which they carry out the promises
made in this House.
an
I put forward a Motion calling upon the
Government to carry out the drainage of
the Bann, and they put forward
Amendment to insert the words "to take
initial steps to deal with the matter." I
accepted that Amendment against the
vote of the Opposition, and I explained
that I was satisfied to trust the Government on that occasion. I think I have
shown the people that, perhaps in a small
way, I have been able to put forward my
views effectively before the Government,
and I think the Government have shown
that if they give a promise they keep to
their promise. They have gone further in
the Report, which we have seen issued,
than the people had a right to expect from
them, and I know that the people in the
devastated areas concerned are very grateful indeed. When the time comes,
whether they are political followers of
mine or of the Opposition-in many cases
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address 84
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Chichester]
that I know they are the latter the
Government will receive their support
because of their gratitude.
I ought to take this opportunity of
saying that the Government have done
their part, and it now lies with the people
of Ulster, and if I may add my words to
those spoken by the Prime Minister
yesterday I would hope from the bottom
of my heart that those representatives
chosen directly by the people to look
after their interests should deliberate
well and carefully before they reject a
scheme such as I have reason to believe
the Government are going to put forward.
As I say, even if they think that these
terms are not as generous as they might
be, I trust they will think very carefully, at any rate, before rejecting them,
and will consult with the Government on
the matter. I cannot see how it is
possible for hon. Members opposite to
say that the Government are not attempting, in the first place, to deal with the
vital question of the drainage of the Bann
and, in the second place, to give employment to the large number of unemployed
throughout the Six Counties.
I would like to take this opportunity of
thanking the Government for the additional assistance which has been promised
to agriculture. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We do not know what may be
still in the minds of the Government. We
do know that yesterday the Prime
Minister, in giving us some details as to
what they proposed to do, said that he
could also give us some little hope that
there might be more. I would like to say
that the additional grant in aid of agricultural rates will be received with gratitude throughout the Six Counties by those
sorely depressed, sorely taxed, and sorely
rated people. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) At the same time I would like to
say that we are looking forward with
great anxiety and great hope to any other
help which may be forthcoming.
believe that the Government realize that
the farmers are almost on their beam
ends, and certainly unless some assistance
had been forthcoming I hardly care to
visualize the possibilities and prospects in
the country this year.
I notice that mention is made in the
King's Speech of a proposal for the registration of Nursing and Maternity
Homes. I can only say I am more than
glad that the Government are going to take
this matter up. I do not propose to say
anything further until I see the Bill dealing with this subject. I am also very
glad to see that they are going to introduce Measures dealing with the adoption
of children and legitimacy. I hope that
in this way we will keep in step with
England, for up to the present moment
we have lagged somewhat behind in this
direction.
I will not detain the House any longer,
but if I may just go back to the one point
I have raised I would say that I do thank
the Government for having taken steps,
at any rate, to give the people of Ulster
an opportunity of dealing with the evil
of flooding which has lain so heavily on
them for generations. If the people of
Ulster will only rise to the occasion-and
I believe they will then we will have
accomplished something that will redound
to the credit not only of the Government,
but of the citizens of the whole Six
Counties.
Mr. HARBISON: I wish I could
speak in as optimistic a tone as the hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) who
has just sat down. Before this Session
opened I had hoped that there would be
something tangible done or proposed
by the Ministry. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I have searched through the
Gracious Speech and I can find nothing
except one or two little doles that, placed
on the surface on the plane of the difficulties that the people have to meet, could
hardly be seen by a powerful microscope.
I come from an agricultural district
and also a semi-industrial district. We
are suffering now on the agricultural side
for the sins of this Government. The
farmers have burdens laid upon them
that, as far as I can see-and I yield to
no man in this House as to my knowledge
of the conditions of the people; I have
lived my lifetime amongst them, and in
the part of the country where I live I
know the greater part at least of their
personal affairs. I know the difficulties
from which the farmer at present
is suffering. I would venture to
estimate that there are not more
than twenty or thirty per cent. of
the farmers of Northern Ireland at
the present time solvent. The noble Lord
(Viscount Craigavon) stated that they
had information especially from the banks
as to the condition of the farming classes
L
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
7 MARCH 1928
in the North, or the community at large.
I know their condition, and there is
hardly a farmer at the present time who
would be granted £1 of an advance from
the bank without at least £10 of security.
I know also that the banks which did
heretofore advance money have lost very
heavily in their advances to the farming
community.
I say that the farmers are suffering
for the sins of this Government. In
the first place they carried a Land Purchase Act that laid upon the farmer a
burden that he should not bear, at least
twenty to thirty per cent. higher than he
should have to bear. Contrast that with
the situation in that country which we

I need hardly tell the House-I am sure

the history of the right of the fishermen.
to fish in Lough Neagh and what

these lessees, these vested owners, against
a certain decision in the Irish Courts.
It went to the House of Lords, and there
was not a man living at the time that
decision was given that did not look upon
it-I say this with all due respect and
deference to the House of Lords-with
suspicion. The court consisted of seven
judges, and the decision of the court was
four to three against the fishermen, and
amongst the three was the highest legal
authority in the land. The Lord
Chancellor of England decided with the
fishermen that they had from time
immemorial the immemorial right to fish
there. And the boon this Government is
going to give these fishermen is practically
to deprive them of fishing in the Lough
for ever. Well, I would like the Government to reconsider it before bringing in
their Bill. They have the power to fix
The rates, and to fix them in such a way

by the putting on of prohibitive tariffs

Minister of Commerce. Several attempts

I hope that in the near future the

share, but for some reason or other the
Government have refused to carry out

The development of agriculture and

only hope for the reduction of the

I think the Government would be well

An inquiry, as I have said, would not

bad
results, but that is the fault of the

have been found out only by time and

Another matter which is causing an
uproar in the Six Counties is the persecution of motor-car owners. I regret the
Minister of Finance is not present to
hear my remarks on this subject. A
particularly glaring case is that of the
Derry motor-car owners who have to pay
the Free State duty as well as the taxation imposed by the Northern Government on their cars. As most of their
traffic goes into the Free State they must
either pay the double tax or give up their
business. This means a great blow to
the holiday and tourist traffic. If you
impose such big restrictions on these
people how can you expect them to give
cheap and attractive fares sufficient to
bring tourists here. The tourists complain that the prices of hackney cars and
buses are high, but if the Government
will condemn cars which are known to be
perfectly sound and these men have to
borrow money to buy new cars it is impossible for them to give cheap and
reasonable fares.
I was expecting to see foreshadowed in
the King's Speech an Amending Bill to
relieve the persecution which is at present
going on against the bus and hackney
car owners and against the motor trade
generally, but it appears that the Government is confident of its position. It
would not be so confident if there was a
by-election. There is general discontent
all over the Six Counties, in both agricultural and industrial areas, and the
Government should at once take steps to
have these grievances remedied.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. George Henderson]
remarked, this discussion has largely
ranged on subjects outside the Gracious
Speech from the Throne, but I think that
is not very much to be wondered at because there is very little substance in the
Speech. The debate centred round other
questions of vital importance. The hon.
and learned Member for Armagh, who
so ably seconded the Address in Reply,
in an apologetic way, said in regard to
the meagreness of the programme outlined in the Speech that legislation was
sometimes like a dose of medicine, that
the less you took of it the better for you.
If he means that we had sufficient legislation that entailed burdens on agriculture and industry, I would be in agree.
ment with him, because I feel there have
been enough burdens placed on agriculture and industry, and that they are
more than they can bear. Surely there
are other great measures of reform that
might have been dealt with in the King's
Speech.
There is the question of expenditure.
In a Session like this when we are not so
busily engaged in legislation we might
have overhauled the whole question of
expenditure. I was glad to see the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn), who used to occupy a seat beside
me, back in his place on the other side
of the House, and joining in the flood
of eloquent oratory that issues from this
House. I do not know that the atmosphere of his present seat makes him quite
as useful a Member as he was when he
sat beside me. I remember that when he
occupied a seat here he was most zealous
about economy and about the absolute
necessity for overhauling the expenditure
in this area. Since he has got to the
other side of the House his ardour has
damped down. I have really the most
friendly recollection of the hon. Member
when I came to this House, a sort of
orphan. He took a fatherly interest in
me, and it was really through his tuition
I got to know something of the rules and
usages of this House. Now that he has
come back to the genial atmosphere of
this House there are great hopes for him
still.
In trying to justify the programme in
the King's Speech, the strongest recommendation the Prime Minister could get
was that there was really no controversial
matter in it, and that what we wanted
most at the present time was peace and
good fellowship, all pulling together.
But the Prime Minister seems to be a man
of very variable moods, and he can easily
change from an atmosphere of peace into
a most warlike atmosphere when he tries
to crush relentlessly any expression of
political opinion in this area other than
his own.
Mr. COLLINS: Hear, hear.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: It
seems to me the Prime Minister must be
suffering from an attack of nerves, because he has gathered his faithful around
him and chalk-marked the political line.
He has issued an ultimatum that if they
will not toe his line he will put down the
reins. Is that not a wonderful position
for a Prime Minister to occupy? "As
long as I am top dog and there is no
chance of anybody coming into competition with me I am willing to be Prime
Minister, but if you do not give me that
position I will throw down the reins and
retire to my tent." That is really
typical of the ascendancy party in this
area.
The hon. and learned Member for
Armagh (Mr. Davison) said the first step
necessary for the Government was to
realize the state of affairs in the agricultural industry. That has really been the
great trouble. The Government have
seemed so much out of touch with agricultural opinion and agricultural conditions that they have failed to realize the
seriousness of the state of affairs. Take
the reference to agriculture in the King's
Speech. What is there definite in it?
What does it mean? It may mean something or it may mean nothing. In other
directions definite promises are made by
the Government as to what they intend
to do, but the reference to agriculture is
an entirely indefinite matter and ends up
with a pious, Micawber-like hope that
something will turn up. That is the
extent of the reference to agriculture
made in the King's Speech.
There should have been a serious attempt on the part of the Government to
get to the root causes and to give real

effort should be made to develop our
dairying industry. We are all glad to

to the increase in the quantity of milk.
I do not know whether those are general

figures or whether they apply only to

the Minister of Agriculture has said they

Could there not have been something

time the farmers have been suffering from
a lack of capital owing to four or five bad
seasons and owing to falling prices and the
high cost of production. They have done.
something, but they have done it in a

many of our small farmers are really the
worst housed people in our area.
This is
a question that has been raised time and
again in this House by the hon. Member

Could not something be done along the

is being spent on unproductive purposes.
for the relief of unemployment at the
present time for providing cheap lime for

This other scheme that is now before

the Bann being harnessed to produce

But I do think it is a dangerous thing

the two schemes together. It seems to

say there are

Now since that time some proceedings
have taken place in the Summons Court. I
do not want to discuss this afternoon the
merits either of Mrs. Whan's or the Walker's case, but I want to point out in fairness to those on this side of the House
that we did interest ourselves in this case.
We thought the woman was wrongfully
convicted-and some of us I believe think
so still-but the whole point is that the
Leader of the Opposition in his statement
to-day says he thinks it is time someone
took this matter up, and I think in fairness to ourselves I should say that we did
take this matter up. I want to say
candidly here and now that I refuse to
be a party to any proceeding that is going
to make political capital out of the Whan
case. It has been going from one side
of the House to the other. It was in
our hands at one time and we did ail we
possibly could, and I could tell hon. Members of the Opposition something that
might shock them if they heard what some
of those legal people said about them
when the case was in our hands. Now
that it has gone from our hands to their
hands they probably will be telling them
what they think about us now. I want
it to be clearly understood that we pushed
this case as far as we possibly could, and
if it failed at the police court the fault
was not ours. We did all we possibly
could do in connection with the affair.
That is all I have to say on this question,
but before I sit down I would like to remind the Members of the Opposition of

hon. Members not to put too much dependence in lawyers' statements.

I have most carefully read the records
of these proceedings and I can find no
evidence whatever of any impropriety in
the conduct of this case. It turned, of
course, entirely upon the credibility of
witnesses. The Walkers, on the one hand.
swore that this assault had taken place;
Mrs. Whan, on the other hand, alleged
that it had not taken place, and she produced witnesses to prove an alibi. It
was not believed by the jury, and everyone, I think, in this House knows perfectly well that the Attorney-General or
counsel who represented the Crown are
not and cannot be called upon to form any
personal opinion as to whether persons
who are charged and tried are guilty or
not guilty. It is entirely a matter for
the jury before whom prisoners come. In
this particular case the verdict was given
against Mrs. Whan. So far as this case
itself is concerned I can find in the record
absolutely nothing to suggest that the case
was not perfectly and fairly represented,
that Mrs. Whan was not adequately defended, and it was entirely a matter for
the jury to make up their minds as to
which of the two parties were telling the
truth with reference to this assault.

I am quite prepared to admit that the

there are various other matters that one

The hon. Member made a pretty lengthy
reference to the matter of labour-saving
machinery. I do not know exactly where
he stands in that matter. Obviously the
employers of Northern Ireland must adopt
modern methods of production, otherwise
the cost of production in Northern Ireland
would be much higher than the cost of
production of similar commodities
throughout the world. Therefore, I maintain, that in order that employment may
be given to our people here, it is absolutely
necessary that our cost of production
should be in harmony with the cost of production in other countries. None of us
want to see wages cut in order to produce
that result, but still the result has got
to be attained, and my opinion, for what it
is worth, is that, short of cutting wages,
it can only be attained by adopting
modern methods of production. Take, as
an example. the question of hand looms.
The hand loom industry was of very substantial importance in Northern Ireland
some years ago. Well, the mechanical loom
came along and trade was changed from
one class of loom to the other. Supposing
the employers had been so short-sighted as
not to adopt the power loom, I think the
linen trade would have about left Northern Ireland altogether by this time.
I do not think there is any other matter the hon. Member referred to that I

say that the Department's activities are
not carried out in a sympathetic and impartial way; in fact, the charge very often
brought against me is that it is too sympathetic. However, I put the one charge
against the other, and take them both for
what they are worth.

CLAUSE 2 (Prevention of obstruction
to view at corners).
(1) Where a local authority are of
opinion that it is necessary, for the prevention of danger arising from obstruction to the view of persons using a road
maintainable by the authority, to impose
restrictions with respect to any land at
or near any corner or bend or road junction in such road, the local authority
may serve a notice-
(a) upon the owner or occupier of the
land directing him to alter the height
or character of any wall (not being
a wall forming part of the structure
of a permanent edifice), fence or hedge.
thereon so as to cause it to conform
with any requirements specified in the
notice; or
(b) upon every owner, occupier and
lessee of the land restraining them,
either absolutely or subject to such
conditions as may be specified in the
notice, from permitting any building,
wall, fence or hedge to be erected or
planted on the land:
Provided that-
(i) there shall be annexed to any notice
served under this section a plan showing the land to which the notice relates; and
*
*
*
*
(3) If any person upon whom notice
has been served under this section objects to comply with any requirement of
the notice, or objects to any restriction
imposed thereby, he may, within twentyone days after the receipt of the notice,
send his objection in writing, stating the
grounds thereof, to the authority by
whom the notice was served, and thereupon the question whether the notice
shall be withdrawn as respects any requirement or restriction objected to shall
be determined, if the parties so agree, by
a single arbitrator appointed by them,
or, in default of such agreement as
aforesaid, shall be determined by the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
*
*
If any question arises whether compensation is payable under this provision, the question shall be decided by
the county court having jurisdiction
where the land is situate, and a county
court shall have jurisdiction to deal with
any such question, notwithstanding
that, by reason of the amount of claim
or otherwise, the case would not, but for
this provision, be within the jurisdiction
of a county court.

Hon. Members are aware that as the
Bill left this House, it provided that
where a dispute arose as to whether certain work was to be done or not, it was
with the option of the local authority or
the owner to agree as to an arbitrator,
